Every order-sensitive item runs twice with options swapped; native typed models also swap labels; ten configurations repeat under extra seeds and batch 16. We find widespread stereotype alignment, order-dependent answers, and confidence that tracks instability rather than bias. In BBQ, 97 of 143 model-by-category scores are significant and 94 aligned, while the commercial reference abstains on 99.5% of ambiguous items, hiding aligned probability mass. Option swaps flip 0.0% to 72.6% of choices; typed scoring stays below 10% except Laya (22-33%), and untuned letter prompting reaches 73%. CrowS-Pairs preference spans 0.496 to 0.816, and boolean answers can be decided by position (1.00 versus 0.005). SilverSpoon judgments shift toward lower-SES labels in five of eight decision models, inherited from the 9B backbone or induced by tuning. Audits must permute options and reverse questions by default; order-invariant scoring should become a procurement requirement.

AI.tldr: The paper audits demographic bias in System One decision models, which return typed, probability-scored answers without a human in the loop, across BBQ, CrowS-Pairs and SilverSpoon with twelve models and 1,638,000 decisions. It finds widespread stereotype alignment, order-dependent answers and confidence that tracks instability rather than bias.
AI.motivation: System One decision models are entering production with answers executed automatically, but no multi-model audit on established bias benchmarks existed.
AI.method: The three benchmarks are adapted to the typed interface, with twelve models plus a no-thinking ablation. Every order-sensitive item is run twice with options swapped, native typed models also swap labels, and ten configurations are repeated under extra seeds and batch size 16.
AI.result: In BBQ, 97 of 143 model-by-category scores are significant and 94 are aligned, while the commercial reference abstains on 99.5% of ambiguous items, hiding aligned probability mass. Option swaps flip 0.0% to 72.6% of choices, with typed scoring below 10% except Laya at 22-33%. CrowS-Pairs preference spans 0.496 to 0.816, and boolean answers can be decided by position. SilverSpoon judgments shift toward lower-SES labels in five of eight decision models.
AI.conclusion: Audits should permute options and reverse questions by default, and order-invariant scoring should become a procurement requirement for System One decision models.

title: Robustness Starts with the Objective: Designing and Certifying Robust LLM-Generated Heuristics
summary: LLMs are increasingly used to design heuristics for computer systems. However, most synthesis frameworks evaluate candidates by their average performance, which can mask severe regressions on specific workloads. Even adding adversarial training inputs doesn't eliminate these regressions, and percentile objectives (e.g., optimizing for the 95th percentile) overlook how severe regressions can be beyond the selected threshold. We present TAILOR, a framework that guides LLM synthesis using the Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR) of the cost difference between each candidate and an existing baseline on the same workload. This paired CVaR measures the average difference over the worst fraction of workloads. We show that a negative paired CVaR guarantees improvements in both average performance and tail optimality gap relative to the unknown optimum, without ever computing that optimum. We find that TAILOR achieves the best mean--tail trade-off among the synthesis objectives we evaluate across three case studies: Azure GPU batch admission, Azure VM packing, and server placement. Tested across seven diverse optimization benchmarks, TAILOR produces heuristics that are certified with 99% confidence to improve both average performance and tail optimality gaps over the baseline in six of them. On these six benchmarks, TAILOR also outperforms known robust, human-designed alternatives in the tail while achieving better or comparable average-performance improvement over the baseline.

AI.tldr: TAILOR guides LLM synthesis of computer-systems heuristics with the paired conditional value at risk of the cost difference between each candidate and a baseline on the same workloads. A negative paired CVaR certifies improvement in average performance and tail optimality gap, and TAILOR gives the best mean-tail trade-off across three case studies and seven benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLM-designed heuristics are usually judged by average performance, which can hide severe regressions on specific workloads, and adversarial inputs and percentile objectives do not fully address tail regressions.
AI.method: The authors use paired CVaR over the worst fraction of workloads of the cost difference between each candidate and an existing baseline, to guide LLM synthesis. They show that negative paired CVaR guarantees improvement in average performance and tail optimality gap relative to the unknown optimum, without computing the optimum.
AI.result: On Azure GPU batch admission, Azure VM packing and server placement, TAILOR achieves the best mean-tail trade-off among the evaluated synthesis objectives. Across seven optimization benchmarks, its heuristics are certified with 99% confidence to improve both average performance and tail optimality gaps over the baseline in six of them, and on these six it beats known robust human-designed alternatives in the tail.
AI.conclusion: Using a paired tail-risk objective during LLM synthesis yields heuristics with certified improvements on both average and tail performance.

title: Agentic Context Management for Multi-Turn Human-AI Conversations
summary: LLMs degrade in multi-turn conversation partly because of context pollution: the model's own earlier outputs stay in context and anchor later turns, so an early misreading of the user's intent can persist after the user corrects it. Assistant omission (AO), dropping every assistant message, removes this pollution but fails when interaction is referential: later turns refer back to drafts, decisions, and tool-call results that exist only in assistant turns. We propose Agentic Conversation Context Curation (AC3), a training-free method in which a separate analyzer (1) consolidates the task specification from the user's messages alone, (2) audits the assistant's prior outputs against it, and (3) edits the context, either appending the analysis or discarding the assistant side and rebuilding the context from the specification. A second finding: pollution is contagious. An analyzer that sees the assistant's reasoning while extracting the specification can do worse than no intervention, and instructing it to ignore them did not close the gap, so we exclude assistant turns structurally. On Lost in Conversation (replaying difficulty-selected instances), where AO is an oracle by construction, AC3 closes 55-84% of the gap between full context and AO on three of four tasks and exceeds AO on the fourth, and an LLM that faithfully summarizes the history does not reproduce the gain even with more compute. On real WildChat conversations, a GPT-5-mini judge prefers AC3's next turn over both full context and AO in every configuration of our main table, though this preference depends on the judge; on CollabLLM results are mixed. In stateful tool use (tau2-bench), AO collapses to 0% on every model; AC3 does not collapse, though it falls slightly behind full context. Detector studies show that Reset removes injected pollution but is not span-selective: the gain comes from rebuilding the specification.

AI.tldr: Agentic Conversation Context Curation (AC3) is a training-free method that stops context pollution in multi-turn conversations by using a separate analyzer that extracts the task specification from user messages only and audits assistant outputs against it. It closes 55-84% of the gap between full context and assistant omission on three of four Lost in Conversation tasks and keeps stateful tool use from collapsing.
AI.motivation: LLMs degrade in multi-turn conversation because their earlier outputs anchor later turns. Assistant omission removes this pollution but fails when later turns refer back to drafts, decisions or tool results that exist only in assistant turns.
AI.method: A separate analyzer consolidates the task specification from the user's messages alone, audits the assistant's prior outputs against it, and edits the context either by appending the analysis or by discarding the assistant side and rebuilding the context from the specification. Assistant turns are excluded structurally, because an analyzer that sees assistant reasoning can perform worse than no intervention.
AI.result: On Lost in Conversation, AC3 closes 55-84% of the gap between full context and assistant omission on three of four tasks and exceeds assistant omission on the fourth. On WildChat, a GPT-5-mini judge prefers AC3's next turn in every configuration of the main table, though this depends on the judge, and CollabLLM results are mixed. On tau2-bench, assistant omission collapses to 0% on every model, while AC3 does not collapse but falls slightly behind full context.
AI.conclusion: Rebuilding the task specification, rather than selectively removing spans, drives the gain. The pollution is contagious, so the analyzer should be kept away from assistant turns.

title: WeSearch: A Unified Model-Centric Retrieval Framework for WeChat Search
summary: We present WeSearch, a unified, model-centric retrieval framework for large-scale, continuously evolving content search. Prevailing methods assign documents fixed hierarchical Semantic IDs, implicitly assuming each document follows a single coherent semantic path-an assumption that often breaks down for multi-topic documents. WeSearch instead retrieves query-relevant clusters and then ranks atomic documents within the resulting query-specific candidate space, decoupling candidate pruning from fine-grained relevance modeling. Combined with relevance-aware training, compact document representations, and incremental index updates, this design enables weekly-or daily when needed-model refreshes. Deployed as the primary semantic retrieval path in WeChat Search alongside a lexical syntax tree, WeSearch shows consistent one-week A/B gains on corpora from hundreds of millions to billions of documents, and a one-month full-traffic A/B test confirms stable improvements of +0.68% CTR and +2.27% per-user article clicks, together with a 41% reduction in retrieval resource cost and a 19 ms reduction in graphic-text retrieval latency. WeSearch is now fully deployed in WeChat Search, serving 100% of production traffic.

AI.tldr: WeSearch is a model-centric retrieval framework for WeChat Search that retrieves query-relevant clusters and then ranks atomic documents within them, instead of relying on fixed hierarchical Semantic IDs. It is the primary semantic retrieval path in production and serves 100% of traffic after a one-month full-traffic A/B test.
AI.motivation: Fixed hierarchical Semantic IDs assume each document follows one coherent semantic path, which breaks for multi-topic documents in large, continuously changing content collections.
AI.method: WeSearch first retrieves query-relevant clusters and then ranks atomic documents inside the query-specific candidate space, decoupling candidate pruning from fine-grained relevance modeling. It combines relevance-aware training, compact document representations and incremental index updates, which allow weekly or daily model refreshes, and runs alongside a lexical syntax tree.
AI.result: One-week A/B tests show consistent gains on corpora from hundreds of millions to billions of documents. A one-month full-traffic A/B test shows +0.68% CTR and +2.27% per-user article clicks, a 41% reduction in retrieval resource cost and a 19 ms reduction in graphic-text retrieval latency.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling cluster-level candidate pruning from document-level ranking gives gains in quality, cost and latency at industrial scale.

title: Skill++: Towards Lifelong Agents via Routing-Aware Skill Refinement
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents extend their capabilities with skills, each with a name, a description, and a body. Under progressive disclosure, an LLM router selects skills by name and description alone and loads only the selected bodies. Skill libraries grow continually as users and agents add new skills. Because the router relies on this metadata, a similar new skill can displace an earlier one, breaking previously correct routing even though the earlier skill and the router are unchanged. This routing interference is aggravated for public skills, whose descriptions may not match their bodies. We formulate the problem as lifelong skill routing, a class-incremental continual learning problem. A solution must keep earlier skills selectable without suppressing new ones. Existing approaches fall short, since continually retraining the router risks catastrophic forgetting and rewriting methods either ignore similar skills or require per-skill feedback. We therefore propose Skill++, which rewrites only the name and description of each incoming skill, without router training or labeled data. The new description states what the body supports, how the skill differs from its closest predecessor, and what related work it excludes. As a library grows to 731 skills over ten sessions, Skill++ selects all required skills for 76.3% of queries, versus 36.4% under the original metadata. Across three benchmarks and five LLM routers, it outperforms all compared approaches, and its gains carry over to the Codex CLI agent harness.

AI.tldr: Skill++ fixes routing interference in lifelong LLM agents by rewriting only the name and description of each incoming skill, without router training or labeled data. Over ten sessions growing to 731 skills, it selects all required skills for 76.3% of queries versus 36.4% under the original metadata.
AI.motivation: LLM routers select skills by name and description, so a new similar skill can displace an earlier one and break correct routing. Continual retraining of the router risks catastrophic forgetting, and existing rewriting methods either ignore similar skills or need per-skill feedback.
AI.method: The authors formulate lifelong skill routing as class-incremental continual learning. Skill++ rewrites each incoming skill's description to state what the body supports, how it differs from its closest predecessor and what related work it excludes, without router training or labeled data.
AI.result: With a library of 731 skills over ten sessions, Skill++ selects all required skills for 76.3% of queries versus 36.4% under the original metadata. Across three benchmarks and five LLM routers it outperforms all compared approaches, and the gains carry over to the Codex CLI agent harness.
AI.conclusion: Metadata rewriting that separates similar skills is an effective, training-free way to keep earlier skills selectable as libraries grow.

title: Conic Certification of Transformer Attention
comment: 56 pages, 5 figures, 6 tables. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Attention is the computational core of large language models, yet the verifiers that bound how far an attention head's output can move under input perturbations give no guarantee on how loose their bounds are. A weak certificate therefore cannot be told apart from a fragile model. We develop a conic programming theory of attention certification that supplies this guarantee. We prove that the difficulty lies not in the softmax but in the bilinear interaction of a varying query with the keys. This interaction makes certification NP-hard over boxes and inapproximable once the attention logits can move by a constant amount. A fixed query or listed token substitutions, by contrast, make the exact worst case efficiently computable. An exponential cone moment relaxation then certifies a head with an error bounded quadratically in the perturbation radius by computable quantities, an order that cannot be improved. We also show that relaxations that treat a network one operation at a time, linear bound propagation among them, pay on second-order terms a sum of per-operation maxima instead of one coupled maximum. Computational results on GPT-2 indicate that the theory carries over to a trained model. Against exact worst cases with the query fixed, the certificate attains the predicted second-order accuracy. It is tighter than linear bound propagation on every head, and the looseness of bound propagation tracks the predicted per-operation excess.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a conic programming theory for certifying how much a transformer attention head's output can change under input perturbations. It shows that certification is NP-hard over boxes because of the bilinear query-key interaction, and an exponential cone moment relaxation gives a certificate with quadratic error in the perturbation radius that is tighter than linear bound propagation on every tested head of GPT-2.
AI.motivation: Verifiers for attention give no guarantee on how loose their bounds are, so a weak certificate cannot be distinguished from a fragile model.
AI.method: The authors analyze the bilinear interaction of a varying query with the keys and prove hardness results. They then build an exponential cone moment relaxation that certifies a head with error bounded quadratically in the perturbation radius by computable quantities. They also analyze operation-by-operation relaxations such as linear bound propagation and test on GPT-2.
AI.result: Certification is NP-hard over boxes and inapproximable once attention logits can move by a constant amount, while a fixed query or listed token substitutions make the exact worst case efficiently computable. Against exact worst cases with the query fixed, the certificate attains the predicted second-order accuracy and is tighter than linear bound propagation on every head.
AI.conclusion: The theory carries over to a trained model, and operation-by-operation relaxations pay a sum of per-operation maxima on second-order terms rather than one coupled maximum.

title: TVP: TV is Almost All You Need for Speculative Decoding
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference with a drafter whose proposed tokens are verified by the target model in parallel. Under lossless speculative sampling, a draft token is accepted with probability one minus the total variation (TV) distance between the target and draft distributions, yet drafters are often trained with cross-entropy (CE) or KL. We first show that under matched and well-tuned training, TV matches or surpasses several published draft-training objectives when fine-tuning, and a fixed TV and KL mixture does the same when training from scratch. We identify two remaining problems, TV's vanishing gradients on undercovered tokens and the prefix products that starve later positions in acceptance-length objectives. To address both, we derive TVP, a loss family based on expected acceptance length, whose power parameter interpolates between coverage and acceptance oriented objectives. Annealing the power from zero to one gives the highest or tied-highest acceptance length across three drafter architectures and three target models, including longer drafts and block verification. TVP improves acceptance length over CE by 9.8% when fine-tuning, and over the public DFlash2 training recipes by 6.2 to 12.9%.

AI.tldr: TVP is a loss family for speculative decoding drafters, based on expected acceptance length, whose power parameter interpolates between coverage-oriented and acceptance-oriented objectives. Annealing the power from zero to one gives the highest or tied-highest acceptance length across three drafter architectures and three target models.
AI.motivation: Drafters are usually trained with cross-entropy or KL, while lossless speculative sampling accepts a draft token with probability one minus the total variation distance. TV itself has vanishing gradients on undercovered tokens and prefix products that starve later positions in acceptance-length objectives.
AI.method: The authors first show that under matched, well-tuned training TV matches or surpasses several published draft-training objectives in fine-tuning, and that a fixed TV and KL mixture does the same from scratch. They then derive TVP from expected acceptance length, with a power parameter that is annealed from zero to one, and test on longer drafts and block verification.
AI.result: TVP improves acceptance length over cross-entropy by 9.8% when fine-tuning and over the public DFlash2 training recipes by 6.2 to 12.9%. It gives the highest or tied-highest acceptance length across three drafter architectures and three target models.
AI.conclusion: Annealing a coverage-to-acceptance objective addresses the gradient and prefix-product problems of TV and gives better drafters for speculative decoding.

title: Sparse Autoencoder Attribution Graphs Are Decided at the Margin
summary: Attribution graphs over the features of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are used to predict what an ablation does and are compared across training seeds. A TopK SAE keeps the largest preactivations at each token, and a feature's margin is its preactivation's distance to the cutoff. On five public TopK SAE pairs from three Pythia models, zeroing one feature moves a next layer feature across the cutoff in 0.74 of cases or more, and the crossings carry most of the response's energy. Over writes that scale a feature's code by three factors, the graph built on the features active beforehand has a median relative error of 0.247 or more. The margin graph adds the first order change to every preactivation and reranks, at the same cost, and errs by at most 0.033. At the median, the crossing features' decoded change is 1.24 times the model's own change in norm or more. Between seeds of one testbed, sparse maps between features explain 0.85 of a graph's energy on its active features, and 0.47 once the other seed's graph keeps only its own. The largest model studied is pythia-160m.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that attribution graphs over TopK sparse autoencoder features are decided by features near the activation cutoff, since zeroing one feature crosses the cutoff for a next-layer feature in 0.74 or more of cases. A margin-based graph that adds the first-order change to every preactivation reranks at the same cost and errs by at most 0.033.
AI.motivation: Attribution graphs over SAE features are used to predict ablation effects and to compare training seeds, but graphs built only on features active beforehand can be badly wrong when activations move across the TopK cutoff.
AI.method: On five public TopK SAE pairs from three Pythia models, the authors zero features and measure crossings of the cutoff by next-layer features, and scale feature codes by three factors to compare graph errors. The margin of a feature is its preactivation's distance to the cutoff, and the margin graph adds the first-order change to every preactivation before reranking.
AI.result: The graph built on features active beforehand has a median relative error of 0.247 or more under writes. The margin graph errs by at most 0.033. The crossing features' decoded change is 1.24 times the model's own change in norm or more at the median. Between seeds, sparse maps explain 0.85 of a graph's energy on active features, and 0.47 once the other seed's graph keeps only its own features. The largest model studied is pythia-160m.
AI.conclusion: Feature activity near the TopK cutoff drives attribution graph responses, so margin-aware graphs are a cheap correction, and cross-seed comparisons need care.

title: Heirloom: Carrying a Phone's Personalization Across Base-Model Generations
summary: On-device language models can learn a user's preferences through adapters trained on private data. However, a base-model upgrade may change the layers or vocabulary, leaving the personal adapter incompatible. Replacing it with a non-personal adapter loses much of the personalization, while retraining requires retaining the user's labeled history. We present Heirloom, a system that transfers a personal adapter to a new base model on the phone without retaining labels. Heirloom uses the old personal model as a teacher, collecting its predictions on stored unlabeled inputs, vendor-provided prompts, or prompts generated by the new base. It then unloads the old base and trains an adapter for the new model to match those predictions, keeping only one base model in memory at a time. We evaluate Heirloom across three generation upgrades from two model families, an architecture-preserving refresh, and three personalization tasks. On movie tagging, migration from stored inputs maintains pre-upgrade accuracy and differs from labeled retraining by at most 1.7 percentage points across the three upgrades. On a phone's neural processing unit (NPU), a fixed-length migration for the 4B upgrade takes 38 minutes and consumes 20% of the battery end to end, making the stored-input setting feasible during overnight charging.

AI.tldr: Heirloom transfers a personal on-device adapter to a new base model on the phone without retaining labels, using the old personal model as a teacher on stored unlabeled inputs, vendor prompts or prompts generated by the new base. On movie tagging, migration from stored inputs keeps pre-upgrade accuracy within 1.7 percentage points of labeled retraining across three upgrades.
AI.motivation: A base-model upgrade can make a personal adapter incompatible, and replacing it with a non-personal adapter loses much of the personalization, while retraining needs the user's labeled history.
AI.method: The old personal model acts as a teacher, producing predictions on stored unlabeled inputs, vendor-provided prompts or prompts generated by the new base. The old base is then unloaded and an adapter for the new model is trained to match those predictions, so only one base model is in memory at a time.
AI.result: Across three generation upgrades from two model families, an architecture-preserving refresh and three personalization tasks, migration from stored inputs maintains pre-upgrade accuracy on movie tagging and differs from labeled retraining by at most 1.7 points. On a phone NPU, a fixed-length migration for the 4B upgrade takes 38 minutes and uses 20% of the battery end to end, which makes the stored-input setting feasible overnight.
AI.conclusion: Label-free teacher-student distillation can carry personal adapters across base-model generations on-device at practical cost.

title: Learning Timeline-Preserving Speech-to-Speech Translation
summary: Speech-to-speech translation (S2ST) increasingly preserves what is said and how it sounds, but not necessarily when speech and silence occur. For dubbing and other temporally grounded applications, matching total duration is not enough: speech and pauses must also occur at corresponding moments. We formulate timeline-preserving S2ST, which aims to preserve the source endpoint and salient internal pauses on a shared absolute timeline. We present TransDubber, an end-to-end autoregressive system that learns this temporal structure directly from aligned target waveforms, without inference-time frame-level timing control or post-hoc temporal correction. To provide this supervision, we construct 642K exactly duration-matched English-Chinese speech pairs by translating and synthesizing target speech on source-defined temporal scaffolds. Training combines a progressive supervised curriculum with verifier-guided reinforcement learning to balance translation quality and temporal alignment. On a 4,353-utterance test set spanning read and spontaneous speech, TransDubber increases the proportion of translations within 2% of the source duration from 25.6% to 61.5% and pause-alignment F1 from 0.118 to 0.550 compared with UniSS, while maintaining competitive translation quality. Our analysis shows that aligned supervision establishes timeline following, while reinforcement learning refines temporal precision and partially offsets the translation-quality cost of strict synchronization. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of our data and training framework for timeline-preserving S2ST. Audio samples, code, datasets, and pretrained models are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: TransDubber is an end-to-end autoregressive speech-to-speech translation system that learns to preserve the source timeline, meaning the endpoint and salient internal pauses on a shared absolute timeline, from aligned target waveforms. On a 4,353-utterance test set it raises the share of translations within 2% of source duration from 25.6% to 61.5% and pause-alignment F1 from 0.118 to 0.550 compared with UniSS.
AI.motivation: Speech-to-speech translation preserves content and voice but not the timing of speech and silence, which matters for dubbing and other temporally grounded uses where matching total duration is not enough.
AI.method: The authors construct 642K exactly duration-matched English-Chinese speech pairs by translating and synthesizing target speech on source-defined temporal scaffolds. Training combines a progressive supervised curriculum with verifier-guided reinforcement learning, with no inference-time timing control or post-hoc correction.
AI.result: Compared with UniSS on a 4,353-utterance test set spanning read and spontaneous speech, TransDubber raises the share of translations within 2% of source duration from 25.6% to 61.5% and pause-alignment F1 from 0.118 to 0.550, while keeping translation quality competitive.
AI.conclusion: Aligned supervision establishes timeline following, and reinforcement learning refines temporal precision and partly offsets the translation-quality cost of strict synchronization.

title: ConstraintMatch: Compositional Image-Text Matching through Constrained Regional Evidence Selection
summary: Local image--text matching can find strong evidence for individual concepts yet favor captions with incorrect attribute--entity bindings. We introduce ConstraintMatch, a training-free inference method that turns entity-level regional consistency into an explicit matching cost. On the same frozen condition--region similarity matrix, it compares independent crop selection for each category and attribute with a shared crop choice within each entity. Their gap quantifies the score advantage obtained by relaxing the shared-region constraint. Spatial references from the same image calibrate this gap by keeping category evidence fixed while jointly shifting an entity's attribute maps. Per-entity clipping prevents cancellation across residuals, and the scaled mean cost is subtracted from global similarity. ConstraintMatch uses pooled embeddings, and spatial calibration requires no additional encoder calls. With parameters fixed per backbone across tasks, ConstraintMatch improves over global matching by 7.70 percentage points on full ARO Attribute and 5.63 points on held-out SugarCrepe++ attribute swaps, averaged across Qwen~2B and CORE~2B. Against SGI adapted to the same 13-crop budget, the respective gains are 4.85 and 3.51 points. Controlled analyses distinguish the effects of shared-region matching and candidate score calibration. The results establish entity-level evidence selection as a practical scoring principle for compositional multimodal retrieval.

AI.tldr: ConstraintMatch is a training-free inference method for compositional image-text matching that scores entity-level regional consistency, so that each entity's category and attribute share one crop choice. It improves over global matching by 7.70 points on ARO Attribute and 5.63 points on held-out SugarCrepe++ attribute swaps, averaged across two backbones.
AI.motivation: Local image-text matching finds strong evidence for individual concepts but can prefer captions with incorrect attribute-entity bindings.
AI.method: On the same frozen condition-region similarity matrix, ConstraintMatch compares independent crop selection for each category and attribute with a shared crop choice within each entity, and uses the gap between them as a matching cost. Spatial references from the same image calibrate this gap, per-entity clipping prevents cancellation, and the scaled mean cost is subtracted from global similarity. It uses pooled embeddings and needs no extra encoder calls.
AI.result: With parameters fixed per backbone, ConstraintMatch improves over global matching by 7.70 points on full ARO Attribute and 5.63 points on held-out SugarCrepe++ attribute swaps, averaged across Qwen 2B and CORE 2B. Against SGI adapted to the same 13-crop budget, the gains are 4.85 and 3.51 points.
AI.conclusion: Entity-level evidence selection is a practical scoring principle for compositional multimodal retrieval.

title: ODC: Orthogonal Drift Correction for Improved Text-to-Image Semantic Alignment at Inference
comment: Accepted to Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR) 2026
summary: Text-to-image models have achieved remarkable success in generating high-quality images from textual descriptions. However, they often struggle with "semantic drift," where the generated output fails to precisely align with complex or nuanced text prompts. While recent approaches have attempted to address semantic errors regarding attribute binding or object presence, there remains a gap for a more holistic method that addresses these issues by directly refining the text embeddings of the initial user prompt. In this work, we introduce Orthogonal Drift Correction (ODC), an inference-time guidance method designed to mitigate semantic drift without requiring model retraining or additional user inputs. ODC guides image generation through a two-stage process. In the first stage, it identifies the semantic drift by evaluating the initially generated image against the user prompt in a shared vision-language embedding space. It then isolates the component of this drift vector that is orthogonal to the prompt's direction and translates it back into text via a vocabulary-based surrogate mechanism. In the second stage, it produces refined text conditioning for a second generation pass by feeding both the initial text embedding and the re-embedded drift representation into an adaptive rank-reduced concept removal module. Our experiments demonstrate that ODC consistently improves prompt-image alignment, increasing CLIP scores by up to 5.4% over the baseline on the COALBench-300 and PartiPrompts benchmarks. Furthermore, on the T2I-CompBench complex subset, ODC improves the average 3-in-1 score by 4.5% over the competing methods. As a plug-and-play module, ODC offers a practical and efficient method for improving the reliability of text-to-image models. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Orthogonal Drift Correction (ODC) is an inference-time method that reduces semantic drift in text-to-image generation by refining the prompt embedding. It increases CLIP scores by up to 5.4% over the baseline on COALBench-300 and PartiPrompts and improves the T2I-CompBench complex-subset 3-in-1 score by 4.5% over competing methods.
AI.motivation: Text-to-image models often fail to align precisely with complex or nuanced prompts, and prior fixes target attribute binding or object presence rather than the whole prompt embedding.
AI.method: ODC generates an image, measures the drift between it and the prompt in a shared vision-language embedding space, and keeps the component of the drift orthogonal to the prompt direction. That component is translated back into text through a vocabulary-based surrogate. In a second pass, the initial text embedding and the re-embedded drift go into an adaptive rank-reduced concept removal module to produce refined conditioning. It needs no retraining.
AI.result: ODC increases CLIP scores by up to 5.4% over the baseline on COALBench-300 and PartiPrompts, and improves the average 3-in-1 score on the T2I-CompBench complex subset by 4.5% over competing methods.
AI.conclusion: As a plug-and-play module needing no retraining or extra user input, ODC is a practical way to improve prompt-image alignment.

title: Fewer Tokens, More Answers: Verifiable-Reward Tuning of an Ornith-Style VLM for Multi-View Driving QA
summary: Reasoning-enabled model derivatives must turn intermediate deliberation into a usable answer within a deployment budget. We study that transition in an Ornith checkpoint adapted to multi-camera driving question answering with verifiable rewards. Paired archived outputs show that, on a selected 400-question development screen with a 256-token cap, GRPO increases answer extraction from 78.25% to 90.25% and accuracy from 55.50% to 63.75%. Of 39 wrong-to-correct transitions, 33 begin with an unextractable base response. The base's 87 unextractable responses all reach the token cap. Checkpoint-verified reconstruction on those same questions gives a much smaller first-pass accuracy gain at 512 tokens: +0.75 percentage points, versus +8.25 at 256. A later answer-cued continuation is analyzed separately; it helps the base more and narrows the adapter difference. On the full 2,511-question development set, this recovery-enabled pipeline reduces mean generated tokens from 108.6 to 47.1, while the paired accuracy interval includes zero gain. We frame these findings as adaptation of answer delivery under finite budgets, with explicit selection and provenance limits. Ornith's self-scaffolding lineage and newer reasoning-enabled derivatives such as Bonsai motivate the problem, but our measured results concern Ornith alone and do not establish a shared architectural mechanism or cross-model transfer.

AI.tldr: The paper adapts an Ornith VLM to multi-camera driving question answering with verifiable-reward GRPO and shows that the gain comes from converting deliberation into extractable answers within a token budget. On a 400-question development screen with a 256-token cap, GRPO raises extraction from 78.25% to 90.25% and accuracy from 55.50% to 63.75%, while on the full 2,511-question development set mean generated tokens drop from 108.6 to 47.1 with no accuracy gain whose interval excludes zero.
AI.motivation: Reasoning-enabled models must turn intermediate deliberation into a usable answer within a deployment budget, and the transition from deliberation to answer delivery is not well studied.
AI.method: The authors compare archived paired outputs of the base and GRPO-trained Ornith checkpoints on a selected 400-question development screen with a 256-token cap, and run checkpoint-verified reconstruction at 512 tokens. They also analyze a later answer-cued continuation and evaluate a recovery-enabled pipeline on the full 2,511-question development set, with explicit selection and provenance limits.
AI.result: Of 39 wrong-to-correct transitions, 33 begin with an unextractable base response, and all 87 unextractable base responses reach the token cap. Reconstruction at 512 tokens gives +0.75 points of first-pass accuracy versus +8.25 at 256. On the full development set, the pipeline reduces mean generated tokens from 108.6 to 47.1, while the paired accuracy interval includes zero gain.
AI.conclusion: The findings concern adaptation of answer delivery under finite budgets for Ornith alone and do not establish a shared mechanism or cross-model transfer, for example to Bonsai.

title: When 200 OK Is Not an Answer: Silent Fetch Failures in Agentic Web Content Acquisition
summary: Web agents and answer engines fetch pages at question time, and liveness checks of cited sources treat an HTTP 200 response as success. We measure how often that assumption fails and what it does to measurements built on fetched pages. We fetched 10,307 URLs in three days with a polite static client and a rendered browser client: pages from 1,507 sites in five strata, random non-existent paths on every site, and the 4,795 URLs cited by expert-verified claims in ExpertQA. We define a taxonomy of what a 200 response contains, label the static 200 responses automatically, and check the labels against 300 items reviewed by an LLM-based assistant; a human check of 60 of them retained every reviewed usability label after discussion. By the automatic labels, 20.9% of the pages that a static client receives with status 200 do not contain the page's main content: app shells, bot challenges, block pages, error and placeholder pages, and partial content. On the held-out test split, the reviewed sample lowers this estimate from 25.5% to 20.0%. 13.1% of the sites whose random-path probe was answered returned 200. The error propagates: for the cited sources, treating 200 as content overstates the share of claim-source pairs that can be checked against live content by 12.2 points and inflates the apparent silent citation-drift rate from 5.8% to 21.9%. Cheap heuristics catch most of it. Text length, probe comparison and redirect-to-root, combined and tuned on held-out sites, recover 86% of unusable reviewed responses at a false-alarm rate near 5%. Content-reading detectors perform comparably: the best, the text classifier, gains five to seven points of recall at more than twice the false-alarm rate. We argue that agents and their evaluations should report fetch outcomes explicitly instead of inferring them from the status line and will release the labelled data and code.

AI.tldr: The paper measures how often a successful HTTP 200 response from a web fetch contains no usable main content, finding that about 20.9% of static-client 200 responses are unusable and that treating 200 as content inflates apparent silent citation drift from 5.8% to 21.9%. Simple heuristics on text length, probe comparison and redirect-to-root recover 86% of unusable responses at a false-alarm rate near 5%.
AI.motivation: Web agents and answer engines and liveness checks of cited sources assume that an HTTP 200 means success, and the paper tests how often this fails and how it affects measurements built on fetched pages.
AI.method: The authors fetch 10,307 URLs over three days with a static client and a rendered browser client, covering pages from 1,507 sites in five strata, random non-existent paths on every site, and 4,795 URLs cited by expert-verified claims in ExpertQA. They define a taxonomy of 200 responses, label static 200 responses automatically, and check labels against 300 items reviewed by an LLM-based assistant, with a human check of 60 items.
AI.result: By automatic labels, 20.9% of static-client 200 pages lack main content, and on the held-out split the reviewed sample lowers this from 25.5% to 20.0%. 13.1% of sites answered random-path probes with 200. Treating 200 as content overstates the share of claim-source pairs checkable against live content by 12.2 points. Combined length, probe and redirect heuristics recover 86% of unusable reviewed responses at a false-alarm rate near 5%, and content-reading detectors perform comparably.
AI.conclusion: Agents and their evaluations should report fetch outcomes explicitly rather than infer them from the status line, and the authors will release the labeled data and code.

title: Multi-Turn Semantic Caching for Low-Cost LLM Serving
summary: Semantic caching lowers the cost of serving large language models (LLMs) by reusing stored responses for similar requests. In multi-turn conversations, whether a cached response is acceptable depends on both conversations' histories, which embedding similarity of requests and histories predicts poorly (AUC 0.62--0.74 on five workloads). We therefore learn the \emph{reuse risk}, the probability that a cached response is unacceptable, from judge feedback, and choose a budgeted set of conversation states to cache by weighing the generation cost a reuse avoids against a price for unacceptable reuse. We propose CUCB-SC-MT, which learns a cache from logged conversations with a suboptimality guarantee, and CLCB-LS-MT, which learns online and has $\tilde O(\sqrt N)$ regret over $N$ requests when conversation states recur. On math-tutoring (SocraTeach) and movie-ticketing (Taskmaster-3) conversations, both achieve lower loss than prior semantic caching approaches: ContextCache, multi-turn variants of ElastiCache and vCache, and single-turn semantic caching at every cache budget. With 1,000 cache entries, CLCB-LS-MT avoids 35--41\% of the generation cost through acceptable reuses, against at most 22--25\% for the baselines, and lowers estimated serving latency by 19--35\%.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes learned semantic caching for multi-turn LLM conversations, estimating the reuse risk from judge feedback and choosing a budgeted set of conversation states to cache. With 1,000 cache entries, CLCB-LS-MT avoids 35-41% of generation cost through acceptable reuses versus at most 22-25% for baselines and lowers estimated latency by 19-35%.
AI.motivation: Whether a cached response is acceptable in a multi-turn conversation depends on both conversations' histories, which embedding similarity predicts poorly (AUC 0.62-0.74 on five workloads).
AI.method: The authors learn the reuse risk, the probability that a cached response is unacceptable, from judge feedback. They propose CUCB-SC-MT, which learns a cache from logged conversations with a suboptimality guarantee, and CLCB-LS-MT, which learns online with regret of order sqrt(N) when conversation states recur. The cache choice weighs the generation cost a reuse avoids against a price for unacceptable reuse.
AI.result: On SocraTeach math tutoring and Taskmaster-3 movie ticketing, both methods achieve lower loss than ContextCache, multi-turn variants of ElastiCache and vCache, and single-turn semantic caching at every budget. With 1,000 entries, CLCB-LS-MT avoids 35-41% of generation cost, against at most 22-25% for baselines, and lowers estimated latency by 19-35%.
AI.conclusion: Learning reuse risk from judge feedback and caching conversation states under a budget gives better cost savings than similarity-based multi-turn caching.

title: Concept-Guided Prompting Strategies Increase Diversity in LLM-Generated Recipe Populations
summary: Novelty in solution generation supports automated discovery, but LLM outputs can remain repetitive. To address this, we propose a simple concept-guided prompting method that generates thematic concepts before responses within each of these concepts. To demonstrate, we generated 1,000 recipes for a recipe book task and compared the results against a human-authored corpus. Two naive prompting strategies were compared as baselines. Concept-guided prompting outperformed both baselines in all cases and reached semantic coverage of 47.0% versus 35.1% and 13.1% in respective prior-title and nonce prompt strategies. These findings suggest broader population exploration and diversity, but remain contained to this specific task. Further work is needed to determine the quality of solutions and generalizability.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes concept-guided prompting, which generates thematic concepts before responses for each concept, to increase diversity in LLM-generated recipes. Across 1,000 recipes it reaches semantic coverage of 47.0%, versus 35.1% and 13.1% for two naive baselines.
AI.motivation: LLM outputs can be repetitive, which limits novelty in solution generation for automated discovery.
AI.method: The authors generate 1,000 recipes for a recipe book task using concept-guided prompting, which first produces thematic concepts and then responses within each concept. They compare against a human-authored corpus and two naive baselines, prior-title prompting and nonce prompting.
AI.result: Concept-guided prompting outperforms both baselines in all cases and reaches semantic coverage of 47.0%, versus 35.1% for prior-title and 13.1% for nonce prompting.
AI.conclusion: The approach suggests broader population exploration and diversity, but the results are limited to this task, and solution quality and generalizability remain to be determined.

title: Does Random Search Discover Task Experts? Revisiting Neural Thickets
summary: Pretrained models are typically viewed as generalists, requiring bespoke post-training to achieve task-specific expertise. Gan & Isola (2026) recently proposed a striking alternative: that pretrained models lie in a dense neural thicket of task specialists, which can be surfaced with simple Gaussian weight perturbations. We examine this neural thicket of task-specific experts and identify several key findings that question this perspective. First, we find that the apparent lift of the best-of-N selected perturbation decays quickly with selection-set size m, strongly suggesting overfitting to the selection questions. In fact, for 10 of the 12 model-task pairs we study, a simple null model of pure selection noise predicts more than 75 percent of the top expert's reward lift. Second, the top experts' advantage often vanishes on held-out questions or remains within the run-to-run variability of the unperturbed pretrained model. Third, we find that majority voting over the top-K selected perturbations, termed RandOpt(N, K) by Gan & Isola (2026), is often matched or outperformed by majority voting over K samples from the base model. Overall, our results suggest that random weight perturbations may be ineffective at uncovering task experts around pretrained models, and that task adaptation requires more sophistication than random search. Code and artifacts are available at this http URL.

AI.tldr: The paper revisits the neural thicket claim that Gaussian weight perturbations of pretrained models surface task experts, finding that best-of-N gains largely reflect overfitting to the selection set. A null model of pure selection noise predicts more than 75% of the top expert's reward lift for 10 of 12 model-task pairs.
AI.motivation: Gan and Isola (2026) proposed that pretrained models lie in a dense thicket of task specialists reachable by simple random perturbations, which would make bespoke post-training unnecessary. The authors test this claim.
AI.method: The authors vary the selection-set size m, evaluate top experts on held-out questions, compare them with run-to-run variability of the unperturbed model, and compare majority voting over top-K perturbations, termed RandOpt(N, K), with majority voting over K base-model samples.
AI.result: The best-of-N lift decays quickly with selection-set size m. For 10 of 12 model-task pairs a null model of pure selection noise predicts more than 75% of the top expert's lift. Top experts' advantage often vanishes on held-out questions or stays within run-to-run variability of the base model. Majority voting over top-K perturbations is often matched or outperformed by majority voting over base samples.
AI.conclusion: Random weight perturbations may be ineffective at finding task experts around pretrained models, and task adaptation needs more than random search.

title: Geometry of Confabulation and Refusal in Small Language Models
comment: 35 pages, 16 figures, 19 tables. Code, data, and the ConfabQA benchmark: this https URL
summary: Faced with an unanswerable question, small language models can either refuse or confabulate: confidently produce a wrong answer. Can the hidden state before the first generated token provide a clue? Can we flip confabulations into refusals? I introduce ConfabQA, a 784-item benchmark whose obscure-pre-cutoff category breaks the typical correctness/knowledge-cutoff confound and map the geometry of the hidden state with linear probes, a sparse autoencoder (SAE), and direct optimization of intervention directions. On Qwen3-1.7B and Gemma 2 2B the probe separates upcoming refusals from confabulations well beyond prompt features (+7.4/+16.3 pp); on Llama 3.2 3B the ConfabQA margin is within fold-to-fold spread, but a direct refusal probe on PopQA and TriviaQA recovers +18-25 pp. On Qwen I closely inspect three candidate directions for the refusal vector: probe-recovered, Qwen-Scope SAE feature, and directly optimized. Although the three directions are pairwise 50-81 degrees apart, a push at or below the state's own norm along any of them flips most confabulations into refusal openings dominated by the "As..." family. Forcing the opener without touching the hidden state yields the same one-in-three judged-refusal rate as any push. The opposite push collapses refusals mostly into confabulations, yet leaves originally correct answers intact, so the direction gates the opening speech act rather than the knowledge behind it. Confabulations do not resolve into a concentrated feature in a dictionary or a token signature on Qwen3-1.7B. Scoring every probe on the margin over the strongest of four prompt-feature baselines extracts the hidden state's own contribution. Correctness signal is model-dependent and portable only for Llama 3.2 3B: 81% of the probe's margin over test majority survives transfer between ConfabQA, PopQA, and TriviaQA. Benchmark, judge, and code are released.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether the hidden state before the first generated token predicts whether a small language model will refuse or confabulate on unanswerable questions, and whether steering it can turn confabulations into refusals. Linear probes separate upcoming refusals from confabulations on Qwen3-1.7B and Gemma 2 2B, and pushing along a refusal direction flips most confabulations into refusal openings.
AI.motivation: Small models can either refuse or confidently give wrong answers to unanswerable questions, and it is unclear whether the hidden state carries information about which will happen.
AI.method: The author introduces ConfabQA, a 784-item benchmark with an obscure pre-cutoff category, and studies the hidden state with linear probes, a sparse autoencoder and direct optimization of intervention directions. The three refusal directions on Qwen (probe-recovered, a Qwen-Scope SAE feature and directly optimized) are compared, and the signal is scored against four prompt-feature baselines.
AI.result: The probe separates upcoming refusals from confabulations beyond prompt features by +7.4 points on Qwen3-1.7B and +16.3 points on Gemma 2 2B. On Llama 3.2 3B the ConfabQA margin is within fold-to-fold spread, but a refusal probe on PopQA and TriviaQA recovers +18-25 points. The three Qwen directions are pairwise 50-81 degrees apart, yet pushes along any of them flip most confabulations into refusal openings. The opposite push turns refusals into confabulations and leaves originally correct answers intact.
AI.conclusion: The direction gates the opening speech act rather than the underlying knowledge, and correctness signals are model-dependent and portable only for Llama 3.2 3B, where 81% of the probe's margin survives transfer.

title: What Do LLM Judges Actually Verify? Matched Controls and Record Gaps for Document Currency
comment: 37 pages, 6 figures, including a 13-page supplementary case study. Code, data and all judge replies: this https URL
summary: LLM judges often check, against an amendment record, whether the documents an answer cites are still in force. Such records are rarely complete. From a table of replacements, our test generates matched answers citing a replaced document, its successor, the replaced document before its replacement, and an older document that a newer one updated without replacing; it removes links from the record and scores each finding by its stated reason. On 48 replacements from the IETF RFC index, judges given a correct record caught nearly every replaced citation, as a lookup would. On the 24 faults whose link we removed, every judge caught more from the texts alone than with the record: Gemini 3.1 Pro 23/24 against 1/24, GPT-5.5 23/24 against 9/24, Claude Opus 4.5 17/24 against 9/24 and Gemma 4 26B 13/24 against 0/24. The drop recurred on a second draw of removed links. Most misses carried no finding; in an exploratory run with a conflict code, only Gemini used it often. Rewording the gap as "no replacement recorded" did not help; presenting the record as an unverified note, or warning that it was incomplete, restored most lost catches for Gemini, GPT-5.5 and Claude (significant after correction for the first two) but at most 5 of 13 for Gemma; where catches returned, so did false alarms on updates. With both texts, judges mostly told replacements from updates; every update flagged had a near-identical title. A descriptive case study on Indian rooftop-solar rules is appended; we release the harness.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether LLM judges check the currency of cited documents against an amendment record or from the texts alone, finding that with an incomplete record judges catch far fewer replaced citations. On the 24 faults where links were removed, every judge caught more from the texts alone than with the record, for example Gemini 3.1 Pro at 23/24 versus 1/24.
AI.motivation: LLM judges often rely on an amendment record to check whether cited documents are still in force, but such records are rarely complete, and it is unclear what the judges actually verify.
AI.method: From a table of replacements in the IETF RFC index with 48 replacements, the authors generate matched answers citing a replaced document, its successor, the replaced document before replacement, and an older document updated without replacement. They remove links from the record and score each finding by its stated reason. They test record framings, including presenting the record as unverified or warning that it is incomplete, and append a descriptive case study on Indian rooftop-solar rules.
AI.result: With a correct record, judges caught nearly every replaced citation. On the 24 faults whose links were removed, every judge caught more from texts alone than with the record: Gemini 3.1 Pro 23/24 against 1/24, GPT-5.5 23/24 against 9/24, Claude Opus 4.5 17/24 against 9/24, and Gemma 4 26B 13/24 against 0/24. Presenting the record as unverified or warning it is incomplete restored most lost catches for Gemini, GPT-5.5 and Claude, but at most 5 of 13 for Gemma, and the returned catches came with false alarms on updates.
AI.conclusion: Judges mostly tell replacements from updates when both texts are given, but they depend on record completeness in ways that a correct record hides, and their verification should not be assumed from record lookups alone.

title: Are Fake Citations a Form of Reward Hacking? A Pre-Registered Study of Post-Training and Citation Cues
comment: 49 pages, 3 figures, 20 tables. Code and data: this https URL (archived at doi:https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23845528)
summary: Post-trained language models fabricate citations at high rates. We ask whether that is reward hacking: scoring well on a proxy for scholarship while doing worse on what it stands for. We ran four pre-registered experiments on 900 frozen questions (US federal case law, computationally adjacent scientific literature, and medical literature) across twelve open-weights checkpoints covering four post-training stages of three model families, then refit on fifteen. The clearest result holds the weights fixed and changes only the prompt. Asking for citations raises fabrication sharply in post-trained checkpoints and not in base ones: a 47.8-point interaction on twelve checkpoints (Holm-adjusted p = 2e-34) and 41.5 points on fifteen, in all three domains. A length-matched control separates the citation cue from a demand for a longer answer, so the effect is specific to citations, not verbosity. Post-training also raises fabrication overall, from 4.8% to 56.7%, but our registered prediction that it would rise most where fabrication is most tempting did not hold. A preference model trained only on surface citation features prefers post-trained output 86% of the time, and holding citation count fixed shows it rewards quantity. Our answer: possibly, but not proven. Post-trained models produce fabricated citations at far higher rates when asked for sources, and a naive evaluator that counts sources without checking them would prefer their output for citing more. But the targeted pattern we registered did not appear, and plain instruction-following could explain the same results. Proving that the reward causes fabrication needs an experiment that changes the reward during training, which this study does not do. Pre-registration: doi:https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/S53HY. Code and data: this https URL

AI.tldr: Across four pre-registered experiments on 900 frozen questions and twelve open-weight checkpoints, asking for citations raises fabrication sharply in post-trained models but not base models, with a 47.8-point interaction on twelve checkpoints. The authors conclude fake citations may be reward hacking but this is not proven, since the registered targeted pattern did not appear.
AI.motivation: Post-trained language models fabricate citations at high rates, and the authors ask whether this is reward hacking, that is, scoring well on a proxy for scholarship while doing worse on what it stands for.
AI.method: The authors run four pre-registered experiments on 900 frozen questions in US federal case law, computationally adjacent science and medical literature, across twelve open-weight checkpoints from four post-training stages of three model families, then refit on fifteen. A length-matched control separates citation requests from requests for longer answers, and a preference model trained on surface citation features is tested with citation count held fixed.
AI.result: Asking for citations raises fabrication in post-trained checkpoints and not in base ones, with a 47.8-point interaction on twelve checkpoints (Holm-adjusted p = 2e-34) and 41.5 points on fifteen, in all three domains. Post-training raises fabrication overall from 4.8% to 56.7%, but the predicted larger rise where fabrication is most tempting did not appear. A surface-feature preference model prefers post-trained output 86% of the time and rewards citation quantity.
AI.conclusion: Post-trained models fabricate citations at far higher rates when asked for sources, and a naive evaluator would prefer this output, but proving that reward causes fabrication needs training-time reward interventions that this study does not perform, and instruction-following could explain the results.

title: Learning by Doing: Autonomously Compiling and Curating Agent Skills from Verified Traces
summary: Memory systems for production LLM agents mostly store semantic memory (facts about users and domains) or episodic memory (earlier interactions). Research systems such as Trace2Skill, WikiSkill, and SkillRevise learn procedures from agent runs, package them as Skills, and evaluate them on benchmarks. We describe Zep Agent Skills, a production service that gives deployed agents this procedural memory. The service uses only verified attempts as evidence, cites the supporting events for each field of a Skill, and governs the admission and distribution of each Skill version. The service records each task attempt as a Trace with ordered events, an outcome, and a verification strength. A compiler with separate Reflector and Curator roles turns verified Traces into versioned Skills. Scans and admission gates control which candidates become active, and verified use outcomes change the search rank of each Skill. The Agent Skills format is an open standard that Anthropic originated and donated to the Agentic AI Foundation, so any host of the format can load a compiled Skill. Agents retrieve Skills through lexical search with progressive disclosure, over an API or MCP. We evaluate Zep Agent Skills on $\tau^3$-bench banking, AppWorld, and EnterpriseOps-Gym. Skills compiled from the Traces of a teacher model increase the pass rate of three weaker executor models on the same tasks, at every reasoning effort, by 4.5 to 18.8 points. Most of the gain is on the tasks that the teacher solved. On ALFWorld, Skills compiled from the runs of a small model give a gain similar to or larger than the gain that prior work reports for continuous fine-tuning, with no training.

AI.tldr: Zep Agent Skills is a production service that compiles verified agent task traces into versioned, cited procedural Skills, governed by admission gates and ranked by verified use outcomes. Skills compiled from a teacher model's traces raise the pass rate of three weaker executor models on tau3-bench banking, AppWorld and EnterpriseOps-Gym by 4.5 to 18.8 points.
AI.motivation: Production LLM agent memory mostly stores semantic or episodic memory, while research systems learn procedures from runs but are evaluated on benchmarks rather than deployed.
AI.method: The service records each attempt as a Trace with ordered events, an outcome and a verification strength. A compiler with separate Reflector and Curator roles turns verified Traces into versioned Skills, scans and admission gates decide which candidates become active, and verified use outcomes change each Skill's search rank. Agents retrieve Skills by lexical search with progressive disclosure, over an API or MCP, and each field of a Skill cites its supporting events.
AI.result: Skills compiled from a teacher model's traces increase the pass rate of three weaker executor models on the same tasks, at every reasoning effort, by 4.5 to 18.8 points, mostly on tasks the teacher solved. On ALFWorld, Skills compiled from a small model's runs give a gain similar to or larger than the gain prior work reports for continuous fine-tuning, with no training.
AI.conclusion: Verified, governed procedural memory can improve deployed agents without training, and the Agent Skills format is an open standard that any compatible host can load.

title: When Should an Agent Refresh? Adaptive Index Reuse for Efficient Long-Horizon Reasoning
summary: Language agents read code, tool output, and dialogue in contexts that grow at every step. Dynamic sparse attention lets a small indexer choose the earlier tokens each query attends to, but the indexer still scores the whole prefix at every layer. Cross-layer reuse methods such as IndexCache rerun the indexer at only some layers, with one fixed pattern for every input. In an agent, the relevant evidence can change abruptly when a traceback or test result arrives, so fresh selections matter more at some steps than at others. We propose Adaptive Index Reuse (AIR), which keeps IndexCache's execution and learns, for each segment of an agent episode, how many layers refresh their selection. A small controller reads signals from completed computation and the latest tool event, chooses a pattern from a nested library, and learns from terminal task reward under an expected compute budget. On Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 with a 128K context, AIR improves success over the strongest static schedule at matched cost on SWE-bench Verified (27.0% to 32.4%), Terminal-Bench 2.0, and three $\tau^2$-bench domains, and it lowers time per successful task on all five. Across 50 backbone, context, and benchmark settings, it matches or exceeds that schedule in 44.

AI.tldr: Adaptive Index Reuse (AIR) learns, for each segment of an agent episode, how many layers should refresh their dynamic sparse-attention index, and so reduces indexer cost while keeping task success. On Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 with a 128K context it improves success over the strongest static schedule at matched cost on SWE-bench Verified from 27.0% to 32.4%, and lowers time per successful task on all five benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Dynamic sparse attention indexers rescore the whole prefix at every layer, and cross-layer reuse such as IndexCache uses one fixed refresh pattern for all inputs, even though agent evidence changes abruptly when tool output arrives.
AI.method: AIR keeps IndexCache's execution and adds a small controller that reads signals from completed computation and the latest tool event, picks a refresh pattern from a nested library, and learns from terminal task reward under an expected compute budget.
AI.result: On SWE-bench Verified AIR improves success from 27.0% to 32.4% over the strongest static schedule at matched cost, and it also improves on Terminal-Bench 2.0 and three tau2-bench domains while lowering time per successful task on all five. Across 50 backbone, context and benchmark settings it matches or exceeds that schedule in 44 of them.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, per-segment refresh schedules can beat fixed cross-layer reuse for long-horizon agent reasoning at matched compute.

title: Can Large Language Model Agents Learn by Watching Tutorial Videos?
summary: Humans continuously acquire knowledge from carefully crafted materials such as books and tutorial videos, carrying that understanding into future tasks. Millions of such instructional videos are uploaded online every day, yet LLM agents remain unable to exploit this ever-expanding wealth of human teaching. Their capabilities are frozen after training, while parameter updates at scale remain prohibitively expensive. This raises the central question: can LLM agents learn from this vast instructional resource without parameter updates? We introduce Tutorial Agentic Learning (TAL), a nonparametric continual-learning paradigm that consolidates tutorial videos into a persistent, structured tutorialbook memory through a two-stage adversarial process that harvests hard, video-grounded questions and uses them to refine the memory. At inference time, TAL retrieves through a Table-of-Contents (TOC) tree, tying retrieval directly to the model's reasoning rather than to embedding similarity. To study this setting, we introduce VidLearn, a multimodal QA benchmark built from 72 chess tutorial videos spanning 12 openings. On VidLearn, TAL outperforms all evaluated baselines and improves monotonically as more videos are consumed, achieving up to 113% and 91% relative gains over the corresponding vanilla MLLMs on the training and test splits, respectively. In actual gameplay, TAL reaches a stronger opening-phase position than its vanilla counterpart in 69% of head-to-head games. Evaluation in a second domain further demonstrates the generality of TAL. Together, these results highlight instructional videos as a scalable resource for parameter-update-free agent continual learning.

AI.tldr: Tutorial Agentic Learning (TAL) lets LLM agents learn from tutorial videos without parameter updates by consolidating them into a structured tutorialbook memory and retrieving through a table-of-contents tree. On the VidLearn chess benchmark built from 72 tutorial videos, it reaches up to 113% and 91% relative gains over vanilla MLLMs on training and test splits.
AI.motivation: LLM agents remain frozen after training, and parameter updates at scale are too expensive, while vast amounts of instructional video are available online.
AI.method: TAL consolidates tutorial videos into a persistent, structured tutorialbook memory through a two-stage adversarial process that harvests hard, video-grounded questions and uses them to refine the memory. At inference it retrieves through a table-of-contents tree, tied to the model's reasoning rather than embedding similarity. The authors introduce VidLearn, a multimodal QA benchmark built from 72 chess tutorial videos spanning 12 openings.
AI.result: On VidLearn, TAL outperforms all evaluated baselines and improves monotonically as more videos are consumed, with up to 113% and 91% relative gains over the corresponding vanilla MLLMs on training and test splits. In gameplay, TAL reaches a stronger opening-phase position than its vanilla counterpart in 69% of head-to-head games, and a second domain shows generality.
AI.conclusion: Instructional videos are a scalable resource for parameter-update-free continual learning of agents.

title: See, Think, Use: Diagnosing Perception and Reasoning Failures in VLMs
summary: We present See, Think, Use, a protocol that traces each answer of a vision-language model to perception, reasoning or the use of perception. The diagnosis shows a developer which stage to improve and directs test-time compute to the stage that fails. Benchmarks score the final answer, and an answer that rests on the image earns the same credit as a guess or a memorized prior. The protocol asks the model two extra questions per item and needs no access to its weights. A localization probe asks for a box around every instance and measures seeing, and a text-replacement probe answers from a description and measures thinking. Use is the rate at which the answer follows the model's own perception across counterfactual image pairs. The rate needs no answer labels, because the question and its prior are the same on both images. On two model families and six datasets the protocol shows that the knob that helps follows the task family. Answers follow the model's perception except on images that contradict a common prior, and asking the model to localize first repairs this failure when its boxes are right. Allocating compute by the measured stages comes close to the best uniform policy at lower cost and beats a random allocation of the same compute wherever a knob raises the short stage. We will release the code, the prompts and the per-question outputs.

AI.tldr: See, Think, Use is a protocol that traces each vision-language model answer to perception, reasoning, or use of perception, using a localization probe, a text-replacement probe and counterfactual image pairs. It shows which stage to improve and directs test-time compute to the failing stage, with models mostly answering from their own perception except on images that contradict a common prior.
AI.motivation: Benchmarks score only the final answer, so an answer grounded in the image earns the same credit as a guess or a memorized prior, and developers cannot tell which stage to improve.
AI.method: The protocol asks two extra questions per item. A localization probe requests a box around every instance to measure seeing, and a text-replacement probe answers from a description to measure thinking. Use is the rate at which the answer follows the model's own perception across counterfactual image pairs, which needs no answer labels because the question and prior are the same on both images. The protocol needs no access to model weights.
AI.result: On two model families and six datasets, the knob that helps follows the task family. Answers follow perception except on images that contradict a common prior, and asking the model to localize first repairs this failure when its boxes are right. Allocating compute by the measured stages comes close to the best uniform policy at lower cost and beats random allocation wherever a knob raises the short stage.
AI.conclusion: Diagnosing which stage fails gives a cheaper and more targeted way to allocate test-time compute for VLMs than uniform policies.

title: Sweep Less, Steer More: Using Activation Steering Geometry for Reduced Hyperparameter Search
summary: Representation steering methods like difference-in-means (DIM) offer a lightweight approach to controlling LLM behavior, but their effectiveness varies widely across concepts, datasets, and layers, making principled deployment costly without exhaustive hyperparameter sweeps. We build on the discriminability index $d'$, a compute-cheap geometric measure of how well contrastive training activations separate along the steering direction. Across five behaviors on 3 models, we demonstrate uses beyond its established role as a dataset-level steerability predictor. First, in the multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) setting, we show that $d'$ reliably identifies performant layers at which to steer, eliminating the need for a layer-wise sweep. Second, we extend this analysis to open-ended multi-token generation, and find that $d'$ remains successful for layer selection across different settings. Lastly, we test whether the position of a generated token's representation on the DIM line predicts steering success on that individual example. In the MCQA setting, this works for high-$d'$ datasets but is inconsistent across behaviors, models, and training-token choices in open-ended generation. This highlights that methods developed and conclusions drawn in single-token MCQA settings do not necessarily transfer to open-ended generation.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the discriminability index d', a cheap geometric measure of how well contrastive activations separate along a difference-in-means steering direction, can select steering layers and partly predict steering success. It finds this works for multiple-choice settings, but per-example predictions are inconsistent in open-ended generation.
AI.motivation: Difference-in-means steering works unevenly across concepts, datasets and layers, and principled deployment normally needs costly hyperparameter sweeps.
AI.method: Across five behaviors on three models, the authors use d' beyond its use as a dataset-level steerability predictor. They test it for layer selection in multiple-choice question answering, extend it to open-ended multi-token generation, and check whether a generated token's position on the difference-in-means line predicts steering success on that example.
AI.result: In multiple-choice QA, d' reliably identifies performant steering layers and removes the need for a layer-wise sweep. In open-ended generation d' remains successful for layer selection. The per-example position predicts success for high-d' datasets in multiple-choice QA but is inconsistent across behaviors, models and training-token choices in open-ended generation.
AI.conclusion: Conclusions from single-token multiple-choice settings do not necessarily transfer to open-ended generation.

title: VLMs Read Aloud: The Gap Between Recognizing and Using Visual Text
summary: Visual-text compression renders long contexts as images and is engineered around how much of the text a vision-language model (VLM) can recover. Yet recovered text is not usable text. VLMs can transcribe the text in an image word for word and still fail to answer from it; given back their own transcript, they answer nearly as well as from the original text. We call this difference the read-use gap. Recognizing and using visual text have different resolution requirements: Qwen3-VL-8B's recognition saturates at 15-pixel characters while use catches up only at 24 pixels, and scaling from 2B to 32B raises recognition without narrowing the gap. Putting the evidence into words closes it: thinking VLMs recite the evidence in their thinking, and their own transcript, written without seeing the question, recovers most of what thinking adds. In a preregistered held-out test, the gap ranks how much eight VLMs gain from their own words over pixels (Spearman $\rho$ = 0.86), which recognition rates do not. We propose ALOUD, which spends visual resolution on finding and recognizing evidence and language tokens on using it. Without keeping the source text, it doubles the accuracy of a frozen Qwen3-VL-8B on long documents compressed 5x and 10x: at 5x, from 27.7% to 54.8%, near the original text's 58.5%, with a context smaller than the compressed pages themselves. For less than the cost of reading the original text, it leads at equal budget every method that does without it, at every level, and beats AGAR and VERA, which paste the original text back; at 5x it also beats LensVLM-9B, which is trained and keeps the original text. Visual-text compression is limited not by how much text a model can recover, but by how much it can use.

AI.tldr: The paper shows a read-use gap in vision-language models: they can transcribe rendered text but fail to use it, and the proposed ALOUD method spends visual resolution on finding evidence and language tokens on using it.
