AI.motivation: Live website evaluation suffers from changing content, access restrictions and limited coverage of authenticated workflows, while existing synthetic environments often lack functional depth and visual fidelity.
AI.method: The environments are built through task-driven human-agent collaboration: they evolve as new tasks expand their functional scope, coding agents implement the changes, and human contributors audit visual fidelity, functional correctness and task validity. The environments run deterministically.
AI.result: The suite comprises 3,518 tasks, including multi-step and post-authentication workflows that existing works often fail to cover. A Qwen 4B-level GUI agent trained with RL in WebHarbor generalizes to unseen tasks and performs competitively with leading open-source GUI web agents across four benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: WebHarbor provides reliable evaluation and cost-efficient RL environments, and the code and data are publicly released.

title: A Generalized Sparse Fuzzy Clustering Framework with Automated Cluster Cardinality Estimation Ability
comment: 25 pages, highlights, 14 figures, under review in Elsevier journal
summary: Fuzzy clustering provides a robust framework for handling ambiguous and overlapping data boundaries, yet its traditional formulation generates entirely dense membership assignments that limit noise resilience and prevent estimating the true number of clusters, when it is unknown. To address these limitations, we introduce in this paper the Generalized Sparse Fuzzy Clustering (GSFC) framework, which incorporates a continuous sparsity penalty into the fuzzy objective function. Because closed-form solutions are precluded by the simultaneous presence of fuzzifier and sparsity exponents, we propose an efficient primal-dual bisection search coupled with specialized analytic pathways to rigorously enforce the partition constraint while organically driving trace memberships to exact zero. This mathematically enforced sparsity empowers the algorithm to autonomously estimate the true number of clusters by dynamically pruning redundant clusters, provided that it is initialized by a larger than the true number of clusters. Furthermore, we integrate a virtual noise sink to insulate outliers from the rest of the data points. The usage of the proposed framework is also extended to line segment detection. Extensive empirical evaluations across synthetic toy datasets, high-noise geometric stress tests, and real-world benchmarks (UCI wine dataset and hyperspectral images) demonstrate that GSFC effectively exceeds conventional fuzzy benchmarks while autonomously resolving cluster cardinality. Additionally, it significantly outperforms existing sparse possibilistic and probabilistic soft-clustering alternatives in line detection tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Generalized Sparse Fuzzy Clustering (GSFC), which adds a continuous sparsity penalty to the fuzzy clustering objective so that memberships can reach exact zero. The sparsity lets the algorithm estimate the number of clusters itself by pruning redundant ones, and it is reported to outperform conventional fuzzy methods.
AI.motivation: Traditional fuzzy clustering produces dense membership assignments, which limit noise resilience and make it impossible to estimate the true number of clusters when it is unknown.
AI.method: GSFC adds a continuous sparsity penalty to the fuzzy objective. Since fuzzifier and sparsity exponents rule out a closed-form solution, the method uses a primal-dual bisection search with analytic special cases to enforce the partition constraint. A virtual noise sink isolates outliers, and the framework is extended to line segment detection.
AI.result: On synthetic toy data, high-noise geometric tests and real benchmarks (UCI wine and hyperspectral images), GSFC outperforms conventional fuzzy benchmarks and estimates the cluster count when initialized with more clusters than the true number. In line detection it significantly outperforms sparse possibilistic and probabilistic soft-clustering alternatives.
AI.conclusion: Sparsity enforced mathematically gives fuzzy clustering both noise robustness and automatic cluster-count estimation, provided the initial cluster number is an overestimate.

title: Beyond the Last Layer: Global Inter-Layer Aggregation for AI-Generated Image Detection
summary: The rapid development of generative models has made AI-generated images increasingly close to real images. It has also brought several challenges to detectors, including rapid generator updates, large changes in data distribution, and limited cross-dataset generalization. Many existing methods based on pretrained vision encoders primarily use the global representation from the last layer, potentially leaving useful information from intermediate layers underexplored. To address this issue, we propose Global Inter-Layer Aggregation (GILA). GILA extracts global representations from different depths of a frozen encoder, models interactions among layer representations through inter-layer self-attention, and adaptively aggregates the resulting contextualized representations. The method is not tied to a single pretraining objective and does not require fine-tuning the pretrained encoder. We evaluated GILA on three vision backbones with different pretraining objectives, ten seen generators, and three external datasets. The experimental results show that GILA makes better use of multi-layer information in pretrained encoders and improves detection performance and cross-dataset generalization.

AI.tldr: GILA (Global Inter-Layer Aggregation) improves AI-generated image detection by extracting global representations from several depths of a frozen pretrained encoder and fusing them with inter-layer self-attention. It improves detection and cross-dataset generalization without fine-tuning the encoder.
AI.motivation: Many detectors built on pretrained vision encoders use only the final layer's global representation, which may leave useful information from intermediate layers unused, and generalization across generators and datasets is limited.
AI.method: GILA extracts global representations from different depths of a frozen encoder, models interactions among these layer representations with inter-layer self-attention, and adaptively aggregates the contextualized representations. It does not depend on a single pretraining objective and does not require fine-tuning the encoder.
AI.result: Evaluated on three vision backbones with different pretraining objectives, ten seen generators and three external datasets, GILA makes better use of multi-layer information and improves detection performance and cross-dataset generalization.
AI.conclusion: Aggregating intermediate-layer information across a frozen encoder is a simple way to strengthen detectors of AI-generated images.

title: Output-Aware Block Influence: Jacobian-Lens Weighting for Depth Pruning
summary: Depth pruning removes entire transformer blocks and therefore depends on a reliable criterion for identifying which blocks can be removed. Block Influence (BI) ranks blocks by how minimally they rotate the hidden state. However, local redundancy does not necessarily imply downstream irrelevance. We address this limitation using the Jacobian Lens (J-Lens) neural artifact, a map transporting perturbations at a layer to the final residual stream. At a common sparsity level, pruning scores applying J-Lens transportation to $BI$, what we call $J-BI$, were found to improve post-pruning accuracy by up to 19 points over $BI$ while reducing damage to perplexity for Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B-IT, and Gemma-3-12B-IT. We also perform a single-block ablation study and use J-Lens probing to explain why the proposed scores improved performance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes J-BI, which scores transformer blocks for depth pruning by applying Jacobian Lens transport to Block Influence (BI). At a common sparsity level it improves post-pruning accuracy by up to 19 points over BI on Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B-IT and Gemma-3-12B-IT, while reducing perplexity damage.
AI.motivation: Depth pruning depends on a reliable criterion for which blocks to remove. BI ranks blocks by how little they rotate the hidden state, but local redundancy does not imply downstream irrelevance.
AI.method: The Jacobian Lens (J-Lens) maps perturbations at a layer to the final residual stream. Applying this transport to BI gives the pruning score J-BI. The paper also runs a single-block ablation study and uses J-Lens probing to explain the gains.
AI.result: At a common sparsity level, J-BI improves post-pruning accuracy by up to 19 points over BI and reduces damage to perplexity on Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B-IT and Gemma-3-12B-IT.
AI.conclusion: Weighting blocks by their downstream effect through J-Lens gives a better depth-pruning criterion than local block influence alone.

title: Learning to bid and bundle: a posterior-sampling agent for online retail
comment: 37 pages, 5 figures; online supplement included as an ancillary file. Under review at Expert Systems with Applications
summary: An online retailer launching a perishable product bids for sponsored-search clicks, discounts a bundle with an always-stocked staple and displays its remaining stock, which raises willingness to pay. It knows neither how clicks respond to its bid nor how strong and dispersed its market is, and learns both over repeated seasons from data its own decisions censor: a zero bid reveals nothing about paid clicks, and choices follow only clicks. We design a posterior-sampling agent for it. Each period it draws a market from an exact posterior and posts the bid and discount of that market's exactly solved season plan, so every action is one a fully informed seller could take. In a simulated online florist it has the lowest regret averaged over markets. In weak markets it gives up 12% to 23% of one season's revenue over 500 seasons, four to seven times less than drawing once per season. A planner acting on point estimates can stop bidding and never learn that bidding pays. The agent escapes after about three seasons on average, against fifty with one draw per season. Where displayed scarcity keeps willingness to pay above the posted price, the discount needs no learning. Customers waiting for the discount to return to its recent level look like lost sales, so frequent waiting makes the agent underrate its market. One discount per season removes waiting at a cost of 5.9% of clairvoyant revenue in a weak market and none in a strong one.

AI.tldr: The paper designs a posterior-sampling agent that learns, over repeated seasons, how clicks respond to bids and how strong the market is, while choosing bids and bundle discounts for a perishable product. It has the lowest regret averaged over markets in a simulated online florist.
AI.motivation: A seller launching a perishable product does not know how clicks respond to its bid or how strong its market is, and its own decisions censor the data it learns from: zero bids reveal nothing and choices reveal only clicks.
AI.method: Each period the agent draws a market from an exact posterior and posts the bid and discount of that market's exactly solved season plan, so every action is one a fully informed seller could take. Displayed stock is used to raise willingness to pay alongside a bundle with a staple product.
AI.result: In weak markets the agent gives up 12% to 23% of one season's revenue over 500 seasons, four to seven times less than drawing once per season. It escapes a poor market after about three seasons on average, against fifty with one draw per season. A planner using point estimates can stop bidding and never learn that bidding pays. One discount per season removes waiting at a cost of 5.9% of clairvoyant revenue in a weak market and none in a strong one.
AI.conclusion: Posterior sampling with actions drawn from fully informed plans learns the market far faster than per-season sampling, while avoiding the lock-in that point-estimate planning can cause.

title: Early Stopping in Large Reasoning Models: A Survey and Empirical Audit of Efficiency and Reliability
summary: Large reasoning models can improve accuracy by generating longer reasoning traces, but some of this computation may be unnecessary. Early-stopping methods aim to stop once enough reasoning is available to answer. Evaluating these methods requires accounting for the cost of deciding when to stop and the reliability of the resulting answer. We evaluate different methods across five reasoning models on mathematical and scientific reasoning, code generation, and factuality tasks by using a shared rollout replay protocol. We introduce Target-Integrated Token Efficiency (TITE) to measure efficiency relative to the oracle across accuracy targets. We also examine correctness at later exit positions, transfer across models and tasks, post-stop reasoning continuation, and retained justification quality. In our experiments, correctness can decrease at later positions beyond what the fitted decoding-noise model predicts. Reliability checks also reveal continued reasoning after forced termination and weaker supporting reasoning in some correct early-stopping outputs. The implementation can be found in this https URL.

AI.tldr: This survey and empirical audit evaluates early-stopping methods for large reasoning models across five models and four task families, using a shared rollout replay protocol. It introduces Target-Integrated Token Efficiency (TITE) and finds that correctness can decline at later exit positions and that some reasoning continues after forced termination.
AI.motivation: Early stopping can cut unnecessary reasoning tokens, but evaluating it requires accounting for the cost of deciding when to stop and for the reliability of the resulting answer.
AI.method: Methods are compared on five reasoning models across mathematical and scientific reasoning, code generation and factuality tasks using a shared rollout replay protocol. TITE measures efficiency relative to an oracle across accuracy targets. The study also checks correctness at later exit positions, transfer across models and tasks, post-stop reasoning and the quality of retained justifications.
AI.result: Correctness can decrease at later exit positions beyond what the fitted decoding-noise model predicts. Reliability checks reveal continued reasoning after forced termination and weaker supporting reasoning in some correct early-stopped outputs.
AI.conclusion: Efficiency gains from early stopping should be judged together with reliability, since accuracy and justification quality can degrade in ways that efficiency metrics alone do not show.

title: PatchScout: Thematic Web Data Collection via Information Foraging
comment: 10 pages, 1 figure, to be published in Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 2026
summary: Researchers often need web corpora that are not answers to a single query, but reusable collections of documents spanning many decentralized sources. We refer to this problem as thematic web data collection: assembling semantically relevant documents that share a common theme but are scattered across heterogeneous and structurally disconnected regions of the web. Existing approaches, including traversal-based methods and LLM-driven web agents, are limited by local exploration or short-horizon stopping, preventing comprehensive collection. We formulate this task as a long-horizon information foraging problem over query-induced semantic patches, where the central challenge is deciding when to continue local exploitation and when to switch to new regions. We propose PatchScout, a multi-agent framework that instantiates a class of patch-switching policies to balance local exploitation and adaptive patch switching under a fixed budget. Experiments on four live-web topics show that PatchScout substantially improves yield and domain coverage over traversal-based and search-augmented reasoning agent baselines. In an applied social science setting with an incomplete prior collection, PatchScout discovers 102 previously unidentified entities, illustrating its ability to expand existing thematic datasets.

AI.tldr: PatchScout is a multi-agent framework for thematic web data collection that treats the task as long-horizon information foraging over query-induced semantic patches. It improves yield and domain coverage over traversal-based and search-augmented agent baselines and found 102 previously unidentified entities in a social science application.
AI.motivation: Researchers need reusable web corpora spanning many decentralized sources. Traversal methods and LLM web agents are limited by local exploration or short-horizon stopping, which prevents comprehensive collection.
AI.method: The task is formulated as a foraging problem over query-induced semantic patches, where the central decision is when to keep exploiting the current patch and when to switch. PatchScout instantiates a class of patch-switching policies that balance exploitation and switching under a fixed budget.
AI.result: On four live-web topics, PatchScout substantially improves yield and domain coverage over traversal-based and search-augmented reasoning agent baselines. In a social science setting with an incomplete prior collection, it discovers 102 previously unidentified entities.
AI.conclusion: Patch-switching policies can expand existing thematic datasets by reaching regions of the web that local exploration would miss.

title: Reimagining Text-to-SQL: A Survey of Large Language Model Architectures and Strategies
summary: Text-to-SQL systems translate natural language questions into executable SQL queries, democratizing access to relational data. Early approaches relied on handcrafted rules and template matching, while subsequent neural methods introduced encoder-decoder architectures, schema linking, and constrained decoding to handle increasingly complex queries. The emergence of large language models (LLMs), exemplified by systems such as ReFoRCE, Agentar-Scale-SQL, Snowflake's Arctic-Text2SQL-R1, and the modular XiYan-SQL framework, has dramatically advanced the field, pushing execution accuracy to new state-of-the-art levels on challenging benchmarks such as Spider, Spider 2.0, and BIRD. In parallel, modular frameworks decompose the task into sub-problems (schema retrieval, sketch-based generation, repair, and ranking), while agentic systems coordinate multiple specialized agents that communicate and dynamically allocate sub-tasks. This survey systematically reviews these LLM-driven approaches within a unified taxonomy of five paradigms (in-context learning, supervised and parameter-efficient fine-tuning, agentic and tool-augmented orchestration, retrieval-augmented generation, and reinforcement learning) and characterizes them by model granularity (monolithic vs. modular), level of supervision (zero-shot, fine-tuned, or reinforcement-based), and reasoning style (direct decoding vs. decomposed multi-step reasoning). We further analyze evaluation metrics, datasets, and open challenges, including domain generalization, efficiency, and real-world deployment, and we examine the role of the semantic layer in production systems. As LLMs increasingly access sensitive databases, we also discuss responsible AI practices. We survey over 100 papers and technical resources, focusing on work published between 2022 and 2026.

AI.tldr: This survey reviews LLM-driven text-to-SQL systems within a taxonomy of five paradigms and characterizes them by granularity, supervision and reasoning style. It covers over 100 papers and technical resources from 2022 to 2026 and discusses evaluation, open challenges and responsible AI practices.
AI.motivation: Text-to-SQL has moved from handcrafted rules and neural encoder-decoder models to LLM systems, and the field needs a unified view of how these approaches differ.
AI.method: The survey uses a taxonomy of five paradigms: in-context learning, supervised and parameter-efficient fine-tuning, agentic and tool-augmented orchestration, retrieval-augmented generation and reinforcement learning. Systems are characterized by model granularity (monolithic vs. modular), level of supervision and reasoning style (direct decoding vs. decomposed multi-step reasoning).
AI.result: The survey reviews systems such as ReFoRCE, Agentar-Scale-SQL, Arctic-Text2SQL-R1 and XiYan-SQL, which push execution accuracy to new state-of-the-art levels on Spider, Spider 2.0 and BIRD. It also analyzes evaluation metrics, datasets and open challenges, including domain generalization, efficiency and deployment.
AI.conclusion: Text-to-SQL research is converging on modular and agentic designs, and the survey highlights the semantic layer and responsible use over sensitive databases as open issues.

title: AuroraWorld: Structured 4D World Modeling for Exo-to-Ego Video Generation in Robot Manipulation
summary: Egocentric observations provide a robot-centric view of manipulation processes, capturing contact interactions and object-state changes that are important for visuomotor policy learning but difficult to observe from external cameras. However, collecting such data at scale remains expensive due to additional hardware requirements and platform-specific deployment costs. Synthesizing egocentric observations from large-scale exocentric manipulation videos provides a scalable alternative. However, existing methods struggle to synthesize physically consistent and policy-relevant egocentric videos under substantial viewpoint transformations, severe occlusions, complex object interactions, and inherently sparse observations from available exocentric viewpoints.

AI.tldr: AuroraWorld is a structured 4D world model for synthesizing egocentric robot-manipulation video from exocentric videos. The abstract as provided states only the problem it addresses, so its method and results are not given here.
AI.motivation: Egocentric views capture contact and object-state changes useful for visuomotor policy learning, but collecting them at scale is costly. Existing synthesis methods struggle to produce physically consistent and policy-relevant egocentric video under large viewpoint changes, severe occlusion, complex object interactions and sparse exocentric observations.
AI.method: The abstract as provided does not describe the method beyond calling it a structured 4D world modeling approach for exo-to-ego video generation.
AI.result: The abstract as provided does not report results.
AI.conclusion: Exo-to-ego synthesis from large exocentric manipulation datasets is presented as a scalable alternative to collecting egocentric data directly.

title: Neurons Are All You Need
summary: For decades, artificial neural networks have operated under the assumption that durable, learned capability resides exclusively in adaptive synaptic parameters, primarily due to the established neurobiology of synaptic connectivity. This design forces models to remain stateless during deployment, incurring well-known limitations such as catastrophic forgetting and expensive retraining. However, recent neurobiological research by Glanzman and colleagues, and others, shows that memories can be transferred between individual organisms in a synaptically independent manner. Inspired by this research, we sought to demonstrate memory transfer of persistent memory between AI model instances, leveraging a neurocentric version of memory. In this paper, we propose NURESA (Neural Unit with Retentive Self-Adaptive Architecture), a novel neural layer that eschews sole reliance on synaptic weight updating by introducing persistent intra-unit memory as a first-class, computational primitive. By structurally separating computation from persistent memory, NURESA enables autonomous memory accumulation and consolidation into transferable stores of memory registers. Experiments across MLP, GPT-2, and modern frontier models like Qwen2.5 demonstrate qualitatively new capability: zero-shot transfer of learned capability into a naive model instance without retraining or access to the original training data; this transfer is enabled by a sparse set of parameters in NURESA's memory register that the model selects on its own based on which neurons were most active. The memory transfer capability of NURESA also protects against domain loss when transformer models undergo learning via fine-tuning. Finally, the memory transfer process completes in approximately one minute even for transformer models with millions to billions of parameters, producing a transfer file orders of magnitude smaller than the original model.

AI.tldr: NURESA is a neural layer that keeps persistent intra-unit memory alongside synaptic weights, and the paper reports zero-shot transfer of learned capability between model instances. The transfer uses a sparse set of memory-register parameters selected by the model and completes in about one minute.
AI.motivation: Artificial neural networks store durable capability only in synaptic weights, which leaves models stateless at deployment and prone to catastrophic forgetting and costly retraining. Neurobiology shows that memories can transfer between organisms independently of synapses.
AI.method: NURESA separates computation from a persistent memory with intra-unit memory registers as a first-class primitive. Memory accumulates and consolidates into transferable stores, and the model selects the sparse set of register parameters to transfer based on which neurons were most active.
AI.result: Experiments on MLP, GPT-2 and Qwen2.5 report zero-shot transfer of learned capability into a naive instance without retraining or the original data. The memory transfer also protects against domain loss during fine-tuning, and the transfer completes in about one minute, producing files orders of magnitude smaller than the model.
AI.conclusion: Persistent memory separate from synaptic weights could make learned capability portable between model instances, though the abstract presents this as a qualitatively new capability that needs broader validation.

title: MemU-Bench: Benchmarking GUI Agents on Long-Horizon User Interactions
summary: Existing Graphical User Interface (GUI) benchmarks predominantly rely on precise and stateless user instructions. In everyday usage, however, instructions are often \emph{vague and history-dependent}: users omit the exact details of their past operations because they no longer remember them, leaving the agent to recover the missing context from long and noisy interaction histories. To bridge this evaluation gap, we introduce \textbf{MemU-Bench}, a mobile benchmark of \textbf{118 vague tasks} grounded in 29 long-horizon user trajectories, where agents must distill raw interaction streams into memory and retrieve the missing context on demand, with task outcomes verified against serialized application databases. Alongside Success Rate, we incorporate Interaction Efficiency (IE) and Success weighted by Path Length (SPL) to expose agents that succeed by exhaustively searching across different applications rather than by \emph{genuinely recalling} the history. Evaluations show that without user history, state-of-the-art systems struggle under such ambiguity: the best-performing Gemini-3.1-Pro achieves an SPL of only 16.4\%, and end-to-end GUI agents fall below 5\%. To address this, we further propose \textbf{AppMem}, a training-free framework that distills user history into a \emph{structured, app-centric} memory bank, tracks interrupted intents across application switches, and selectively retrieves relevant memories via target-app inference. AppMem raises the SPL of GPT-5.5 from 15.7\% to 66.9\% (\textbf{+51.2\%}), outperforms a naive summary baseline by 9.3\%, and delivers consistent gains across evaluated backbones.

AI.tldr: MemU-Bench is a mobile GUI benchmark of 118 vague, history-dependent tasks built on 29 long-horizon user trajectories, with outcomes verified against application databases. The best model scores an SPL of only 16.4%, and AppMem, a training-free memory framework, raises GPT-5.5 from 15.7% to 66.9%.
AI.motivation: Existing GUI benchmarks use precise, stateless instructions, whereas real users give vague instructions that depend on past operations they no longer remember.
AI.method: The benchmark adds Interaction Efficiency and Success weighted by Path Length (SPL) to expose agents that succeed by exhaustive search rather than by recalling history. AppMem distills user history into a structured, app-centric memory bank, tracks interrupted intents across application switches and retrieves memories by target-app inference.
AI.result: Without user history, state-of-the-art systems struggle: the best, Gemini-3.1-Pro, reaches an SPL of 16.4%, and end-to-end GUI agents fall below 5%. AppMem raises GPT-5.5's SPL from 15.7% to 66.9% (+51.2 points), outperforms a naive summary baseline by 9.3% and gives consistent gains across the evaluated backbones.
AI.conclusion: Long-horizon memory is a key missing capability for GUI agents on vague instructions, and the benchmark exposes it while AppMem offers a training-free remedy.

title: From Cross-Section to Cross-Omics: Conditional Cell Nucleus Image Editing in Spatial Transcriptomics
summary: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) platforms simultaneously measure gene expression and capture cell nucleus images at single-cell resolution. A fundamental property of tissue preparation introduces a confounding relationship between the two measurement modalities: sectioning a three-dimensional tissue into a thin slice produces a two-dimensional cross-section whose area depends on the cutting angle. Larger cross-sections expose more cytoplasm, yielding higher mRNA counts, while pathomics features such as nuclear area are measured directly from the same 2D boundary. This sectioning geometry creates an apparent correlation between gene expression and pathomics that reflects the measurement process rather than independent biology. Existing gene-to-image methods generate cell images from gene features but do not support condition-driven editing of existing images across both omics layers. We apply the Manifold-Aware Diffusion (MAD) framework to this dual-omics editing setting, enabling targeted modification of one feature group while preserving the other. Evaluated on podocyte cells from CosMx SMI kidney tissue, MAD achieves MAE=0.6636 and FID=25.19 for pathomics editing, outperforming all compared baselines. A controlled simulation study further confirms that the VAE component in MAD better preserves cross-group independence than CCDM (MAD without VAE).

AI.tldr: The paper applies Manifold-Aware Diffusion (MAD) to conditional editing of cell nucleus images in spatial transcriptomics, modifying pathomics features or gene-related features while preserving the other. On podocyte cells from CosMx SMI kidney tissue, MAD reaches MAE 0.6636 and FID 25.19 for pathomics editing.
AI.motivation: Sectioning tissue creates a geometric confound in which cross-section area links gene expression and nuclear morphology. Existing gene-to-image methods generate cells from gene features but do not edit existing images across both omics layers.
AI.method: MAD, a manifold-aware diffusion framework, is applied to dual-omics editing so that one feature group can be modified while the other is preserved. A VAE component is part of MAD, and the compared variant without it is called CCDM.
AI.result: On podocyte cells from CosMx SMI kidney tissue, MAD achieves MAE 0.6636 and FID 25.19 for pathomics editing and outperforms all compared baselines. A controlled simulation shows that the VAE component preserves cross-group independence better than CCDM.
AI.conclusion: Condition-driven editing across omics layers is feasible, and the VAE component helps keep the two feature groups separate.

title: RE-SciVQA: Improving Scientific VQA With Context-Relevant Retrieval and Lightweight MLLM Adaptation
summary: A deep understanding of scientific literature often relies on interpreting figures that contain key information beyond the main text. Leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to extract insights from these figures can significantly accelerate knowledge discovery. Existing works on Scientific Visual Question Answering rely on resource-intensive training pipelines that are often inaccessible and require large computational resources. Instead of designing complex architectures, we propose RE- SciVQA, which focuses on improving the quality of retrieved context and fine-tuning small LLMs with parameter-efficient LoRA training. Using a simple query expansion step, relevant section headers are appended to the original question to improve the retrieval coverage. In addition, a simple adjustment of similarity scores is applied using figure references and caption alignment. On the SciVQA benchmark, RE-SciVQA achieves a ROUGE-1 F1 score of 73.9%, outperforming chart-focused models such as UniChart (14.7%), ChartGemma (6.9%), and Matcha-ChartQA (6.3%). Our relevance-enhanced RAG setup also improves the exact match by 11.9% and the fuzzy match by 29.5% compared with a standard RAG baseline, resulting in an overall gain of 14.3%. We also examine closed-ended infinite visual questions, a category in which chart-understanding models often struggle. Our experiments show that using plot digitization instead of synthetic captions leads to an 18.5% improvement for this question type.

AI.tldr: RE-SciVQA improves scientific visual question answering with better retrieval context and parameter-efficient LoRA fine-tuning of small LLMs, avoiding complex architectures. It reaches a ROUGE-1 F1 of 73.9% on SciVQA and outperforms chart-focused models such as UniChart, ChartGemma and Matcha-ChartQA.
AI.motivation: Scientific VQA methods rely on resource-intensive training pipelines that are often inaccessible, and chart-understanding models struggle with infinite visual question types.
AI.method: A query expansion step appends relevant section headers to the question to improve retrieval coverage. Similarity scores are adjusted using figure references and caption alignment. Small LLMs are fine-tuned with LoRA, and plot digitization replaces synthetic captions for some question types.
AI.result: On SciVQA, RE-SciVQA reaches a ROUGE-1 F1 of 73.9%, against UniChart (14.7%), ChartGemma (6.9%) and Matcha-ChartQA (6.3%). Its relevance-enhanced RAG improves exact match by 11.9% and fuzzy match by 29.5% over a standard RAG baseline, for an overall gain of 14.3%. Plot digitization gives an 18.5% improvement on closed-ended infinite visual questions.
AI.conclusion: Better retrieval context and lightweight adaptation can match or beat heavier chart-focused systems on scientific VQA.

title: OmniPiano: Diverse Dexterous Piano-Playing Challenges for Standard, Robust, Safe, and Multi-Agent RL
summary: Dexterous robotic manipulation remains a major challenge in robotics, exemplified by piano playing, which requires coordinated control of fingers and provides a demanding testbed for reinforcement learning (RL). Although previous work established a benchmark for robotic piano playing, it is restricted to two hands and does not support unified evaluation. To address this gap, we introduce OmniPiano, a benchmark that provides one to up to five Shadow Hands and supports standard, robust, safe, and multi-agent RL within a shared piano-playing task family. OmniPiano is developed for scalable and diverse piano-playing tasks with configurable perturbations, explicit safety constraints, and decentralized cooperation settings. Particularly, to facilitate usability and extendability, OmniPiano adopts a highly modular design and provides comprehensive tasks to support RL study of task performance, robustness, safety, and cooperation in dexterous control. With at least 912 task settings and 36 baseline algorithms, OmniPiano further incorporates LLM-based agents to broaden the evaluation scope and reveal new insights. Extensive evaluations show that state-of-the-art RL algorithms and frontier LLM-based agents still struggle on challenging piano-playing tasks, even under standard RL settings, highlighting substantial room for improvement in dexterous control. The code, dataset, tutorial, and demo are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: OmniPiano is a benchmark for dexterous piano playing with one to five Shadow Hands, supporting standard, robust, safe and multi-agent RL in a shared task family. It provides at least 912 task settings and 36 baseline algorithms, and state-of-the-art RL and frontier LLM agents still struggle on it.
AI.motivation: Previous robotic piano benchmarks are limited to two hands and lack unified evaluation across task performance, robustness, safety and cooperation.
AI.method: The benchmark is modular and offers configurable perturbations, explicit safety constraints and decentralized cooperation settings. It also incorporates LLM-based agents to broaden the evaluation.
AI.result: With at least 912 task settings and 36 baseline algorithms, state-of-the-art RL algorithms and frontier LLM-based agents still struggle on challenging piano-playing tasks, even under standard RL settings.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark shows substantial room for improvement in dexterous control, and code, dataset, tutorial and demo are released.

title: Taurus: LLM-in-the-Loop CT Annotation Matches Coding Agents at Half the Cost
comment: 24 pages (10 main text, 12 appendix), 8 figures, 10 tables
summary: Dense labels of the aorta in CT are slow to draw, and the public aortic CT datasets that could stand in for them each label different structures under their own conventions. Large language model (LLM) agents can now write code and read images. We asked whether such a model labels these scans better as a free-form agent that writes its own segmentation code, or inside a harness, where an automated pass labels the scan and the model reviews the result. We built a harness, Taurus, and compared it with free-form agents by blind label recovery: we withheld the human labels of six public datasets (939 volumes) and scored every approach against each dataset's own classes. In the first version of Taurus, the model's review raised the primary metric on only two of six datasets, by less than the noise between two reviews of the same case. A free-form agent running Claude Opus 5.5 scored higher on most datasets. Moving what the free-form agents did well into the automated pass then carried most of the gain on 38 held-out cases. The final version smooths the label surfaces with a fixed rule and checks for the large errors the automated pass tends to make, such as an aneurysm drawn to half its size. Each check that fires puts a multiple-choice question to the model, with candidate corrections drawn on the scan. It matched the surface smoothness of the human references, and in the primary metric we found no difference from the free-form Opus agent, at under half its cost, $1.22 against $2.71 per case. Most of what made Taurus competitive came from the harness and its automation rather than from the language model itself. Taurus shows that this kind of annotation can be automated, so that expert time can move from drawing labels to checking them.

AI.tldr: Taurus is an LLM-in-the-loop harness for CT aorta annotation in which an automated pass labels the scan and the model reviews the result. Its final version matches the primary metric of a free-form Claude Opus 5.5 agent at under half the cost, $1.22 against $2.71 per case.
AI.motivation: Dense aortic CT labels are slow to draw, and public datasets each label structures under their own conventions. The paper asks whether an LLM labels scans better as a free-form coding agent or inside a harness.
AI.method: Taurus pairs an automated labeling pass with a model review. Its final version smooths label surfaces with a fixed rule and checks for large errors, asking the model multiple-choice questions with candidate corrections drawn on the scan when a check fires. It is compared with free-form agents by blind label recovery on six public datasets (939 volumes).
AI.result: In the first version, model review raised the primary metric on only two of six datasets, by less than review-to-review noise. A free-form Opus 5.5 agent scored higher on most datasets, and moving its strengths into the automated pass carried most of the gain on 38 held-out cases. The final version matches the human references' surface smoothness and shows no difference from the free-form Opus agent on the primary metric, at $1.22 against $2.71 per case.
AI.conclusion: Most of Taurus's competitiveness comes from the harness and its automation rather than the language model, so expert time can shift from drawing labels to checking them.

authors: Multi-Center Cooperative Clinical Study Group for "Lesion-Phenotype Brain Mapping in Acute Stroke"
title: A generative foundation model for computational brain imaging
summary: Computational brain imaging is constrained by a mismatch between increasingly diverse tasks and scarce, heterogeneous clinical data. Although existing brain foundation models transfer pretrained representations, their knowledge remains entangled within model-specific features and fixed architectures. This paper proposes BrainGFM, a generative foundation model that extends knowledge transfer beyond representation reuse through a reusable and reconfigurable brain-imaging prior. By pretraining on a corpus of about 1.3 million MRI and CT slices, BrainGFM supported task-aligned data synthesis for low-data predictive learning and task-adapted post-training for image reconstruction. Across 48 downstream tasks, BrainGFM improved segmentation and classification under limited supervision and achieved high-fidelity image enhancement across heterogeneous imaging conditions. Multicenter clinical validation involving 4,796 stroke patients across two internal and four external centers demonstrated its applicability to three clinically relevant tasks around stroke cohorts. Blinded reader assessments showed that BrainGFM-generated FLAIR images approached acquired FLAIR in overall diagnostic quality. In a human-AI collaboration study, BrainGFM assistance yielded a 14% relative improvement in mean radiologist stroke-subtyping accuracy. These findings support generative priors as a reusable foundation for heterogeneous computational brain-imaging applications.

AI.tldr: BrainGFM is a generative foundation model for brain imaging, pretrained on about 1.3 million MRI and CT slices, that serves as a reusable prior for data synthesis and image reconstruction. It improves 48 downstream tasks under limited supervision and was validated on 4,796 stroke patients across six centers.
AI.motivation: Brain foundation models transfer pretrained representations, but their knowledge stays entangled with model-specific features and fixed architectures, while clinical data is scarce and heterogeneous.
AI.method: BrainGFM is a generative model pretrained on about 1.3 million MRI and CT slices. It is used for task-aligned data synthesis in low-data predictive learning and for task-adapted post-training for image reconstruction.
AI.result: Across 48 downstream tasks, BrainGFM improves segmentation and classification under limited supervision and achieves high-fidelity enhancement across heterogeneous imaging conditions. In validation on 4,796 stroke patients across two internal and four external centers, blinded readers judged its generated FLAIR images to approach acquired FLAIR in diagnostic quality, and assistance gave a 14% relative improvement in radiologist stroke-subtyping accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Generative priors can serve as a reusable foundation for heterogeneous computational brain-imaging applications.

title: Automated Theorem Generation in First-Order Logic by Construction from Triangular Standard Contradictions
summary: Automated theorem generation (ATG) seeks to construct new theorems rather than merely prove given conjectures. Existing approaches typically generate candidate statements that require subsequent proof or formal verification. We propose a constructive framework for ATG in first-order logic based on triangular standard contradictions. The method constructs minimally unsatisfiable clause sets from selected first-order literals, then forms theorems by retaining some clauses as premises and taking the negation of one clause, or a conjunction of clauses, as the conclusion. Minimal unsatisfiability ensures that the remaining premises are satisfiable, avoiding trivial inference by explosion, while unsatisfiability of the full set guarantees the resulting entailment. Theorems are therefore correct by construction, without a separate proof procedure for each instance. Extending the previously developed $\Delta_1$ generator, we introduce seven methods, $\Delta_2$--$\Delta_8$, forming a unified family of eight theorem-generation methods. Four generators, $\Delta_1$--$\Delta_4$, have been implemented and released. We also formulate a general $\Delta$-class method encompassing the family. Combinatorial analysis demonstrates the capacity to generate large numbers of distinct theorems systematically. This framework offers a principled foundation for automated theorem discovery and the construction of logically guaranteed knowledge.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a constructive framework for automated theorem generation in first-order logic, building theorems from minimally unsatisfiable clause sets so that they are correct by construction. It extends an earlier generator to eight methods, of which four are implemented and released.
AI.motivation: Existing automated theorem generation typically produces candidate statements that still need proof or formal verification, which adds a separate step for each instance.
AI.method: Minimally unsatisfiable clause sets are built from selected first-order literals. Some clauses are kept as premises and the negation of one clause, or a conjunction of clauses, becomes the conclusion. Minimal unsatisfiability keeps the premises satisfiable and avoids trivial inference by explosion. The Delta-1 generator is extended with methods Delta-2 to Delta-8, and a general Delta-class method encompasses the family.
AI.result: Delta-1 to Delta-4 have been implemented and released. Combinatorial analysis shows the framework can systematically generate large numbers of distinct theorems.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a principled foundation for automated theorem discovery and for constructing logically guaranteed knowledge.

title: Quantifying Local and Global Fidelity of Nonlinear Embeddings
summary: Dimension reduction methods are chosen by a common claim: t-SNE and UMAP preserve local structure, and PCA preserves global structure. Checking it on given data takes local and global scores on one scale and a test that compares two maps. Both scores come from one curve. The locality profile is the chance-corrected share of each point's k nearest neighbors that a map keeps, over all neighborhood sizes. Its value at k = 10 is the local fidelity L, and its mean over 30 to 50 percent of the data is the global fidelity G. We prove that at the midpoint the profile is the agreement on which half of the data is near each point, a rank correlation of the distances. Because L and G are one statistic, two maps can be tested against each other. The LG reversal test applies to any two dimension reduction methods. It decides, with a block-jackknife p-value, whether one map is more local and the other more global, and returns the scale at which to change maps. On 156 maps of twelve datasets with up to 1.38 million points, G agrees with established global scores at 0.89 and 0.96, and 2,000 points estimate it. The test confirms the usual claim on seven datasets. On both retail datasets and both rolled-up manifolds, it finds the neighbor embeddings more global. In an agent memory of one million passages, the two maps cross at 150,000 passages (p = 2.6e-5). Applications span pathology, single cells, supply chains and AI agent memory.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a single curve-based statistic that measures both local fidelity L and global fidelity G of nonlinear embeddings, and a LG reversal test that compares two dimension reduction maps. On 156 maps of twelve datasets, the test confirms the usual claim on seven datasets and finds the neighbor embeddings more global on the retail datasets and rolled-up manifolds.
AI.motivation: The common claim that t-SNE and UMAP preserve local structure while PCA preserves global structure is usually checked without a single scale for local and global scores or a test comparing two maps.
AI.method: The locality profile is the chance-corrected share of each point's k nearest neighbors kept by a map, over all neighborhood sizes. Its value at k = 10 is L and its mean over 30 to 50 percent of the data is G. The LG reversal test uses a block-jackknife p-value to decide whether one map is more local and the other more global, and returns the scale at which to switch maps.
AI.result: G agrees with established global scores at 0.89 and 0.96, and 2,000 points estimate it. The test confirms the usual claim on seven datasets, and on both retail datasets and both rolled-up manifolds it finds the neighbor embeddings more global. In an agent memory of one million passages, the two maps cross at 150,000 passages (p = 2.6e-5).
AI.conclusion: L and G from one statistic make map choice testable, and the scale at which to switch maps can be identified.

title: Beyond Semantic IDs: Atomic Creator Tokens for Large-Scale Generative Recommendation
summary: Recommending creators that a user does not yet follow is a cold-start problem: from hundreds of thousands of popular creators and only a short trail of prior engagements, the system must predict the next creator worth surfacing. The prevailing generative recommendation recipe tokenizes each creator into a \emph{Semantic ID} (SID) by quantizing a frozen embedding and trains a language model to generate SIDs. We show that this SID layer, not the language model, is the binding constraint. The creator-to-SID map is many-to-one, so colliding creators must be resolved by a popularity tie-break that caps creator-level recall and favors already-popular creators, and the frozen quantizer stops the training gradient from reaching the creator representation. We propose Atomic Creator Token (ACT), which gives every creator its own vocabulary token trained end-to-end. The map is bijective, so collisions are impossible and inference is a direct top-$k$ over creator logits. In a controlled comparison on production data in which the token layer is the only variable, ACT improves creator-level Recall@15 by 19.8 points ($1.84\times$) over a matched SID baseline, still leads when the SID codebook is enlarged $64\times$, and serves at ${\sim}2.7\times$ lower per-user latency. The advantage carries over to the public KuaiRand dataset, where ACT is the only method that beats a global-popularity baseline, provided each creator token sees enough training examples. In a live A/B test, ACT is directionally positive on every reported metric against both the SID-enhanced and the classic production rankers.

AI.tldr: Atomic Creator Token (ACT) gives every creator in a generative recommender its own vocabulary token trained end-to-end, instead of a shared Semantic ID. In a controlled production comparison it improves creator-level Recall@15 by 19.8 points (1.84x) over a matched SID baseline.
AI.motivation: Recommending creators a user does not yet follow is a cold-start problem. The usual Semantic ID quantization is many-to-one, so colliding creators need a popularity tie-break, and the frozen quantizer blocks gradients from reaching the creator representation.
AI.method: ACT assigns each creator a separate token trained end-to-end. The creator-to-token map is bijective, so collisions cannot occur and inference is a direct top-k over creator logits.
AI.result: With the token layer as the only variable on production data, ACT improves creator-level Recall@15 by 19.8 points (1.84x) over a matched SID baseline and still leads when the SID codebook is enlarged 64x. It serves at about 2.7x lower per-user latency. On KuaiRand it is the only method that beats a global-popularity baseline when each creator token has enough training examples. A live A/B test is directionally positive on every reported metric.
AI.conclusion: The token layer, not the language model, is the binding constraint in SID-based generative recommendation, and per-creator tokens remove it.

title: Efficient NPN Classification for Large Functions using Graph Neural Network
summary: Two Boolean functions are considered NPN equivalent if one can be transformed into the other by negating inputs, permuting inputs, or negating the output. Efficient NPN classification is valuable in fields such as logic synthesis, quantum computing, and information theory. However, exact NPN classification demands exhaustive enumeration of all possible input permutations and negations. Its complexity grows exponentially, making it impractical for larger functions with more inputs. In this paper, we introduce the first learning-based formulation for NPN classification by recasting it as NPN action prediction. Our method represents Boolean functions as AND-Inverter Graphs (AIGs) and applies a bidirectional heterogeneous graph neural network to predict input negations, output negation, and input permutations. To mitigate the non-canonicity of logic networks, we further introduce graph rewriting techniques that reduce structural ambiguity and recover useful symmetries before prediction. Experimental results show that NPN action prediction is learnable, that the resulting canonicalization quality improves over heuristic baselines, and that on practical benchmarks our method approaches exact methods on tractable cases while scaling to functions with up to 16 inputs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the first learning-based formulation of NPN classification, predicting input negations, output negation and input permutations with a bidirectional heterogeneous graph neural network over AND-Inverter Graphs. The method approaches exact methods on tractable cases and scales to functions with up to 16 inputs.
AI.motivation: Exact NPN classification enumerates all input permutations and negations, so its cost grows exponentially and it is impractical for functions with many inputs.
AI.method: Boolean functions are represented as AND-Inverter Graphs and processed by a bidirectional heterogeneous graph neural network that predicts the NPN action. Graph rewriting reduces structural ambiguity and recovers useful symmetries before prediction.
AI.result: NPN action prediction is learnable, and the canonicalization quality improves over heuristic baselines. On practical benchmarks the method approaches exact methods on tractable cases and scales to functions with up to 16 inputs.
AI.conclusion: Recasting NPN classification as action prediction offers a learned route to canonicalization for large functions where exact enumeration fails.

title: Dependence-Aware Risk Assessment and Optimal Design of AI-Agent Safeguard Systems
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on safeguards to prevent unauthorized actions while preserving legitimate service. However, existing risk assessments often focus on individual safeguard performance while overlooking dependence among safeguard decisions. This paper develops a dependence-aware framework for risk assessment and optimal design of multi-component AI safeguard systems, jointly selecting configurations and operating policies for sequential layered screening and selective verification. We establish stochastic comparisons of layered-screening error probabilities and invocation costs under lower-orthant ordering. For selective verification, we characterize exactly which policies have error probabilities and review costs that respond monotonically to stronger dependence under supermodular ordering. For a fixed first stage and reviewer, we show that the optimal routing map is a two-threshold rule in the first-stage likelihood ratio. An accompanying open-source software package, Dependence-Aware Policy Optimization Algorithms (DAPOA), facilitates the practical implementation of the proposed framework. Numerical experiments show that ignoring dependence can lead to inaccurate risk assessments and infeasible safeguard designs, with independence-based selections violating security requirements in six of eight scenarios. An empirical study using four LLM safeguards on benchmark-derived agent actions further demonstrates the practical implications of dependence modeling. Under the principal operating setting, dependence-aware selection lowers held-out total cost by 39.6% relative to independence-based selection.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a dependence-aware framework for risk assessment and optimal design of multi-component AI safeguard systems, and shows that ignoring dependence between safeguard decisions can yield inaccurate risk estimates and infeasible designs. Under the principal setting, dependence-aware selection lowers held-out total cost by 39.6%.
AI.motivation: Existing risk assessments of LLM agent safeguards examine individual components and overlook dependence among their decisions.
AI.method: The framework jointly selects configurations and operating policies for sequential layered screening and selective verification. It gives stochastic comparisons of error probabilities and invocation costs under lower-orthant ordering, and characterizes which policies respond monotonically to dependence under supermodular ordering. For a fixed first stage and reviewer, the optimal routing is a two-threshold rule on the first-stage likelihood ratio. The DAPOA open-source package implements it.
AI.result: Ignoring dependence can make independence-based selections violate security requirements in six of eight scenarios. In an empirical study using four LLM safeguards on benchmark-derived agent actions, dependence-aware selection lowers held-out total cost by 39.6% under the principal operating setting.
AI.conclusion: Modeling dependence among safeguard decisions is necessary for accurate risk assessment and cost-effective safeguard design.

title: CalVLA: Shaping Native Confidence in Vision-Language-Action Policies with Outcome Supervision
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at the Science of Physical AI Safety (SPAIS) Workshop, CoRL 2026
summary: Can a vision-language-action (VLA) policy signal likely task failure from its own action probabilities? We introduce CalVLA, which shapes native action-token confidence using successful and failed rollouts and an Action-Confidence Alignment (ACal) squared margin-ranking loss. Low-rank adapters update OpenVLA-7B without an auxiliary failure detector. Observations are paired within tasks at similar normalized elapsed times, not necessarily equivalent physical progress. On a held-out test split from 500 LIBERO-10 configurations, adapted confidence achieves a joint failure-discrimination AUROC of $0.7392\pm0.0480$ over three seeds, averaging scores at 130 and 260 steps. Frozen-policy probes reach 0.6146--0.6436, but superiority over the linear probe is statistically inconclusive. For the same confidence summary, AUROC rises from 0.4485 before adaptation to 0.7327 after adaptation. Mean task success decreases from 58% to 55%. These results show improved failure discrimination, not improved control or established safety benefits.

AI.tldr: CalVLA adapts OpenVLA-7B with low-rank adapters so that its native action-token confidence signals likely task failure, without an auxiliary failure detector. Adapted confidence reaches a failure-discrimination AUROC of 0.7392 on a held-out LIBERO-10 split, but the paper says this is not improved control or established safety.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether a vision-language-action policy can flag likely failure from its own action probabilities, and whether such confidence can be shaped using rollout outcomes.
AI.method: The method shapes native action-token confidence with successful and failed rollouts and an Action-Confidence Alignment (ACal) squared margin-ranking loss. Observations are paired within tasks at similar normalized elapsed times, and low-rank adapters update OpenVLA-7B.
AI.result: On a held-out test split from 500 LIBERO-10 configurations, adapted confidence reaches a joint failure-discrimination AUROC of 0.7392 ± 0.0480 over three seeds. Frozen-policy probes reach 0.6146 to 0.6436, a difference from the linear probe that is statistically inconclusive. AUROC rises from 0.4485 before adaptation to 0.7327 after, and mean task success falls from 58% to 55%.
AI.conclusion: The results show better failure discrimination, not improved control or established safety benefits.

title: Hacking or Just Failing? A More Capable LLM Monitor Better Separates Reward Hacking from Honest Failure
comment: 14 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables. Code, data and pre-registrations: this https URL
summary: An agent's visible score can exceed its real progress because it gamed the score or because it simply made mistakes, so a useful reward-hacking monitor must tell the two apart. We built a sandboxed task in which an agent can game a completion score, labelled every episode by replaying it and repairing the final state counterfactually, and ran five pre-registered studies. On 60 episodes from a Llama 3.1 8B agent, small local monitors (Llama 3B and 8B) did not separate exploit attempts from honest failures with the same score gap: prompt changes traded missed exploits for false alarms, and the pre-registered primary monitor reached AUC 0.64. On identical inputs, Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite, which completed 9/10 clean tasks against 2/10 for the 8B model, met our pre-registered criterion (AUC 0.80, 95% interval [0.66, 0.93]; 1/35 honest failures flagged); with only 14 exploit episodes, this estimate is uncertain. On an exploit that no prompt names, Gemini usually described the action correctly yet never flagged it, in 5 and then 25 new episodes, even when manipulation was defined by its effect on the score. Given the full trace, the 8B monitor flagged all 25 replication episodes and none of 25 honest look-alikes, but its explanations described actions that had not occurred; given additional structured evidence, it also flagged 15 of the 25 look-alikes. A two-rule deterministic check caught every known exploit. We release the environment, labels, pre-registrations and per-judgement logs.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether LLM monitors can separate reward hacking from honest failure in a sandboxed task, finding that a more capable monitor (Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite) reaches AUC 0.80 where small local monitors do not. Smaller monitors fail on the same inputs, and a two-rule deterministic check caught every known exploit.
AI.motivation: An agent's visible score can exceed its real progress either by gaming the score or by making mistakes, so a useful reward-hacking monitor must distinguish the two.
AI.method: The authors built a sandboxed task where an agent can game a completion score, labeled each episode by replaying it and counterfactually repairing the final state, and ran five pre-registered studies. Local Llama 3B and 8B monitors and Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite were compared on 60 episodes from a Llama 3.1 8B agent, with a two-rule deterministic check as a baseline.
AI.result: The pre-registered primary local monitor reaches AUC 0.64. Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite meets the pre-registered criterion with AUC 0.80 (95% interval [0.66, 0.93]) and flags 1/35 honest failures, though with only 14 exploit episodes the estimate is uncertain. Gemini often describes exploit actions correctly yet does not flag them on an unnamed exploit. Given the full trace, the 8B monitor flags all 25 replication episodes and none of 25 honest look-alikes, but its explanations describe actions that did not occur. A two-rule deterministic check caught every known exploit.
AI.conclusion: Monitor capability matters for separating exploitation from honest failure, but explanation quality and the uncertainty of small samples still limit how far the results can be trusted.

title: Nonconformal Distortion and Local Orientation Reversal in the Fourier Circuit of a Modular-Addition Transformer
summary: We study the local differential geometry of a Fourier-based modular-addition circuit in a one-layer transformer whose algorithm has previously been reverse-engineered. For each of the five key Fourier frequencies, we restrict the model's multilayer perceptron (MLP) contribution to a corresponding Fourier input plane and readout, and measure its directional Beltrami coefficient under continuous input perturbations. Whereas nondegenerate restrictions of ideal complex multiplication are conformal, the trained maps exhibit nonconformal distortion (median $|\mu|=0.304$--$0.446$), spatial organization in the Beltrami argument, and regions of local orientation reversal. The median across frequencies decreases from $0.939$ at initialization to $0.390$ after training. The key-frequency planes also show lower median distortion than most random-plane controls, although their distributions overlap and the coordinate frames differ in conditioning. Across 500 checkpoints in one training run, most of the aggregate reduction in Beltrami magnitude occurs before the principal increase in the measured Fourier-circuit formation. At the individual-input level, Beltrami magnitude shows negligible association with the correct-logit margin ($|\rho|\leq0.026$). Late-checkpoint measurements across six runs show comparable distortion for most selected frequencies. These results provide a quantitative characterization of local deformation in a frequency-projected component of an identified neural circuit, complementary to its algorithmic reconstruction.

AI.tldr: The paper measures the local differential geometry of the Fourier modular-addition circuit in a one-layer transformer, finding that its MLP maps are nonconformal and contain regions of local orientation reversal. Median Beltrami distortion falls from 0.939 at initialization to 0.390 after training.
AI.motivation: The Fourier circuit of this transformer has been reverse-engineered algorithmically, but its local geometric deformation has not been quantified.
AI.method: For each of five key Fourier frequencies, the MLP contribution is restricted to a Fourier input plane and readout, and the directional Beltrami coefficient is measured under continuous input perturbations. Comparisons include random-plane controls and 500 checkpoints from one training run, with late-checkpoint measurements across six runs.
AI.result: The trained maps are nonconformal, with median |mu| between 0.304 and 0.446, and show regions of local orientation reversal. The median across frequencies falls from 0.939 at initialization to 0.390 after training. Most of the reduction happens before the main increase in Fourier-circuit formation, and Beltrami magnitude shows negligible association with the correct-logit margin (|rho| <= 0.026).
AI.conclusion: The paper gives a quantitative characterization of local deformation in a frequency-projected component of an identified circuit, complementary to its algorithmic reconstruction.

title: OmniMechanism Design for Human-AI Collaboration with Impressionable Minds
summary: As AI systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, effectively integrating human expertise with AI outputs is critical for reliable decision-making. A substantial body of theoretical work studies optimal mechanisms for human-AI collaboration (HAC), focusing on when to involve humans and how to combine their expertise with AI predictions. However, these approaches largely overlook a key factor highlighted by empirical evidence: human judgments are impressionable and can vary depending on how AI outputs are presented. For example, when AI systems defer decisions to humans, revealing or withholding the AI prediction can significantly influence human judgments. Moreover, existing work neglects deployment-time variability, where conditions, particularly the cost of eliciting human input, may differ substantially from those observed during training. To address these challenges, we introduce a rigorous and theoretically grounded framework for human-AI collaboration, termed collaborative omnimechanism design, based on a novel and computationally efficient contextual bandit variant of boosting for outcome indistinguishability. In particular, we reduce a calibration-type outcome indistinguishability condition to weighted calibration, providing a novel time-efficiency result, bypassing the high-dimension curse induced by complicated collaboration methods and outcome space. Our framework provides a principled characterization of human impressionability and introduces a unified optimization scheme that enables robust and adaptable decision-making across diverse query costs and evaluation objectives without retraining. We evaluate the framework in three HAC settings, examining adaptation to query costs and prediction objectives without retraining, and show that its induced policies perform comparably to or better than the evaluated baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes collaborative omnimechanism design for human-AI collaboration, which models how human judgments depend on how AI outputs are presented and adapts to changing query costs without retraining. It is built on a contextual bandit variant of boosting for outcome indistinguishability and performs comparably to or better than the evaluated baselines.
AI.motivation: Theoretical work on human-AI collaboration overlooks that human judgments are impressionable, depending on whether AI predictions are shown, and that deployment-time query costs can differ from training conditions.
AI.method: The framework is a contextual bandit variant of boosting for outcome indistinguishability. It reduces a calibration-type outcome indistinguishability condition to weighted calibration, which gives a time-efficient algorithm that avoids the high-dimensional cost of complicated collaboration methods and outcome spaces.
AI.result: Across three human-AI collaboration settings, the induced policies adapt to query costs and prediction objectives without retraining and perform comparably to or better than the evaluated baselines.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling human impressionability and optimizing across query costs gives a principled and adaptable approach to human-AI collaboration.

title: Exo: An Architecture for Self-Improving Systems at Runtime
summary: Agent harnesses govern how language models act in an environment; designing their policies by hand is difficult, while automated techniques require representative datasets and costly executions. We present Exo, an agent runtime architecture for safe learning during ongoing work that collapses the optimization loop into task execution, allowing agents to revise both their harness and their strategies for further improvement. A minimal protected mechanism layer preserves execution history and governs policy activation while the harness evolves through inspectable code changes. On long-running objectives in an open-world game, Exo reduces model cost by 12-53% relative to Codex and Pi in standalone runs and 45-82% in transfer runs, while matching task completion rates. Compared with the same starting policy without the ability to edit policy, Exo reduces held-out model cost by 35-61% on AppWorld and SREGym with comparable correctness, cutting AppWorld's mean task time by 13% and SREGym's median diagnosis time by 35%. On Continual Learning Bench coding tasks, model cost including learning falls by 14%, with both policies resolving every issue.

AI.tldr: Exo is an agent runtime architecture that folds policy optimization into task execution, letting agents revise their harness and strategies during ongoing work. It reduces model cost by 12% to 53% against Codex and Pi in standalone runs and by 45% to 82% in transfer runs, while matching task completion rates.
AI.motivation: Hand-designed agent harness policies are difficult to write, while automated optimization needs representative datasets and costly executions.
AI.method: A minimal protected mechanism layer preserves execution history and governs policy activation, while the harness evolves through inspectable code changes. Agents can edit their own policies during the task.
AI.result: On long-running open-world game objectives, Exo cuts model cost by 12% to 53% relative to Codex and Pi in standalone runs and by 45% to 82% in transfer runs, while matching task completion. Against the same starting policy without policy editing, it reduces held-out model cost by 35% to 61% on AppWorld and SREGym with comparable correctness, cuts AppWorld mean task time by 13% and SREGym median diagnosis time by 35%. On Continual Learning Bench coding tasks, model cost including learning falls by 14%.
AI.conclusion: Safe learning during execution can reduce agent cost and improve efficiency without a separate optimization stage.

title: Compression Technique Interactions in Small Language Models: A Factorial Ablation Study
summary: Deploying small language models on resource-constrained hardware requires compression, yet practitioners lack systematic guidance on how quantization, pruning, and post-compression recovery interact when combined. We present a factorial ablation study evaluating 72 compression configurations across four SLM architectures (2.7B-7B parameters), extended with a 48-configuration ordering analysis, benchmark accuracy validation on 30 compressed models, and robustness checks including multi-seed validation and full-corpus perplexity evaluation. INT8 quantization is effectively lossless (<0.5% accuracy degradation), while NF4 quantization combined with L1 magnitude pruning causes model collapse in all 16 tested combinations. LoRA-based fine-tuning reduces degraded perplexity by up to 97% after aggressive pruning; an ablation against standard fine-tuning without a teacher model shows the recovery is driven by LoRA adaptation itself rather than the distillation signal. Compression ordering shows no significant effect among viable configurations (ANOVA p = 0.96) but determines viability for NF4+pruning combinations. INT8 quantization alone provides 40-45% memory reduction with no quality loss. On-device CPU deployment via this http URL confirms these findings transfer off the GPU: 4-bit quantization runs 46-54% faster than 8-bit for a perplexity difference under 0.5 points, while un-structured pruning yields no CPU latency or memory benefit, consistent with its dense storage format.

AI.tldr: A factorial study of 72 compression configurations across four small language models (2.7B to 7B parameters) finds that INT8 quantization is effectively lossless, while NF4 with L1 pruning collapses in all 16 tested combinations. LoRA recovery after aggressive pruning cuts degraded perplexity by up to 97%.
AI.motivation: Practitioners lack systematic guidance on how quantization, pruning and post-compression recovery interact when combined for deployment on resource-constrained hardware.
AI.method: The factorial ablation covers 72 configurations across four SLM architectures, extended with a 48-configuration ordering analysis, accuracy checks on 30 compressed models, and robustness checks with multi-seed validation and full-corpus perplexity. An ablation compares LoRA with standard fine-tuning that has no teacher model.
AI.result: INT8 quantization loses under 0.5% accuracy and gives 40% to 45% memory reduction. NF4 with L1 magnitude pruning causes model collapse in all 16 tested combinations. LoRA fine-tuning reduces degraded perplexity by up to 97% after aggressive pruning, and the recovery is driven by LoRA itself rather than the distillation signal. Compression ordering shows no significant effect among viable configurations (ANOVA p = 0.96). On CPU, 4-bit quantization runs 46% to 54% faster than 8-bit with a perplexity difference under 0.5 points, and unstructured pruning gives no CPU latency or memory benefit.
AI.conclusion: The findings transfer from GPU to CPU deployment, with INT8 quantization as a safe choice and ordering mattering only for NF4 plus pruning combinations.

title: Few Trials, Many Metrics: Beta Mixtures for Low-Budget AI Evaluation
summary: Evaluating a stochastic AI system often requires many repeated samples per instance, especially for metrics defined over long horizons. Recent work has shown that modeling instance-level success probabilities with a Beta distribution recovers Pass@$k$ from far fewer samples than direct estimation. We show that this framework supports a broader range of evaluation targets. We fit a mixture of Beta distributions by marginal maximum likelihood, with the number of components chosen by BIC. From that one fit, we compute Pass$^k$ and AUC@$k$ at any horizon in closed form. We also derive delta-method confidence intervals for these metrics and for Pass@$k$, which require no additional model calls. Treating configurations rather than tasks as instances extends the same model to sensitivity analysis. For repeated success metrics, we find that mixture priors yield more accurate estimators than naive estimation across competition mathematics and graduate-level science benchmarks when extrapolating beyond the observed number of trials, and the resulting intervals cover the full-data reference. When prompts are treated as instances, it estimates the distribution of prompt sensitivity more accurately than a comparable item-response baseline without external covariates. Direct estimators remain preferable once trials reach the target horizon.

AI.tldr: The paper fits a mixture of Beta distributions to instance-level success probabilities by marginal maximum likelihood, deriving Pass^k and AUC@k in closed form and delta-method confidence intervals from one fit. It supports low-budget evaluation of stochastic AI systems and is more accurate than naive estimation when extrapolating beyond the observed number of trials.
AI.motivation: Evaluating stochastic AI systems needs many repeated samples per instance, especially for long-horizon metrics, and earlier Beta-based work only recovered Pass@k.
AI.method: A mixture of Beta distributions is fit by marginal maximum likelihood, with the number of components chosen by BIC. From that single fit, Pass^k and AUC@k are computed at any horizon in closed form, and delta-method confidence intervals are derived for these metrics and for Pass@k without extra model calls. Configurations can be treated as instances for sensitivity analysis.
AI.result: For repeated success metrics, mixture priors give more accurate estimators than naive estimation on competition mathematics and graduate-level science benchmarks when extrapolating beyond the observed number of trials, and the intervals cover the full-data reference. With prompts as instances, the model estimates prompt sensitivity more accurately than an item-response baseline without external covariates. Direct estimators remain preferable once trials reach the target horizon.
AI.conclusion: One mixture fit supports a broader set of evaluation targets, though direct estimation is better when enough trials are available.

title: To Jev or Not to Jev: When Can System-1 Decision Models Replace LLM Judges?
