AI.conclusion: Isoform-aware cross-modal JEPA alignment is presented as a promising direction for genomic foundation model pretraining.

title: DELBERT-2: Pretrained Fingerprint Language Models for DEL Protein Binder Prediction
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures, 2026 Workshop on Generative and Agentic AI for Biology (ICML 2026)
summary: We present DELBERT-2, a pretrained fingerprint language model that converts sparse molecular fingerprints into unified token sequences using a ModernBERT encoder trained with masked language modelling on 2.5M molecules from the AIRCHECK DEL corpus. We evaluate across six targets (WDR91, WDR12, SETDB1, PLCZ1, LRRK2, DCAF7) under three out-of-distribution (OOD) protocols: hierarchical cluster splits probe chemical novelty, library splits test cross-library transfer, and building-block splits assess compositional generalization. DELBERT-2 consistently improves PR-AUC and NDCG@1000 relative to LightGBM ensemble baselines and transformers trained from scratch, with the largest gains in stringent OOD regimes. DELBERT-2 achieves 13.28+/-3.72 enrichment factor at top-100 vs. 12.36+/-3.75 for no-pretraining (p=0.040), representing 7.4% improvement and 13x enrichment over random selection. These results demonstrate that fingerprint-centric self-supervised learning effectively improves hit prioritization under distribution shift, enabling practical DEL virtual screening. Code is available at \hyperlink{this https URL}{DELBERT-2}.

AI.tldr: DELBERT-2 is a pretrained fingerprint language model, a ModernBERT encoder trained with masked language modelling on 2.5M molecules, for DEL protein binder prediction. It improves PR-AUC and NDCG@1000 over LightGBM and from-scratch transformers, most strongly under out-of-distribution splits.
AI.motivation: Molecular fingerprints are sparse, and DEL virtual screening must generalize under distribution shift, including chemical novelty, cross-library transfer and compositional building-block changes.
AI.method: Sparse fingerprints are converted into unified token sequences and a ModernBERT encoder is pretrained with masked language modelling on 2.5M molecules from the AIRCHECK DEL corpus. Evaluation uses six targets (WDR91, WDR12, SETDB1, PLCZ1, LRRK2, DCAF7) under hierarchical cluster, library and building-block splits.
AI.result: DELBERT-2 reaches an enrichment factor at top-100 of 13.28 +/- 3.72, versus 12.36 +/- 3.75 without pretraining (p=0.040), a 7.4% improvement and 13x enrichment over random selection. It consistently improves PR-AUC and NDCG@1000 relative to LightGBM and from-scratch transformers, with the largest gains in stringent OOD regimes.
AI.conclusion: Fingerprint-centric self-supervised learning improves hit prioritization under distribution shift, which supports practical DEL virtual screening.

title: OCELOT: Planetary-Scale Species Distribution Modeling with Satellite Foundation Embeddings
summary: Large-scale repositories of species observations now contain billions of occurrence records from around the world, but these sightings cluster heavily in human-accessible areas. Existing models use only a small fraction of these records and are not evaluated on extrapolating to remote, unvisited regions--where species distribution models can be used as geographic priors to help classify data from camera traps and acoustic recorders. We scale relative occurrence species distribution models by training a multimodal implicit neural representation network called OCELOT that fuses spatial coordinates with satellite foundation embeddings on two orders of magnitude more observations than previous work: 2 billion GBIF records across 100,000 taxa. Scaling to this regime requires co-designing the data pipeline, taxonomic representation, loss formulation, and model architecture: spatiotemporal thinning and sub-linear cell sampling correct for spatial redundancy and observer bias, while an additive taxonomic readout shares representations across species, genera, and families to improve predictions for rare taxa. To evaluate performance in remote areas, we benchmark geographic extrapolation using the NDCG metric on spatial block holdouts up to 600 km. Satellite foundation embeddings improve extrapolation by 51% over coordinate-only models and outperform classical bioclimatic rasters. The resulting model also matches or outperforms existing baselines on established interpolation benchmarks, demonstrating that optimizing for geographic extrapolation does not compromise in-distribution accuracy.

AI.tldr: OCELOT is an implicit neural representation that fuses coordinates with satellite foundation embeddings to model species distributions at planetary scale, trained on 2 billion GBIF records across 100,000 taxa. Satellite embeddings improve geographic extrapolation by 51% over coordinate-only models.
AI.motivation: Species occurrence records cluster in human-accessible areas, and existing models use only a small fraction of the data and are not evaluated on extrapolating to remote, unvisited regions, where they would serve as geographic priors for camera trap and acoustic data.
AI.method: Scaling requires co-designing spatiotemporal thinning and sub-linear cell sampling to correct spatial redundancy and observer bias, an additive taxonomic readout that shares representations across species, genera and families, a loss formulation, and an architecture. Extrapolation is benchmarked with NDCG on spatial block holdouts up to 600 km.
AI.result: Satellite foundation embeddings improve geographic extrapolation by 51% over coordinate-only models and outperform classical bioclimatic rasters. The model matches or outperforms existing baselines on interpolation benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Optimizing for geographic extrapolation does not compromise in-distribution accuracy, which supports OCELOT as a planetary-scale geographic prior for species distribution modeling.

title: Quantization of Large Models with Weight Outliers and Sparsity
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on On-Device Intelligence: Foundation Models under Real-World Constraints
summary: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces the memory burden of large model deployment by casting the high precision trained weights to fewer bits. While this promotes memory-efficient inference, it also incurs quantization error that impairs model performance. To compensate for quantization error, the present contribution decomposes the original trained weights into a quantized matrix, a low-rank component, and a sparse matrix that accounts for outlier rows in the weights. Due to analytical intractability and the discrete structure of the decomposition, a simulated annealing search is employed to explore candidate decompositions while avoiding poor local minima. Numerical tests demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach across a broad suite of large language models, including Llama 3.2 1B, Llama 3.2 3B, Llama 3.1 8B, and Qwen2.5 7B, evaluated on natural language generation benchmarks using 4-bit NF4 and FP4 quantizers. The novel method can markedly outperform direct quantization while incurring minimal memory overhead.

AI.tldr: The paper decomposes trained LLM weights into a quantized matrix, a low-rank component and a sparse outlier-row matrix, searched by simulated annealing, to reduce post-training quantization error. It reports that the method markedly outperforms direct quantization with minimal memory overhead.
AI.motivation: Post-training quantization reduces memory for large model deployment but introduces quantization error that degrades performance, and direct quantization leaves this error uncompensated.
AI.method: Weights are decomposed into a quantized matrix, a low-rank term and a sparse matrix capturing outlier rows; because the discrete decomposition is analytically intractable, simulated annealing explores candidate decompositions while avoiding poor local minima.
AI.result: Tests on Llama 3.2 1B, Llama 3.2 3B, Llama 3.1 8B and Qwen2.5 7B with 4-bit NF4 and FP4 quantizers on natural language generation benchmarks show the method markedly outperforms direct quantization at minimal memory overhead.
AI.conclusion: The decomposition with outlier-row sparsity and annealed search is an effective way to reduce 4-bit quantization error in LLMs without large memory cost.

title: A Framework for Task-Agnostic Counterfactual Fairness in Transformers through Activation Steering
summary: Bias in transformer-based models is a growing concern as these architectures become more prevalent in automated decision-making systems, such as prediction models for hiring, lending, and clinical treatment recommendation. Mechanistic interpretability (MI) is a growing body of work that measures meaningful causal effects of activations on model output by identifying human-interpretable features encoded in model activations. When such features correspond to sensitive attributes, they provide a direct way to quantify the bias those attributes introduce and to causally intervene to mitigate it. However, counterfactual fairness (CF) methods have not been systematically adapted to this setting of intervening on interpretable mechanisms in transformers. We propose a framework, Mechanistic Interpretability for Counterfactual Fairness (MICF), that utilizes MI tools to reformulate CF constraints in terms of transformer activations, unifying former approaches into a single pipeline for fairness analysis in transformers. MICF does not require a prior causal model or specific transformer architecture. We evaluate MICF on real-world tabular data and show that CF can be improved across different prediction tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MICF, a framework that uses mechanistic interpretability tools to express counterfactual fairness constraints in terms of transformer activations. It reports that counterfactual fairness can be improved across different prediction tasks on real-world tabular data.
AI.motivation: Counterfactual fairness methods have not been systematically adapted to intervening on interpretable mechanisms inside transformers, and existing approaches are fragmented and often rely on a prior causal model.
AI.method: MICF reformulates counterfactual fairness constraints in terms of transformer activations using interpretability tools that identify features encoding sensitive attributes, unifying prior approaches into one pipeline without requiring a causal model or a specific architecture.
AI.result: MICF is evaluated on real-world tabular data across several prediction tasks, where counterfactual fairness is improved; the abstract gives no numerical results.
AI.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability offers a general, architecture-agnostic route to causally intervening on bias in transformers for fairness analysis.

title: RaMMOBO: Random Max-Margin Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization
summary: Multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) maximizes $M$ expensive black-box objectives with the goal of approximating the Pareto set, whose objective vectors cannot be improved in one component without sacrificing another. A common quality measure is hypervolume, the volume in objective space dominated by these vectors relative to a reference point. Expected hypervolume improvement (EHVI) directly targets this metric and is one-step Bayes-optimal, but its standard computation scales exponentially with $M$, making it prohibitively expensive for many-objective problems. We introduce random max-margin multi-objective Bayesian optimization (RaMMOBO), whose acquisition function lower-bounds EHVI while requiring only linear cost in $M$ to evaluate. RaMMOBO measures the volume of a max-margin box contained in a candidate's hypervolume-improvement region and averages over random reweightings of the objective space, yielding a utility that is strictly Pareto-monotone on hypervolume-improving outcomes. It naturally handles noisy observations and different probabilistic surrogates and supports efficient gradient-based optimization. Across synthetic and real-world benchmarks, RaMMOBO matches or outperforms state-of-the-art methods, with largest gains at higher $M$, with acquisition optimization up to two orders of magnitude faster than qLogNEHVI. Our implementation is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RaMMOBO, a multi-objective Bayesian optimization acquisition function that lower-bounds expected hypervolume improvement at linear cost in the number of objectives. It reports matching or outperforming state-of-the-art methods, with the largest gains at higher objective counts and acquisition optimization up to two orders of magnitude faster than qLogNEHVI.
AI.motivation: Expected hypervolume improvement is one-step Bayes-optimal for hypervolume but its standard computation scales exponentially with the number of objectives, which makes it prohibitive for many-objective problems.
AI.method: The acquisition function measures the volume of a max-margin box inside a candidate's hypervolume-improvement region and averages over random reweightings of the objective space, giving a utility that is strictly Pareto-monotone on hypervolume-improving outcomes; it handles noise, different surrogates and gradient-based optimization.
AI.result: Across synthetic and real-world benchmarks RaMMOBO matches or outperforms state-of-the-art methods, with largest gains at higher M, and acquisition optimization is up to two orders of magnitude faster than qLogNEHVI.
AI.conclusion: A linear-cost lower bound on EHVI makes hypervolume-based multi-objective Bayesian optimization practical for many-objective problems.

title: Cyber-physical attack detection approaches in the wide-area measurement system
summary: Improving situational awareness within the Smart Grid is an effective preventive measure to detect potential anomalies, and avoid their adverse consequences. A wide area measurement system (WAMS) based Phasor Measurement Unit (PMU) can assist in improving visibility within the grid by collecting relevant measurements including magnitude, phase angle, frequency, voltage, and current, with a precise GPS-based timestamp. So far, there are more than 2500 PMUs deployed in the North American power grid, where each of which generates between 30 and 60 samples/s, roughly 1.5 TB/month of streamed data. Thus, processing such large PMU streams requires expensive computational resources and faster algorithms. This paper provides state-of-the-art cyber and physical anomalies in the WAMS and analyses their impact on the integrity and availability of the system. Next, it investigates the current anomaly detection approach in historical and streaming PMU data, including conventional machine learning and hybrid approaches, and assesses their advantages and main drawbacks. Lastly, it sheds light on the importance of handling missing PMU data and concept drifts.

AI.tldr: This survey reviews cyber and physical anomalies in wide-area measurement systems built on phasor measurement units, and assesses conventional machine learning and hybrid anomaly detection methods for historical and streaming PMU data. It highlights missing data and concept drift as key open challenges.
AI.motivation: PMU deployments in the smart grid generate very large volumes of streaming data, which demand expensive computation and faster algorithms, while anomalies threaten the integrity and availability of situational awareness.
AI.method: The paper surveys state-of-the-art cyber and physical anomalies in WAMS, analyses their impact on integrity and availability, and reviews current detection approaches for historical and streaming PMU data, comparing their advantages and drawbacks.
AI.result: The abstract reports no experimental results; it notes that more than 2500 PMUs are deployed in North America, each producing 30 to 60 samples per second, about 1.5 TB per month in total.
AI.conclusion: Handling missing PMU data and concept drift is important for reliable anomaly detection in WAMS, and existing methods still have notable drawbacks.

title: C3: Speech-Guided KV Retrieval for Long-Context SpeechLLM Inference
summary: Speech language models encode audio at a much higher rate than text, causing the KV cache to dominate the memory, bandwidth, and decoding cost of long-form generation. KV retrieval can reduce per-step access by attending to only a query-dependent subset of the cache, but existing methods are designed primarily for text and do not account for the structure of audio attention. We first show that retrieval errors may compound autoregressively into generation drift. We then analyze full audio attention during long-form generation and identify three properties relevant to retrieval: unequal attention concentration across query heads, non-contiguous audio support, and temporal continuity across decoding steps. Guided by these observations, we propose $C^3$(Cluster-Compete-Compete), which organizes audio KVs in a hierarchical key-space index, lets query heads sharing a KV head compete for a common retrieval budget, and adaptively reallocates retrieval resolution through paired split-merge updates. Across long-form speech recognition, translation, and summarization on four SpeechLLMs, $C^3$ achieves the strongest overall performance among retrieval methods under comparable final-KV access budgets, with particularly large gains in the tight-budget regime, while improving long-context decoding efficiency and accelerator-memory scaling.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes C3, a KV-cache retrieval method for long-form SpeechLLM inference that organizes audio KV entries in a hierarchical index and lets query heads compete for a shared retrieval budget. It reports the strongest overall performance among retrieval methods under comparable KV access budgets across four SpeechLLMs, with large gains in the tight-budget regime.
AI.motivation: Audio tokens are encoded at a much higher rate than text, so the KV cache dominates memory and decoding cost, while existing KV retrieval methods are designed for text and ignore the structure of audio attention, and their errors can compound into generation drift.
AI.method: C3 (Cluster-Compete-Compete) organizes audio KVs in a hierarchical key-space index, lets query heads sharing a KV head compete for a common retrieval budget, and adaptively reallocates retrieval resolution through paired split-merge updates, guided by observed unequal head concentration, non-contiguous audio support and temporal continuity.
AI.result: Evaluated on long-form speech recognition, translation and summarization across four SpeechLLMs, C3 achieves the strongest overall performance among retrieval methods under comparable final-KV access budgets, with particularly large gains at tight budgets, and improves long-context decoding efficiency and accelerator-memory scaling.
AI.conclusion: Audio-specific retrieval design, rather than text-oriented KV retrieval, is needed to make long-context SpeechLLM decoding efficient without generation drift.

title: Decomposing Irregular Time Series into Interpretable Temporal Patterns with Mixture-of-Experts
summary: Irregularly-spaced sequential data, such as transaction logs, encode multi-scale temporal structure that is critical for prediction but difficult to recover explicitly with standard sequence models, which often trade interpretability for performance. We introduce MoTIF, an interpretable framework using mixture-of-experts (MoE) attention to decompose irregular time series into temporal patterns spanning minute-to-year scales. Each expert is trained via temporal alignment that induces attention specialization to a designated cyclical or within-range pattern, with label-free routing supervision that learns to activate the correct expert from patterns present in the data. On synthetic data with known temporal structure, MoTIF recovers correct routing well above chance (0.389/0.829 for range/cyclical patterns vs. 0.091 random) and outperforms all baselines, including a standard transformer and an unspecialized MoE, on next-value prediction. On a public credit card transaction dataset, MoTIF achieves higher macro-F1 than all baselines for next-amount prediction. Its learned routing reveals structure a black-box model cannot: transactions are governed primarily by intraday and short-interval rhythms, while fraudulent transactions show bursty, calendar-agnostic timing versus the steadier periodicity of legitimate ones. On downstream fraud detection, MoTIF matches standard transformer and MoE baselines and clearly outperforms recent sequential recommendation models used as embedding baselines. These results show that decomposing temporal structure into interpretable, expert-specific patterns need not sacrifice predictive accuracy, offering a practical route to sequence models that are both accurate and auditable in high-stakes settings. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MoTIF, an interpretable mixture-of-experts attention model that decomposes irregular time series into temporal patterns from minute to year scales. It reports competitive prediction and fraud detection accuracy while its learned routing reveals interpretable transaction structure.
AI.motivation: Irregularly spaced sequences such as transaction logs contain multi-scale temporal structure that matters for prediction, but standard sequence models trade interpretability for performance and do not expose this structure explicitly.
AI.method: Each expert in an MoE attention layer is trained through temporal alignment to specialize in a designated cyclical or within-range pattern, with label-free routing supervision that learns to activate the correct expert from patterns present in the data.
AI.result: On synthetic data, routing recovers correct patterns well above chance (0.389 and 0.829 for range and cyclical patterns versus 0.091 random) and outperforms baselines on next-value prediction; on a public credit card dataset MoTIF gives higher macro-F1 than all baselines for next-amount prediction and matches transformer and MoE baselines on fraud detection, clearly beating sequential recommendation embeddings.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing temporal structure into expert-specific patterns need not sacrifice accuracy, offering auditable sequence models for high-stakes settings such as fraud detection.

title: DEPLOY-RL: Active Boundary Discovery and Conservative Certification for Deployable Reinforcement Learning in Safety-Critical Continuous Processes
comment: 8 pages; published in IJCAI-ECAI 2026, AI4Tech track. This version adds a publication notice
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) policies often outperform classical controllers in simulation, yet rarely reach production in safety-critical processes. The barrier is that there is no principled way to answer "Is this policy safe to deploy?" with statistical guarantees. We introduce DEPLOY-RL, a post-training certification framework built on one key insight: deployment certification requires discovering where failures occur (boundary discovery), not measuring how much everywhere (uniform reconstruction). Our contributions: (1) a contract-coupled acquisition function that concentrates sampling on certification-critical boundaries, achieving approximately 2x sample efficiency with a semi-empirical ambiguity reduction bound (domain-calibrated convergence guarantee); (2) conformal risk control providing finite-sample false-go guarantees (<= alpha) under explicit deployment contracts; (3) a three-way decision framework (Deploy/No-Deploy/Abstain) with fail-safe PID/MPC fallback. In simulations on papermaking (industrial digital twin) and Tennessee Eastman (public benchmark), DEPLOY-RL achieves 4.4% false-go rate (vs. 8.6% for the best baseline) while retaining 88.6% policy coverage, the only method achieving <5% false-go with >85% coverage among 14 baselines under our evaluation protocol.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes DEPLOY-RL, a post-training certification framework that finds where RL policies fail and issues Deploy, No-Deploy or Abstain decisions with conformal false-go guarantees. In simulations on papermaking and Tennessee Eastman, it reaches a 4.4% false-go rate versus 8.6% for the best baseline while keeping 88.6% policy coverage.
AI.motivation: RL policies that outperform classical controllers in simulation rarely reach production in safety-critical processes because there is no principled statistical way to certify that a policy is safe to deploy.
AI.method: A contract-coupled acquisition function concentrates sampling on certification-critical failure boundaries, conformal risk control provides finite-sample false-go guarantees under explicit deployment contracts, and a three-way decision rule falls back to a PID or MPC controller when abstaining.
AI.result: On a papermaking digital twin and the Tennessee Eastman benchmark, DEPLOY-RL achieves a 4.4% false-go rate versus 8.6% for the best baseline with 88.6% policy coverage, and is the only one of 14 baselines with under 5% false-go and above 85% coverage; it claims about 2x sample efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Targeting boundary discovery rather than uniform reconstruction makes statistical deployment certification of RL policies practical for safety-critical continuous processes.

title: On the Limits of Test-Time Compute for Self-Evaluation
comment: 30 pages, 22 figures, Code: this https URL
summary: Self-verification and aggregation have emerged as popular approaches for bridging the gap between pass@1 and pass@N. However, increasing the number of candidates does not consistently narrow the gap between final-answer accuracy and pass@N. To understand this limitation, we use ranking error to measure how reliably models distinguish their correct generations from incorrect ones. We show that ranking error admits a bias-variance decomposition, with both components shaped by algorithmic design choices and inference compute. Across our experiments, additional compute reduces variance, while bias initially decreases before approaching a plateau. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Scorpio, a simple and general method that jointly scores randomly grouped candidates. Across math, code, and puzzle benchmarks, Scorpio improves verification, tree search, and aggregation. For verification, Scorpio improves accuracy over the strongest baseline by up to 7 percentage points while matching or exceeding that baseline's peak accuracy with 17-42% lower inference cost. For tree search, using Scorpio to score partial solutions and select the final answer improves accuracy by up to 10 percentage points over prior methods. Finally, Scorpio improves the scaling of aggregation-based methods by 11 percentage points on coding tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper analyses why extra test-time compute fails to close the gap between pass@1 and pass@N, decomposing ranking error into bias and variance, and proposes Scorpio, which jointly scores randomly grouped candidates. It reports gains in verification, tree search and aggregation across math, code and puzzle benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Self-verification and aggregation are popular for narrowing the gap between pass@1 and pass@N, but adding candidates does not consistently close it, and the reasons are not well understood.
AI.method: Ranking error, which measures how reliably a model separates its correct from incorrect generations, is decomposed into bias and variance shaped by algorithm design and inference compute; guided by this, Scorpio jointly scores randomly grouped candidates.
AI.result: Scorpio improves verification accuracy over the strongest baseline by up to 7 percentage points and matches its peak accuracy with 17 to 42% lower inference cost; for tree search it improves accuracy by up to 10 points over prior methods; for aggregation it improves coding tasks by 11 points.
AI.conclusion: Joint scoring of grouped candidates reduces the variance and bias of self-evaluation, improving verification, search and aggregation under a given compute budget.

title: MXCode: Vector Quantization for MX-Native Inference at Scale
summary: Memory capacity and bandwidth are major bottlenecks in LLM inference, motivating weight compression beyond conventional 4-bit quantization. Vector quantization (VQ) enables approximately 2-bit weight storage but often relies on codebooks incompatible with native FP4 computation. We introduce MXCode (MX-Native Codebook Quantization), a framework bridging ultra-low-bit VQ compression with MicroXcaling (MX)-native FP4 computation. MXCode proposes three strategies: PostScale, which quantizes learned codebooks to MXFP4; PreScale, which extracts MX scales before codebook learning; and PreScale+, which further compresses these scales using VQ. These strategies explore tradeoffs among quantization quality, scale overhead, and codebook granularity. All reconstruct MX-native W4A4 operands without materializing intermediate high-precision weights. We evaluate MXCode on Qwen3 (235B), DeepSeek-R1 (671B), and GLM-5.2 (753B) using the Microsoft MX Emulation Library. MXCode achieves approximately 2 bits per weight with competitive, workload-dependent model quality. On GB300 hardware, experiments with Qwen3 (235B) show approximately 50% lower model-load memory than Native FP4 while maintaining near-Native-FP4 serving throughput. Under memory-constrained prefix reuse, P90 TTFT improves by up to 94.5%. These results demonstrate software-based reconstruction on existing FP4 hardware and inform the development of future MX-native inference systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MXCode, which combines ultra-low-bit vector quantization of LLM weights, at about 2 bits per weight, with MX-native FP4 computation so that the reconstruction runs without intermediate high-precision weights. It reports roughly 50% lower model-load memory than native FP4 on GB300 for Qwen3 235B with near-native serving throughput.
AI.motivation: Memory and bandwidth limit LLM inference, and VQ compression at about 2 bits relies on codebooks that are incompatible with native FP4 computation.
AI.method: Three strategies are proposed: PostScale quantizes learned codebooks to MXFP4, PreScale extracts MX scales before codebook learning, and PreScale+ further compresses those scales with VQ; all reconstruct MX-native W4A4 operands.
AI.result: On Qwen3 235B, DeepSeek-R1 671B and GLM-5.2 753B with the Microsoft MX Emulation Library, MXCode reaches about 2 bits per weight with competitive quality; on GB300, Qwen3 235B shows about 50% lower model-load memory than native FP4 and near-native FP4 throughput, and P90 TTFT improves by up to 94.5% under memory-constrained prefix reuse.
AI.conclusion: Software reconstruction of VQ-compressed weights can run on existing FP4 hardware, pointing toward MX-native inference systems.

title: TileWeave: Heterogeneous Tiling for Sparse Prefill on Mobile SoCs
summary: Smartphone applications increasingly require large language models to process long contexts, whereas high prefill latency and memory demands constrain local inference. Block-sparse attention reduces computation and memory traffic, but its irregular selections conflict with mobile NPUs' preference for large, regular tiles. Efficient execution must exploit cross-query reuse while avoiding redundant computation and preserving selections needed for accuracy. In this paper, we present TileWeave, which partitions sparse attention by this cross-query reuse: highly shared key blocks run in coarse NPU tiles, while low-reuse blocks run on the GPU only for the query blocks that selected them. In addition, we design an NPU-native pooled-key selector that keeps selection inexpensive, and a runtime that publishes GPU partials in the order the NPU consumes them and merges them in its existing output store. On RULER, HeteroSparse matches XAttention's accuracy with Qwen3-1.7B and improves it with Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct; its mean LongBench scores match XAttention as well. On Snapdragon SM8750 and SM8850 phones, it achieves 1.35--3.23$\times$ faster full-model prefill than XAttention over 1k--16k tokens and up to 1.58$\times$ faster than dense attention.

AI.tldr: The paper presents TileWeave, which splits block-sparse prefill attention between a mobile NPU and GPU according to cross-query key reuse, speeding up long-context prefill on Snapdragon phones. It reports 1.35 to 3.23 times faster full-model prefill than XAttention over 1k to 16k tokens.
AI.motivation: On-device LLM prefill with long contexts is slow and memory-heavy, and irregular block-sparse selections conflict with mobile NPUs' preference for large regular tiles.
AI.method: Highly shared key blocks run in coarse NPU tiles while low-reuse blocks run on the GPU only for the query blocks that selected them; an NPU-native pooled-key selector keeps selection cheap, and a runtime publishes GPU partial results in the order the NPU consumes them and merges them into the NPU's output store.
AI.result: On RULER the method matches XAttention's accuracy with Qwen3-1.7B and improves it with Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, and matches XAttention on mean LongBench scores; on Snapdragon SM8750 and SM8850 it achieves 1.35 to 3.23 times faster full-model prefill than XAttention over 1k to 16k tokens and up to 1.58 times faster than dense attention.
AI.conclusion: Partitioning sparse attention by cross-query reuse across heterogeneous mobile processors makes long-context on-device prefill faster without losing accuracy.

title: RankLane: Efficient MoE Prefill on Accelerators with Ranked Expert Capacities
summary: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models expand model capacity by activating only a subset of experts for each token. On accelerators with static execution plans, expert capacities and placement are fixed before routing reveals each expert's load. Uniform worst-case capacities waste work on padding; smaller capacities tied to expert identities can overflow. We present RankLane, which ranks each device's experts by current load and assigns them to fixed-capacity lanes. Runtime indices select experts and token rows while tier populations, shapes and device placement remain fixed. An aggregation graph preserves device ownership and reduces each token's local contributions on one core. Routing calibration and measured execution costs guide tier selection; overflowing chunks rerun at full capacity. We evaluate full-model prefill of Qwen3-30B-A3B and Gemma 4 26B-A4B with MXFP6 weights on four Cloud AI 100 Ultra SoCs, using 128-2048-token chunks and including overflow detection and in-program recovery support. Against a dense baseline, RankLane achieves end-to-end prefill speedups of 1.27-4.18x on Qwen3 and 1.93-3.46x on Gemma.

AI.tldr: The paper presents RankLane, an MoE prefill scheme for static-plan accelerators that ranks experts by current load and assigns them to fixed-capacity lanes. It reports end-to-end prefill speedups of 1.27 to 4.18 times on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 1.93 to 3.46 times on Gemma 4 26B-A4B against a dense baseline.
AI.motivation: On accelerators with static execution plans, expert capacities and placement are fixed before routing reveals each expert's load, so uniform worst-case capacities waste work on padding while expert-tied smaller capacities can overflow.
AI.method: Each device's experts are ranked by current load and assigned to fixed-capacity lanes; runtime indices select experts and token rows while tier populations, shapes and device placement stay fixed, with an aggregation graph preserving device ownership, routing calibration guiding tier selection, and overflowing chunks rerun at full capacity.
AI.result: Full-model prefill of Qwen3-30B-A3B and Gemma 4 26B-A4B with MXFP6 weights on four Cloud AI 100 Ultra SoCs, with 128 to 2048-token chunks, gives end-to-end speedups of 1.27 to 4.18 times on Qwen3 and 1.93 to 3.46 times on Gemma against a dense baseline.
AI.conclusion: Load-ranked fixed-capacity lanes let MoE prefill on static accelerators avoid padding waste and overflow failures, yielding substantial end-to-end speedups.

title: A Spectral Renormalization-Group View of Learning
summary: We study how the layers in deep neural networks (NNs) converge, using Wilsonian Renormalization-Group (RG) ideas to organize the spectral picture. During training, these layers often develop heavy-tailed power-law (PL) spectra, and the strongest checkpoints often appear near the PL exponent $\alpha\approx 2$. This pattern raises a simple question: why should this value mark a well-trained layer? The answer is both statistical and physical. Our statistical hypothesis is that $\alpha=2$ marks the boundary between stable if not optimal learning and overfitting via non-self-averaging. The physical answer is that the same value makes the spectral energy gain scale evenly across logarithmic spectral scales, which is the proposed Wilsonian marginal condition. We then apply the ERG trace-log condition, the proposed SETOL theory, which we justify by taking volume-preserving, scale-invariant transformations to remove arbitrary layer scale along the proposed RG flow. The resulting spectral RG flow connects the HTSR and SETOL theories to optimizers such as Muon, and motivates a new optimizer extension, WW-PGD. Together, these results point toward a spectral Renormalization-Group view of learning, in which NNs may approach shared spectral structure in the settings studied here.

AI.tldr: The paper uses Wilsonian renormalization-group ideas to argue that power-law exponent alpha of about 2 marks well-trained neural network layers, and derives a spectral RG view connecting HTSR and SETOL theories to optimizers such as Muon. It also proposes a new optimizer extension, WW-PGD.
AI.motivation: Trained layers often develop heavy-tailed power-law spectra with the strongest checkpoints near alpha of about 2, and there is no explanation for why this value should indicate good training.
AI.method: The paper proposes a statistical hypothesis that alpha equal to 2 separates stable learning from overfitting via non-self-averaging, and a physical argument that it gives a Wilsonian marginal condition; it applies the ERG trace-log condition (the proposed SETOL theory) under volume-preserving, scale-invariant transformations along a spectral RG flow.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative experimental results; it states that the framework connects HTSR and SETOL to optimizers such as Muon and motivates the WW-PGD optimizer extension.
AI.conclusion: The results point toward a spectral renormalization-group view of learning in which networks may approach shared spectral structure, with an optimizer consequence still to be validated.

title: Local Spatial TreeSHAP: Geographically Explainable AI Revealing Urbanization-Dependent Spatial Heterogeneity in Flood Resilience
summary: Urban flood resilience emerges from complex interactions among natural, built, and socio-economic systems, yet most recovery policies implicitly assume that resilience mechanisms are spatially uniform. To address this gap, this study develops a spatially explainable machine learning framework that integrates geographically weighted random forests with a novel Local Spatial TreeSHAP algorithm, enabling nonlinear resilience mechanisms to be identified and interpreted at the community scale. The framework is applied to 779 communities affected by the July 2023 extreme rainstorm in Beijing. Results reveal that resilience mechanisms exhibit substantially stronger spatial heterogeneity than the underlying physical and socio-economic conditions themselves, with SHAP-value spatial autocorrelation decreasing by 66.2% on average relative to predictor variables. Three distinct resilience regimes emerge across the urbanization gradient. Highly urbanized communities benefit from synergistic interactions among commercial infrastructure and accommodation services; transitional medium urbanized communities are constrained by infrastructure-development mismatches that create facility gaps despite continued urban expansion; and low urbanized communities are dominated by ecological and topographic thresholds, where adverse interactions between transportation and river-network structures undermine recovery capacity. Field investigations and interviews with 12 stakeholders corroborate these patterns. By linking geographically weighted machine learning with locally grounded attribution analysis, the proposed framework provides a new pathway for uncovering spatially varying resilience mechanisms and translating them into place-based recovery strategies under increasing climate extremes.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Local Spatial TreeSHAP, a geographically weighted random forest explanation framework for flood resilience across 779 Beijing communities hit by the July 2023 rainstorm. It finds that resilience mechanisms are far more spatially heterogeneous than the underlying conditions and identifies three urbanization-dependent resilience regimes.
AI.motivation: Recovery policies implicitly assume resilience mechanisms are spatially uniform, which is not tested for urban flood resilience.
AI.method: The framework combines geographically weighted random forests with a new Local Spatial TreeSHAP algorithm to identify and interpret nonlinear resilience mechanisms at community scale, and attributes the results with field investigations and stakeholder interviews.
AI.result: For 779 communities affected by the July 2023 Beijing rainstorm, SHAP-value spatial autocorrelation decreases by 66.2% on average relative to predictor variables, and three resilience regimes emerge: highly urbanized areas benefit from synergy among commercial and accommodation services, medium urbanized areas face infrastructure-development mismatches, and low urbanized areas are dominated by ecological and topographic thresholds; interviews with 12 stakeholders corroborate these patterns.
AI.conclusion: Spatially varying resilience mechanisms can be uncovered with locally grounded attribution, supporting place-based recovery strategies under increasing climate extremes.

title: CLiS: Plug-and-Play Attention Acceleration for Video Diffusion on TPUs via Certified Stabilization
summary: High-resolution video diffusion relies on attention over long token sequences, making attention efficiency critical to generation latency. Our analysis identifies repeated maximum reductions and accumulator rescaling in online softmax as a bottleneck in long-context TPU attention. We propose CLiS (Certified Loop-invariant Stabilization), a training-free, plug-and-play optimization for video diffusion inference. CLiS fixes per-row stabilizers before the KV loop and certifies numerical safety per head, falling back to online softmax when certification fails. It integrates into existing fused-attention kernels without changing model weights or architecture. On Wan 2.2 and LTX-2 across TPU v6e and TPU7x, CLiS reduces diffusion transformer (DiT) step latency by up to 19.6% relative to tuned online softmax without measurable quality loss. Controlled TPU adaptations of prior GPU stabilization methods show performance or numerical-safety limitations. Preliminary causal LLM experiments also show up to 13.5% higher training throughput in continued pretraining and 7.7% in supervised fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CLiS, a training-free, plug-and-play attention optimization for video diffusion on TPUs that fixes per-row softmax stabilizers before the KV loop and falls back to online softmax when certification fails. It reports up to 19.6% lower diffusion transformer step latency on Wan 2.2 and LTX-2 without measurable quality loss.
AI.motivation: Repeated maximum reductions and accumulator rescaling in online softmax are a bottleneck for long-context attention in high-resolution video diffusion on TPUs, and prior GPU stabilization methods show performance or numerical-safety limitations when adapted to TPUs.
AI.method: Per-row stabilizers are fixed before the KV loop and numerical safety is certified per head, with online softmax as fallback; it integrates into existing fused-attention kernels without changing weights or architecture.
AI.result: On Wan 2.2 and LTX-2 across TPU v6e and TPU7x, CLiS reduces DiT step latency by up to 19.6% relative to tuned online softmax without measurable quality loss; preliminary causal LLM experiments show up to 13.5% higher continued-pretraining throughput and 7.7% in supervised fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Certified loop-invariant stabilization can speed up TPU attention for video diffusion and offers preliminary benefits for LLM training.

title: Learning to evolve by matching velocities
summary: Learning the continuous-time evolution of nonlinear dynamical systems relies on trajectory-based objectives, which require simulating the learned dynamics during training and backpropagating through the numerical scheme, at a cost that grows with the rollout horizon. We show that trajectory-based objectives degenerate as the rollout horizon increases, hindering gradient-based optimization, and that the numerical scheme biases the learned dynamics by constraining the spectrum of the learned Jacobian to its absolute stability region. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Velocity Matching (VM), a simulation-free objective that relies on piecewise-linear interpolation and stochastic collocation, and approximates the velocity population risk to second order in the sampling step. We develop a theoretical framework for velocity-based learning, introducing stability estimates that control trajectory errors in terms of velocity errors, which enable us to establish universal and continuous-time approximation results when the learned velocity field is parameterized by deep neural networks. Building on a bias-variance decomposition of the VM objective, we show that its higher-order approximation of the velocity population risk yields a consistent minimizer; that it relates to the residual of an A-stable continuous-stage Runge-Kutta scheme, thus connecting VM to implicit integration without requiring any implicit solve; and that it implicitly matches the action of the learned Jacobian to that of the true one along the observed trajectories, without requiring access to the underlying velocity field or its Jacobian. Numerical experiments on nonlinear ordinary differential equations and semi-discretized time-dependent partial differential equations show that VM improves accuracy over trajectory-based objectives, while avoiding both the cost of simulation and the instabilities of long rollouts.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Velocity Matching, a simulation-free training objective for learning continuous-time nonlinear dynamics that avoids backpropagating through rollouts. It reports better accuracy than trajectory-based objectives on ODEs and semi-discretized PDEs while avoiding simulation cost and long-rollout instability.
AI.motivation: Trajectory-based objectives degenerate as the rollout horizon grows, and the numerical scheme biases the learned dynamics by constraining the learned Jacobian spectrum to the scheme's stability region.
AI.method: Velocity Matching uses piecewise-linear interpolation and stochastic collocation to approximate the velocity population risk to second order in the sampling step, with a bias-variance analysis that relates it to the residual of an A-stable continuous-stage Runge-Kutta scheme and implicitly matches Jacobian action along observed trajectories.
AI.result: Numerical experiments on nonlinear ODEs and semi-discretized time-dependent PDEs show that VM improves accuracy over trajectory-based objectives while avoiding simulation cost and long-rollout instability; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Learning velocity fields directly, with stability and universal approximation guarantees, offers an accurate and simulation-free alternative to trajectory-based training of learned dynamics.

title: Compositional Self-Improvement: Promises and Pitfalls
summary: Although self-improvement is becoming increasingly important as tasks become more complex, models struggle to generate reliable supervision for harder, out-of-distribution instances. One way to address this challenge is to exploit compositional structure: models often solve simpler subproblems more reliably than full problems, so their subproblem predictions can be composed into supervision for harder ones. We systematically study when this kind of composed supervision supports self-improvement and when it fails. Our controlled experiments identify three failure modes: unreliable subproblem predictions, errors introduced by composition, and limited supervision coverage. Beyond controlled settings, these findings carry over to more realistic coding and reasoning tasks: composed labels are more accurate than direct self-generated labels and improve performance even on compositions longer than those seen during training, while the failure modes remain visible. Further, although these failure modes often keep compositional self-improvement from fully succeeding on its own, a short SFT warmup with compositional self-improvement can bootstrap reinforcement learning on tasks that require composing skills the model already has, particularly when direct exploration rarely succeeds. Together, these findings characterize when compositional self-improvement can provide sufficiently reliable supervision to expand model capabilities.

AI.tldr: The paper studies when compositional self-improvement, which composes subproblem predictions into supervision for harder tasks, supports or fails to support model self-improvement. It reports that composed labels are more accurate than direct self-labels and that a short SFT warmup can bootstrap reinforcement learning on compositional tasks.
AI.motivation: Models struggle to produce reliable supervision for harder, out-of-distribution instances, while they solve simpler subproblems more reliably, but when composed supervision works has not been characterized.
AI.method: Controlled experiments identify three failure modes (unreliable subproblem predictions, errors introduced by composition, and limited supervision coverage), and the findings are checked on coding and reasoning tasks, including combining an SFT warmup with compositional self-improvement before reinforcement learning.
AI.result: On realistic coding and reasoning tasks, composed labels are more accurate than direct self-generated labels and improve performance even on compositions longer than those in training, while the failure modes remain visible; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Compositional self-improvement can supply sufficiently reliable supervision to expand capabilities in some regimes, especially when direct exploration rarely succeeds.

title: Stochastic learning flow: moment equations for stochastic gradient descent at finite step size
summary: Analytical theories of learning in deep networks often assume gradient flow, discarding the finite step size and batch noise of stochastic gradient descent (SGD). Starting from the discrete update, we derive continuous-time equations for the mean and covariance of the parameter distribution under a Gaussian closure for a general stochastic learning, to first order in the learning rate $\eta$. Applying these stochastic learning flow (SLF) equations to SGD, we show that the mean descends an effective loss regularized by the covariance and loss curvature, while the covariance, unlike in stochastic differential equation approximations, becomes unstable at curvature $2/\eta$. In SGD ensembles of linear and nonlinear networks, SLF predicts learning curves and mean trajectories more accurately than gradient flow and captures the covariance dynamics, failing where the parameter distribution becomes strongly non-Gaussian. In the full-batch limit, the edge of stability corresponds to a stationary point of the coupled sharpness-covariance dynamics, recovering self-stabilization and central flow, and batch-to-batch curvature fluctuations lower this threshold under SGD.

AI.tldr: The paper derives moment equations for SGD at finite step size, giving continuous-time flows for the mean and covariance of the parameter distribution. It reports that the mean follows an effective loss regularized by covariance and curvature, and that the covariance becomes unstable at curvature 2/eta, unlike gradient flow or SDE approximations.
AI.motivation: Analytical theories of deep-network learning usually assume gradient flow and discard the finite step size and batch noise of SGD, which matter in practice.
AI.method: Starting from the discrete SGD update, the authors derive continuous-time equations for the mean and covariance of the parameters under a Gaussian closure, to first order in the learning rate eta, and analyse the resulting stochastic learning flow.
AI.result: In SGD ensembles of linear and nonlinear networks, the stochastic learning flow predicts learning curves and mean trajectories more accurately than gradient flow and captures covariance dynamics, failing where the parameter distribution becomes strongly non-Gaussian; in the full-batch limit it recovers self-stabilization and central flow.
AI.conclusion: Finite-step-size moment equations explain how batch noise lowers the edge-of-stability threshold under SGD, improving on gradient-flow theories of learning dynamics.

title: Ensemble Classification and Cancer-Specific Gene Signatures from Quality-Aware Hybrid Gene Selection in TCGA RNA-Seq data
comment: 17 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables and 1 supplementary file
summary: Gene-expression classifiers of cancer type are usually developed and validated within one cohort using random splits. Starting from a quality-aware hybrid Boruta selector from earlier work, we developed and evaluated ensemble classifiers and cancer-specific gene signatures. Using 10,469 TCGA tumours of 33 types, we compared five learners and three ensembles under decision rules fixed in advance, reran the selection in site-grouped cross-validation, transferred a breast-cancer subtype panel to 3273 tumours of the independent SCAN-B cohort, and built five-gene stage~I tumour versus adjacent-normal panels for nine cancer types. Logistic regression (LR) was the most accurate and best-calibrated single learner (balanced accuracy 0.943 on the locked test set). Stacking added at most 0.006 with 1000 genes but improved on LR in every fold with a minimal 100-gene panel; a hierarchical model did not reduce within-group confusion. Site-grouped validation lowered balanced accuracy by 0.027, almost entirely in colon and rectal cancer (0.008 without them and the untestable LAML). On SCAN-B, the subtype panel reached 0.855, close to the 50 PAM50 genes (0.876). Stage~I panels reached ROC AUC >= 0.99 in held-out patients and detected most later-stage tumours. Ensembles help most with a minimal panel; with 1000 genes, a calibrated linear model suffices.

AI.tldr: The paper develops ensemble classifiers and cancer-specific gene signatures from a quality-aware hybrid Boruta gene selector, using 10,469 TCGA tumours of 33 types. It reports that logistic regression is the most accurate single learner and that ensembles help mainly with minimal gene panels.
AI.motivation: Gene-expression cancer classifiers are usually developed and validated within one cohort using random splits, which may overstate their generalization.
AI.method: Five learners and three ensembles are compared under pre-set decision rules, selection is rerun in site-grouped cross-validation, a breast-cancer subtype panel is transferred to 3273 SCAN-B tumours, and five-gene stage I tumour-versus-normal panels are built for nine cancer types.
AI.result: Logistic regression reaches balanced accuracy 0.943 on the locked test set; stacking adds at most 0.006 with 1000 genes but improves on LR in every fold with a 100-gene panel; site-grouped validation lowers balanced accuracy by 0.027; on SCAN-B the subtype panel reaches 0.855 versus 0.876 for 50 PAM50 genes; stage I panels reach ROC AUC of at least 0.99 in held-out patients.
AI.conclusion: With 1000 genes a calibrated linear model suffices, while ensembles matter most for minimal gene panels.

title: Integer-Exact Microscaling: Running MXFP4 Language Models on INT8 Matrix Units
comment: 22 pages, 3 figures, 13 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: On hardware whose fastest matrix datapath is INT8$\times$INT8, such as the Neural Accelerators of Apple's M5 GPUs, 4-bit weights must become INT8 operands. Existing MXFP4 kernels already map FP4 (E2M1) values to integers by doubling them, but apply every 32-element block scale inside the reduction. We show when no per-block work is needed: a row of MXFP4 weights is exactly one INT8 vector times one power-of-two scale if its block exponents span at most three, so a linear layer becomes a single INT8 GEMM with one rescale per output. Enforcing the condition adds at most 1/16 of a row's largest rounding error to the blocks it changes, and real weights already satisfy it: 97.9-99.97% of rows across seven models, including 99.93% of the 95M rows of a 125B-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next. The resulting spread-constrained MXFP4 files stay standard MXFP4. With integer instead of power-of-two block multipliers, an integer-exact format (16-wide blocks, multipliers 1..10, 4.26 bits) runs as one exact INT8 GEMM and is more accurate than NVFP4 (4.5 bits) with its standard scale rule on five small models, within 0.06 perplexity of NVFP4 with scale search. On Qwen3.8-Flash-Next's routed experts with INT8 activations it is as close to the FP8 model as NVFP4 with scale search (KL divergence 0.0557 vs. 0.0553) and closer than MLX's MXFP4 and affine INT4; with every matrix quantized it solves 94.8% of GSM8K vs. 91.0% for MLX's MXFP4. Quantizing only the 74k routed expert matrices (96% of the parameters) to either of our formats with INT8 activations costs at most 0.2% perplexity. A complete W4A8 system on the M5 produces outputs bit-identical to the quantized reference; prefill is 1.34-1.74x faster than MLX on a dense model, 1.10-1.57x on two MoE models up to 35B parameters and 1.22-1.29x on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, where shared non-GEMM work bounds the gain.

AI.tldr: The paper shows how MXFP4 language-model weights can be converted to INT8 operands so that a linear layer runs as one exact INT8 GEMM per row, targeting Apple M5 Neural Accelerators. It reports prefill 1.10 to 1.74 times faster than MLX across dense and MoE models.
AI.motivation: On hardware whose fastest matrix datapath is INT8 by INT8, 4-bit MXFP4 weights must be converted, but existing kernels apply every 32-element block scale inside the reduction, adding per-block work.
AI.method: The paper proves that a row of MXFP4 weights equals one INT8 vector times one power-of-two scale when its block exponents span at most three, and enforces this spread constraint on weights, which stay standard MXFP4; an integer-exact 16-wide block format with multipliers 1 to 10 at 4.26 bits is also proposed.
AI.result: Real weights satisfy the condition for 97.9 to 99.97% of rows across seven models; the integer-exact format is more accurate than NVFP4 (4.5 bits) on five small models; on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with INT8 activations it has KL divergence 0.0557 versus 0.0553 for NVFP4 with scale search, and solves 94.8% of GSM8K versus 91.0% for MLX MXFP4; the complete W4A8 system is bit-identical to the quantized reference and gives prefill 1.34 to 1.74 times faster than MLX on a dense model and 1.10 to 1.57 times on MoE models.
AI.conclusion: Spread-constrained MXFP4 allows exact INT8 GEMM with a single rescale per output, making 4-bit inference efficient on INT8-native matrix units with little accuracy cost.

title: VoirDire: Counterfactual Calibration for Reliable LLM-as-a-Judge Aggregation
summary: LLM-as-a-judge systems often aggregate multiple judges to improve evaluation reliability. However, judge agreement can reflect shared biases toward verbosity, formatting, or fluency rather than the intended evaluation target. Addressing these shared biases is challenging because observational judge outputs alone cannot distinguish agreement driven by target quality from agreement driven by nuisance attributes. We introduce VoirDire, an intervention-calibrated aggregation method for LLM-judge panels. VoirDire applies controlled interventions that vary specified surface attributes while aiming to preserve the evaluation target; it then uses paired changes in judge scores to identify nuisance-sensitive directions. It attenuates these directions and selects aggregation weights that retain variation across items while penalizing sensitivity to the interventions, making the final consensus less dependent on superficial features. We show theoretically that observational judge outputs alone cannot identify which shared direction is target-relevant, while paired interventions provide the contrast needed to identify nuisance-sensitive variation. We evaluate VoirDire on 12 datasets spanning continuous scoring, binary classification, and pairwise preference. Compared with the existing LLM-judge aggregation baselines, VoirDire reduces MAE by up to 26.8% on continuous-score tasks and improves accuracy by up to 5.3 percentage points on binary and preference tasks. These findings suggest that counterfactual interventions provide an additional means of improving the reliability and controllability of LLM-based evaluation beyond merely relying on observed judge agreement.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes VoirDire, an aggregation method for LLM-as-a-judge panels that uses paired interventions on surface attributes to down-weight shared nuisance biases such as verbosity. It reports up to 26.8% lower MAE on continuous-score tasks and up to 5.3 points higher accuracy on binary and preference tasks across 12 datasets.
AI.motivation: Judges can agree because of shared biases toward verbosity, formatting or fluency rather than target quality, and observational judge outputs alone cannot distinguish these cases.
AI.method: Controlled interventions vary specified surface attributes while aiming to preserve the target; paired changes in judge scores identify nuisance-sensitive directions, which are attenuated, and aggregation weights are chosen to retain item variation while penalizing sensitivity to interventions.
AI.result: Compared with existing LLM-judge aggregation baselines on 12 datasets spanning continuous scoring, binary classification and pairwise preference, VoirDire reduces MAE by up to 26.8% on continuous-score tasks and improves accuracy by up to 5.3 percentage points on binary and preference tasks.
AI.conclusion: Counterfactual interventions give a means, beyond observed agreement, to make LLM-based evaluation more reliable and controllable.

title: Where Does EEG Help Wearable Freezing of Gait Detection?
summary: Freezing of gait (FoG) detectors built on inertial measurement units (IMUs) are accurate while the legs move, but they become unreliable when the legs are nearly still, which is exactly when akinetic freezing, voluntary stopping, and standing must be told apart. Electroencephalography (EEG) captures motor-planning activity that leg sensors cannot, but EEG is impractical for daily use. We ask where EEG helps: as an input at inference time, or only during pretraining, so that the deployed detector still needs only IMUs. We assemble a pretraining corpus of synchronized EEG and IMU recordings (5 datasets, 184 people, 94 hours) and compare six settings that differ only in the modalities used for pretraining and as model input, each with tuned hyperparameters and five independent pretraining runs. On the BXHC FoG dataset (leave-one-patient-out, 10 patients with FoG), adding EEG as input raises FoG F1 from 0.663 to 0.740 (9 of 10 patients improve), and the gain in ranking performance is confined to the quartile of windows with the least leg movement (AUROC +0.063). Pretraining the IMU encoder jointly with EEG improves an IMU-only detector both within the cohort (FoG F1 0.663 to 0.705) and when it is trained on a small cohort and tested on another (FoG F1 +0.083, all 10 test patients improve). Repeating the study with PD-only and healthy-only pretraining corpora, each with its own hyperparameter search, shows that IMU-based detection is robust to the corpus, whereas the benefit of aligning EEG with IMU requires both. Cross-cohort analysis further shows that detectors trained without annotated voluntary stops classify nearly all stops as freezing. Finally, on PD versus non-PD classification in three external datasets, joint EEG+IMU pretraining improves PD detection from walking EEG over EEG-only pretraining (AUROC 0.750 vs. 0.683), while IMU-based detection does not depend on the pretraining.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether EEG helps wearable freezing-of-gait detection, finding that EEG as an inference-time input or as joint pretraining signal improves IMU-based detection, with the gains concentrated in windows of little leg movement. It reports FoG F1 rising from 0.663 to 0.740 with EEG input on the BXHC dataset.
AI.motivation: IMU-based freezing-of-gait detectors become unreliable when the legs are nearly still, which is exactly when akinetic freezing, voluntary stopping and standing must be distinguished, and EEG could help but is impractical for daily use.
AI.method: A corpus of synchronized EEG and IMU recordings (5 datasets, 184 people, 94 hours) is used to compare six settings that differ in pretraining modalities and model input, each with tuned hyperparameters and five independent pretraining runs, evaluated leave-one-patient-out.
AI.result: On BXHC with 10 FoG patients, adding EEG as input raises FoG F1 from 0.663 to 0.740, improving 9 of 10 patients, with the AUROC gain confined to the least-movement quartile (+0.063); joint EEG and IMU pretraining raises IMU-only F1 from 0.663 to 0.705 and improves cross-cohort F1 by 0.083; on PD versus non-PD classification in three external datasets, joint pretraining raises AUROC from 0.683 to 0.750.
AI.conclusion: EEG is most useful during pretraining, with joint EEG and IMU pretraining producing an IMU-only detector that stays deployable, while EEG at inference adds accuracy only in low-movement windows.

title: Beyond Blackwell: Constrained Data Processing Inequalities
summary: We study the comparison of statistical experiments from a decision-theoretic standpoint, working with Markov transitions as basis-free linear maps on dual spaces. Our starting observation is that the data-processing inequality, that adding noise to an experiment cannot lower its Bayes risk, is the functoriality of fibrewise minimisation over a presheaf of decision rules: the rules available after an experiment form a presheaf, garbling acts on it by precomposition, and a risk functional is a natural transformation from it to the ordered reals. The argument refers to neither probabilities nor expected values, and it survives replacing the decision presheaf by a sub-presheaf of admissible rules. Any constraint imposed on the strategy that a rule induces fairness, unbiasedness, is automatically of this form, and so yields a data-processing inequality with no counterpart in the unconstrained Blackwell theory. Our main result is their quantitative companion. For constraints closed under post-processing we define a constrained deficiency and prove a constrained randomization theorem: one experiment dominates another on every admissible decision problem exactly when the constrained deficiency is small. The classical theorem is the case of no constraint, where the identity is itself an admissible rule; in general it is not, and the constrained deficiency is an optimisation over the coarsenings of an experiment that render it compliant. Specialising to equalized odds, we exhibit a pair of experiments that unconstrained Bayes risk identifies at a given loss and prior but that the constrained risk separates, giving a one-line certificate of Blackwell-incomparability. We work throughout with finite sets.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a constrained data-processing inequality and a constrained randomization theorem for statistical experiments under decision-rule constraints such as fairness or unbiasedness, using a presheaf view of decision rules. It shows that equalized-odds-constrained risk separates experiments that unconstrained Bayes risk cannot distinguish.
AI.motivation: Classical Blackwell comparison of experiments does not cover constraints on decision rules, such as fairness or unbiasedness, and the constrained setting is not known to obey a data-processing inequality.
AI.method: Markov transitions are treated as basis-free linear maps on dual spaces, the decision rules form a presheaf that garbling acts on by precomposition, and for constraints closed under post-processing a constrained deficiency is defined as an optimisation over coarsenings of an experiment.
AI.result: The paper proves a constrained randomization theorem for finite sets: one experiment dominates another on every admissible decision problem exactly when the constrained deficiency is small; for equalized odds it exhibits a pair of experiments that unconstrained Bayes risk cannot separate but constrained risk does.
AI.conclusion: Constraints on decision rules yield their own data-processing inequalities and a quantitative Blackwell theory that is strictly richer than the unconstrained case.

title: Efficient and Scalable Multi-View Masked Autoencoder for Heterogeneous Graph Self-Supervised Learning
comment: Accepted in IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems
summary: Recent years have witnessed the flourishing of self-supervised learning on heterogeneous graphs, e.g., masked autoencoder-based methods. However, existing methods suffer from three issues, including the prohibitive computational cost of constructing meta-path-induced subgraphs, the limitations of uniform random masking, and the suboptimal objective of reconstructing potentially noisy or uninformative original node features. To address these issues, we propose the Multi-View Masked Auto Encoder (MVMAE), a novel, efficient, and scalable framework for heterogeneous graph self-supervised learning. First, MVMAE introduces a novel multi-view mask-then-reconstruct strategy. Instead of masking individual nodes or features, MVMAE randomly masks entire meta-path views and guides the model to reconstruct their representations from remaining visible views. This approach shifts the learning objective to a high-level and semantic task, providing a more robust and informative supervisory signal that is effective even when initial node features are absent or flawed. Then, to handle the computational demands, MVMAE employs an efficient offline aggregation mechanism that pre-computes and reuses representations for each meta-path view, completely avoiding the costly construction of meta-path-induced subgraphs. Next, to fuse the representations of each view, MVMAE uses a Transformer-based multi-view fusion encoder to capture the complex correlations between views, and a deliberately simple MLP decoder to compel the encoder to learn highly expressive and robust node representations. Extensive experiments on six real-world datasets, including three large-scale graphs, demonstrate that MVMAE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art self-supervised and even semi-supervised baselines, confirming its superior effectiveness and scalability. Our source code is released at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MVMAE, a masked autoencoder for heterogeneous graphs that masks entire meta-path views and reconstructs them from the remaining views, avoiding costly meta-path subgraph construction. It reports consistent gains over self-supervised and some semi-supervised baselines on six datasets, including three large graphs.
AI.motivation: Existing heterogeneous-graph masked autoencoders have prohibitive cost for building meta-path-induced subgraphs, uniform random masking is limited, and reconstructing noisy node features gives a weak objective.
AI.method: Entire meta-path views are randomly masked and their representations are reconstructed from visible views; representations are precomputed offline per meta-path, fused by a Transformer-based multi-view encoder, and decoded by a simple MLP.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on six real-world datasets, including three large-scale graphs, show that MVMAE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art self-supervised and some semi-supervised baselines; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Masking at the level of semantic meta-path views gives an efficient and scalable self-supervised objective that remains effective when node features are absent or flawed.

title: When Does Spatial Cooperation Help? Contamination Regimes in Decentralized Online Spectrum Anomaly Learning
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Extended version of a paper accepted to IEEE MILCOM 2026, Workshop S4: Smart Systems for Signal Intelligence, Sensing, and Electromagnetic Spectrum Operations, including the proofs omitted from the conference version
summary: Learning-based spectrum monitors adapt online to benign propagation changes, but persistent rogue transmissions can gradually become incorporated into the learned background. Spatially distributed receivers provide additional evidence for detecting such anomalies, while decentralized model mixing can also spread contamination to receivers with clean measurements. We study this tradeoff using a decentralized online learner with sample gating and model sharing. We show that, without defenses, contamination propagation is governed by the occupancy rate and is independent of cross-receiver correlation. In contrast, the benefit of spatial fusion depends strongly on correlation and the detector operating point, so cooperation can either improve or degrade detection. We also show that fragmented transmissions can evade gating based on temporally smoothed statistics. Combining smoothed and per-sample gating substantially improves robustness to such intermittent contamination.

AI.tldr: The paper analyses when spatial cooperation among receivers helps or hurts online anomaly detection of rogue transmissions in spectrum monitoring. It shows that contamination spread depends on occupancy rate rather than cross-receiver correlation, and that combining smoothed and per-sample gating improves robustness.
AI.motivation: Online learned spectrum monitors can gradually absorb persistent rogue transmissions into their background model, and decentralized model mixing can spread that contamination to clean receivers.
AI.method: A decentralized online learner with sample gating and model sharing is analysed, establishing the effect of occupancy rate and cross-receiver correlation on contamination propagation and on the benefit of spatial fusion, and testing gating based on temporally smoothed statistics combined with per-sample gating.
AI.result: Without defenses contamination propagation is governed by occupancy rate and is independent of cross-receiver correlation; spatial fusion can improve or degrade detection depending on correlation and operating point; fragmented transmissions can evade smoothed-statistic gating, and combining smoothed and per-sample gating substantially improves robustness; the abstract gives no numbers.
AI.conclusion: Cooperation among receivers is not uniformly beneficial, and robust decentralized spectrum monitoring needs combined gating to resist intermittent contamination.

title: From Weeks to Hours: Fast and Principled SFT Data Generation for Reasoning LLMs
summary: Reasoning-oriented post-training enables large language models (LLMs) to solve complex tasks via multi-step inference. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on high-quality reasoning traces is a particularly efficient approach, but its effectiveness depends critically on careful data curation. Existing pipelines rely on a costly generate-then-filter paradigm: large pools of long reasoning traces are produced by multiple teacher models and subsequently filtered for difficulty and diversity using additional LLMs, often requiring weeks of computation. In this work, we propose SFTProbe, a fundamentally different approach that bypasses this pipeline by directly predicting the quality of reasoning data. We show that a brief LoRA-based adaptation, combined with evaluating loss on only 5% of each reasoning trace, suffices to estimate both difficulty and diversity. SFTProbe is grounded in a geometric view of post-training, where pretrained LLMs lie in a low-rank, anisotropic loss basin. By probing this basin via low-rank perturbations, we construct compact loss signatures whose clustering captures diversity, while loss at curvature inflection points provides a robust proxy for difficulty. We also provide a simple criterion for teacher selection. Empirically, our approach reduces data curation time from weeks to hours while maintaining or improving performance. Remarkably, on mathematical reasoning, 5k generated examples match the highly filtered 89k-example in OpenThoughts-Math dataset, and 7.5k generated examples outperforms it by 2.5% in accuracy. We further introduce a high-quality physics reasoning dataset, and use it to train a model that outperforms an IPhO 2025 silver-medal-winning model. The code and the dataset are released at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SFTProbe, which selects SFT reasoning data by directly predicting difficulty and diversity from a brief LoRA adaptation and loss on 5% of each trace, replacing costly generate-then-filter pipelines. It reports that 5k generated examples match the 89k-example OpenThoughts-Math dataset on math reasoning and that a 7.5k set outperforms it by 2.5% in accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing SFT data pipelines generate large pools of long reasoning traces with several teacher models and then filter them with additional LLMs, which can take weeks of computation.
AI.method: A brief LoRA adaptation is trained and loss is evaluated on only 5% of each reasoning trace; clustering of low-rank loss signatures captures diversity, and loss at curvature inflection points serves as a difficulty proxy, guided by a geometric view of a low-rank anisotropic loss basin and a simple teacher-selection criterion.
AI.result: On mathematical reasoning, 5k generated examples match the highly filtered 89k-example OpenThoughts-Math dataset and 7.5k examples outperform it by 2.5% in accuracy; a physics reasoning dataset is also released and used to train a model that outperforms an IPhO 2025 silver-medal-winning model.
AI.conclusion: Predicting data quality directly from loss geometry cuts curation time from weeks to hours while maintaining or improving reasoning performance.

title: TabAbax: A Tabular Foundation Model Technical Report
summary: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) enable in-context prediction on unseen tabular datasets without task-specific training. Mechanistic work has shown that increasing the depth of the ICL Transformer yields weak gains, leaving the main headroom for gains in the synthetic pretraining prior and column-row encoder upstream of the ICL backbone. We introduce TabAbax, a TFM built on TabICLv2 that focuses all modifications on these two upstream components. On the prior side, we further improve the quality and complexity of the synthetic pretraining prior. On the encoder side, a two-pass column-row stack strengthens cross-feature interactions before row compression, using learned Fourier scalar encoding from TabFM and Causilo.
