AI.result: The solution relates training error and generalization error to the curvatures of the empirical risk landscape, showing how memorization and generalization emerge during learning. The free energy predicts the training and generalization errors in the long-time limit of the learning dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The work adds a learning-dynamics perspective on the mechanism of in-context learning within this analyzed linear-attention setting.

title: MarkovTS: Pretrained State-Transition Representations for Zero-Shot Time Series Generation
summary: Across heterogeneous real-world domains, time-series generation supports simulation, model development, and data augmentation by generating sequences that preserve target-domain statistics and temporal dependencies when real observations are scarce or costly. However, existing methods predominantly address in-domain generation, limiting their reuse in unseen domains. We study reference-conditioned zero-shot time series generation: target domains are unseen during pretraining, generation uses a single target-domain reference sequence, and no model parameters are updated. MarkovTS characterizes sequence evolution through local morphologies and their ordered transitions at multiple temporal scales. Its pretrained encoder quantizes normalized time-series patches into multiscale morphological states with a state codebook, while a transition codebook encodes contextual transitions between adjacent intervals. These transferable state-transition representations condition a pretrained flow-matching model. At generation, the frozen model combines a reference-derived condition with independent Gaussian noise to produce stochastic samples that retain the reference's temporal organization. Across 12 unseen target datasets, MarkovTS outperforms strong baselines in most distributional comparisons and generates diverse, reference-consistent sequences. As downstream augmentation, its samples yield overall gains across forecasting, classification, and anomaly detection benchmarks and diverse model families. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes MarkovTS, which uses pretrained state-transition representations to condition a frozen flow-matching model, generating time series for unseen domains from a single reference sequence without parameter updates.
AI.motivation: Existing time-series generation methods mostly address in-domain generation, which limits their reuse in unseen domains where real observations are scarce or costly.
AI.method: A pretrained encoder quantizes normalized patches into multiscale morphological states with a state codebook, and a transition codebook encodes transitions between adjacent intervals; these representations condition a pretrained flow-matching model that combines a reference-derived condition with Gaussian noise at generation time.
AI.result: Across 12 unseen target datasets, MarkovTS outperforms strong baselines in most distributional comparisons and generates diverse, reference-consistent sequences. As downstream augmentation, its samples yield overall gains across forecasting, classification and anomaly detection benchmarks and diverse model families.
AI.conclusion: Transferable state-transition representations enable zero-shot, reference-conditioned generation that also helps downstream tasks as data augmentation.

title: HieraNTP: Structured Risk Representations for Time-Series Anomaly Detection via Hierarchical Next-Token Prediction
summary: Time-series anomaly detection commonly converts deviations from learned temporal regularities into anomaly scores. This practice can conflate violations of temporal regularity with task-specific anomaly judgments: the same deviation may be anomalous under one task definition and benign under another. Aggregating heterogeneous deviations into a single score before task-specific adaptation can obscure the evidence needed to distinguish these cases. We introduce HieraNTP, a Hierarchical Next-Token Prediction framework that separates self-supervised predictive modeling from task-specific risk interpretation. HieraNTP pretrains a hierarchical tokenizer and a causal next-token predictor to capture temporal regularities at multiple scales. It then organizes prediction discrepancies into a structured risk representation, preserving complementary evidence across temporal scales in token, local-statistic, and observation spaces. A task-adaptive detector uses anomaly labels to select and combine this evidence for the target task. Across anomaly detection benchmarks, HieraNTP improves VUS-PR by 12.0% on TSB-AD-U and 15.5% on TSB-AD-M relative to the strongest baselines, and achieves the highest composite score on both TAB tracks, with controlled comparisons supporting the value of retaining distinct evidence. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes HieraNTP, a hierarchical next-token prediction framework for time-series anomaly detection that keeps structured risk evidence across temporal scales, letting a task-adaptive detector combine it using anomaly labels.
AI.motivation: Aggregating heterogeneous prediction deviations into a single anomaly score conflates violations of temporal regularity with task-specific anomaly judgments and can obscure the evidence needed to distinguish them.
AI.method: A hierarchical tokenizer and a causal next-token predictor are pretrained self-supervised; prediction discrepancies are then organized into a structured risk representation across token, local-statistic and observation spaces, and a task-adaptive detector uses anomaly labels to select and combine this evidence.
AI.result: HieraNTP improves VUS-PR by 12.0% on TSB-AD-U and 15.5% on TSB-AD-M relative to the strongest baselines, and achieves the highest composite score on both TAB tracks.
AI.conclusion: Retaining distinct evidence across temporal scales before task-specific adaptation is valuable for time-series anomaly detection.

title: ISBC: Interpretable Sparse Binary Coding of Pretrained Text Embeddings
summary: Pretrained text embeddings encode semantic structure in high-dimensional continuous spaces whose coordinates are difficult to interpret. We introduce Interpretable Sparse Binary Coding (ISBC), which learns a small set of binary dimensions from frozen embeddings without taxonomy labels or downstream outcomes. A trainable encoder and affine decoder combine reconstruction with controls on activity, factor utilization, dependence, and activation uncertainty. Individual bits and their conjunctions select overlapping document groups; complete activation profiles provide finer contexts for conditional comparisons. We evaluate these representations across corpora, backbones, and code configurations through reconstruction, geometry, predictive probes, and document inspection. Empirical cases identify both distinctions within existing categories and shared content across their boundaries. In a mixed-domain corpus, the most frequent profiles predominantly identify source collections, while selected within-source comparisons reveal sentiment and migration contrasts. Selected associations persist in additional documents encoded without refitting. In an engagement application, bits alone improve prediction of log-transformed outcomes over a constant reference, while their combinations identify within-event content contrasts associated with engagement. The results support using binary coordinates and their combinations for empirical interpretation, with complete profiles providing a fine, partly initialization-dependent description rather than a unique discrete taxonomy.

AI.tldr: Introduces Interpretable Sparse Binary Coding (ISBC), which learns a small set of binary dimensions from frozen text embeddings without taxonomy labels or downstream outcomes, so that individual bits and their conjunctions select interpretable document groups.
AI.motivation: Pretrained text embedding coordinates are high-dimensional and difficult to interpret, and the method is designed to need no taxonomy labels or downstream outcomes.
AI.method: A trainable encoder and an affine decoder combine reconstruction with controls on activity, factor utilization, dependence and activation uncertainty; individual bits, their conjunctions and complete activation profiles are used to describe document groups.
AI.result: In a mixed-domain corpus, the most frequent profiles mostly identify source collections, while within-source comparisons reveal sentiment and migration contrasts; selected associations persist in additional documents encoded without refitting. In an engagement application, bits alone improve prediction of log-transformed outcomes over a constant reference.
AI.conclusion: Binary coordinates and their combinations support empirical interpretation, with complete activation profiles giving a fine, partly initialization-dependent description rather than a unique discrete taxonomy.

title: Jet-QSparse: Accelerating Agentic LLM Inference with 4-Bit Sparse Attention
summary: Long-horizon reasoning and agentic workloads strain KV-cache capacity and decode attention throughput. We present Jet-QSparse, a training-free method that combines compact NVFP4 cache storage with native FP4 query-key computation on Blackwell tensor cores. A dense scan scores the full key history and selects 128-token blocks for sparse FP16 value aggregation with FP32 accumulation, preserving higher precision in the output-forming step while enabling contiguous tile loads. Calibrated key centering and at most two BF16 pages per sequence and layer address quantization error; FP8 prefill uses a temporary arena while the persistent cache is packed directly from BF16 activations. Across four hybrid LLMs, a budget of 128 blocks per KV head shows no detected accuracy loss on the evaluated mathematical reasoning, coding, and agentic benchmarks, although some smaller budgets incur losses. With 64 blocks, Qwen3.8-27B achieves a $1.94\times$ end-to-end decode speedup over dense BF16 at 128K context and batch size 16 on one GB300, and the measured Qwen KV pools provide $2.58$-$2.76\times$ BF16's token capacity.

AI.tldr: Proposes Jet-QSparse, a training-free method that speeds up agentic LLM decoding with NVFP4 KV-cache storage, FP4 query-key computation on Blackwell tensor cores, and sparse attention over selected 128-token blocks.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon reasoning and agentic workloads strain KV-cache capacity and decode attention throughput.
AI.method: A dense scan scores the full key history and selects 128-token blocks for sparse FP16 value aggregation with FP32 accumulation; calibrated key centering and at most two BF16 pages per sequence and layer address quantization error, and the persistent cache is packed directly from BF16 activations.
AI.result: Across four hybrid LLMs, a budget of 128 blocks per KV head shows no detected accuracy loss on the evaluated mathematical reasoning, coding and agentic benchmarks, while some smaller budgets incur losses. With 64 blocks, Qwen3.8-27B achieves a 1.94x end-to-end decode speedup over dense BF16 at 128K context and batch size 16 on one GB300, and the measured Qwen KV pools give 2.58-2.76x BF16's token capacity.
AI.conclusion: Compact FP4 caching combined with sparse block selection can speed up long-context agentic decoding without detected accuracy loss at moderate budgets.

title: Hierarchical Asynchronous Federated Learning over Space-Air-Ground Integrated Networks
summary: With the emerging 6G paradigm where AI services operate over decentralized and resource-constrained edge infrastructure, performance of distributed learning algorithms remains a significant challenge. This paper proposes HAFL, a Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite-assisted hierarchical asynchronous Federated Learning (FL) framework, enabling resource-limited terrestrial clients to collaborate via Ground-Satellite Links (GSLs). Within this framework, LEO satellites serve multiple roles: as edge servers aggregating and broadcasting models, as clients accelerating training, and as high-throughput relays managing inter-satellite routing through Inter-Satellite Links (ISLs). Unlike conventional synchronous Jacobian-type updates, HAFL employs asynchronous Gauss-Seidel-type updates to enhance convergence speed. We provide theoretical convergences for convex, strongly convex, and nonconvex objectives, respectively, and formulate optimization problems to jointly determine optimal hyperparameters to minimize global training latency. Evaluations demonstrate that HAFL achieves faster initial convergence and comparable final performance for benchmark DNNs and datasets, offering promising FL systems across remote areas with 6G technologies, but much less global rounds and communication cost.

AI.tldr: Proposes HAFL, a LEO-satellite-assisted hierarchical asynchronous federated learning framework over space-air-ground networks that uses asynchronous Gauss-Seidel-type updates to speed convergence.
AI.motivation: Resource-limited terrestrial clients need to collaborate on federated learning over 6G edge infrastructure, and conventional synchronous Jacobi-type updates converge slowly.
AI.method: LEO satellites act as edge servers that aggregate and broadcast models, as clients that accelerate training, and as high-throughput relays managing inter-satellite routing; optimization problems jointly determine hyperparameters to minimize global training latency.
AI.result: Convergence is established for convex, strongly convex and nonconvex objectives. HAFL achieves faster initial convergence and comparable final performance on benchmark DNNs and datasets, with far fewer global rounds and communication cost.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a promising route to federated learning in remote areas under 6G, with faster early convergence at lower communication cost.

title: ParaBlock++: Communication-Computation Parallel Blockwise Hierarchical Federated Learning
comment: A journal version extended from the published conference version
summary: In the emerging 6G paradigm, where AI-driven services operate over decentralized and resource-constrained infrastructures, the convergence of distributed learning algorithms remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces $\mathrm{ParaBlock}$++, a low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite-assisted hierarchical federated learning (HFL) framework, enabling resource-limited terrestrial clients to collaboratively engage in federated learning (FL) via ground-satellite links (GSLs) supported by LEO satellite megaconstellations. Within this architecture, LEO satellites serve multiple roles: as edge servers aggregating and broadcasting models, as clients accelerating training, and as high-throughput relays managing inter-satellite routing through inter-satellite links (ISLs). Departing from conventional synchronous Jacobian-type updates, $\mathrm{ParaBlock}$++ employs asynchronous BCD-type updates to enhance convergence speed. We provide theoretical convergence guarantees for convex, strongly convex, and non-convex objectives, and formulate optimization problems to determine optimal cluster resource allocation and model partitioning for minimizing global training latency. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that $\mathrm{ParaBlock}$++ achieves faster initial convergence and comparable final performance for deep neural networks (DNNs) such as ResNet-18, offering promising directions for federated learning across geographically remote areas enabled by 6G technologies, but much less global rounds and communication cost.

AI.tldr: Proposes ParaBlock++, a LEO-satellite-assisted hierarchical federated learning framework that uses asynchronous BCD-type (block coordinate descent) updates instead of synchronous Jacobi-type updates to speed convergence.
AI.motivation: In 6G systems where AI services run over decentralized, resource-constrained infrastructure, the convergence of distributed learning algorithms remains a significant challenge.
AI.method: LEO satellites serve as edge servers, clients and relays over ground-satellite and inter-satellite links; optimization problems determine cluster resource allocation and model partitioning to minimize global training latency.
AI.result: Convergence guarantees are given for convex, strongly convex and non-convex objectives. For DNNs such as ResNet-18, ParaBlock++ achieves faster initial convergence and comparable final performance, with far fewer global rounds and communication cost.
AI.conclusion: Asynchronous block updates in satellite-assisted hierarchical federated learning offer faster early convergence for geographically remote clients under 6G.

title: Entropy-Regularized Reinforcement Learning for the Regime-Switching Consumption-Investment Problem
summary: This paper establishes an entropy-regularized reinforcement learning (ERRL) framework for the continuous-time consumption-investment problem under a regime-switching market model with general utility functions. By incorporating randomized exploratory policies and Shannon entropy regularization into the stochastic optimal control formulation, we derive closed-form representations for the optimal exploratory consumption and investment strategies. Specifically, the optimal investment strategy follows a multivariate Gaussian distribution, whereas the optimal consumption strategy takes the form of a Gibbs measure---which specializes to a Gamma distribution under logarithmic utility and a non-standard exponential distribution under power utility. Crucially, our theoretical analysis reveals that the classical deterministic optimal decisions correspond to the mode---rather than the mean---of these exploratory distributions. Furthermore, we establish the convergence of the exploratory value function to its classical unregularized counterpart as the temperature parameter vanishes. For algorithmic design, we develop a continuous-time q-learning framework grounded in a novel continuous-time q-function, prove the policy improvement theorem, and establish martingale characterizations for both on-policy and off-policy learning. We find that parameterizing the actor network based on theoretical distribution families can help accelerate convergence and enhance numerical stability. Furthermore, numerical experiments across regime-switching environments provide empirical support for our theoretical findings, demonstrating stable loss convergence as well as the monotonicity and concavity of the learned value functions.

AI.tldr: Establishes an entropy-regularized reinforcement learning framework for continuous-time consumption-investment under a regime-switching market, deriving closed-form exploratory policies and a continuous-time q-learning algorithm.
AI.motivation: Continuous-time consumption-investment problems under regime switching with general utility functions need an exploration-aware formulation with theoretical support for RL algorithms.
AI.method: Randomized exploratory policies with Shannon entropy regularization are added to the stochastic optimal control formulation; a continuous-time q-function underpins q-learning, with martingale characterizations for on-policy and off-policy learning, and the actor network is parameterized by the theoretical distribution families.
AI.result: The optimal investment strategy is multivariate Gaussian and the optimal consumption strategy is a Gibbs measure, which is Gamma under logarithmic utility and a non-standard exponential under power utility. The classical deterministic decisions correspond to the mode, not the mean, of these exploratory distributions, and the exploratory value function converges to the classical one as the temperature vanishes. Numerical experiments show stable loss convergence and the monotonicity and concavity of learned value functions, and parameterizing the actor on these families accelerates convergence and improves stability.
AI.conclusion: Entropy-regularized exploration yields closed-form optimal policies in this setting, and theory-based actor parameterization helps learning.

title: Infinite Worlds from One Example: What Local Generators Must Share
comment: 35 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables; further results in a supplementary file (47 pages, ancillary)
summary: Seeded noise lets games generate any region of an unbounded world on demand. We ask what such a generator needs when every small window must come from one example, the constraint behind Wave Function Collapse. The difficulty is that local constraints can require agreement over arbitrary distances: in a brick wall, each row keeps its place between the mortar lines. We study local generators, each cell a fixed function of the randomness near it. When the constraints carry a quantity that varies across the example, no generator that applies one rule, ignoring position, to independent randomness at every cell can be both exactly valid and faithful to the example's statistics, however far each cell reads. At radius r, staying faithful forces forbidden windows at a density of at least order 1/r, and a construction attains this order. To vary the quantity between exactly valid worlds, a generator needs randomness shared along its direction. We give a finitely checkable condition under which row types drawn from the seed and the position modulo a fixed period suffice for exact validity without learning. A search over the example's patches certifies these quantities and names the input each needs. Across 52 public examples of Wave Function Collapse and 27 from other implementations, it certifies only examples where a learned generator on independent randomness stays far from valid after repair. Given that input, a neural cellular automaton and a diffusion model become valid on 10 and 8 of the 12 certified examples that receive one, and on none from independent randomness. Valid means at most one forbidden window in a thousand after repair. With octaves of seeded noise elsewhere, the automaton is valid on 45 of the 52 public examples and 21 of the 27 from other implementations, and repair keeps random access.

AI.tldr: Shows that a local generator built from one example cannot be both exactly valid and faithful to the example's statistics if it applies one position-independent rule to independent randomness, and gives a finitely checkable condition under which shared row-type randomness suffices.
AI.motivation: Wave Function Collapse-style generation needs every local window to come from one example, but local constraints can require agreement over arbitrary distances, as in a brick wall where each row keeps its place between mortar lines.
AI.method: Local generators are studied as fixed functions of the randomness near each cell; the sufficient condition uses row types drawn from the seed and the position modulo a fixed period, and a search over the example's patches certifies the quantities and names the input each generator needs.
AI.result: At radius r, faithfulness forces forbidden windows at a density of at least order 1/r, and a construction attains this order. Across 52 public WFC examples and 27 from other implementations, the method certifies only examples where a learned generator on independent randomness stays far from valid after repair. Given the certified input, a neural cellular automaton and a diffusion model become valid on 10 and 8 of the 12 certified examples that receive it, and on none from independent randomness; with octaves of seeded noise elsewhere, the automaton is valid on 45 of 52 public examples and 21 of 27 from other implementations. Valid means at most one forbidden window in a thousand after repair.
AI.conclusion: Varying a constrained quantity between exactly valid worlds requires randomness shared along the generator's direction, and repair keeps random access.

title: Efficient Conformal Calibration for Paired Recommendation Decisions
summary: Risk control can suppress useful changes to a frozen recommendation rule. We study how to recover valid activation from the same observed fractional losses. Two specified internal calibrators can lose efficiency by compressing losses into their sum or clipping auxiliary inverse counts before averaging. We propose Averaged Conformal Risk Calibration, or ACRC, which averages before clipping. A product identity proves expected-risk validity, while pointwise bounds characterize the additional activation. For fixed populations sampled without replacement, we connect activation to signed utility under heterogeneous users and switching constraints. Near the budgets, positive population mean gain and the stated nondegeneracy conditions give positive leading-order utility increments despite sampling dependence. Across six datasets, changing only calibration improves discounted net utility by $0.010226$ over raw and $0.008337$ over RB. A separately frozen Jester confirmation gives $0.011025 \pm 0.001082$ over raw with the rule and filter fixed, using a five-seed approximate 95 percent paired interval. Against information-matched SCoRE selecting risk or reward scores, the mean utility difference is $+0.015934 \pm 0.001440$. These gains use more mean realized risk within the declared budgets. Upstream failures delimit the benefit: efficient calibration releases useful modifications when the proposals themselves have value.

AI.tldr: Proposes Averaged Conformal Risk Calibration (ACRC), which averages fractional losses before clipping to recover valid activation of useful changes to a frozen recommendation rule under risk control.
AI.motivation: Risk control can suppress useful changes to a frozen recommendation rule, and existing internal calibrators lose efficiency either by compressing losses into their sum or by clipping auxiliary inverse counts before averaging.
AI.method: ACRC averages before clipping; a product identity proves expected-risk validity, pointwise bounds characterize the additional activation, and activation is linked to signed utility under heterogeneous users and switching constraints for populations sampled without replacement.
AI.result: Across six datasets, changing only the calibration improves discounted net utility by 0.010226 over raw and 0.008337 over RB. A separately frozen Jester confirmation gives 0.011025 ± 0.001082 over raw (five-seed approximate 95% paired interval), and +0.015934 ± 0.001440 against information-matched SCoRE. The gains use more mean realized risk within the declared budgets.
AI.conclusion: Efficient calibration releases useful modifications when the proposals themselves have value; upstream failures delimit the benefit.

title: On Sparse Graph Limits for Neural Combinatorial Optimization
summary: Graph neural networks are often trained on small graphs and deployed on larger ones, raising the question of which graph information must be preserved for combinatorial optimization values to transfer across sizes. We establish size-transfer guarantees for normalized graph optimization values using finite collections of energy features. For affine objectives, including MAX-CUT, coloring defect, and independent-set density, differences in task value are controlled by discrepancies in normalized scalar energy probes on all bounded-degree graphs. For general Lipschitz objectives, such as those with balance penalties, an additional representation error appears; this error vanishes on hyperfinite graph families but can remain bounded away from zero on expanders. Thus, at fixed degree bound, state space, Lipschitz constant, and target accuracy, a finite energy representation independent of graph size suffices universally for affine tasks and asymptotically for general Lipschitz tasks on hyperfinite families. These results yield prediction guarantees under explicit conditions on encoder accuracy, readout stability, and representation coverage, together with statistical generalization bounds. Theoretically, we prove Shapley-Folkman bounds with sharp parameter dependence, including a dimension-free $\ell_2$ regime, and realize the resulting energy features with a fixed-weight message-passing network using random node initialization on bounded-treewidth graphs. Experiments with exact solvers and trained models test the resulting transfer guarantees.

AI.tldr: Gives size-transfer guarantees for neural combinatorial optimization, showing that a finite set of graph-size-independent energy features suffices for affine tasks such as MAX-CUT, and asymptotically for general Lipschitz tasks on hyperfinite families.
AI.motivation: GNNs trained on small graphs and deployed on larger ones raise the question of which graph information must be preserved for combinatorial optimization values to transfer across sizes.
AI.method: Normalized graph optimization values are controlled by finite collections of energy features, using Shapley-Folkman bounds; a fixed-weight message-passing network with random node initialization realizes these features on bounded-treewidth graphs, and statistical generalization bounds are derived.
AI.result: For affine objectives such as MAX-CUT, coloring defect and independent-set density, task-value differences are controlled by discrepancies in normalized scalar energy probes on all bounded-degree graphs. For general Lipschitz objectives such as those with balance penalties, an additional representation error appears that vanishes on hyperfinite families but can remain bounded away from zero on expanders. Experiments with exact solvers and trained models test the transfer guarantees.
AI.conclusion: At fixed degree bound, state space, Lipschitz constant and target accuracy, a finite energy representation independent of graph size suffices universally for affine tasks and asymptotically for general Lipschitz tasks on hyperfinite families.

title: Synergetic Autonomous Intelligence: Three Axioms for Recursive Semi-Closed Learning
summary: We introduce Synergetic Autonomous Intelligence (SAI), a theory and design program for learning systems that form, preserve, revise, and compose relations while continuing to learn. SAI is built on three axioms: consequential distinctions must not become orphaned (U); identity is determined by future-faithful continuation under a declared contract (I); and unresolved defects are repaired by the least lawful local completion at the lowest admitted grade (L). We model a model, agent, tool, team, or environment boundary as a recursive semi-closed system with a Kernel-Ring representation, a Compile-Open-Participate cycle, and a typed residual comparing actual with claimed continuation. Under explicit finite or affine contracts, we establish relative consistency and conditional non-redundancy of U/I/L, characterize a contract-relative semantic quotient, construct an exact joint stochastic refinement, derive a constrained residual contraction, prove finite-horizon continued-service viability, and give an executed-intervention identification result with an observational-confounding boundary. We define GRC-Close as the generative and repair schema for this contract. The framework also gives finite contracts for action-effect-feedback loop re-entry, partial failure, duplicate-effect idempotency, replay, concurrent delivery, causal uncertainty, and threshold-radix state representation. KREIT, the Kernel-Ring Equilibrium Information Theory layer, treats information as a typed, resource-bounded distinction; the control layer authorizes, executes, audits, and updates actions across cloud-edge-end scales. These results establish a common contract-level vocabulary for representation, relation, memory, action, communication, explanation, coordination, and growth, while marking the assumptions and open boundaries required for later generalization.

AI.tldr: Presents Synergetic Autonomous Intelligence (SAI), a theory and design program for learning systems built on three axioms (U, I, L) and a Kernel-Ring representation, with contract-level results on consistency, viability and identification.
AI.motivation: Learning systems must form, preserve, revise and compose relations while continuing to learn, and the paper aims to give representation, relation, memory, action, communication and coordination a common contract-level vocabulary.
AI.method: The axioms are: consequential distinctions must not become orphaned (U); identity is determined by future-faithful continuation under a declared contract (I); unresolved defects are repaired by the least lawful local completion at the lowest admitted grade (L). Components include a Kernel-Ring representation, a Compile-Open-Participate cycle, a typed residual and GRC-Close, a generative and repair schema.
AI.result: Under explicit finite or affine contracts, the paper establishes relative consistency and conditional non-redundancy of U/I/L, a constrained residual contraction, finite-horizon continued-service viability, and an executed-intervention identification result with an observational-confounding boundary. Finite contracts are given for action-effect-feedback loop re-entry, partial failure, duplicate-effect idempotency, replay, concurrent delivery and causal uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a common vocabulary at the contract level while marking the assumptions and open boundaries needed for later generalization.

title: Change the Funnel, Not Who May Submit: Engineering Peer Review for the Flood
summary: Every reviewer knows the feeling: more papers each cycle, three full reviews for each of them, and a suspicion that near the accept line the outcome is luck. The numbers bear it out. NeurIPS received 30,709 submissions in 2026, more than three times as many as in 2021, and reviewing them took some 184,000 expert hours, or 92 years of researchers' time. Three-quarters of those hours went to papers that were rejected. And when NeurIPS twice had the same papers reviewed by two committees, the second rejected half of what the first accepted. Conferences are responding by limiting who may submit. We simulated that answer, and an alternative, in a model calibrated to the NeurIPS experiments. The limits save little and select no better, and those based on a past acceptance fall mostly on new authors. The alternative changes how papers are judged, spending full reads only where a decision turns on them. In a staged funnel, an automated quality check first turns back papers that are not ready. The rest are ranked by their value, from short summaries, by readers that each submission brings. Only the finalists get a full read, which checks their claims and settles the final ranking. The staged funnel needs a little over half of today's expert hours, accepts 95.5% of papers in the top 3-10% (against 74% today), and makes nearly every top-0.5% paper a spotlight or oral. And because every paper brings its own reader, the funnel keeps pace with the flood.

AI.tldr: Simulates a staged, value-ranked review funnel for conference peer review that needs a little over half of today's expert hours and places more top papers in the accept tiers than current practice.
AI.motivation: Reviewing about 184,000 expert hours of NeurIPS submissions (30,709 in 2026) yields outcomes that look like luck near the accept line, and when two committees reviewed the same papers, the second rejected half of what the first accepted; conferences respond by limiting who may submit.
AI.method: A model calibrated to the NeurIPS experiments compares submission limits with a staged funnel in which an automated quality check first turns back unready papers, the rest are ranked from short summaries by readers each submission brings, and only finalists get a full read that checks claims and settles the final ranking.
AI.result: Submission limits save little and select no better, and those based on past acceptance fall mostly on new authors. The staged funnel needs a little over half of today's expert hours, accepts 95.5% of papers in the top 3-10% (against 74% today), and makes nearly every top-0.5% paper a spotlight or oral.
AI.conclusion: Changing how papers are judged, rather than who may submit, can keep review feasible as submissions grow.

title: Scute: Exact Batched Serving for PEFT Adapters Beyond LoRA
summary: Existing serving systems for large language models batch requests for many different LoRA adapters on one GPU. However, these systems reject adapters from other parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as DoRA, (IA), VeRA and OFT. One solution to this is to convert these adapters to LoRA, but this induces a significant memory and accuracy cost. Instead, we show that, under some modifications, a batched LoRA kernel can serve all of these methods exactly and efficiently. We achieve this by writing each method in one normal form, a LoRA computation with six slots for an adapter's own vectors and matrices. Some slots can merge into an adapter's weights at load time; the others remain live and induce a cost. We give ways to efficiently pay this cost and predict it from a zero-parameter byte model. We package this system, Scute, and build it on top of vLLM. Scute serves all five methods, coming as checkpoints from the Hugging Face PEFT library, in one batch, and it matches that library with a mean error of at most 1.5% of each adapter's effect. Under a burst of requests on an RTX A6000, a mix of these methods takes 5-17% more decode time than the same number of LoRA adapters. Furthermore, using Scute, the same GPU can serve 64 to 1024 (IA) and VeRA adapters at 1.5x to at least 2.5x the request rate of their LoRA conversions.

AI.tldr: Proposes Scute, a batched serving system built on vLLM that serves exactly several PEFT adapter types (DoRA, IA3, VeRA, OFT and LoRA) in one batch by writing each method in a six-slot LoRA normal form.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-adapter serving systems batch only LoRA adapters, and converting other PEFT adapters to LoRA costs significant memory and accuracy.
AI.method: Each method is written in one normal form, a LoRA computation with six slots for the adapter's own vectors and matrices; some slots merge into the weights at load time, while the others stay live and add a cost that is paid efficiently and predicted by a zero-parameter byte model.
AI.result: Scute matches the Hugging Face PEFT library with a mean error of at most 1.5% of each adapter's effect. Under a burst of requests on an RTX A6000, a mix of these methods takes 5-17% more decode time than the same number of LoRA adapters, and the same GPU serves 64 to 1024 IA3 and VeRA adapters at 1.5x to at least 2.5x the request rate of their LoRA conversions.
AI.conclusion: A batched LoRA kernel with a normal form can serve several PEFT methods exactly and efficiently without converting them to LoRA.

title: Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting in Task-Free Federated Continual Forecasting via Two-Tier Replay under Concept Drift
comment: Peer-reviewed and accepted for presentation at the AGCS 2026 conference
summary: Federated time-series forecasting is increasingly important in applications where temporal data are distributed across privacy-sensitive clients, such as environmental monitoring, smart cities, and industrial sensing. A central limitation of current continual-learning protocols is that they usually assume predefined task boundaries, whereas deployed forecasting systems receive an uninterrupted stream and must decide autonomously when adaptation is necessary. This paper addresses catastrophic forgetting in task-free federated forecasting under concept drift. We introduce a drift-aware continual-learning protocol in which each client monitors prediction-window RMSE, calibrates a robust median threshold from the offline base period, and triggers adaptation only after persistent degradation. To mitigate forgetting, we propose a TwoTierReplay mechanism that separates fixed offline representative memory from online memory. The offline tier preserves long-term knowledge learned during the base phase, while the online tier captures recent distributional changes after drift. Experiments on the Beijing Multi-Site Air- Quality dataset with 12 clients, three forecasting targets, and three horizons show that TwoTierReplay achieves the best stability-plasticity score in all nine target-horizon configurations. It improves over the strongest baseline by approximately 11.4%. These results suggest that explicit temporal structuring of replay memory is a practical and effective mechanism for task-free federated continual forecasting.

AI.tldr: Proposes a drift-aware, task-free federated forecasting protocol with TwoTierReplay, which separates fixed offline memory from online memory to mitigate catastrophic forgetting under concept drift.
AI.motivation: Continual-learning protocols usually assume predefined task boundaries, whereas deployed forecasting systems receive uninterrupted streams and must decide autonomously when adaptation is needed.
AI.method: Each client monitors prediction-window RMSE, calibrates a robust median threshold from the offline base period, and triggers adaptation only after persistent degradation; TwoTierReplay keeps a fixed offline representative memory for base-phase knowledge and an online memory for recent post-drift changes.
AI.result: On the Beijing Multi-Site Air-Quality dataset with 12 clients, three forecasting targets and three horizons, TwoTierReplay achieves the best stability-plasticity score in all nine target-horizon configurations, improving over the strongest baseline by about 11.4%.
AI.conclusion: Explicit temporal structuring of replay memory is a practical and effective mechanism for task-free federated continual forecasting.

title: Zero-Gated Cross-Attention
summary: Injecting non-text modalities into frozen language models often introduces early optimization instability, making it difficult to separate architectural gains from transient training dynamics. We introduce Inductively Gated Cross-Attention (IGCA), a zero-initialized cross-attention bridge that preserves pretrained model behavior at initialization while enabling gradual multimodal conditioning. Integrated across six decoder layers of frozen Falcon-40B, open_llama_30b, and Bloom-7b1 backbones (with 40,404,961,288 trainable adapter parameters used during training), IGCA acts as an exact algebraic no-op at initialization with a maximum output discrepancy of 0.00e+00. Over 59,500 training steps on Falcon-40B, the training loss decreases from 3.9403 to 0.0007 (with final ten step losses of [0.0001, 0.0003, 0.0005, 0.0002, 0.0005, 0.0011, 0.0005, 0.0006, 0.0005, 0.0007]). On held-out evaluation, the best gate-on checkpoint achieves a loss of 2.2201 compared to 4.3469 for the gate-off baseline -- a 48.9% reduction (2.1268 nats) -- while average held-out loss improves from 4.3423 to 2.2498 (1.9075 nats) with a mean gate magnitude of $\vert{}\tanh(\alpha)\vert{} = 0.0713$.

AI.tldr: Introduces Inductively Gated Cross-Attention (IGCA), a zero-initialized cross-attention bridge that injects non-text modalities into frozen language models without changing their behaviour at initialization.
AI.motivation: Injecting non-text modalities into frozen language models often causes early optimization instability, which makes architectural gains hard to separate from transient training dynamics.
AI.method: IGCA is integrated across six decoder layers of frozen Falcon-40B, open_llama_30b and Bloom-7b1 backbones, with 40,404,961,288 trainable adapter parameters as stated in the abstract; the gate is zero-initialized, so IGCA is an exact algebraic no-op at initialization.
AI.result: The maximum output discrepancy at initialization is 0.00e+00. Over 59,500 training steps on Falcon-40B, training loss falls from 3.9403 to 0.0007, with the final ten step losses between 0.0001 and 0.0011. On held-out evaluation, the best gate-on checkpoint reaches a loss of 2.2201 against 4.3469 for the gate-off baseline (a 48.9% reduction), and average held-out loss improves from 4.3423 to 2.2498, with mean gate magnitude |tanh(alpha)| of 0.0713.
AI.conclusion: Zero-gated initialization gives stable, gradual multimodal conditioning of frozen language models, with held-out gains reported for this setup.

title: World Models Need Not Be Right to Rank Policies Right: Relative Bounds and Audit Limits
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Accepted as a poster at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on World Models in Physical AI
summary: Selecting a reinforcement-learning (RL) policy usually requires additional environment interaction, while learned world models offer cheap but potentially biased evaluations. This raises two distinct questions: can shared model errors preserve pairwise rankings despite poor absolute values, and do they make a small number of real audits more informative? We derive an exact pairwise simulation identity and a relative bound separating common-mode Bellman residuals from policy-specific error. The analysis motivates RAVEL (Relative Auditing of Value Errors in Learned models), a selective policy tournament whose eliminations use held-out real outcomes. We test 45 SAC, TD3, and PPO policies per task in DMC cheetah-run and walker-walk. At rollout horizon 500, model rankings remain strong (Kendall tau = 0.962 and 0.800), and same-run differential-error ratios are 0.674 and 0.106. Yet mean paired audit-error correlations are only 0.007 and 0.090, and pairing changes standard deviation by -2.5 percent and +1.9 percent. Simultaneous intervals attain 99.98 percent and 99.75 percent coverage, but certify only 13.2 percent and 0 percent of decisions at eight audits. RAVEL improves low-budget walker-walk regret, whereas real-only successive halving is better at the largest budget, rejecting the precommitted twofold efficiency target. Frozen-model optimization lowers real return without increasing predicted return on average. Thus ranking fidelity, useful audit covariance, and upward model exploitation are distinct properties, separated in part by closed-loop trajectory divergence.

AI.tldr: Shows that learned world models can preserve pairwise policy rankings despite poor absolute value estimates, and introduces RAVEL, a selective policy tournament that eliminates policies using held-out real outcomes.
AI.motivation: Selecting an RL policy usually requires environment interaction, while learned world models are cheap but biased; the question is whether shared model errors preserve rankings and whether a few real audits can become more informative.
AI.method: An exact pairwise simulation identity and a relative bound separate common-mode Bellman residuals from policy-specific error; RAVEL uses held-out real outcomes for eliminations. Forty-five SAC, TD3 and PPO policies per task are tested on DMC cheetah-run and walker-walk.
AI.result: At rollout horizon 500, model rankings remain strong (Kendall tau of 0.962 and 0.800). Mean paired audit-error correlations are only 0.007 and 0.090, and simultaneous intervals certify only 13.2% and 0% of decisions at eight audits. RAVEL improves low-budget walker-walk regret, whereas real-only successive halving is better at the largest budget. Frozen-model optimization lowers real return without increasing predicted return on average.
AI.conclusion: Ranking fidelity, useful audit covariance and upward model exploitation are distinct properties, separated in part by closed-loop trajectory divergence.

title: Lightweight Representation Learning for Low Tucker Rank Tensors
summary: Low Tucker rank tensors provide compact representations of multidimensional dependencies, but standard learning pipelines can incur substantial computational and memory overhead from redundant intermediate quantities. We reduce this overhead without modifying the underlying representation objective or parameterization. Our approach combines three complementary components: (i) sequential extraction of only task-required spectral components, avoiding unnecessary full decompositions; (ii) factor-wise multilinear contractions without materializing large Kronecker operators; and (iii) compact latent-state updates without storing full ambient tensor iterates. These components preserve the algebraic operations and learning trajectories of the original algorithms while reducing their computational and memory footprints. Across five low Tucker rank tensor estimators, our implementations match the original trajectories to numerical precision (relative discrepancies of $10^{-16}$ to $10^{-13}$), while reducing per-iteration runtime by up to $3.12\times$ and resident memory by up to $616\times$ ($99.8\%$) on the main order-3 benchmark at $n=100$, with memory reductions exceeding $900\times$ across the full evaluation suite. These results show that substantial computational redundancy can be eliminated from Tucker representation learning without changing the underlying model or learned representation.

AI.tldr: Reduces the computational and memory overhead of learning low Tucker rank tensor representations without changing the objective or parameterization, matching the original learning trajectories to numerical precision.
AI.motivation: Standard pipelines for low Tucker rank tensors incur substantial overhead from redundant intermediate quantities, such as unnecessary full decompositions, large Kronecker operators and full ambient tensor iterates.
AI.method: Three components: sequential extraction of only the task-required spectral components; factor-wise multilinear contractions without materializing large Kronecker operators; and compact latent-state updates that avoid storing full ambient tensor iterates.
AI.result: Across five low Tucker rank tensor estimators, the implementations match the original trajectories to relative discrepancies of 1e-16 to 1e-13. On the main order-3 benchmark at n=100, per-iteration runtime drops by up to 3.12x and resident memory by up to 616x (99.8%), with memory reductions exceeding 900x across the full evaluation suite.
AI.conclusion: Substantial computational redundancy can be removed from Tucker representation learning without changing the underlying model or the learned representation.

title: TRIAGE: Reliability- and Load-Conditioned Escalation for Two-Tier LLM Serving with a Semantic Evidence Judge
summary: Two-tier LLM serving escalates selected requests from a small model to a large one, but prompt-based routers cannot see whether retrieved evidence supports an answer, and they treat the GPU cost of an escalation as constant. We study TRIAGE, which conditions escalation on a post-generation reliability state and on a load-dependent GPU price, and we report both what held and what did not on one A40 serving Qwen2.5-7B and 32B (AWQ) under VLLM. Escalation cost rose 21.9x from 1 to 10 requests/s but showed no monotone dependence on KV-cache headroom, and a pre-registered claim that the reliability state detects corrupted evidence (AUROC>=0.70) was falsified at 0.571, although any prompt-only router scores exactly 0.500 by construction. Post hoc, a semantic evidence judge raised detection to 0.846 (0.926 on never-served items) and predicted wrong small-model answers at AUROC 0.90-0.96 on RGB and three RouterBench model pairs; the resulting cascade stayed within about 3 pp of GPT-4 at 79.5% lower API cost for GPT-3.5->GPT-4, yet fell below random routing for open-model pairs with 2-3x price ratios. End to end, the 7B->32B pair showed only a +2.88 pp held-out gap, so the allocator rightly declined to escalate and the headline is a null that a small pre-launch gate failed to expose.

AI.tldr: Studies TRIAGE, a two-tier LLM serving policy that conditions escalation from a small model to a large one on a post-generation reliability state and a load-dependent GPU price; the pre-registered reliability claim is falsified, while a post-hoc semantic evidence judge performs well.
AI.motivation: Prompt-based routers cannot see whether retrieved evidence supports an answer, and they treat the GPU cost of an escalation as constant.
AI.method: Qwen2.5-7B and 32B (AWQ) are served under vLLM on one A40, with escalation conditioned on a reliability state and a load-dependent GPU price; a semantic evidence judge is added post hoc and evaluated on RGB and three RouterBench model pairs.
AI.result: Escalation cost rose 21.9x from 1 to 10 requests/s with no monotone dependence on KV-cache headroom. The pre-registered claim that the reliability state detects corrupted evidence (AUROC of at least 0.70) was falsified at 0.571. Post hoc, the semantic judge raised detection to 0.846 (0.926 on never-served items) and predicted wrong small-model answers at AUROC 0.90-0.96; the cascade stayed within about 3 pp of GPT-4 at 79.5% lower API cost for GPT-3.5 to GPT-4 but fell below random routing for open-model pairs with 2-3x price ratios. The 7B to 32B pair showed only a +2.88 pp held-out gap.
AI.conclusion: The end-to-end headline is a null result: the allocator rightly declined to escalate, and a small pre-launch gate failed to expose this.

title: Fast and Exact Relative-Position Attention via Structure-Aware Kernels
summary: Relative-position attention mechanisms offer compelling alternatives to RoPE across various transformer architectures, delivering superior performance in domains such as audio. These mechanisms typically modify attention scores by adding content-position or bias-position terms. Unlike RoPE, which encodes position via per-token rotations directly on the queries and keys, relative-position terms generally require pairwise offset-dependent computation or lookups, complicating their integration into fused attention kernels and introducing severe memory, bandwidth, and compute overheads as sequences scale. To address this bottleneck, we propose an exact attention algorithm that incorporates additive relative-position terms into FlashAttention-style tiled computation. Our method (1) uses offset-aware tiling to avoid redundant indexing and memory accesses, (2) computes only the necessary key/query-relation products and reuses them across token pairs in both forward and backward passes, and (3) uses offset-based gradient sharding and aggregation, eliminating atomic contention. We provide a unified, efficient Triton implementation across diverse relative-position attention mechanisms and evaluate it against naive and specialized implementations. For 8K-token sequences, our method speeds up the forward (backward) pass by 1.8-6.4$\times$ (2.0-21$\times$) and reduces peak memory up to 2.9-128$\times$ (1.4-54$\times$) over the strongest baseline for each mechanism, enabling long-context end-to-end transcription that is 1.8$\times$ faster and uses 2.4$\times$ less memory. Our method thus provides a drop-in, hardware-efficient solution for scaling relative-position attention transformers.

AI.tldr: Proposes an exact FlashAttention-style Triton kernel for attention with additive relative-position terms, using offset-aware tiling and offset-based gradient sharding, with large speed and memory gains at 8K tokens.
AI.motivation: Relative-position attention is an alternative to RoPE, but its pairwise offset-dependent terms complicate fused attention kernels and add memory, bandwidth and compute overheads as sequences scale.
AI.method: Offset-aware tiling avoids redundant indexing and memory accesses; only the necessary key/query-relation products are computed and reused across token pairs in both forward and backward passes; offset-based gradient sharding and aggregation eliminate atomic contention. A unified Triton implementation covers diverse relative-position mechanisms.
AI.result: For 8K-token sequences, the forward (backward) pass is 1.8-6.4x (2.0-21x) faster and peak memory is reduced 2.9-128x (1.4-54x) relative to the strongest baseline for each mechanism. On long-context end-to-end transcription, the method is 1.8x faster and uses 2.4x less memory.
AI.conclusion: The method is a drop-in, hardware-efficient solution for scaling relative-position attention transformers.

title: Satisfied, Not Solving: Wireheading of Bounded Homeostatic Rewards in Reinforcement Learning
comment: 33 pages, 5 figures, 11 tables. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Bounded intrinsic rewards are often assumed to be safe from exploitation: if a signal can yield at most a fixed amount, gaming it should not pay. We test this for a homeostatic satiation reward, in which needs build up and relieving them is rewarding, and give the agent a cheap action that resets its needs. In MiniGrid DoorKey-8x8, PPO agents with this action solved 2 of 80 seeds, against 71 of 80 on the same seeds without it; in KeyCorridorS3R1, 0 of 20 against 20 of 20. Their policies stayed near uniform. The reward does not ask for this: a telescoping argument caps any policy's satiation return at the needs' starting drive, and a post-hoc computation shows that, at every growth rate we trained, a solving trajectory beats that cap on all sampled layouts. In DoorKey with advantage normalization on, a satisfaction signal the agent could fill itself was worse than none (11 of 20 solved with task reward alone, 1 of 20 with the tamperable signal), and a per-press cost of 0.1 restored the task in every seed. Farming of positive reward cycles appeared in DoorKey but not persistently in KeyCorridorS3R1. All predictions were pre-registered, and hash-locked from round 3 on; 9 of our 23 hypotheses were not supported, and we report each.

AI.tldr: Shows that a bounded homeostatic satiation reward can still be exploited: PPO agents given a cheap action that resets their needs learn to satisfy the signal rather than solve the task in MiniGrid DoorKey and KeyCorridor.
AI.motivation: Bounded intrinsic rewards are often assumed to be safe from exploitation, and the paper tests this assumption for a homeostatic satiation reward.
AI.method: PPO agents are trained with and without a cheap needs-resetting action on MiniGrid DoorKey-8x8 and KeyCorridorS3R1; a telescoping argument bounds any policy's satiation return, a post-hoc computation checks solving trajectories against that cap, and all predictions were pre-registered and hash-locked from round 3 on.
AI.result: With the action, PPO agents solved 2 of 80 seeds in DoorKey versus 71 of 80 without it, and 0 of 20 versus 20 of 20 in KeyCorridorS3R1; their policies stayed near uniform. In DoorKey with advantage normalization, a tamperable satisfaction signal was worse than none (1 of 20 solved versus 11 of 20 with task reward alone), and a per-press cost of 0.1 restored the task in every seed. Nine of 23 pre-registered hypotheses were not supported.
AI.conclusion: A bounded reward does not guarantee safety from exploitation, and a small per-action cost can restore task solving in these settings.

title: Zeroth-Order Policy Optimization for Scheduling in Queueing Networks
summary: Reinforcement learning in queueing network scheduling presents significant challenges because of the countably infinite state space and the high stochasticity in transitions. In this paper, we propose zeroth-order policy optimization algorithms that are easy to implement and rely solely on estimates of the average cost, a single scalar quantity, without requiring the estimation of value or advantage functions. Our analysis focuses on back-pressure guarded policies and establishes uniform smoothness of the average cost objective with respect to the policy parameters. Building on this property, we establish finite-time convergence guarantees to an $\epsilon$-stationary policy for the proposed algorithms. Numerical experiments on multiple queueing networks, including systems beyond classical exponential service distribution, demonstrate competitive performance, outperforming gradient-based RL methods like PPO and traditional queueing baselines.

AI.tldr: Proposes zeroth-order policy optimization for queueing network scheduling that relies only on estimates of the average cost, with finite-time convergence to an epsilon-stationary policy for back-pressure guarded policies.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning for queueing network scheduling faces a countably infinite state space and highly stochastic transitions, and estimating value or advantage functions is difficult.
AI.method: Zeroth-order policy optimization uses only a scalar estimate of the average cost; uniform smoothness of the average cost with respect to the policy parameters is established for back-pressure guarded policies.
AI.result: Finite-time convergence guarantees to an epsilon-stationary policy are established. On multiple queueing networks, including systems beyond classical exponential service distributions, the method is competitive and outperforms gradient-based RL methods such as PPO and traditional queueing baselines.
AI.conclusion: Zeroth-order optimization offers a simple, provably convergent alternative for scheduling in queueing networks.

title: GraCo: A Unified Toolkit of Graph Coarsening Algorithms and Metrics
summary: Graph coarsening aims to reduce a graph to a smaller one that preserves chosen properties of the original. It is increasingly used to scale graph learning to large graphs, as a non-differentiable step applied once before training. Many coarsening methods have been proposed in recent years, each with its own implementation, notation and evaluation. In this work, we introduce GraCo, a unified toolkit of graph coarsening methods. It relies on a single definition: a coarsening is fixed by a partition of the nodes and by the Laplacian the coarsened graph is consistent with. The coarsened graph, and the reduction and lifting matrices that map signals from the original graph to the coarsened one and back, follow from these two choices. We implement 17 methods from the literature and a random baseline, grouped into five families, with the same notation, inputs and outputs. We also build a collection of metrics from different papers, applicable to any coarsening. We check the implementations on a synthetic stochastic block model, then we report the runtime and peak memory of each method on Cora, PubMed, ogbn-arxiv and ogbn-products. GraCo is open-source and available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Presents GraCo, an open-source unified toolkit that implements 17 graph coarsening methods and a random baseline under one definition based on a node partition and a Laplacian, together with a collection of metrics.
AI.motivation: Graph coarsening methods come with separate implementations, notation and evaluation protocols, which makes them hard to compare.
AI.method: A coarsening is fixed by a partition of the nodes and the Laplacian that the coarsened graph is consistent with, which determine the coarsened graph and the reduction and lifting matrices; the 17 methods in five families share the same notation, inputs and outputs, and metrics from different papers are implemented.
AI.result: The implementations are checked on a synthetic stochastic block model, and runtime and peak memory are reported for each method on Cora, PubMed, ogbn-arxiv and ogbn-products.
AI.conclusion: A single common interface makes coarsening methods and metrics comparable across the literature.

title: A Batched Hartigan's $k$-Means Clustering
comment: To appear in the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Hartigan's $k$-means algorithm has theoretical advantages over the standard Lloyd's variant, which has become synonymous with "$k$-means". Yet, Hartigan's algorithm is far slower in practice due to its inherently sequential calculations. We devise a Batched Hartigan's method that enables vectorized calculation by exploiting the triangle inequality to expose a set of parallel-safe updates and a smaller set of sequential updates. This makes Hartigan's method competitive with Lloyd's in execution speed for the first time.

AI.tldr: Proposes a Batched Hartigan's k-means algorithm that vectorizes Hartigan's method by using the triangle inequality to separate parallel-safe updates from a smaller set of sequential ones, making it competitive with Lloyd's algorithm in execution speed.
AI.motivation: Hartigan's k-means has theoretical advantages over Lloyd's variant, but it is far slower in practice because its calculations are inherently sequential.
AI.method: The triangle inequality exposes a set of parallel-safe updates and a smaller set of sequential updates, which enables vectorized calculation.
AI.result: The abstract claims that Hartigan's method is competitive with Lloyd's in execution speed for the first time; no benchmark figures are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Batched updates make Hartigan's k-means a speed-competitive alternative to Lloyd's algorithm.

title: Mathematical Formulation and Comparative Performance Evaluation of Machine Learning Algorithms for Maize Land Suitability Prediction
summary: Addressing the food needs of a growing population is one of the major challenges of developing countries like Ethiopia. Various policies aimed at increasing food production have been enacted by governments and development partners. Although efforts in this regard have been made, there is still inadequate emphasis on increasing food production through the use of high technology practices. Precision agriculture using technology has been utilized to increase crop yield. Precision agriculture also relies on identifying land for a crop, which is a key factor that affects crop yield. Traditional methods of assessing land suitability for crop production are time-consuming, costly and unreliable. Against this background, the aim of this study was to assess the potential of machine learning (ML) in improving the speed and accuracy of assessing land suitability for maize, a staple crop in Ethiopia, as compared to traditional methods. The study is investigated in three areas (Burie, Shindi and Tilili) in the Amhara region. Data collection was done through the local agriculture offices and survey teams. The data were coded, scaled and balanced. Various feature extraction techniques, which included Univariate Feature Selection(UFS), Recursive Feature Elimination with Cross-Validation(RFECV) and Sequential Feature Selection(SFS), and various classifiers, which were K-nearest neighbor (KNN), gradient boosting (GB),random forest (RF) with mathematical formulations were employed. The best models were constructed through combining GBOOST and SFS and achieved an accuracy of 99.41% and 99.35% for both precision and recall. Our results showed that using machine learning is a reliable method of assessing land suitability for maize in Ethiopia. Keywords: Maize, Gradient boosting,Land suitability,Machine learning, Mathematical formulations

AI.tldr: Compares KNN, gradient boosting and random forest classifiers, with univariate, RFECV and sequential feature selection, for maize land suitability prediction in three Amhara areas of Ethiopia; the best model, GBoost with SFS, reports 99.41% accuracy.
AI.motivation: Traditional land-suitability assessment for maize is time-consuming, costly and unreliable, and Ethiopia needs faster methods to support food production.
AI.method: Field data from local agriculture offices and survey teams in Burie, Shindi and Tilili were coded, scaled and balanced; three feature-selection techniques and three classifiers were compared, with mathematical formulations given for each.
AI.result: The best models combine GBOOST with SFS, achieving 99.41% accuracy and 99.35% for both precision and recall.
AI.conclusion: The authors report that machine learning is a reliable method for assessing maize land suitability in Ethiopia.

title: Learning What to Ask and What to Believe: Distilling a Variational Bayesian Agent into Language Models
summary: Interactive tasks such as eliciting a user's preferences or diagnosing a hidden mechanism require an agent to track its uncertainty over a latent state, ask informative questions and act on the answers. Language models have no explicit mechanism for this, whereas Bayesian information seeking provides one through posterior inference and expected information gain (EIG), and we ask whether it can be distilled into an 8B language model. Our teacher, a lightweight Bayesian agent with a sequential variational belief and EIG query selection, matches or approaches exact and particle references on three task families. We generate synthetic interactions with the teacher on episodes disjoint from the benchmark and fine-tune \Student{} to reproduce its queries and its belief state as a structured scratchpad. On three Multi-Turn Puzzles tasks the student raises Circuit Decoding from 0.00 to 0.93 success, lowers the normalized rank of the recommended film from 0.50 to 0.10 and cuts word guessing from 32 to 3.4 attempts, exceeding the strongest reported language models on the two comparable tasks. Exposing the belief state closes much of the gap where the decision is an implicit computation rather than a read-out of the interaction; in matched teacher contrasts, EIG supervision consistently outperforms random querying, whereas greater inference fidelity does not uniformly improve the distilled student; a 70B language-model teacher does not match the Bayesian teacher in downstream student performance, and the learned skill does not transfer to an unseen task family. Variational Bayesian information seeking can thus be amortized into a language model by transferring the belief state that drives its questions and decisions.

AI.tldr: Distills a variational Bayesian information-seeking teacher into an 8B language model, which learns to ask informative questions and to maintain an explicit belief state as a structured scratchpad.
AI.motivation: Interactive tasks require tracking uncertainty over a latent state and asking informative questions, and language models have no explicit mechanism for this.
AI.method: A lightweight Bayesian teacher with a sequential variational belief and expected-information-gain (EIG) query selection generates synthetic interactions on episodes disjoint from the benchmark; the student is fine-tuned to reproduce its queries and its belief state.
AI.result: On three Multi-Turn Puzzles tasks, the student raises Circuit Decoding success from 0.00 to 0.93, lowers the normalized rank of the recommended film from 0.50 to 0.10, and cuts word-guessing attempts from 32 to 3.4, exceeding the strongest reported language models on the two comparable tasks. EIG supervision consistently outperforms random querying in matched teacher contrasts; a 70B language-model teacher does not match the Bayesian teacher in student performance; the learned skill does not transfer to an unseen task family.
AI.conclusion: Variational Bayesian information seeking can be amortized into a language model by transferring the belief state that drives its questions and decisions.

title: LoRAForge: Co-Designing Post-Hoc Compression and Execution for Efficient Multi-LoRA Serving
summary: Multi-LoRA serving allows many task-specific adapters to share a common base model, but scaling to large adapter fleets introduces substantial storage, loading, and execution overheads. Post-hoc compression can reduce the memory footprint of trained LoRA adapters, yet smaller ranks do not automatically translate into faster serving. For instance, padding, factor access, and generic kernels can obscure the retained low-rank structure, while independently recompressing thousands of modules also incurs significant preparation overhead. We present LoRAForge, a system connecting batched factor construction to rank-specialized execution through an explicit retained-rank representation. It supports two allocation policies: uniform retention ratios (LoRAForge-U) and spectral-energy budget allocation (LoRAForge-S). Both share FlashTSQR factor construction and the same serving backend. FlashTSQR exploits parallelism across modules and row tiles, accelerating factor construction by up to $2.28\times$ over matched library QR. In a fixed-work Qwen control, the shared runtime adds $1.17$--$1.22\times$ throughput across both compressed policies, with negligible gains on original adapters. Across 85 trained open-weighted Qwen and Llama adapters, the spectral policy's floored quality configuration retains about 7.7% of adapter parameters with fleet-average score drops of at most 1.2 points on a 0--100 scale. The same rank-floored $1/12$ spectral exports achieve substantial token-throughput gains on both AMD and NVIDIA GPUs.

AI.tldr: Proposes LoRAForge, which connects batched post-hoc LoRA compression with rank-specialized execution, retaining about 7.7% of adapter parameters with fleet-average score drops of at most 1.2 points in the spectral floored configuration.
AI.motivation: Smaller LoRA ranks do not automatically speed up multi-LoRA serving, because padding, factor access and generic kernels obscure the retained low-rank structure, and independently recompressing thousands of modules is costly.
AI.method: Batched factor construction (FlashTSQR) feeds an explicit retained-rank representation executed by a shared serving backend; two allocation policies are offered: uniform retention ratios (LoRAForge-U) and spectral-energy budget allocation (LoRAForge-S).
AI.result: FlashTSQR accelerates factor construction by up to 2.28x over matched library QR. In a fixed-work Qwen control, the shared runtime adds 1.17-1.22x throughput across both compressed policies. Across 85 trained open-weight Qwen and Llama adapters, the spectral policy's floored quality configuration retains about 7.7% of adapter parameters with fleet-average score drops of at most 1.2 points on a 0-100 scale, and the rank-floored 1/12 spectral exports achieve token-throughput gains on both AMD and NVIDIA GPUs.
AI.conclusion: Co-designing compression with execution turns post-hoc LoRA compression into real serving throughput gains.

title: Learning momenta for Hamiltonian-based models
summary: There has been increasing interest in methodologies that incorporate physics priors into neural network architectures to enhance their modeling capabilities. Among these methodologies, Hamiltonian neural networks (HNNs) and their variants have gained considerable attention. These architectures explicitly encode Hamiltonian mechanics both in their structure and loss function, resulting in desirable properties and additional modeled information. A crucial limitation of HNNs is their reliance on data on the target system's generalized momenta. This severely hampers their applicability when the analytical form of the generalized momenta is unknown, which frequently is the case in real-world applications. The goal of the present work is to develop a general extension of Hamiltonian-based architectures that addresses this issue by simultaneously learning the system's generalized momenta, Hamiltonian structure, and dynamics from data. The proposed architecture learns the generalized momenta when their analytical form is unknown, and only (potentially non-sequential) data on the state and its derivatives is available. A dissipative mass-spring system, a double pendulum, and a rolling disk under nonholonomic constraints are considered as canonical examples to assess the performance of the proposed architecture.

AI.tldr: Proposes an extension of Hamiltonian-based neural architectures that learns the generalized momenta, the Hamiltonian structure and the dynamics jointly from data, for systems whose analytic momenta are unknown.
AI.motivation: Hamiltonian neural networks rely on data about the target system's generalized momenta, which limits their use in real-world applications where the analytic form of the momenta is usually unknown.
AI.method: The architecture learns the generalized momenta when their analytic form is unknown, using only potentially non-sequential data on the state and its derivatives.
AI.result: Evaluation uses three canonical examples: a dissipative mass-spring system, a double pendulum and a rolling disk under nonholonomic constraints. The abstract gives no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: The approach extends Hamiltonian-based architectures to settings where momenta are not known analytically; the abstract reports no quantitative evidence.

title: Best-of-Both-Worlds FTRL for Linear Bandits: The Interplay of Information Acquisition, Corruption, and Geometry
summary: We study \textit{best-of-both-worlds} (BOBW) algorithms for linear bandits, which aim to simultaneously guarantee $\gO(\sqrt T)$ regret in the adversarial regime and $\gO(\log T)$ regret in the stochastic regime over $T$ rounds. For finite action sets, we introduce \emph{information-acquisition follow-the-regularized-leader} (\IAFTRL{}), the first BOBW algorithm based purely on the follow-the-regularized-leader (FTRL) framework that attains an $\gO(\cstar\log T)$-type regret in the stochastic regime, where $\cstar$ is the information-acquisition complexity that characterizes instance-dependent optimality in linear bandits, while retaining the $\gO(\sqrt{T})$ regret guarantee in the adversarial regime. This resolves the open problem posed in~\cite{LeeEtAl2021,KongZ023,ItoT23,ZhaoItoLi2025}.

AI.tldr: Introduces IAFTRL, the first best-of-both-worlds algorithm built purely on the FTRL framework for finite-action linear bandits, attaining O(c* log T)-type regret in the stochastic regime and O(sqrt(T)) regret in the adversarial regime.
AI.motivation: Achieving both O(sqrt(T)) adversarial and O(log T) stochastic regret for linear bandits with FTRL was an open problem posed in prior work.
AI.method: Information-acquisition follow-the-regularized-leader (IAFTRL), where c* is the information-acquisition complexity that characterizes instance-dependent optimality in linear bandits.
AI.result: The algorithm attains O(c* log T)-type regret in the stochastic regime while retaining the O(sqrt(T)) guarantee in the adversarial regime.
AI.conclusion: Information-acquisition complexity gives an instance-dependent best-of-both-worlds guarantee for finite-action linear bandits within the FTRL framework.

title: When Does Exploration Prevent Collapse? Three Regimes and the Path of the Reward in Self-Consistency Training
summary: Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) adapts a model without labels by rewarding answers that agree with the majority, but it collapses the policy onto its majority answer and can remove the correct answer from the samples. Exploration can prevent this collapse, yet its strength is chosen by trial and error, and how the training algorithm changes the required strength is unclear. We model training on a single problem as a continuous flow of the logits of a softmax policy and analyze which policies are stable as the exploration coefficient varies. Only collapsed policies are stable below a lower boundary and only policies spread over many answers above an upper boundary, and we derive these boundaries in closed form for an agreement reward with smoothing toward the uniform policy, compute them for the majority reward of TTRL on policies with one leading answer and bound them with interval arithmetic for actions on ordered bins. We prove that under exact gradients, the learning rate and, in a mean-field model, the normalization of GRPO leave these boundaries unchanged when exploration passes through them together with the reward but shift them when exploration bypasses them. Exact sums on these policies then show that a bonus for rare answers needs a coefficient above $1/\log(G-1)$ for groups of $G$ samples before the normalization and about two to three times that after it. In free-form TTRL on MATH-500, a bonus placed before the normalization prevented collapse and kept more correct answers among the samples, although it lowered pass@1.
