A complexity research case study establishes an exact theorem: for every complex tensor of order n >= 2 and rank greater than two, the minimum Nullstellensatz certificate degree for its original two-term decomposition equations is 3n. This includes an infinite family whose every flattening has rank at most two. The exploration develops an explicit boundary certificate, a balanced transfer lemma, and an exhaustive argument using classical rank-two geometry. A parallel branch gives bounds 3m + 3 <= delta_m(I_m, N) <= 3m + 6 for every nonzero nilpotent m by m matrix. Six graph revisions record the progression from inherited results to these theorems, with exact arithmetic checks and a replayable exploration history. We present the RRE representation and protocol, the mathematical proofs, visualizations of graph evolution, and a research agenda for shared human-AI exploration, cumulative reuse, and education.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Recursive Reasoning Exploration (RRE), a framework that organizes mathematical research as evolving reasoning graphs, and uses it in a case study to prove that the minimum Nullstellensatz certificate degree for two-term tensor decomposition equations of order n >= 2 and rank above two is 3n. A parallel branch bounds delta_m(I_m, N) between 3m + 3 and 3m + 6 for nonzero nilpotent m by m matrices.
AI.motivation: Large collections of manuscripts make it easier to reuse arguments but harder to keep hypotheses, check claims and understand how results were obtained. The authors want cumulative mathematical research with a record of claims, premises, counterexamples and revisions.
AI.method: RRE links claims and jointly required premises to research targets, attempted arguments, counterexamples, checks and revisions. Each investigation can generate further targets, and its supported outcomes become available to later investigations. The complexity case study uses an explicit boundary certificate, a balanced transfer lemma and an exhaustive argument based on classical rank-two geometry, with exact arithmetic checks and six graph revisions recording the progression.
AI.result: The exact theorem states that for every complex tensor of order n >= 2 and rank greater than two, the minimum Nullstellensatz certificate degree for its original two-term decomposition equations is 3n, including an infinite family whose every flattening has rank at most two. The nilpotent-matrix branch gives 3m + 3 <= delta_m(I_m, N) <= 3m + 6.
AI.conclusion: RRE offers a representation and protocol for shared human-AI mathematical exploration with replayable histories, and the authors propose a research agenda on cumulative reuse and education.

title: ZeroGraph: Compositional Blockwise Training via Materialized Boundary Supervision
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures. Code available at this https URL
summary: Blockwise learning can remove online gradient dependencies across depth, but independently optimized blocks need not compose into a useful model. We present ZeroGraph, a systems transformation for pretrained-model conversion and distillation that materializes a frozen teacher's coherent boundary trajectory as a versioned dataset. Each partition then trains with disjoint parameters, optimizer state, random state, and checkpoints, replacing live cross-depth dependencies with persistent supervision. Experiments separate learning quality from systems behavior. On GPT-2 Large, an unanchored objective reduces denoising error by 99.44%, yet assembled held-out cross-entropy worsens from 3.63 to 10.48 and context use becomes negative. A six-arm TinyLlama study identifies clean teacher-boundary regression as the successful interface; the tested noisy objective fails with cached or online targets. The clean recipe passes quality and context-use gates across three Qwen2.5-1.5B seeds and on a 3.086B Qwen2.5 model. In an objective-matched comparison, cached and online targets are bitwise identical. Cached jobs are faster after materialization, but a 618.31 s cache-build cost prevents wall-time break-even through 16 measured reuses. Boundary-shift tests show tolerance to intermediate representation mismatch, and an interrupted block resumes to a bitwise-identical final state without rerunning unaffected blocks. In the tested pretrained-model conversion and distillation setting, cross-depth semantic dependence can move from online optimization into persistent data.

AI.tldr: The paper presents ZeroGraph, a systems transformation that materializes a frozen teacher's boundary trajectory as a versioned dataset, so that partitions of a pretrained model can be trained independently with disjoint parameters. A clean teacher-boundary regression recipe passes quality and context-use gates across three Qwen2.5-1.5B seeds and a 3.086B Qwen2.5 model, though cache building costs 618.31 s and prevents wall-time break-even through 16 reuses.
AI.motivation: Blockwise learning can remove online gradient dependencies across depth, but independently optimized blocks need not compose into a useful model, and the authors want to convert and distil pretrained models in that setting.
AI.method: A frozen teacher's coherent boundary trajectory is materialized as a versioned dataset. Each partition then trains with disjoint parameters, optimizer state, random state and checkpoints, so live cross-depth dependencies become persistent supervision. A six-arm TinyLlama study compares objectives, and an objective-matched comparison contrasts cached and online targets.
AI.result: On GPT-2 Large an unanchored objective reduces denoising error by 99.44%, yet assembled held-out cross-entropy worsens from 3.63 to 10.48 and context use becomes negative. The clean teacher-boundary regression is identified as the successful interface, and the tested noisy objective fails with cached or online targets. Cached and online targets are bitwise identical in the matched comparison. Cached jobs are faster after materialization, but the 618.31 s cache build prevents wall-time break-even through 16 measured reuses. An interrupted block resumes to a bitwise-identical final state.
AI.conclusion: In this conversion and distillation setting, cross-depth semantic dependence can move from online optimization into persistent data, provided the boundary objective is clean.

title: TIGER: Learning from Researcher Taste to Generate Tailored Research Ideas
summary: In pairwise comparisons where each judge chooses between an idea generated by its corresponding TIGER-8B policy and one generated by GPT-4.1, the three LLM researchers select the TIGER-8B idea in 56.6%-68.4% of 76 comparisons per researcher. PhD1 and PhD2 select the TIGER-8B idea in 19 of 30 pairs (63.3%) and 17 of 30 pairs (56.7%), respectively. All six directed cross-policy comparisons likewise favor the judge's matched TIGER-8B policy over an off-target policy, supporting the use of individual preference feedback for tailored research ideation.

AI.tldr: The paper reports a pairwise study in which three LLM researchers, and two PhD judges, choose between ideas from a TIGER-8B policy trained on individual researcher taste and ideas from GPT-4.1. The TIGER-8B idea is preferred in 56.6% to 68.4% of comparisons for the LLM judges, and in 63.3% and 56.7% for the two PhD judges.
AI.motivation: The authors want to tailor research-idea generation to an individual researcher's preferences, which requires that individual preference feedback can steer the generator.
AI.method: Each judge chooses between an idea from the judge's matched TIGER-8B policy and one from GPT-4.1, with 76 comparisons per LLM researcher. The two PhD judges each make 30 pairwise comparisons. The authors also run six directed cross-policy comparisons, in which a judge compares its matched policy with an off-target policy.
AI.result: The three LLM researchers select the TIGER-8B idea in 56.6% to 68.4% of 76 comparisons each. PhD1 and PhD2 select it in 19 of 30 pairs (63.3%) and 17 of 30 pairs (56.7%). All six directed cross-policy comparisons favour the judge's matched TIGER-8B policy over an off-target policy.
AI.conclusion: The results support the use of individual preference feedback for tailored research ideation, since each judge prefers the policy matched to its own taste.

title: Can LLMs Reliably Evaluate Themselves? A Probabilistic VC Framework
comment: 34 pages, 6 figures, 8 tables. Non-archival paper at the NeurIPS 2025 Workshop on Bridging Language, Agent, and World Models for Reasoning and Planning (LAW 2025)
summary: As large language models (LLMs) find increasing use in critical applications, evaluating their ability to assess their own outputs has become crucial. We present a theoretical and empirical framework that examines whether LLMs can differentiate between correct and incorrect solutions while maintaining properly calibrated confidence. Building on classical Vapnik-Chervonenkis (VC) theory, we adapt it to probabilistic predictors through two complexity metrics: Probabilistic VC (PVC), which measures a model's ability to confidently classify across problem types, and Calibration-aware PVC (C-PVC), which additionally demands alignment between confidence scores and actual success rates. Unlike Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and Actual Error (AE), these measures give an integrated assessment of self-evaluation expressiveness and calibration, with sample complexity bounds and generalization guarantees comparable to classical VC theory. We test eleven 7-8B models on 360 original mathematical reasoning problems, TruthfulQA, and CommonsenseQA. Each model chooses between two of its own generated solutions and reports its confidence, with ground truth determined by an ensemble of larger models. The results show a systematic inverse relationship: models with greater self-evaluation expressiveness have weaker calibration. s1.1-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct achieve the highest PVC-VUS scores, while JiuZhang3.0-7B is best calibrated, with the lowest ECE and the smallest PVC-VUS gap. The trade-off persists across architectures, training paradigms, and domains, pointing to a fundamental challenge in developing self-reflective LLMs, and our framework offers practical tools for diagnosing it.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Probabilistic VC (PVC) and Calibration-aware PVC (C-PVC) to measure whether LLMs can reliably evaluate their own solutions, and finds a systematic inverse relationship in which models with greater self-evaluation expressiveness have weaker calibration. Eleven 7-8B models are tested on mathematical reasoning, TruthfulQA and CommonsenseQA.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are used in critical applications, their ability to assess their own outputs has become crucial. Existing measures such as Expected Calibration Error and Actual Error do not give an integrated view of self-evaluation expressiveness and calibration.
AI.method: The authors adapt Vapnik-Chervonenkis theory to probabilistic predictors through PVC, which measures confident classification across problem types, and C-PVC, which additionally requires confidence scores to match actual success rates, with sample-complexity bounds. Each model chooses between two of its own generated solutions and reports confidence, on 360 original mathematical problems, TruthfulQA and CommonsenseQA, with ground truth from an ensemble of larger models.
AI.result: s1.1-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct achieve the highest PVC-VUS scores, while JiuZhang3.0-7B is best calibrated, with the lowest ECE and the smallest PVC-VUS gap. The trade-off persists across architectures, training paradigms and domains.
AI.conclusion: The inverse relationship between expressiveness and calibration points to a fundamental challenge in building self-reflective LLMs, and the framework offers practical diagnostic tools for it.

title: The 3-Tier Integrated Technology Risk Model for Occupational Safety and Health
summary: This paper presents the 3-Tier Integrated Technology Risk Model, a progressive framework for Occupational Safety and Health (OSH) management that integrates Job Safety Analysis (JSA), dynamic risk assessment using leading and lagging indicators, and predictive analytics powered by Large Language Models (LLMs). The model provides organizations with a structured pathway to evolve from static, reactive safety practices to a sophisticated, predictive safety paradigm. Each tier builds upon the previous one, creating a comprehensive, data-driven approach that enables just-in-time training and preemptive risk mitigation.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the 3-Tier Integrated Technology Risk Model, a progressive framework for occupational safety and health that combines Job Safety Analysis, dynamic risk assessment with leading and lagging indicators, and LLM-based predictive analytics. The abstract gives a conceptual description and reports no empirical evaluation.
AI.motivation: Organizations rely on static, reactive safety practices, and the authors want a structured path toward a predictive, data-driven safety paradigm that supports just-in-time training and preemptive risk mitigation.
AI.method: The model has three tiers, and each builds upon the previous one. The tiers integrate Job Safety Analysis, dynamic risk assessment using leading and lagging indicators, and predictive analytics powered by Large Language Models.
AI.result: The abstract reports no experimental or numerical results.
AI.conclusion: The authors present the model as a comprehensive, data-driven approach that enables just-in-time training and preemptive risk mitigation, but the abstract gives no evidence for its effectiveness.

title: Beyond Binary Detection: Type-Aware Hallucination Analysis and Hierarchical Detection in Financial Question Answering
summary: Large language models are increasingly used to answer questions over financial filings, where an unfaithful answer can mislead investment, compliance, or client decisions. Hallucination detectors are a common safeguard, but they are usually evaluated with a single binary score that reveals neither which kinds of errors analysesed nor why. This paper studies hallucination detection on PHANTOM, a long-context benchmark built from SEC filings, at the level of hallucination type. We first analyze 15,443 paired hallucinated and faithful answers without any detector and find that hallucinated answers are more than twice as long as faithful ones, and that lexical grounding separates the two classes only because faithful answers are bimodal. We then generate hallucinations in nine financially motivated categories, confirm each with a separate verification pass, and diagnose an LLM-based detector on 4,086 usable examples. Generation success varies from 66.3% to 100% across categories. The detector reaches 80.2% binary accuracy but only 44.7% subtype accuracy, never assigns two of the nine categories, and misses between 5.3% and 46.8% of hallucinations depending on category; these misses are unrelated to input length but rise with how far an answer departs from the correct one. Guided by this diagnosis, we propose a two-stage hierarchical detector that first decides whether an answer is hallucinated and then assigns a subtype, raising binary accuracy to 95.6% and subtype accuracy to 56.1%. The results show that type-level evaluation exposes detector weaknesses that aggregate metrics conceal.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates hallucination detection on PHANTOM, a long-context financial QA benchmark built from SEC filings, at the level of hallucination type. A two-stage hierarchical detector raises binary accuracy to 95.6% and subtype accuracy to 56.1%, from 80.2% and 44.7% for the original LLM-based detector.
AI.motivation: Hallucination detectors are usually evaluated with a single binary score, which does not reveal which kinds of errors they miss or why, and unfaithful financial answers can mislead investment, compliance and client decisions.
AI.method: The authors analyse 15,443 paired hallucinated and faithful answers without a detector, then generate hallucinations in nine financially motivated categories, confirm each with a separate verification pass, and diagnose an LLM-based detector on 4,086 usable examples. Guided by this diagnosis they propose a two-stage hierarchical detector that first decides whether an answer is hallucinated and then assigns a subtype.
AI.result: Hallucinated answers are more than twice as long as faithful ones. The original detector reaches 80.2% binary accuracy but only 44.7% subtype accuracy, never assigns two of the nine categories, and misses between 5.3% and 46.8% of hallucinations depending on category. Generation success varies from 66.3% to 100% across categories. The hierarchical detector reaches 95.6% binary accuracy and 56.1% subtype accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Type-level evaluation exposes detector weaknesses that aggregate metrics conceal, and a hierarchical design guided by that diagnosis improves both binary and subtype detection.

title: Data-Scarce, Multi-Granular, Multimodal: Benchmark Design for Biosynthetic Gene Clusters
comment: 43 pages, including references and appendices. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations and Datasets Track)
summary: Biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) are co-located genes that encode the biosynthesis of specialized metabolites, an important source of antibiotics, anticancer agents, immunosuppressants, and agricultural bioactives. Deep learning, particularly self-supervised foundation models, has spurred interest in BGC sequence modeling, but evaluation has lagged behind: existing benchmarks often rely on coarse classification over small curated datasets, providing limited discrimination among models and insight into downstream utility. We propose a benchmark-design framework in which an informative benchmark should be discriminative, separating models with statistical confidence, and applicable, spanning scientifically meaningful tasks under different levels of generalization. We instantiate this framework as BGC-Bench, which derives five tasks from MIBiG, ranging from A-domain substrate prediction to BGC-molecule retrieval, evaluates them under genotype- and phenotype-shift splits, includes an active-learning setting for label-scarce discovery, and is easily extensible to new tasks and encoders. BGCs further provide a shared testbed across granularities and modalities: BGC-Bench compares twelve encoders on nucleotide, amino-acid, or Pfam-domain sequences, including compositional baselines for each input type, and combines BGC and chemical encoders for cross-modal retrieval. No single representation dominates: the best granularity depends on the biological scale of the task, and pretrained encoders do not consistently outperform other representations across tasks and splits. Active-learning experiments show that most tasks remain data-limited, encoder rankings change with labeling budget, and acquisition strategies yield modest gains. These results show that BGC model evaluation requires task-diverse, shift-aware benchmarks, and the framework can be generalized to benchmark design beyond BGCs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a benchmark-design framework for biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) and instantiates it as BGC-Bench, with five tasks derived from MIBiG and twelve encoders compared across nucleotide, amino-acid and Pfam-domain inputs. No single representation dominates, and most tasks remain data-limited under active learning.
AI.motivation: Evaluation of BGC sequence models has lagged behind their development, since existing benchmarks often use coarse classification on small curated datasets that give limited discrimination among models and little insight into downstream utility.
AI.method: The framework requires a benchmark to be discriminative, separating models with statistical confidence, and applicable, spanning scientifically meaningful tasks at different generalization levels. BGC-Bench derives five tasks from MIBiG, from A-domain substrate prediction to BGC-molecule retrieval, evaluates them under genotype- and phenotype-shift splits, and includes an active-learning setting. It compares twelve encoders on nucleotide, amino-acid or Pfam-domain sequences, with compositional baselines, and combines BGC and chemical encoders for cross-modal retrieval.
AI.result: No single representation dominates, the best granularity depends on the biological scale of the task, and pretrained encoders do not consistently outperform other representations across tasks and splits. Most tasks remain data-limited, encoder rankings change with labelling budget, and acquisition strategies yield modest gains.
AI.conclusion: BGC model evaluation requires task-diverse, shift-aware benchmarks, and the framework can be generalized to benchmark design beyond BGCs.

title: Toward Agentic AI-Ready Workflows in Built Environment Organizations: Knowledge Structures and Interoperability Challenges
summary: The rise of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) in the built environment is shifting attention from isolated AI tools toward autonomous systems that reason, plan, and act across project and organizational workflows. The effectiveness of such systems depends not only on large language model capabilities, but also on the readiness of heterogeneous data environments across the Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC) sector. These environments combine structured sources, such as CAD and BIM models, schedules, cost databases, and asset registers, with unstructured ones, including technical reports, design narratives, planning and policy documents, contracts, meeting minutes, and risk registers. This paper reviews how built environment data can be organized to support agentic AI-ready workflows, focusing on knowledge structures, interoperability, and access and integration mechanisms such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Drawing on existing literature, it examines approaches proposed to organize structured and unstructured data and considers how such data can be contextualized and made accessible to AI agents in a reliable manner. The paper synthesizes current perspectives, highlights challenges around fragmentation and interoperability, and identifies open questions for future research on AI-compatible information management in the built environment.

AI.tldr: The paper reviews how built-environment data can be organized to support agentic AI-ready workflows in the architecture, engineering and construction (AEC) sector, focusing on knowledge structures, interoperability and access mechanisms such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and the Model Context Protocol (MCP). It highlights fragmentation and interoperability challenges and identifies open research questions.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI in the built environment is moving from isolated tools toward autonomous systems, but the effectiveness of such systems depends on the readiness of heterogeneous AEC data, both structured (CAD and BIM models, schedules, cost databases, asset registers) and unstructured (reports, contracts, minutes, risk registers).
AI.method: This is a literature review. It examines approaches proposed to organize structured and unstructured data, considers how such data can be contextualized and made accessible to AI agents reliably, and synthesizes current perspectives.
AI.result: The abstract reports no new empirical results. It identifies fragmentation and interoperability as the main challenges and lists open questions for AI-compatible information management in the built environment.
AI.conclusion: Agentic AI readiness in the built environment depends as much on data organization and interoperability as on LLM capability, and these are the areas the authors identify for future research.

title: SGR-OPSD: Learning from Subgoal Plans with Graph-Regularized Credit Assignment for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: OPSD provides dense supervision for agentic reinforcement learning through privileged information feedback. However, existing privileged information often lacks explicit task-progression planning, while teacher-student log-probability gaps reflect shifts in model preference rather than true task progress. To address these limitations, we propose Subgoal-Guided Graph-Regularized OPSD (SGR-OPSD), a framework that combines subgoal supervision with interaction-derived evidence for turn-level credit assignment. Specifically, SGR-OPSD uses LLM-generated subgoal plans to provide dense action-level guidance, converting them into advantage weights via a constrained, KL-regularized objective. To ground credit in observed outcomes, we construct a Subgoal Progress Graph that estimates empirical returns from sampled transition frequencies. The graph compares empirical action returns against the state average to derive preferences that calibrate the teacher's credit weights. Evaluated on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA across two model scales (Qwen2.5-3B and 7B), SGR-OPSD consistently outperforms GRPO and strong self-distillation baselines, improving success rates over GRPO by up to 7.4 percentage points and reaching 85.8% on ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-7B. Ablation studies confirm that subgoal guidance and graph-based weight calibration are key to these performance gains.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SGR-OPSD, which combines LLM-generated subgoal plans with a Subgoal Progress Graph built from interaction data to assign turn-level credit in agentic reinforcement learning. It outperforms GRPO and strong self-distillation baselines on ALFWorld, WebShop and Search-QA, reaching 85.8% on ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-7B.
AI.motivation: OPSD gives dense supervision through privileged information, but existing privileged information often lacks explicit task-progression planning, and teacher-student log-probability gaps reflect shifts in model preference rather than true task progress.
AI.method: SGR-OPSD uses LLM-generated subgoal plans to give dense action-level guidance, converting them into advantage weights through a constrained, KL-regularized objective. A Subgoal Progress Graph estimates empirical returns from sampled transition frequencies, and compares empirical action returns against the state average to calibrate the teacher's credit weights.
AI.result: Evaluated on ALFWorld, WebShop and Search-QA with Qwen2.5-3B and 7B, SGR-OPSD consistently outperforms GRPO and strong self-distillation baselines. It improves success over GRPO by up to 7.4 percentage points and reaches 85.8% on ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-7B. Ablations confirm that subgoal guidance and graph-based weight calibration are key.
AI.conclusion: Grounding credit in observed outcomes, alongside subgoal supervision, improves turn-level credit assignment for agentic reinforcement learning.

title: RecGroupMemory: Feedback-Aware Cohort Memory for E-Commerce Recommendation
summary: Cohort memory can support LLM-based recommendation planning through group-level user profiles and advice. As outcome feedback becomes available, this guidance may need to be updated while preserving the underlying observations. We present RecGroupMemory, a workflow that provides this memory to an orchestration LLM and separates memory construction from feedback-based revision. It uses feedback from the previous day to revise decision guidance, while validation checks keep selected source values unchanged. Online comparisons were conducted among Taobao users with low purchasing power selected by the business team. Relative to a no-memory baseline, memory without feedback and memory with feedback showed increases of 1.58% and 1.78%, respectively, in the number of guided transaction users.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RecGroupMemory, a workflow that gives an orchestration LLM cohort-level memory for e-commerce recommendation and revises its guidance from the previous day's feedback while keeping source values unchanged. In online tests among low-purchasing-power Taobao users, memory with feedback increased guided transaction users by 1.78% over a no-memory baseline.
AI.motivation: Cohort memory can support LLM-based recommendation planning, but as outcome feedback arrives the guidance may need revising while the underlying observations are preserved.
AI.method: RecGroupMemory separates memory construction from feedback-based revision. It uses the previous day's feedback to revise decision guidance, and validation checks keep selected source values unchanged. Online comparisons were run among Taobao users with low purchasing power selected by the business team.
AI.result: Relative to a no-memory baseline, memory without feedback increased the number of guided transaction users by 1.58%, and memory with feedback increased it by 1.78%.
AI.conclusion: Feedback-based revision of cohort memory gives a small additional gain over memory alone in this online setting, with the gains reported as relative increases from one deployment.

title: RLiD: Reinforcement Learning in the Decision Plane for Language Agents and LLMs
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has improved the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) across a wide range of tasks. However, token-level RL assigns an action's advantage to the entire generated response, including tokens specifying the parsed action, reasoning chains, and malformed content. Although the environment executes only the parsed action, variation in how the action is expressed in natural language can introduce additional variance into policy-gradient estimates. We propose RLiD (Reinforcement Learning in the Decision plane), a framework that directly optimizes the probabilities of executable action options. RLiD compiles observations, an optional compact memory, and a labeled action menu into the model input, and uses a large decision model (LDM) to select an action in a single forward pass. By eliminating autoregressive token generation and bypassing action parsing, RLiD avoids invalid action outputs and improves RL rollout efficiency. Our analysis shows that, within a fixed text policy, marginalizing over alternative realizations of the same action removes a zero-mean gradient component without changing the expected update. We further distill trained LDM policies into generative LLMs through supervision on their action trajectories. Experiments on ARC, Countdown, and Sokoban demonstrate improved performance or lower computational cost across several settings. On ALFWorld, the complete training and distillation pipeline reaches 99.3% success in 12.7 H100 GPU-hours, compared with 86.6% in 17.3 GPU-hours for token-level RL of the same LLM. With compiled memory, our strongest Qwen2.5-1.5B LDM and distilled generative LLM achieve 100% success on all 134 unseen and 140 seen ALFWorld evaluation games.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RLiD, which optimizes the probabilities of executable action options directly, so that a large decision model picks an action in one forward pass without autoregressive generation or action parsing. On ALFWorld, the full pipeline reaches 99.3% success in 12.7 H100 GPU-hours, against 86.6% in 17.3 GPU-hours for token-level RL of the same LLM.
AI.motivation: Token-level RL assigns an action's advantage to the whole generated response, including parsing tokens, reasoning and malformed content, though the environment executes only the parsed action. Variation in how the same action is phrased adds variance to policy-gradient estimates.
AI.method: RLiD compiles observations, an optional compact memory and a labelled action menu into the model input, and a large decision model selects an action in a single forward pass. The authors show that, within a fixed text policy, marginalizing over alternative realizations of the same action removes a zero-mean gradient component without changing the expected update. Trained decision-model policies are further distilled into generative LLMs through supervision on their action trajectories.
AI.result: Experiments on ARC, Countdown and Sokoban show improved performance or lower computational cost across several settings. On ALFWorld the complete pipeline reaches 99.3% success in 12.7 H100 GPU-hours, against 86.6% in 17.3 GPU-hours for token-level RL. With compiled memory, the strongest Qwen2.5-1.5B decision model and its distilled generative LLM achieve 100% success on all 134 unseen and 140 seen ALFWorld evaluation games.
AI.conclusion: Optimizing executable action options avoids invalid outputs and improves rollout efficiency, and the distilled generative LLM retains the gains.

title: Think Globally, Generate Personally: Multi-View Thinking with Adaptive Generation for Generative Recommendation
summary: Semantic-ID-based (SID) generative recommendation (GR) represents each item as a sequence of discrete tokens and predicts the next item through autoregressive SID generation. However, existing methods face two challenges. First, insufficient shared context modeling for user sequences: full-history and recent behaviors provide overlapping yet complementary evidence, but modeling them within a single sequence may dilute current cues, whereas processing them through separate streams may fail to coordinate them. Second, insufficient personalized adaptation in progressive SID decisions: although decoder states evolve with generated prefixes, existing models typically use a shared output-side transformation across recommendation instances, without explicitly selecting a transformation suited to the current user need. To address these challenges, we propose Multi-View Thinking with Adaptive Generation (MV-Thinker), a framework that Thinks Globally and Generates Personally. First, Multi-View Temporal Thinking uses view-specific thinking queries and readers over overlapping full-history and recent-history views, coordinating both sources into complementary user-conditioned contexts before SID generation. Second, Hierarchical Residual Adaptation organizes lightweight adapters into nested residual paths before a shared vocabulary projection, adaptively transforming context-bearing decoder states for SID decisions. Extensive experiments on four public datasets demonstrate that MV-Thinker consistently outperforms strong discriminative and generative recommendation baselines across multiple ranking metrics. The implementation code and datasets are available on: this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MV-Thinker, a generative recommendation model for semantic-ID sequences that combines multi-view temporal thinking over full-history and recent-history views with hierarchical residual adaptation of decoder states. It consistently outperforms strong discriminative and generative baselines on four public datasets across multiple ranking metrics.
AI.motivation: In semantic-ID generative recommendation, modelling full-history and recent behaviour in one sequence may dilute current cues, separate streams may fail to coordinate them, and a shared output transformation ignores the user need at each progressive SID decision.
AI.method: Multi-View Temporal Thinking uses view-specific thinking queries and readers over overlapping full-history and recent-history views, coordinating both into complementary user-conditioned contexts before SID generation. Hierarchical Residual Adaptation organizes lightweight adapters into nested residual paths before a shared vocabulary projection, adaptively transforming context-bearing decoder states.
AI.result: MV-Thinker consistently outperforms strong discriminative and generative recommendation baselines across multiple ranking metrics on four public datasets. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Thinking globally over multiple history views and generating personally through adaptive residual adapters improves semantic-ID generative recommendation. Code and datasets are stated to be available.

title: MAGAR: Multimodal Agents for GUI-Based 3D Mechanical Assembly and Minimal Rework
summary: A GUI command can be correct at the interface level yet still produce an incorrect assembly. An agent must identify the relevant components, respect their structural relationships, and determine which parts should move during recovery. We introduce MAGAR-Bench, a benchmark of 4,000 multimodal samples from 26 assembly families that separates Assembly Decision, Atomic Action, and Minimal Rework. For rework, the objective counts distinct moved parts within the validated recovery candidate set for each state, rather than the number of actions. We also introduce MAGAR, a selective correction framework built on a frozen policy obtained by supervised fine-tuning. Its key design matches correction granularity to output dependencies. Structured candidates revise assembly fields and rework scope, while complete action candidates keep native GUI primitives coupled with their parameters. A learned selector retains the original prediction unless a candidate passes a task-specific intervention threshold. On recorded states from held-out assembly families, MAGAR improves Overall, the task-balanced aggregate, from 37.50 to 41.39, with gains on all three tasks. Across 209 interventions, 70 correct an error and 22 introduce one. These results support task-specific correction while highlighting the remaining tradeoff between fixing errors and preserving reliable predictions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MAGAR-Bench, a 4,000-sample multimodal benchmark for GUI-based 3D mechanical assembly, and MAGAR, a selective correction framework over a frozen supervised policy that revises predictions only when a candidate passes an intervention threshold. On held-out assembly families, the Overall score rises from 37.50 to 41.39, with gains on all three tasks.
AI.motivation: A GUI command can be correct at the interface level yet still produce an incorrect assembly, so agents must identify relevant components, respect structural relationships and choose which parts to move during recovery.
AI.method: MAGAR-Bench separates Assembly Decision, Atomic Action and Minimal Rework, and its rework objective counts distinct moved parts within the validated recovery candidate set. MAGAR uses a frozen supervised fine-tuned policy. Structured candidates revise assembly fields and rework scope, complete action candidates keep GUI primitives with their parameters, and a learned selector keeps the original prediction unless a candidate passes a task-specific threshold.
AI.result: On recorded states from held-out assembly families, MAGAR improves Overall, the task-balanced aggregate, from 37.50 to 41.39, with gains on all three tasks. Across 209 interventions, 70 correct an error and 22 introduce one.
AI.conclusion: Task-specific correction helps, but there remains a trade-off between fixing errors and preserving reliable predictions.

title: Benchmark of THReD: Evaluating an LLM Agent and Its Preprocessing Tools for Turning Electronic Health Records into AI-Ready Datasets
comment: 35 pages, 3 figures, and 22 tables. Code, task definitions, and per-episode results are available on Zenodo via the DOI provided in the DOI field
summary: LLM agents are increasingly built into data-analysis software, yet little evidence shows how reliably they preprocess clinical data or whether the tools they invoke give correct, reproducible output. We report a benchmark of THReD, a web-based system that turns electronic health record (EHR) extracts into AI-ready datasets through a chat agent whose proposed steps run only after user confirmation. The agent benchmark has 141 tasks (100 templates) in seven categories, including goal-level requests, failure recovery, requests calling for no action, schema variation and prompt injection through the data, on synthetic tables calibrated to a regional health information exchange; success is judged by checks on the produced data. Over 2,550 episodes with Claude Haiku 5.5 in four context configurations, the deployed agent completed 92.7% (95% CI 88.1-96.4) of tasks on its first answer, abstained on every advice request, recovered from every injected fault, and never proposed an action requested by planted text. Without the data profile, completion fell to 58.0%; goal-level requests were hardest (80.6%). Six experiments on real records of two chronic-disease cohorts and on synthetic data at scale validate the tools: 91-92% of inferred patient classes and 99.7-99.8% of inferred vital-sign labels were correct in masked reconstruction; a dictionary builder combining curated dictionaries with LLM suggestions mapped 99.0% of 2,208 raw variants correctly; all 2,176 replays of 128 saved pipelines gave byte-identical files under pinned dependencies; subgroup differences in inference accuracy vanished within facility and lookup key; and the same-day consolidation rule changed 90-day emergency revisit rates by up to 3.2 points without shifting cohort composition by more than one point. Processing time grew roughly linearly to 5.5 million records while the prompt stayed at about 13 thousand tokens.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks THReD, a web-based system whose chat agent turns EHR extracts into AI-ready datasets, and validates its deterministic tools on real and synthetic records. The deployed agent completes 92.7% of 141 tasks on its first answer, recovers from every injected fault and never acts on requests planted in the data.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are increasingly built into data-analysis software, but there is little evidence on how reliably they preprocess clinical data or whether their tools give correct, reproducible output.
AI.method: The agent benchmark has 141 tasks (100 templates) in seven categories, including goal-level requests, failure recovery, no-action requests, schema variation and prompt injection through the data, on synthetic tables calibrated to a regional health information exchange. Over 2,550 episodes with Claude Haiku 5.5 in four context configurations were scored by checks on the produced data. Six tool experiments use real records of two chronic-disease cohorts and synthetic data at scale.
AI.result: The deployed agent completed 92.7% (95% CI 88.1-96.4) of tasks on its first answer, abstained on every advice request, recovered from every injected fault and never proposed an action requested by planted text. Without the data profile, completion fell to 58.0%, and goal-level requests were hardest at 80.6%. In masked reconstruction, 91-92% of inferred patient classes and 99.7-99.8% of inferred vital-sign labels were correct. The dictionary builder mapped 99.0% of 2,208 raw variants correctly. All 2,176 replays of 128 saved pipelines gave byte-identical files, and processing time grew roughly linearly to 5.5 million records with a prompt of about 13 thousand tokens.
AI.conclusion: The agent and its tools are reliable enough for this preprocessing setting within the tested conditions, and the data profile is essential to agent completion.

title: Towards Multi-Value Alignment via Value Localization in LLMs
summary: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with multiple, potentially conflicting human values remains challenging, as existing multi-objective alignment methods often require costly fine-tuning and provide limited insight into the internal mechanisms underlying value-related behaviors. In this work, we investigate multi-value alignment from a mechanistic interpretability perspective by identifying value-sensitive attention heads (value heads) in LLMs. Using a probing-based value localization framework, we discover sparse sets of attention heads associated with diverse dimensions, spanning both human values (e.g., harmlessness, honesty) and stylistic preferences (e.g., coherence, complexity). Analyses across multiple LLM families reveal functional specialization and structured interactions among value heads, including conflicts between certain values. Targeted head ablations further induce substantial, value-specific behavioral changes, providing causal evidence of their functional importance. Building on these findings, we propose an inference-time activation steering strategy that enables controllable alignment with individual values or combinations of values without updating the underlying model parameters, supported by theoretical analysis. Experiments across multiple value alignment benchmarks demonstrate effective single- and multi-value control while largely preserving non-target model performance. Our findings connect mechanistic interpretability with flexible multi-value alignment, offering a foundation for more interpretable and pluralistic LLM behavior. The code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies value-sensitive attention heads in LLMs with a probing-based localization framework and proposes inference-time activation steering that controls individual or combined values without changing model parameters. Head ablations produce value-specific behaviour changes, and steering gives effective single- and multi-value control while largely preserving non-target performance.
AI.motivation: Multi-objective alignment methods for multiple, potentially conflicting human values often need costly fine-tuning and give limited insight into the internal mechanisms behind value-related behaviour.
AI.method: From a mechanistic interpretability perspective, the authors use a probing-based value localization framework to find sparse sets of attention heads associated with values such as harmlessness and honesty, and with stylistic preferences such as coherence and complexity. They analyse these heads across LLM families, perform targeted head ablations, and propose an inference-time activation steering strategy, supported by theoretical analysis.
AI.result: Analyses across several LLM families reveal functional specialization and structured interactions among value heads, including conflicts between some values. Targeted head ablations induce substantial, value-specific behavioural changes. Steering gives effective single- and multi-value control across several value alignment benchmarks while largely preserving non-target performance.
AI.conclusion: The findings link mechanistic interpretability with flexible, multi-value alignment without updating model parameters, offering a foundation for more interpretable and pluralistic LLM behaviour. The code is available.

title: AttentionIndex: Accelerating Learned Sparse Attention with a Causal Inverted-File Index
summary: Learned sparse attention, used in production models such as DeepSeek-V4 and GLM-5, lets each query attend to only k keys chosen by a lightweight indexer, but the indexer still scores every key in the prefix. At one million tokens, this selection takes more than half of prefill time. Two-stage selection over contiguous blocks, as in HiSA, reduces this cost, but its recall declines as context grows at a fixed candidate budget. We present AttentionIndex, which routes each query over an inverted-file index that groups indexer keys by similarity and refines the candidates with the native indexer score. AttentionIndex builds the index during prefill, making new keys searchable immediately, reusing previous clustering to keep maintenance cheap, and exposing each query only to clusters built from its own prefix. On GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash at one million tokens, AttentionIndex delivers 1.3-1.8 times the prefill throughput of exhaustive selection, and at throughput within 5% of HiSA, it recovers 17.0 and 10.0 percentage points more of the exhaustive top-k, respectively. AttentionIndex also improves accuracy on long-context benchmarks by up to 18.4 percentage points over HiSA at the same candidate budget.

AI.tldr: AttentionIndex speeds up learned sparse attention by routing each query over an inverted-file index of indexer keys, so it no longer scores every key in the prefix. At one million tokens it gives 1.3-1.8 times the prefill throughput of exhaustive selection.
AI.motivation: The lightweight indexer in learned sparse attention still scores every key in the prefix, which takes more than half of prefill time at one million tokens. The existing two-stage block selection (HiSA) loses recall as context grows at a fixed candidate budget.
AI.method: The method groups indexer keys by similarity into an inverted-file index built during prefill, so new keys are searchable immediately. It reuses previous clustering to keep maintenance cheap, exposes each query only to clusters from its own prefix, and refines the candidates with the native indexer score.
AI.result: On GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash at one million tokens, AttentionIndex gives 1.3-1.8 times the prefill throughput of exhaustive selection. At throughput within 5% of HiSA, it recovers 17.0 and 10.0 percentage points more of the exhaustive top-k, and it improves long-context benchmark accuracy by up to 18.4 points over HiSA at the same candidate budget.
AI.conclusion: Indexing the indexer's keys with an inverted file makes sparse attention selection cheap at long context while keeping recall close to exhaustive top-k, which narrows the cost-recall trade-off of block-based selection.

title: A balloon effect: ban one channel and a hidden trait finds another
comment: 30 pages, 9 figures, 2 Extended Data figures, 8 Extended Data tables; Supplementary Information included. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Language models trained on the outputs of other models can acquire traits that those outputs never mention, such as a preference for an animal carried by lists of numbers. Such subliminal learning can pass on unwanted traits. The intuitive defence is to find and forbid the tokens through which a trait shows, but how a trait's trace behaves under such bans, and what of it a student learns, has not been resolved. We closed a trait's outlets one by one in two stress tests, a preference chain and a name chain, across two models, six output formats and 16 traits. Bans did not remove the trait. Much as squeezing a balloon in one place makes it bulge in another, the trait moved to wherever the format still allowed, an effect we call the balloon effect. Decomposing this transfer, which bans on surface features cannot stop, down to single heads and neurons, we show that it can be cut at the circuit that writes the trait into the output. Patching that circuit while the teacher writes numbers stopped the chains, sharply reduced the overt name leak and halved the trait passed to a student, whereas the same number of random heads produced no detectable reduction. These results give a mechanistic account of how unwanted hidden traits are transferred and a route to preventing it.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that banning the surface tokens that carry a hidden trait does not remove the trait from a model's outputs; the trait moves to whichever format is still allowed. It then cuts the transfer by patching the specific circuit that writes the trait into the output.
AI.motivation: Subliminal learning can pass unwanted traits from teacher to student through outputs that never mention them. The intuitive defence of forbidding the tokens that show the trait had not been tested, and how the trait behaves under such bans was unresolved.
AI.method: The authors close a trait's output channels one by one in two stress tests, a preference chain and a name chain, across two models, six output formats and 16 traits. They then decompose the transfer down to individual attention heads and neurons and patch the circuit that writes the trait into the output, comparing against the same number of random heads.
AI.result: Bans did not remove the trait; it shifted to the formats still allowed, which the authors call the balloon effect. Patching the identified circuit stopped the chains, sharply reduced the overt name leak, and halved the trait passed to a student, while patching random heads gave no detectable reduction.
AI.conclusion: Hidden trait transfer can be mechanistically explained and cut at the circuit that writes the trait into the output, which offers a route to prevent it, while surface-level bans are shown to be insufficient.

title: When Prediction Shapes the Future: A BlueSky Agenda for Reflexive Time Series Analysis
comment: Accepted to the ICDM 2026 BlueSky Track
summary: Time-series models are increasingly deployed in operational systems (e.g., inventory management and clinical care) where predictions trigger interventions that alter future observations, producing records we term AI-shaped trajectories. This sequence-prediction coupling deepens as such systems evolve into agents that autonomously predict, act, and remember across long horizons. Such AI-shaped trajectories support immediate performance monitoring, but turn ambiguous once reused as passive data. An algorithm may then misread a prediction-prevented stockout as naturally stable demand, or an averted medical crisis as a false alarm. This ambiguity then propagates into everything built on the record, from retraining and agent memory to downstream predictive tasks. As a result, systems may internalize these intervention effects as natural phenomena, drifting further from the truth at every closed-loop cycle. In this Blue Sky paper, we advocate an agenda for reflexive time-series analysis that shifts the analytical object from the intervention-agnostic sequence to the prediction-action-observation loop. The agenda requires closed-loop provenance to track the operational context (e.g., predictions, policies, and actions), sequence identification to estimate how those actions affect future values under explicit causal assumptions, and closed-loop evaluation to separate intrinsic process prediction from policy-driven effects. This foundation is essential for integrating autonomous agents into such loops at scale, enabling the joint learning of intervention effects and intrinsic dynamics for robust temporal representations.

AI.tldr: This Blue Sky paper argues that time-series data produced under prediction-triggered interventions, which it calls AI-shaped trajectories, should not be reused as passive data. It proposes a reflexive analysis agenda centred on the prediction-action-observation loop.
AI.motivation: Predictions in deployed systems trigger interventions that change future observations, so the recorded sequences mix intrinsic dynamics with intervention effects. Models trained on such records can treat these effects as natural phenomena and drift from the truth with each closed-loop cycle.
AI.method: The paper proposes an agenda with three components: closed-loop provenance that records predictions, policies and actions; sequence identification that estimates action effects under explicit causal assumptions; and closed-loop evaluation that separates intrinsic process prediction from policy-driven effects.
AI.result: The paper reports no experiments; it is a position paper that describes the problem with examples such as a prediction-prevented stockout and an averted medical crisis.
AI.conclusion: Reflexive time-series analysis is presented as a foundation for integrating autonomous agents into prediction loops at scale and for learning intervention effects and intrinsic dynamics jointly to obtain robust temporal representations.

title: Cumulative and Audited Guardrail Tool Evolution for LLM Agent Safety
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate in open-world environments where safety risks cannot be fully predefined. However, most existing guardrail mechanisms remain static, relying on fixed rules, prompts, or classifiers that generalize poorly to emerging risks. Here we present EVOLVE, a tool-level self-evolving defense framework that formulates agent security as a process of cumulative security evolution. Inspired by how human societies transform experiences into transferable protective knowledge, EVOLVE externalizes security knowledge into executable guardrail tools that are continuously inherited, independently audited, and iteratively refined through lifelong interaction. Across multiple benchmarks, backbone models, and embodied environments, EVOLVE consistently outperforms existing defenses across diverse risk scenarios with +22\% average F1 score. We further validate the framework in real-world robotic and autonomous agent systems. Our results suggest that scalable agent safety may require continuously evolving defense systems rather than static guardrails.

AI.tldr: EVOLVE is a tool-level self-evolving guardrail framework for LLM agents that stores security knowledge as executable guardrail tools which are inherited, audited and refined over time. The paper reports a 22% average F1 gain over existing defences.
AI.motivation: Most guardrails are static, relying on fixed rules, prompts or classifiers that generalise poorly to emerging risks that cannot be predefined in open-world environments.
AI.method: EVOLVE externalises security knowledge into executable guardrail tools that are continuously inherited across interactions, independently audited, and iteratively refined through lifelong interaction. The design is inspired by how human societies turn experience into transferable protective knowledge.
AI.result: Across multiple benchmarks, backbone models and embodied environments, EVOLVE consistently outperforms existing defences with a 22% average F1 improvement. The framework is also validated in real-world robotic and autonomous agent systems.
AI.conclusion: The authors argue that scalable agent safety may require continuously evolving defence systems rather than static guardrails.

title: FORGE: Fault-Oriented Rework Code Generation for Executable Interlocking Assembly
summary: Large language models have demonstrated strong capabilities in structured reasoning and code generation, yet identifying an assembly fault does not guarantee the ability to generate executable rework programs. In interlocking assemblies, a locally plausible repair program may violate blocking dependencies, omit required recovery operations, or terminate in an incorrect configuration. We identify this challenge as fault-conditioned executable rework generation, where models must jointly reason about structural failures and generate programs that restore constrained assembly states. To benchmark this capability, we introduce FORGE-Bench, containing 4,000 tasks across 26 interlocking assemblies with five assemblies held out for evaluating generalization to unseen structures. We further propose FORGE (Fault-Oriented Rework Code Generation for Executable Interlocking Assembly), a structured state-to-program framework that decomposes rework generation into Rework Structuring and Action Grounding. Rework Structuring captures fault-induced recovery dependencies, while Action Grounding maps these dependencies into state-conditioned executable actions. Experiments show that locally reasonable repair code is insufficient for reliable assembly recovery, and that connecting structural recovery reasoning with executable action realization is essential for verified target restoration.

AI.tldr: FORGE targets fault-conditioned executable rework generation for interlocking assemblies, where a locally plausible repair program may break blocking dependencies. It introduces FORGE-Bench with 4,000 tasks across 26 assemblies and a framework that separates rework structuring from action grounding.
AI.motivation: Identifying an assembly fault does not guarantee that a model can produce an executable repair program, because local repairs can violate blocking dependencies, omit recovery steps or end in the wrong configuration.
AI.method: FORGE decomposes rework generation into Rework Structuring, which captures fault-induced recovery dependencies, and Action Grounding, which maps those dependencies into state-conditioned executable actions. The benchmark FORGE-Bench has 4,000 tasks across 26 assemblies, with five held out to test generalisation to unseen structures.
AI.result: The experiments show that locally reasonable repair code is insufficient for reliable assembly recovery. The abstract reports no specific numeric results.
AI.conclusion: Linking structural recovery reasoning with executable action realisation is essential for verified restoration of the target assembly state.

title: EEFA: A Framework for the Ethical Evaluation of AI Agents
summary: The rapid deployment of autonomous AI agents across consequential domains including healthcare, legal services, nancial management, and enterprise workows has created an urgent governance challenge. While the eld of AI evaluation has produced sophisticated benchmarks for measuring agent capability, these frameworks measure exclusively what agents can do rather than how they do it. The ethical dimensions most critical to responsible agent deployment, in- cluding respect for human autonomy, harm avoidance, transparency and non-deception, privacy compliance, and accountability, are systematically absent from current evaluation practice. This paper addresses that gap through three contributions. First, a structured literature review of twelve leading AI agent benchmarks characterizes the ethical dimensions those bench- marks do and do not measure. Second, the Ethical Evaluation Framework for AI Agents (EEFA) is introduced as a comprehensive, operationalizable instrument for ethical agent evaluation, grounded in established AI ethics principles and designed for use by developers, auditors, and regulators. Third, a reproducible validation protocol is specied for applying the EEFA to deployed agent systems, with illustrative test scenarios across all ve framework dimensions. The EEFA is organized across ve primary dimensions: Autonomy Preservation, Harm Avoid- ance, Transparency and Non-Deception, Privacy Compliance, and Accountability and Traceabil- ity. The framework maps directly onto the requirements of the EU AI Act and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, positioning it as a practical compliance assessment instrument for high-risk AI applications. Empirical application of the framework across diverse benchmarks and agent systems is identied as a priority direction for future work.

AI.tldr: EEFA is a framework for the ethical evaluation of AI agents, organised around five dimensions: autonomy preservation, harm avoidance, transparency and non-deception, privacy compliance, and accountability and traceability. The paper also reviews twelve agent benchmarks for the ethical dimensions they cover.
AI.motivation: Agent benchmarks measure what agents can do but not how they do it, so ethical dimensions such as human autonomy, harm avoidance and privacy are largely absent from current evaluation practice, despite growing deployment in high-stakes domains.
AI.method: The paper contributes a structured literature review of twelve leading agent benchmarks, the EEFA instrument grounded in AI ethics principles, and a reproducible validation protocol with illustrative test scenarios for all five dimensions.
AI.result: The paper reports no empirical application of EEFA across benchmarks or agent systems; it states this is a priority for future work. The framework is mapped onto the requirements of the EU AI Act and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework.
AI.conclusion: EEFA is positioned as a practical compliance assessment instrument for high-risk AI applications, pending empirical validation.

title: Probing Local Conditional Fit for Diffusion Model Membership Inference
summary: Membership inference determines whether a candidate example was used to train a text-to-image diffusion model and is an important tool for auditing training-data use. We identify a directional membership signal in \emph{conditional prediction shifts}, the changes in predicted noise under alternative text conditions at a fixed noisy input: whether movement toward the alternative prediction initially lowers or raises the denoising loss from its value under the original caption. Members exhibit less room for such local improvement. To quantify this response, we propose \emph{LoFIT} (Local Conditional Fit), which measures the initial response of the denoising loss along normalized prediction shifts and aggregates it across multiple text conditions and diffusion states. LoFIT requires no target-model gradients and can be computed using only forward queries to the denoiser. Evaluations on four datasets show improved membership discrimination across fine-tuned and pretrained models. LoFIT distinguishes members early in fine-tuning, while the naive denoising-loss baseline remains near chance. Controlled comparisons show that the membership signal is concentrated in the first-order response, with little discrimination from prediction-shift magnitude alone.

AI.tldr: LoFIT is a membership inference method for text-to-image diffusion models that uses the first-order response of the denoising loss to shifts in predicted noise under alternative text conditions. It needs only forward queries to the denoiser and no target-model gradients.
AI.motivation: Auditing whether an example was used to train a diffusion model needs signals that work without model gradients. The naive denoising-loss baseline stays near chance early in fine-tuning.
AI.method: For a fixed noisy input, LoFIT measures how the denoising loss initially responds when moving along normalised prediction shifts between the original caption and alternative text conditions. It aggregates this response across multiple text conditions and diffusion states.
AI.result: Evaluations on four datasets show improved membership discrimination across fine-tuned and pretrained models. LoFIT separates members early in fine-tuning, where the naive baseline is near chance, and the signal is concentrated in the first-order response rather than shift magnitude alone.
AI.conclusion: Members show less room for local improvement under conditional prediction shifts, so this directional signal offers a gradient-free way to audit training-data use in diffusion models.

title: BasisKV: Value Latents for Communication and Key Routing
summary: Long-context large language model (LLM) inference is increasingly constrained by the cost of maintaining an ever-growing KV-cache. Low-rank K/V projections provide a promising way to compress the KV-cache with minimal quality loss, but prior work has largely optimized KV-cache compression in isolation, leaving distributed inference, especially with tensor parallelism where attention computation is partitioned across multiple GPUs, largely underexplored. We make two observations: (i) tensor-parallel communication is an important cost when deploying low-rank KV-cache compression in distributed inference; and (ii) Value compression can be associated with the output projection, allowing the same low-rank Value representation to reduce both Value-cache width and tensor-parallel communication. Based on these observations, we propose BasisKV, a low-rank KV-cache compression method for communication-intensive, long-context LLM inference. BasisKV jointly optimizes the low-rank factors across per-GPU attention partitions against the complete attention output, rather than fitting each partition in isolation. The compressed Value cache is further reused to help identify which Key pages should be accessed: it predicts part of the Key information needed for routing, while a Key-specific residual stores what cannot be recovered from Value. The original Keys are then retrieved only for the selected pages to compute exact QK scores. Across multiple LLM families and system settings, BasisKV achieves a better quality--efficiency tradeoff than existing low-rank baselines, reaching up to 1.42x end-to-end speedup under 8-GPU tensor-parallel inference. Our code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: BasisKV is a low-rank KV-cache compression method for tensor-parallel long-context inference. It uses one low-rank Value representation to reduce both Value-cache width and communication, and reuses the compressed Values to route Key page access. It reaches up to 1.42x end-to-end speedup on 8-GPU tensor-parallel inference.
AI.motivation: Prior low-rank KV-cache work optimises compression in isolation and largely ignores tensor-parallel communication, which becomes a significant cost in distributed long-context inference.
AI.method: The low-rank factors are optimised jointly across per-GPU attention partitions against the complete attention output. The compressed Value cache predicts part of the Key information used for routing, a Key-specific residual stores what Values cannot recover, and original Keys are fetched only for selected pages to compute exact QK scores.
AI.result: Across multiple LLM families and system settings, BasisKV gives a better quality-efficiency trade-off than existing low-rank baselines, with up to 1.42x end-to-end speedup under 8-GPU tensor-parallel inference.
AI.conclusion: Value compression linked to the output projection can reduce both memory and tensor-parallel communication, making low-rank KV-cache compression practical for distributed long-context serving.

title: Parallelism-Aligned Pruning and Round-Aware Context Reuse for On-Device Multimodal Agents
summary: On-device multimodal agents are limited by two deployment mismatches: pretrained attention structures may not divide evenly across the compute cores of an edge accelerator, causing irregular partitions; and standard prefix caching keeps historical visual tokens in the persistent KV cache, whose capacity grows with the number of rounds. We present PARC, which combines parallelism-aligned structured pruning with lifetime-aware KV-cache reorganization. At the model level, it uses first-order Taylor importance and grouped-query-attention-aware selection to make attention dimensions divisible by the target core count while preserving the query-to-key/value ratio and head dimension. At runtime, it separates the system prompt, persistent text history, and transient visual observations by lifetime, updating text history during tool execution so that historical images leave the persistent cache and more interaction rounds fit a fixed budget. On 2,062 GUI actions, the incremental interface shows no accuracy regression, and task-aware recovery training restores 98.7% of the action-type accuracy gap and the coordinate hit rate to the original level. Under seven-core deployment, hardware-aligned pruning reduces vision-encoder latency by 11.4%, improves decoding throughput by 23.8%, and lowers per-heap high-water memory by 12.7%; a parameter-matched control confirms that the speedup stems mainly from core alignment rather than parameter reduction.

AI.tldr: PARC makes on-device multimodal agents faster and leaner by combining parallelism-aligned structured pruning with lifetime-aware KV-cache reorganisation. Under seven-core deployment it cuts vision-encoder latency by 11.4% and raises decoding throughput by 23.8%.
AI.motivation: Pretrained attention structures often do not divide evenly across the cores of an edge accelerator, and standard prefix caching keeps historical visual tokens in the persistent KV cache, so the cache grows with the number of interaction rounds.
AI.method: Structured pruning uses first-order Taylor importance and grouped-query-attention-aware selection so that attention dimensions divide by the target core count while the query-to-key/value ratio and head dimension are kept. At runtime, the system separates the system prompt, persistent text history and transient visual observations by lifetime, and updates text history during tool execution so historical images leave the persistent cache.
AI.result: On 2,062 GUI actions, the incremental interface shows no accuracy regression, and task-aware recovery training restores 98.7% of the action-type accuracy gap and the coordinate hit rate to the original level. Under seven-core deployment, pruning reduces vision-encoder latency by 11.4%, improves decoding throughput by 23.8% and lowers per-heap high-water memory by 12.7%, and a parameter-matched control attributes the speedup mainly to core alignment.
AI.conclusion: Aligning pruning with hardware core counts and freeing transient visual tokens from the persistent cache lets on-device agents fit more interaction rounds in a fixed memory budget.

title: Widening Harm Evaluation Coverage with a Judge that Reads the World
summary: An agent acting in a stateful environment can leave evidence of harm in two places: the record of what it did and said, or the world it changed. Safety evaluations for discovering harm examine one or the other in limited ways, using either an LLM judge over the trajectory or deterministic checks over the final state. Although LLM-based verifiers that inspect the environment exist, they have been used to verify task completion, not to detect and confirm harm in a safety setting. We address this gap with an LLM that has read-only access to the environment state and is given a harm taxonomy. We evaluate this approach in three environments: two from DecodingTrust-Arena and one from OSWorld. We hold the judge model and harm taxonomy fixed, varying only what the judge observes: the trajectory, read-only tools for inspecting the environment, or both channels together. In the two DecodingTrust-Arena environments, combining the trajectory and state-only judges recalls 94 percent of confirmed harms, compared with 53 percent for the trajectory judge alone. On OS-Harm, the union recalls 77 percent, compared with 67 percent. A single judge given both channels does not perform better and produces more false negatives than the state-only judge. We also record disagreements and find that the two channels miss different episodes. These results suggest that combining verdicts from two channel-specific judges is a robust and flexible approach to detecting and verifying harm in agentic settings.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a harm-detection judge with read-only access to the environment state, and shows that combining a trajectory judge with a state-only judge recalls more confirmed harms than either alone. Results come from three agent environments.
AI.motivation: Harm evaluations usually check either the agent's trajectory with an LLM judge or the final state with deterministic checks, and LLM verifiers that inspect the environment have so far been used to verify task completion rather than detect harm.
AI.method: The authors hold the judge model and harm taxonomy fixed and vary only what the judge observes: the trajectory, read-only tools for inspecting the environment, or both. They evaluate on two DecodingTrust-Arena environments and OS-Harm from OSWorld, and compare a single judge given both channels with a union of two channel-specific judges.
AI.result: In the two DecodingTrust-Arena environments, the combined trajectory and state-only judges recall 94% of confirmed harms, against 53% for the trajectory judge alone. On OS-Harm the union recalls 77%, against 67%. A single judge given both channels performs no better and has more false negatives than the state-only judge.
AI.conclusion: Combining verdicts from two channel-specific judges is a robust and flexible way to detect and verify harm in agentic settings, because the two channels miss different episodes.

title: Measuring AI Agents as Teammates with Collaborative Intelligence
comment: 51 pages, 19 figures, 11 tables. Website: this https URL
summary: Progress in AI is often measured by what a single model can do on its own. Yet teams of AI agents are starting to make breakthroughs and discoveries in science, medicine, mathematics and software engineering. As AI begins to work in teams of agents and people, the ability to collaborate becomes a core part of their intelligence. Research on human teams has measured this ability for decades. Inspired by this, we introduce the Collaborative Intelligence Benchmark, which measures how well an AI agent works as a teammate. It contains 240 tasks across 8 dimensions of teamwork, from refusing an unsafe shortcut to checking the work that a weaker model leaves behind. Each task comes from a real record or an existing benchmark, from aviation accident reports and clinical cases to coding tasks and negotiations, and has a programmatically verifiable outcome. To isolate teamwork from individual capability, models are scored only on tasks that they can solve by themselves when they have full information. We evaluate 18 closed- and open-weight models and find that every model, across sizes and families, has clear weaknesses as a teammate, with the best model scoring only 82.2 out of 100. Frontier models almost always refuse unsafe shortcuts and report misconduct, yet they cave under interpersonal pressure, reaching the best overall deal in only 14% of conflicts, and their pass rate drops from 97% to 81% when they take over a task in which a weaker model has cheated. Crucially, general capability does not guarantee good teamwork, as models with nearly the same capability score differ by up to 11 points as teammates. The benchmark includes 160 public tasks with code and data, along with 80 held-out tasks for evaluation. As AI agents increasingly work alongside other agents and people, the ability to collaborate effectively is becoming a crucial capability to measure and develop.

AI.tldr: The Collaborative Intelligence Benchmark measures how well an AI agent works as a teammate, using 240 verifiable tasks across eight teamwork dimensions. Evaluating 18 models, the paper finds every model has clear weaknesses as a teammate, and the best scores 82.2 out of 100.
AI.motivation: AI progress is usually measured by solo capability, yet agents increasingly work in teams with other agents and people, and teamwork ability is not captured by single-model evaluation.
AI.method: Tasks are drawn from real records or existing benchmarks, including aviation accident reports, clinical cases, coding tasks and negotiations, each with a programmatically verifiable outcome. To isolate teamwork from individual capability, models are scored only on tasks they can solve alone with full information. The benchmark has 160 public tasks and 80 held-out tasks.
AI.result: Across 18 closed- and open-weight models, the best scores 82.2 out of 100. Frontier models almost always refuse unsafe shortcuts and report misconduct, but they reach the best overall deal in only 14% of conflicts under interpersonal pressure. Their pass rate drops from 97% to 81% when taking over a task in which a weaker model has cheated. Models with nearly equal capability differ by up to 11 points as teammates.
AI.conclusion: General capability does not guarantee good teamwork, so collaboration needs to be measured and developed as a distinct capability.

title: InterFuse: Interaction-Guided Adaptive Fusion of Heterogeneous Models for Payment Risk Ranking
summary: Payment platforms use view-specific models trained on transaction attributes, behavioral histories, and relational structures to rank transactions under limited review budgets. However, existing fusion methods often focus on prediction scores or interactions among model representations, with less attention to how these interactions should guide aggregation using each model's original prediction and input coverage. To address this limitation, we propose InterFuse, a fusion framework that uses a shared fusion state from cross-model interaction to guide transaction-adaptive aggregation. InterFuse encodes each model's representation, prediction score, and input coverage as a model-specific token, using learned states for unavailable outputs. Availability-aware attention updates these tokens and produces a shared fusion state. This state then guides aggregation over available models using their updated representations, original predictions, and input coverage.
