We evaluate InterFuse on an industrial payment replay and three public financial benchmarks using the same upstream models across fusion methods. InterFuse achieves the highest top-ranked recall and AUC on all four datasets, improving Recall@1% by 1.11-8.09 percentage points over the strongest baselines. Ablations show the benefits of cross-model interaction and adaptive aggregation, while industrial analyses find larger interaction gains when model predictions disagree. Additional analyses examine robustness to missing outputs and the trade-off between ranking gains and fusion latency.

AI.tldr: InterFuse is a fusion framework for heterogeneous payment-risk models that uses cross-model interaction to guide transaction-adaptive aggregation. It achieves the highest top-ranked recall and AUC on all four evaluated datasets, with Recall@1% improved by 1.11-8.09 points over the strongest baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing fusion methods focus on prediction scores or interactions among representations, paying less attention to how those interactions should guide aggregation using each model's prediction and input coverage, which matters when review budgets are limited.
AI.method: Each model's representation, prediction score and input coverage form a model-specific token, with learned states for unavailable outputs. Availability-aware attention updates these tokens into a shared fusion state, which then guides weighted aggregation over the available models.
AI.result: Evaluated on an industrial payment replay and three public financial benchmarks with the same upstream models, InterFuse achieves the highest top-ranked recall and AUC on all four datasets, improving Recall@1% by 1.11-8.09 points over the strongest baselines. Gains are larger when model predictions disagree, and the paper also reports robustness to missing outputs and a latency trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Guiding aggregation with cross-model interaction and per-transaction availability improves ranking for payment risk under limited review budgets.

title: SearchInject: Retrieval Exposure Control for Indirect Prompt Injection in Language-Model Search
comment: 6 pages, 3 tables, 6 graphs. Accepted at IEEE ICCC 2026. Author accepted manuscript. Reproducibility artifact: this https URL
summary: An indirect prompt injection can affect a search-augmented large language model only after its carrier page reaches model context. SearchInject controls this admission decision with a joint score combining retrieval relevance, search-abuse cues, instruction likelihood, and two relevance interactions. A quarantine threshold is selected under an empirical 0.5% clean-candidate false-quarantine constraint on a calibration split. Evaluation uses 300 held-out SciFact queries and held-out payload categories within four construction families already represented during development. Across 1,200 query-family outcomes per retriever, top-10 target exposure falls from 0.9408 to 0.1583 for BM25, from 0.9158 to 0.1508 for a normalized hybrid, and from 0.8450 to 0.1375 for latent semantic analysis. These are relative reductions of 83.2-83.7%; the largest absolute change in clean normalized discounted cumulative gain at rank 10 is 0.0018. The frozen threshold yields clean test false-quarantine rates of 0.59-0.65%, above the empirical calibration constraint. A query-level analytical reanalysis accounts for the repeated construction outcomes under an independent-query assumption. A separate 104-case generation follow-up records context removal but no confirmed undefended hijacks under a post hoc endpoint, so it cannot estimate a reduction in attack success. The evidence supports retrieval exposure control within the evaluated construction families; the benefit of the interaction terms at matched clean cost remains unresolved.

AI.tldr: SearchInject is an admission-control method that quarantines retrieved pages before they reach a search-augmented LLM's context, cutting top-10 target exposure of indirect prompt injections by about 83% across three retrievers. The benefit of the interaction terms remains unresolved.
AI.motivation: An indirect prompt injection can affect a search-augmented model only once its carrier page enters the context, so controlling that admission decision is the target of the defence.
AI.method: A joint score combines retrieval relevance, search-abuse cues, instruction likelihood and two relevance interactions. The quarantine threshold is chosen on a calibration split under an empirical constraint of 0.5% false quarantine on clean candidates. Evaluation uses 300 held-out SciFact queries and held-out payload categories within four construction families seen during development.
AI.result: Top-10 target exposure falls from 0.9408 to 0.1583 for BM25, from 0.9158 to 0.1508 for a normalised hybrid, and from 0.8450 to 0.1375 for latent semantic analysis, which are relative reductions of 83.2-83.7%. The largest absolute change in clean nDCG@10 is 0.0018. Clean test false-quarantine rates are 0.59-0.65%, above the calibration constraint, and a 104-case generation follow-up shows no confirmed undefended hijacks, so it cannot estimate a reduction in attack success.
AI.conclusion: The evidence supports retrieval exposure control within the evaluated construction families, but the benefit of the interaction terms at matched clean cost is still unresolved.

title: Parametric CAD Bench v3: Evaluating Agentic Parametric CAD Authoring from Text and Engineering Drawings
comment: 31 pages, 12 figures, 11 tables. Benchmark: this https URL ; tasks and leaderboard: this https URL ; scoring code: this https URL
summary: Producing an executable CAD script is not sufficient to establish that an agent has satisfied an engineering design request. Evaluation must also consider the resulting geometry, specified dimensions, and native CAD modeling history. We present Parametric CAD Bench v3, a 100-task benchmark comprising 30 text-to-CAD creation tasks, 30 text-to-CAD create-and-edit tasks, and 40 tasks that reconstruct mechanical parts from engineering drawings. Agents operate in a pinned FreeCAD environment and submit native CAD artifacts to a separate programmatic verifier. The primary metric is mean continuous task reward, combining geometry similarity and specification consistency rather than binary task success. A September 24, 2026 snapshot covers 13 model-agent systems; Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 achieves the highest overall point estimate, 61.03%, and an image-to-CAD mean reward of 84.66%. These measurements describe complete systems, not isolated model capabilities. We release versioned tasks, evaluation configurations, and inspectable result artifacts.

AI.tldr: Parametric CAD Bench v3 is a 100-task benchmark for agentic parametric CAD authoring from text and engineering drawings, scored by a continuous reward on geometry and specification consistency. Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 gets the highest overall point estimate, 61.03%.
AI.motivation: An executable CAD script does not establish that an agent met an engineering request, so evaluation must consider resulting geometry, specified dimensions and native CAD modelling history.
AI.method: The benchmark has 30 text-to-CAD creation tasks, 30 create-and-edit tasks and 40 tasks that reconstruct mechanical parts from engineering drawings. Agents work in a pinned FreeCAD environment and submit native CAD artifacts to a separate programmatic verifier, and the primary metric is mean continuous task reward.
AI.result: A September 24, 2026 snapshot covers 13 model-agent systems. Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 scores highest overall at 61.03% and an image-to-CAD mean reward of 84.66%.
AI.conclusion: The results describe complete systems rather than isolated model capabilities, and versioned tasks, configurations and inspectable artifacts are released for reproduction.

title: UPSHIFT: User Preference Steering from Human-AI Interaction Feedback Traces
summary: Personalizing large language model assistants requires adapting their responses to individual users, including the selection of content, reasoning approach, level of detail, and form of presentation. Such preferences are often latent, becoming visible only when users respond to an initial answer and request revisions. We investigate whether these feedback trajectories can be converted into a reusable personalization signal without explicit preference profiles or labels, prompt-time access to interaction histories, or model parameter updates. We introduce UPSHIFT (User Preference Steering from Human-AI Interaction Feedback Traces), a training-free method that compares the hidden representations of initial and feedback-conditioned responses within each session, averages the resulting trajectory displacements across a user's sessions, and injects the aggregated preference direction when answering a new query. The method is motivated by the implicit-preference hypothesis: although an individual conversational transition may reflect topic progression or task-specific correction, changes that recur across sessions retain a component that captures how the user wants responses to be adjusted. We validate the preference-representation capability of UPSHIFT on PrefEval. In evaluations with 40 simulated users, every tested configuration improves preference alignment over the unsteered baseline on held-out topics for both Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B; the best configuration increases macro-averaged Elo from 1364.0 to 1605.2 and from 1341.9 to 1591.8, respectively. Matched-user and positive-versus-negative controls further demonstrate that these gains arise from the user-specific preference direction and its learned orientation. These results show that interaction histories can provide compact, reusable supervision for lightweight personalization.

AI.tldr: UPSHIFT personalises LLM assistants without training or explicit profiles by averaging the hidden-state displacements between initial and feedback-conditioned responses across a user's sessions, then injecting that direction into new answers. It raises macro-averaged Elo on PrefEval for Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B.
AI.motivation: User preferences are often latent and show up only when users revise an answer. The paper asks whether these feedback trajectories can be turned into reusable personalisation signals without labels, interaction-history prompts or parameter updates.
AI.method: Within each session, the method compares hidden representations of the initial response and the feedback-conditioned response. It averages the trajectory displacements across a user's sessions, which the implicit-preference hypothesis suggests retain the recurring preference component, and injects the aggregated direction when answering a new query.
AI.result: With 40 simulated users, every tested configuration improves preference alignment over the unsteered baseline on held-out topics. The best configuration raises macro-averaged Elo from 1364.0 to 1605.2 on Qwen3-8B and from 1341.9 to 1591.8 on Qwen3-32B, and matched-user and positive-versus-negative controls attribute the gain to the user-specific direction.
AI.conclusion: Interaction histories can provide compact, reusable supervision for lightweight personalisation.

title: Chain of Faith: Policy-Internal Rewards for Reasoning Reliance
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) explanations can sound plausible while having little influence on a model's final answer. We study four rewards that use the policy's own signals to encourage reliance on generated reasoning: gradient sensitivity, confidence gaps, progressive confidence gains, and reasoning--prompt swaps. We add each reward to group relative policy optimization (GRPO) and evaluate two small instruction-tuned models on GSM8K and StrategyQA using reasoning edits, paraphrases, and prompt hints. Several configurations increase answer reliance to reasoning edits, while effects on accuracy and paraphrase robustness vary. We also observe answer copying at a high reward weight and high reliance in decomposition settings with poor task accuracy. The study compares practical objectives for reasoning reliance, confirms the trade-off between reliance and performance, and proposes four lightweight rewards that can improve reasoning reliance.

AI.tldr: The paper studies four rewards that use a policy's own signals to make chain-of-thought more influential on the final answer, and adds each to GRPO. Several configurations increase reliance on reasoning edits, with trade-offs in accuracy and paraphrase robustness.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-thought explanations can sound plausible while having little influence on the final answer, and the paper asks which practical objectives can increase reliance on generated reasoning.
AI.method: The four rewards are gradient sensitivity, confidence gaps, progressive confidence gains and reasoning-prompt swaps, each added to group relative policy optimisation (GRPO). Two small instruction-tuned models are evaluated on GSM8K and StrategyQA using reasoning edits, paraphrases and prompt hints.
AI.result: Several configurations raise answer reliance to reasoning edits, while effects on accuracy and paraphrase robustness vary. Answer copying appears at a high reward weight, and high reliance with poor task accuracy appears in decomposition settings.
AI.conclusion: The study confirms a trade-off between reliance and performance and proposes four lightweight rewards that can improve reasoning reliance.

title: Auditing Representation-Space Fraud Detection: A Bayesian IRL Framework for Calibrated Uncertainty and Its Limits
summary: Shilling detectors for recommender systems are almost always evaluated by one number, detection AUROC, with no account of when it can be trusted. We audit representation-space detection with VEIL (Variational Evaluation via Inverse-reinforcement Learning), a pairwise (Bradley-Terry) Bayesian reward-inference framework over frozen encoder embeddings, following the Bayesian auditing paradigm for LLM alignment [1]: (A) a base posterior; (B) a hierarchical ARD extension with learned confidence; and (C) a label-routed organic/attacker mixture used as an evidence-accumulation this http URL prove (Proposition 1) that no detector built on a representation invariant to a transformation of user profiles can outperform chance against an attack that is indistinguishable from organic profiles under that this http URL is near-perfect against synthetic-structure attacks (AUROC 0.936-1.000) but collapses under donor-mimicry, which clones a real user's item set and splices in 1-3 target items. Performance falls to chance on MovieLens-1M (0.48-0.51), partially degrades on Amazon Musical Instruments, and degrades least on this http URL-mimicry is not undetectable: a non-learned baseline, based on each profile's maximum raw item-set Jaccard similarity to any other profile, reaches AUROC 0.92-0.97 (average precision 0.50-0.57) on all four donor-mimicry configurations, including ML-1M, where every embedding-based score is at this http URL signal is present in the raw profiles, but LightGCN's representation discards it, placing injected profiles closer to their true donor than its zero-propagation MF reduction does (distance 1.98 vs. 3.09). Severity varies by dataset, encoder, and detection method, with no single axis predicting the others. The limit lies in the representation, not the attack, and raw-similarity checks are a necessary complement to any learned detector.

AI.tldr: VEIL is a Bayesian inverse-reinforcement-learning auditor for shilling detection in recommender systems. It is near-perfect against synthetic attacks but falls to chance against donor-mimicry, while a simple raw item-set Jaccard baseline still detects it with AUROC 0.92-0.97.
AI.motivation: Shilling detectors are usually reported by a single detection AUROC with no account of when they can be trusted, and representation-space detectors may miss attacks that look like organic profiles.
AI.method: VEIL is a pairwise Bradley-Terry Bayesian reward-inference framework over frozen encoder embeddings, with a base posterior, a hierarchical ARD extension with learned confidence, and a label-routed organic/attacker mixture. The paper proves that no detector built on a representation invariant to a transformation of user profiles can beat chance against attacks indistinguishable from organic profiles under that transformation.
AI.result: VEIL reaches AUROC 0.936-1.000 against synthetic-structure attacks but collapses under donor-mimicry, falling to 0.48-0.51 on MovieLens-1M and partially degrading on Amazon Musical Instruments. A non-learned maximum raw item-set Jaccard baseline reaches AUROC 0.92-0.97 with average precision 0.50-0.57 on all four donor-mimicry configurations, including ML-1M. LightGCN's representation discards the signal, which remains present in the raw profiles.
AI.conclusion: The limitation lies in the representation rather than the attack, and raw-similarity checks are a necessary complement to any learned detector.

title: Reap: Uncovering Monte Carlo proof search with a lightweight model
summary: We present Reap, an open framework for learning and analyzing formal proof search in Lean4. Reap implements policy-value-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search directly in Lean, sharing proof-state transitions, AND-OR search, and replay verification between inference and training rollouts. Structured action logs expose how neural predictions and tactic execution interact during search. Using this framework, we train Reaper-1, a 1.7B-parameter policy-value model, through continued pre-training, supervised tactic learning, and iterative search-based reinforcement learning. Using a separate premise selector, the final system solves 79.9% of miniF2F-test at pass@32, establishing state-of-the-art performance among open provers of comparable size while remaining competitive with substantially larger models. Beyond improved solve rates, our results suggest that RL strengthens the prover's ability to organize proofs around useful intermediate results, favoring substantial advances over repeated local adjustments. This more directed proof construction is accompanied by increasingly elaborate tactic programs: fewer explicit search decisions are needed, while more work is performed within each decision. The resulting trade-off between search effort and tactic execution cost provides insight into how learning changes the prover's problem-solving strategy.

AI.tldr: Reap is an open framework that runs policy-value-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search directly in Lean 4, and its 1.7B-parameter prover Reaper-1 solves 79.9% of miniF2F-test at pass@32. The paper claims state of the art among open provers of comparable size.
AI.motivation: Learning and analysing formal proof search in Lean 4 needs an integrated environment in which neural predictions and tactic execution can be studied together.
AI.method: Reap shares proof-state transitions, AND-OR search and replay verification between inference and training rollouts, and produces structured action logs. Reaper-1 is trained through continued pre-training, supervised tactic learning and iterative search-based reinforcement learning, with a separate premise selector.
AI.result: The final system solves 79.9% of miniF2F-test at pass@32, which the paper reports as state of the art among open provers of comparable size and competitive with substantially larger models. RL is reported to favour organising proofs around useful intermediate results, with fewer search decisions and more tactic work per decision.
AI.conclusion: RL shapes the prover's problem-solving strategy, trading search effort for more elaborate tactic execution, which gives insight into how learning changes proof search.

title: Human-Oriented World Model
summary: Supporting a person over repeated interactions requires interpreting their current state in context and anticipating its subsequent evolution. We formulate the \emph{Human-Oriented World Model} (HOWM) as a conceptual framework centered on task-relevant human states and their evolution. HOWM connects current observations and individual history with environmental and social context to organize continuing state estimation, personalized dynamics prediction, and action support. Dynamic expectations and new observations jointly inform the current estimate, which in turn anchors personalized forecasts based on shared knowledge and individual experience. An external policy relates forecasts under alternative conditions to the person's goals, preferences, and constraints when considering support. Actual responses and outcomes provide evidence for revising the state estimate and personal dynamic patterns, thereby informing subsequent estimation, prediction, and support. We illustrate the framework through hypothetical training and learning scenarios. Our research agenda asks whether accumulated interaction experience improves subsequent estimation and prediction, and whether using the model helps the person pursue their goals over time.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Human-Oriented World Model (HOWM), a conceptual framework that estimates a person's task-relevant state over time and predicts its personalised evolution to support them. It is illustrated through hypothetical scenarios and sets out a research agenda, with no experiments reported.
AI.motivation: Supporting a person across repeated interactions requires interpreting their current state in context and anticipating how it will change, which existing frameworks do not organise into one loop.
AI.method: HOWM links current observations and individual history with environmental and social context to drive continuing state estimation, personalised dynamics prediction and action support. An external policy relates forecasts under alternative conditions to the person's goals, preferences and constraints, and actual responses revise both the state estimate and personal dynamic patterns.
AI.result: The paper gives no empirical results; it illustrates the framework through hypothetical training and learning scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The research agenda asks whether accumulated interaction experience improves estimation and prediction, and whether using the model helps people pursue their goals over time.

title: GeoGuesser Bench: Benchmarking Vision-Language Agents on Interactive Geolocation
summary: Vision-language model (VLM) agents that act in the open world need two abilities: world knowledge to interpret what they see, and exploration to find what they cannot yet see. We study how agents combine the two through interactive visual geolocation. GeoGuesser Bench contains 282 tasks in an offline Street View environment where agents rotate, zoom, and move between real panoramas. Its three task types shift the balance from knowledge to exploration: agents (1) report the coordinates of their starting location, (2) name the enclosing street, city, state, or country, or (3) find, read, and count nearby objects. The coordinate tasks in (1) also include 42 real GeoGuessr World Championship rounds, whose expert guesses provide a human reference. We evaluate 23 VLMs: the best accuracy is 62.5% on place naming and 35.0% on object finding, and the best agent averages 4352.4 GeoGuessr points on the championship rounds, against 4770.3 for the better expert in each round. Beyond these headline numbers, world knowledge and exploration are only weakly correlated across models: agents that localize well do not necessarily explore well. To understand where agents fail, we categorize their errors into vision, navigation, and tool-use failures. Further ablations show that the strongest agents, such as Claude Opus 4.8, still perform well with limited views, while weaker agents degrade; customizing the environment thus adjusts task difficulty. The environment's verifiable rewards and restorable state also support training, and our Planner-Worker-Compressor harness cuts planner tokens by 57-61% by compacting the interaction history. We hope GeoGuesser Bench and its environment serve as a high-quality foundation for simulating real-world exploration at scale.

AI.tldr: GeoGuesser Bench is a benchmark of 282 interactive geolocation tasks in an offline Street View environment for testing vision-language agents on world knowledge and exploration. The best model reaches 62.5% accuracy on place naming and 35.0% on object finding.
AI.motivation: Open-world VLM agents need both world knowledge to interpret what they see and exploration to find what they cannot yet see, and the two abilities have not been measured together.
AI.method: Agents can rotate, zoom and move between real panoramas. Three task types shift emphasis from knowledge to exploration: reporting the starting coordinates, naming the enclosing street, city, state or country, and finding, reading and counting nearby objects. The coordinate tasks include 42 real GeoGuessr World Championship rounds with expert guesses as a human reference, and a Planner-Worker-Compressor harness compacts the interaction history.
AI.result: Across 23 VLMs, the best accuracy is 62.5% on place naming and 35.0% on object finding. The best agent averages 4352.4 GeoGuessr points on the championship rounds, against 4770.3 for the better expert in each round. World knowledge and exploration are only weakly correlated across models, and the harness cuts planner tokens by 57-61%.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark and its environment are offered as a foundation for simulating real-world exploration at scale, with verifiable rewards and restorable state that also support training.

title: Beyond Answers, Traces, and Efficiency: Evidence for Adaptive Reasoning
summary: Current AI systems are evaluated as reasoners through final-answer accuracy, reasoning traces, process supervision, and computational or human-relative efficiency. Yet these measures do not establish whether reasoning adapts when tasks or evidence change. We distinguish across-task adaptivity, where acquired abstractions transfer or recombine across novel problems, fromwithin-task adaptivity, where hypotheses and actions are revised in response to new observations, feedback, or counterexamples. Using ARC-AGI as a diagnostic case study rather than an alignment benchmark, we examine what existing measures leave unresolved when test-time search, sampling, or adaptation affects performance. We propose intervention-oriented evaluation that tests abstraction transfer and hypothesis revision under controlled changes to tasks and evidence, with explicit reporting of test-time procedures and budgets. This perspective supports evaluating systems for robustness, responsiveness to corrective feedback, and auditability under changing conditions.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that current reasoning evaluations, based on final answers, traces and efficiency, cannot show whether reasoning adapts when tasks or evidence change. It proposes intervention-oriented evaluation of abstraction transfer and hypothesis revision, using ARC-AGI as a diagnostic case study.
AI.motivation: Final-answer accuracy, reasoning traces, process supervision and efficiency do not establish whether a system adapts across tasks or within a task, especially when test-time search, sampling or adaptation affects performance.
AI.method: The paper separates across-task adaptivity, where abstractions transfer or recombine to novel problems, from within-task adaptivity, where hypotheses and actions are revised after new observations, feedback or counterexamples. It examines ARC-AGI as a diagnostic case and proposes evaluation that applies controlled changes to tasks and evidence, with explicit reporting of test-time procedures and budgets.
AI.result: The paper reports no new experimental results; it is a perspective that uses ARC-AGI as a case study.
AI.conclusion: The proposed evaluation supports assessing robustness, responsiveness to corrective feedback and auditability of systems under changing conditions.

title: Human-Supervised Artificial Intelligence Researchers in Electric Power Systems: Knowledge, Physics, Simulation, and Governance for Large Language Models
summary: Conclusions in power-system research require a clear evidential basis. Researchers need to understand the data sources, modelling assumptions, and solution procedures to assess the conditions under which a conclusion holds. Large language models (LLMs) can help researchers extract information from documents and translate research requests into code and tool calls, but their outputs still require physical validation. Focusing on human-supervised artificial intelligence (AI) researchers, this review examines power-system LLM applications and related scientific workflows, together with physics-grounded power AI studies, to discuss the conditions for using LLMs in scientific research. In the proposed knowledge-physics-simulation-governance framework, LLMs translate information and coordinate tasks, simulators and validation tools test models, and experts retain authority over critical assumptions, safety boundaries, and final conclusions. Research processes should preserve materials for review so that claims can be traced to their sources, computations can be reproduced, and failed attempts and approvals can be examined. On this basis, a staged development roadmap and requirements for research reporting are proposed. Evaluation should focus on research artifacts and their validation to assess whether LLMs can improve the efficiency of power-system research within clearly defined permissions.

AI.tldr: This review examines LLM applications in power-system research and proposes a knowledge-physics-simulation-governance framework in which LLMs translate and coordinate tasks while simulators validate and human experts keep authority over assumptions and conclusions.
AI.motivation: Power-system conclusions need a clear evidential basis, and LLM outputs for tasks such as document extraction and code generation still require physical validation before they can support research.
AI.method: The review covers power-system LLM applications, related scientific workflows and physics-grounded power AI studies. It proposes a staged development roadmap and requirements for research reporting, under which research materials are preserved so claims can be traced, computations reproduced and failed attempts examined.
AI.result: The paper reports no experimental results; its outputs are a framework, a staged roadmap and reporting requirements, with evaluation focused on research artefacts and their validation.
AI.conclusion: LLMs may improve the efficiency of power-system research when used within clearly defined permissions and with expert oversight of critical assumptions and conclusions.

title: MURFormer: Attention-Based Lightweight Multi-Scale Uncertainty-Guided Refinement Framework for PPG Denoising
comment: Submitted to IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics (JBHI) on 11 May 2026; currently under review
summary: Photoplethysmography (PPG) is a widely used physiological signal for its convenience but is highly susceptible to motion artifacts that degrade waveform quality and limit downstream analysis. This paper proposes MURFormer, a lightweight multi-scale uncertainty-guided refinement framework for PPG denoising through noisy-to-clean PPG mapping. MURFormer employs a newly proposed Multi-Scale Attention-Conv Fusion (MACF) block, which is designed to efficiently capture multi-scale temporal dynamics of PPG, as the fundamental building block and performs uncertainty-guided two-pass refinement prioritizing unreliable regions. The method was evaluated on the publicly available CIME dataset and on a Daily Activities dataset collected in this work, comprising paired noisy-clean PPG recordings from 24 subjects. Experimental results show that MURFormer improves both signal quality and physiological fidelity over the raw noisy input, yielding 129\% and 105\% relative signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) improvements, and 66\% and 81\% relative reductions in heart-rate mean absolute error (MAE), on the Daily Activities and CIME datasets, respectively. MURFormer also outperforms an existing denoising baseline on both datasets with a relatively small parameter count while preserving beat-level timing and waveform morphology. In addition, the model maintains strong denoising performance across varying input window lengths, suggesting that MURFormer is an effective and robust framework for practical PPG denoising. The implementation of MURFormer is publicly available at this https URL

AI.tldr: MURFormer is a lightweight attention-based network for PPG denoising that uses uncertainty-guided two-pass refinement with multi-scale attention-convolution blocks. It raises SNR by 129% and 105% and cuts heart-rate MAE by 66% and 81% on its two datasets, relative to the noisy input.
AI.motivation: Photoplethysmography is convenient but highly sensitive to motion artefacts, which degrade waveform quality and limit downstream analysis.
AI.method: The core block, Multi-Scale Attention-Conv Fusion (MACF), captures multi-scale temporal dynamics of PPG. The model performs noisy-to-clean mapping with uncertainty-guided two-pass refinement that prioritises unreliable regions.
AI.result: Evaluated on the public CIME dataset and a Daily Activities dataset of paired noisy-clean recordings from 24 subjects, MURFormer gives 129% and 105% relative SNR improvements and 66% and 81% relative reductions in heart-rate MAE on Daily Activities and CIME respectively. It also outperforms an existing denoising baseline on both datasets with a small parameter count and keeps denoising strong across window lengths.
AI.conclusion: MURFormer improves signal quality and physiological fidelity, preserving beat timing and waveform morphology, and is presented as an effective and robust denoiser for practical use.

title: AffToM: Benchmarking Recursive Affective Theory of Mind in Dynamic Multi-Party Interactions
summary: Understanding emotion in realistic social interactions requires more than recognizing facial expressions or assigning affective labels. The same event can elicit different emotions depending on what each participant knows, what they believe others know or feel, and how these nested mental states evolve over time. Existing benchmarks largely study higher-order epistemic Theory of Mind (ToM) and multimodal emotion reasoning in isolation, leaving recursive affective reasoning under asymmetric and dynamically changing information underexplored. Therefore, we introduce AffToM, a benchmark for affective ToM with 1,922 test pairs and 19,759 training pairs. AffToM evaluates Individual Affective Reasoning (IAR), which infers emotions from events and socio-cognitive context, and Multi-party Affective Reasoning (MPAR), which recursively tracks participants' nested beliefs and emotions as new evidence emerges. We develop an event-driven multi-agent generation pipeline grounded in dynamic character interaction graphs that explicitly capture event sequences, interpersonal relations, and mental-state updates. Furthermore, we propose AffToM-R1, a two-stage post-training framework combining supervised fine-tuning with perspective-aware rubric-guided reinforcement learning. Experiments show that MPAR remains challenging, with even the strongest evaluated MLLM achieving less than 60% accuracy, while AffToM-R1 improves MPAR accuracy by 13.38 percentage points over its base model. Our dataset is available at: this https URL.

AI.tldr: AffToM is a benchmark for recursive affective theory of mind in multi-party interactions, with 1,922 test pairs and 19,759 training pairs. It also proposes AffToM-R1, which raises multi-party affective reasoning accuracy by 13.38 points over its base model, while the strongest evaluated MLLM stays below 60%.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks study epistemic theory of mind and multimodal emotion reasoning separately, leaving recursive affective reasoning under asymmetric, changing information largely unexplored.
AI.method: The benchmark has two parts: Individual Affective Reasoning, which infers emotions from events and socio-cognitive context, and Multi-party Affective Reasoning, which tracks participants' nested beliefs and emotions as evidence emerges. An event-driven multi-agent pipeline grounded in dynamic character interaction graphs generates the data. AffToM-R1 combines supervised fine-tuning with perspective-aware, rubric-guided reinforcement learning.
AI.result: Multi-party affective reasoning remains hard, with the strongest evaluated MLLM below 60% accuracy. AffToM-R1 improves multi-party accuracy by 13.38 percentage points over its base model.
AI.conclusion: Recursive affective reasoning under shifting information is a challenging gap that the benchmark and training framework are designed to measure and address.

title: Is your LLM an Agressive Narcissist with Depression? Analyzing Psychological Portraits of Large Language Models
summary: Nowadays, interaction with AI requires caution not only regarding the factual reliability of generated content but also regarding personality markers that models may implicitly transmit during dialogue that can subtly influence users' perception of information. In this paper, we conduct a large-scale experimental study in which 22 large language models complete 11 psychological inventories. Furthermore, we investigate correlations between human and model responses to track the adjustments made for the users who interact with them on a daily basis. The results show that LLMs exhibit coherent and relatively stable psychological patterns. Personality traits remain largely consistent, whereas emotional and symptomatic dimensions are more variable, with anxiety and neuroticism emerging as dominant tendencies. Model explanations further suggest that LLMs generate internally consistent and safety-oriented profiles while also reflecting correlations with the users they regularly interact with.

AI.tldr: The paper administers 11 psychological inventories to 22 LLMs and finds coherent, fairly stable personality profiles, with anxiety and neuroticism as dominant tendencies. It also reports correlations between model responses and human responses.
AI.motivation: LLMs may transmit personality markers that subtly shape how users perceive information, and the paper asks whether these markers are stable and whether they track the users models interact with.
AI.method: The study is a large-scale experiment in which 22 LLMs complete 11 psychological inventories. It measures correlations between human and model responses and inspects model explanations of their profiles.
AI.result: LLMs show coherent and relatively stable psychological patterns. Personality traits stay largely consistent, while emotional and symptomatic dimensions vary more, with anxiety and neuroticism emerging as dominant tendencies. Model explanations describe internally consistent, safety-oriented profiles that also reflect correlations with users they regularly interact with.
AI.conclusion: LLM personality profiles are relatively stable but carry tendencies that can influence users, so the authors argue they warrant attention in deployment.

title: Stage-aware Multimodal Brain Graph Contrastive Learning for Neurodegenerative Disorder Diagnosis
summary: Neurodegenerative disorders are characterized by their progressive nature, with distinct stages that require precise identification and tracking of progression trajectories for accurate diagnosis. However, existing diagnostic methods often fail to fully capture the unique brain patterns associated with different stages, limiting their ability to effectively target specific stages of the disorders. To address this issue, we propose a Stage-aware Multimodal Brain Graph Contrastive Learning (smBGC) method. Specifically, smBGC introduces a stage-aware feature enhancement strategy to capture stage-specific features across all progression stages, enabling the generation of stage-aware multimodal brain graph representations. In addition, smBGC incorporates a stage-adaptive brain graph augmentation approach within a graph contrastive learning framework, facilitating multimodal fusion and improving the model's capability to distinguish between different disorder stages. Experiments on two real-world datasets demonstrate the superior performance of smBGC in various neurodegenerative disorder diagnosis tasks compared with state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: smBGC is a stage-aware multimodal brain graph contrastive learning method for diagnosing neurodegenerative disorders across progression stages. It reports superior performance over state-of-the-art methods on two real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing diagnostic methods often miss the brain patterns specific to different disease stages, which limits their ability to target particular stages of progression.
AI.method: smBGC adds a stage-aware feature enhancement strategy that captures stage-specific features and produces stage-aware multimodal brain graph representations. It uses a stage-adaptive brain graph augmentation within a graph contrastive learning framework to fuse modalities and separate disorder stages.
AI.result: Experiments on two real-world datasets show superior performance over state-of-the-art methods across various neurodegenerative disorder diagnosis tasks. The abstract gives no specific numeric results.
AI.conclusion: Stage-aware multimodal graph contrastive learning improves the distinction between disorder stages for diagnosis.

title: DrawOffer: Evidence-Grounded Longitudinal User-State Modeling for Career Support
comment: 9 pages, 4 tables. Evaluation code and aggregate results: this https URL . Core engine private; not all experiments independently reproducible
summary: Career-support assistants must distinguish user claims from evidence of current ability and withhold judgments when evidence is insufficient. DrawOffer separates language-model observation extraction from deterministic inference over source-linked records to maintain uncertain ability estimates, experience assessments, and revisable issues. We evaluate 102 fictional personas with 580 scored checkpoints, a historical full-context and Mem0 comparison, and three auxiliary knowledge-tracing datasets. On 37 test personas, DrawOffer passes 169/210 checkpoints; checkpoint-defined issue precision and recall are 0.875 and 0.636. Across three development simulations, 87.0% of checkpoint verdicts agree, including persistent failures. A cache-only development ablation replacing answer-evidence requirements with confidence-only settlement reduces majority-vote passes from 306 to 293 of 370 and issue precision from 0.927 to 0.725. Equalizing positive source weights improves predictive metrics without changing total passes; removing decay gives mixed results. These findings support an exploratory systems contribution centered on evidence sufficiency. Developer-authored scenarios, unmatched baseline models, historical test exposure, and incomplete public artifacts limit generalization and independent reproduction.

AI.tldr: DrawOffer is an evidence-grounded longitudinal user-state model for career-support assistants. It separates LLM observation extraction from deterministic inference over source-linked records, and passes 169 of 210 checkpoints on 37 test personas.
AI.motivation: Career-support assistants must distinguish user claims from evidence of current ability and withhold judgments when evidence is insufficient, which existing memory approaches do not handle well.
AI.method: The LLM extracts observations, and a deterministic inference step over source-linked records maintains uncertain ability estimates, experience assessments and revisable issues. It is evaluated on 102 fictional personas with 580 scored checkpoints, against a historical full-context baseline and Mem0, plus three auxiliary knowledge-tracing datasets.
AI.result: On 37 test personas, DrawOffer passes 169/210 checkpoints, with checkpoint-defined issue precision 0.875 and recall 0.636. Across three development simulations, 87.0% of checkpoint verdicts agree. An ablation that replaces answer-evidence requirements with confidence-only settlement lowers issue precision from 0.927 to 0.725.
AI.conclusion: The results support an exploratory systems contribution centred on evidence sufficiency, though developer-authored scenarios, unmatched baselines, historical test exposure and incomplete artefacts limit generalisation and reproduction.

title: Analysing the Narrative Paradox through Formal Models and Properties in Interactive Narrative
summary: Interactive narratives aim to let players influence the unfolding of a story while preserving a coherent and satisfying narrative progression. This creates a central tension, commonly described as the narrative paradox, between player autonomy and narrative control. Experience Managers (EMs) manage the story by determining how the narrative progresses in response to player behaviour. Although this paradox is widely discussed, it is rarely modelled in a way that supports systematic analysis, simulation, and comparison across management strategies. This paper proposes a formal framework for modelling and analysing the narrative paradox as a trade-off between interdependent properties shaped by EM decisions. We represent interactive narrative behaviour through an extended state-transition system in which world states are connected by player actions and system events. From this model, we formalize key properties involved in the paradox such as the player agency, EM controllability, author intent, and robustness, and define quantitative indicators derived from simulated plans. These indicators make it possible to compare EM strategies according to their ability to balance freedom, control, and narrative satisfaction. A case study compares different EM policies, showing how simulations can reveal correlations and conflicts between properties and identify compromise zones in the design space. This work contributes a reusable modelling and analysis framework for studying the narrative paradox and evaluating heterogeneous interactive narratives on shared formal grounds, with a focus on supporting the comparison and testing of EM strategies.

AI.tldr: The paper gives a formal framework for the narrative paradox in interactive narrative, modelling the trade-off between player agency and narrative control as interdependent properties over an extended state-transition system. A case study compares Experience Manager policies and identifies compromise zones.
AI.motivation: The tension between player autonomy and narrative control is widely discussed but rarely modelled in a way that supports systematic analysis, simulation and comparison of management strategies.
AI.method: Interactive narrative behaviour is represented as an extended state-transition system in which world states are linked by player actions and system events. Properties such as player agency, EM controllability, author intent and robustness are formalised, and quantitative indicators are derived from simulated plans.
AI.result: A case study compares different EM policies and shows how simulations reveal correlations and conflicts between properties and identify compromise zones in the design space. The paper reports no numeric results in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The framework is a reusable basis for comparing and testing Experience Manager strategies across heterogeneous interactive narratives on shared formal grounds.

title: Offline Approximate Value Iteration: A Reinforcement Learning Approach for Satellite Constellation Deployment
summary: This paper introduces a reinforcement learning-based approximate dynamic programming approach to optimize the deployment of Walker-type satellite constellations under uncertainties, including launch failures and satellite malfunctions. We formulate the problem as a Markov Decision Process that incorporates low-injection orbit launches, continuous low-thrust orbit raising, and variable satellite loads. We adopt the offline approximate value iteration solution method, using linear function approximation with basis functions and action pruning strategies to substantially reduce the computational and memory requirements for finding optimal decision policies. Preliminary results demonstrate convergence to policies with low expected costs and deployment times, both of which are lower than those of a rolling-horizon baseline, showcasing a novel application of approximate dynamic programming in space logistics.

AI.tldr: The paper applies offline approximate value iteration with linear function approximation to plan the deployment of Walker-type satellite constellations under launch failures and satellite malfunctions. Preliminary results show lower expected cost and deployment time than a rolling-horizon baseline.
AI.motivation: Constellation deployment under uncertainty is a sequential decision problem, and exact dynamic programming is computationally heavy for it.
AI.method: The deployment is modelled as a Markov decision process covering low-injection orbit launches, continuous low-thrust orbit raising and variable satellite loads. Offline approximate value iteration uses basis functions and action pruning to reduce computation and memory.
AI.result: Preliminary results show convergence to policies with low expected costs and deployment times, both lower than those of a rolling-horizon baseline. The abstract gives no numeric values.
AI.conclusion: Approximate dynamic programming is shown as a novel approach to space logistics, though the results are described as preliminary.

title: Predictive Safety Guardrails Do Not Always Make LLM Agents Safer
summary: Large language model agents increasingly take consequential actions in digital and physical environments, where safety risks may emerge only after multiple interaction steps. This has motivated world-model-driven predictive safety guardrails, which anticipate future consequences before execution. However, existing evaluations largely focus on end-to-end safety outcomes, leaving unclear whether safety gains arise from reliable prediction and faithful use of predicted risks. In this work, we systematically diagnose the prediction-to-action pipeline along three dimensions: how world-model predictions are integrated into decision making, whether the predictions themselves are reliable, and whether their content is faithfully used. Across seven policy models and two safety environments, we find that stronger prediction involvement does not yield monotonic safety gains and can reduce task completion while substantially increasing inference cost. We further find that world-model predictions remain insufficiently reliable, especially over longer horizons, where safety prediction degrades substantially relative to near-term forecasting. Finally, we find that safety gains can persist even under corrupted predictions, while locally verified predictions still leave subsequent safety violations, showing that predictive content is not faithfully incorporated into the decision process. Together, these findings expose a fundamental prediction-to-action gap in current predictive guardrails: producing more or seemingly accurate foresight is insufficient unless that foresight is both reliable and faithfully translated into safer decisions.

AI.tldr: The paper diagnoses the prediction-to-action pipeline of world-model-driven predictive safety guardrails for LLM agents, and finds that stronger prediction involvement does not give monotonic safety gains. Predictions are less reliable over long horizons and are not faithfully used in decisions.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations focus on end-to-end safety outcomes, leaving unclear whether safety gains come from reliable prediction and faithful use of predicted risks.
AI.method: The authors diagnose three dimensions across seven policy models and two safety environments: how world-model predictions are integrated into decisions, whether the predictions are reliable, and whether their content is faithfully used, including under corrupted predictions.
AI.result: Stronger prediction involvement does not yield monotonic safety gains and can reduce task completion while raising inference cost. Safety prediction degrades substantially over longer horizons relative to near-term forecasting. Safety gains persist under corrupted predictions, and locally verified predictions still leave later safety violations.
AI.conclusion: A prediction-to-action gap exists in current predictive guardrails, so more or seemingly accurate foresight is insufficient unless it is reliable and faithfully translated into safer decisions.

title: RxnMiner: A Multimodal Agent for Structured Reaction Data Extraction from Chemistry Figures
comment: 54 pages, 4 figures in the main text. Homepage: this https URL ; Code: this https URL ; Benchmark: this https URL ; Dataset: this https URL
summary: Reaction data underpin machine learning for reaction prediction, condition recommendation, and retrosynthetic planning, yet extracting these data from literature figures still requires substantial manual effort. Many figures encode multiple experiments through shared templates, substituent tables, and product grids. Recovering concrete reaction records therefore requires molecular recognition, association of evidence with individual experimental entries, and reconstruction of indirectly specified participants. We present RxnMiner, a multimodal agent system that combines an expert-informed extraction procedure with a chemistry toolbox to coordinate these operations. The agent reads molecular structures, resolves shared and entry-specific evidence, and instantiates participants from templates to assemble source-linked reaction records. We also introduce ChemRxn-Bench, a benchmark of 603 reaction figures with 8,547 manually annotated and reviewed reaction records, evaluated under a common protocol for exact molecular identity and reactant-product pairing. On this benchmark, with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next as the backbone, RxnMiner raises stereochemistry-aware reaction macro-F1 from 21.0% under direct prediction to 71.0%, compared with 25.0% for the strongest existing extraction system. Across five backbones, it also outperforms the same base agent without the extraction procedure and chemistry toolbox by 9.4 to 25.5 points. Applied without human intervention to 10,107 literature figures, RxnMiner produces a silver corpus of 88,202 source-linked reaction records.

AI.tldr: RxnMiner is a multimodal agent that extracts structured reaction records from chemistry figures by combining an expert-informed procedure with a chemistry toolbox. It raises stereochemistry-aware reaction macro-F1 to 71.0% on ChemRxn-Bench, against 25.0% for the strongest existing system.
AI.motivation: Reaction data needed for machine learning are still extracted from literature figures by hand, and figures encode many experiments through shared templates, substituent tables and product grids that require reconstruction.
AI.method: The agent recognises molecular structures, resolves shared and entry-specific evidence, and instantiates participants from templates to build source-linked reaction records. The authors also introduce ChemRxn-Bench, with 603 reaction figures and 8,547 annotated and reviewed records, evaluated on exact molecular identity and reactant-product pairing.
AI.result: With Qwen3.8-Flash-Next as backbone, RxnMiner raises stereochemistry-aware reaction macro-F1 from 21.0% under direct prediction to 71.0%, against 25.0% for the strongest existing extraction system. Across five backbones it outperforms the same base agent without the procedure and toolbox by 9.4 to 25.5 points. Applied to 10,107 literature figures, it produces a silver corpus of 88,202 source-linked records.
AI.conclusion: Structured, source-linked extraction from chemistry figures is feasible at scale, producing a silver corpus without human intervention.

title: Think with Skills: Pseudocode Planning Before Execution for Advanced Reasoners
summary: Language model agents often struggle with complex tasks even when equipped with expert-written skills. Such skills encode declarative knowledge, whereas successful execution requires procedural knowledge tailored to the task at hand. Natural language skills may leave conditions and dependencies implicit, and tasks involving multiple skills further require agents to coordinate intermediate results and execution order. We introduce Think with Skills, a method that trains reasoning models to turn relevant skill descriptions into task-specific pseudocode plans before execution. The pseudocode explicitly represents operations, conditions, intermediate results, and dependencies, providing a structured bridge from skill descriptions to agent actions. We construct training data that pairs tasks and skills with pseudocode plans and execution trajectories, use supervised fine tuning to initialize this behavior, and further optimize end-to-end task performance with Group Relative Policy Optimization. On SkillsBench, Think with Skills raises task success from 35.0% to 62.0%. These results show that proceduralizing expert knowledge before execution substantially improves skill use.

AI.tldr: Think with Skills trains reasoning models to turn relevant skill descriptions into task-specific pseudocode plans before execution. On SkillsBench it raises task success from 35.0% to 62.0%.
AI.motivation: Agents often fail at complex tasks even with expert-written skills, because skill descriptions are declarative and leave conditions, dependencies and intermediate results implicit, whereas execution needs procedural knowledge.
AI.method: The pseudocode represents operations, conditions, intermediate results and dependencies. Training data pairs tasks and skills with pseudocode plans and execution trajectories, supervised fine-tuning initialises the behaviour, and Group Relative Policy Optimization further improves end-to-end task performance.
AI.result: On SkillsBench, task success rises from 35.0% to 62.0%.
AI.conclusion: Proceduralising expert knowledge before execution substantially improves how agents use skills.

title: CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvement for Production Customer-Service Agents
summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) in production agents involves transforming accumulated experience into reliable model updates while adapting to evolving business policies. We present CARE (Customer-service Agent Retrospective and Evolve), a grounded RSI framework that operationalizes this process in customer service. Its goal is to replace a frontier proprietary incumbent with an in-house mid-sized model that continues learning after deployment. After a one-time cold start on governed production traces, the current model serves production traffic alongside the incumbent, and its own failures drive the next update. A 24/7 inspection process establishes failures through evidence-blinded, independently reviewed judgments. Attribution separates model errors from defects in Skills, tools, or the harness, routing component failures to repair. Model-attributable trajectories are truncated at the first erroneous decision and paired with verified repairs. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) then updates the model using the same model as teacher, with the diagnosis and repair supplied as privileged information unavailable to the student. To support continued evolution as business requirements change, training mixes failures from different Skill/SOP versions, each judged against the policy in force when it occurred. Candidates run an executable simulation test compiled from the latest SOP and then frozen, followed by offline inspection of the resulting traces. Promotion requires a combined simulation-and-inspection score at least at parity with the deployed version, confirmation through an online comparison with the incumbent, and human approval.

AI.tldr: CARE is a grounded recursive self-improvement framework for a production customer-service agent, aiming to replace a frontier proprietary model with an in-house mid-sized model that keeps learning after deployment. Updates come from attributed failures, and promotion needs simulation, online comparison and human approval.
AI.motivation: Production agents need to turn accumulated experience into reliable model updates while adapting to changing business policies, and the goal is to replace a frontier proprietary incumbent with an in-house model.
AI.method: After a cold start on governed production traces, the current model serves traffic alongside the incumbent. Independent, evidence-blinded inspection judges failures, and attribution separates model errors from Skill, tool or harness defects. Failing trajectories are truncated at the first error and paired with verified repairs, and on-policy self-distillation uses the same model as teacher with the diagnosis and repair as privileged information. Candidates must pass an executable simulation compiled from the latest SOP and an offline inspection, then an online comparison and human approval.
AI.result: The abstract reports no numeric results.
AI.conclusion: CARE describes a process for continual, governed improvement of a deployed customer-service model, with promotion gated by simulation, inspection, online comparison and human approval.

title: SpecOPD: Branch-Parallel On-Policy Distillation for Speculative Decoding
summary: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates large language model inference by reducing the sequential cost of token-by-token generation. Advanced SD methods reduce proposal cost with parallel drafters that predict entire blocks in one forward pass, but overall speedup still depends on acceptance length. On-policy distillation (OPD) can push well-trained drafters beyond acceptance-length plateaus, yet conventional pipelines collect supervision through sequential draft-and-verify rollouts. Our key insight is that on-policy supervision need not inherit these dependencies: a draft block can be supervised using only its reference prefix and draft-sampled history. We propose SpecOPD, a branch-parallel OPD framework that parallelizes draft sampling and target supervision across independent branches drawn from the evolving drafter policy at reference anchors. We pack these branches into proposal trees to share target-prefix computation, using tree masks for full attention, branch-consistent indexer groups for sparse attention, and indexed state replay for linear attention to preserve each branch's history. We train the drafter with an E2E-TV surrogate that directly targets acceptance length. Our study spans 8B full-attention (GQA), 27B full-linear (GQA--GDN), and 125B sparse-linear (QSA--GDN) targets, three parallel draft architectures (DFlash, DSpark, and DFlash V2), and four task domains (dialogue, coding, mathematics, and agentic). SpecOPD achieves up to 41.45% higher mean acceptance length, $16.09\times$ supervised-token throughput over sequential-rollout OPD under native configurations, and up to $3.56\times$ generation speedup over autoregressive decoding.

AI.tldr: SpecOPD parallelises draft sampling and target supervision for on-policy distillation of speculative-decoding drafters by using branch-parallel proposal trees. It reports up to 41.45% higher mean acceptance length and up to 3.56x generation speedup over autoregressive decoding.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation can push drafters past acceptance-length plateaus, but its sequential draft-and-verify rollouts are expensive. The paper observes that on-policy supervision of a draft block needs only its reference prefix and draft-sampled history.
AI.method: SpecOPD branches draft sampling and target supervision from the evolving drafter policy at reference anchors and packs the branches into proposal trees. It uses tree masks for full attention, branch-consistent indexer groups for sparse attention and indexed state replay for linear attention, and trains with an E2E-TV surrogate that targets acceptance length. The study covers 8B GQA, 27B GQA-GDN and 125B QSA-GDN targets, three parallel draft architectures and four task domains.
AI.result: SpecOPD achieves up to 41.45% higher mean acceptance length, 16.09x supervised-token throughput over sequential-rollout OPD under native configurations, and up to 3.56x generation speedup over autoregressive decoding.
AI.conclusion: Branch-parallel on-policy distillation can make drafter training much cheaper while improving acceptance length across architectures and domains.

title: TLAPS-Bench: Formally Proving Correctness of Real-World System Specifications with TLA+ Proof System
comment: 35 pages (10-page main text, references, and appendix), 7 figures, 20 tables. Benchmark and harness: this https URL
summary: TLAPS-Bench is a benchmark and execution harness for constructing machine-checked proofs for real-world system specifications in TLA+ with agentic AI. Proving correctness of complex system specifications requires discovering inductive invariants, reasoning about intricate state transitions, and decomposing proofs into tractable obligations. TLAPS-Bench provides a proof harness that supports iterative proof development atop the TLA+ Proof System (TLAPS), where agents are equipped with proof tools and libraries, with safeguards against reward hacking. Using the harness, we have employed AI agents to prove desired properties for important system specifications that were not proved before, spanning cache coherence, Byzantine consensus, and write-ahead logs. TLAPS-Bench contains 265 proof targets (each encodes a property to prove) from 95 TLA+ specifications of real-world systems. We evaluated frontier AI agents, represented by Codex with GPT models, on a subset of 70 proof targets across 12 specifications. The highest-scoring model, GPT-6.1 Sol (max), proved 31 (44.3%) proof targets. The results show challenges and opportunities in end-to-end proof development.

AI.tldr: TLAPS-Bench is a benchmark and execution harness for agents building machine-checked TLA+ proofs of real-world system specifications. The best evaluated agent, GPT-6.1 Sol (max), proves 31 of 70 tested proof targets (44.3%).
AI.motivation: Proving correctness of complex system specifications needs invariant discovery, reasoning about state transitions and decomposition into tractable obligations, and this process is not yet handled end to end by agents.
AI.method: The harness supports iterative proof development on the TLA+ Proof System, with proof tools and libraries and safeguards against reward hacking. The benchmark has 265 proof targets from 95 real-world TLA+ specifications, and Codex with GPT models is evaluated on 70 targets across 12 specifications.
AI.result: The highest-scoring model, GPT-6.1 Sol (max), proves 31 of the 70 targets (44.3%). The agents also proved properties for system specifications, spanning cache coherence, Byzantine consensus and write-ahead logs, that had not been proved before.
AI.conclusion: End-to-end proof development for real-world specifications shows both challenges and opportunities for agentic AI.

title: Value-Conditioned Proposal Acquisition for Test-Time Reasoning
summary: Sampling and selection spend test-time compute inside a candidate pool, but they cannot recover a correct answer that never enters it. We introduce ValueFormation, a test-time policy that decides after each primary-model draw whether to stop, continue sampling, or acquire one proposal from a heterogeneous reasoning specialist. The three actions are compared on one cost-regularized value scale learned from vote-state features; the calibration is frozen across tasks and primary models, and acquired proposals are accepted only through a frozen posterior comparison. On held-out MATH-500, one Llama-fitted calibration improves over the strongest of eight identically evaluated baselines by more than fifteen points for each of three 8B primaries and transfers unchanged to Qwen3-14B. Removing acquisition lowers Llama MATH accuracy by 20.43 points, while same-trace and same-access replays attribute the gain to state-conditioned acquisition rather than specialist access alone. Where primary coverage is high, as on GSM8K, acquisition is rare and gains mainly come from cheaper allocation; on MBPP, a fixed code route attains the top accuracy at the lowest interaction cost. Varying the token price monotonically reduces calls without retraining.

AI.tldr: ValueFormation is a test-time policy that decides after each draw whether to stop, keep sampling, or acquire a proposal from a heterogeneous reasoning specialist. On held-out MATH-500 it beats the strongest of eight baselines by more than fifteen points on three 8B primary models.
AI.motivation: Sampling and selection spend test-time compute only inside a candidate pool, so they cannot recover a correct answer that never enters it.
AI.method: A cost-regularised value scale learned from vote-state features compares the three actions, and the calibration is frozen across tasks and primary models. Acquired proposals are accepted only through a frozen posterior comparison.
AI.result: One Llama-fitted calibration improves over the strongest of eight baselines by more than fifteen points for each of three 8B primaries and transfers unchanged to Qwen3-14B. Removing acquisition lowers Llama MATH accuracy by 20.43 points. On GSM8K acquisition is rare and gains come mainly from cheaper allocation, and on MBPP a fixed code route gives the top accuracy at the lowest interaction cost.
AI.conclusion: State-conditioned acquisition of specialist proposals, rather than specialist access alone, drives the gains, and the token price can be varied to reduce calls without retraining.

title: Integrating Domain Adaptation and Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Saline-Alkali Land Reclamation Planning
summary: Reclamation of saline-alkali land requires management plans that account for soil and water conditions, treatment evidence, and financial constraints. This study develops Wenyao, an agricultural decision-support system integrating domain adaptation with retrieval-augmented generation. A bilingual corpus of 8,664 research papers was processed using a 110-indicator schema to construct SA-Bench, comprising 4,860 paper-level planning instances. A QwQ-32B model was adapted through low-rank supervised fine-tuning and combined with case retrieval for budget-conditioned planning. Evidence extraction achieved an F1-score of 0.83 on 300 expert-annotated papers. Without retrieval, Wenyao achieved 95.83% accuracy on 936 source-disjoint multiple-choice questions, compared with 87.93% for the strongest general-purpose baseline; removing explanatory supervision reduced accuracy to 89.42%. Matched-evidence comparisons across 69 region-budget cases supported complementary contributions from adaptation and retrieval. In a blind assessment by 31 experts, Wenyao with retrieval obtained the highest mean scores for objectives and projected outcomes, whereas GPT-5 scored highest for cost estimates. These findings support literature-informed reclamation planning with professional review, while ongoing field monitoring will assess soil and crop responses.

AI.tldr: Wenyao is an agricultural decision-support system for saline-alkali land reclamation that combines domain adaptation of QwQ-32B with retrieval of case studies. It reaches 95.83% accuracy on 936 multiple-choice questions, against 87.93% for the strongest general-purpose baseline.
AI.motivation: Reclamation planning must account for soil and water conditions, treatment evidence and financial constraints, which general-purpose models do not handle reliably.
AI.method: A bilingual corpus of 8,664 papers is processed with a 110-indicator schema to build SA-Bench, with 4,860 paper-level planning instances. QwQ-32B is adapted by low-rank supervised fine-tuning and combined with case retrieval for budget-conditioned planning.
AI.result: Evidence extraction reaches an F1-score of 0.83 on 300 expert-annotated papers. Without retrieval, Wenyao reaches 95.83% accuracy on 936 source-disjoint multiple-choice questions, against 87.93% for the strongest general-purpose baseline, and 89.42% without explanatory supervision. In a blind assessment by 31 experts, Wenyao with retrieval scores highest on objectives and projected outcomes, while GPT-5 scores highest on cost estimates.
AI.conclusion: The findings support literature-informed reclamation planning with professional review, and field monitoring is still needed to assess soil and crop responses.

title: JABER: Sequential Quality Control for Human-AI Data Annotation under Shared Bias
summary: High-quality annotations are essential for training and evaluating artificial intelligence (AI) systems. Quality control (QC) often acquires additional human or AI judgments before accepting a label. Nevertheless, shared biases can cause correlated judgments, leading conventional methods to mistake repeated agreement for independent evidence of correctness. To address this challenge, we propose JABER (Joint Alias-Preserving Belief for Evidence Routing), a bias-aware sequential QC framework that maintains a joint Bayesian posterior over label correctness and shared biases to guide evidence acquisition and termination decisions. Building on this posterior, we develop a finite-horizon algorithm that selects evidence-acquisition and termination actions to minimize expected QC loss under resource constraints. Our theoretical analysis shows that conditional-independence updating can become arbitrarily confident in an incorrect label under persistent shared bias. We further identify when repeated inspections cannot distinguish a correct label from an incorrect label supported by shared bias, when obtaining a new label can resolve this ambiguity, and why modeling the dependence between label correctness and shared bias can be necessary for QC decisions. Our experiments show that JABER reduces expected QC loss by an average of 4.65% compared with a method maintaining separate label correctness and bias probabilities when shared bias makes repeated inspections unreliable. Further, JABER's finite-horizon planning, which evaluates outcomes of successive QC actions, reduces expected QC loss by an average of 10.05% compared with a one-step lookahead method. In real-API experiments on FEVER, JABER achieves zero labeling errors while reducing QC costs by 2.67% and 16.99% compared with marginal-based belief modeling and one-step lookahead methods, respectively.

AI.tldr: JABER is a sequential quality-control framework for human-AI annotation that maintains a joint Bayesian posterior over label correctness and shared bias, so repeated agreement is not mistaken for independent evidence. It cuts expected QC loss by 4.65% against a separate-belief method and 10.05% against one-step lookahead.
AI.motivation: Shared biases among annotators or AI judges produce correlated judgments, and conventional conditional-independence updating can become arbitrarily confident in an incorrect label under persistent shared bias.
AI.method: JABER maintains a joint posterior over label correctness and shared biases to choose evidence-acquisition and termination actions. A finite-horizon algorithm minimises expected QC loss under resource constraints, and the analysis identifies when repeated inspections cannot separate a correct label from one supported by shared bias.
AI.result: JABER reduces expected QC loss by an average of 4.65% against a method keeping separate correctness and bias probabilities, and by 10.05% against one-step lookahead. On real-API experiments on FEVER it achieves zero labelling errors while reducing QC costs by 2.67% and 16.99% against marginal-based belief modelling and one-step lookahead respectively.
AI.conclusion: Modelling the dependence between label correctness and shared bias can be necessary for quality-control decisions when shared bias makes repeated inspections unreliable.

title: Bridging Low-Level Image Fusion and High-Level Semantic Understanding
summary: Remote sensing image fusion and semantic interpretation are usually optimized separately, so reconstruction quality need not preserve downstream retrieval utility. We propose LANCE, which uses structured language as an explicit, indexable semantic state. A frozen vision-language model maps the input to a closed-vocabulary text record; a language-conditioned generator fuses the imagery; and a dense verifier with a differentiable continuous summarizer re-describes the output. Text-text consistency and anti-collapse contrastive text-mask losses with negative queries close the loop without dense annotations or VLM fine-tuning. A variational EM formulation yields a per-step contraction result under regularity assumptions, distinguishing semantic faithfulness from verifier overfitting. Across seven test sets on GF2, QuickBird, WorldView-III, and WorldView-II, LANCE improves reduced-scale reference metrics by up to 11.7% (median 2.1%) over the strongest learning baseline. Independent evaluation using a held-out VLM and a supervised aerial detector yields gains of +6.4 mAP and +0.072 open-vocabulary F1 over the closest competitor. Text perturbations, cross-verifier transfer, and pseudo-RGB ablations examine the mechanisms underlying these gains. The framework connects image fusion to verifiable semantic representations for multimodal retrieval and knowledge management.

AI.tldr: LANCE uses structured language as an indexable semantic state to couple remote-sensing image fusion with semantic understanding, closing the loop with a verifier and text-consistency losses. It improves reduced-scale reference metrics by up to 11.7% (median 2.1%) over the strongest learning baseline.
AI.motivation: Remote-sensing image fusion and semantic interpretation are usually optimised separately, so reconstruction quality does not guarantee downstream retrieval utility.
AI.method: A frozen vision-language model maps the input to a closed-vocabulary text record, and a language-conditioned generator fuses the imagery. A dense verifier with a differentiable continuous summariser re-describes the output, and text-text consistency and anti-collapse contrastive text-mask losses with negative queries close the loop without dense annotations or VLM fine-tuning.
AI.result: Across seven test sets on GF2, QuickBird, WorldView-III and WorldView-II, LANCE improves reduced-scale reference metrics by up to 11.7% (median 2.1%) over the strongest learning baseline. With an independent held-out VLM and a supervised aerial detector, it gains +6.4 mAP and +0.072 open-vocabulary F1 over the closest competitor.
AI.conclusion: The framework links image fusion to verifiable semantic representations for multimodal retrieval and knowledge management, with a variational EM formulation giving a per-step contraction result under regularity assumptions.

title: What makes a theorem interesting? Operationalizing interestingness for open-ended exploration
summary: An agent that explores, whether it generates conjectures or research ideas, must decide which of them are worth keeping. This judgment of interestingness is usually delegated to a hand-picked proxy or to a language model, neither of which is known to correspond to what humans actually value. I study it for mathematical theorems, by observing which results mathematicians single out in formal libraries and in papers.
