I model each way of singling out results as an evaluator that weights features of a result's statement, its proof and dependencies, and split its weights into a shared and a subjective part. In formalized mathematics, ex-ante features predict these selections as well as a large language-model judge, and the two complement each other. Interestingness is also largely shared. One set of weights, carried mostly by structural features such as the length of the statement and of the proof and the subfields the proof draws on, accounts for most of the signal and transfers in part across formal libraries. What remains subjective depends on practices and individual authors more than on subfields. The judge's advantage lies in its knowledge of the canon, and neither the judge nor the features rely on memory of the papers. The approach, which infers what a community finds interesting from what it singles out, can be applied to other sciences.

AI.tldr: The paper operationalises interestingness for mathematical theorems by modelling which results mathematicians single out in formal libraries and papers as weighted feature evaluators. Structural features predict these selections as well as an LLM judge, and much of the signal is shared across communities.
AI.motivation: An agent that generates conjectures or research ideas must decide which results are worth keeping, but this judgment is usually handed to a hand-picked proxy or a language model, and neither is known to match what humans value.
AI.method: Each way of singling out results is modelled as an evaluator that weights features of a result's statement, proof and dependencies, split into a shared part and a subjective part. The features are ex-ante, and they are compared with a large language-model judge across formal libraries.
AI.result: In formalised mathematics, ex-ante features predict selections about as well as a large language-model judge, and the two complement each other. A shared weight set, carried mainly by structural features such as statement and proof length and the subfields the proof draws on, accounts for most of the signal and transfers in part across formal libraries. The judge's advantage lies in its knowledge of the canon.
AI.conclusion: Interestingness is largely shared within a community and can be inferred from what it singles out, with the approach potentially applicable to other sciences.

title: Why Tabular Foundation Models Excel on Relational Data They Have Never Seen
summary: Given a relational database (RDB) storing heterogeneous tabular information, how can we predict missing (or future) values in some target column of interest? As candidate targets are numerous in enterprise settings, it is preferable to avoid learning a new model from scratch each time there is a new prediction task. Frozen foundation models (FMs) based on in-context learning (ICL) and RDB-specific pre-training provide a viable solution, but the ideal design still remains largely unresolved. Perhaps unexpectedly, preliminary evidence has recently shown that existing single-table FMs (aka TFMs), when combined with suitable parameter-free relational encoders, can be quite competitive in practice despite zero exposure to RDB pre-training or relational data of any kind. In this work we first empirically confirm this phenomenon with a more diverse array of experiments. We then turn to our main contribution, namely, surfacing multiple complementary explanations for why TFMs behave so effectively. These explanations ultimately hinge on innate synergies whereby parameter-free encoders map relational effects to fixed-length embeddings that loosely mimic distributions for which TFMs were originally designed; in so doing, desirable single-table properties transfer to relational settings (e.g., convergent posterior predictive distributions). Collectively, our analysis forges new pathways for improving RDB FMs, particularly when we prioritize interpretability and inevitable integration within agentic systems.

AI.tldr: Shows that single-table tabular foundation models (TFMs), combined with parameter-free relational encoders, predict missing values in relational databases competitively despite no relational pre-training, and offers several complementary explanations for why.
AI.motivation: Predicting values in relational databases across many enterprise targets would otherwise need a new model per task; frozen foundation models based on in-context learning and RDB-specific pre-training are promising, but their ideal design is unresolved and the reason single-table models transfer to relational data was unexplained.
AI.method: The authors first confirm the effect empirically across a more diverse set of experiments, then analyse it: parameter-free encoders map relational effects to fixed-length embeddings that loosely mimic the distributions TFMs were designed for, so single-table properties such as convergent posterior predictive distributions carry over.
AI.result: The phenomenon is confirmed across a more diverse array of experiments, and multiple complementary explanations are surfaced; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: The analysis is intended to guide improvements to relational database foundation models, with emphasis on interpretability and integration into agentic systems.

title: CAREFUL-Bench: Effect-Aware, Judge-Free Evaluation of Multi-Turn LLM Function Calling
summary: The multi-turn checker of the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) evaluates final state correctness but ignores the effects of intermediate calls: extra calls are free, function documentation does not describe side effects, and the scripted user never responds to proposals. Consequently, models asking for confirmation before destructive actions are penalized; 260 of 734 reference turns in the base category perform destructive actions without confirmation. We make BFCL effect-aware without replacing it. We infer effect declarations for all 128 functions by executing them in BFCL simulators and comparing state changes, with destructive writes identified by three annotators. A judge-free replay scorer reproduces official results across all 800 reference trajectories while reporting unrequested destructive calls, duplicate writes, redundant reads, surplus steps, and their token costs. We also introduce a confirmation-aware protocol with a deterministic simulated user. Across 11 open models, effect-aware scoring preserves the official ranking but reveals substantial differences in execution quality: the leading model loses 14.0 points due to unrequested destructive calls, while surplus steps consume up to 28% of input tokens. Adding effect hints to function documentation has no impact on eight evaluated models. Allowing the simulated user to respond recovers up to four points for models that seek confirmation. However, the best model completes only six of 576 conversations requiring destructive actions with explicit confirmation. These results expose a key limitation of current function-calling benchmarks: they cannot distinguish between asking for clarification and obtaining permission before potentially destructive actions.

AI.tldr: Makes the BFCL multi-turn function-calling evaluation effect-aware and judge-free, scoring unrequested destructive calls and confirmation behaviour, and shows that current benchmarks cannot distinguish asking for clarification from obtaining permission.
AI.motivation: The BFCL multi-turn checker judges only final state correctness and ignores the side effects of intermediate calls; the scripted user never responds, so models that ask for confirmation before destructive actions are penalised.
AI.method: Effect declarations for all 128 functions are inferred by executing them in BFCL simulators and comparing state changes, with destructive writes identified by three annotators. A judge-free replay scorer reports unrequested destructive calls, duplicate writes, redundant reads, surplus steps and their token costs, and a confirmation-aware protocol adds a deterministic simulated user.
AI.result: The scorer reproduces official results across all 800 reference trajectories and preserves the official ranking of 11 open models. The leading model loses 14.0 points to unrequested destructive calls, surplus steps consume up to 28% of input tokens, effect hints in documentation have no impact on eight models, and a simulated user recovers up to four points for confirmation-seeking models. The best model completes only six of 576 conversations requiring destructive actions with explicit confirmation.
AI.conclusion: Current function-calling benchmarks cannot distinguish asking for clarification from obtaining permission before potentially destructive actions, which exposes a key limitation of these benchmarks.

title: BLPO: Beyond-Local Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
comment: 18 pages, 8 figures. Code available at this https URL
summary: Long-horizon tasks require large language model (LLM) agents to coordinate interdependent actions, a capability central to automating complex workflows. Stepwise group-based reinforcement learning provides finer credit than trajectory-level supervision, but reliable comparisons must account for differences in interaction history. Enforcing this consistency within the limited rollouts of each task can leave insufficient support for estimating action preferences. We propose Beyond-Local Policy Optimization (BLPO), which estimates task-progress advantages from experience shared across tasks and training updates. We summarize trajectory prefixes into task-progress states and abstract actions by their function, allowing corresponding decisions from different tasks to contribute to shared estimates. To control bias and noise from heterogeneous tasks, we accumulate context-relative returns in a global memory with balanced aggregation and reliability weighting. These global advantages complement local comparisons over normalized actions and trajectory-level credit without a learned critic or additional rollouts. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop with 1.5B and 7B policies show improved task success over the evaluated baselines under matched training budgets. Further analyses show faster learning and shorter trajectories with little computational overhead.

AI.tldr: Proposes BLPO, a policy optimisation method for long-horizon LLM agents that estimates task-progress advantages from experience shared across tasks, without a learned critic or additional rollouts.
AI.motivation: Stepwise group-based RL gives finer credit than trajectory-level supervision, but reliable comparisons need consistent interaction history, and within each task's limited rollouts this leaves too little support for estimating action preferences.
AI.method: Trajectory prefixes are summarised into task-progress states and actions are abstracted by function, so corresponding decisions from different tasks contribute to shared estimates; context-relative returns are accumulated in a global memory with balanced aggregation and reliability weighting, and complement local comparisons over normalised actions and trajectory-level credit.
AI.result: Under matched training budgets, BLPO improves task success over the evaluated baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop with 1.5B and 7B policies; further analyses show faster learning and shorter trajectories with little computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: Experience shared across tasks can supply useful advantage estimates for stepwise RL on long-horizon agent tasks at low cost.

title: PRIME: Predictive Routing of Interventions by Modeling Effects for Scientific Ideation
summary: Feedback-driven iteration is widely used to improve LLM-generated scientific ideas, but existing systems either leave revision decisions implicit in generation, align revisions with feedback-localized weaknesses, or restrict action selection to system-specific operations. This is problematic because problems, hypotheses, and solutions are interdependent: the location where a weakness manifests does not itself determine the revision scope that will produce a better successor. We term this phenomenon diagnosis-intervention mismatch. We introduce Predictive Routing of Interventions by Modeling Effects (PRIME), a plug-and-play feedback-to-revision decision layer for existing scientific ideators. PRIME operates in three stages: (1) Structural Attribution interprets feedback over the problem-hypothesis-solution structure without fixing a revision target; (2) Counterfactual Routing constructs alternative scope-conditioned interventions and compares their projected successor utility and risks through lightweight rollouts; and (3) Intervention Execution compiles the selected intervention into an ordered generator-facing plan with semantic actions, preservation constraints, and dependency requirements for successor generation. We validate diagnosis intervention mismatch on 112 human-annotated idea-feedback pairs. Across four benchmarks, two ideators, and fixed- and open-problem settings, PRIME improves successor quality and routing reliability over strong baselines; removing counterfactual routing reduces quality from 3.463 to 1.960 and increases route regret from 0.426 to 1.929, confirming cross-scope effect modeling as the primary source of its gains.

AI.tldr: Introduces PRIME, a plug-and-play decision layer that turns feedback on LLM-generated scientific ideas into revisions by choosing the revision scope through counterfactual routing, rather than revising at the location where the weakness appears.
AI.motivation: Existing feedback-driven idea revision leaves revision decisions implicit, aligns revisions with feedback-localised weaknesses, or restricts actions to system-specific operations, ignoring that problems, hypotheses and solutions are interdependent (diagnosis-intervention mismatch).
AI.method: PRIME has three stages: Structural Attribution interprets feedback over the problem-hypothesis-solution structure without fixing a revision target; Counterfactual Routing builds scope-conditioned interventions and compares their projected successor utility and risks through lightweight rollouts; Intervention Execution compiles the chosen intervention into an ordered plan with semantic actions, preservation constraints and dependency requirements.
AI.result: Across four benchmarks, two ideators and fixed- and open-problem settings, PRIME improves successor quality and routing reliability over strong baselines. Removing counterfactual routing reduces quality from 3.463 to 1.960 and raises route regret from 0.426 to 1.929; the mismatch itself is validated on 112 human-annotated idea-feedback pairs.
AI.conclusion: Cross-scope effect modelling is the primary source of PRIME's gains, supporting the view that revision scope should be chosen by predicted effects rather than by where the weakness shows up.

title: Networked AI: Architecture, Theory, and Applications
summary: Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly large-scale deep learning, have been driven by monolithic or offline training on massive curated datasets. While successful, these approaches face structural limitations: escalating data and computational demands, limited online adaptability, and a lack of system-level intelligence in open, non-stationary environments. This paper presents Networked AI - a networked intelligent system composed of interacting, heterogeneous, and continuously evolving AI agents. We establish a hierarchical layered architecture comprising an Agent Layer for heterogeneous capability construction, an Interaction Layer for signal-processing-guided online data extraction, and a Regulation Layer for stability-constrained collective evolution. Foundations in data science, signal processing, and system control are hereby synthesized into a unified theoretical framework of Networked AI, providing superior data efficiency, intelligence efficiency, interpretability, and scalability. Theoretical and experimental analysis demonstrates that Networked AI can approach near-linear scaling in resource demand, in contrast to the exponential increase in standalone end-to-end systems. It provides not only online adaptation to out-of-distribution environmental novelties, but also the autonomous evolution towards application-specific intelligence. Application frontiers are discussed for IoT spaces, embodied, spatial, and industrial intelligences, as well as the cellular infrastructure and beyond. Key open challenges are identified towards realizing locally autonomous, collectively intelligent, continuously evolving, globally regulated Networked AI.

AI.tldr: Proposes Networked AI, a hierarchical architecture of interacting, heterogeneous and continuously evolving AI agents, and argues it can approach near-linear scaling in resource demand while adapting online to out-of-distribution change.
AI.motivation: Monolithic or offline training on massive curated datasets faces escalating data and computational demands, limited online adaptability and a lack of system-level intelligence in open, non-stationary environments.
AI.method: The architecture has three layers: an Agent Layer for heterogeneous capability construction, an Interaction Layer for signal-processing-guided online data extraction, and a Regulation Layer for stability-constrained collective evolution; the framework synthesises data science, signal processing and system control into one theory.
AI.result: Theoretical and experimental analysis is reported to show near-linear scaling in resource demand, in contrast to exponential growth for standalone end-to-end systems; the abstract gives no specific figures.
AI.conclusion: Networked AI is presented as a unified framework for data efficiency, interpretability and scalability, with application frontiers in IoT, embodied, spatial and industrial intelligence and cellular infrastructure, and key open challenges remain.

title: Towards a Trustworthy and Governable Internet of Agentics: An Architectural Perspective on Protocols, Systems, and Services
summary: Large language model applications are increasingly being organized as tool-using and multi-agent workflows rather than as isolated chat interfaces. This perspective paper examines the architectural problem that follows from that shift: agents may reason, invoke tools, and delegate work, but dependable deployment still requires interoperability across frameworks, runtimes, data boundaries, and organizational control domains. We study this problem through the lens of the \emph{Internet of Agentics} (IoA), an emerging service-computing view in which heterogeneous agents are treated as governable service participants rather than only as stand-alone model endpoints. The paper organizes the landscape as a three-layer progression: from today's fragmented agent ecosystem, to interoperable agents, and ultimately to trustworthy and governable autonomy. First, it examines the protocol stack centered on the Agentic AI Foundation, including MCP for agent--tool interaction; A2A for agent--agent coordination; this http URL and Skills-style procedural manifests; and discovery, transport, and trust mechanisms such as AGNTCY and SLIM. Second, it reviews the systems abstractions that make agents deployable as service components, including logical agent architectures, orchestration patterns, gateways, registries, runtime control loops, and hardware-aware inference infrastructure. Third, it situates these developments within services computing, arguing that agentic systems reinterpret classical concerns from SOA and microservices---discovery, composition, governance, pricing, and trust---at the level of cognitive capabilities rather than deterministic functions.

AI.tldr: A perspective paper that frames agents as governable service participants and organises the emerging protocol, systems and services-computing landscape into a three-layer progression toward trustworthy, governable autonomy.
AI.motivation: LLM applications are shifting to tool-using multi-agent workflows, but dependable deployment requires interoperability across frameworks, runtimes, data boundaries and organisational control domains.
AI.method: Through the Internet of Agentics lens, the paper reviews the protocol stack (MCP, A2A, procedural manifests, AGNTCY and SLIM, centred on the Agentic AI Foundation), the systems abstractions that make agents deployable (orchestration patterns, gateways, registries, runtime control loops) and links these to classical SOA and microservices concerns.
AI.result: As a perspective paper it reports no experimental results; its contribution is a structured survey and conceptual framing of the landscape.
AI.conclusion: Agentic systems reinterpret service concerns such as discovery, composition, governance, pricing and trust at the level of cognitive capabilities rather than deterministic functions.

title: A Fine-Grained Hierarchy and Benchmark for State Tracking in Language Models
summary: Theoretical limitations of transformers on state tracking---the ability to track information about entities or variables over long contexts---have motivated new recurrent language modeling (LM) architectures such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN). These architectures have, in particular, been benchmarked against the $S_5$ word problem, a theoretically hard state-tracking task that captures abilities such as code evaluation under arbitrary variable assignment. It, however, remains open whether other, simpler forms of state tracking might both be more relevant in practice and already explain observed differences between these architectures. We propose evaluating state tracking using a hierarchy of word problems with four increasing levels of difficulty: r-trivial, corresponding to immutable assignment to variables in programming; aperiodic, where assignments are mutable; soluble, where assignments are self-referential; and general finite state tracking. Theoretically, we show that the class of problems transformers are thought to length-generalize on does not even contain all aperiodic state tracking. On the other hand, we prove that GDN with positive eigenvalues expresses all aperiodic problems, and the regular languages recognized by certain transformers are precisely all soluble ones, thus providing a fine-grained picture of state tracking capabilities of various architectures. Taking these ideas to practice, we construct StateBench, a 4-tier long-horizon state-tracking benchmark. Our systematic direct training experiments across architectures largely align with theoretical expectation, albeit with interesting observations at very large scale length-generalization. Additionally, we also evaluate pretrained models---both open hybrid and closed frontier ones---on StateBench, finding that none of them robustly solves even soluble state tracking, suggesting a direction for future improvement.

AI.tldr: Proposes a four-level hierarchy of word problems for state tracking in language models, proves architectural expressivity results, and introduces StateBench, a long-horizon benchmark on which no tested pretrained model robustly solves even soluble state tracking.
AI.motivation: Recurrent architectures such as Gated DeltaNet have been benchmarked on the S5 word problem, but it is unclear whether simpler forms of state tracking are more relevant in practice and explain the observed differences between architectures.
AI.method: Word problems are ordered as r-trivial (immutable variable assignment), aperiodic (mutable assignment), soluble (self-referential assignment) and general finite state tracking; the paper gives theoretical results on which architectures express each class and runs direct training experiments across architectures.
AI.result: The class of problems transformers are thought to length-generalise on does not contain all aperiodic state tracking; GDN with positive eigenvalues expresses all aperiodic problems; certain transformers recognise exactly the soluble regular languages. Direct training largely matches theory, with some observations at very large-scale length generalisation. Open hybrid and closed frontier pretrained models all fail to robustly solve even soluble tasks on StateBench.
AI.conclusion: Current models have clear room to improve on basic state tracking, and the hierarchy gives a finer-grained picture of which architectures can track which kinds of state.

title: LUCA: A Synthetic World for Experimental Reasoning
comment: 20 pages (9 pages main text, remainder appendix), 6 figures, 14 tables. NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Evaluation of Interactive Agents; non-archival
summary: An experimental agent can succeed for the wrong reasons. Evaluations, however, often focus on the outcome, not the experiments, evidence, and inferences that produced it. We introduce LUCA, a configurable synthetic world for evaluating this process under fully known ground truth. Agents learn unknown regulatory systems through budgeted experimentation, then predict unseen interventions, diagnose hidden faults, and attempt rescues. This setup allows us to evaluate experiment selection, prediction, diagnosis, and intervention separately. Across seven frontier LLMs and three baselines, these capabilities dissociate sharply. Agents frequently rescue malfunctioning systems while diagnosing the wrong fault; diagnosis varies 7x across models while prediction varies only 1.4x. Models also adopt surprisingly different experimental strategies, and greater exploration does not reliably yield better performance. In one failure mode, agents often perform the experiment needed to distinguish competing causes, but still fail to use the resulting evidence. LUCA turns these hidden failures into measurable behaviours, providing a controlled environment to study where experimental agents succeed and fail. Code: this https URL.

AI.tldr: Introduces LUCA, a synthetic world with fully known ground truth that evaluates experimental agents on experiment selection, prediction, diagnosis and intervention separately, finding that these capabilities dissociate sharply across seven frontier LLMs.
AI.motivation: Evaluations focus on outcomes rather than the experiments, evidence and inferences that produced them, so an experimental agent can succeed for the wrong reasons.
AI.method: Agents learn unknown regulatory systems through budgeted experimentation, then predict unseen interventions, diagnose hidden faults and attempt rescues, so each capability is evaluated separately in a configurable environment.
AI.result: Across seven frontier LLMs and three baselines, agents often rescue malfunctioning systems while diagnosing the wrong fault; diagnosis varies 7x across models while prediction varies 1.4x. Models adopt different experimental strategies, and more exploration does not reliably yield better performance. In one failure mode, agents run the experiment needed to distinguish competing causes but still fail to use the evidence.
AI.conclusion: Hidden failures become measurable behaviours, giving a controlled environment in which to study where experimental agents succeed and fail.

title: From Local Skills to Long-Horizon Web Tasks: Progressive Skill Exploration for LLM Web Agents
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are driving autonomous agents toward real-world environments, with the Web emerging as one of the most representative interaction scenarios. However, training Web agents with naive exploration remains challenging: successful trajectories are rare, and the sparse terminal rewards make it difficult for agents to obtain useful feedback from failed trajectories. Inspired by skill acquisition theory, we propose Skill-Composed Progressive Exploration (SCOPE), a short-to-long learning framework for long-horizon Web agents that decomposes complex task exploration into a gradual expansion process from local skills to complete task-solving capability. Specifically, SCOPE iteratively explores around local skills: Skill Discovery extracts reusable local skills and failure experiences from historical rollouts; Skill Orchestration composes discovered skills into high-level skill chains; and Skill Expansion leverages failure experiences aligned with the current skill chain to guide the agent toward exploring new subskills. Through this process, SCOPE progressively constructs task-completing skill chains across rollouts and internalizes them into the policy parameters through agentic on-policy distillation. Extensive experiments on WebArena, WebVoyager, and WebShop show that SCOPE consistently improves exploration dynamics and achieves 3.9% to 18.6% relative gains over the strongest baselines in each setting.

AI.tldr: Proposes SCOPE, a short-to-long training framework for LLM web agents that progressively builds task-completing skill chains from local skills and internalises them into the policy parameters.
AI.motivation: Naive exploration rarely produces successful trajectories for Web agents, and sparse terminal rewards give failed trajectories little useful feedback.
AI.method: SCOPE iterates Skill Discovery (extracting reusable local skills and failure experiences from rollouts), Skill Orchestration (composing skills into high-level chains) and Skill Expansion (using failures aligned with the current chain to explore new subskills), then distils the discovered chains into the policy through agentic on-policy distillation.
AI.result: On WebArena, WebVoyager and WebShop, SCOPE consistently improves exploration dynamics and achieves 3.9% to 18.6% relative gains over the strongest baseline in each setting.
AI.conclusion: Gradual expansion from local skills to complete task-solving capability is an effective way to train long-horizon web agents under sparse rewards.

title: ComplianceAtlas: A Taxonomy-Driven Agentic AI Framework for Automated AI Act Gap Analysis and Remediation
summary: Assessing regulatory compliance for high-risk AI systems requires systematic identification of technical gaps such as missing controls, in- adequate processes, or shallow evaluation of practices. Compliance officers typically admin- ister structured questionnaires collecting evi- dence of current practices, where organizations respond with descriptions of their existing pro- cesses, technical capabilities, and architectural choices. However, translating these compli- ance questionnaire responses into typed, ac- tionable gap diagnoses remains unsystematic. In this paper, we present a literature-grounded taxonomy of technical compliance gaps cover- ing areas such as accuracy, robustness, logging, and human oversight, and embed it in GapTo- Compliance, a two-stage agentic framework coordinating two specialized agents: a Gap Extraction Agent that performs hierarchical rea- soning from compliance areas to specific gap types, and a Remediation Planning Agent that ranks remediation actions from a remediation catalog via multi-signal scoring combining se- mantic similarity, regulatory alignment, and effort estimation. We evaluate this framework against four automatic compliance gap detec- tion baselines across 9 AI systems and 6 AI families. Our approach achieves a gap-type F1 of 0.831 (vs. 0.533 for the strongest baseline) and remediation P@5 of 0.872 (vs. 0.635 for retrieval methods), demonstrating promising potential for automated compliance workflows. The structured agent coordination reveals a path toward human-in-the-loop compliance systems where automated gap extraction reduces expert burden while maintaining auditability, and the taxonomy-driven design enables extension to emerging regulatory frameworks beyond

AI.tldr: Presents a taxonomy of technical compliance gaps and GapToCompliance, a two-agent framework that turns questionnaire responses into typed AI Act gap diagnoses and ranks remediation actions.
AI.motivation: Translating compliance questionnaire responses for high-risk AI systems into typed, actionable gap diagnoses is currently unsystematic.
AI.method: A literature-grounded taxonomy covers areas such as accuracy, robustness, logging and human oversight. A Gap Extraction Agent performs hierarchical reasoning from compliance areas to specific gap types; a Remediation Planning Agent ranks catalogue actions by combining semantic similarity, regulatory alignment and effort estimation.
AI.result: Over 9 AI systems from 6 AI families, the framework reaches a gap-type F1 of 0.831 versus 0.533 for the strongest of four automatic baselines, and remediation P@5 of 0.872 versus 0.635 for retrieval methods.
AI.conclusion: Structured agent coordination points toward human-in-the-loop compliance systems that reduce expert burden while keeping decisions auditable, and the taxonomy-driven design is meant to extend to emerging regulatory frameworks.

title: CUA-Master: Scaling Computer-use Agents through Open-World Recursive Improvements
summary: Despite recent advances in CUAs, their development remains constrained by the limited diversity, controllability, and reliability of interaction data. Moreover, conventional optimization pipelines lack iterative feedback, while existing recursive improvement approaches often rely on self-generated experiences, limiting ability expansion and yielding diminishing returns. To address these challenges, we introduce CUA-Master, a nested double-loop recursive improvement framework. At the system level, an outer world-data-model flywheel continuously incorporates open-world corpus and leverages evolving model weaknesses to guide subsequent data construction and optimization iterations. At the data level, an inner flywheel couples open-world seeding and autocatalytic propagation. The former mines authentic workflows as seed tasks from instructional videos, and employs visual-semantic dual-path trajectory reconstruction; The latter transforms these seeds into reusable primitives for controllable synthesis of diverse, complex, and verifiable tasks. To enable efficient and reliable trajectory collection, we further introduce a feedback-guided snapshot-rollback retry mechanism in various real environments. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CUA-Master-27B achieves competitive performance across GUI-only and GUI-CLI hybrid benchmarks, scoring 80.2 on OSWorld Verified, 36.9 on OSWorld 2.0, 43.9 on WeaveBench, and 25.0 on Agents' Last Exam. Our framework also substantially improves the quality and efficiency of data synthesis, and exhibits continuous gains across recursive iterations.

AI.tldr: Proposes CUA-Master, a nested double-loop recursive improvement framework for computer-use agents, with a 27B model scoring 80.2 on OSWorld Verified.
AI.motivation: Computer-use agent development is constrained by the limited diversity, controllability and reliability of interaction data, and existing recursive methods rely on self-generated experience, which limits ability expansion and gives diminishing returns.
AI.method: An outer world-data-model flywheel folds in open-world corpora and uses evolving model weaknesses to guide data construction. An inner flywheel couples open-world seeding (workflows mined from instructional videos, with visual-semantic dual-path trajectory reconstruction) with autocatalytic propagation of seeds into reusable primitives; a feedback-guided snapshot-rollback retry mechanism collects trajectories in real environments.
AI.result: CUA-Master-27B scores 80.2 on OSWorld Verified, 36.9 on OSWorld 2.0, 43.9 on WeaveBench and 25.0 on Agents' Last Exam, with competitive performance on GUI-only and GUI-CLI hybrid benchmarks; data synthesis quality and efficiency improve, with continuous gains across recursive iterations.
AI.conclusion: Open-world data flywheels can sustain gains across recursive iterations for computer-use agents without relying solely on self-generated experience.

title: Toward Knowledge-Centric AI: Discovering, Internalizing, and Using Explicit Knowledge Across Agents and Generations
summary: Knowledge is how understanding accumulates across people and generations: durable records that outlive their producers and that others can check, combine, teach, and correct. AI agents are now built and run by many independent users and organizations, and each agent is upgraded, replaced, or retired within months. Yet what an agent learns stays trapped in model parameters, a transient context window, or a system-specific memory store that is appended to and retrieved from rather than processed. We argue that the next generation of AI should be knowledge-centric, built around an explicit, continuously evolving knowledge layer independent of any single agent. In this loop, agents discover knowledge from their environments and trajectories; the layer internalizes it by turning fragmented, heterogeneous records and experience into composable, revisable understanding; and agents across systems and generations use the result and return new outcomes for revision. While discovery and use have advanced rapidly with large language model agents, internalization remains the bottleneck. We argue that internalization should become a persistent object of training and maintenance-centered on condition-preserving conceptualization of events and deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning across noisy, heterogeneous representations (text, tables, graphs, rules, and programs). To power this layer, we call for knowledge foundation models that provide shared neural capacity for knowledge computation, and outline a research agenda showing how an explicit knowledge layer delivers reuse, cost efficiency, auditability, and continuity across agent generations.

AI.tldr: A position paper arguing that AI should be knowledge-centric, built around an explicit, continuously evolving knowledge layer independent of any single agent, and identifying internalisation of knowledge as the bottleneck.
AI.motivation: Knowledge that agents learn stays trapped in model parameters, transient context windows or system-specific memory stores, so it is not reusable, checkable or retained across agent generations; discovery and use have advanced rapidly, but internalisation has not.
AI.method: The paper describes a loop in which agents discover knowledge, the layer internalises it by turning heterogeneous records into composable, revisable understanding, and agents reuse the result and return new outcomes. It proposes training and maintaining internalisation through condition-preserving conceptualisation of events and deductive, inductive and abductive reasoning over text, tables, graphs, rules and programs, powered by knowledge foundation models.
AI.result: The paper is a position paper and reports no experiments; it outlines a research agenda for an explicit knowledge layer.
AI.conclusion: An explicit knowledge layer is argued to deliver reuse, cost efficiency, auditability and continuity across agent generations.

title: Auto-Research Agent on MSA Organization to Improve Protein-Protein Complex Structure Prediction
summary: Protein-complex structure prediction with AlphaFold 3 depends on MSA content, depth, and cross-chain pairing. Current pipelines apply uniform recipes, typically maximizing depth and pairing by species, yet even whether cross-chain pairing helps AF3 remains contested. We show that the value of both depth and pairing is strongly target-dependent, so no single recipe is optimal across interfaces. We introduce an autonomous agent that treats a frozen AF3 as a black-box experimental instrument. For each target, the agent formulates biological hypotheses, analyzes and reorganizes the MSA, and iteratively refines sequence selection and pairing using predictor label-free signals alone. On 1{,}015 protein--protein interfaces from three benchmarks released after AF3's training cutoff, the agent improves overall interface DockQ over AF3's default pipeline and fixed MSA recipes on every benchmark, while using on average 60\% fewer MSA sequences than the default. Gains are largest for inter-species heteromers, where species-based pairing is unreliable: mean DockQ increases from 0.465 to 0.612 on FoldBench and from 0.482 to 0.562 on HD439. The improvements arise from both sequence construction and pairing policy, including deliberate this http URL results recast MSA design as a target-specific problem and show that an autonomous agent can adapt it at test time through biological reasoning and self-directed, confidence-guided experimentation.

AI.tldr: An autonomous agent treats a frozen AlphaFold 3 as a black-box instrument and reorganises the MSA for each target, improving protein-complex DockQ on three benchmarks while using on average 60% fewer MSA sequences than the default pipeline.
AI.motivation: AF3 pipelines apply uniform MSA recipes that maximise depth and pair chains by species, but the value of depth and cross-chain pairing is target-dependent, and even whether cross-chain pairing helps AF3 is contested.
AI.method: For each target, the agent formulates biological hypotheses, analyses and reorganises the MSA, and iteratively refines sequence selection and pairing using only label-free signals from the predictor.
AI.result: On 1,015 protein-protein interfaces from three benchmarks released after AF3's training cutoff, overall interface DockQ improves over the default pipeline and fixed MSA recipes on every benchmark, with 60% fewer sequences on average. Mean DockQ for inter-species heteromers rises from 0.465 to 0.612 on FoldBench and from 0.482 to 0.562 on HD439.
AI.conclusion: MSA design is a target-specific problem, and an agent can adapt it at test time through biological reasoning and confidence-guided experimentation.

title: Axion 1.0: Open Agent Foundation Models, Simplified
summary: We introduce Axion 1.0, a fully open agent foundation model that combines strong and broad agentic capabilities with a remarkably simple training recipe. Axion 1.0 is trained in only three stages: two lightweight supervised fine-tuning stages followed by reinforcement learning, without dedicated mid-training, direct preference optimization (DPO), or on-policy distillation (OPD). The first SFT stage develops strong self-contained reasoning through model-aware data construction, where we synthesize challenging problems and adversarially strengthen them based on the base model's own successful solution strategies. The second stage extends these capabilities to tool-dependent reasoning through a scalable pipeline for constructing diverse and automatically verifiable tasks grounded in real-world data sources and deterministic computation. Finally, reinforcement learning further strengthens long-horizon reasoning and interaction with external tools and environments. Despite this compact training recipe, Axion 1.0 achieves strong performance across a broad suite of agentic benchmarks and is competitive with leading commercial models on several of them. Equally importantly, Axion 1.0 is open beyond model weights: we release the complete recipe, including data construction, generation, filtering, verification, prompts, and training code, enabling the entire development process to be reproduced and extended. Axion 1.0 demonstrates that strong agent foundation models can be both open and simple, offering a practical and reproducible path toward advancing open agentic intelligence.

AI.tldr: Presents Axion 1.0, a fully open agent foundation model trained in three stages (two SFT stages followed by RL) and released with its full recipe, claimed to be competitive with leading commercial models on several agentic benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Agent foundation models are usually built with more complex pipelines involving mid-training, DPO or on-policy distillation, and open releases often omit the recipe needed to reproduce them.
AI.method: The first SFT stage builds self-contained reasoning through model-aware data construction, synthesising hard problems and adversarially strengthening them based on the base model's own successful solution strategies. The second SFT stage extends this to tool-dependent reasoning with automatically verifiable tasks grounded in real data and deterministic computation. RL then strengthens long-horizon reasoning and interaction with tools and environments.
AI.result: Strong performance across a broad suite of agentic benchmarks and competitive with leading commercial models on several of them; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Strong agent foundation models can be both open and simple, and the released data construction, filtering, verification, prompts and training code make the development process reproducible and extensible.

title: ScienceCUA: Resource-to-Skill Construction and Execution-Guided Skill Evolution for Scientific Computer Use Agents
summary: Computer-use agents for scientific software require application-specific expertise. Much of this expertise is documented in human-authored software manuals and web pages. However, turning these resources into executable, reusable skills remains challenging due to mismatches between documented and deployed software versions and differences in scope between documentation coverage and task requirements. We introduce ScienceCUA, a two-stage framework combining resource-to-skill construction with execution-guided skill evolution. First, ScienceCUA identifies tasks supported by the software from its documentation, infers operational trajectories, and generalizes them into reusable Skills. Command catalogs, syntax constraints, and shortcuts are organized separately as References for on-demand lookup. Then, ScienceCUA uses execution feedback to drive skill self-evolution by contrasting successful and failed trajectories for the same task, identifying deficiencies, revising existing skills or adding new ones, and updating the skill library only after repeated validation in real environments. To enable reliable evaluation without benchmark noise or task leakage, we introduce two improved benchmarks. ScienceBoard-Verified provides an audited and corrected basis for measuring task performance, while ScienceBoard-VE separates skill evolution from final testing through disjoint evolution and test tasks and further supports native-agent evaluation. Experiments show that the initial Skills and References improve average task success rate by up to 7.23 percentage points over the base model, while skill self-evolution increases the total gain over the baseline to as much as 17.12 percentage points. ScienceCUA turns software documentation into an evolving set of executable skills and queryable references, offering a practical way for general-purpose agents to use scientific software reliably and at scale.

AI.tldr: Proposes ScienceCUA, which converts software manuals and web documentation into executable skills and references for computer-use agents, then evolves those skills by contrasting successful and failed trajectories.
AI.motivation: Scientific software needs application-specific expertise that is documented in manuals, but turning these resources into executable, reusable skills is hard because of version mismatches and scope differences between documentation and task requirements.
AI.method: Stage one identifies tasks supported by the software from its documentation, infers operational trajectories and generalises them into Skills, with command catalogues, syntax constraints and shortcuts stored separately as References. Stage two contrasts successful and failed trajectories for the same task, revises or adds skills, and updates the library only after repeated validation in real environments. The ScienceBoard-Verified and ScienceBoard-VE benchmarks separate skill evolution from final testing.
AI.result: The initial Skills and References raise average task success by up to 7.23 percentage points over the base model, and skill self-evolution increases the total gain to as much as 17.12 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Software documentation can be turned into an evolving set of executable skills and queryable references, giving general-purpose agents a practical route to reliable use of scientific software.

title: Top-$k$ Retrieval Leaves Memory Value Undetermined
summary: A memory-augmented agent must decide which memories to keep, merge and retrieve, and its only evidence of their value is its retrieval log: the memories it retrieved in each episode and whether it succeeded. Existing methods assign every memory a value from this log, even when the log cannot separate one memory's contribution from another's. We treat the log as an experiment that nobody designed and ask which memory values it determines. Two counts answer this before any outcome is observed: how often each memory was retrieved, and how often each pair was retrieved together. From these counts, we prove that top-$k$ retrieval leaves every memory value undetermined, however many episodes are logged, and that a question with its own memories, asked once, determines at most one of their values. On fourteen standard memory benchmarks, no memory value is determined in any of 55 configurations. Both causes are choices about retrieval. We introduce LEDGER, which estimates each determined Shapley value in closed form with a confidence interval and reports every other value as undetermined. It merges memories with identical histories without losing a determined value, and it retrieves so that the next log determines more. On pooled HotpotQA, LEDGER raises the fraction of memories determined from 0.001 to 0.797, at a cost of 2.6 accuracy points on HotpotQA and with a gain of 2.7 on LoCoMo.

AI.tldr: Shows that top-k retrieval leaves memory values undetermined and introduces LEDGER, which estimates determined Shapley values in closed form with confidence intervals and reports all other values as undetermined.
AI.motivation: Memory-augmented agents assign memory values from their retrieval logs, but existing methods give every memory a value even when the log cannot separate one memory's contribution from another's.
AI.method: The retrieval log is treated as an experiment nobody designed, and two counts are used: how often each memory is retrieved and how often each pair is retrieved together. LEDGER computes each determined Shapley value in closed form with a confidence interval, merges memories with identical histories without losing a determined value, and retrieves so that the next log determines more values.
AI.result: Top-k retrieval is proved to leave every memory value undetermined however many episodes are logged, and no memory value is determined in any of 55 configurations across fourteen standard memory benchmarks. On pooled HotpotQA, the fraction of determined memories rises from 0.001 to 0.797, at a cost of 2.6 accuracy points on HotpotQA, with a gain of 2.7 on LoCoMo.
AI.conclusion: Memory values are determined only through choices about retrieval, so retrieval should be designed to make the logged evidence informative.

title: From FAIR to AI-FAIR Metadata-First Infrastructure for AI-Enabled Science
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, Code available at: this https URL
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies and their capabilities have advanced rapidly over the past few years, leading to widespread interest and adoption in the biological and ecological sciences. However, the data infrastructure and computational resources that provide the foundation for AI workflows in ecology and biodiversity science remain fragmented. Moreover, the flow of value remains largely unidirectional: data move from collectors, through repositories and aggregators into models, and finally to research products or management actions. The derived value, such as corrected taxonomies, annotations, quality flags, and insights, rarely returns to source communities. We propose an extension of the original FAIR principles to address the needs of AI-ready infrastructure: the AI-FAIR metadata criteria, which place AI-enabled science in the context of a bidirectional Question-Data-Model triangle. This framework is designed to facilitate large-scale content-based analysis across diverse collections and ensure that the scientists generating the data benefit from the AI-enabled advances built on their data. Alongside these criteria, we introduce an agentic evaluation workflow that both rates existing datasets on the AI-FAIR and traditional FAIR criteria and provides actionable feedback where critical metadata is missing or incomplete. This modular dataset evaluation tool, paired with a domain-appropriate checklist, translates these principles into a reusable assessment of machine-learning readiness, AI-readiness for specified tasks, traceability, and ethical and CARE-aligned stewardship. Through this approach we aim to create a community-informed system to close the model data loop, so that AI also enriches data to further enable scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: Extends the FAIR principles to AI-FAIR metadata criteria for AI-ready ecology and biodiversity infrastructure, and introduces an agentic workflow that rates datasets and gives feedback where critical metadata is missing.
AI.motivation: Data infrastructure for AI in ecology and biodiversity is fragmented, and value flows one way: corrected taxonomies, annotations and insights rarely return to the source communities.
AI.method: The AI-FAIR criteria place AI-enabled science in a bidirectional Question-Data-Model triangle. An agentic evaluation workflow scores datasets against AI-FAIR and traditional FAIR criteria with a domain-appropriate checklist, covering machine-learning readiness, task-specific AI readiness, traceability and ethical, CARE-aligned stewardship.
AI.result: The abstract describes a framework and a modular evaluation tool but reports no quantitative evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The aim is a community-informed system that closes the model-data loop, so that AI also enriches data and further enables scientific discovery.

title: The SIMPLE Law for Energy Cost of LLM Inference
comment: Submitted to Future Generation Computer Systems
summary: Generative AI is billed per token, yet tokens are not equally expensive. Each token enters the KV-cache and raises the cost of those that follow, so energy grows non-linearly along a sequence whose tokens look identical. No analytical model states what a token costs, and the most accurate SOTA model is a fit, not a law: it absorbs architecture into fitted coefficients, requiring per-LLM fitting. We derive closed-form expressions of the computational and memory-access complexity of LLM inference in terms of architectural hyperparameters, covering MHA and GQA, and compare a family of analytical models of increasing granularity. From these, we obtain the SIMPLE Inference Model to Predict LLMs Energy (SIMPLE), a four-parameter law that separates prefill from decode, and decode into KV-cache cost and next-token computation. Over traces of 13 dense LLMs from six families on NVIDIA H100 GPUs, it attains R2 = 0.969 and 11.97% MAPE, 3.1-3.5x below the SOTA, without per-LLM calibration. The SIMPLE law explains as well as predicts: prefill energy grows quadratically with the hidden dimension, so larger LLMs suffer most from long inputs; and more aggressive GQA KV grouping reduces the per-token energy by up to 3x relative to standard MHA. Increasing the reasoning token budget pushes output length beyond the analytically derived energy minimum, driving super-linear energy growth; although accuracy grows with the budget, energy grows faster, so Intelligence per Joule peaks at an intermediate budget and falls by up to 3.14x across a 4.0x reasoning-budget range. Agentic serving raises energy per request by 13.0x relative to non-agentic ones, driven by the growth of both the prefill and the KV-cache terms with input length; while prefix caching removes most of the prefill cost (-93%), the KV-cache term is unaffected, so even a cached agentic request costs 4.8x more.

AI.tldr: Derives closed-form complexity expressions for LLM inference and a four-parameter SIMPLE law that predicts energy per request without per-model calibration, reaching R2 = 0.969 and 11.97% MAPE over 13 dense LLMs on H100 GPUs.
AI.motivation: Each token enters the KV cache and raises the cost of the tokens after it, so energy grows non-linearly along a sequence; the most accurate existing model is a fit that needs per-LLM coefficients rather than a law.
AI.method: Closed-form computational and memory-access complexity in terms of architectural hyperparameters, covering MHA and GQA. The SIMPLE law separates prefill from decode and decomposes decode into KV-cache cost and next-token computation; it is validated on traces from 13 dense LLMs from six families on NVIDIA H100 GPUs.
AI.result: R2 = 0.969 and 11.97% MAPE, 3.1 to 3.5 times below the SOTA without per-LLM calibration. Prefill energy grows quadratically with hidden dimension, and more aggressive GQA reduces per-token energy by up to 3x relative to MHA. Intelligence per Joule peaks at an intermediate reasoning budget and falls by up to 3.14x across a 4.0x budget range. Agentic serving raises energy per request by 13.0x; prefix caching removes 93% of the prefill cost, but a cached agentic request still costs 4.8x more.
AI.conclusion: The law both explains and predicts energy use, showing that reasoning budgets and agentic workloads drive energy costs sharply upward.

title: Mixed-Methods Exploration of Sociotechnical Factors to Improve Adoption of Crime-Reporting Apps in Urban Communities
summary: Crime-reporting mobile applications can enhance community safety and engagement in urban areas, yet their adoption remains low, partly because developers prioritize technological features over residents' social realities. This study used an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design to identify and validate the sociotechnical factors that drive adoption. Two focus groups and an analysis of 660 app reviews revealed that users' initial sense of usefulness fades, whereas sustained engagement depends on perceived value (PV), comprising six dimensions: safety, anonymity, recency, autonomy, camaraderie, and accessibility. A survey of 505 urban residents, analyzed with PLS-SEM, validated PV as a formative higher-order construct formed by four of these dimensions (safety, anonymity, autonomy, and camaraderie). PV was the strongest predictor of behavioral intention, ahead of effort expectancy, facilitating conditions, and performance expectancy, and behavioral intention strongly predicted actual use. The model explained 75% of the variance in behavioral intention and 51% in actual use. The findings offer design principles for community-centered crime-reporting technologies.

AI.tldr: A mixed-methods study identifies sociotechnical factors behind the adoption of urban crime-reporting apps, finding that perceived value, built from safety, anonymity, autonomy and camaraderie, predicts behavioural intention and actual use.
AI.motivation: Crime-reporting apps can enhance community safety and engagement, but adoption remains low because developers prioritise technological features over residents' social realities.
AI.method: An exploratory sequential design: two focus groups and an analysis of 660 app reviews identified six perceived-value dimensions (safety, anonymity, recency, autonomy, camaraderie and accessibility). A survey of 505 urban residents, analysed with PLS-SEM, validated perceived value as a formative higher-order construct formed by four of them (safety, anonymity, autonomy and camaraderie).
AI.result: Perceived value was the strongest predictor of behavioural intention, ahead of effort expectancy, facilitating conditions and performance expectancy, and behavioural intention strongly predicted actual use. The model explains 75% of the variance in behavioural intention and 51% in actual use.
AI.conclusion: Community-centred design principles for crime-reporting technologies should target perceived value, particularly its safety, anonymity, autonomy and camaraderie components.

title: Can We Stop the Backtest Yet? Anytime-Valid Promotion Tests for Adaptive Financial Research Agents
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at ICAIF 2026, Milan, Italy
summary: Financial research agents can generate and monitor trading rules faster than a human can document the resulting selection process. Candidates appear at data-dependent times, weak rules are abandoned, and promising ones are watched until they cross a reporting threshold. We introduce PROMOTE, a protocol that assigns every candidate predictable testing wealth at birth and accumulates a cost-aware e-process only from subsequent returns. If lifetime allocations sum to at most one, a weighted Ville argument bounds the probability of ever promoting a rule whose declared bounded net score has always had nonpositive conditional mean. The result permits dependent candidates, adaptive births, and indefinite monitoring. We audit the implementation in two settings. A retrospective pseudo-out-of-sample replay contains 24 panel--rule hypotheses, 3,000 shared-sign null paths, injected alternatives, and public ETF and industry data. Repeated unadjusted tests produce a family crossing in 94.5% of null paths, versus 0.0% for PROMOTE; at a 15-bp aligned ETF-component perturbation, PROMOTE has 70.1% target power and median crossing session 2,327. A separate exact mean-zero experiment lets an agent select candidate identities and birth times from past scores; the funded gate has 1.77% false-family crossings across 3,000 programs. The market replay produces zero promotions after costs. The certificate controls historical false promotion under the declared null; it is not a certificate that an earlier edge remains profitable at deployment. AI-use disclosure. Generative AI tools, including OpenAI Codex, assisted manuscript preparation. For this preprint version, Codex assisted with LaTeX editing, author and venue metadata, compilation, and layout checks.

AI.tldr: Introduces PROMOTE, an anytime-valid promotion protocol for adaptive financial research agents that bounds the probability of promoting a rule whose declared net score has nonpositive conditional mean, even with dependent candidates and indefinite monitoring.
AI.motivation: Research agents generate and monitor trading rules faster than a human can document the selection process; candidates appear at data-dependent times and promising rules are watched until they cross a threshold, which inflates false promotions under standard tests.
AI.method: Each candidate is assigned predictable testing wealth at birth and accumulates a cost-aware e-process only from subsequent returns. If lifetime allocations sum to at most one, a weighted Ville argument bounds the probability of ever promoting a rule with nonpositive conditional mean.
AI.result: In a pseudo-out-of-sample replay with 24 panel-rule hypotheses and 3,000 shared-sign null paths, repeated unadjusted tests produce a family crossing in 94.5% of null paths versus 0.0% for PROMOTE; under a 15 bp aligned ETF-component perturbation, PROMOTE has 70.1% target power. In an exact mean-zero experiment the funded gate has 1.77% false-family crossings across 3,000 programs, and the market replay produces zero promotions after costs.
AI.conclusion: The certificate controls historical false promotion under the declared null, but it does not show that an earlier edge remains profitable at deployment.

title: PhoneValue-Bench: A Multimodal Benchmark and Datasets for Consumer Smartphone Recommerce Valuation
summary: As consumer smartphone recommerce scales, buyers must quote binding repurchase prices from seller-uploaded multi-view photos and diagnostic screenshots before devices reach the warehouse. Accurate remote valuation requires fusing noisy cosmetic evidence with identity, battery, lock, and channel risk from screenshots and staff forms, since an error in any modality changes both grade and payout. However, existing multimodal resources mainly target general VLM competence, screen reading, or factory defect detection, and largely overlook staff-aligned trade-in fields, dual appearance/staff ground truth, and executable valuation scorecards. This gap stems from two challenges: (1) the lack of large-scale real trade-in data with audited dual annotations and a compact ranking benchmark kept separate from training labels, and (2) the need to jointly reason over unordered multi-view cosmetics and diagnostic screens under operational deduction rules. To address these challenges, we propose PhoneValue-Bench, a dual-GT evaluation suite with tier-gated scorecards, together with PhoneValue-Corpus, a matched weakly labeled training set of over twenty thousand orders and hundreds of thousands of captioned images. We further present ValueAgent, a staged perception-fusion-valuation reference pipeline aligned with production inspection, plus an executable public scorer and submission schema. Experiments show that ValueAgent reaches a measured 84.1/100 on Bench-Full, with 97.0 appearance fill and 54.1 staff-field fill, establishing a practical dual-GT benchmark for multimodal recommerce valuation.

AI.tldr: Introduces PhoneValue-Bench, a dual-ground-truth benchmark with tier-gated scorecards for multimodal smartphone recommerce valuation, together with PhoneValue-Corpus, a weakly labelled training set, and the ValueAgent reference pipeline.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal resources focus on general VLM competence, screen reading or factory defect detection, and overlook staff-aligned trade-in fields, dual appearance and staff ground truth, and executable valuation scorecards; large-scale audited trade-in data is lacking.
AI.method: PhoneValue-Bench pairs dual ground truth with tier-gated scorecards in a compact ranking benchmark kept separate from training labels. PhoneValue-Corpus is a matched weakly labelled set of over twenty thousand orders and hundreds of thousands of captioned images. ValueAgent is a staged perception-fusion-valuation pipeline aligned with production inspection, released with an executable public scorer and submission schema.
AI.result: ValueAgent reaches a measured 84.1/100 on Bench-Full, with 97.0 appearance fill and 54.1 staff-field fill.
AI.conclusion: The suite establishes a practical dual-ground-truth benchmark for multimodal recommerce valuation.

title: Training-free Conditional Object Composition for Multi-object Image Generation with Diffusion Models
comment: Accepted for oral presentation at TAAI 2026
summary: Multi-object image generation in text-to-image diffusion models remains challenging, as existing approaches struggle to reliably generate all objects specified in a prompt. Compositional approaches that generate objects independently often fail to capture the interactions among them, whereas joint generation methods tend to suffer from inter-object interference. In this work, we propose a training-free framework, termed conditional object composition, that relaxes joint generation methods by taking one step back toward compositional approaches. Our framework decomposes the generation of $N$ objects into two stages: it first generates a subset of $N-1$ objects and then composes the remaining object conditioned on the generated content. To enable effective composition, we adopt an inpainting-based formulation with layout guidance to preserve existing regions and encourage spatially coherent placement. To address the challenge of selecting which objects to generate separately, we introduce an attention-based scoring mechanism based on cross-attention maps and further explore the use of off-the-shelf object detectors. We evaluate our method on multi-object image generation using the widely adopted MS COCO dataset. Experimental results show that our approach achieves competitive or improved performance compared to existing methods, particularly as the number of objects increases. Further studies highlight the importance of the proposed design choices. The source code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: A training-free framework for multi-object text-to-image generation that generates N-1 objects first and then composes the remaining object conditioned on them, using inpainting with layout guidance.
AI.motivation: Compositional methods that generate objects independently miss their interactions, joint generation suffers from inter-object interference, and existing approaches struggle to reliably generate all objects named in a prompt.
AI.method: Generation of N objects is split into two stages. An inpainting-based formulation with layout guidance preserves existing regions and encourages spatially coherent placement, and an attention-based score computed from cross-attention maps, optionally with off-the-shelf object detectors, selects which objects to generate separately.
AI.result: On MS COCO, the approach achieves competitive or improved performance relative to existing methods, particularly as the number of objects increases.
AI.conclusion: Relaxing joint generation toward compositional generation improves multi-object image generation without any training, and the proposed design choices matter.

title: UniCaMo: Unified Camera and Motion Control for Video Diffusion Models
comment: Qualitative videos are available on our project page: this https URL
summary: We present \textbf{UniCaMo}, an unified framework for joint control of camera and object motion in image-and-text-to-video diffusion models. Given a reference image, text prompt, sparse 3D object trajectories, and a 3D camera trajectory, UniCaMo constructs motion-consistent input noise that directly encodes the desired motion. Our 3D-grounded noise construction combines reference-derived noise propagation with a spherical Gaussian noise representation for newly revealed regions, providing a simple and effective motion prior without requiring reconstruction of unseen scene geometry. UniCaMo requires no architectural modifications or dedicated control modules and can be adapted using lightweight LoRA fine-tuning with low training data volume. Experiments on standard controllable video generation benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art motion controllability and high visual quality with minimal inference overhead.

AI.tldr: Presents UniCaMo, which jointly controls camera and object motion in image-and-text-to-video diffusion by constructing motion-consistent input noise, requiring no architectural changes and only lightweight LoRA fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: The goal is joint control of camera and object motion without modifying the architecture or reconstructing the geometry of unseen scene regions.
AI.method: Given a reference image, a text prompt, sparse 3D object trajectories and a 3D camera trajectory, 3D-grounded noise construction combines reference-derived noise propagation with a spherical Gaussian noise representation for newly revealed regions, providing a motion prior. The model is adapted with LoRA using low training data volume.
AI.result: The method reports state-of-the-art motion controllability and high visual quality on standard controllable video generation benchmarks, with minimal inference overhead; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Motion-consistent input noise is presented as a simple and effective motion prior for joint camera and object control.

title: Beyond Temporal Overlap: Consumer-Aware Evaluation of Sign-Language Segmentation across Three Corpora
comment: Submitted to IEEE FG 2027. 9 pages, 4 figures. Supplementary material included
summary: Sign-language segmentation divides continuous signing into clips. In this study, the downstream consumer is a frozen recognizer that assigns one sign label to each predicted clip. Existing metrics instead compare predicted clips with manually annotated boundaries. They do not directly measure whether a clip preserves the visual evidence needed by the recognizer or whether the segmenter produces too many clips. We therefore ask whether overlap metrics and this consumer prefer the same segmenter. We evaluate 27 outputs from three segmentation architectures, three random seeds, and three corpora. Controlled boundary edits separate the effect of removing sign evidence from that of adding surrounding context. Overlap predicts recognition on average, but it does not always determine model choice. At the same intersection-over-union, different recognizers can prefer the shorter or the longer clip. The real outputs reveal two operating regimes. On DGS, overlap, recognition, and sequence error select the same model. On BSL, recognition-based selection recovers and recognizes more reference signs but increases word error rate (WER). Dicta-Sign shows the reverse trade-off: WER selection reduces in-vocabulary WER by 31.17 points but misses more recognizable signs. Segmenters should therefore be evaluated on four axes: temporal agreement, reference recovery, clip recognition, and sequence error, rather than on overlap alone.

AI.tldr: Argues that sign-language segmenters should be judged by whether their clips serve a frozen recognizer, showing that overlap metrics do not always select the same model as recognition-based criteria.
AI.motivation: Existing metrics compare predicted clips with manually annotated boundaries, so they do not measure whether clips preserve the visual evidence a recognizer needs or whether the segmenter produces too many clips.
AI.method: Evaluates 27 outputs from three segmentation architectures, three random seeds and three corpora, with controlled boundary edits that separate the effect of removing sign evidence from that of adding surrounding context, comparing overlap, recognition and sequence error.
AI.result: Overlap predicts recognition on average but does not always determine model choice; at the same IoU, different recognizers can prefer shorter or longer clips. On DGS, overlap, recognition and sequence error select the same model. On BSL, recognition-based selection recovers and recognises more reference signs but increases word error rate (WER). On Dicta-Sign, WER selection reduces in-vocabulary WER by 31.17 points but misses more recognisable signs.
AI.conclusion: Segmenters should be evaluated on four axes (temporal agreement, reference recovery, clip recognition and sequence error) rather than on overlap alone.

title: Answer Correction with Verifiable Rewards: A Gemma-Family Study of Multi-View Driving QA
summary: Multi-camera driving question answering provides a discrete test of vision-language models, but post-training gains can reflect changed selected answers or improved answer extraction. We investigate this distinction within the Gemma model family using archived, task-linked WaymoQA evaluations. A zero-shot diagnostic on 5,519 test questions spans effective-small, mixture-of-experts, unified, and dense checkpoints, with serving differences disclosed rather than interpreted as architecture effects. The strongest controlled evidence is a matched-harness Gemma-4-12B base/GRPO pair: accuracy rises from 73.78% to 75.43%, a gain of 1.65 percentage points with a scene-cluster bootstrap interval of [+0.84, +2.41]. There are 215 improvements and 124 regressions; 213 improvements start from an extractable but incorrect base answer, and only two recover previously unextractable responses. Crossing correctness with extraction state shows why correct noncompliant outputs cannot be counted as prediction errors. Category counts reveal a critical safety asymmetry: routine perception gains (+5.93 pp) mask a regression in safety-critical hazard prediction (-1.82 pp), demonstrating that unweighted outcome rewards can trade off rare edge cases for aggregate accuracy. Reward saturation describes sampled training dynamics rather than an architectural ceiling. A separate archived Gemma-31B thinking comparison yields no detected average improvement, with uncertainty that does not establish equivalence. These results support a modest answer-selection gain for the recorded tuning configuration and a reproducible diagnostic accounting, without attributing corrected labels to specific grounding mechanisms or claiming superiority over matched supervised tuning.

AI.tldr: A Gemma-family study on multi-view driving QA finds that a 1.65-point GRPO gain comes from changed selected answers, and that routine perception gains mask a regression in safety-critical hazard prediction.
AI.motivation: Post-training gains on multi-camera driving QA may reflect changed selected answers or improved answer extraction, and these two sources need to be separated.
AI.method: A zero-shot diagnostic on 5,519 WaymoQA test questions across Gemma checkpoints, with serving differences disclosed; a matched-harness Gemma-4-12B base versus GRPO comparison with a scene-cluster bootstrap; crossing of correctness with extraction state; and category-level accounting of errors.
AI.result: Accuracy rises from 73.78% to 75.43% (a gain of 1.65 points, scene-cluster bootstrap interval [+0.84, +2.41]), with 215 improvements and 124 regressions; 213 improvements start from an extractable but incorrect base answer. Routine perception gains are +5.93 points while safety-critical hazard prediction regresses by 1.82 points. A Gemma-31B thinking comparison detects no average improvement.
AI.conclusion: The gain supports a modest answer-selection improvement for the recorded tuning configuration, and unweighted outcome rewards can trade rare edge cases for aggregate accuracy.

title: Running a 20B Video Diffusion Transformer on Consumer Hardware: A Deployment and Measurement Report for MiniMax H3 on Apple Silicon
comment: Also published as a Zenodo record, DOI https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23803987
summary: We report the end-to-end deployment and measurement of MiniMax H3, a 20.38-billion-parameter video diffusion transformer (DiT) - the count measured from the safetensors headers of the Q8 checkpoint as deployed locally (Section 3.2) - running entirely on consumer Apple Silicon hardware: an Apple Mac mini with M5 Pro chip and 64 GiB of unified memory. Using the official bf16-to-Q8 (8-bit, group size 64) quantization path executed locally on the machine, we produced a working text-to-video pipeline with no cloud dependency. We document the full deployment procedure, including two non-trivial blockers and their fixes, and report measured figures for build time, peak memory, and per-clip render latency across four resolution tiers (Draft 384x640 through Native 768x1344). A 15.08-second 576x1024 clip rendered in 4838.49 seconds with a measured MLX peak of 27.467 GiB. We further operated the system as an unattended production pipeline, completing 17 clips in 26.49 hours with zero render failures. A blind human review of the 17 production clips (generation prompts withheld) averaged 3.12, 3.18, and 2.94 out of 5 for structural integrity, temporal consistency, and visible artifacts. All figures in this report are our own measurements except where explicitly labeled as third-party data. This is a systems/empirical report; we make no claim of model innovation.

AI.tldr: A systems report on running MiniMax H3, a 20.38-billion-parameter video diffusion transformer quantised to Q8, entirely on a Mac mini with an M5 Pro chip and 64 GiB of unified memory, with measured build time, memory, latency and production reliability.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to document a full deployment and measurement of a large video DiT on consumer Apple Silicon hardware with no cloud dependency.
AI.method: The official bf16-to-Q8 (8-bit, group size 64) quantisation path is run locally.
