The deployment procedure is documented, including two blockers and their fixes, and build time, peak memory and per-clip latency are measured across four resolution tiers from Draft 384x640 to Native 768x1344; the system is then operated as an unattended production pipeline.
AI.result: A 15.08-second 576x1024 clip renders in 4838.49 seconds with a measured MLX peak of 27.467 GiB; 17 clips are completed in 26.49 hours with zero render failures. A blind human review averages 3.12, 3.18 and 2.94 out of 5 for structural integrity, temporal consistency and visible artifacts respectively.
AI.conclusion: The paper is a systems and empirical report that makes no claim of model innovation; it documents what local video generation on consumer hardware can achieve in practice.

title: Toward Counterfactual Learning for Selective Re-Examination in Agentic Visual Search
summary: Visual search over high-resolution images requires a vision-language model (VLM) not only to determine where to inspect, but also whether another observation is warranted before committing to an answer. Existing prompting, demonstrations, and outcome-based reinforcement learning can encourage re-examination, yet do not directly supervise whether it is beneficial at a particular search state. We introduce ReSee, a benchmark of re-examination decisions comprising 3,227 visual-search trajectories and 8,827 explicit commit-or-re-examine decisions, with counterfactual adjudication that distinguishes states where additional inspection is warranted from those where commitment is preferable. Building on this formulation, we propose CARE (Counterfactual Advantage for Re-Examination), a decision-level reinforcement learning method that compares paired continuations under commit and re-examine verdicts from the same search state. Their cost-aware return difference estimates the counterfactual value of an additional observation and is assigned only to the corresponding verdict tokens, providing localized credit for whether search should continue. Experiments expose limited re-examination selectivity in existing VLMs and show that CARE significantly improves accuracy and decision selectivity over GRPO across two backbones, with higher accuracy and fewer visual requests on six unseen OOD benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Introduces ReSee, a benchmark of commit-or-re-examine decisions in visual search, and CARE, a decision-level RL method that uses counterfactual return differences to supervise whether another observation is warranted.
AI.motivation: Prompting, demonstrations and outcome-based RL can encourage re-examination, but none directly supervises whether re-examination is beneficial at a particular search state.
AI.method: ReSee comprises 3,227 visual-search trajectories and 8,827 explicit commit-or-re-examine decisions with counterfactual adjudication. CARE compares paired continuations under commit and re-examine verdicts from the same search state, and assigns the cost-aware return difference only to the corresponding verdict tokens.
AI.result: Experiments expose limited re-examination selectivity in existing VLMs. CARE significantly improves accuracy and decision selectivity over GRPO across two backbones, with higher accuracy and fewer visual requests on six unseen OOD benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Localised counterfactual credit gives a supervised signal for when an additional observation is worth its cost during high-resolution visual search.

title: Wave Forcing: Towards Speed-of-Light Streaming Video Generation
summary: Real-time long-video generation requires continuous output with consistent appearance and natural motion. Existing chunk-wise autoregressive methods face challenges in both generation efficiency and long-video quality: serialized denoising and history-cache refresh require two forward passes even with one-step denoising, and longer rollouts can degrade quality and cause camera drift. We propose Wave Forcing (WF), which co-designs generation, training, and execution for continuous video output with multi-step denoising. WF uses chunk-wise causal attention to access earlier, cleaner chunks before their denoising is complete, and distributes staggered denoising and cache-refresh stages across full-model replicas to achieve 1F1C: one output chunk per concurrent forward round after pipeline fill. To adapt the model to this continuous generation process, we develop a three-stage training procedure that successively introduces mixed-noise denoising, motion supervision, and causal adaptation using self-generated history. To execute this process efficiently, Wave Runtime (WaveRT) uses Wave Parallelism (WP) for early K/V delivery and communication-computation overlap, together with optimized kernels and pipelined VAE decoding. Experiments on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B show that 5-step WF maintains overall quality comparable to Rolling Forcing while achieving higher Dynamic Degree on both short and long videos. Our system efficiency experiments show that 4-step WF achieves 147.6 DiT FPS and 134.8 end-to-end FPS on eight H200 GPUs, yielding 7.07x the single-GPU end-to-end throughput. In DiT-only tests with matched SageAttention+W8A8 backends, denoising steps, and GPU counts, WP delivers up to 2.53x the throughput of the faster of the Ulysses and Ring context-parallel baselines across six model scales (1.3B-14B).

AI.tldr: Proposes Wave Forcing, a co-designed generation, training and runtime system for streaming video that yields one output chunk per concurrent forward round after pipeline fill, reaching 134.8 end-to-end FPS on eight H200 GPUs with 4-step denoising.
AI.motivation: Chunk-wise autoregressive video generators need two forward passes per chunk for serialised denoising and history-cache refresh, and longer rollouts degrade quality and cause camera drift.
AI.method: Chunk-wise causal attention accesses earlier, cleaner chunks before their denoising completes, and staggered denoising and cache-refresh stages are distributed across full-model replicas (1F1C). A three-stage training procedure introduces mixed-noise denoising, motion supervision and causal adaptation using self-generated history. The Wave Runtime (WaveRT) uses Wave Parallelism for early K/V delivery and communication-computation overlap, with optimised kernels and pipelined VAE decoding.
AI.result: On Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, 5-step WF maintains overall quality comparable to Rolling Forcing with higher Dynamic Degree on short and long videos. 4-step WF reaches 147.6 DiT FPS and 134.8 end-to-end FPS on eight H200 GPUs, 7.07x the single-GPU end-to-end throughput. Wave Parallelism delivers up to 2.53x the throughput of the faster of the Ulysses and Ring context-parallel baselines across six model scales (1.3B-14B).
AI.conclusion: Co-designing generation, training and execution removes the extra forward pass per chunk and enables near-continuous streaming video output.

title: Learning to Group and Order: Cross-Instance Self-Supervised RL for Vision-Centric MLLMs
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training has become an important paradigm for improving multimodal large language models (MLLMs), especially with automatically verifiable rewards. Self-supervised visual pretext tasks provide such rewards without human annotations. However, existing methods mainly exploit within-instance structure, offering limited supervision for cross-instance discrimination and fine-grained comparison. We introduce Group-and-Order Self-Supervised Reinforcement Learning (GO-SSL), a cross-instance jigsaw framework for vision-centric MLLM post-training. Given two visual instances, GO-SSL mixes their local elements and trains the model to group them by instance of origin while recovering the order within each group, coupling instance-level comparison with spatial, temporal, or geometric structure recovery. This paired formulation turns the same unlabeled data into richer verifiable supervision through diverse pairings, shuffles, and a random-to-hard curriculum. We instantiate GO-SSL mainly on cross-image jigsaw tasks and further extend it to 3D depth and video temporal ordering. Across diverse benchmarks, GO-SSL consistently improves over the base MLLM and prior self-supervised post-training baselines, with clear gains in fine-grained perception and spatial understanding. Further evaluations across model scales and families support its generality. These results suggest that cross-instance comparison provides a useful self-supervised RL signal for improving transferable visual understanding in MLLMs. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes GO-SSL, a cross-instance jigsaw self-supervised RL method for vision-centric MLLMs in which the model groups mixed local elements by instance of origin and recovers their order, improving over the base model and prior self-supervised baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing self-supervised visual pretext rewards mainly exploit within-instance structure, which gives limited supervision for cross-instance discrimination and fine-grained comparison.
AI.method: Given two visual instances, their local elements are mixed and the model is trained to group them by origin while recovering the order within each group, coupling instance comparison with spatial, temporal or geometric structure recovery. It is instantiated mainly on cross-image jigsaw tasks and extended to 3D depth and video temporal ordering, using diverse pairings, shuffles and a random-to-hard curriculum.
AI.result: Consistent improvements over the base MLLM and prior self-supervised post-training baselines across diverse benchmarks, with clear gains in fine-grained perception and spatial understanding; generality is supported across model scales and families. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Cross-instance comparison provides a useful self-supervised RL signal for improving transferable visual understanding in MLLMs.

title: FilmTogether: Cinematic Video Generation from Low-Cost Inputs
comment: 14 pages. Project page: this https URL
summary: The widespread adoption of mobile devices has democratized video recording, but a stark aesthetic divide persists between casual, low-cost captures and high-cost cinematic productions. Bridging this gap requires upgrading heterogeneous production elements, such as lighting, specialized costumes, and materials, without altering the core layout, identity, and temporal motion of the original footage. However, this task is heavily bottlenecked by two important challenges: 1) Lacking a high-quality paired training data specifically designed to handle complex low-to-high appearance shifts. 2) Ignoring the capacity of current video editing models to perceive and enhance the multiple low-cost compositions. To address these issues, we present CineCraft-120K, a large-scale dataset of aligned low- and high-cost video pairs annotated with pair-aware editing prompts. CineCraft-120K features a diverse, high-resolution and high-cost Cinematic Crafting bank spanning decades of media production, meticulously taxonomized into 5 broad domains and 23 fine-grained sub-categories. It also provides element-level mapping between low- and high-cost counterparts, offering pair-aware rich textual prompts that precisely detail the required aesthetic transformations while anchoring structural layout. Architecturally, we propose a simple yet effective dual-memory feature adapter, where a text-memory expands semantic capacity for low2high appearance changes, and a hint memory supplies layer-wise visual feature corrections of high-cost element before context injection. Extensive experiments and ablation studies demonstrate the superiority of CineCraft-120K for low-to-high-cost video editing, alongside the effectiveness of our dual-memory adapter.

AI.tldr: Introduces CineCraft-120K, a dataset of aligned low-cost and high-cost video pairs with pair-aware editing prompts, and a dual-memory feature adapter for upgrading casual footage to a cinematic look while preserving layout, identity and motion.
AI.motivation: Turning casual mobile footage into cinematic footage requires paired training data for complex low-to-high appearance shifts, and current video editing models do not perceive and enhance multiple low-cost compositions.
AI.method: The dataset draws on a Cinematic Crafting bank spanning decades of media production, taxonomised into 5 broad domains and 23 fine-grained sub-categories, with element-level mapping between low- and high-cost counterparts and pair-aware textual prompts. The dual-memory adapter has a text memory that expands semantic capacity for low-to-high appearance changes and a hint memory that supplies layer-wise visual feature corrections of high-cost elements before context injection.
AI.result: Extensive experiments and ablation studies are said to demonstrate the superiority of CineCraft-120K for low-to-high-cost video editing and the effectiveness of the dual-memory adapter; the abstract gives no numbers.
AI.conclusion: Paired, element-aligned data together with the dual-memory adapter enables low-to-high-cost video editing that keeps the original layout, identity and temporal motion.

title: ZOPGA-KD: Zeroth Order PGA Guided Data Free Knowledge Distillation
summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) enables the transfer of learned representations from a large teacher network to a small student network. In foundational KD, the student network uses the original training data of the teacher model to accomplish this task. However, due to privacy concerns, the original training data is often not available. To overcome this reliance on original training data, several data-free knowledge distillation methods have been developed. Some of these methods operate in the white-box setting, and a few methods generate synthetic data by training a generator network. White-box methods use the teacher model's parameters to obtain a synthetic dataset. To avoid relying on teacher parameters, some methods use computationally expensive generative approaches to obtain such a dataset. There also exist certain black-box methods that generate the synthetic data without accessing teacher parameters. These methods are also computationally intensive. We propose a data-free knowledge distillation method that utilizes just the teacher's output logits and does not require access to its architecture, parameters, or gradients. We generate synthetic data via Projected Gradient Ascent (PGA) starting from smooth random noise signals. Required gradients are obtained through zeroth-order gradient estimation rather than backpropagating through the teacher's parameters. The student is then trained on these synthetically generated samples. We evaluate the proposed method on several benchmark datasets and show that the distillation performance is comparable with approaches that have access to the teacher model parameters.

AI.tldr: Proposes ZOPGA-KD, a data-free knowledge distillation method that uses only the teacher's output logits, generating synthetic samples by projected gradient ascent with zeroth-order gradient estimation.
AI.motivation: Original training data is often unavailable for privacy reasons; existing white-box methods need teacher parameters, generative methods are computationally expensive, and black-box methods are also computationally intensive.
AI.method: Synthetic data is produced by projected gradient ascent from smooth random noise signals, with gradients obtained by zeroth-order estimation on the teacher's logits rather than by backpropagating through the teacher. The student is then trained on these synthetic samples.
AI.result: On several benchmark datasets, distillation performance is comparable to approaches that have access to the teacher's parameters; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Logit-only zeroth-order access is sufficient for competitive data-free distillation without the teacher's architecture, parameters or gradients.

title: UI-UG 2: Advancing Mobile UI Understanding and Generation with Fine-Grained Supervision and Reinforcement Learning
comment: 30 pages, 17 figures, 10 tables, including references and appendices
summary: Mobile UI understanding and generation require both fine-grained component perception and reliable structured synthesis. Inspired by the unified direction introduced by UI-UG, we present UI-UG 2, a compact 4B-parameter multimodal large language model (MLLM) that advances mobile UI Understanding and Generation with broader task coverage, a front-end-aligned taxonomy, and online render-aware reinforcement learning. UI-UG 2 constructs a multi-source understanding corpus from RICO, VINS, Android in the Wild, and Android Control, annotated with an 80-category two-level UI taxonomy aligned with front-end component semantics, and pairs it with over 5,000 requirement-screenshot-JSON tuples for progressive structured UI generation through a domain-specific language (DSL). For understanding, UI-UG 2 introduces decomposed rewards for category prediction, OCR fidelity, color recognition, dense grounding, and GUI grounding. Unlike the offline Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)-style generation optimization in UI-UG, UI-UG 2 optimizes generation through end-to-end online Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO): sampled DSL outputs are rendered with a Playwright-based server-side pipeline and evaluated using LLM-as-a-Judge and contrastive preference ranking. Experiments show that UI-UG 2 achieves the strongest referring and dense-grounding results among the evaluated models on our 80-category benchmark, and achieves the best composite generation score among compared models at a compact scale (4B). More importantly, we observe a consistent understanding-to-generation transfer: adding fine-grained UI perception supervision improves generation quality under a fixed training budget, suggesting that component-level semantics provide a shared representational foundation for both tasks.

AI.tldr: Presents UI-UG 2, a compact 4B multimodal LLM for mobile UI understanding and generation, trained with decomposed rewards for understanding and online GRPO with a rendering pipeline for generation, and reports that fine-grained perception supervision improves generation.
AI.motivation: Mobile UI understanding and generation require fine-grained component perception and reliable structured synthesis; the predecessor UI-UG optimised generation with offline DPO-style methods.
AI.method: A multi-source understanding corpus from RICO, VINS, Android in the Wild and Android Control, annotated with an 80-category two-level taxonomy, and over 5,000 requirement-screenshot-JSON tuples for structured generation through a DSL. Understanding uses decomposed rewards for category prediction, OCR, colour recognition, dense grounding and GUI grounding. Generation uses online GRPO: sampled DSL outputs are rendered with a Playwright-based pipeline and scored by LLM-as-a-Judge and contrastive preference ranking.
AI.result: UI-UG 2 achieves the strongest referring and dense-grounding results among the evaluated models on the 80-category benchmark, and the best composite generation score among compared models at the 4B scale. Adding fine-grained UI perception supervision improves generation quality under a fixed training budget.
AI.conclusion: Component-level semantics provide a shared representation that transfers from understanding to generation.

title: What Helps Denoising Can Hurt Memory: Rethinking History in Long Video Generation
summary: Autoregressive video generators produce long videos block by block, using historical context to maintain temporal consistency. After denoising, a committing pass encodes each clean block into keys and values (KV) that later blocks read, and the same clean block can be encoded into different KV depending on the history it reads. We therefore study historical context not only as a condition for denoising but also as an input to committing. Older historical context that supports denoising can harm subsequent generation when read during committing. At fixed context size and temporal positions, older historical context lowers mean clip-to-clip Subject Consistency. Across 5 generator configurations supporting longer contexts, consistency rises, plateaus, and then declines as committing context expands. Motivated by these findings, we propose Commit Forcing, a training-free rule that organizes committing into a chain. During committing, each block reads only the preceding block's stored KV, so older historical context reaches new entries only through the chain. We apply this rule to 6 pretrained generators. On 60-second VBench, Commit Forcing improves Quality and Total on all 6 generators, by up to 1.27 Quality points and 1.10 Total points. Long-range consistency gains extend to 240-second videos. In a blinded comparison on 120-second LongLive videos, Commit Forcing achieves win rates of 83.5% for subject and scene consistency and 82.9% for overall preference against the base generator, excluding ties.

AI.tldr: Proposes Commit Forcing, a training-free rule that restricts each block's committing pass to read only the preceding block's stored KV, improving long-video consistency and VBench quality across six pretrained generators.
AI.motivation: In autoregressive video generation, older historical context that supports denoising can harm subsequent generation when it is read during the committing pass, lowering clip-to-clip Subject Consistency.
AI.method: The committing pass is organised into a chain in which each block reads only the preceding block's stored KV, so older context reaches new entries only through the chain. The rule is applied to six pretrained generators without training.
AI.result: On 60-second VBench, Quality and Total improve on all six generators by up to 1.27 and 1.10 points. Long-range consistency gains extend to 240-second videos. In a blinded comparison on 120-second LongLive videos, win rates against the base generator are 83.5% for subject and scene consistency and 82.9% for overall preference, excluding ties.
AI.conclusion: Restricting committing context to a chain preserves useful history while avoiding the harm it does to consistency.

title: PSF-Informed Reconstruction: An Enhanced 2D Directional Filtered Backprojection Method for Cone-Beam Rotary Computed Laminography
summary: Cone-beam rotary computed laminography (CL) presents a viable alternative to cone-beam CT for imaging objects with high aspect ratios. Conventional reconstruction techniques, such as CL-FBP and CL-FDK, often yield suboptimal results charac?terized by pronounced superimposition artifacts, reduced contrast,and blurred edges, primarily due to their reliance on 1D row-wise filtering along detector rows. To address these limitations and improve reconstruction quality, we proposed a novel 2D directional filtered backprojection (DFBP) method based on the point spread function (PSF). First, an exact expression for the projection process is derived by establishing the relationship between a reconstructed pixel and its corresponding projection point on the detector. Second, a revised backprojection process incorporating two weighting factors is introduced to counteract the nonlinearity inherent in conventional backprojection, leading to a simplified PSF formulation. Third, to circumvent the computational burden of 3D image space filtering,an approximate method by linearizing the coordinate relationship in Fourier space under some assumptions is developed that transfers the 3D filtering operation to the 2D projection space. This approach facilitates the derivation of a formally simple yet effective 2D direc?tional filter, which integrates a 2D von Hann window and a 2D sinc window. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method produces reconstructions with superior contrast, sharper boundaries,and fewer superimposition artifacts compared to CL-FBP and CL?FDK. Moreover, it enables more accurate recovery of internal structures, such as bubble defects and electronic components.

AI.tldr: Proposes a 2D directional filtered backprojection method for cone-beam rotary computed laminography, based on the point spread function, which gives sharper boundaries and fewer superimposition artefacts than CL-FBP and CL-FDK.
AI.motivation: Conventional laminography reconstructions (CL-FBP and CL-FDK) rely on 1D row-wise filtering along detector rows, which produces superimposition artefacts, reduced contrast and blurred edges.
AI.method: An exact projection expression links reconstructed pixels to their detector points. A revised backprojection with two weighting factors counteracts the nonlinearity of conventional backprojection and gives a simplified PSF formulation. The 3D filtering is approximated by linearising the coordinate relation in Fourier space and moved into 2D projection space as a 2D directional filter combining a 2D von Hann window and a 2D sinc window, which avoids the computational burden of 3D filtering.
AI.result: Reconstructions show superior contrast, sharper boundaries and fewer superimposition artefacts than CL-FBP and CL-FDK, with more accurate recovery of internal structures such as bubble defects and electronic components. The abstract gives no quantitative metrics.
AI.conclusion: The PSF-based 2D directional filtering is presented as an accurate alternative to conventional laminography reconstruction that avoids 3D filtering.

title: 4K Image Super-Resolution on Mobile NPUs: Mobile AI 2026 Challenge Report
summary: Image super-resolution is widely used on mobile devices for upscaling various types of image data. This creates a need for efficient deep learning-based models that are not only performant but can also be deployed on neural processing units (NPUs) present in the majority of mobile and IoT chipsets. In this Mobile AI challenge, we address this problem and propose the participants to design fast solutions that can upsample images from Full HD to 4K resolution while running on popular mobile NPUs from Qualcomm and MediaTek. For this, the participants were provided with the DIV2K dataset and trained models to do an efficient 3X image upscaling. The competition had two tracks: in the first track, the models had to be fully quantized (INT8), and the runtime of all models was evaluated on the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 NPU. In the second track, the participants were developing floating-point solutions that were evaluated on the MediaTek Dimensity 9500 NPU. Top solutions proposed in this challenge are able to reconstruct 4K images under 5 milliseconds while reaching a PSNR score of 30 dB. A comprehensive description of the models developed in the challenge is provided in this paper.

AI.tldr: Reports the Mobile AI 2026 challenge on efficient 3x image super-resolution from Full HD to 4K on mobile NPUs, where top solutions reconstruct 4K images in under 5 ms at a PSNR of 30 dB.
AI.motivation: Mobile devices need efficient deep super-resolution that runs on the NPUs found in most phone and IoT chipsets, not only accurate models.
AI.method: Participants were given DIV2K and trained models for 3x upscaling. Track 1 required fully INT8-quantised models evaluated on the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 NPU; track 2 used floating-point models evaluated on the MediaTek Dimensity 9500 NPU.
AI.result: Top solutions reconstruct 4K images in under 5 milliseconds while reaching a PSNR of 30 dB.
AI.conclusion: The report documents the models developed in the challenge, showing fast 4K upscaling is feasible on current mobile NPUs.

title: Efficient Image Denoising on Smartphone GPUs: Mobile AI 2026 Challenge Report
summary: Image denoising is a fundamental problem in mobile photography. Despite a large number of solutions proposed for this task, the majority of them are trained on synthetically produced noisy images, and are additionally too computationally heavy for processing full-resolution images on mobile devices. This creates a need for efficient deep learning-based models that are not only performant but can also be deployed on constrained mobile hardware. In this Mobile AI challenge, we address this problem and propose the participants to design fast solutions that can denoise Full HD resolution photos while running on popular smartphone GPUs from Qualcomm and Arm. For this, the participants were provided with a large-scale dataset consisting of noisy-clean image pairs captured in the wild. The runtime of all models was evaluated on the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 and Dimensity 9500 chipsets with the Adreno and Mali GPUs, respectively. Top solutions proposed in this challenge are able to perform high-quality image denoising under 100 milliseconds on both platforms while reaching a PSNR score of over 37 dB. A comprehensive description of the models developed in the challenge is provided in this paper.

AI.tldr: Reports the Mobile AI 2026 challenge on efficient denoising of Full HD photos on smartphone GPUs, where the best solutions denoise in under 100 ms on both platforms at over 37 dB PSNR.
AI.motivation: Most denoisers are trained on synthetic noise and are too computationally heavy for full-resolution processing on mobile devices, so efficient models trained on real noisy photos are needed.
AI.method: Participants were given a large-scale dataset of noisy-clean image pairs captured in the wild. Runtimes were measured on the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 (Adreno GPU) and the Dimensity 9500 (Mali GPU).
AI.result: Top solutions denoise Full HD photos in under 100 ms on both platforms while reaching over 37 dB PSNR.
AI.conclusion: The challenge report documents the models developed, showing that high-quality on-device denoising on phone GPUs is achievable.

title: Robust Pixel-wise Digital Image Correlation under Large Motions and Illumination Variations via a Global-to-Local Hybrid Neural Field
summary: Digital image correlation (DIC) is a widely used non-contact technique for full-field displacement measurement. Data-driven deep-learning DIC offers rapid inference but may generalize poorly to unseen speckle patterns, deformation modes, noise levels, and illumination conditions. Classical optimization-based DIC and recent image-constrained neural formulations avoid labeled displacement data, yet their convergence and accuracy remain vulnerable to initialization, large rigid-body motion, fine non-uniform deformation, and gray-value disturbances. This paper presents a global-to-local hybrid neural DIC framework for robust pixelwise measurement. Stage 1 estimates a dominant in-plane rigid transformation through coarse rotation search, phase correlation, and masked refinement, providing a reliable initialization under large translation and rotation. Stage 2 represents the residual displacement with a hybrid Kolmogorov-Arnold network (KAN) and multilayer perceptron (MLP), and optimizes it using a valid-overlap, illumination-robust structural loss. The local gray-value model explicitly accommodates multiplicative and additive intensity changes. Simulated and real experiments demonstrate accurate and stable displacement recovery under noise, non-uniform deformation, large rotation, illumination variation, and degraded imaging conditions.

AI.tldr: Proposes a global-to-local hybrid neural DIC framework that first estimates a rigid transform by rotation search and phase correlation, then refines the residual displacement with a hybrid KAN-MLP network under an illumination-robust structural loss.
AI.motivation: Data-driven DIC generalises poorly to unseen speckle patterns, deformation modes, noise levels and illumination, while classical and image-constrained neural DIC are sensitive to initialisation, large rigid motion and gray-value disturbances.
AI.method: Stage 1 estimates a dominant in-plane rigid transformation through coarse rotation search, phase correlation and masked refinement. Stage 2 represents the residual displacement with a hybrid Kolmogorov-Arnold network and multilayer perceptron, optimised with a valid-overlap, illumination-robust structural loss and a local gray-value model that accommodates multiplicative and additive intensity changes.
AI.result: Simulated and real experiments show accurate and stable displacement recovery under noise, non-uniform deformation, large rotation, illumination variation and degraded imaging. The abstract gives no numbers.
AI.conclusion: The global-to-local hybrid approach gives robust pixel-wise displacement measurement without labelled displacement data.

title: Grounding Across Views: Cross-View Referring Reasoning for Visual Grounding
summary: Cross-view object geo-localization (CVOGL) aims to localize a target in a satellite image from an observation captured under another viewpoint. Existing methods typically specify the query with a click point or bounding box, marking the target region but underusing the semantic attributes and relations conveyed by natural language. Moreover, referring expressions are often viewpoint-dependent, making query-view descriptions difficult to ground directly in the satellite image. In this paper, we formulate cross-view visual grounding (CVVG), extending conventional point- or box-prompted CVOGL to instance grounding jointly guided by a referring expression and a visual exemplar. We present GAV (Grounding Across Views), a view-aware framework for selectively transferring visual and linguistic evidence across views. Its core is view-aware referring reasoning: target-centered descriptions are derived from the marked query image, checked for target-category consistency, and augmented with a direction-free role cue. Exemplar prompting, cross-view alignment, and scene-level discrimination ground this semantic evidence in a satellite instance. GAV achieves a new state of the art on MoP-UAV with 62.55% Acc@0.5. We also introduce CVOGL-Text, a benchmark for text-guided grounding from street- and drone-view queries to satellite images. GAV outperforms the click-point baseline by 7.09 and 6.79 Acc@0.25 points on the street- and drone-view splits, respectively, demonstrating robustness to larger viewpoint gaps. The code and annotations will be publicly released.

AI.tldr: Formulates cross-view visual grounding, which localises a satellite instance from a referring expression and a visual exemplar, and proposes GAV, which reaches 62.55% Acc@0.5 on MoP-UAV.
AI.motivation: Cross-view object geo-localisation uses click points or boxes that underuse linguistic attributes and relations, and referring expressions are viewpoint-dependent, so they are hard to ground directly in satellite images.
AI.method: GAV is a view-aware framework built on view-aware referring reasoning: target-centred descriptions are derived from the marked query image, checked for target-category consistency and augmented with a direction-free role cue. Exemplar prompting, cross-view alignment and scene-level discrimination ground this evidence in a satellite instance. The paper also introduces CVOGL-Text for text-guided grounding from street- and drone-view queries.
AI.result: GAV achieves a new state of the art on MoP-UAV with 62.55% Acc@0.5, and outperforms the click-point baseline by 7.09 and 6.79 Acc@0.25 points on the street- and drone-view splits.
AI.conclusion: Selectively transferring visual and linguistic evidence across views makes text-guided grounding robust to larger viewpoint gaps.

title: CuPH: Parallel Cubical Persistent Homology via Level-Synchronous Component Tracking
summary: Persistent homology (PH) is a mathematically principled multi-scale topological descriptor of shape and connectivity in data. It is widely applied in image classification, segmentation, and shape analysis across medical and aerial imaging, providing structural information that pixel-wise deep learning may overlook. Standard cubical PH decomposes an image into cubical cells (vertices, edges, and squares) and reduces them sequentially in filtration order. This sequential reduction has $\Theta(n)$ parallel depth for an $n$-pixel image, limiting within-image GPU parallelism and constraining its use in topology-aware deep learning. We introduce CuPH, a GPU-based parallel algorithm for computing cubical PH on 2D images that operates directly on pixels rather than cubical cells. CuPH buckets pixels by filtration values, activates them with a level-synchronous sweep, and tracks connected components with a lock-free union-find method. We prove that CuPH produces persistence diagrams identical to standard cubical PH on integer inputs, with a stability bound for floating-point inputs. CuPH reduces parallel depth from $\Theta(n)$ to $O(L\log n)$ for an image with $L$ intensity levels. We implement the level sweep as a single CUDA kernel, eliminating cross-level kernel-launch overhead. Empirically, CuPH is $18.6$--$99.6\times$ faster than the existing GPU baseline (CMP). As a drop-in PH backend, CuPH accelerates topology-aware classification ($4.2$--$16.7\times$) and segmentation ($8.3$--$44\times$) while preserving accuracy. It also enables computing full-image PH losses on high-resolution images, improving segmentation Dice by $2.2$--$4.6$ points over patch-local PH baselines and accelerating training by $25$--$31\times$.

AI.tldr: Introduces CuPH, a GPU algorithm for 2D cubical persistent homology that works on pixels with a level-synchronous sweep and lock-free union-find, reducing parallel depth from Theta(n) to O(L log n) and running 18.6 to 99.6 times faster than the CMP GPU baseline.
AI.motivation: Standard cubical persistent homology reduces cells sequentially in filtration order, giving Theta(n) parallel depth for an n-pixel image; this limits GPU parallelism within an image and constrains topology-aware deep learning.
AI.method: CuPH buckets pixels by filtration value, activates them with a level-synchronous sweep and tracks connected components with a lock-free union-find. The level sweep is a single CUDA kernel, which avoids cross-level kernel-launch overhead. The method is proved to give persistence diagrams identical to standard cubical PH on integer inputs, with a stability bound for floating-point inputs.
AI.result: 18.6 to 99.6 times faster than the existing GPU baseline CMP. As a drop-in backend it accelerates topology-aware classification by 4.2 to 16.7 times and segmentation by 8.3 to 44 times while preserving accuracy; full-image PH losses improve segmentation Dice by 2.2 to 4.6 points over patch-local PH baselines and speed up training by 25 to 31 times.
AI.conclusion: CuPH makes full-image persistent homology losses practical on high-resolution images for topology-aware learning.

title: QVR3D: Query-Guided Visual Reasoning for Training-Free 3D Grounding
summary: 3D visual grounding localizes objects in 3D scenes from natural language descriptions, requiring reasoning over semantics, spatial relationships, and multi-view observations. Training-free approaches avoid costly annotations but often rely on explicit scene transformation or scene-level frame selection, which may waste limited visual capacity on query-irrelevant regions. We observe that effective grounding should prioritize observations that provide evidence for the query rather than uniformly represent the entire scene. Based on this insight, we introduce QVR3D, a query-guided visual reasoning framework that operates on RGB-D observations using off-the-shelf foundation models. QVR3D combines Query-Guided Maximum Coverage (QGMC) for selecting complementary query-relevant views with Grounding Probability Estimation (GPE) that integrates instance confidence, attribute consistency, and relationship consistency. The framework supports both single- and multi-object grounding without task-specific adaptation. Experiments on ScanRefer and Nr3D achieve state-of-the-art zero-shot performance, while QGMC also improves frame efficiency across multiple 3D vision-language tasks. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes QVR3D, a training-free 3D visual grounding framework on RGB-D observations that selects query-relevant views and estimates grounding probability from instance, attribute and relationship consistency, reaching state-of-the-art zero-shot results on ScanRefer and Nr3D.
AI.motivation: Training-free 3D grounding often relies on explicit scene transformation or scene-level frame selection, which can waste limited visual capacity on query-irrelevant regions.
AI.method: Query-Guided Maximum Coverage (QGMC) selects complementary query-relevant views, and Grounding Probability Estimation (GPE) integrates instance confidence, attribute consistency and relationship consistency, using off-the-shelf foundation models and supporting single- and multi-object grounding.
AI.result: State-of-the-art zero-shot performance on ScanRefer and Nr3D; QGMC also improves frame efficiency across multiple 3D vision-language tasks.
AI.conclusion: Prioritising observations that give evidence for the query, rather than uniformly covering the scene, is effective for training-free 3D grounding.

title: StreamDuo: A Live Commentator and a Research Agent for Unseen Games
summary: Streaming video LLMs can now commentate live gameplay, but they are trained and tested on the same games. We study cross-game streaming commentary, in which a model trained on one game commentates games it has never seen, and find that current commentators transfer their timing but not their knowledge of the game world. We propose StreamDuo, which pairs a trainable commentator with a frozen research agent that reads the wiki of the game being played. When the commentator sees something it cannot name, it sends the current frames, and the research agent returns a few wiki entries two seconds later while the stream continues. We train only the commentator, on a single game, in two stages. Information-gain labels teach it to ask only where an answer would help it say what the human caster said, and on-policy self-distillation from a copy of itself that sees the ideal answer teaches it to use noisy answers. Trained on Baldur's Gate 3 and tested on ten unseen games, StreamDuo raises entity recall from 0.082 to 0.116 over Proact-VL trained on the same data, cuts source-game leakage from 9.9% to 1.0%, and achieves the best timing and the highest judged liveliness and overall quality among streaming models.

AI.tldr: StreamDuo pairs a trainable live commentator for streaming video with a frozen research agent that retrieves wiki entries for unfamiliar game content, so the commentator can transfer to games it was never trained on. Trained on Baldur's Gate 3 only, it outperforms Proact-VL on entity recall and source-game leakage across ten unseen games.
AI.motivation: Streaming video LLM commentators are trained and tested on the same games, and the authors find that existing commentators transfer their timing to unseen games but not their knowledge of the game world.
AI.method: The commentator is trained alone in two stages on a single game. Information-gain labels teach it to request help only where an answer would change its commentary, and on-policy self-distillation from a copy that sees the ideal answer teaches it to use noisy answers. At inference, when the commentator cannot name something, it sends the current frames to a frozen research agent that reads the game wiki and returns entries about two seconds later while the stream continues.
AI.result: On ten unseen games, StreamDuo raises entity recall from 0.082 to 0.116 over Proact-VL trained on the same data and cuts source-game leakage from 9.9% to 1.0%. It achieves the best timing and the highest judged liveliness and overall quality among streaming models.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval from an external knowledge source, with the commentator trained to ask only when it helps, is a practical way to make live game commentary generalize across games.

title: What Does a Safety Label Measure? Auditing Situational-Safety Benchmarks for Multimodal LLMs
summary: Situational-safety benchmarks label each scene SAFE or UNSAFE and score a multimodal large language model (MLLM) against that label, usually by judging its free-form answer, and these scores guide deployment. We ask what such a label measures. A label score can come from the scene, the request or the benchmark's own files. We propose the Benchmark Card, seven measured fields that tell them apart, and fill it for six benchmarks. Only MSSBench chat leaks the label through its image files: image size alone reaches 82.3% accuracy, matching or beating six of seven commercial models. Elsewhere the signal outside the scene comes from design. In MOSSBench the item partition fixes the label, and on HoliSafe the request alone ranks pairs about as well as the scene. On our corrected chat split, the size rule falls to chance. We then introduce the Spot-Stop decomposition, which compares ranking with labelling on pairs of a safe and an unsafe scene. It splits the gap above a label-swap null into three parts: a threshold part, overlap between safe and unsafe scores, and order that holds only within a pair. Most of fourteen open MLLMs rank better than they label, beyond what their AUROC predicts. On chat, one shared threshold repairs a third to a half of the excess, and label-free recentering recovers it on balanced batches. Recentering on unlabelled scenes of the same situation improves ranking on VSCBench for 13 of 14 models.

AI.tldr: The paper audits what situational-safety benchmarks for multimodal LLMs actually measure, showing that label scores can come from shortcuts in the benchmark files or design rather than from the scene. It introduces a Benchmark Card, a Spot-Stop decomposition of the ranking-versus-labelling gap, and a recentering fix.
AI.motivation: Situational-safety benchmarks label scenes SAFE or UNSAFE and their scores guide deployment, but it is unclear whether a label score reflects the scene, the request, or artifacts of the benchmark itself.
AI.method: The authors propose a Benchmark Card with seven measured fields and fill it for six benchmarks. They introduce the Spot-Stop decomposition, which compares ranking with labelling on pairs of safe and unsafe scenes and splits the gap above a label-swap null into a threshold part, overlap between safe and unsafe scores, and within-pair order.
AI.result: On MSSBench chat, image file size alone reaches 82.3% accuracy, and on MOSSBench the item partition fixes the label. On the corrected chat split the size rule falls to chance. Most of fourteen open MLLMs rank better than they label. On chat, one shared threshold repairs a third to a half of the excess, and label-free recentering recovers it on balanced batches. Recentering on unlabelled scenes of the same situation improves ranking on VSCBench for 13 of 14 models.
AI.conclusion: Benchmark scores for MLLM situational safety can be dominated by artifacts and design choices, so benchmarks should be audited for what their labels measure before scores guide deployment.

title: GESTALT: Fast, Generalizable Histopathology Image Synthesis from Gene Expression with Pretrained Pathology Foundation Models
comment: Accepted at WACV 2027. 10 pages (8 main paper + 2 references), 4 figures. 8 pages of supplementary material
summary: Spatial transcriptomics measures gene expression while preserving where each cell sits in the tissue. The inverse, what a given transcriptomic state looks like, is less explored but equally useful: it lets researchers visualize the morphological consequence of a molecular state and interpret a spatial assay's molecular calls against real tissue structure. GeneFlow, the current state of the art on the Xenium gene expression-to-image benchmark, trains a model from scratch, incurring a high cost on every new target dataset it is applied to. We instead propose GESTALT, which reformulates gene expression-to-image synthesis as predicting a pathology foundation model's image embedding. A lightweight gene-token transformer predicts this embedding from multi-cell gene expression, and a frozen or LoRA-adapted diffusion decoder (PixCell) renders it as an image. Because this visual knowledge is reused rather than relearned, GESTALT trains in a fraction of the time. In both multi-cell and single-cell settings, our method outperforms the SoTA on perceptual metrics across all three Xenium datasets. Beyond improved image quality, GESTALT natively synthesizes at 1024 x 1024, and is evaluated in three generalization settings: zero-shot transfer across gene panels and datasets, held-out patients and disease states, and transfer across studies and tissue sources. Coupled with a statistical model of spatial expression, GESTALT also provides, to our knowledge, the first paired synthesis of cell-resolved transcriptomic fields and tissue images with explicit control over cell type, density, and composition. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: GESTALT synthesizes histopathology images from spatial gene expression by predicting a pathology foundation model's image embedding and rendering it with a diffusion decoder. It trains much faster than the prior state of the art, GeneFlow, and performs better on perceptual metrics on three Xenium datasets.
AI.motivation: GeneFlow, the state of the art on the Xenium gene expression-to-image benchmark, trains a model from scratch for each new target dataset, which is expensive, and the inverse problem of mapping transcriptomic states to tissue appearance is less explored.
AI.method: GESTALT reformulates expression-to-image synthesis as predicting a pathology foundation model's image embedding. A lightweight gene-token transformer predicts this embedding from multi-cell gene expression, and a frozen or LoRA-adapted diffusion decoder (PixCell) renders it. A statistical model of spatial expression is coupled to the generator for explicit control.
AI.result: GESTALT outperforms the state of the art on perceptual metrics across all three Xenium datasets in both multi-cell and single-cell settings. It natively synthesizes 1024 x 1024 images and is evaluated under zero-shot transfer across gene panels and datasets, held-out patients and disease states, and transfer across studies and tissue sources.
AI.conclusion: Reusing visual knowledge from a pathology foundation model reduces training cost and enables paired synthesis of cell-resolved transcriptomic fields and tissue images with control over cell type, density and composition.

title: SHield: Watermarking 4D Gaussian Splatting via Spherical Harmonic Coefficient Perturbation
summary: 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) models are computationally expensive to train but distributed as easily copied parameter files. Existing watermarks protect these assets by fine-tuning the scene against a neural decoder to extract bit strings from rendered video, a heavy process vulnerable to the temporal dynamics of dynamic scenes. However, if the threat model targets the redistributed file itself, verification can be vastly simplified. Because the canonical Spherical-Harmonic (SH) coefficients of 4DGS are time- and view-invariant, parameter-space perturbations can be recovered via deterministic arithmetic. We propose **SHield**, the first non-blind, decoder-free watermarking approach that natively embeds full-resolution RGB images into 4DGS files. SHield tiles a zero-mean payload across the SH coefficients of a key-selected Gaussian subset, applying a brief anchored optimization to preserve visual fidelity. To verify ownership, it geometrically re-associates the key using canonical Gaussian centres to survive file tampering and recovers the payload in closed form. Across 30 scenes (D-NeRF, HyperNeRF, DyNeRF), SHield guarantees near-perfect payload recovery (Pearson $r \geq 0.991$) on all 150 tested models with a mean rendering penalty of $\leq 0.13$~dB. Held-out evaluation yields perfect detection on 400 true trials and zero false positives across $1{,}600$ wrong-subset null trials. We also strictly bound the method's robustness: SHield survives INT8 quantization and $30\%$ opacity pruning for the image payload, and on aggressive SH-degree-1 truncation bit payloads are still decodable.

AI.tldr: SHield is a decoder-free watermarking method for 4D Gaussian Splatting files that embeds full-resolution RGB images in the spherical harmonic coefficients, which are time- and view-invariant. It recovers the payload in closed form with near-perfect fidelity and survives quantization and pruning for image payloads.
AI.motivation: Existing 4DGS watermarks fine-tune the scene against a neural decoder that extracts bits from rendered video, a heavy process that is vulnerable to the temporal dynamics of dynamic scenes. When the threat is the redistributed file itself, verification can be simpler.
AI.method: SHield tiles a zero-mean payload across the SH coefficients of a key-selected Gaussian subset, with a brief anchored optimization to preserve visual fidelity. Ownership is verified by re-associating the key through canonical Gaussian centres, which lets it survive file tampering, and the payload is recovered by arithmetic.
AI.result: Across 30 scenes from D-NeRF, HyperNeRF and DyNeRF, payload recovery reaches Pearson r of at least 0.991 on all 150 models with a mean rendering penalty of at most 0.13 dB. Held-out evaluation gives perfect detection on 400 true trials and zero false positives over 1,600 wrong-subset null trials. The image payload survives INT8 quantization and 30% opacity pruning, and bit payloads remain decodable under aggressive SH-degree-1 truncation.
AI.conclusion: Parameter-space watermarking of 4DGS files offers a simple, non-blind and decoder-free ownership check, with robustness characterized for common file-level modifications.

title: Modeling Fat-shift for Improved Head Segmentation from MRI Scans using a Probabilistic Model
summary: Personalized computational head models for biophysical simulations rely on accurate whole-head segmentations from T1-weighted (T1w) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans. While T1w scans provide excellent contrast for intracranial anatomy, extracerebral tissues have partly almost no signal (compact bone) and also suffer from the so-called chemical shift artifact, which affects the fatty tissues in MRI and causes them to spatially shift in the frequency encoding direction of the scan. This artifact occurs primarily in two structures of the head: the spongy bone, a fatty compartment inside the compact bone, and the subcutaneous fat, located directly underneath the skin. The frequency-encoding direction is often set in the superior-inferior direction, causing the fatty tissues to shift down and, as a result, making the skull appear thinner than it actually is. Existing segmentation methods do not model this artifact, consequently leading to inaccurate labeling of the skull and scalp, which introduces a bias in biophysical simulations. The direction and magnitude of the fat-shift can be determined from the scan parameters, thus making it possible to explicitly model the shift and to recover the correct anatomy. This study introduces a probabilistic model that uses variational inference to segment head and brain structures from a T1w scan while accounting for the fat-shift artifact. The proposed Fat-shift-informed Label Optimization of the Whole head (FLOW) method reconstructs extracerebral anatomy more accurately than a fat-shift-agnostic segmentation approach while maintaining high segmentation accuracy in all other structures. FLOW-based fat-shift corrected segmentations significantly reduce bias in electric field simulations compared to a segmentation method that does not model the shift.

AI.tldr: FLOW is a probabilistic variational segmentation method for T1-weighted head MRI that models the chemical shift (fat-shift) artifact, which displaces fatty tissue and makes the skull look thinner. It yields more accurate extracerebral anatomy than fat-shift-agnostic segmentation and reduces bias in electric field simulations.
AI.motivation: Personalized head models for biophysical simulation need accurate whole-head segmentation, but existing methods ignore the chemical shift artifact, which mislabels the skull and scalp and biases simulations.
AI.method: The method is a probabilistic model trained with variational inference that segments head and brain structures while explicitly accounting for the fat-shift artifact. The shift direction and magnitude are derived from the scan parameters, so the model can recover the correct anatomy.
AI.result: FLOW reconstructs extracerebral anatomy more accurately than a fat-shift-agnostic approach while keeping high accuracy on other structures. Fat-shift corrected segmentations significantly reduce bias in electric field simulations compared with a segmentation method that does not model the shift.
AI.conclusion: Modeling known acquisition physics in the segmentation improves the anatomical accuracy of head models and the reliability of downstream electric field simulations.

title: Reproducing INP-Former: Reconstructing Intrinsic Normal Prototypes for Industrial Anomaly Detection
comment: Reproducibility study. 12 pages of main text (excluding references and appendix), 14 tables. Code available at this https URL
summary: We reproduce the central claims of INP-Former, a reconstruction-based method for multi-class industrial anomaly detection. INP-Former extracts Intrinsic Normal Prototypes (INPs) from each test image and uses them to guide a decoder that reconstructs normal features, without a stored memory bank. Using the authors' released code, we reproduce the reported performance on MVTec AD and VisA and extend the evaluation to MVTec AD 2, where image AUROC with the default settings is 63.4, compared with 99.7 on MVTec AD. On MVTec AD, a five-seed ablation shows that most of the performance comes from the INP mechanism, while the two auxiliary losses add small changes whose direction depends on the metric. A paired comparison with both losses disabled confirms the benefit of INP on MVTec AD 2. The default of six prototypes transfers less well: the plateau beyond four prototypes reproduces on MVTec AD and VisA, but on MVTec AD 2 a single prototype outperforms six in AU-PRO on the public split and on both hidden test splits. We also measure practical trade-offs in resolution, backbone size, training length, and LoRA adaptation, and examine performance by defect size, lighting condition, and a stricter AU-PRO limit. Several conclusions from the original benchmarks, including the default prototype count, do not carry over to harder data. Code: this https URL

AI.tldr: This reproduction study checks the central claims of INP-Former for multi-class industrial anomaly detection and extends it to the harder MVTec AD 2. The reported performance reproduces on MVTec AD and VisA, but several conclusions, including the default of six prototypes, do not carry over to MVTec AD 2.
AI.motivation: INP-Former is a reconstruction-based anomaly detector without a memory bank, and its original claims were established on the older benchmarks, so it was unclear whether they hold on harder data.
AI.method: The authors use the released code and reproduce results on MVTec AD and VisA, extend the evaluation to MVTec AD 2, run a five-seed ablation on MVTec AD, and add a paired comparison with both auxiliary losses disabled. They also measure resolution, backbone size, training length, LoRA adaptation, defect size, lighting condition and a stricter AU-PRO limit.
AI.result: Image AUROC with default settings is 63.4 on MVTec AD 2, against 99.7 on MVTec AD. On MVTec AD most performance comes from the INP mechanism, and the auxiliary losses make small, metric-dependent changes. On MVTec AD 2 a single prototype beats six in AU-PRO on the public and both hidden splits.
AI.conclusion: Conclusions from original anomaly detection benchmarks, including the default prototype count, may not transfer to harder industrial data, so defaults should be re-checked on new benchmarks.

title: Context-Shielded Backdoor Attack against Large Vision-Language Models
summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) routinely use inference-time visual-token compression to prune hundreds of patch tokens down to a compact budget. Existing LVLM backdoors fire whenever a triggered image appears, whereas prior deployment-triggered attacks activate only when model weights are quantized or pruned. However, conventional LVLM backdoors exhibit nearly 100% attack success rate (ASR) under full-token inference, immediately exposing compromised checkpoints during pre-deployment auditing. We reveal context stripping: surrounding clean visual tokens suppress an embedded trigger at full length, whereas token pruning strips this context away and activates the backdoor. Motivated by this finding, we propose StripWake, a projector-only backdoor that remains dormant under full-token auditing yet activates across unseen compressors. Specifically, StripWake pairs clean-supervised full-token views with target-supervised randomized compressed views, and aligns early visual attention with a frozen benign teacher to preserve clean utility. On LLaVA-1.5-7B across nine unseen compressors, StripWake stays dormant at 0.4% full-token ASR yet achieves 94.0%-99.7% compressed ASR across five primary compressors without CIDEr loss.

AI.tldr: StripWake is a projector-only backdoor for large vision-language models that stays dormant under full-token inference but activates when inference-time visual-token compression is applied. It reaches 94.0% to 99.7% attack success under compression while staying at 0.4% under full-token auditing.
AI.motivation: Conventional LVLM backdoors fire at near 100% attack success under full-token inference and are therefore easy to expose in pre-deployment audits, while earlier deployment-triggered attacks depend on weight quantization or pruning.
AI.method: The authors identify context stripping, in which surrounding clean visual tokens suppress an embedded trigger, and token pruning removes that context. StripWake pairs clean-supervised full-token views with target-supervised randomized compressed views and aligns early visual attention with a frozen benign teacher to preserve clean utility.
AI.result: On LLaVA-1.5-7B across nine unseen compressors, StripWake has 0.4% full-token ASR and 94.0% to 99.7% compressed ASR across five primary compressors, without CIDEr loss.
AI.conclusion: Backdoors that depend on visual-token compression can evade full-token auditing, so auditing must cover the compressed inference paths that deployments actually use.

title: StreamClarify: Proactive Clarification for Grounded Streaming Video Question Answering
summary: Streaming video question answering (QA) requires real-time reasoning over continuous video streams under strict latency and active-context budgets. Current streaming vision-language models (VLMs) often give confident yet ungrounded answers when queries are ambiguous or have false premises, or when relevant visual evidence is no longer in the active context. Proactive clarification can help, but must satisfy the same latency and memory constraints. We present StreamClarify, a training-free framework for grounded streaming QA that combines a pre-answer uncertainty check with hierarchical memory. The check uses the entropy of a binary pre-answer judgment as a lightweight uncertainty score to decide whether to answer directly or request clarification. To support re-answering, a temporal-pyramid KV cache maintains a bounded active visual context, while a CPU-side semantic retrieval archive provides access to historical frames. We further construct StreamClarify-QA, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,837 QA pairs from StreamBench and OVO-Bench, spanning standard, referential ambiguity, and unanswerable scenarios. Across three VLM backbones, StreamClarify improves Macro accuracy by up to 8.2 points over backbone-matched baselines. At comparable trigger rates, entropy-based selection achieves more than 18 points higher precision than random selection in identifying initially incorrect answers. Under oracle user guidance, clarification improves Macro accuracy by up to 3.5 points. We also report a controlled, oracle-assisted Qwen3-VL simulation on Ambiguous QA with generated questions and referent-only user replies, where the entropy-gated condition improves accuracy by 8.3 points.

AI.tldr: StreamClarify is a training-free framework for streaming video question answering that decides whether to answer or ask for clarification using the entropy of a binary pre-answer judgment. It uses a bounded KV cache and a CPU-side retrieval archive, and improves Macro accuracy by up to 8.2 points.
AI.motivation: Streaming vision-language models often give confident but ungrounded answers to ambiguous or false-premise queries, or when the relevant evidence has left the active context, and clarification must meet the same latency and memory limits.
AI.method: A pre-answer uncertainty check uses the entropy of a binary judgment to decide between answering directly and requesting clarification. A temporal-pyramid KV cache keeps a bounded active visual context, and a semantic retrieval archive on the CPU gives access to historical frames. The authors also build StreamClarify-QA, a benchmark of 1,837 QA pairs from StreamBench and OVO-Bench covering standard, referential ambiguity and unanswerable cases.
AI.result: Across three VLM backbones, StreamClarify improves Macro accuracy by up to 8.2 points over backbone-matched baselines. At comparable trigger rates, entropy-based selection is more than 18 points more precise than random selection at finding initially incorrect answers. Oracle user guidance adds up to 3.5 points, and an oracle-assisted Qwen3-VL simulation on ambiguous QA gains 8.3 points.
AI.conclusion: Entropy-gated clarification is a cheap way to improve grounding in streaming video QA under tight resource budgets.

title: DriftingPlanner: Drifting Generative Models for One-Step Trajectory Planning in End-to-End Autonomous Driving
summary: End-to-end planners decode the ego trajectory either by coordinate regression, which is fast but blends plausible maneuvers into one trajectory that may follow none of them, or by diffusion and flow matching, which model the trajectory distribution but need several inference steps. Drifting models move this iteration into training: a one-step generator learns to follow an attraction--repulsion field between generated and ground-truth samples. Drifting was developed for class-conditional image generation, where every class supplies many positive samples. In planning, every scene is its own condition. Pooling scenes would attract the generated trajectories of one scene to the ground truth of unrelated scenes, whereas computing the field per scene leaves a single positive, the expert trajectory. Mutual repulsion then holds the generated trajectories on a shell around it, so any single generated trajectory deviates from the ground truth. We present DriftingPlanner, a trajectory planner trained with the drifting loss alone, without any coordinate regression term. It computes the field per scene and removes the shell at inference: it decodes every noise vector together with its negation in one batched pass, and averaging each antithetic pair cancels the linear part of the displacement from the shell center. On NAVSIM navtest, DriftingPlanner reaches a state-of-the-art 93.75 PDMS, and with single-step inference its drifting decoder comes within 0.13 PDMS of the best diffusion or flow matching setting, which needs ten inference steps.

AI.tldr: DriftingPlanner is an end-to-end autonomous driving planner that generates trajectories in one step using a drifting loss, computed per scene without coordinate regression. It reaches 93.75 PDMS on NAVSIM navtest, and its single-step decoder comes within 0.13 PDMS of the best ten-step diffusion or flow matching setting.
AI.motivation: Coordinate regression blends plausible maneuvers into one trajectory that may match none of them, while diffusion and flow matching model the distribution but need several inference steps. Drifting models were developed for class-conditional image generation, and pooling positives across scenes would attract trajectories to unrelated ground truth.
AI.method: The field is computed per scene, so the expert trajectory is the only positive. Mutual repulsion keeps generated trajectories on a shell around it. At inference, each noise vector is decoded together with its negation in one batched pass, and averaging each antithetic pair cancels the linear part of the displacement from the shell centre.
AI.result: On NAVSIM navtest, DriftingPlanner reaches a state-of-the-art 93.75 PDMS, and with single-step inference it is within 0.13 PDMS of the best diffusion or flow matching setting, which uses ten inference steps.
AI.conclusion: Moving iterative refinement into training with a per-scene drifting loss allows one-step trajectory planning that approaches multi-step generative planners.

title: [Re] Pure Noise to the Rescue of Insufficient Data
comment: Reproducibility study of Zada et al. (arXiv:2112.08810). Published in ReScience C 9(2), #45 (2023), ML Reproducibility Challenge 2022. 15 pages. Code: this https URL
summary: We examine the main claims of Zada, Benou, and Irani (2021), which states that in an image classification task with imbalanced training data, (i) using pure noise to augment minority-class images encourages generalization by improving minority-class accuracy. This method is paired with (ii) a new batch normalization layer that normalizes noise images using affine parameters learned from natural images, which improves the model's performance. Moreover, (iii) this improvement is robust to varying levels of data augmentation. Finally, the authors propose that (iv) adding pure noise images can improve classification even on balanced training data. We implemented the training pipeline from the description of the paper using PyTorch and integrated authors' code snippets for sampling pure noise images and batch normalizing noise and natural images separately. We reproduced the main claims that (i) oversampling with pure noise improves generalization by improving the minority-class accuracy, (ii) the proposed batch normalization (BN) method outperforms baselines, (iii) and this improvement is robust across data augmentations. Our results also support that (iv) adding pure noise images can improve classification on balanced training data. However, additional experiments suggest that the performance improvement from OPeN may be more orthogonal to the improvement caused by a bigger network or more complex data augmentation.

AI.tldr: This reproduction study checks the claims of Zada et al. (2021) that pure-noise augmentation (OPeN) with a separate batch normalization for noise improves minority-class accuracy on imbalanced image classification. The authors reproduce most claims but find the gains may overlap with those from a larger network or stronger augmentation.
AI.motivation: The original paper reported that pure-noise oversampling, paired with a new batch normalization layer, improves generalization on imbalanced data and even on balanced data, and the claims needed independent verification.
AI.method: The authors reimplement the training pipeline in PyTorch from the paper description and integrate the authors' code snippets for sampling pure noise images and batch normalizing noise and natural images separately. They test the claims across augmentation levels and on balanced training data.
AI.result: The authors reproduce the minority-class accuracy gains from oversampling with pure noise, the advantage of the proposed batch normalization over baselines, and robustness across data augmentations. Adding pure noise also improves classification on balanced data. Additional experiments suggest the improvement from OPeN may be largely orthogonal to gains from a bigger network or more complex augmentation.
AI.conclusion: The main claims hold, but the reported improvement should be compared against capacity and augmentation controls before it is attributed to pure noise.

title: IMPACT: Image-Conditioned Motion with Physics-Aware Collision and Trajectory Guidance for Video Generation
summary: Visually realistic video generation does not guarantee physically consistent motion. Generated objects may exhibit implausible collision responses or rebounds without energy dissipation, while even physically valid motion predictions may not be faithfully realized during synthesis. We propose \textbf{IMPACT}, a physics-state-driven image-to-video framework that addresses these challenges by coupling explicit dynamics prediction with complementary sparse--dense physical guidance. A learnably calibrated Physics State Generator unifies continuous free-flight dynamics with discrete collision responses, linking impact timing, post-impact velocity, rebound attenuation, and eventual settling within a coherent physical-state sequence. To translate this evolution into effective generative constraints, IMPACT derives sparse trajectories and dense region-level motion priors from the same physical rollout. Sparse trajectories constrain global object displacement, while dense priors guide diffusion sampling to encourage coherent object-region motion and suppress unwanted background changes. Their shared physical basis coordinates global and local motion guidance to reduce prediction--generation mismatch. Experiments on 100 controlled sphere--plane collision scenes spanning different material combinations and visual environments demonstrate improved physical plausibility over representative general-purpose, physics-grounded, and motion-controllable baselines. The project repository is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: IMPACT is an image-to-video framework that makes generated object collisions physically plausible by coupling a physics-state generator with sparse trajectories and dense region-level motion priors derived from one physical rollout. It improves physical plausibility over general-purpose, physics-grounded and motion-controllable baselines on 100 sphere-plane collision scenes.
AI.motivation: Visually realistic video generators do not guarantee physically consistent motion, producing implausible collision responses, rebounds without energy loss, or physically valid motion that is not realized in the generated video.
AI.method: A learnably calibrated Physics State Generator links impact timing, post-impact velocity, rebound attenuation and settling into one physical-state sequence. Sparse trajectories constrain global object displacement, and dense priors guide diffusion sampling toward coherent object-region motion while suppressing background changes.
AI.result: On 100 controlled sphere-plane collision scenes spanning different materials and visual environments, IMPACT shows improved physical plausibility over the compared general-purpose, physics-grounded and motion-controllable baselines.
AI.conclusion: Sharing a single physical rollout between global and local guidance reduces the mismatch between predicted physics and generated motion.

title: Vocabulary Aligned Explanations for Computer Vision Models
summary: Optimizing vision models for accuracy does not force the model to learn and utilize human-understandable and domain-specific concepts and rules. We propose explaining image classifications through domain-specific concepts, visual evidence, and expert knowledge expressed as logical rules. We introduce FLUENT (Framework for Localized, Uncertainty-Aware Explanations in Normative Terminology), a post-hoc framework that ranks expert-authored rules combining jointly required, alternative, and absent concepts. To account for prediction errors, FLUENT combines predicted labels and concept states with empirically estimated likelihoods and concept priors. It scores each rule by calculating support over satisfying assignments to the concepts mentioned in that rule, then normalizes these scores to express relative confidence among candidate explanations. The selected rule is illustrated through occlusion-based highlights for positive concept mentions in the query image and localized examples in retrieved reference images for negative mentions. These illustrations are intended to show end users unfamiliar with the domain what the concepts named in an explanation look like. FLUENT combines domain knowledge and model accuracy, and delivers visual concept highlights and explicit rule confidence to explain an image in the vocabulary of an application domain.

AI.tldr: FLUENT explains image classifications with expert-authored logical rules over domain concepts, ranking candidate rules by support under predicted labels and concept likelihoods and illustrating them with visual highlights and reference examples. It aims to give explanations in an application domain's vocabulary with explicit confidence.
AI.motivation: Optimizing vision models for accuracy does not make them learn or use human-understandable, domain-specific concepts and expert rules, so explanations are often not in the vocabulary of the domain.
AI.method: FLUENT is a post-hoc framework that ranks expert rules combining jointly required, alternative and absent concepts. It combines predicted labels and concept states with empirically estimated likelihoods and concept priors, scores each rule by support over satisfying assignments of its concepts, and normalizes the scores into relative confidence. Positive concepts are shown by occlusion highlights on the query image, and negative concepts by localized examples from retrieved reference images.
AI.result: The abstract describes the framework and its outputs (concept highlights and explicit rule confidence) but reports no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: Combining expert rules with model predictions and their uncertainty can produce domain-language explanations with visual evidence that end users unfamiliar with the domain can follow.

title: SpecUltra: A Unified Foundation Model for Heterogeneous Spectral Images
summary: Spectral imagery, including hyperspectral image (HSI) and multispectral image (MSI), exhibits substantial heterogeneity in band numbers, wavelengths, spectral resolutions, hindering unified modeling and cross-sensor transfer. From the perspective of imaging physics, these heterogeneous observations can be regarded as discrete measurements of an underlying continuous spectrum acquired through different sampling processes. Motivated by this perspective, we propose SpecUltra, a unified foundation model for heterogeneous spectral images. Specifically, SpecUltra employs 3D convolutional tokenization and wavelength-aware 3D RoPE to encode relative wavelength and spatial relationships, enabling fine-grained spatial-spectral modeling within a shared coordinate system. We further construct MultiHyper-200K, a large-scale multi-sensor HSI dataset, and pretrain SpecUltra using auxiliary-token-assisted mask image modeling (MIM), where a level token indicates the radiometric product type and register tokens absorb sensor- and acquisition-dependent variations. To bridge the spectral-granularity gap between HSI and MSI, we introduce Spectral Kernel Transformation (SKT), which transfers pretrained knowledge in parameter space by constructing MSI embedding kernels from fine-grained HSI-pretrained kernel slices. This design preserves pretrained spectral priors while maintaining compatibility with the pretrained backbone. Experiments on HSI and MSI classification and segmentation benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art or competitive performance across disparate sensors and downstream tasks.
