AI.tldr: SpecUltra is a unified foundation model for hyperspectral and multispectral images with different band counts and wavelengths, using wavelength-aware 3D RoPE and 3D convolutional tokenization. It transfers knowledge from hyperspectral pretraining to multispectral data by constructing MSI embedding kernels from HSI kernel slices.
AI.motivation: Spectral images vary widely in band number, wavelength and resolution across sensors, which hinders unified modeling and cross-sensor transfer. The authors treat heterogeneous observations as discrete samples of one underlying continuous spectrum.
AI.method: The model uses 3D convolutional tokenization and wavelength-aware 3D RoPE in a shared coordinate system. It is pretrained on the newly built MultiHyper-200K dataset with auxiliary-token-assisted masked image modeling, where a level token marks the radiometric product type and register tokens absorb sensor-specific variation. Spectral Kernel Transformation bridges the HSI-MSI granularity gap by transferring pretrained parameters.
AI.result: The abstract reports state-of-the-art or competitive performance on HSI and MSI classification and segmentation benchmarks across different sensors and downstream tasks, without specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: A single pretrained backbone with wavelength-aware encoding and parameter-space kernel transfer can serve heterogeneous spectral sensors.

title: RadPose: ISAC-based RF 3D Human Pose Estimation
summary: Human pose estimation under adverse lighting and occlusion conditions remains challenging for camera- and LiDAR-based systems. Although mmWave radars provide robustness to illumination and occlusion, they rely on dedicated hardware and licensed spectrum, limiting scalability. In this paper, we present RadPose, a learning-based monostatic integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) framework that enables mmWave communication devices to perform 3D human pose estimation. Unlike specialized radars, RadPose leverages monostatic full-duplex operation to extract channel impulse responses (CIRs) directly from standard OFDM communication signals, generating 3D radio point clouds without additional sensing hardware. To address the sparsity and noise of RF observations, RadPose employs a cross-frame transformer-based pose inference network with semantic-guided spatial attention and target-driven temporal attention for robust spatio-temporal aggregation. It further adopts a joint-aware inverse kinematics refinement module based on graph convolution to enforce skeletal topology, bone-length consistency, and anatomical plausibility. Extensive experiments demonstrate RadPose achieves competitive accuracy compared to state-of-the-art radar-based approaches while maintaining robust performance in unseen and occluded scenarios. The dataset and source code are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: RadPose estimates 3D human pose with mmWave signals from a monostatic ISAC system, extracting channel impulse responses from standard OFDM communication signals without dedicated radar hardware. It reports accuracy competitive with state-of-the-art radar-based methods, including in occluded and unseen scenarios.
AI.motivation: Camera and LiDAR pose estimation degrades in poor lighting and occlusion, and mmWave radars are robust but need dedicated hardware and licensed spectrum, which limits scalability.
AI.method: A learning-based monostatic ISAC framework uses full-duplex operation to produce 3D radio point clouds from OFDM channel responses. A cross-frame transformer with semantic-guided spatial attention and target-driven temporal attention aggregates the sparse, noisy observations, and a graph-convolution inverse kinematics module enforces skeletal topology, bone-length consistency and anatomical plausibility.
AI.result: RadPose achieves accuracy competitive with state-of-the-art radar-based approaches and maintains robust performance in unseen and occluded scenarios. The abstract gives no numerical results.
AI.conclusion: Communication devices with ISAC capability could perform 3D human pose estimation without specialized sensing hardware, which would improve scalability.

title: ContactCut: A Partition-Aware Contact Selection Framework for False-Merge Correction in Connectomics
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures. Submitted to the IEEE International Symposium on Biomedical Imaging (ISBI) 2027
summary: Localized false-merge correction in connectomics requires converting an identified error into an executable native 3D partition. Still, neither intermediate correction predictions nor seeded graph solvers alone determine which native source-sink constraints should define that partition. We formulate this problem as a 3D-native partition-aware contact selection problem: selecting candidate contacts based on the complete partitions they induce. Our solution comprises two components: ContactCut (CC)-Auto, which uses learned single-contact selection, and ContactCut (CC)-Search, which enables bounded paired-contact search, generates compact alternatives, and applies learned panel ranking. On historical two-way false-merge corrections from MICrONS and FlyWire, CC-Auto improves failure-aware 3D partition (FA-3D Part.) mIoU by 5.9 and 3.4 points over the strongest graph-based controls and by 12.5 and 10.0 points over the best learned baselines. A MICrONS-trained ranker transfers to FlyWire with negligible degradation. CC-Search expands oracle reachability and prioritizes near-oracle alternatives. The code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: ContactCut is a partition-aware contact selection framework for correcting false merges in connectomics, selecting cut contacts by the complete 3D partitions they induce rather than by individual predictions. It improves FA-3D partition mIoU over graph-based and learned baselines on MICrONS and FlyWire, and a ranker trained on MICrONS transfers to FlyWire.
AI.motivation: Localized false-merge correction needs to turn an identified error into an executable native 3D partition, but intermediate correction predictions and seeded graph solvers alone do not decide which source-sink constraints should define that partition.
AI.method: ContactCut-Auto uses learned single-contact selection. ContactCut-Search performs bounded paired-contact search, generates compact alternatives and applies learned panel ranking.
AI.result: On historical two-way false-merge corrections from MICrONS and FlyWire, CC-Auto improves FA-3D Part. mIoU by 5.9 and 3.4 points over the strongest graph-based controls, and by 12.5 and 10.0 points over the best learned baselines. The MICrONS-trained ranker transfers to FlyWire with negligible degradation, and CC-Search expands oracle reachability.
AI.conclusion: Selecting contacts by the partitions they induce, rather than by per-contact scores, improves the correction of false merges in connectomics.

title: Resolve, Clear, or Defer: Training-Free Active Prototype Triage for Ecological Detection Pipelines
comment: Accepted to the IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV 2027), Main Conference. 27 pages including supplementary material
summary: Ecological monitoring increasingly relies on camera traps and aerial surveys that generate large image collections. High-recall animal detectors can localize candidate animals at scale. However, they also produce many detections that still require expert review, including false positives, ambiguous cases, and animals difficult to identify at the species level. Since exhaustive review requires substantial effort, we propose training-free active prototype triage, where reviewed detections become reusable evidence to (1) Resolve supported foreground classes, (2) Clear likely background false positives, or (3) Defer insufficiently supported cases for expert review. Across camera-trap and aerial datasets, foreground recognition and false-positive rejection benefit from different pretrained representations: BioCLIP2 provides foreground evidence while DINOv3 provides background evidence, reducing erroneous foreground clearing while improving automatic foreground recovery. Deferring unsupported cases avoids the higher error rates caused by forced decisions. Compared with confidence-thresholded multiclass k-NN and uncertainty-sampling logistic regression, prototype triage improves foreground recovery while maintaining competitive or lower review burden. Acquisition goes beyond class discovery: even after classes are represented, prototype choice determines how reliably evidence propagates through the remaining detections. Our results suggest that once animal localization reaches high recall, the challenge shifts from finding animals to deciding which examples to review, how to reuse them, and when evidence does not support an automatic decision.

AI.tldr: Active prototype triage uses reviewed detections as reusable evidence to resolve foreground classes, clear background false positives, or defer unsupported cases to experts, without training. Using BioCLIP2 for foreground evidence and DINOv3 for background evidence, it improves foreground recovery over k-NN and uncertainty sampling with similar or lower review burden on camera-trap and aerial data.
AI.motivation: High-recall animal detectors produce many detections that still need expert review, and exhaustive review is costly. Existing approaches such as confidence-thresholded k-NN and uncertainty-sampling logistic regression do not handle the trade-off between automatic decisions and deferral well.
AI.method: The authors propose training-free active prototype triage, in which reviewed detections become prototypes that resolve, clear or defer new detections. Different pretrained representations are used for foreground and background evidence, and unsupported cases are deferred rather than forced into a decision.
AI.result: Across camera-trap and aerial datasets, the combination of BioCLIP2 and DINOv3 reduces erroneous foreground clearing while improving automatic foreground recovery. Deferral avoids the higher error of forced decisions. Prototype triage improves foreground recovery compared with k-NN and logistic regression baselines while keeping review burden competitive or lower.
AI.conclusion: Once detectors reach high recall, the main challenge is deciding which examples to review, how to reuse them, and when evidence is insufficient for an automatic decision.

title: Label-Free Localization and Test-Time Suppression of CLIP's Typographic Circuits
summary: CLIP-based Vision-Language Models have become cornerstones of modern multimodal systems. The cross-modal contrastive objective equips the CLIP vision encoder to both see objects and read text. These two abilities induce an entanglement between the encoding of lexical and semantic shapes, creating a distinctive vulnerability to typographic attacks, in which rendered text overrides an image's semantic content with its literal meaning. The black-box nature of these encoders has prevented a mechanistic interpretation of such entanglement. We introduce a head-decomposed Sparse Dictionary Learning (SDL) architecture that, by design, decomposes individual attention heads into interpretable, head-specific latents. Based on this inductive disentanglement, we re-purpose Clarity Score and propose normalized Text Attribution Score, which are both label-free, to identify attention heads that carry typographic information. As a causal validation of successful circuit separation, we perform a mechanistic intervention that reweighs attention away from the patch tokens in the identified lexical heads at test-time. Experiments show that the intervention effectively recovers object classification under typographic attack and, across five CLIP variants and four typographic benchmarks, achieves up to 46.9% improvement while incurring up to 1% accuracy loss in general image perception, outperforming prior supervised and training-free methods. Expanding on the mechanistic intervention, we propose a test-time adaptive attention head routing to further reduce the impact on performance at matched robustness, pushing beyond the Pareto frontier of current robustness-perception tradeoff.

AI.tldr: The paper mechanistically localizes typographic attack circuits in CLIP using head-decomposed sparse dictionary learning and label-free attribution scores, then reweights attention away from patch tokens in the identified heads at test time. This recovers object classification under typographic attack, with up to 46.9% improvement and up to 1% loss in general perception.
AI.motivation: The entanglement of lexical and semantic encodings in CLIP makes it vulnerable to typographic attacks, in which rendered text overrides visual content, and the black-box nature of the encoder has prevented a mechanistic account of this entanglement.
AI.method: A head-decomposed Sparse Dictionary Learning architecture decomposes each attention head into head-specific latents. Clarity Score is re-purposed and a normalized Text Attribution Score is proposed, both label-free, to identify heads that carry typographic information. A test-time intervention reweights attention away from patch tokens in those lexical heads, and a test-time adaptive head routing is proposed to reduce the impact on perception.
AI.result: Across five CLIP variants and four typographic benchmarks, the intervention achieves up to 46.9% improvement under typographic attack with up to 1% accuracy loss in general image perception, outperforming prior supervised and training-free methods. Adaptive head routing further reduces the perception cost at matched robustness.
AI.conclusion: Typographic vulnerability can be localized to specific attention heads without labels and mitigated by a causal test-time intervention, improving the robustness-perception trade-off.

title: AR-RRG: Anatomy-Guided Retrieval-Driven Radiology Report Generation
summary: Radiology report generation (RRG) streamlines clinical workflows and alleviates the burden of radiologists' documentation. Standard vision-language models capture global visual cues and lack fine-grained alignment between anatomical regions and diagnostic text. Most retrieval-augmented methods retrieve complete historical reports, introducing redundant noise and severe vision-text mismatches that trigger clinically risky hallucinations and missed lesions. In this paper, we introduce AR-RRG, an anatomy-guided retrieval-driven method for the generation of radiology reports. AR-RRG consists of two core modules: the anatomy-aware self-training lesion detection network (ASLDNet) and the retrieval-driven radiology report generation (RRRG). ASLDNet leverages anatomy-aware spatial verification (ASV) and class-adaptive dynamic thresholding (CDT) via self-training, delivering accurate lesion localization to support subsequent generation. As the generative branch of AR-RRG, RRRG eliminates clinical hallucinations through dual-granularity retrieval (DR) and complements missing lesions with a neighborhood consensus (NC) mechanism. A parallel continuous visual perception (PCVP) stream converts radiographs into visual tokens through fixed medical encoding and resampling. Multi-scale text and visual features are fused, followed by LoRA-efficient large language model tuning to generate clinically consistent, visually grounded radiology reports. Extensive evaluations on MS-CXR, MIMIC-CXR, and IU X-Ray demonstrate that AR-RRG consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods across mainstream metrics. Our code will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: AR-RRG generates radiology reports by combining an anatomy-aware lesion detector with retrieval of fine-grained reports rather than whole historical reports, and a LoRA-tuned language model. It reports consistent gains over state-of-the-art methods on MS-CXR, MIMIC-CXR and IU X-Ray.
AI.motivation: Standard vision-language report generators capture global cues but lack fine-grained alignment between anatomical regions and diagnostic text, and retrieving complete historical reports adds noise and vision-text mismatch that leads to hallucinations and missed lesions.
AI.method: ASLDNet is a self-training lesion detector using anatomy-aware spatial verification and class-adaptive dynamic thresholding. The generative branch RRRG uses dual-granularity retrieval to reduce hallucination and a neighborhood consensus mechanism to add missing lesions. A parallel perception stream turns radiographs into visual tokens, and multi-scale text and visual features are fused before LoRA-based LLM tuning.
AI.result: The abstract states that AR-RRG consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods across mainstream metrics on MS-CXR, MIMIC-CXR and IU X-Ray, without giving specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Anatomy-guided, fine-grained retrieval combined with lesion localization can reduce hallucinations and missed lesions in automated radiology report generation.

title: AbacusGS: Gaussian Splatting without Per-Splat Sorting
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting sorts every splat by depth in every frame. Viewers that draw splats with the hardware rasterizer and sort them on the CPU, as most web and mobile viewers do, spend most of the frame time in this sort. We present AbacusGS, which stores the blending order of a 3DGS scene in the scene layout. AbacusGS groups the splats into octree boxes of at most 128 splats and stores each box in order along an axis chosen at write time. In each frame, AbacusGS sorts only the visible boxes, and one dot product per box decides whether the box is read forward or backward. A short order-aware fine-tuning converts an existing 3DGS model, and the over operator of 3DGS stays unchanged. On 13 standard scenes, AbacusGS loses 0.13 dB PSNR on average against an equally fine-tuned 3DGS model. In an OpenGL viewer that orders splats on the CPU, AbacusGS renders frames 4.5 times faster than per-splat sorting. We also present a compact format of 17 bytes per splat and a CUDA tile renderer that use the same order. The code will be released.

AI.tldr: AbacusGS stores a blending order in the layout of a 3D Gaussian Splatting scene, so viewers do not need to sort every splat per frame. It renders about 4.5 times faster than per-splat CPU sorting in an OpenGL viewer, at an average cost of 0.13 dB PSNR on 13 standard scenes.
AI.motivation: Viewers that rasterize splats in hardware but sort them on the CPU, as most web and mobile viewers do, spend most of the frame time on depth sorting.
AI.method: Splats are grouped into octree boxes of at most 128 splats, and each box is stored in order along an axis chosen at write time. Each frame sorts only visible boxes, and one dot product per box decides whether to read it forward or backward. A short order-aware fine-tuning converts an existing 3DGS model, and the over operator is unchanged. A compact 17-byte-per-splat format and a CUDA tile renderer use the same order.
AI.result: On 13 standard scenes AbacusGS loses 0.13 dB PSNR on average against an equally fine-tuned 3DGS model. In an OpenGL viewer that sorts on the CPU, it renders frames 4.5 times faster than per-splat sorting.
AI.conclusion: Precomputing blending order in the scene layout removes most of the per-frame sorting cost for a small quality loss, which benefits web and mobile viewers.

title: CUFormer: Modality-Aware CT-Ultrasound Point Cloud Registration for Orthopedic Navigation
summary: Registering intraoperative Ultrasound (US) bone-surface point clouds to preoperative Computed Tomography (CT) models can support radiation-free orthopedic navigation. Differences in imaging physics produce distinct surface sampling patterns, complicating cross-modal feature matching. Bone strongly reflects ultrasound and casts an acoustic shadow, so US captures only the probe-facing bone surface and leaves most CT points unmatched. This partial coverage makes correspondences ambiguous on near-symmetric bones. We propose CUFormer, a modality-aware registration framework. We introduce a Modality-Aware Transformer (MAT) that encodes input modality through identity embeddings and updates features through modality-specific adapters within a shared geometric matcher. We model imaging visibility and use predicted reference-side visibility to weight coarse and fine correspondences. CUFormer achieves the lowest mean registration errors among evaluated methods on two CT-US datasets, UltraBones100k and UltraBonesHip, and the CT-RGB-D dataset SpineDepth. On UltraBones100k, it reaches mean rotation error 4.53$^\circ$, translation error 3.19\,mm, and Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) 2.54\,mm, reducing RMSE by 65.8\% relative to the best-performing baseline by this metric. These results demonstrate CUFormer's effectiveness in aligning partial bone surfaces with preoperative CT across anatomical sites.

AI.tldr: CUFormer is a modality-aware registration framework that aligns intraoperative ultrasound bone-surface point clouds with preoperative CT models, using a Modality-Aware Transformer and visibility-weighted correspondences. It attains the lowest mean registration errors among evaluated methods on two CT-US datasets and SpineDepth, with RMSE reduced by 65.8% relative to the best baseline on UltraBones100k.
AI.motivation: Ultrasound captures only the probe-facing bone surface because of strong reflection and acoustic shadowing, so it leaves most CT points unmatched, and near-symmetric bones make correspondences ambiguous.
AI.method: The Modality-Aware Transformer encodes input modality with identity embeddings and updates features through modality-specific adapters within a shared geometric matcher. The method models imaging visibility and uses predicted reference-side visibility to weight coarse and fine correspondences.
AI.result: On UltraBones100k, CUFormer reaches mean rotation error 4.53 degrees, translation error 3.19 mm and RMSE 2.54 mm, reducing RMSE by 65.8% relative to the best baseline. It also achieves the lowest mean errors on UltraBonesHip and the CT-RGB-D dataset SpineDepth.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling modality and imaging visibility enables accurate alignment of partial bone surfaces with preoperative CT for radiation-free orthopedic navigation.

title: MoPort: A View-Aware 2D Interface for Motion Language Models
summary: Motion language models (MoLMs) encode 3D human motion as discrete tokens for language-based understanding. Deploying them on monocular video raises two problems. Pose detection yields 2D joint sequences, leaving a dimensional gap from the 3D motion used in training. Moreover, the 2D observation changes with the camera viewpoint, while the depth lost in projection makes the 2D pose ambiguous across viewpoints. We propose MoPort, a view-aware 2D interface that enables MoLMs to take 2D observations as input. We introduce Paired View Alignment (PVA), which gives two views of the same motion a shared 3D teacher target and directly constrains the consistency of their latents, so that 2D observations from different viewpoints are mapped to a consistent semantic representation. Camera-Modulated Encoding (CME) estimates the camera extrinsics from the 2D sequence and uses them to modulate encoding, providing the 2D latents with geometric information about the viewpoint. MoPort achieves R@1 of 0.5674 on HumanML3D and 0.3286 on KIT-ML, outperforming all evaluated baselines. On HumanML3D, its R@1 decreases only from 0.5763 on in-distribution viewpoints to 0.5585 on out-of-distribution viewpoints. We validate portability on three downstream MoLMs. Furthermore, on the real-world RGB video dataset Fit3D, MoPort achieves 80.36\% accuracy. Code will be released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: MoPort is a view-aware 2D interface that lets motion language models take monocular 2D pose sequences as input instead of 3D motion, using paired view alignment and camera-modulated encoding. It achieves R@1 of 0.5674 on HumanML3D and 0.3286 on KIT-ML, and holds up under out-of-distribution viewpoints.
AI.motivation: Motion language models are trained on 3D motion, but monocular video yields 2D joint sequences whose appearance depends on the camera viewpoint, and depth lost in projection makes the 2D pose ambiguous across viewpoints.
AI.method: Paired View Alignment gives two views of the same motion a shared 3D teacher target and constrains the consistency of their latents. Camera-Modulated Encoding estimates the camera extrinsics from the 2D sequence and uses them to modulate encoding, providing geometric information about the viewpoint.
AI.result: MoPort achieves R@1 of 0.5674 on HumanML3D and 0.3286 on KIT-ML, outperforming all evaluated baselines. On HumanML3D its R@1 falls only from 0.5763 in-distribution to 0.5585 on out-of-distribution viewpoints. It transfers to three downstream MoLMs and achieves 80.36% accuracy on the real-world RGB video dataset Fit3D.
AI.conclusion: A view-aware 2D interface can make 3D-trained motion language models usable on monocular video with limited viewpoint sensitivity.

title: GSExplorer: Interactive World Generation with a Persistent 3D Gaussian World State
summary: Interactive world generation requires both accurate local control and stable scene consistency over long rollouts. Existing methods improve local generation through camera or geometry conditioning and extend historical context with memory mechanisms. However, long-horizon exploration remains challenging as target-view guidance becomes incomplete and inconsistencies accumulate across repeated scene updates. We present \textbf{GSExplorer}, a generation--reconstruction framework built around a persistent 3D Gaussian world state. At each step, the current 3DGS scene provides multimodal rendering conditions for a condition-driven video generator, while camera geometry is injected through a separate Relative Ray Encoding branch. Generated videos are then fed back to a SLAM-based reconstruction backend, where inconsistency filtering prevents conflicting content from corrupting the scene and cross-chunk bundle adjustment improves spatial alignment across generation steps. We further design a data-construction pipeline that reproduces realistic 3DGS degradation during scene extrapolation, yielding 293K training pairs of degraded multimodal renderings and real target videos. GSExplorer achieves the best overall performance among the compared methods on both single-step and three-step WorldScore evaluation, with strong camera control and consistency across both settings, including a Camera Control score of 99.07 in single-step extrapolation. On 481-frame leave-and-return rollouts, it also shows strong revisit consistency, demonstrating the value of maintaining a reliable 3D world state for continued exploration.

AI.tldr: GSExplorer is an interactive world generator that keeps a persistent 3D Gaussian world state, rendering it as conditions for a video generator and feeding generated videos back into a SLAM-based reconstruction with inconsistency filtering. It achieves the best overall WorldScore on single-step and three-step evaluation, with a Camera Control score of 99.07 in single-step extrapolation.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon interactive world generation suffers from incomplete target-view guidance and accumulating inconsistencies across repeated scene updates, which existing camera conditioning and memory mechanisms do not fully address.
AI.method: The current 3DGS scene supplies multimodal rendering conditions for a condition-driven video generator, and camera geometry is injected through a separate Relative Ray Encoding branch. Generated videos go to a SLAM reconstruction backend with inconsistency filtering and cross-chunk bundle adjustment. A data pipeline reproduces realistic 3DGS degradation to build 293K training pairs.
AI.result: GSExplorer achieves the best overall performance among the compared methods on single-step and three-step WorldScore, with strong camera control and consistency. It reaches a Camera Control score of 99.07 in single-step extrapolation and shows strong revisit consistency over 481-frame leave-and-return rollouts.
AI.conclusion: Maintaining a persistent 3D world state that is updated through reconstruction is valuable for consistent long-horizon exploration.

title: Band2Net: Frequency-to-Network Transport Distillation for fMRI-Privileged, EEG-Only Session-Condition Decoding
summary: Functional MRI resolves large-scale brain networks but is expensive and stationary, whereas EEG is portable but poorly localised. We treat fMRI as privileged information, available during training and absent at deployment, with EEG and fMRI acquired from the same participants under matched conditions but not simultaneously. Band2Net encodes EEG into five frequency-specific connectivity graphs and fMRI into seven canonical network tokens from a frozen teacher, and solves a balanced entropic transport problem between the two token sets that gives each EEG band its own fMRI target. In subject-grouped cross-validation on the PsiConnect psilocybin data set, Band2Net reaches 0.801 ROC-AUC for EEG-only session-condition decoding, 5.0 AUC points (95% CI 1.8-8.2) above an EEG-only student. Although its margins over a single shared plan, a KL-relaxed plan and label-free network descriptors remain unresolved, secondary comparisons favour band-specific transported targets over logit, global-feature, contrastive and pooled-target distillation, though not after Holm correction.

AI.tldr: Band2Net distills fMRI-derived network knowledge into an EEG-only model for decoding session condition, using entropic transport between EEG frequency-band graphs and fMRI network tokens. It reaches 0.801 ROC-AUC on the PsiConnect psilocybin dataset, 5.0 points above an EEG-only student, though some margins are unresolved after correction.
AI.motivation: fMRI resolves large-scale networks but is expensive and stationary, while EEG is portable but poorly localized. fMRI is available only during training, and EEG and fMRI were acquired from the same participants under matched conditions but not simultaneously.
AI.method: EEG is encoded into five frequency-specific connectivity graphs, and fMRI into seven canonical network tokens from a frozen teacher. A balanced entropic transport problem links the two token sets so that each EEG band gets its own fMRI target.
AI.result: In subject-grouped cross-validation on PsiConnect, Band2Net reaches 0.801 ROC-AUC for EEG-only session-condition decoding, 5.0 AUC points (95% CI 1.8 to 8.2) above an EEG-only student. Band-specific transported targets are favored over logit, global-feature, contrastive and pooled-target distillation, but not after Holm correction, and margins over a single shared plan remain unresolved.
AI.conclusion: Band-specific transport of privileged fMRI targets may help EEG-only decoding, though the evidence for its advantage over simpler alternatives is not yet conclusive.

title: TopoDPO: Dense Preference Alignment for Structure-Sensitive Aerial Referring Segmentation
summary: Preference optimization for multimodal segmentation faces a granularity mismatch: dense masks contain spatially heterogeneous preference signals, whereas image-level objectives assign one shared nonlinear weight to all spatial margins. We introduce TopoDPO, a topology-aware dense preference alignment framework for structure-sensitive aerial referring segmentation. Topo-Prior mines informative preference pairs using connected-component discrepancy and macro-corner recall, while the dense objective applies the preference penalty to each local margin before spatial aggregation against a frozen supervised reference. On Topo-RS-Hard, a 4590-instance structural stress set, TopoDPO improves intersection over union (IoU) from 50.91% to 51.24% over image-level direct preference optimization (DPO) and reduces Betti-0 error from 1.34 to 0.90; paired image-cluster bootstrap intervals against image-level DPO exclude zero for all five reported metrics. Matched supervised controls and a complete factorial analysis separate the effects of topology-aware pair mining, localized correction, and dense reference-relative preference weighting. An unfiltered stratification over all 39,244 validation records further shows the clearest structural gains on samples with moderate or severe pre-alignment component-count errors. The code is publicly available at: this https URL.

AI.tldr: TopoDPO applies dense, topology-aware preference optimization to aerial referring segmentation, mining preference pairs by connected-component discrepancy and macro-corner recall and weighting each local margin. On a 4,590-instance structural stress set it raises IoU from 50.91% to 51.24% over image-level DPO and reduces Betti-0 error from 1.34 to 0.90.
AI.motivation: Image-level preference objectives assign a single nonlinear weight to all spatial margins, although dense masks contain spatially heterogeneous preference signals, so structurally important errors are underweighted.
AI.method: Topo-Prior mines informative preference pairs using connected-component discrepancy and macro-corner recall. The dense objective applies the preference penalty to each local margin before spatial aggregation, against a frozen supervised reference. A factorial analysis separates topology-aware pair mining, localized correction and dense reference-relative weighting.
AI.result: On Topo-RS-Hard, TopoDPO improves IoU from 50.91% to 51.24% over image-level DPO and reduces Betti-0 error from 1.34 to 0.90. Paired bootstrap intervals against image-level DPO exclude zero for all five reported metrics. The clearest gains appear on samples with moderate or severe pre-alignment component-count errors.
AI.conclusion: Dense, localized preference weighting combined with topology-aware pair mining improves structural accuracy in referring segmentation, with modest absolute IoU gains.

title: Text-Assisted Event Stream Visual Place Recognition via Multi-Scale Spatiotemporal Optimal Transport
comment: 17 pages including appendix, 4 figures. Submitted to ICLR 2027
summary: Benefiting from the high dynamic range, high temporal resolution, and low energy consumption of event cameras, low-altitude economic research leveraging event cameras has become a popular topic. Several existing attempts introduce natural-language descriptions into visual place recognition (VPR) to mitigate the sparsity of structural spatial information inherent to event cameras. Nevertheless, these methods still fail to fully address two core challenges: effectively encoding event streams and semantically aligning event streams with text. In this paper, we propose a multi-scale spatial-temporal optimal transport approach, MSTOT-EPR, to address these challenges. Specifically, given event streams and scene text information, we first adopt a visual encoder and a text encoder to extract respective feature representations. We then apply optimal-transport constraints to achieve cross-modal alignment. We then design a cross-modal bottleneck fusion module to further fuse bimodal features. Furthermore, we develop multi-scale spatial optimal transport and inter-frame temporal optimal transport modules to mine high-quality spatial-temporal event features for scene recognition. Extensive experiments on the NYC-Event-VPR and EPRBench datasets fully validate the effectiveness of our proposed framework for event-based VPR. The source code of this paper will be released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: MSTOT-EPR is a text-assisted event-camera visual place recognition method that aligns event streams with scene text via optimal transport and fuses them with a cross-modal bottleneck. It applies multi-scale spatial and inter-frame temporal optimal transport to mine spatio-temporal event features, and is evaluated on NYC-Event-VPR and EPRBench.
AI.motivation: Event cameras offer high dynamic range and temporal resolution, but their sparse spatial structure is hard to recognize, and existing text-assisted VPR methods fail to encode event streams well or to align them semantically with text.
AI.method: A visual encoder and a text encoder extract features, and optimal-transport constraints align the two modalities. A cross-modal bottleneck fusion module combines the bimodal features. Multi-scale spatial optimal transport and inter-frame temporal optimal transport modules then mine spatio-temporal event features for scene recognition.
AI.result: The abstract states that extensive experiments on NYC-Event-VPR and EPRBench validate the framework for event-based VPR, without giving numerical results.
AI.conclusion: Optimal-transport alignment of event streams with text, combined with spatio-temporal event modeling, is an effective approach to event-based place recognition.

title: Spend the Bits Where the Tiny Objects Are: Rate-Utility Region Coding for Aerial Detection
summary: Bandwidth-limited aerial cameras must compress their images before a remote detector can find the many tiny objects in them. Threshold-based region-of-interest (ROI) coding sends only confidently detected regions, and because tiny objects provide limited visual evidence and often score low, it can discard the regions that contain them. We propose rate-utility region coding (RUO), which sends a region when its expected detection utility justifies its measured byte cost, choosing to drop it or to send it at low or high quality with one multiplier shared across images. RUO trains no model, uses a standard image codec and decodes in a few milliseconds. On all 1,610 VisDrone-DET test-dev images, RUO uses 42.4% fewer bits than a tuned threshold-based ROI coder, averaged over their shared tiny-object average precision (AP) range. RUO also needs fewer bits for tiny objects than the AV1 Image File Format (AVIF), High Efficiency Video Coding (HEVC) and three published learned codecs, and its advantage over threshold-based ROI coding persists when the sender and receiver use different detectors. For AP over all object sizes RUO needs 25.4% more bits than the tuned ROI coder, because its allocation drops large regions first at low rates, so it suits tasks that target tiny objects. We plan to release the code.

AI.tldr: RUO is a rate-utility region coder for aerial imagery that sends a region only when its expected detection utility justifies its byte cost, choosing to drop it or send it at low or high quality. On VisDrone-DET test-dev it uses 42.4% fewer bits than a tuned threshold-based ROI coder at matched tiny-object AP, but 25.4% more bits for all object sizes.
AI.motivation: Threshold-based ROI coding sends only confidently detected regions, and because tiny objects provide weak evidence and often score low, it can discard exactly the regions that contain them.
AI.method: RUO trains no model, uses a standard image codec and decodes in a few milliseconds. It decides per region between dropping it and sending it at low or high quality, using one multiplier shared across images to trade expected detection utility against measured byte cost.
AI.result: On all 1,610 VisDrone-DET test-dev images, RUO uses 42.4% fewer bits than a tuned threshold-based ROI coder, averaged over their shared tiny-object AP range. It needs fewer bits for tiny objects than AVIF, HEVC and three published learned codecs, and the advantage persists when sender and receiver use different detectors. For AP over all sizes it needs 25.4% more bits than the tuned ROI coder.
AI.conclusion: Utility-aware region allocation spends bits where tiny objects are, which suits tasks that target small objects, though it is less efficient when large objects matter as well.

title: Recoverability-Aware Evaluation of Diffusion Video Inpainting and Object Removal
summary: Video inpainting for object removal is scored over the whole hole, although the background behind the object is visible in other frames of the shot for some hole pixels and in no frame for others. A whole-hole score therefore mixes copying with generation and cannot show which of the two a remover does well. To separate the two, we propose recoverability-stratified evaluation, in which a point tracker run on the clean video labels each hole pixel by whether and how far away it is observed, so that fidelity and temporal stability can be reported per stratum against a copy reference. To reuse the observed content, we also propose evidence-guided sampling (EGS), which blends tracked colors into the clean-latent prediction of a video diffusion remover without training. On DAVIS, the perceptual advantage of three diffusion removers over flow propagation shrinks where the content is visible a few frames away (LPIPS difference-in-differences +0.046 to +0.056 against E2FGVI-HQ), and real paired captures show the same pattern for two of them. Their DAVIS hole warping error is two to four times that of ProPainter, and copying along clean-video tracks lowers their recoverable LPIPS by a quarter to two fifths. EGS closes 43% and 56% of the gap to this copy reference on held-out DAVIS when its colors come from clean-video tracks. With colors tracked on the masked input, a pre-registered confirmation finds no gain on MiniMax-Remover and a loss on ROSE. Diffusion removers thus leave observed content unused on DAVIS, and training-free reuse does not yet hold with tracked evidence.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes recoverability-stratified evaluation for video object-removal inpainting, separating hole pixels by whether the background is visible in other frames, and evidence-guided sampling that reuses tracked colors in a diffusion remover. It finds diffusion removers leave observed content unused on DAVIS, and training-free reuse does not yet help with tracked evidence.
AI.motivation: Whole-hole scores mix copying visible background with generating unseen content, so they cannot show which of the two a remover does well.
AI.method: A point tracker run on the clean video labels each hole pixel by whether and how far away it is observed, and fidelity and temporal stability are reported per stratum against a copy reference. Evidence-guided sampling blends tracked colors into the clean-latent prediction of a video diffusion remover without training.
AI.result: On DAVIS, the perceptual advantage of three diffusion removers over flow propagation shrinks where content is visible a few frames away, and their hole warping error is two to four times that of ProPainter. EGS closes 43% and 56% of the gap to the copy reference on held-out DAVIS when colors come from clean-video tracks. With colors tracked on the masked input, a pre-registered confirmation finds no gain on MiniMax-Remover and a loss on ROSE.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion removers leave recoverable content unused, and training-free reuse of tracked evidence does not yet hold up when the evidence is tracked on the masked input.

title: Accurate automated photo-identification of Near Eastern and European fire salamanders
summary: Photo-identification underpins non-invasive capture-recapture monitoring of amphibians, but manual identification becomes slow and error-prone as reference libraries grow. Focusing on the Near Eastern fire salamander (Salamandra infraimmaculata), we developed a pipeline based on zero-shot local-feature matching (SuperPoint and LightGlue) without species-specific training and evaluated it on $2{,}440$ field photographs from Haifa and Tel Dan in northern Israel. We isolated the yellow spot pattern, scored image similarity by the number of high-confidence keypoint matches, which reduced a confound whereby many-spotted individuals accumulate spurious matches, and assigned identities across the database by two-tier clustering. Pipeline-assisted expert review corrected misidentifications, reducing the number of identities by almost a quarter. On held-out individuals, the pipeline ranked the correct individual first for $95.2\%$ of queries and recovered identities with an ARI of $0.958$. Without modification, it reached $95.1\%$ and $91.7\%$ top-1 accuracy on two datasets of the European fire salamander (Salamandra salamandra) and recognised $93.7\%$ of recaptures in one of them, compared with $38$-$77\%$ for five established programs and $93.9\%$ for visual inspection. Zero-shot local-feature matching thus offers amphibian monitoring a re-identification tool that needs no training data, transfers between related species, scales to databases of over a thousand individuals, and can audit existing databases before capture-recapture analysis.

AI.tldr: A zero-shot local-feature pipeline using SuperPoint and LightGlue identifies individual Near Eastern fire salamanders from yellow spot patterns without species-specific training. It ranks the correct individual first for 95.2% of held-out queries and transfers to European fire salamanders with 91.7% to 95.1% top-1 accuracy.
AI.motivation: Manual photo-identification for capture-recapture monitoring of amphibians becomes slow and error-prone as reference libraries grow.
AI.method: The authors isolate the yellow spot pattern and score similarity by the number of high-confidence keypoint matches, which reduces the bias toward heavily spotted individuals. Identities across the database are assigned by two-tier clustering, and expert review is assisted by the pipeline.
AI.result: On 2,440 field photographs from Haifa and Tel Dan, the pipeline ranks the correct individual first for 95.2% of held-out queries and recovers identities with an ARI of 0.958. Without modification it reaches 95.1% and 91.7% top-1 accuracy on two European fire salamander datasets, and recognizes 93.7% of recaptures in one of them, compared with 38% to 77% for five established programs and 93.9% for visual inspection.
AI.conclusion: Zero-shot local-feature matching gives amphibian monitoring a re-identification tool that needs no training data, transfers between related species, scales to over a thousand individuals, and can audit existing databases.

title: MedNet and U$^2$-ViT: A Nested Vision Transformer Diffusion Framework for Diverse Medical Images Generation
summary: The scarcity of diverse, high-quality medical images remains a significant bottleneck in advancing AI-driven medical diagnostics and treatment planning. Traditional datasets often suffer from class imbalances, limited disease coverage, and insufficient variations in imaging conditions - challenges that hinder the development of robust, generalizable models. To address this, we introduce MedNet, a large-scale, multi-modal text-to-image dataset spanning 61 disease categories with 160 classes, covering both humans and animals. We built this with images from trusted public repositories, ensuring data diversity, quality, and ethical compliance. Additionally, we propose U$^2$-ViT, a novel diffusion-based text-to-image generation architecture arranging Vision Transformers (ViTs) in a nested U-Net structure to enhance the generation of diverse, and high-fidelity medical images. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that our model achieves the best Fr'echet Inception Distance (FID) score compared to state-of-the-art models. The source code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: MedNet is a 61-disease-category text-to-image dataset of medical and animal images built from public repositories, and U2-ViT is a diffusion architecture that nests Vision Transformers in a U-Net structure to generate medical images. The authors report the best FID compared with state-of-the-art models.
AI.motivation: Medical imaging datasets suffer from class imbalance, limited disease coverage and narrow imaging conditions, which hinders robust and generalizable diagnostic models.
AI.method: MedNet is a large-scale multi-modal text-to-image dataset spanning 61 disease categories with 160 classes, covering humans and animals, and built from trusted public repositories. U2-ViT is a diffusion-based text-to-image architecture that arranges ViTs in a nested U-Net structure.
AI.result: The model achieves the best Frechet Inception Distance compared with state-of-the-art models, according to the abstract, which gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: A diverse, public-source medical image dataset together with a nested ViT-U-Net diffusion architecture is proposed as a basis for generating more diverse, high-fidelity medical images.

title: NatureFusion: Rethinking Infrared and Visible Image Fusion as Natural Complementary Enhancement
summary: In the absence of ground truth, most existing infrared and visible image fusion methods pursue fidelity to the source images and directly superimpose two physically distinct modalities. As a result, salient infrared targets appear as bright patches of thermal radiation pasted onto the scene. These patches obscure the original color and texture of the targets, so the fused images look unnatural to human observers and deviate from the data distribution learned by vision models pretrained on visible images. Therefore, we redefine infrared and visible image fusion as natural complementary enhancement rather than source fidelity, and propose NatureFusion, which exploits cross-modal complementary cues to infer a clear and natural visible-style image from low-quality visible and infrared image pairs. Specifically, to address the lack of ground truth, we employ a generative foundation model as the teacher to directly generate visually natural fused images for supervision. Furthermore, to fully distill the teacher's generative capability while reducing computational cost, we fine-tune a pretrained generative model with conditional flow matching through a light-weight fusion adapter. Last but not least, to further improve downstream performance without sacrificing natural appearance, we freeze the fusion adapter and introduce a detector-supervised task adapter that strengthens the complementary contribution of infrared. Extensive comparisons with seven multi-modal fusion and seven single-modality enhancement methods demonstrate that NatureFusion generates visually natural fused images with the best perceptual quality. Detection and segmentation models pretrained on visible images achieve substantially higher accuracy on our fused images than on those of any competing method.

AI.tldr: NatureFusion reframes infrared and visible image fusion as natural complementary enhancement, using a generative foundation model as teacher to produce natural fused images and a light fusion adapter with conditional flow matching. A detector-supervised task adapter then strengthens the infrared contribution, and detectors pretrained on visible images perform better on its outputs.
AI.motivation: Existing fusion methods superimpose infrared targets as bright thermal patches that look unnatural and deviate from the data distribution that vision models were pretrained on.
AI.method: Without ground truth, a generative foundation model supplies supervision by generating visually natural fused images. A pretrained generative model is fine-tuned with conditional flow matching through a light-weight fusion adapter. The fusion adapter is then frozen and a detector-supervised task adapter is added to strengthen the complementary infrared cues.
AI.result: Compared with seven multi-modal fusion and seven single-modality enhancement methods, NatureFusion produces visually natural fused images with the best perceptual quality. Detection and segmentation models pretrained on visible images achieve substantially higher accuracy on its outputs than on those of any competing method.
AI.conclusion: Treating fusion as natural complementary enhancement rather than source fidelity yields images that look natural to people and work better with downstream vision models.

title: Special and General Computational Aesthetics
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Presented at the 2026 CCF Chinese Conference on Computational Art (CCAC 2026), Jinan, China, October 2026; to appear in the conference proceedings
summary: Computational aesthetics is a field at the intersection of computer science, artificial intelligence, aesthetics, and other disciplines. As AI has developed, the field has formed relations of inclusion, intersection, or support with computational art, AI art, AI aesthetics, AI-generated content (AIGC), computational creativity, affective computing, and neuroaesthetics. Without distinguishing scope, objectives, and methods, it may be narrowed to image aesthetic quality assessment or expanded into an umbrella term for AI's involvement in art. We analyze its internal structure and its relations with neighboring concepts, and propose a two-level scope: special computational aesthetics (SCA) and general computational aesthetics (GCA). SCA centers on aesthetic measurement and aesthetic process modeling. The former primarily corresponds to "Aesthetic Perception": computationally identifying and representing aesthetic attributes and predicting human aesthetic evaluations; the latter primarily to "Aesthetic Understanding": computationally describing, testing, and explaining how human aesthetic perception and judgment are formed. GCA extends this core to include "Aesthetic Generation," namely artistic generation guided by computational aesthetic models. Some computational aesthetic tasks can also use non-AI methods. Research in this scope using AI algorithms and models we define as AI aesthetics, which may involve the special core and the general extension. "Aesthetic Generation" intersects with AIGC, AI art, and computational creativity, but belongs to the general extension defined here only when computational aesthetic models substantively constrain, guide, or optimize artwork generation. We also draw on Feng Peng's discussion of the computability of beauty, aesthetic experience, and art as a theoretical reference for clarifying boundaries between computational aesthetics and related concepts.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a two-level scope for computational aesthetics, special computational aesthetics (SCA) for aesthetic measurement and process modeling, and general computational aesthetics (GCA), which adds aesthetic generation guided by aesthetic models. It clarifies boundaries with AI art, AIGC and computational creativity.
AI.motivation: The field's scope has been unclear: without distinguishing scope, objectives and methods, it may be narrowed to image quality assessment or expanded into an umbrella term for AI in art.
AI.method: The authors analyze the field's internal structure and its relations to neighboring concepts. SCA corresponds to aesthetic perception and aesthetic understanding, and GCA adds aesthetic generation. AI-based work in this scope is defined as AI aesthetics, and the paper draws on Feng Peng's discussion of the computability of beauty as a theoretical reference.
AI.result: The abstract reports no experiments or quantitative results; its contribution is conceptual.
AI.conclusion: A two-level scope separates measurement and understanding of aesthetics from aesthetically guided generation, which clarifies what counts as computational aesthetics.

title: EgoMo3R: Joint Egocentric Motion and Scene Reconstruction
comment: NeurIPS 2026. Project Page: this https URL
summary: Understanding holistic 3D human motion and the surrounding environment from egocentric video is fundamental for applications in AR/VR and robotics. Although these tasks are inherently coupled, existing methods treat them separately. In particular, egocentric motion reconstruction methods typically assume access to metric, gravity-aligned camera trajectories from specialized inertial sensors. Recovering such trajectories from monocular egocentric video remains a significant challenge due to rapid head movements and motion blur. We present EgoMo3R, a joint optimization framework that simultaneously reconstructs 3D human motion and scene geometry from casual egocentric video. It leverages the robustness of low-level visuo-geometric primitives, including monocular depth, optical flow, and point tracks, integrated with a diffusion-based human motion prior via first-order optimization. We propose an alternating optimization scheme that establishes a synergistic feedback loop: scene reconstruction provides physical grounding and trajectory conditioning for the motion prior, while the motion prior regularizes the camera trajectory and anchors the scene in a metric, gravity-aligned world frame. We evaluate EgoMo3R on the highly dynamic sequences of the EgoExo4D and Nymeria datasets and show that it outperforms specialized baselines in both 3D scene reconstruction and egocentric motion estimation.

AI.tldr: EgoMo3R jointly reconstructs 3D human motion and scene geometry from casual egocentric video by alternating optimization between scene reconstruction and a diffusion-based human motion prior. It outperforms specialized baselines in scene reconstruction and egocentric motion estimation on EgoExo4D and Nymeria.
AI.motivation: Egocentric motion methods usually assume metric, gravity-aligned trajectories from inertial sensors, and recovering such trajectories from monocular video is hard because of rapid head motion and blur. Motion and scene are tightly coupled but treated separately.
AI.method: The framework uses monocular depth, optical flow and point tracks as low-level visuo-geometric primitives, combined with a diffusion-based human motion prior through first-order optimization. The alternating scheme feeds back scene geometry as physical grounding and trajectory conditioning for the motion prior, while the prior regularizes the camera trajectory and anchors the scene in a metric, gravity-aligned world frame.
AI.result: On the highly dynamic sequences of EgoExo4D and Nymeria, EgoMo3R outperforms specialized baselines in both 3D scene reconstruction and egocentric motion estimation.
AI.conclusion: Joint optimization with a motion prior makes monocular egocentric video yield both metric scene geometry and human motion, without inertial sensors.

title: Zero-shot evaluation of open vision-language models as System 1 decision models on radiology tasks
summary: Purpose: We compared two multimodal System 1 decision models, Clef 27B and d1 3B, with a traditional LLM (Qwen 3.8-27B) on seven radiology tasks covering text, radiographs, CT and MRI. Methods: Three models were compared: Clef, Qwen3.8-27B and d1. Three tasks were interpretation of text and 4 were detection of finding in images. The tasks were: 1. finding presence of finding in CT-RATE chest CT reports; 2. Presence of finding in PadChest chest radiograph reports; 3. the same 18 findings on CT-RATE chest CT but 3D volumes; 4. MR safety status of devices from AccessGUDID device records; 5. line and tube position on RANZCR CLiP chest radiographs; 6. motion-artifact severity on MR-ART T1-weighted brain MRI and 7. sequence identification on BraTS 2021 brain MRI. The primary endpoint was AUROC. There was no fine-tuning of the models on the tasks. Results: All models completed all tests without a failed request. All retrieved findings from reports almost perfectly (AUROC >0.95). Clef ranked higher than its Qwen backbone on CT-RATE volumes and RANZCR lower on MR-ART. The two did not differ on BraTS, GUDID or PadChest, and differed by 0.002 on CT-RATE reports. On BraTS, Clef correctly identified 90 of 100 FLAIR volumes while Qwen never chose it. d1 ranked lower than Clef on six of seven tasks. No model performed well on motion severity. Clef was faster per request than Qwen on tasks with many questions per input. d1 used 3 to 9 times less energy per request than Clef. Conclusions: System 1 models can perform important tasks in radiology with high accuracy, at lower compute cost than LLMs used in the usual way. When an LLM is constrained to a single answer token, its cost and performance is similar to System 1 models unless multiple questions are asked. A 3B System 1 model was close to the 27B models on report text but not on images. No model performed well on motion severity.

AI.tldr: The study compares two multimodal System 1 models, Clef 27B and d1 3B, with the Qwen 27B LLM on seven radiology tasks without fine-tuning. Clef and Qwen perform similarly on most tasks, and the 3B d1 is close to the 27B models on report text but not on images.
AI.motivation: Compute-efficient models that make single-answer decisions could serve radiology tasks at lower cost than LLMs used in the usual way, but their accuracy across text and imaging tasks was unknown.
AI.method: Zero-shot evaluation on seven tasks: finding detection in CT-RATE chest CT reports, PadChest radiograph reports, CT-RATE volumes, MR safety status from AccessGUDID records, line and tube position on RANZCR CLiP, motion-artifact severity on MR-ART, and sequence identification on BraTS 2021. The primary endpoint is AUROC.
AI.result: All models completed all requests. Report-based finding retrieval reaches AUROC above 0.95. Clef ranks higher than Qwen on CT-RATE volumes and lower on MR-ART, and the two do not differ on BraTS, GUDID or PadChest. d1 ranks lower than Clef on six of seven tasks, and d1 uses 3 to 9 times less energy per request than Clef. No model performs well on motion severity.
AI.conclusion: System 1 models can perform important radiology tasks with high accuracy at lower compute cost than LLMs, though a 3B model is competitive only on report text and not on images.

title: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models for Urdu Nastaliq Handwriting Recognition
summary: Handwritten Urdu is hard to recognize because the cursive Nastaliq script has no fixed baseline and no clear character boundaries. We benchmark six systems on the Urdu Nastaliq Handwritten Dataset (UNHD): Tesseract (default configuration), a script-specific recognizer trained on printed Urdu (UTRNet-Large), two open-source vision-language models (VLMs), and two commercial VLMs. All six systems are evaluated without fine-tuning on 2,465 single-line images (Part A), and the four VLMs receive the same fixed prompt (decoding uses temperature 0 where configurable, except for Claude Sonnet 5, whose decoding cannot be configured). Both commercial VLMs reach lower error than the printed-Urdu recognizer and the open-source VLMs. We do not compare against handwriting-trained recognizers, which would likely do better in-domain; we characterize zero-shot behavior, not state of the art. We also describe three distinct failure modes among the ranked systems. In one of them, a commercial model explicitly declines to transcribe a few very hard-to-read images instead of guessing. In a second study (Part B), VLMs correct the output of a separate OCR system using both the source image and the noisy text. Once separated from each model's own reading ability, the benefit is small on Tesseract's output (0.7% to 7.4%) and larger (17.9% and 21.9%) only for the two commercial correctors given UTRNet's text. It appears to depend on how legible the supplied text already is, and a weaker corrector can make a more legible text worse.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks six OCR and vision-language systems on handwritten Urdu Nastaliq text without fine-tuning, finding that the two commercial VLMs have lower error than the printed-Urdu recognizer and the open-source VLMs. It also shows that VLM correction of OCR output helps mainly when the supplied text is already legible.
AI.motivation: Cursive Nastaliq script has no fixed baseline and no clear character boundaries, which makes handwritten Urdu hard to recognize, and zero-shot behavior of current systems on it was uncharacterized.
AI.method: Six systems are evaluated on 2,465 single-line images from UNHD (Part A): Tesseract, UTRNet-Large, two open-source VLMs and two commercial VLMs, with a fixed prompt and temperature 0 where configurable. In Part B, VLMs correct the output of a separate OCR system using the source image and the noisy text.
AI.result: Both commercial VLMs reach lower error than the printed-Urdu recognizer and the open-source VLMs. The authors describe three failure modes, including a commercial model declining to transcribe very hard images. In Part B the correction benefit is small on Tesseract output (0.7% to 7.4%) and larger (17.9% and 21.9%) only for the two commercial correctors on UTRNet output.
AI.conclusion: Zero-shot commercial VLMs read handwritten Urdu better than the compared systems, and VLM correction depends on how legible the supplied text already is, since a weaker corrector can make legible text worse. Handwriting-trained recognizers were not compared.

title: UA-Depth: Uncertainty-Aware Depth Restoration for Material-Agnostic Object Manipulation
summary: Robotic manipulation requires accurate metric depth, yet commodity RGB-D cameras often fail on non-Lambertian objects such as transparent, reflective, and translucent materials, producing holes, structured noise, and biased depth. Most restoration methods produce only a single depth map, treating noisy and reliable regions uniformly for downstream tasks while ignoring regional uncertainty. We present UA-Depth, an uncertainty-aware depth restoration framework that iteratively co-refines depth and pixel-wise uncertainty, and uses uncertainty-gated features to suppress unreliable cues for stable updates. To strengthen zero-shot behavior, UA-Depth leverages a frozen depth foundation model as a prior to initialize missing or unreliable depth, and applies two-stage MAD-weighted log-depth scale normalization to reduce outlier bias in relative-to-metric alignment. We introduce an eight-dataset zero-shot benchmark across diverse scenes, materials, and sensors. Across these benchmarks, UA-Depth achieves the best mean rank among representative baselines, with particularly strong gains on datasets dominated by transparent and reflective objects. Beyond depth metrics, we demonstrate downstream improvements in category-level 6D pose estimation and 6D grasp synthesis by exploiting the predicted uncertainty. \emph{Code, models, and data for training and evaluation will be released upon publication.}

AI.tldr: UA-Depth restores depth for transparent, reflective and translucent objects by iteratively co-refining depth and pixel-wise uncertainty, with uncertainty-gated features and a frozen depth foundation model as prior. It achieves the best mean rank across an eight-dataset zero-shot benchmark and improves 6D pose estimation and grasp synthesis.
AI.motivation: Commodity RGB-D cameras fail on non-Lambertian materials, producing holes, structured noise and biased depth, and most restoration methods output a single depth map that treats noisy and reliable regions alike.
AI.method: The framework iteratively co-refines depth and pixel-wise uncertainty and uses uncertainty-gated features to suppress unreliable cues during updates. A frozen depth foundation model initializes missing or unreliable depth, and two-stage MAD-weighted log-depth scale normalization reduces outlier bias in relative-to-metric alignment.
AI.result: Across an eight-dataset zero-shot benchmark, UA-Depth achieves the best mean rank among representative baselines, with particularly strong gains on datasets dominated by transparent and reflective objects. Downstream, the predicted uncertainty improves category-level 6D pose estimation and 6D grasp synthesis.
AI.conclusion: Explicit uncertainty estimation makes depth restoration more reliable for manipulation of non-Lambertian objects, and the benefit carries over to downstream pose and grasp tasks.

title: dKV Forcing: Separating Generation and Memory Representations through a Differentiable KV Cache
summary: A causal video generator produces two key--value (KV) states for every segment: the KV it uses while denoising that segment, and the KV it writes into the cache for later segments to read. In a pretrained generator the two already differ substantially, later segments attend to them differently, and replacing the written KV with the generation KV degrades the continuation. We propose dKV Forcing (dKV denotes differentiable KV) to learn a dedicated memory representation from its future use: a writer-specific low-rank residual on the shared backbone separates memory writing from generation and is trained through the future reads of what it writes. Learning a write from its future use needs gradients through the cache, which the mutable cache in common use cannot provide. dKV Forcing replaces the training-time cache by persistent differentiable pages with local rematerialization and, in one temporal traversal, computes exactly the gradient that a two-pass reconstruction of the same objective computes. One traversal computes the full memory gradient at $7\%$ generator-update overhead over detached-write training, with $28\%$ less resident memory and $20.8\%$ shorter training cycles than the two-pass reconstruction. Over Self Gradient Forcing (SGF), the same objective trained with the same traversal, writer adaptation raises VBench-Long aesthetic quality by $6.6$ points at 60\,s and $8.5$ points at 240\,s with the highest subject and background consistency, and rollout dropout of the residual keeps most of this gain while restoring the motion of training without write gradients.

AI.tldr: dKV Forcing learns a dedicated memory representation for causal video generation by training a writer-specific low-rank residual through the future reads of the KV cache it writes, using differentiable pages. It improves VBench-Long aesthetic quality over Self Gradient Forcing by 6.6 points at 60 s and 8.5 points at 240 s, at 7% generator-update overhead.
AI.motivation: A causal video generator's cache entries used for denoising and those written for later segments differ, and replacing the written KV with the generation KV degrades continuation. Learning a write from its future use needs gradients through the cache, which common mutable caches cannot provide.
AI.method: A writer-specific low-rank residual on the shared backbone separates memory writing from generation. The training-time cache is replaced by persistent differentiable pages with local rematerialization, so one temporal traversal computes the same gradient as a two-pass reconstruction.
AI.result: One traversal computes the full memory gradient at 7% generator-update overhead over detached-write training, with 28% less resident memory and 20.8% shorter training cycles than the two-pass reconstruction. Over Self Gradient Forcing, writer adaptation raises VBench-Long aesthetic quality by 6.6 points at 60 s and 8.5 points at 240 s with the highest subject and background consistency. Rollout dropout of the residual keeps most of the gain while restoring motion.
AI.conclusion: Training the memory writer through its future reads, with a differentiable cache, improves long-horizon video generation quality at modest cost.

title: GatedVLA with Camera-Based Emergency Braking: AlpaSim E2E Closed Loop Challenge Technical Report
summary: This report presents GatedVLA, our entry for the Physical AI AV (PAI-AV) track. Our learned vision-language-action (VLA) policy pairs the driving-pretrained Qwen-Drive-1.0-4B vision-language model with a layer-wise flow-matching action expert that outputs a 2.5 s horizon of acceleration and curvature controls, augmented with a soft visual mask applied to the expert's cross-attention. Compared to an identically trained baseline, the masked policy achieves comparable overall open-loop error while reducing error on left turns. In local closed-loop evaluation across the same 150 scenes (two rollouts per scene), the visual mask increases the mean scene score from 0.479 to 0.517 (paired difference +0.038, 95% bootstrap CI [-0.018, +0.093], wins/losses 37/26, sign test p = 0.21). Incorporating a rule-based automatic emergency braking (AEB) module at deployment further increases the mean score to 0.599 (+0.082, CI [+0.023, +0.143]) and reduces the mean number of scenes with at-fault collisions from 34.0 to 11.0.

AI.tldr: GatedVLA is a vision-language-action driving policy that adds a soft visual mask to a flow-matching action expert, and a rule-based automatic emergency braking module at deployment. In local closed-loop evaluation the mask lifts the mean scene score from 0.479 to 0.517, and adding AEB raises it to 0.599 while halving at-fault collisions.
AI.motivation: The authors enter the Physical AI AV track of the AlpaSim E2E Closed Loop Challenge, where a learned driving policy must handle closed-loop scenes safely.
AI.method: The policy pairs the driving-pretrained Qwen-Drive-1.0-4B vision-language model with a layer-wise flow-matching action expert that outputs a 2.5 s horizon of acceleration and curvature. A soft visual mask is applied to the expert's cross-attention. A rule-based AEB module is added at deployment.
AI.result: Relative to an identically trained baseline, the masked policy has comparable open-loop error and lower error on left turns. Across 150 scenes with two rollouts each, the mask raises mean scene score from 0.479 to 0.517 (paired difference +0.038, 95% CI -0.018 to +0.093, sign test p = 0.21). AEB raises the mean to 0.599 (+0.082, CI +0.023 to +0.143) and reduces the mean number of scenes with at-fault collisions from 34.0 to 11.0.
AI.conclusion: In this local evaluation the visual mask gain is not statistically significant, while the rule-based braking module gives a significant improvement in score and collision count.

title: MMCoT$^3$: Empowering 3D Scene Understanding with 3D-Text Interleaved Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Accepted to ACM Multimedia 2026
summary: Understanding and reasoning over 3D scenes from point clouds is essential for a broad range of AI applications. Recent 3D large language models have shown promising results, yet they still face two fundamental limitations: (i) insufficient capability for grounded multi-step reasoning in complex 3D scenes, and (ii) a text-centric inference paradigm that lacks effective interaction between textual reasoning and visual evidence. As a result, these models often fail to verify intermediate inferences, disambiguate similar object instances, and avoid hallucinations. To address these limitations, we propose MMCoT$^3$, the first 3D-Text Interleaved Chain-of-Thought (CoT) framework for 3D scene understanding. The core idea is to explicitly interleave textual reasoning with task-relevant 3D evidence, enabling the model to consult scene observations throughout the reasoning process. In addition, since a textual mention in 3D scenes may correspond to multiple candidate objects, naive object-mention alignment can inject incorrect evidence and mislead subsequent reasoning. To mitigate this multi-instance ambiguity, we design an ambiguity-aware evidence aggregation mechanism that uses query-guided cross-attention to fuse candidate object tokens and inject both evidence and ambiguity cues into the reasoning process. To better equip the model with multi-step reasoning capability, we further develop PointCoT, a large-scale 3D-specific CoT instruction tuning dataset with approximately 176.2K instances spanning captioning, question answering, dialogue, and planning tasks. Extensive experiments on six benchmarks show that our method consistently improves performance and achieves state-of-the-art results, validating the effectiveness of our proposed ambiguity-aware 3D-text interleaved reasoning for 3D scene understanding.

AI.tldr: MMCoT3 is a 3D-text interleaved chain-of-thought framework that lets a 3D LLM consult scene evidence during multi-step reasoning, with ambiguity-aware aggregation of candidate object tokens. It introduces PointCoT, a dataset of about 176.2K 3D CoT instructions, and reports state-of-the-art results on six benchmarks.
AI.motivation: 3D LLMs have limited grounded multi-step reasoning and rely on text-centric inference that does not verify intermediate steps against visual evidence, so they fail to disambiguate similar instances and tend to hallucinate.
AI.method: Textual reasoning is explicitly interleaved with task-relevant 3D evidence. Because a textual mention may match several candidate objects, query-guided cross-attention fuses candidate object tokens and injects evidence and ambiguity cues into the reasoning. The authors also build PointCoT, with about 176.2K instances spanning captioning, question answering, dialogue and planning.
AI.result: The method consistently improves performance on six benchmarks and achieves state-of-the-art results, according to the abstract, which gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Ambiguity-aware interleaving of text reasoning with 3D evidence is a effective route to grounded 3D scene understanding.

title: Leveraging 2D Foundation Priors for Generalized Category Discovery under Test-Time Adaptation in 3D LiDAR Segmentation
summary: In autonomous driving, 3D LiDAR semantic segmentation is expected to adapt to evolving environments and recognize previously unseen categories, making generalized category discovery under test-time adaptation (GCD-TTA) an important problem. However, existing works treat GCD and TTA separately, while the limited semantic information in 3D point clouds makes GCD-TTA under domain shift more prone to feature collapse when combining GCD with TTA. To address this issue, we propose a two-stage framework for GCD-TTA in 3D LiDAR semantic segmentation. Specifically, in the first stage, we adaptively aggregate local 3D features according to geometric density variations and obtain reliable pseudo labels under a global class-wise prototype consistency constraint. In the second stage, we cast category discovery as an optimal transport assignment process for globally consistent grouping of novel categories. Meanwhile, semantic features from 2D vision foundation models are fused with 3D point cloud features to enrich 3D semantic information and promote a more separable feature space. Extensive experiments on Synth4D to SemanticKITTI, SynLiDAR to SemanticKITTI, and Synth4D to nuScenes demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework. Under a unified evaluation protocol, our method achieves the best overall mIoU on 9 out of 10 benchmark splits and improves the overall mIoU by up to 12.21 points over the strongest re-implemented baseline.

AI.tldr: A two-stage framework for generalized category discovery under test-time adaptation in 3D LiDAR segmentation uses geometry-aware local features with optimal-transport assignment, and fuses 2D foundation-model features to avoid feature collapse. It improves overall mIoU by up to 12.21 points over the strongest re-implemented baseline and is best on 9 of 10 splits.
AI.motivation: Autonomous driving needs LiDAR segmentation that adapts to changing environments and recognizes unseen categories, but GCD and TTA are treated separately, and the sparse semantics of point clouds make their combination under domain shift prone to feature collapse.
AI.method: In the first stage, local 3D features are aggregated according to geometric density, and reliable pseudo-labels are obtained under a global class-wise prototype consistency constraint. In the second stage, category discovery is cast as an optimal transport assignment for globally consistent grouping of novel categories, and 2D vision foundation model features are fused with 3D features.
AI.result: On Synth4D to SemanticKITTI, SynLiDAR to SemanticKITTI and Synth4D to nuScenes, the method achieves the best overall mIoU on 9 of 10 benchmark splits under a unified protocol, with gains of up to 12.21 points over the strongest re-implemented baseline.
AI.conclusion: Combining optimal transport category discovery with 2D foundation features gives a more separable feature space for unseen-category discovery during test-time adaptation in LiDAR segmentation.

title: GaitFM: A Cross-Modal Foundation Model for Wearable Gait Assessment
