summary: Gait assessment supports the diagnosis, monitoring, and prognosis of diverse movement-related conditions, such as neurological and musculoskeletal disorders. Recent advances in deep learning using everyday wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs) offer an accessible and low-cost approach to automated gait assessment. However, IMU measurements vary substantially across individuals, body locations, and device configurations, while existing deep learning models are typically developed using small, homogeneous datasets for specific clinical tasks, limiting their robustness and generalizability in diverse real-world contexts. Here we present GaitFM, a cross-modal foundation model for gait assessment using IMU sensors. GaitFM improves the generalizability of gait assessment by transferring knowledge from large vision models and pretraining on unlabeled IMU sensor data. We pretrain GaitFM on a large curated dataset comprising about 4,000 participants and 1.23 million gait windows across diverse clinical and daily conditions, sensor modalities, and body locations. GaitFM demonstrates strong performance across 18 gait-related tasks, including 3 gait parameter estimation tasks, 14 disease and gait abnormality detection tasks, and 1 clinical outcome prediction task. Furthermore, GaitFM generalizes across different sensor configurations and body locations, including those commonly used in clinical settings and everyday wearable devices. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of transferring visual knowledge in improving sensor-based gait assessment performance, offering a new promising pathway for addressing data scarcity in the sensor and medical domains.

AI.tldr: GaitFM is a cross-modal foundation model for wearable IMU gait assessment that transfers knowledge from large vision models and pretrains on about 1.23 million unlabeled gait windows from roughly 4,000 participants. It performs strongly across 18 gait-related tasks and generalizes across sensor configurations and body locations.
AI.motivation: IMU measurements vary across individuals, body locations and devices, and existing deep learning models are trained on small, homogeneous clinical datasets, which limits their robustness in real-world settings.
AI.method: GaitFM is pretrained on a large curated dataset spanning diverse clinical and daily conditions, sensor modalities and body locations, and it transfers knowledge from large vision models into IMU-based gait assessment.
AI.result: GaitFM performs strongly across 18 tasks: three gait parameter estimation tasks, 14 disease and gait abnormality detection tasks, and one clinical outcome prediction task. It generalizes across different sensor configurations and body locations, including clinical and everyday wearable settings.
AI.conclusion: Transferring visual knowledge to sensor-based models can improve gait assessment and offers a route around data scarcity in sensor and medical domains.

title: SEALECT: Scene-Conditioned Pose Priors for Plausible Maritime Vessel Retrieval
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027 (Applications Track). 22 pages: 11-page main paper including references, plus 11 pages of supplementary material. Code: this https URL
summary: We address scene-conditioned object retrieval for compositional augmentation in maritime imagery, where strong geometric constraints make appearance-only retrieval produce physically implausible vessel insertions. We propose SEALECT, a retrieval framework that jointly models visual compatibility, vessel pose, scale, and scene geometry through a unified score combining neural similarity, scene-conditioned pose priors, and observed-pose consistency. We construct a maritime scene-pose library and model the pose and scale priors nonparametrically, as a kernel that conditions each prior continuously on the scene with no learned parameters. Across seven maritime benchmarks, our trained scene-conditioned retriever exceeds the strongest appearance encoder (SigLIP 2) in recall (+0.14), and the training-free prior raises geometric plausibility further at negligible recall cost, more than halving the constraint violations of appearance retrieval and outperforming learned foreground-search baselines (GALA-style, DiscoFOS). In a blind study of end-to-end composites (BootPlace placement, DiffHarmony harmonization), SEALECT ranks first among six methods, ahead of random and GALA-style selection and statistically tied with CLIP, DiscoFOS, and DINO.

AI.tldr: SEALECT is a retrieval framework for inserting vessels into maritime imagery that jointly scores visual similarity, scene-conditioned pose and scale priors, and observed-pose consistency so that inserted vessels are physically plausible.
AI.motivation: Appearance-only retrieval for compositional augmentation in maritime scenes produces physically implausible vessel insertions because strong geometric constraints are ignored.
AI.method: The method builds a maritime scene-pose library and models pose and scale priors nonparametrically as a kernel that conditions each prior continuously on the scene, with no learned parameters, and combines it with a trained scene-conditioned retriever in a unified score.
AI.result: Across seven maritime benchmarks the trained retriever exceeds the strongest appearance encoder SigLIP 2 in recall by 0.14, and the training-free prior raises geometric plausibility at negligible recall cost, more than halving constraint violations of appearance retrieval and outperforming GALA-style and DiscoFOS foreground-search baselines; in a blind study of end-to-end composites SEALECT ranks first among six methods and is statistically tied with CLIP, DiscoFOS, and DINO for the runner-up positions.
AI.conclusion: Modelling scene geometry as a parameter-free prior makes retrieval for maritime augmentation substantially more physically plausible without a meaningful loss in recall.

title: Restoring Semantic Fidelity for Training-Free High-Resolution Image Generation in Diffusion Transformers
summary: Diffusion Transformer (DiT)-based text-to-image models have recently achieved remarkable success in image synthesis. However, when directly applied beyond their training resolution, these models often suffer from severe semantic degradation, where meaningful semantic content disappears. Although existing training-free high-resolution generation methods can mitigate this issue, the inherent semantic degradation at high resolutions remains largely unresolved, leading to degraded fine-grained details. Furthermore, widely used structural guidance methods lack modeling of the structure and details in the intermediate trajectory, which degrades the quality of the generated results. In this paper, we propose a training-free framework for high-resolution image generation to address these challenges. First, we propose a text-visual scale-decoupled attention (TVSDA) module, which restores the model's ability to generate semantically meaningful content at high resolutions by preserving the global receptive field of text tokens while aligning the receptive field of image tokens with the training resolution. Second, we propose a structure-detail guidance (SDG) strategy that explicitly models structural information and fine details through scale-wise and temporal-wise guidance, overcoming the limitations of conventional low-resolution guidance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly improves both structural coherence and detail fidelity over existing training-free DiT-based high-resolution generation approaches. The code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a training-free framework for high-resolution image generation with Diffusion Transformers that restores semantic content and improves fine-detail and structural quality beyond the training resolution.
AI.motivation: DiT text-to-image models suffer severe semantic degradation when run beyond their training resolution, and existing training-free high-resolution methods leave this degradation largely unresolved and use low-resolution structural guidance that ignores intermediate trajectory structure and detail.
AI.method: The method combines a text-visual scale-decoupled attention (TVSDA) module, which keeps the global receptive field of text tokens while aligning the receptive field of image tokens with the training resolution, and a structure-detail guidance (SDG) strategy that models structure and fine details through scale-wise and temporal-wise guidance.
AI.result: Extensive experiments reportedly show significant improvements in structural coherence and detail fidelity over existing training-free DiT-based high-resolution generation approaches; the abstract gives no specific numbers or benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling attention scales and guiding with multi-scale and temporal structure offers a training-free route to coherent high-resolution generation from DiT models.

title: Fréchet Oral Distance: A Coordinate-Free Metric and Benchmark for Speech-Driven Oral Animation
summary: Recently, speech-driven facial and oral animation technologies have been used in various fields such as education, speech therapy, and healthcare. But methods to objectively evaluate the quality of generated results are still limited. Accordingly, we propose the Fréchet Oral Distance (FOD), which uses embeddings from an Oral Motion Encoder (OME) and a TIMIT-Vis reference distribution. In experiments, FOD reproduced model rankings similar to the coordinate-based metric, Lip Vertex Error (LVE), and showed trends consistent with user preference. Our framework provides objective and reproducible benchmarking without relying on expensive equipment or subjective evaluation, and it can be extended to compare a variety of 2D/3D models.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Fréchet Oral Distance (FOD), a coordinate-free metric with a TIMIT-Vis reference distribution for evaluating speech-driven oral animation, which reproduces model rankings of the coordinate-based Lip Vertex Error.
AI.motivation: Objective evaluation of speech-driven facial and oral animation is limited, and existing coordinate-based metrics such as Lip Vertex Error require careful coordinate alignment and do not capture overall distribution similarity.
AI.method: FOD compares embeddings from an Oral Motion Encoder (OME) against a reference distribution built from TIMIT-Vis, in the manner of a Fréchet distance, and does not depend on vertex coordinates.
AI.result: FOD reproduces model rankings similar to Lip Vertex Error and shows trends consistent with user preference; the abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: The framework gives objective, reproducible benchmarking without expensive equipment or subjective studies and can be extended to compare 2D and 3D models.

title: Deep Learning for Cervical Cytology Screening: Methods, Algorithms, Challenges and Prospects
summary: Cervical cancer remains a leading cause of cancer death among women, with more than 90\% of deaths occurring in low- and middle-income countries, where cytology screening is constrained by a shortage of trained cytopathologists. Deep learning has made automated cytology screening increasingly feasible, but the literature is fragmented across cell, patch and whole-slide-image scales, task formulations and supervision regimes, hindering comparison and clinical translation. This Review synthesizes the deep learning literature for cervical cytology screening, organizing the field along three axes---data scale, functional task and supervision---and distinguishing two clinical roadmaps: whole-slide-image confidence aggregation and cell-level detection with Bethesda classification. We examine 16 publicly available or publicly documented cytology datasets alongside the CAISHI histopathology dataset, compare quantitative performance while exposing incomparable metrics and data leakage, and assess commercial systems, regulatory status, HPV-era screening pathways and low-resource deployment. Single-cell accuracy on Herlev and SIPaKMeD has plateaued, but this reflects benchmark saturation rather than clinical readiness; prospective and randomized evidence is emerging but remains limited. We consolidate the evidence into five challenge areas---data and benchmarks, architecture and label-efficient learning, trustworthy AI, clinical translation and health economics, and evaluation and reproducibility---and provide an evidence-to-agenda map and a deployment decision matrix. Progress now depends on multi-center benchmarks, externally validated label-efficient methods, calibrated and fair predictions, and pragmatic clinical trials rather than further gains on saturated single-cell benchmarks.

AI.tldr: This review surveys deep learning for cervical cytology screening, organizing the literature along data scale, functional task and supervision and concluding that single-cell benchmark accuracy has plateaued without establishing clinical readiness.
AI.motivation: Cervical cancer mainly burdens low- and middle-income countries where cytopathologists are scarce, and deep learning literature for cytology is fragmented across cell, patch and whole-slide scales, tasks and supervision regimes, which hinders comparison and clinical translation.
AI.method: The review organizes the field along data scale, functional task and supervision, distinguishes whole-slide-image confidence aggregation from cell-level detection with Bethesda classification, examines 16 public or publicly documented cytology datasets with the CAISHI histopathology dataset, and assesses commercial systems, regulation, HPV-era screening pathways and low-resource deployment.
AI.result: Single-cell accuracy on Herlev and SIPaKMeD has plateaued, metrics across studies are often incomparable, and data leakage is exposed; prospective and randomized evidence is emerging but limited.
AI.conclusion: The authors consolidate five challenge areas and call for multi-center benchmarks, externally validated label-efficient methods, calibrated and fair predictions, and pragmatic clinical trials rather than further gains on saturated benchmarks, supported by an evidence-to-agenda map and a deployment decision matrix.

title: RSI-Env: An Open-Ended Environment for Recursive Self-Improvement of Agents
summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) envisions agent systems that autonomously improve their own models and harnesses, with each updated system continuing to improve itself. Existing approaches typically restrict optimization objectives, editable components, or evaluation procedures, limiting open-ended exploration and continuity across generations. We introduce RSI-Env, a persistent environment for coordinated model-harness improvement, supporting autonomous training, harness modification, and retention of research state. An independent Host Controller manages services, evaluation, and versioning. Under Self, each accepted model-harness version takes over the next improvement round. We define three settings that vary goal specificity and access to benchmark feedback: Open-General, Capability-Directed, and Benchmark-Guided. Across these three settings, we compare Self with two fixed external Teachers on seven tasks, starting from Qwen3.8-27B with a minimal harness. Without benchmark feedback, Open-General Self raises GPQA Diamond accuracy from 65.2% to 73.2% and AIME 2026 accuracy from 53.3% to 56.7%. All three Capability-Directed Self runs achieve target-aligned gains. Knowledge Self demonstrates continued improvement across system updates, with SimpleQA accuracy rising from 82.0% to 85.0% and then 88.0%. Benchmark guidance and Teacher benefits vary by task. These results demonstrate RSI-Env's support for open-ended exploration and sustained recursive improvement within the studied runs, while highlighting challenges in preserving gains across capabilities.

AI.tldr: RSI-Env is a persistent environment for recursive self-improvement of agents, in which an accepted model-harness version takes over the next improvement round, and the paper reports gains across seven tasks in three settings.
AI.motivation: Existing recursive self-improvement approaches restrict optimization objectives, editable components or evaluation procedures, which limits open-ended exploration and continuity across generations.
AI.method: An independent Host Controller manages services, evaluation and versioning, and under the Self setting each accepted model-harness version performs the next improvement round; three settings (Open-General, Capability-Directed, Benchmark-Guided) vary goal specificity and access to benchmark feedback, and Self is compared with two fixed external Teachers starting from Qwen3.8-27B with a minimal harness.
AI.result: Without benchmark feedback, Open-General Self raises GPQA Diamond accuracy from 65.2% to 73.2% and AIME 2026 accuracy from 53.3% to 56.7%; all three Capability-Directed Self runs achieve target-aligned gains; Knowledge Self rises on SimpleQA from 82.0% to 85.0% and then 88.0%; benefits of benchmark guidance and Teachers vary by task.
AI.conclusion: The results show sustained recursive improvement within the studied runs, while highlighting that preserving gains across capabilities remains a challenge.

title: Teleoperation System for Service Robots using Virtual Reality Headset and Pose Estimation
summary: This paper presents a teleoperation system for service robots that integrates human pose estimation with virtual reality (VR) to enable intuitive remote control. By using the Mediapipe framework for 2D pose detection and extending it with RGB-D data from the Intel RealSense D455 camera, a comprehensive 3D human pose estimation is achieved. This data is then mapped to the robot's kinematics, allowing the operator to control the robot's movements naturally. A VR interface was developed to provide an immersive perspective, enhancing the operator's situational awareness. Real-world experiments were conducted using the CHARMIE service robot to validate the system's effectiveness in tasks involving object manipulation. While the current system successfully demonstrates the potential of VR-based teleoperation, challenges remain in accurately capturing certain joint angles (e.g., wrist yaw) and ensuring precise mapping between human and robot movements. Future work includes the integration of inertial measurement units (IMUs) for improved rotational tracking and the implementation of more advanced control algorithms. Overall, this research contributes to the development of more intuitive and effective teleoperation systems for service robots, facilitating their deployment in complex and dynamic environments. This work further introduces a novel approach to teleoperation by combining RGB-D sensing with an innovative algorithm for real-time joint angle computation using Mediapipe, enhancing the precision of human-robot motion mapping and enabling immersive control through a VR interface. These contributions represent significant advancements in the field of human-robot interaction, particularly for service robot applications.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a VR teleoperation system for service robots that combines Mediapipe 2D pose detection with RGB-D depth from an Intel RealSense D455 to map a human operator's 3D pose onto robot kinematics, validated on the CHARMIE robot.
AI.motivation: Intuitive remote control of service robots requires capturing the operator's motion accurately and giving an immersive view of the robot's workspace.
AI.method: Mediapipe 2D pose detection is extended with RGB-D data to obtain 3D human pose, a joint-angle computation algorithm maps this to the robot kinematics, and a VR interface provides an immersive perspective.
AI.result: Real-world experiments on the CHARMIE service robot show that the system works for object-manipulation tasks, though some joint angles, such as wrist yaw, are captured inaccurately; the abstract gives no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates the potential of VR-based pose teleoperation for service robots, with future work planned on IMUs for rotational tracking and more advanced control.

title: FinishStrong: Learning to End Well after Imperfect Start in Video Temporal Grounding
summary: A poor start lowers the ceiling, but does not negate the value of finishing well. In autoregressive video temporal grounding, models systematically exhibit an endpoint performance asymmetry, predicting ends significantly worse than starts. A committed flawed start acts as an immutable physical constraint, irreversibly capping the attainable overlap as a sunk loss. While models should minimize the remaining conditional regret, standard post-training paradigms fail to teach this adaptation. Specifically, teacher-forced SFT suffers from strict prefix exposure bias, and holistic trajectory evaluation in standard GRPO inadvertently penalizes conditionally optimal ends if they follow a poor start. To address this, we introduce FinishStrong, a novel two-stage post-training framework explicitly designed to teach optimal continuations. First, Online-start SFT exposes the end prediction to the model's own generated contexts. Second, Conditional-tree GRPO restructures the sampling topology, centering end rewards exclusively within the same-start branch to mathematically isolate the conditional end quality from the inherited start penalty. FinishStrong-9B achieves a state-of-the-art 61.7\% overall IoU on TimeLens-Bench, remarkably outperforming flagship closed-source models like Gemini-3.8-Flash and Qwen3.8-Max. Crucially, when forced to continue from imperfect starts, it reduces the subsequent end prediction error by 36.5\%, proving its exceptional ability to end well after flawed starts. Code will be open.

AI.tldr: FinishStrong is a two-stage post-training framework for autoregressive video temporal grounding that teaches models to predict good end points after imperfect starts, reaching 61.7% overall IoU on TimeLens-Bench with the 9B model.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive grounding models predict ends much worse than starts, and standard post-training fails to teach conditional adaptation to a committed flawed start, because teacher-forced SFT suffers from prefix exposure bias and holistic GRPO penalizes good ends that follow poor starts.
AI.method: Online-start SFT exposes end prediction to the model's own generated contexts, and Conditional-tree GRPO restructures the sampling topology so that end rewards are centred only within the same-start branch, isolating conditional end quality from the inherited start penalty.
AI.result: FinishStrong-9B achieves 61.7% overall IoU on TimeLens-Bench, which the authors state outperforms closed-source models such as Gemini-3.8-Flash and Qwen3.8-Max, and reduces subsequent end-prediction error by 36.5% when continuing from imperfect starts.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning reward and training on the start yields better ends after flawed starts; the code is promised to be released.

title: OCBI: Order-Sensitive Cross-Branch Interaction for Image Manipulation Localization
summary: Image manipulation localization combines semantic structure with forensic traces to identify modified pixels. Within-branch spatial mixing and RGB-guided cross-branch mixing can produce different messages when composed in opposite orders. We propose OCBI, an extension of Co-Transformers that models the discrepancy between these two composition orders for localization. A local cross-branch fusion module uses the commutator of RGB-guided cross-attention and forensic self-attention to add a learnable signed correction to feature transfer. Pixelwise adaptive multiscale aggregation then combines spatial contexts before prediction. OCBI uses the Co-Transformers backbone and supervision. We compare OCBI with retrained Co-Transformers using CASIA-only task training, a 50-epoch budget, and final-epoch evaluation. Across five clean test datasets, OCBI achieves a macro PixelF1 of 0.5773, exceeding the baseline by 0.43 percentage points. Under JPEG compression, Gaussian blur, and resizing on three datasets, its average PixelF1 over 21 dataset-transformation conditions exceeds the baseline by 0.95 percentage points.

AI.tldr: OCBI is an extension of Co-Transformers for image manipulation localization that models the discrepancy between two composition orders of within-branch and cross-branch mixing using a learnable signed correction.
AI.motivation: Within-branch spatial mixing and RGB-guided cross-branch mixing produce different messages depending on composition order, a discrepancy that existing localization models do not exploit.
AI.method: A local cross-branch fusion module uses the commutator of RGB-guided cross-attention and forensic self-attention to add a learnable signed correction to feature transfer, followed by pixelwise adaptive multiscale aggregation before prediction, with the Co-Transformers backbone and supervision.
AI.result: Under a controlled comparison with retrained Co-Transformers (CASIA-only training, 50 epochs, final-epoch evaluation), OCBI reaches a macro PixelF1 of 0.5773 on five clean test datasets, 0.43 percentage points above the baseline, and under JPEG, Gaussian blur and resizing it exceeds the baseline's average PixelF1 by 0.95 points over 21 conditions on three datasets.
AI.conclusion: Modelling the order-dependent discrepancy between compositions gives a modest but consistent gain in manipulation localization, including under common post-processing.

title: Detection Instead of Inversion: T1-T2 Microstructure Quantification With Detection Transformers
comment: 4 pages, 3 figures, 1 table; For submission to IEEE ISBI 2027; Code: this https URL
summary: T1-T2 correlation MRI has strong potential to quantify microstructural compartments without imposing a biological model. Traditionally, full T1-T2 spectra per voxel are reconstructed with an ill-conditioned and time-consuming Inverse Laplace Transform. We propose to view this challenge as an object detection task: A Detection Transformer (DETR) takes 64 TI/TE signals and directly predicts a set of compartments specified by T1, T2, and signal fraction. We achieve a mean average precision mAP@10 of 76.8% on simulated data, outperforming both our previous model design (53.8%) and regularized NNLS (66.1%). We show that our DETR approach outperforms NNLS in almost every setting across compartment count, compartmental signal fraction, and SNR. Reconstruction is orders of magnitude faster than NNLS. The results are fully reproducible from our public code: this http URL

AI.tldr: The paper frames T1-T2 correlation MRI microstructure quantification as object detection, using a Detection Transformer that directly predicts compartments with T1, T2 and signal fraction instead of an inverse Laplace transform.
AI.motivation: Full T1-T2 spectra per voxel from the Inverse Laplace Transform are ill-conditioned and slow, which limits practical microstructure quantification.
AI.method: A DETR takes 64 TI/TE signals per voxel and directly predicts a set of compartments specified by T1, T2 and signal fraction, and is compared with the authors' previous model design and regularized NNLS.
AI.result: On simulated data the DETR reaches mAP@10 of 76.8%, versus 53.8% for the previous design and 66.1% for regularized NNLS, outperforming NNLS in almost every setting of compartment count, signal fraction and SNR, with reconstruction orders of magnitude faster.
AI.conclusion: Detection-style prediction is a faster and more accurate alternative to inversion for T1-T2 microstructure quantification, and the code is public for reproduction.

title: RIFT: Residual-Informed Flow Transfer for One-Step Generative Video Compression
summary: Recent advances in video generation have enabled generative video compression to reconstruct details lost during coding using pretrained spatiotemporal priors. However, a substantial gap remains between codec-induced degradation and the perturbation trajectories learned by flow-matching models. In this paper, we identify a compression-dependent directional mismatch that degradation-strength-based timestep calibration alone cannot resolve. Compressed latents remain strongly aligned across codec operating points, while their reconstruction residuals vary substantially in magnitude and direction. To bridge this gap, we propose RIFT, a Residual-Informed Flow Transfer framework for one-step generative video compression. At its core, RIFT introduces a Residual Geometry Inducer (RGI) that converts the pretrained flow prediction into a content-adaptive restoration update using decoder-visible codec cues. RGI integrates flow-timestep conditioning with a learned full-band residual-strength estimate and content-conditioned direction and gain modulation, aligning the orientation and magnitude of the update with the compression-dependent residual geometry. Extensive experiments on three public video compression benchmarks show that RIFT outperforms competing generative video compression methods. The code is publicly available on RIFT.

AI.tldr: RIFT is a one-step generative video compression framework that uses decoder-visible codec cues to adapt a pretrained flow-matching model's restoration update to the compression-dependent residual geometry, outperforming competing generative methods on three benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Generative video compression reconstructs lost details with pretrained flow-matching priors, but a directional mismatch between codec-induced degradation and the learned perturbation trajectories remains, which degradation-strength timestep calibration alone cannot resolve.
AI.method: The Residual Geometry Inducer (RGI) converts the pretrained flow prediction into a content-adaptive restoration update, integrating flow-timestep conditioning, a learned full-band residual-strength estimate, and content-conditioned direction and gain modulation.
AI.result: RIFT outperforms competing generative video compression methods on three public video compression benchmarks; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Aligning the orientation and magnitude of the restoration update with residual geometry enables effective one-step generative video compression.

title: When Does Latent Prediction Error Support Physical Surprise Claims in Video World Models?
comment: 28 pages, 12 figures, 25 tables. Accepted at the World Models in Physical AI Workshop, NeurIPS 2026
summary: Prediction errors from video world models are often treated as physical surprise, but they can also reflect appearance, static content, motion, or ordinary prediction difficulty. We present an evaluation framework that separates what frozen representations contain, how they organize appearance and physical differences, and what changes a model's own prediction error. On IntPhys2, a benchmark of physically possible and impossible events, we compare representations from latent prediction, masked pixel reconstruction, and simple visual statistics. Appearance remains easy to decode, while V-JEPA2 exposes modest information about whether events are possible or impossible. Looking at the latent geometry, appearance changes become smaller compared with differences between videos, their directions line up more consistently across scenes, and their overlap with physical changes decreases in deeper layers. Across action-conditioned models, incorrect actions raise prediction error, while appearance changes also produce substantial responses. In Physion++ video clips, repeating a single frame can produce higher error than the original clip, while changing color throughout the clip can lower it. Using Kubric, a simulation and rendering framework, we find that impossible events can produce lower error than possible events. A fixed error threshold also incorrectly flags many possible events as impossible. A model can therefore represent physical information and respond to incorrect actions without its native prediction error reliably measuring physical surprise.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether prediction error from video world models can be treated as physical surprise, finding that it is confounded by appearance, motion and prediction difficulty, so the error alone does not reliably measure physical violations.
AI.motivation: Prediction errors from video world models are often read as physical surprise, but they may instead reflect appearance, static content, motion, or ordinary prediction difficulty.
AI.method: The evaluation framework separates what frozen representations contain, how they organize appearance and physical differences, and what changes a model's own prediction error, comparing latent-prediction, masked-pixel-reconstruction and simple visual-statistics representations on IntPhys2, with further analyses on Physion++ clips and Kubric simulations.
AI.result: Appearance is easy to decode while V-JEPA2 exposes modest information about physical possibility; incorrect actions raise prediction error but appearance changes also produce large responses; repeating a frame can raise error and recolouring can lower it in Physion++; impossible Kubric events can yield lower error than possible ones; a fixed error threshold flags many possible events as impossible.
AI.conclusion: A model can represent physical information and respond to incorrect actions without its native prediction error reliably measuring physical surprise.

title: RCFormer: Reliability-aware Context Transformer for Occlusion-Robust Facial Landmark Detection
comment: Accepted at the British Machine Vision Conference (BMVC 2026)
summary: Facial landmark detection has advanced substantially under regular imaging conditions, yet occlusion, poor illumination, and large pose changes remain major sources of error because local facial evidence can become incomplete or misleading. Context-guided latent patch recovery offers a promising way to address this issue by inferring unreliable patch representations from surrounding facial context before heatmap prediction. However, the recovered context can itself be unreliable when it is weakly adapted to the input face, influenced by corrupted neighboring patches, or blended without preserving local spatial coherence. We propose RCFormer, a Reliability-aware Context Transformer for occlusion-robust facial landmark detection. RCFormer strengthens latent patch recovery with three reliability-oriented components: visible-context conditioning (VCC), which adapts the context representation using a visibility-weighted global facial summary; visibility-guided context aggregation (VGCA), which reduces the influence of unreliable source patches during attention; and spatial residual correction (SRC), which refines blended latent features using neighboring patch information. The recovered heatmaps are then used as reliability-aware structural cues for existing landmark detection networks. Experiments show that RCFormer improves heatmap recovery and achieves strong landmark localization results on the WFLW, COFW, and 300W datasets.

AI.tldr: RCFormer is a reliability-aware context transformer that improves occlusion-robust facial landmark detection by making context-guided latent patch recovery aware of visibility, and its recovered heatmaps serve as cues for existing landmark networks.
AI.motivation: Context-guided latent patch recovery can produce unreliable patches when the context is weakly adapted to the input face, influenced by corrupted neighbours, or blended without spatial coherence, which harms landmark detection under occlusion, poor lighting and large pose changes.
AI.method: Three components are added: visible-context conditioning (VCC) adapts context with a visibility-weighted global facial summary, visibility-guided context aggregation (VGCA) reduces the influence of unreliable source patches in attention, and spatial residual correction (SRC) refines blended latent features using neighbouring patch information.
AI.result: The recovered heatmaps improve heatmap recovery and give strong landmark localization on WFLW, COFW and 300W; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Reliability-aware context recovery provides useful structural cues that improve landmark detection under occlusion.

title: LUMEN: Geometry-Guided Diffusion Model for Spatially-Varying HDR Illumination Estimation
summary: Estimating scene illumination from images is challenging as lighting is inherently spatially varying, depending on geometry, occlusion, and light sources. Existing methods incorporate geometric cues by deriving local environment maps or probe-based representations, but largely rely on regression or parametric models, resulting in over-smoothed lighting and limited realism. We revisit spatially-varying illumination estimation from a generative perspective and introduce LUMEN, a geometry-conditioned diffusion framework for synthesizing high-dynamic-range (HDR) environment maps at arbitrary spatial locations from single or multi-view images. Specifically, we reconstruct a coarse 3D scene from input images and render partial environment maps at arbitrary locations to encode visibility and spatial structure. These signals are fused with multi-view image features and fed into a diffusion transformer to generate full HDR environment maps. To train the model, we build a synthetic dataset of 700 indoor scenes with dense spatial supervision, including multi-view RGB images, depth, and HDR illumination at multiple sampled locations. This dataset enables the model to learn spatially consistent lighting distributions across diverse scenes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LUMEN significantly improves visual fidelity and spatial coherence compared to prior approaches.

AI.tldr: LUMEN is a geometry-conditioned diffusion transformer that generates HDR environment maps at arbitrary spatial locations from single or multi-view images, trained on a new synthetic dataset of 700 indoor scenes.
AI.motivation: Regression and parametric methods for spatially varying illumination produce over-smoothed lighting with limited realism, and geometric cues are used only in limited ways.
AI.method: A coarse 3D scene is reconstructed from the input images, partial environment maps are rendered at arbitrary locations to encode visibility and spatial structure, these signals are fused with multi-view image features, and a diffusion transformer generates full HDR environment maps; training uses a synthetic dataset of 700 indoor scenes with multi-view RGB, depth and HDR illumination at sampled locations.
AI.result: The abstract reports that LUMEN significantly improves visual fidelity and spatial coherence over prior approaches but gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: A generative, geometry-conditioned formulation learns spatially consistent lighting distributions across diverse scenes.

title: Z-Cache: Accelerating Diffusion Transformers via Self-Reflection
summary: Diffusion transformers have become the most powerful models for visual generation, but still suffer from massive computation costs. To solve this problem, feature caching has been proposed to cache the features of diffusion models in the previous computation steps and then reuse them in the following caching steps, which brings significant acceleration but also degradation in generation quality. To address this problem, this paper proposes Z-cache as a feature caching method that can maintain high-quality generation through self-reflection. Concretely, we observe that the error from feature caching tends to be sharply reduced after each full computation. Based on this observation, Z-Cache is designed to first predict the features in the future caching steps and then perform a full computation. After that, Z-Cache returns to the caching steps and re-predicts them based on the previous and the current computation steps, which brings correction in features. Experiments demonstrate that with Z-Cache, diffusion transformers achieve comparable generation quality to the original model but with faster inference speed, for instance, 6.22X acceleration on FLUX-dev for text-to-image generation. Our code is released on GitHub.

AI.tldr: Z-Cache is a feature-caching method for diffusion transformers that predicts future cached features, performs a full computation, and then re-predicts the cached steps to correct them, achieving 6.22x acceleration on FLUX-dev with comparable quality.
AI.motivation: Feature caching speeds up diffusion transformers by reusing earlier features, but reuse degrades generation quality.
AI.method: The authors observe that caching error drops sharply after each full computation, so Z-Cache predicts the features for upcoming caching steps, performs a full computation, and then re-predicts those steps from the previous and current computation steps to correct them.
AI.result: With Z-Cache, diffusion transformers achieve generation quality comparable to the original model with faster inference, for example 6.22x acceleration on FLUX-dev for text-to-image generation.
AI.conclusion: Self-reflective correction after full computations allows caching to accelerate diffusion transformers while keeping quality high; the code is released on GitHub.

title: Biological Congruence: Evaluating Microscopy Generation Across Representations
summary: Generative models increasingly produce realistic microscopy images, yet conventional evaluation primarily characterizes visual fidelity and distributional coverage rather than the biological information represented by synthetic data. We introduce biological congruence as an evaluation principle describing whether biologically relevant information forms a coherent description across representations and remains consistent with its empirical biological context. To study this principle, we develop a text-conditioned diffusion framework that jointly generates microscopy images and instance masks, exposing the same generated biological state through conditioning, visual appearance, and instance structure. Across prompt--mask, prompt--image, image--mask, and population-level analyses, we find strongly feature-dependent behavior: density and confluency are consistently preserved, morphology exhibits recurrent disagreement, while nearest-neighbor distance reveals that strong image--mask agreement can coexist with weaker conditioning and population fidelity. Stress testing increasingly unsupported phenotype combinations further shows that target controllability can increase while untargeted phenotypes reorganize and the complete generated state moves toward configurations better supported by real data. These findings demonstrate that generative quality, controllability, cross-representation agreement, and population fidelity capture complementary properties, motivating biological congruence as a relational perspective for evaluating scientific generative models.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces biological congruence as an evaluation principle for generative microscopy, using a text-conditioned diffusion model that jointly generates images and instance masks, and finds that quality, controllability, cross-representation agreement and population fidelity are distinct properties.
AI.motivation: Conventional evaluation of synthetic microscopy images measures visual fidelity and distributional coverage but not whether the biological information is coherent across representations and consistent with real biology.
AI.method: A text-conditioned diffusion framework jointly generates microscopy images and instance masks, exposing the same generated biological state through conditioning, appearance and instance structure, and is analysed through prompt-mask, prompt-image, image-mask and population-level comparisons plus stress tests on unsupported phenotype combinations.
AI.result: Density and confluency are consistently preserved, morphology shows recurrent disagreement, and nearest-neighbour distance shows strong image-mask agreement can coexist with weaker conditioning and population fidelity; under stress tests controllability of targeted phenotypes can rise while untargeted phenotypes reorganize.
AI.conclusion: Generative quality, controllability, cross-representation agreement and population fidelity are complementary, so biological congruence is proposed as a relational criterion for evaluating scientific generative models.

title: Learning-to-Memorize: Dynamic Context Management for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Generation
summary: Autoregressive video generation has achieved impressive results on short clips, yet generating long videos remains challenging due to error accumulation over extended horizons, where each predicted frame depends on potentially imperfect previous frames. Existing approaches typically rely on static context management strategies, such as sliding-window caches that discard early frames or fixed sink frames that permanently preserve initial content. These designs either lose critical long-range context or anchor generation to outdated information, which can lead to degraded fidelity, motion stagnation, and reduced diversity. In this paper, we propose Learning to Memorize (L2M), a learned context memory management framework that dynamically retains, evicts, and evolves historical frames according to predicted importance. The framework consists of an importance prediction router that estimates the relevance of each historical frame, degradation-aware training that improves robustness to noisy or corrupted context, and a dynamic memory initialization and evolution mechanism that updates long-term memory using exponential moving average (EMA) importance scores. This allows high-quality frames to replace stale anchors and enables memory to adapt naturally to scene evolution. Trained with a teacher-student distillation objective and sparsity regularization, L2M makes efficient use of a fixed KV-cache budget while preserving the most informative contextual information. Extensive experiments demonstrate that L2M improves long-horizon video generation quality and temporal consistency over existing baselines, providing a learned strategy for context memory management in long autoregressive video generation.

AI.tldr: Learning to Memorize (L2M) is a learned context-memory manager for long-horizon autoregressive video generation that decides which historical frames to retain, evict or update under a fixed KV-cache budget.
AI.motivation: Static context strategies such as sliding-window caches and fixed sink frames either lose critical long-range context or anchor generation to outdated frames, causing fidelity loss, motion stagnation and reduced diversity over long horizons.
AI.method: An importance prediction router estimates the relevance of each historical frame, degradation-aware training improves robustness to noisy or corrupted context, and a dynamic memory initialization and evolution mechanism updates long-term memory with exponential moving average importance scores; training uses teacher-student distillation and sparsity regularization.
AI.result: The abstract states that L2M improves long-horizon video generation quality and temporal consistency over existing baselines but gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Learned, importance-based context memory management is presented as a strategy for long autoregressive video generation within a fixed cache budget.

title: Advances in Agentic Computer Graphics
summary: Computer graphics is built on code. Large language model (LLM) agents can now generate graphics code and iteratively refine it through various feedback. This capability opens the door to a potentially new paradigm of computer graphics, with graphics algorithms increasingly built around agentic systems to automate progressively complex tasks. Over the past years, research on agentic graphics has expanded rapidly across a diverse range of tasks. This rapid growth makes it increasingly difficult for manual literature reviews to keep pace with new developments. At the same time, similar ideas are often described using different terminology across these tasks, further complicating efforts to develop a systematic understanding of the field. In this report, we address these challenges through two contributions. First, we introduce a unified taxonomy for characterizing agentic systems across diverse computer graphics tasks. Second, we develop an agentic literature system that can assist human researchers in analyzing existing and newly published papers at scale. Building on these contributions, we analyze emerging research trends and discuss open challenges in coordinating agents and tools across graphics tasks, designing interfaces and representations for human-agent collaboration, sustaining long-horizon planning and refinement, and reliably evaluating interactive graphics systems.

AI.tldr: This report proposes a unified taxonomy for agentic systems across computer graphics tasks and a literature-analysis system for reviewing agentic graphics research at scale, and it analyses trends and open challenges.
AI.motivation: LLM agents that generate and refine graphics code are expanding rapidly across many tasks, but terminology varies and manual literature reviews cannot keep pace with the field.
AI.method: The authors introduce a unified taxonomy for characterizing agentic systems across graphics tasks and develop an agentic literature system to help researchers analyse existing and newly published papers at scale.
AI.result: The report analyses emerging research trends and identifies open challenges in coordinating agents and tools, designing interfaces for human-agent collaboration, sustaining long-horizon planning and refinement, and evaluating interactive graphics systems; the abstract gives no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: A shared taxonomy and automated literature tooling are offered as a basis for systematically understanding agentic computer graphics.

title: Prior-Guided Physics-Informed Deep Learning for Fast 4D MRI Reconstruction
summary: Background and purpose: We propose PGPI4MR (prior-guided, physics-informed 4D MRI reconstruction), a deep learning method that leverages information from other respiratory phases or a setup scan, the first 30 s of the same scan, to improve 4D MRI reconstruction without extra scan time. Materials and methods: PGPI4MR is an unrolled network that reconstructs 16 respiratory phases from 60, 30, or 15 s of data, and single 3D volumes, each from 0.29-0.49 s of data, using a setup-scan image. The networks were trained once, on other volunteers, and were not retrained for new volunteers. We evaluated PGPI4MR on measured k-space from three datasets: free-breathing MR-linac (1.5T) and abdominal (3T) scans, and thigh scans with cuff compression (1.5T). All methods, including comparative models, received identical samples and were scored similarly. Results: In vivo, PGPI4MR had the lowest held-out error for 4D MRI at every scan time, and its 16 phases were ready a median of 7.5-13 s after the scan on the 2 GPUs tested. Coupling the 16 respiratory phases reduced the error at 60 s by 9.1% compared with reconstructing each phase alone. For sub-second MRI, the error at 0.49 s was 15.5% lower than that of the best comparison method, classical reconstruction toward the same prior, and on the faster GPU, every 0.29 s window was acquired and reconstructed within 0.5 s. Without retraining, PGPI4MR matched the best methods on the 3T abdominal scans but not on the thigh scans; after retraining on thigh data, it reduced the held-out error by 6.6% relative to the best comparison method. Conclusion: Prior information allowed PGPI4MR to reconstruct 4D and sub-second MRI more accurately than compressed sensing and a published 4D network, within seconds and without extra scan time. This could support 4D MRI for treatment planning and 3D motion monitoring during MR-guided radiotherapy.

AI.tldr: PGPI4MR is an unrolled, physics-informed deep network that reconstructs 4D MRI and sub-second 3D MRI using a prior from other respiratory phases or a setup scan, without extra scan time, and generalises to new volunteers without retraining for some scan types.
AI.motivation: 4D MRI for treatment planning and motion monitoring in MR-guided radiotherapy needs short scans, but short acquisitions yield poor reconstructions, and compressed sensing and a published 4D network are less accurate.
AI.method: PGPI4MR is an unrolled network that reconstructs 16 respiratory phases from 60, 30 or 15 seconds of data, and single 3D volumes from 0.29 to 0.49 seconds, using a setup-scan image as prior; networks are trained once on other volunteers and evaluated on measured k-space from MR-linac, abdominal and thigh datasets.
AI.result: In vivo, PGPI4MR has the lowest held-out error at every scan time, reconstructs its 16 phases a median of 7.5 to 13 seconds after the scan, and reduces error at 60 seconds by 9.1% relative to per-phase reconstruction; at 0.49 seconds its error is 15.5% lower than the best comparison; without retraining it matches the best methods on 3T abdominal scans but not thigh scans, and after retraining on thigh data it reduces held-out error by 6.6% relative to the best comparison.
AI.conclusion: Prior information allows accurate 4D and sub-second MRI within seconds and without extra scan time, which could support treatment planning and 3D motion monitoring during MR-guided radiotherapy.

title: Systematic Evaluation of Robustness in Fine-tuned Models
summary: Our study systematically evaluates the robustness of fine-tuned pre-trained models across different datasets and attack types, aiming to provide insights for researchers in selecting pre-trained models for image classification tasks while prioritizing robustness against potential attacks. Our work explores the influence of fine-tuning pre-trained models with different datasets and attack types on their robustness and overview of the appropriate pre-trained model for image classification based on factors such as computation resources, memory usage, and accuracy on clean data. We fine-tune the models with weights. Evaluate the models on data before any attack and after different attack cases. The study utilizes publicly available image datasets such as MNIST, CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and SVHN to assess the robustness of pre-trained models. The results indicate that the robustness of fine-tuned models varies across different data distributions and sample sizes, emphasizing the need for tailored selection based on specific task requirements. The findings also highlight the varying performance of ResNet50, DenseNet, and MobileNet in defending against attacks on different datasets. Overall, this research provides valuable insights into the robustness of fine-tuned pre-trained models and their suitability for real-world applications in image classification.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates the robustness of fine-tuned pre-trained image classifiers across datasets and attack types, and finds that robustness varies with data distribution and sample size, so model selection should be task-specific.
AI.motivation: Practitioners choosing pre-trained models for image classification need to know how fine-tuning affects robustness to attacks, alongside computation, memory and clean accuracy.
AI.method: Pre-trained models are fine-tuned on MNIST, CIFAR10, CIFAR100 and SVHN, evaluated on clean data and after several attack cases, and the robustness of ResNet50, DenseNet and MobileNet is compared; the abstract does not specify the attack algorithms.
AI.result: Robustness of fine-tuned models varies across data distributions and sample sizes, and the architectures differ in defending against attacks depending on the dataset; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Selection of a pre-trained model for robustness should be tailored to the specific task requirements and to its data.

title: Training-Free Motion-Corrected 3D Brain MRI Reconstruction via Event-Guided References
summary: Head motion causes artefacts in 3D brain MRI and can bias structural measurements. Model-based correction alternates between image and motion estimation, but artefacts in the reconstructed reference can reinforce motion errors. Learned priors can reduce these artefacts but require pretraining and may add test-time computation. We propose EventMC (event-guided motion correction), a training-free method for interleaved Cartesian acquisitions. It iteratively detects motion events and estimates motion using reference images reconstructed from stable intervals. It then refines the image and motion from low to high spatial frequencies. In a fair comparison in simulation (same reconstruction), EventMC's motion estimates improve mean PSNR by up to 4.0 dB over those of the learning-based MotionTTT. A single run of EventMC is up to 7.5 times faster than MotionTTT with less than half the GPU memory. On in vivo motion-corrupted scans, EventMC achieves similar mean image quality to MotionTTT without any training. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: EventMC is a training-free method for correcting head motion in 3D brain MRI from interleaved Cartesian acquisitions, which detects motion events and estimates motion from stable-interval reference images, and it outperforms the learning-based MotionTTT in simulation.
AI.motivation: Head motion causes artefacts in 3D brain MRI that bias measurements, and model-based correction can be corrupted by artefacts in its own reference images, while learned priors need pretraining and extra test-time computation.
AI.method: EventMC iteratively detects motion events and estimates motion using reference images reconstructed from stable intervals, then refines the image and motion from low to high spatial frequencies, with no training.
AI.result: In simulation with the same reconstruction, EventMC's motion estimates improve mean PSNR by up to 4.0 dB over MotionTTT; a single run is up to 7.5 times faster with less than half the GPU memory; on in vivo motion-corrupted scans it achieves similar mean image quality to MotionTTT.
AI.conclusion: A training-free, event-guided approach matches a learning-based method on in vivo data while being faster and lighter, and the code is available.

title: Online Active Learning Architecture for Safety-Critical Control Systems
summary: The transition of information-centric artificial intelligence to safety-critical applications is impeded by the limitations of conventional offline-training paradigms in open-world environments. This paper presents Control AI, an architecture for Online Active Learning (OAL) inspired by the continuous Prediction-Evaluation-Correction process of biological intelligence. The framework combines the hierarchical representation capacity of deep neural networks with the real-time error-feedback adaptation of adaptive control. A prediction model maps sensory input into a latent manifold, an optional latent model represents transitions in that space, and a reconstruction model maps the latent state back to observable signals. Residuals between predictions and measurements provide the internal learning signal. Spatial and temporal cross-reconstruction architectures prevent OAL from collapsing to a trivial identity mapping, while coupled, dual, and localized variants shorten error-transmission paths. Localized predictive coding style OAL is implemented through guidance-backpropagation and target-backpropagation architectures, and hybrid and scaled variants support high-dimensional deployment. The paper focuses on the architectural rationale and the progression from a conceptual feedback loop to practical large-scale configurations.

AI.tldr: Control AI is an architecture for online active learning that treats learning as a continuous prediction-evaluation-correction loop, combining deep networks with adaptive-control-style error feedback for safety-critical settings.
AI.motivation: Conventional offline training is a barrier for applying information-centric AI to safety-critical applications in open-world environments.
AI.method: A prediction model maps sensory input to a latent manifold, an optional latent model represents transitions, and a reconstruction model maps back to observations; residuals provide the learning signal, with spatial and temporal cross-reconstruction to prevent identity collapse and coupled, dual and localized variants, including guidance-backpropagation and target-backpropagation for predictive-coding-style learning.
AI.result: The abstract reports architectural rationale and the progression from a conceptual feedback loop to practical large-scale configurations, with no experimental results given.
AI.conclusion: The paper offers a design framework for online active learning architectures, leaving empirical validation of the proposed variants to the scope of the abstract's claims.

title: SurgQ-VLM: Question-Conditioned Dual-Stream Compression and Answer-Type-Aware Reinforcement for Surgical Video Question Answering
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027 (Applications track). 16 pages: 8-page main paper, references, and supplementary material. Code: this https URL ; Weights: this https URL
summary: Reasoning about surgical video -- which phase is underway, which instruments act, and when events occur -- underpins operative documentation, workflow analysis, and skill assessment. Yet surgical visual question answering is still largely built on single frames and closed labels that cannot express a duration, an ordering, or a count, and the video models that lift the frame limit typically compress every clip the same way regardless of the question, discarding the temporal evidence the answer needs. Worse, the answers are structurally heterogeneous, spanning five incompatible structures -- binary, classification, multi-label, counting, and sentence-temporal -- that no single training signal scores uniformly well. We propose SurgQ-VLM, a two-stage model for surgical video question answering. Stage 1 trains a question-conditioned dual-stream (slow/fast) compressor for a LoRA-adapted Qwen2.5-VL-7B: cross-attention conditions both streams on the question, and each clip's visual tokens shrink 49x from the raw ViT patches (11x vs. post-merge backbone tokens). Stage 2 post-trains with GRPO under an answer-type-aware reward that scores each question on the metric matching its answer structure (micro-F1 for label sets, normalised error for counts, a content-timing blend for temporal windows). On a sealed 21,840-question test split over Cholec80 and CholecT50, SurgQ-VLM reaches 0.779 keyword accuracy and a 10x BLEU-4 gain over zero-shot; GRPO adds 2.5 pp K-Acc (2.0 pp attributable to the answer-type-aware reward), concentrated in the structurally hard types, with answer format unchanged (ROUGE-L). Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: SurgQ-VLM is a two-stage model for surgical video question answering that compresses clips conditioned on the question and then post-trains with GRPO under an answer-type-aware reward, reaching 0.779 keyword accuracy on a sealed test split over Cholec80 and CholecT50.
AI.motivation: Surgical VQA relies on single frames and closed labels, and video models compress every clip the same way regardless of the question, discarding temporal evidence; answer structures also differ across binary, classification, multi-label, counting and temporal types, which a single training signal cannot score well.
AI.method: Stage 1 trains a question-conditioned dual-stream (slow/fast) compressor for a LoRA-adapted Qwen2.5-VL-7B, with cross-attention conditioning both streams on the question and visual tokens shrunk 49x from raw ViT patches (11x relative to post-merge backbone tokens); Stage 2 applies GRPO with a reward that scores each question on the metric matching its answer type.
AI.result: On a sealed split of 21,840 questions, SurgQ-VLM reaches 0.779 keyword accuracy and a 10x BLEU-4 gain over zero-shot; GRPO adds 2.5 percentage points of K-Acc, of which 2.0 points are attributed to the answer-type-aware reward, concentrated in structurally hard types, with answer format unchanged (ROUGE-L).
AI.conclusion: Question-conditioned compression and answer-type-aware rewards jointly improve surgical video question answering, especially for structurally difficult question types.

title: Vision-language classification of Torsades de Pointes risk from pseudo-coloured ECG images: do T-wave morphology and colour context help or hinder?
summary: Contextual prompting is widely presented as a cheap route to better performance from vision models, but the evidence comes largely from benchmarks in which an attribute named in a prompt is also present in the image, confounding the two channels. We investigate the significance of context for a semantically complex biomedical signal classification task using a domain-adapted vision-language model, BiomedCLIP. Building on our previous work that renders electrocardiogram (ECG) signals as colour-enhanced images to flag Torsades de Pointes risk using the QT-nomogram and pseudo-colouring technique, we cross four context strategies with four T-wave morphology label sets, evaluated zero-shot and with a class-balanced linear probe, under five-fold stratified cross-validation on 9,789 images. Zero-shot inference is unusable. Once trained, the colour-enhanced images outperform the colourless ones on every metric: balanced accuracy 0.903 versus 0.825, sensitivity 0.914 versus 0.827, specificity 0.892 versus 0.823, ROC-AUC 0.955 versus 0.888 and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) 0.437 versus 0.311. Crossing colour-in-image with colour-in-prompt separates the confounded channels: the image contributes +0.126 MCC (+0.078 balanced accuracy, +0.067 ROC-AUC) whether or not the prompt names colour, whereas naming it changes nothing under any metric. Context is two-sided: the best prompt set gains 0.008 MCC where colour is present and 0.016 where it is not, while the worst loses 0.017 and 0.013. For a signal rendered as an image, the leverage lies in how the signal is drawn rather than in how it is described - and where the endpoint is an interval measurement, prompts naming T-wave morphology describe the wrong quantity.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that colour-enhanced ECG images give a BiomedCLIP linear probe a clear advantage for Torsades de Pointes risk classification, while mentioning colour in the text prompt has no effect, so the leverage lies in how the signal is drawn.
AI.motivation: Contextual prompting is often presented as a cheap way to improve vision models, but benchmark evidence confounds attributes named in prompts with attributes present in images, and this needs separating for a biomedical signal task.
AI.method: Four context strategies are crossed with four T-wave morphology label sets and with colour-in-image versus colourless rendering of ECGs, evaluated zero-shot and with a class-balanced linear probe under five-fold stratified cross-validation on 9,789 images, using BiomedCLIP.
AI.result: Zero-shot inference is unusable; with a linear probe colour-enhanced images beat colourless ones on every metric, with balanced accuracy 0.903 versus 0.825, ROC-AUC 0.955 versus 0.888 and MCC 0.437 versus 0.311; the image contributes +0.126 MCC whether or not the prompt names colour, and naming colour changes nothing.
AI.conclusion: For signals rendered as images, the way the signal is drawn matters more than how it is described, and prompts naming T-wave morphology describe the wrong quantity when the endpoint is an interval measurement.

title: Spade-SLAM: Sparse Correspondence Anchors for Dense Self-Supervised Visual SLAM
summary: We introduce Spade-SLAM, a self-supervised dense visual SLAM framework that substantially narrows the long-standing performance gap to supervised methods in a zero-shot setting. By demonstrating that high-fidelity tracking can be achieved without explicit ground-truth pose and depth labels, our approach offers a highly effective and label-efficient alternative to fully supervised pretraining. Our core contribution is a complementary sparse-to-dense training regime: While a warping-based photometric loss provides a dense training signal, we stabilize the optimization and suppress drift in ambiguous regions using a sparse correspondence loss derived from image feature matches. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Spade-SLAM significantly improves robustness and accuracy compared to existing self-supervised baselines, closely rivaling SLAM systems trained with explicit pose and depth supervision. The code will be made publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Spade-SLAM is a self-supervised dense visual SLAM framework that uses sparse feature-match correspondences to stabilize photometric training, approaching supervised SLAM systems in a zero-shot setting without ground-truth pose or depth.
AI.motivation: Dense visual SLAM methods trained with supervision perform best, and the gap to self-supervised methods is long-standing; photometric losses alone drift in ambiguous regions.
AI.method: A warping-based photometric loss provides a dense training signal, and a sparse correspondence loss derived from image feature matches stabilizes optimization and suppresses drift in ambiguous regions, forming a sparse-to-dense training regime.
AI.result: Spade-SLAM significantly improves robustness and accuracy over existing self-supervised baselines and closely rivals SLAM systems trained with explicit pose and depth supervision; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Sparse correspondence anchors make label-free dense SLAM a practical alternative to fully supervised pretraining, with code to be released.

title: VLSplat: Vision-Language Guided Object-Centric 3D Gaussian Splatting via Scene Graph
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. Project page: this https URL
summary: Learning semantic representations for 3D Gaussian Splatting has recently emerged as a promising direction for 3D scene understanding. However, existing 2D-to-3D semantic lifting approaches rely primarily on 2D segmentation supervision and lack object-level priors, causing the learned representation to be driven by local mask evidence rather than holistic object structure. In this paper, we present VLSplat, a vision-language guided approach for object-centric semantic lifting in 3D Gaussian Splatting. Our method augments mask-based lifting with object-level semantic priors derived from vision-language models and refines Gaussian representations using an object-group scene graph. The refinement is performed through two language-guided modules: intra-group refinement suppresses semantic noise within object groups, while inter-group acquisition expands object support regions by incorporating structurally relevant candidates from neighboring groups. Extensive experiments on indoor scene datasets demonstrate that VLSplat improves the semantic consistency and structural completeness of object-level categories. Our code and models are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: VLSplat adds vision-language object-level priors and a scene-graph-based refinement to mask-driven semantic lifting in 3D Gaussian Splatting, improving semantic consistency and structural completeness of object categories on indoor scenes.
AI.motivation: Existing 2D-to-3D semantic lifting for Gaussian Splatting relies mainly on 2D segmentation masks and lacks object-level priors, so the learned representation follows local mask evidence rather than holistic object structure.
AI.method: Mask-based lifting is augmented with object-level semantic priors from vision-language models, and Gaussians are refined on an object-group scene graph through intra-group refinement, which suppresses semantic noise within groups, and inter-group acquisition, which expands object support with structurally relevant candidates from neighbouring groups.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on indoor scene datasets show improved semantic consistency and structural completeness of object-level categories; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Language-guided object priors and scene-graph refinement make object-centric semantic 3D Gaussian representations more coherent and complete.

title: Event-Based Optical Flow Constraint via Time-Sliced Plane Fitting
comment: 5 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Accepted for publication at IEEE VCIP 2026 (2026 IEEE International Conference on Visual Communications and Image Processing). (c) 2026 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted. Permission from IEEE must be obtained for all other uses
summary: Event-based optical flow estimation using spatiotemporal planar approximation inherently assumes constant velocity and tends to average out temporal velocity variations. In this paper, we propose a flow estimation method that extends this planar approximation along the temporal axis. The resulting event-based optical flow constraint allows existing variational optical flow formulations to model temporal motion variation. Specifically, we partition the space-time volume into sub-intervals and apply a two-step planar approximation to track object edges consistently. Moreover, a spatial compensation mechanism and a temporal regularization term are incorporated to compensate for edge displacements and temporally stabilize the flow estimation, respectively. The experimental results show that modeling temporal motion variation improves flow estimation accuracy over conventional methods.

AI.tldr: The paper extends planar-fitting-based event optical flow along the temporal axis by partitioning space-time into sub-intervals, producing a constraint that lets variational flow models capture temporal velocity variation.
AI.motivation: Existing event-based planar approximation assumes constant velocity and averages out temporal velocity changes.
AI.method: The space-time volume is split into sub-intervals and a two-step planar approximation tracks object edges, with a spatial compensation mechanism for edge displacement and a temporal regularization term for stabilizing the flow.
AI.result: The experiments show that modelling temporal motion variation improves flow estimation accuracy over conventional methods; the abstract gives no specific numbers or datasets.
AI.conclusion: A temporally resolved event-based flow constraint can be plugged into existing variational optical flow formulations to improve accuracy.

title: Object-Only Is Not Context-Free: A Counterfactual Diagnostic for Context Removal in Object Retrieval
comment: Accepted at WACV 2027. 8 pages plus references and supplementary material (15 pages total). Code and adapter checkpoints: this https URL
summary: Object-centric retrieval pipelines often mask the background before pooling backbone features, aiming for a descriptor that reflects the object rather than its scene. Whether this truly yields an object-only descriptor, however, is rarely tested. We introduce the Keyhole Aperture Probe (KAP), a counterfactual diagnostic that repurposes the ground-truth masks of existing panoptic segmentation datasets (COCO, ADE20K) for retrieval: it holds the pooled object region fixed and varies only the pixels outside it, summarizing a backbone's context dependence in a single number. We find that the pooled object region has already integrated its surround. Replacing the context, with a neutral fill or even a different real scene, changes the descriptor, and when retrieval fails under a blank fill, the descriptor matches plain-background images rather than its own object. Object-only is not context-free. Across ten modern backbones, object-only descriptors retain only about a quarter to two-thirds of their full-image accuracy, and the effect is not unique to Transformer self-attention: a convolutional backbone shows it too. The dependence is also reducible: a lightweight adapter that encourages the descriptor to stay stable as context is removed lowers it and improves full-image instance retrieval on INSTRE, transferring to ILIAS with accuracy improved or preserved. A matched contrastive-fine-tuning control does not reproduce those gains. We release KAP as a simple, backbone-agnostic evaluation protocol to measure and reduce this dependence before deployment.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Keyhole Aperture Probe (KAP), a counterfactual diagnostic showing that masked object descriptors remain dependent on surrounding context, and a lightweight adapter that reduces this dependence and improves instance retrieval.
AI.motivation: Object-centric retrieval often masks the background before pooling backbone features, assuming the result is an object-only descriptor, but this assumption is rarely tested.
AI.method: KAP reuses ground-truth masks from COCO and ADE20K, holds the pooled object region fixed while varying the pixels outside it, and summarizes context dependence in one number; an adapter encourages descriptors to remain stable as context is removed.
AI.result: Across ten modern backbones, object-only descriptors keep about a quarter to two-thirds of their full-image accuracy, the effect appears in convolutional as well as Transformer backbones, and the adapter lowers the dependence and improves full-image instance retrieval on INSTRE, transferring to ILIAS, while a matched contrastive-fine-tuning control does not reproduce the gains.
AI.conclusion: Object-only descriptors are not context-free, and KAP offers a backbone-agnostic protocol to measure and reduce this dependence before deployment.

title: Knowledge-Guided Floodwater Level Reasoning for Cloud-Edge Collaborative Monitoring
summary: Frequent urban floodwater poses a serious threat to the safety and efficiency of intelligent transportation systems. Existing vision-based methods for floodwater level detection face two main limitations. First, the lack of explicit reasoning leads to poor detection performance and little interpretability. Second, these methods struggle to generalize to the complex and varied real-world road scenes seen from different viewpoints. To address this, we reformulate the task as an explicit visual reasoning problem and propose HydroReasoner, a floodwater level reasoning framework designed for cloud-edge collaboration. HydroReasoner builds on Qwen2.5-VL and is trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization. To address the scarcity of reasoning process annotations, we build a floodwater domain knowledge graph HydroKG and design a novel KG path reward. Through deterministic graph traversal over HydroKG, this reward supervises the model's reasoning process at a fine granularity, which improves both reasoning and generalization. For edge deployment, we apply 4-bit quantization to the model, cutting GPU memory usage by 57% and inference latency by 43% while out-of-domain accuracy drops by only 0.2 percentage points. We also propose a confidence-based cloud-edge routing mechanism, which improves system safety and eases the computational load on the cloud. In addition, we build HydroLevel, a floodwater benchmark dataset of 3,000 images, for training and evaluating the model. Experimental results show that HydroReasoner achieves detection accuracy 4.0 and 13.6 percentage points higher than conventional vision baselines in the in-domain and out-of-domain evaluations respectively, with performance dropping by only 4.4 percentage points out of domain.

AI.tldr: HydroReasoner reformulates floodwater level detection as explicit visual reasoning, using GRPO with a knowledge-graph path reward, 4-bit quantization and confidence-based cloud-edge routing, and outperforms conventional vision baselines on in-domain and out-of-domain tests.
