AI.motivation: Existing vision methods for floodwater level detection lack explicit reasoning, which hurts performance and interpretability, and they generalise poorly to varied road scenes and viewpoints.
AI.method: HydroReasoner builds on Qwen2.5-VL and is trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization, using a floodwater knowledge graph HydroKG and a KG path reward computed by deterministic graph traversal; 4-bit quantization is applied for the edge, and a confidence-based cloud-edge routing mechanism is added; the authors also build the 3,000-image HydroLevel benchmark.
AI.result: Detection accuracy is 4.0 points higher than conventional vision baselines in-domain and 13.6 points higher out-of-domain; 4-bit quantization cuts GPU memory by 57% and latency by 43% with only 0.2 points of out-of-domain accuracy loss; out-of-domain performance drops 4.4 points relative to in-domain.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge-graph-guided reasoning with quantized edge deployment and confidence-based routing gives accurate, generalisable and efficient floodwater monitoring within a cloud-edge system.

title: MUPA${}^2$S: Multimodal Unified Perception with Asymmetric Attention for Stress Assessment
summary: Stress is a leading contributor to long-term physical and mental health decline. The automatic assessment of stress is a promising approach for continuous monitoring and mitigating human biases. However, the development of automated systems remains challenging due to the heterogeneity of physiological and behavioral signals. This paper presents MUPA${}^2$S, a multimodal framework for automatic stress assessment that combines facial video and ECG signals within a unified perception architecture. Both modalities are mapped into a shared token representation without modality-specific components, and processed through asymmetric attention comprising segment-local cross-attention and global self-attention across segment states. Experiments on a newly collected 58-subject stress dataset, evaluated under a stratified subject-level protocol, show that facial video achieves 69.44% test accuracy, while ECG-only performance remains close to chance under the proposed representation. Unified Video-ECG fusion achieves a test accuracy of 69.58% at approximately half the number of parameters of feature-level fusion, with negligible additional computational cost. Feature-level fusion does not exceed the video-only baseline, while unified input-level integration provides a parameter-efficient mechanism for jointly processing the two modalities.

AI.tldr: MUPA2S is a multimodal stress assessment framework that maps facial video and ECG into a shared token space processed by asymmetric attention, reaching 69.58% test accuracy with fusion at about half the parameters of feature-level fusion.
AI.motivation: Automatic stress assessment from heterogeneous physiological and behavioural signals is difficult, and existing pipelines use modality-specific components.
AI.method: Both facial video and ECG are mapped to a shared token representation without modality-specific components and processed with asymmetric attention, which combines segment-local cross-attention and global self-attention across segment states.
AI.result: On a newly collected 58-subject stress dataset under a stratified subject-level protocol, facial video alone reaches 69.44% test accuracy, ECG alone stays near chance, and unified video-ECG fusion reaches 69.58% with about half the parameters of feature-level fusion; feature-level fusion does not exceed the video-only baseline.
AI.conclusion: Unified input-level integration is a parameter-efficient way to jointly process video and ECG for stress assessment, though the gain over video alone is small.

title: Multimodal BVP and Respiration for Automated Pain Recognition with Hankel-FCN
summary: Automated pain recognition is a fundamental challenge for the advancement of clinical care and empathetic human-computer interaction, due to the subjective and dynamic nature of pain. In this study, we propose a deep learning framework for objective pain assessment based on multimodal physiological signals from the AI4Pain dataset. The approach focuses on Blood Volume Pulse (BVP) and Respiration (RESP), capturing complementary aspects of autonomic responses to nociceptive stimulation. To explicitly model their temporal dynamics, the signals are transformed into structured trajectory representations using Hankel matrix embeddings, enabling the learning of dynamical patterns beyond conventional time-series representations. These embeddings are processed by modality-specific Fully Convolutional Networks, and their outputs are integrated through a late fusion strategy for three-class classification (No Pain, Low Pain, High Pain). Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves an accuracy of 67.09% and an F1-score of 66.41%, providing competitive performance compared to existing approaches, while relying on no handcrafted feature engineering. Multimodal fusion significantly outperformed either modality alone, and the Hankel embedding showed a trend towards further improvement. Further validation is required to establish generalisability to broader populations and clinical settings.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Hankel-matrix trajectory embedding of blood volume pulse and respiration signals, processed by modality-specific fully convolutional networks with late fusion, for three-level pain recognition on the AI4Pain dataset.
AI.motivation: Pain is subjective and dynamic, and automatic assessment from physiological signals needs to capture the temporal dynamics of autonomic responses without handcrafted features.
AI.method: BVP and RESP signals are converted into structured trajectory representations with Hankel matrix embeddings, processed by modality-specific fully convolutional networks, and combined with late fusion for three-class classification of no, low and high pain.
AI.result: The method achieves 67.09% accuracy and a 66.41% F1-score, competitive with existing approaches; multimodal fusion significantly outperforms either modality alone, and the Hankel embedding shows a trend towards further improvement.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal physiological pain recognition with Hankel embeddings is competitive without handcrafted features, but generalisation to broader populations and clinical settings still needs validation.

title: SurgStream: A Workflow-Anchored Proactive Streaming Framework and Benchmark for Real-Time Surgical Video Understanding
summary: Surgical video understanding is essential for intraoperative assistance such as workflow monitoring, instrument preparation and procedural documentation. Delivering such assistance in real time requires a model to jointly perceive the ongoing scene, remember past surgical events, and respond before clinically relevant moments pass. Existing approaches provide limited support for jointly retaining procedural evidence and deciding when to respond in streaming surgical video. In this work, we propose SurgStream, a workflow-anchored proactive streaming framework for real-time surgical video understanding. We first introduce Workflow-Anchored Memory (WAM) to record structured instrument-action-target observations and fold them into phase-level summaries, providing compact and queryable surgical memory. Deadline-aware Transition Learning (DTL) is then devised to supervise response states within clinical windows, enabling timely responses before procedural deadlines. We further introduce SurgStream-Bench, comprising 11.7K streaming interactions across various tasks covering real-time perception, backward memory queries, forward proactive QA, proactive alerts and caption memory. Experiments on SurgStream-Bench show gains over state-of-the-art methods, especially in memory and forward proactive QA. The source code will be available.

AI.tldr: SurgStream is a workflow-anchored proactive streaming framework for real-time surgical video understanding, pairing structured surgical memory with deadline-aware response learning, and is evaluated on a new 11.7K-interaction benchmark.
AI.motivation: Real-time surgical assistance requires jointly retaining procedural evidence and deciding when to respond in streaming video, which existing approaches support only to a limited extent.
AI.method: Workflow-Anchored Memory (WAM) records structured instrument-action-target observations and folds them into phase-level summaries, and Deadline-aware Transition Learning (DTL) supervises response states within clinical windows; SurgStream-Bench comprises 11.7K streaming interactions covering real-time perception, backward memory queries, forward proactive QA, proactive alerts and caption memory.
AI.result: Experiments on SurgStream-Bench show gains over state-of-the-art methods, especially on memory and forward proactive QA; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Structured, phase-level memory combined with deadline-aware response supervision supports timely proactive surgical video understanding; the source code is promised.

title: Synthetic Realities: Evaluating Human Ability to Distinguish AIGenerated Videos from Real Footage
summary: Recent advances in generative AI have enabled multiple pathways for high-fidelity video synthesis: text-to-video, image-to-video animation, and video outpainting. Empirical side-by-side evaluations of how untrained viewers perceive and distinguish these outputs from real footage remain scarce. In this study, we systematically compare human detection accuracy across these three AI generation techniques within three thematic contexts: historical footage, film and media content, and natural environments. We constructed a balanced stimulus set comprising equal amounts of real and AI-generated videos (18 each). The AI clips were evenly distributed across the three generation methods using Google's Veo 3, Lightricks LTX Video, and Wan VACE. All videos were produced and standardized within the ComfyUI framework to ensure consistent quality and duration. 87 participants judged every clip in a binary forced-choice task ("real" vs. "AI-generated"). Participants correctly identified videos 60% of the time on average. Image-to-video clips were recognized most accurately (79%), followed by real footage (64%), outpainting (49%), and text-to-video (43%). Accuracy also varied by theme: film and historical scenes yielded higher detection rates than environmental clips, which were frequently mistaken for AI. Logistic regression confirmed significant effects of both technique and theme as well as their interaction (p < 0.001), indicating that detection success depends jointly on how the content was generated and what it depicts. Findings reveal a consistent bias toward assuming synthetic origins and highlight that perceptual realism in AI video is shaped more by context than by model type, underscoring the importance of media-literacy approaches and context-aware evaluation tools for navigating increasingly synthetic visual media.

AI.tldr: A controlled study of 87 participants finds that people detect AI-generated videos at 60% accuracy overall, with detection depending on the generation technique and on the thematic context.
AI.motivation: Side-by-side human evaluations of how untrained viewers distinguish outputs from text-to-video, image-to-video and video outpainting from real footage are scarce.
AI.method: An 18-real and 18-AI balanced stimulus set uses clips from Veo 3, LTX Video and Wan VACE, standardized in ComfyUI across historical, film and media, and natural-environment themes, with a binary real-versus-AI forced choice and logistic regression on technique, theme and their interaction.
AI.result: Participants correctly identify videos 60% of the time on average; image-to-video clips are recognized best at 79%, followed by real footage at 64%, outpainting at 49% and text-to-video at 43%; technique, theme and their interaction are all significant at p < 0.001, and environmental clips are often mistaken for AI.
AI.conclusion: Detection depends jointly on how content was generated and what it depicts, with a bias toward assuming synthetic origin, so context-aware evaluation and media literacy matter.

title: NAS-PO: Native Attention-Strategy Policy Optimization for Vision-Language Models
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become an effective post-training paradigm for vision-language models (VLMs). Standard RLVR, however, assigns identical outcome-derived credit to all generated tokens regardless of their perceptual relevance. Recent perception-aware methods estimate visual reliance through image perturbation or masking. These indirect proxies require perturbation branches, while corruption sensitivity does not necessarily identify the visual evidence used for reasoning. We instead shape model perception through native attention, an intrinsic model signal. Rather than treating attention as a post-hoc explanation, we formulate it as a reward-anchored, token-aligned routing signal that encourages attention patterns supporting visually grounded reasoning. To this end, we propose NAS-PO, a Native Attention-Strategy Policy Optimization framework. NAS-PO analyzes native attention with a visual mass policy that quantifies visual allocation and a conditional visual policy that captures spatial routing over visual tokens, making the optimization well-posed. Based on this, Native Attention-Strategy Advantage Shaping (NAS-AS) draws on the visual-mass policy to redistribute signed policy-gradient credit for visually engaged rollouts. The Adaptive Attention-Coupled (AAC) loss then aligns the visual-mass policy on all response tokens and the conditional visual policy on visually active ones, consolidating the visual-routing patterns that drive successful trajectories. Experiments demonstrate that NAS-PO substantially surpasses leading RL-tuned VLMs across 7 out-of-domain reasoning and perception benchmarks, with its effectiveness consistently validated across 8B and 32B. Visual-Routing Sensitivity (VRS) analysis further indicates that the optimized attention prioritizes visually load-bearing regions.

AI.tldr: NAS-PO is a reinforcement learning method for vision-language models that uses native attention as a token-level routing signal to assign visually grounded credit, and it outperforms leading RL-tuned VLMs on seven out-of-domain benchmarks at 8B and 32B.
AI.motivation: Standard RLVR gives all generated tokens the same outcome-derived credit regardless of perceptual relevance, and existing perception-aware methods rely on perturbation or masking proxies that do not identify the visual evidence used for reasoning.
AI.method: Native attention is treated as a reward-anchored, token-aligned routing signal through a visual-mass policy and a conditional visual policy; NAS-AS redistributes signed policy-gradient credit for visually engaged rollouts, and an Adaptive Attention-Coupled loss aligns both policies with visually active tokens.
AI.result: NAS-PO substantially surpasses leading RL-tuned VLMs across seven out-of-domain reasoning and perception benchmarks at 8B and 32B, and Visual-Routing Sensitivity analysis shows the optimized attention prioritizes visually load-bearing regions; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Shaping native attention during RL is an effective way to couple visual grounding with reasoning credit in VLM post-training.

title: Reconstruction as Spatial Evaluation: Diagnosing Cross-View Spatial Intelligence in Large Vision-Language Models
summary: The spatial intelligence of large vision-language models (LVLMs) requires the ability to combine local visual observations into a geometrically consistent representation of the physical world. Many static benchmarks assess isolated spatial judgments, such as relative direction or distance, while interactive embodied evaluations combine perception with exploration, planning, control, and simulator-specific execution. To bridge this gap, we introduce RECONSPATIAL, a benchmark centered on multi-view 3D scene reconstruction across indoor, tabletop, and outdoor environments. Given real multi-view images and target-object queries, LVLMs are required to jointly predict oriented 3D bounding boxes in a shared, camera-anchored metric coordinate frame. Reconstructions are evaluated along two complementary axes: Structure for relative layout and Metric for physical scale and camera-anchored placement. Nine atomic spatial QA tasks, grouped into Geometric Perception and Spatial Relations, probe spatial capabilities involved in joint reconstruction. Offline navigation extends evaluation to path planning. Evaluation of 18 frontier LVLMs reveals a consistent gap between relative scene structure and metric reconstruction; even GPT-6-Astra scores 81.4% on Structure but only 58.7% on Metric. Tracing this gap, diagnostic analyses link atomic spatial capabilities to reconstruction quality and show that relational consistency alone does not ensure metric accuracy. Experiments with 3D map injection further separate scene construction from path planning, revealing how these geometric errors limit navigation success. Finally, spatial fine-tuning yields broad transfer across both spatial and general vision-language benchmarks.

AI.tldr: RECONSPATIAL is a benchmark that evaluates whether large vision-language models can reconstruct geometrically consistent 3D scenes from multi-view images, finding a consistent gap between relative structure and metric accuracy.
AI.motivation: Static spatial benchmarks test isolated judgments such as relative direction or distance, while embodied evaluations entangle perception with planning and simulator-specific execution, so joint spatial reconstruction is not directly tested.
AI.method: LVLMs predict oriented 3D bounding boxes for target objects in a shared, camera-anchored metric frame from multi-view indoor, tabletop and outdoor images, scored on Structure and Metric axes, with nine atomic spatial QA tasks, offline navigation path planning, and 3D map injection experiments.
AI.result: Across 18 frontier LVLMs there is a consistent gap between relative structure and metric reconstruction; GPT-6-Astra scores 81.4% on Structure but 58.7% on Metric; spatial fine-tuning transfers broadly to other spatial and general vision-language benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Relational consistency does not ensure metric accuracy, and geometric reconstruction errors limit navigation, so metric reconstruction is a distinct capability to target.

title: 4D Triangle Splatting Reconstruction of Dynamic Endoscopic Scenes from Monocular Videos
summary: Robust 4D reconstruction of deformable endoscopic scenes from monocular videos remains challenging due to non-rigid tissue deformation, illumination changes, occlusions, and unknown camera trajectories. Reliable dynamic reconstruction of endoscopies could significantly enhance visualization, diagnostic accuracy and intraoperative guidance of minimally invasive procedures. We propose SurgicalTS, a self-supervised triangle-splatting framework for dynamic endoscopic scene reconstruction from static monocular cameras. The scene is represented by a canonical set of triangles jointly optimized with a deformation network. We introduce a quaternion-based deformation model, an improved color parametrization, spatio-temporal priors, and a redefined initialization strategy that improves completeness under occlusions. Extensive evaluation on challenging in-vivo endoscopy videos from diverse procedures shows that SurgicalTS successfully models soft-tissue deformations and tool-tissue interactions over time, while consistently outperforming state-of-the-art methods. Our method also reduces training times while maintaining competitive geometric and photometric accuracy results, highlighting the effectiveness of quaternion-based deformation modelling with physical consistency for robust and efficient 4D reconstruction of endoscopic scenes.

AI.tldr: SurgicalTS is a self-supervised triangle-splatting framework for 4D reconstruction of deforming endoscopic scenes from monocular video, using a quaternion-based deformation model and reporting better results than state-of-the-art methods with shorter training.
AI.motivation: Robust 4D reconstruction of soft tissue from monocular endoscopy is hard because of non-rigid deformation, illumination changes, occlusion and unknown camera trajectories.
AI.method: A canonical set of triangles is jointly optimized with a deformation network, using a quaternion-based deformation model, an improved colour parametrization, spatio-temporal priors and a redefined initialization that improves completeness under occlusion.
AI.result: On in-vivo endoscopy videos from diverse procedures SurgicalTS models soft-tissue deformation and tool-tissue interaction and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, with reduced training time and competitive geometric and photometric accuracy; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Quaternion-based deformation with physical consistency enables robust and efficient 4D endoscopic reconstruction.

title: Unified Loss-Aware Density Control for 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: The efficiency and fidelity of 3D Gaussian Splatting critically depend on adaptive density control, which grows and suppresses Gaussian primitives throughout optimization. However, the standard pipeline still relies on heuristic view-space gradients, scale thresholds, and global opacity resets, rather than explicitly assessing the loss-reducing effect of each split, clone, or opacity update. This mismatch can allocate primitives to already-sufficient regions, miss under-reconstructed structures, and destabilize training through blanket opacity changes. In this work, we recast adaptive density control as a collection of local loss-reduction decisions. We derive efficient Taylor-based per-Gaussian surrogates that predict the objective change caused by three primitive-level operations: splitting, cloning, and opacity decay. This yields a unified loss-aware framework with three components. First, we extend second-order splitting to a normalized joint position-scale space, enabling children to adapt not only their locations but also their anisotropic extents. Second, we formulate duplicate cloning as a surrogate minimization problem, selecting only Gaussians whose duplicated contribution is predicted to improve reconstruction and assigning each child a principled opacity. Third, we replace global opacity reset with selective soft opacity decay that weakens harmful primitives while preserving useful ones. Across standard 3DGS benchmarks, our method produces more targeted primitive allocation and achieves improved rendering quality with comparable or smaller Gaussian budgets compared to baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper recasts adaptive density control for 3D Gaussian Splatting as local loss-reduction decisions, using Taylor-based surrogates to predict the objective change of splitting, cloning and opacity decay, and reports improved rendering with comparable or smaller Gaussian budgets.
AI.motivation: Standard 3DGS density control relies on heuristic view-space gradients, scale thresholds and global opacity resets, which can allocate primitives to already-sufficient regions, miss under-reconstructed structures and destabilize training.
AI.method: Efficient Taylor-based per-Gaussian surrogates predict the loss change of three operations: second-order splitting extended to a normalized joint position-scale space, duplicate cloning formulated as surrogate minimization with a principled child opacity, and selective soft opacity decay replacing the global reset.
AI.result: Across standard 3DGS benchmarks the method produces more targeted primitive allocation and improved rendering quality with comparable or smaller Gaussian budgets than baselines; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Loss-aware local decisions make adaptive density control more targeted and stable for 3D Gaussian Splatting.

title: UniGS-SLAM: Monocular Gaussian SLAM with Enhanced Geometry and Open-Vocabulary Semantics
summary: Monocular semantic SLAM aims to reconstruct scene geometry and build semantic maps from RGB observations. Existing Gaussian-based methods often attach semantic labels or features to evolving Gaussian primitives, making semantic fusion difficult to maintain and increasing reconstruction overhead. Hybrid Gaussian--voxel representations provide more stable semantic support, but often rely on RGB-D input or known poses and do not revise historical semantic evidence after geometry updates. We present UniGS-SLAM, an RGB-only framework that decouples open-vocabulary semantics from Gaussian reconstruction while preserving bidirectional interaction. Foundation priors enhance monocular depth and pose estimation, while semantic observations are fused into an independent sparse voxel map with observation provenance, enabling historical contributions to be revised as reconstruction evolves. The fused semantics further guide Gaussian filtering and local surface refinement. Experiments on Replica, ScanNet, and KITTI-360 show leading tracking, rendering, and geometric reconstruction performance among representative RGB-only methods, together with strong open-set semantic mapping on Replica and ScanNet. We also achieve a 2.37-fold reconstruction speedup over the fastest compared semantic SLAM baseline. Project page: this https URL.

AI.tldr: UniGS-SLAM is an RGB-only monocular Gaussian SLAM framework that decouples open-vocabulary semantics into an independent sparse voxel map with observation provenance, reporting leading tracking and reconstruction and a 2.37-fold speedup over the fastest semantic SLAM baseline.
AI.motivation: Gaussian-based semantic SLAM struggles to maintain semantic fusion on evolving primitives, and hybrid Gaussian-voxel methods often need RGB-D input or known poses and cannot revise historical semantic evidence after geometry updates.
AI.method: Foundation priors enhance monocular depth and pose estimation, semantic observations are fused into an independent sparse voxel map that stores observation provenance so historical contributions can be revised, and the fused semantics guide Gaussian filtering and local surface refinement.
AI.result: Experiments on Replica, ScanNet and KITTI-360 show leading tracking, rendering and geometric reconstruction among RGB-only methods, strong open-set semantic mapping on Replica and ScanNet, and a 2.37-fold reconstruction speedup over the fastest compared semantic SLAM baseline.
AI.conclusion: Decoupled, provenance-aware semantic voxel mapping with bidirectional interaction gives accurate and faster RGB-only semantic SLAM.

title: Learning to Look: A Foundation for Visual Understanding
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) suffer from visual hallucination, such as saying an object that is not present in an image. We ask a more fundamental question: whether a VLM is even aware of where it is looking before understanding the semantic meaning in the image. We formulate this question as a LOOK task: identifying which parts of its visual input were available to the model. We construct the task in a self-supervised way without manually labeling the available region to the model. Our experiments show that existing VLMs fail to localize the visible region. We further show that fine-tuning VLMs on the proposed LOOK task improves a model's awareness of visual input.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a LOOK task that tests whether a vision-language model knows which parts of its visual input are available to it, finding that existing VLMs fail it and that fine-tuning on the task improves visual awareness.
AI.motivation: VLM visual hallucination may be linked to a more basic failure: the model may not be aware of where it is looking before interpreting semantic content.
AI.method: The LOOK task asks the model to identify which parts of its visual input were available to it, constructed in a self-supervised way without manually labelling the visible region.
AI.result: Existing VLMs fail to localize the visible region, and fine-tuning VLMs on the LOOK task improves their awareness of visual input; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Visual-input awareness is a foundational capability that can be trained with a self-supervised task, with potential benefits for reducing hallucination.

title: Scene-Adaptive Readout and Decoding in Diffusion Driving VLAs
summary: Diffusion driving vision-language-action models repeatedly execute the backbone at every denoising stage, incurring substantial inference cost, while it remains unclear whether all scenes require the same decoding computation. To distinguish when a trajectory becomes readable from how much further refinement it requires, we analyze trajectory readout across network depth and decoding progress. We identify a depth-decoding dissociation in which late-layer representations already support useful trajectory readout after the first forward sweep, whereas early-layer representations benefit more from continued decoding. We further find that both the preferred readout layer and decoding depth vary across scenes. Based on these observations, we propose a scene-adaptive readout and decoding framework. A scene-conditioned readout MoE adaptively weights and combines trajectory predictions from layer-specific late-layer representations after a single backbone sweep, while an adaptive decoding policy applies additional native refinement only when required by the scene. We evaluate our framework on two diffusion driving VLAs across the Waymo E2E and nuScenes benchmarks. Our method improves validation RFS by up to 0.56 while also improving test performance, and achieves an end-to-end speedup of up to $6.0\times$ on Waymo E2E, while consistently reducing trajectory error on nuScenes. These results demonstrate that scene-level readout and decoding allocation improves planning quality while avoiding unnecessary decoding. Our code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper proposes scene-adaptive readout and decoding for diffusion driving VLAs, using a scene-conditioned mixture of experts over late-layer readouts after one backbone sweep and adaptive extra refinement, reaching up to 6.0x end-to-end speedup on Waymo E2E.
AI.motivation: Diffusion driving VLAs run the backbone at every denoising step, which is costly, and it is unclear whether every scene needs the same decoding computation.
AI.method: The authors identify a depth-decoding dissociation in which late-layer representations support trajectory readout after one sweep while early layers benefit from more decoding; a scene-conditioned readout MoE combines layer-specific late-layer predictions, and an adaptive decoding policy applies extra native refinement only when a scene requires it.
AI.result: On two diffusion driving VLAs evaluated on Waymo E2E and nuScenes, validation RFS improves by up to 0.56 with test gains as well, end-to-end speedup reaches up to 6.0x on Waymo E2E, and trajectory error is consistently reduced on nuScenes.
AI.conclusion: Allocating readout and decoding per scene improves planning quality while avoiding unnecessary decoding computation.

title: EarthJev: Calibrated, Non-Generative Answers to Natural-Language Questions about Sentinel-2 Land Cover
comment: 16 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables. Code and model: this https URL
summary: Vision-language models for remote sensing answer questions about satellite images by generating text: every answer costs a decoding loop, has to be parsed back to an option, and comes without a usable probability. We present EarthJev, a 0.8B-parameter model that answers typed questions about multispectral Sentinel-2 patches without generating any token. All 12 bands enter the vision encoder of Qwen3.5-0.8B through a widened input layer initialised from the RGB kernels, and, following the open OneJev recipe, the answer is read from the logits of the option letters at a single position and trained with cross-entropy plus Brier score. Under a pre-specified analysis plan, we compare it with the same backbone fine-tuned to generate the answer and with three multimodal language models fine-tuned with LoRA, all trained on the same 70,890 questions from 5% of BigEarthNet v2.0 and timed in one job on the same GPU; VQA models that classify over a fixed answer vocabulary are reported as a reference for the cost of answering only the questions seen in training. EarthJev answers a question in 19.9 ms, 4.3 to 8.7 times faster than the multimodal language models and 6.8 times faster than its own backbone used generatively; when all the questions about an image are asked together, it answers them in 42.8 ms, 3.7 to 10.1 times faster than the batched generative models. On 36,028 test questions it reaches 86.0% accuracy (three seeds), 0.6 and 1.2 points below the two 2B multimodal models and 3.5 points below the remote-sensing EarthDial-4B, with answers that are valid by construction and calibrated probabilities (ECE 0.006). Replacing the nine non-RGB bands with their mean costs 4.5 points, so the model uses the multispectral input, and in an ablation training the whole vision encoder raises accuracy to 88.4% at the same cost. Code and model: this https URL

AI.tldr: EarthJev is a 0.8B multispectral vision-language model that answers typed questions about Sentinel-2 patches by reading option-letter logits at a single position, with no generated tokens, and reaches 86.0% accuracy with calibrated probabilities at 19.9 ms per answer.
AI.motivation: Generative vision-language models for remote sensing need a full decoding loop per answer, must parse answers back to options, and provide no usable probabilities.
AI.method: All 12 Sentinel-2 bands enter a Qwen3.5-0.8B vision encoder through a widened input layer initialised from RGB kernels, and the answer is read from option-letter logits at a single position, trained with cross-entropy plus Brier score on 70,890 questions from 5% of BigEarthNet v2.0, compared with generative fine-tuning and LoRA-tuned multimodal language models under a pre-specified plan.
AI.result: EarthJev answers a question in 19.9 ms, 4.3 to 8.7 times faster than the multimodal language models and 6.8 times faster than its own generative backbone; it reaches 86.0% accuracy over three seeds on 36,028 test questions, 0.6 and 1.2 points below the two 2B multimodal models and 3.5 points below EarthDial-4B, with ECE 0.006; replacing non-RGB bands with their mean costs 4.5 points, and training the whole vision encoder raises accuracy to 88.4%.
AI.conclusion: Non-generative, logit-based answering yields valid-by-construction and calibrated outputs at much lower latency, at a modest accuracy cost relative to the larger 2B models, and the multispectral input is used.

title: CNN-Based Retinal OCT Classification: Research Gap Analysis and a From-Scratch Baseline, ED126-A
summary: Automated classification of retinal pathologies from Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) images remains challenging because diagnostically relevant morphological patterns may exhibit substantial inter-class similarity. Although high classification accuracies have been reported on benchmark OCT datasets, cross-study comparison is limited by heterogeneous evaluation protocols and by the limited characterization of compact convolutional neural network (CNN) baselines trained from random initialization. This study addresses this gap through two contributions. First, it provides a focused review of CNN-based retinal OCT classification and identifies methodological considerations relevant to controlled benchmarking. Second, it presents ED126-A, a purpose-built four-class CNN baseline trained from scratch under a documented experimental protocol on the Kermany labeled OCT dataset. The model contains 1,241,380 total parameters, including 1,239,460 trainable parameters, and is evaluated using training-dynamics analysis, class-wise performance metrics, confusion-matrix analysis, confidence analysis, t-SNE representation-space visualization, Grad-CAM, hierarchical feature-map analysis, and one-vs-rest ROC/Precision-Recall analysis. On the image-level held-out test set, ED126-A achieved 95.03% accuracy, with a macro-F1 of 0.9205 and a weighted-F1 of 0.9521. The principal class-conditional limitation occurred for Drusen, which attained a recall of 0.9605 but a precision of 0.7493 and an F1-score of 0.8419. The confusion matrix identified Normal to Drusen and CNV to Drusen as major error channels. These results support the use of ED126-A as a documented from-scratch reference baseline and provide an empirical basis for controlled evaluation of transfer learning, increased depth, attention, multi-scale feature fusion, and calibration in subsequent studies.

AI.tldr: The paper reviews CNN-based retinal OCT classification and provides ED126-A, a four-class CNN baseline trained from scratch on the Kermany OCT dataset, reaching 95.03% test accuracy.
AI.motivation: Reported OCT classification accuracies are hard to compare because evaluation protocols differ, and compact CNN baselines trained from random initialization are poorly characterized.
AI.method: The authors give a focused review of CNN-based OCT classification and identify benchmarking considerations, then build a 1.24M-parameter four-class CNN trained from scratch under a documented protocol and analyzed with training dynamics, confusion matrices, confidence analysis, t-SNE, Grad-CAM, feature-map analysis and one-vs-rest ROC/PR curves.
AI.result: On the image-level held-out test set the model reaches 95.03% accuracy, macro-F1 0.9205 and weighted-F1 0.9521; Drusen is the weakest class, with recall 0.9605 but precision 0.7493 and F1 0.8419, and Normal-to-Drusen and CNV-to-Drusen are the main confusions.
AI.conclusion: ED126-A is offered as a documented from-scratch reference baseline and a basis for controlled later comparisons of transfer learning, depth, attention, multi-scale fusion and calibration.

title: MoEDDI: Semantic Mixtures of Experts for Long Tailed Drug Drug Interaction Prediction
summary: Descriptor-based drug--drug interaction (DDI) models typically apply a single global predictor despite heterogeneous physicochemical evidence and severely long-tailed labels. We introduce \textbf{MoEDDI (Mixture-of-Experts for Drug--Drug Interaction prediction)}, a chemically organized mixture-of-experts that routes overlapping descriptor families using low-dimensional statistics and combines their sparse top-$2$ mixture with a global T-DDI pathway through a residual logit correction. The residual parameterization can exactly preserve a supplied T-DDI checkpoint at initialization, although the evaluated models are trained from scratch. Across complete test partitions with 178, 86, and 92 classes, MoEDDI improves macro-F1 over reproduced seed-2026 T-DDI baselines from 0.8284 to 0.8485, 0.4729 to 0.6536, and 0.1807 to 0.4671. On the 3,780-feature corpus, the lowest-support group (89 classes with fewer than 50 test examples) shows the largest mean classwise gain (+3.30 F1 points). Calibration improves on one corpus but worsens on two. These single-seed results support semantic conditional specialization while motivating matched ablations and distribution-shift evaluation.

AI.tldr: MoEDDI is a chemically organized mixture-of-experts for drug-drug interaction prediction that improves macro-F1 over reproduced single-seed T-DDI baselines on three long-tailed test partitions.
AI.motivation: Descriptor-based DDI models use one global predictor despite heterogeneous physicochemical evidence and severely long-tailed label distributions.
AI.method: MoEDDI routes overlapping descriptor families through experts chosen by low-dimensional statistics, combines a sparse top-2 expert mixture with a global T-DDI pathway via a residual logit correction, and can exactly preserve a supplied T-DDI checkpoint at initialization.
AI.result: Across test partitions with 178, 86 and 92 classes, macro-F1 rises from 0.8284 to 0.8485, 0.4729 to 0.6536 and 0.1807 to 0.4671 over reproduced seed-2026 T-DDI baselines; on the 3,780-feature corpus the lowest-support group gains +3.30 F1 points on average, while calibration improves on one corpus and worsens on two.
AI.conclusion: The single-seed results support semantic conditional specialization, but matched ablations and distribution-shift evaluation are still needed.

title: Unified dynamics of training, learning, inference, and reinforcement in neural networks
summary: Despite their remarkable success, neural networks remain largely black boxes, and the mechanisms underlying their behavior are still poorly understood. Nine nanoGPT experiments established training-learning-inference relations: realized updates elicit state-dependent finite-amplitude responses; learning persistently reorganizes distributed functional support, with target-specific readout-boundary crossings determining capability transitions; inference recruits learned support without changing the learned state. Factors identified in the fifth experiment yielded a direct predictor of post-update capability transitions, achieving 91.43% accuracy and 91.49% four-way macro recall across 5,088 targets. We tested these relations and prediction across five additional neural architectures. In a seventh system, concentrated correct feedback eroded previously mastered skills; rebalanced feedback restored their accuracy from 70.31% to 99.48%. Linking inference consequences to subsequent training closes these relations into unified training-learning-inference-reinforcement dynamics.

AI.tldr: Across nine nanoGPT experiments and five further architectures, the paper links training, learning, inference and reinforcement in neural networks and predicts post-update capability transitions with 91.43% accuracy.
AI.motivation: Neural networks are largely black boxes, and the mechanisms linking updates, learned state and inference behavior are poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors run nine nanoGPT experiments to establish training-learning-inference relations, derive a direct predictor of post-update capability transitions from factors found in the fifth experiment, test it on five other architectures, and examine feedback-driven reinforcement in a seventh system.
AI.result: The predictor reaches 91.43% accuracy and 91.49% four-way macro recall across 5,088 targets; in the seventh system concentrated correct feedback erodes mastered skills, and rebalanced feedback restores accuracy from 70.31% to 99.48%.
AI.conclusion: Linking inference consequences to later training closes the relations into unified training-learning-inference-reinforcement dynamics.

title: MAPLE: A Multimodal Mobile Agent with Playbook-Learned Experience
summary: Autonomous agents powered by vision-language models (VLMs) show great potential in navigating mobile graphical user interfaces (GUIs) to complete complex tasks. However, existing paradigms face fundamental scalability bottlenecks: fine-tuning requires massive high-fidelity datasets or prohibitive training time and compute, while gradient-free approaches rely on custom static heuristics or costly trial-and-error trajectory exploration where feedback is deferred until the end of execution. To address these limitations, we introduce MAPLE (Multimodal Agent with Playbook-Learned Experience), a novel gradient-free multi-agent framework that enables dynamic, step-wise experience sharing and execution-time prompt evolution. Unlike traditional action-reflection architectures that depend on costly, post-hoc self-reflection, MAPLE enables agents to cross-reference and distribute runtime insights in real time at each operational step. This dynamic exchange eliminates blind trial-and-error looping and steers agents along direct, grounded interaction paths. Extensive evaluations on the AndroidWorld and MobileWorld benchmarks demonstrate that MAPLE achieves state-of-the-art performance on complex, long-horizon mobile tasks, while proving scalable and adaptable across novel environments.

AI.tldr: MAPLE is a gradient-free multi-agent framework for mobile GUI agents that shares runtime experience step by step and evolves prompts during execution, reporting state-of-the-art results on AndroidWorld and MobileWorld.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning VLM agents needs large high-fidelity datasets or heavy compute, while gradient-free methods rely on static heuristics or costly trial-and-error where feedback arrives only at the end of execution.
AI.method: MAPLE (Multimodal Agent with Playbook-Learned Experience) lets agents cross-reference and distribute runtime insights at each operational step and performs execution-time prompt evolution, replacing post-hoc action-reflection loops.
AI.result: The abstract reports state-of-the-art performance on complex, long-horizon mobile tasks on the AndroidWorld and MobileWorld benchmarks, and scalability to novel environments; no numeric scores are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Real-time step-wise experience sharing can avoid blind trial-and-error and steer mobile agents along grounded interaction paths without gradient training.

title: FACET: Feasibility-Automaton Complete Enumeration and Truncation-Free Scoring of Molecular Formulas from MS/MS
summary: Determining the neutral molecular formula of a precursor ion from its tandem mass (MS/MS) spectrum is the first step in identifying an unknown small molecule. Existing methods trade recall, whether the correct formula is among the candidates, against the cost of examining each candidate. Methods that examine each candidate in depth must first shorten the list, by limiting element counts or truncating it, and that is where the correct formula is lost. End-to-end regressors are fast but guarantee neither validity nor recall. We present FACET, which separates deciding which formulas to consider from deciding which one to choose. A feasibility automaton builds a formula one element count at a time and admits exactly the formulas that fit the precursor mass and satisfy the ring-and-double-bond and valence constraints. Run as an exhaustive search, it enumerates the complete feasible set, so every candidate is valid and recall is fixed by the chemical constraints rather than by a trained model. A small neural scoring head then ranks every feasible formula from one pass of a pretrained spectrum encoder, so no candidate is discarded. On the NPLIB1 benchmark FACET reaches top-1 accuracies of $0.859$ with the adduct known and $0.729$ with it unknown, compared with $0.766$ and $0.660$ for the strongest established method, and its recall is the highest. On the external CASMI 2022 set its recall is $1.000$, and with the adduct unknown it is the most accurate of the methods compared.

AI.tldr: FACET determines neutral molecular formulas from MS/MS spectra by exhaustively enumerating all chemically feasible formulas and ranking them with a neural head, improving top-1 accuracy on NPLIB1 and CASMI 2022.
AI.motivation: Existing formula-identification methods lose the correct formula either by truncating or limiting candidate lists before in-depth scoring, or by using end-to-end regressors that guarantee neither validity nor recall.
AI.method: A feasibility automaton builds formulas one element count at a time and admits exactly those that fit the precursor mass and satisfy ring-and-double-bond and valence constraints; a small neural scoring head then ranks every feasible formula using one pass of a pretrained spectrum encoder, with no candidate discarded.
AI.result: On NPLIB1, top-1 accuracy is 0.859 with the adduct known and 0.729 with it unknown, versus 0.766 and 0.660 for the strongest established method, with the highest recall; on CASMI 2022 recall is 1.000 and, with the adduct unknown, it is the most accurate of the methods compared.
AI.conclusion: Fixing the candidate set with chemical constraints rather than a trained model makes recall guaranteed and every candidate valid, which improves formula identification.

title: Learned Surrogates of Three-Dimensional Magnetohydrodynamic Turbulence
summary: Three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence, the flow of astrophysical and fusion plasmas, is costly to simulate. We present, to our knowledge, the first learned surrogates of three-dimensional resistive MHD turbulence, and compare three standard backbones in that role: a convolutional UNet, a shifted-window transformer and a Fourier neural operator. They are trained as autoregressive emulators of decaying MHD turbulence at a resolution of $128^3$ and Reynolds numbers of 1000, 3000 and 6000, on 500 simulations per Reynolds number, each with one two-stage procedure, single steps and then short rollouts, and stopped by one rule. Over a window of about one large-eddy turnover time, the UNet and the transformer reach relative velocity errors of 0.018 to 0.053 and keep the current sheets, the enstrophy, the current density and the energy spectra of the simulation; which of the two is the more accurate depends on the Reynolds number, the UNet leading at 3000 and 6000 and the transformer at 1000. Applied with the same backbones and training procedure to two public benchmarks, the models reach the lowest error reported to date on the isotropic turbulence set of FactFormer, 39% below the best published model. On the compressible MHD set of The Well, their rollout errors are a third to a half below those of the best of The Well's baselines. They also match a 1.3 B-parameter pretrained foundation model in its rollout windows, with 20-62 times fewer parameters. The code, the configuration of every model, the evaluation scripts and the data generator with the seed of every simulation will be released upon publication.

AI.tldr: The paper builds learned surrogates for three-dimensional resistive MHD turbulence with UNet, shifted-window transformer and Fourier neural operator backbones, and finds UNet and transformer errors of 0.018 to 0.053 over about one large-eddy turnover time.
AI.motivation: Simulating three-dimensional MHD turbulence for astrophysical and fusion plasmas is costly, and learned surrogates for this regime had not been studied.
AI.method: The three backbones are trained as autoregressive emulators at 128^3 resolution and Reynolds numbers 1000, 3000 and 6000, using 500 simulations per Reynolds number with a two-stage procedure of single steps followed by short rollouts and one stopping rule.
AI.result: The UNet and transformer reach relative velocity errors of 0.018 to 0.053 and preserve current sheets, enstrophy, current density and energy spectra, with the UNet more accurate at Re 3000 and 6000 and the transformer at Re 1000; on FactFormer's isotropic turbulence set the models reach the lowest reported error, 39% below the best published model, and on The Well's compressible MHD set their rollout errors are a third to a half below the best baselines; they match a 1.3B-parameter pretrained foundation model with 20-62 times fewer parameters.
AI.conclusion: Standard backbones with a common training procedure can serve as accurate, parameter-efficient surrogates for 3D MHD turbulence, and code, configurations, evaluation scripts and data generator are promised on publication.

title: State-Augmented Learning for Post-Deployment Adaptation of Coexisting O-RAN Applications
comment: submitted to IEEE Transactions on Mobile Computing
summary: Fixed control policies in Open RAN can require retraining when service requirements, traffic loads, or interacting applications change. We propose ATTUNE, a state-augmented learning method for an energy saving application that coexists with a learned mobility load balancing application under a service constraint. ATTUNE conditions the energy saving policy on a Lagrange multiplier and updates this scalar during operation using measured service degradation, while keeping both applications' network parameters fixed. To train a single policy across service requirements, ATTUNE samples target service levels uniformly and maps them to multipliers through an adaptive table. This procedure accounts for policy-dependent multiplier responses and improves energy savings compared with training over a widened fixed multiplier range. We characterize the induced distribution of service levels and the convergence and fluctuations of the online update. An exact finite-window identity establishes convergence of average measured degradation to the target when the projection corrections vanish on average. Simulations show that a single ATTUNE policy achieves energy savings comparable to policies trained separately for each service requirement. It adapts to changes in the target, load, and partner application without retraining, increases energy savings at light load, and maintains target tracking for separately trained application pairs. No statistically significant increase in cell switching is detected in the evaluated comparisons.

AI.tldr: ATTUNE trains one energy-saving O-RAN policy conditioned on a Lagrange multiplier that is updated online from measured service degradation, so it adapts to changing service targets without retraining.
AI.motivation: Fixed Open RAN control policies need retraining when service requirements, traffic or co-located applications change.
AI.method: ATTUNE conditions the energy-saving policy on a Lagrange multiplier updated during operation from measured service degradation, samples target service levels uniformly and maps them to multipliers through an adaptive table, keeping both co-located applications' parameters fixed.
AI.result: A single policy achieves energy savings comparable to separately trained policies, adapts to changes in target, load and partner application without retraining, increases savings at light load, and maintains target tracking; no statistically significant increase in cell switching is detected.
AI.conclusion: State-augmented learning with an online multiplier update offers post-deployment adaptation of an energy-saving O-RAN application, with convergence of average degradation to the target established under stated conditions.

title: Toward Executable Multi-framework Front-end Code Generation with Self-Correction
summary: Generating codes from UI screenshots has recently benefited from MLLMs, yet existing methods centered on HTML targets and transfer poorly to multi-frameworks such as React, Vue, and Angular. However, unlike HTML, which does not entail compilation issues, generating executable code in multi-framework settings is more challenging due to framework-specific differences in syntax and failure modes, as well as the need to maintain global consistency across files. To address this problem, we study executable multi-framework front-end code generation and propose MESCoder, a tree-structured self-corrective generation framework. Our method first extracts a structural scaffold from the screenshot and then constructs sub-trees and assembly relations step by step, transforming large project generation into a sequence of localized decisions. On top of this scaffold, we introduce a unified Project Agent that continuously revises its own partial project under runtime sandbox feedback and dynamically chooses between local repair and cluster level repair. For training, we adopt a two-stage strategy that first initializes the policy offline to learn basic multi-framework generation and repair priors, and then refines it with online reinforcement learning to optimize long horizon executability and final page quality. The resulting framework models multi-framework executability as a conditioned project state transition process and improves the stability and quality of complex front end generation through self correction. Experiments show that our method improves executability, while narrowing the visual-fidelity gap to HTML-based generation. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: MESCoder generates executable multi-framework front-end code (React, Vue, Angular) from UI screenshots using tree-structured self-correction and a project agent trained offline and then with online reinforcement learning.
AI.motivation: Screenshot-to-code methods centre on HTML, which does not face compilation issues, and transfer poorly to frameworks whose syntax, failure modes and cross-file consistency demands are harder.
AI.method: The framework extracts a structural scaffold from the screenshot, builds sub-trees and assembly relations step by step, and uses a unified Project Agent that revises its partial project from runtime sandbox feedback by choosing between local and cluster-level repair; training is offline initialization followed by online RL for long-horizon executability and page quality.
AI.result: The abstract reports improved executability and a narrower visual-fidelity gap to HTML-based generation; no numeric results are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Modelling executability as a conditioned project state transition with self-correction improves the stability and quality of complex front-end generation.

title: ERIA: An Instruction-Optimized Agent for Clinical EEG Reporting
summary: Clinical EEG interpretation requires integrating technical quality, background and behavioral states, interictal and ictal abnormalities, and overall clinical context across long recordings. We introduce ERIA (EEG Reporting and Instruction-Optimized Agent), a locally deployable framework in which a single 27B language-model controller analyzes whole-recording EEGs by orchestrating specialized parametric and signal-processing tools. ERIA combines learned tools for background abnormality, sleep-wake state, seizure-like activity, and interictal epileptiform discharges with deterministic spectral, amplitude, symmetry, montage, and signal-quality analyses. Rather than fine-tuning the controller or using multi-agent orchestration, ERIA keeps the controller weights, specialist tools, and safety constraints fixed and optimizes only its natural-language analysis policy with GEPA (Genetic-Pareto), using feedback from expert-written EEG reports. GEPA improves physician-aligned whole-recording report quality over the raw policy, and the optimized policy transfers to external EEG benchmarks. On CerebraGloss-Bench and BrainBench Foundational Analysis, ERIA remains competitive with the models evaluated in the original benchmarks. These results show that specialist tools and language-level policy optimization can extend the clinical and general EEG capabilities of a single locally executable model while preserving local inference and traceable tool use.

AI.tldr: ERIA is a locally deployable EEG reporting agent built on a single 27B language-model controller that orchestrates specialist tools, with only its natural-language analysis policy optimized by GEPA.
AI.motivation: Clinical EEG interpretation over long recordings needs integration of many features, and existing approaches typically fine-tune the controller or use multi-agent orchestration, which this work avoids to keep local inference and traceable tool use.
AI.method: The controller combines learned tools for background abnormality, sleep-wake state, seizure-like activity and interictal epileptiform discharges with deterministic spectral, amplitude, symmetry, montage and signal-quality analyses; controller weights, tools and safety constraints stay fixed while GEPA (Genetic-Pareto) optimizes the analysis policy using feedback from expert-written reports.
AI.result: GEPA improves physician-aligned whole-recording report quality over the raw policy and transfers to external EEG benchmarks; on CerebraGloss-Bench and BrainBench Foundational Analysis ERIA remains competitive with the models evaluated in the original benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Specialist tools combined with language-level policy optimization can extend the clinical and general EEG capabilities of one locally executable model while keeping inference local and tool use traceable.

title: Sensitivity Inflation from Cross-Record Precision Routing in Private Quantized Fine-Tuning
summary: Private fine-tuning of large language models increasingly pairs DP-SGD with low-rank adapters on frozen, quantized backbones, and every such stack inherits one unstated premise: frozen layers keep each record's clipped gradient a function of that record alone. We show that LLM.int8 breaks this premise. It routes outlier activation columns to a higher-precision path using a union over the whole batch, so one record decides how every other record's activations are computed, even though the weights are frozen and the quantization scales are per row. We bound the resulting sensitivity inflation, state a record-isolation contract that restores the standard bound, and define record-owned precision dispatch that meets it with the same GEMMs as batched LLM.int8, so isolation needs no extra arithmetic. We then audit the native CUDA stack (bitsandbytes, PEFT, Opacus) against four matched controls. A constructed LoRA-Opacus witness reaches $15.0\times$ the add/remove bound. On pretrained OPT-125M with natural text, other records alter 20% of record-layer precision splits at batch size 16. An exploratory re-clipping analysis finds 10 of 64 candidate neighbors above the bound once every gradient is clipped; the top pair, revalidated natively, reaches $1.065C$ while every control stays within $C$, and forcing one layer's outlier mask removes the excess. A two-million-draw audit of the released adapters yields $\varepsilon$ lower bounds ($3.25$ at $\delta=10^{-5}$) below the advertised guarantee ($4.38$). Resolving an excess this small at the release level would take about 200 times more draws, whereas checking the sensitivity contract directly exposes it in a few native runs, which makes contract checking the practical audit for private quantized training.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that LLM.int8 routes outlier columns using batch-wide information, which inflates per-record sensitivity in DP-SGD fine-tuning, and proposes record-owned precision dispatch that restores the standard privacy bound at no extra arithmetic cost.
AI.motivation: Private fine-tuning stacks assume frozen quantized layers keep each record's clipped gradient a function of that record alone, an assumption that the paper tests against LLM.int8 with DP-SGD and LoRA.
AI.method: The authors bound the sensitivity inflation, state a record-isolation contract, define record-owned precision dispatch that uses the same GEMMs as batched LLM.int8, and audit the CUDA stack (bitsandbytes, PEFT, Opacus) against four matched controls, including a constructed LoRA-Opacus witness and a two-million-draw audit of released adapters.
AI.result: A constructed witness reaches 15.0 times the add/remove bound; on pretrained OPT-125M, other records alter 20% of record-layer precision splits at batch size 16; re-clipping finds 10 of 64 candidate neighbors above the bound, with the top pair reaching 1.065C while controls stay within C; the audit gives epsilon lower bounds of 3.25 at delta 1e-5 against an advertised 4.38.
AI.conclusion: Checking the sensitivity contract directly exposes the excess in a few native runs, whereas statistical release-level audits would need about 200 times more draws, making contract checking the practical audit for private quantized training.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Joint Generative Modeling of Fault Event Sequences and Sensor Time Series in Solar PV Plants
comment: Author preprint of a paper accepted to IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering; 18 pages including supplementary appendix
summary: This paper presents a multimodal generative model designed to simulate a solar energy plant system for predictive maintenance and fault prediction. We propose a novel approach to enhance system generation through conditional generation by leveraging both event sequences and time-series data and improve next event prediction. The framework employs a Transformer Hawkes Process (THP) to encode event data and an iTransformer to encode time-series data, integrated via a co-attention mechanism that effectively captures cross-modal dependencies between discrete events and continuous signals. From these integrated representations, we employ two specialized decoders for simulation: a Conditional Latent Diffusion Model (CLDM) for modeling future sensor trajectories and the Score Matching-based UnceRtainty quantiFication for Transformer Hawkes Process (SMURF-THP) for high-fidelity event prediction. This dual-decoder strategy supports uncertainty-aware, history-conditioned simulation by rolling the model forward for a specified number of generation iterations, producing finite stochastic scenarios rather than deterministic extrapolations over the full observational record. Evaluated on a comprehensive dataset from the Red Rock Solar Site in Arizona, our approach improves aggregate event-prediction F1 relative to baselines and supports applications in predictive maintenance, fault detection, and energy optimization for solar power systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multimodal generative model that jointly models solar plant fault event sequences and sensor time series, with uncertainty-aware simulation and improved next-event prediction F1 on Red Rock Solar Site data.
AI.motivation: Predictive maintenance for solar plants needs models that jointly capture discrete fault events and continuous sensor signals and produce uncertainty-aware scenarios rather than deterministic extrapolations.
AI.method: A Transformer Hawkes Process encodes events and an iTransformer encodes time series, integrated by co-attention; a Conditional Latent Diffusion Model generates future sensor trajectories and SMURF-THP provides score-matching-based uncertainty for event prediction, and rolling the model forward yields stochastic scenarios.
AI.result: The approach improves aggregate event-prediction F1 relative to baselines on a comprehensive dataset from the Red Rock Solar Site in Arizona; the abstract gives no specific values.
AI.conclusion: The framework supports predictive maintenance, fault detection and energy optimization for solar power systems through history-conditioned stochastic simulation.

title: Causal Optimal-Transport Attention: Positional Priors and Length Extrapolation
comment: 40 pages, 5 figures; code: this https URL
summary: Causal masking obstructs the column balancing used by optimal-transport (OT) attention. We study a prefix-consistent unbalanced operator and characterize the positional prior it induces. Under bounded scores, for any fixed balancing strength $\rho<1$, its fixed point dilutes attention: every fixed window receives a vanishing share as the context grows. For constant scores, we derive an exact scale-invariant prior. We then classify positional encodings by whether their distant attention mass remains bounded away from one. Discrete window-mass bounds quantify the finite-length dilution of summable log-distance priors near exponent one. Preregistered experiments with 25M- and 100M-parameter language models establish improved loss extrapolation over softmax; exploratory comparisons favor an explicit distance bias at a fraction of the cost. CABLE outperforms RoPE with evaluation-time YaRN on every seed at three training lengths. Changing only the bias beyond the training length moves long-context loss in the predicted direction on all 30 tested checkpoints. Even with exponents constrained above one, many heads approach the summability boundary during training. A margin selected by prior-only calculations for a specified window, length range and growth tolerance controls distant-mass growth in the tested setting. These results connect loss extrapolation to positional decay over the lengths actually evaluated.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes causal optimal-transport attention, showing that its fixed point dilutes distant attention with context length and proposing a distance bias (CABLE) that improves length extrapolation over softmax and RoPE with YaRN.
AI.motivation: Causal masking breaks the column balancing used by OT attention, and the positional prior induced by the resulting prefix-consistent unbalanced operator was uncharacterized, which matters for loss extrapolation beyond training length.
AI.method: The authors derive the positional prior of a prefix-consistent unbalanced operator, including an exact scale-invariant prior for constant scores, classify positional encodings by whether distant attention mass stays bounded away from one, and run preregistered experiments with 25M- and 100M-parameter language models.
AI.result: The operator improves loss extrapolation over softmax; CABLE outperforms RoPE with evaluation-time YaRN on every seed at three training lengths; changing only the bias beyond training length moves long-context loss in the predicted direction on all 30 tested checkpoints.
AI.conclusion: Loss extrapolation is linked to positional decay over the evaluated lengths, and a prior-based margin can control distant-mass growth in the tested setting.

title: FedUDG: Federated Domain Generalization with Unlabeled Clients
summary: Federated domain generalization (FDG) aims to learn models that generalize reliably to out-of-distribution (OOD) environments without centralizing client's data. However, existing FDG methods assume that all source clients have labeled data, limiting their ability to leverage the abundant unlabeled client data available in practice. To address this limitation, we propose FedUDG. At the federation level, FedUDG utilizes a parameter-functional differentiation strategy that maintains a semantic anchor updated solely using ground-truth labels. The remaining parameters absorb knowledge from unlabeled domains under bounded aggregation, preventing domain-biased noise from eroding the class semantics. Within each unlabeled client, FedUDG utilizes a student-teacher framework with two complementary objectives: (1) semantic self-training on high-confidence samples, using the functional differentiation between the semantic anchor and classifier to constrain the model to learn semantically pure and cross-domain stable features; and (2) label-free representation distillation on all unlabeled samples to stabilize learning under appearance variations. Together, these objectives guide the model toward a transferable feature space, while mitigating overfitting to domain-specific characteristics. Furthermore, to address the lack of systematic evaluation of FDG under formal privacy constraints, we develop a sample-level differentially private extension, DP-FedUDG, to quantify the trade-off between privacy and OOD generalization. Across four evaluation protocols, FedUDG consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. The code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: FedUDG extends federated domain generalization to unlabeled clients using a semantic anchor updated only from labeled data and student-teacher self-training, and includes a differentially private variant, DP-FedUDG.
AI.motivation: Existing federated domain generalization methods assume every source client has labeled data, which leaves abundant unlabeled client data unused.
AI.method: At the federation level a parameter-functional differentiation keeps a semantic anchor updated only from ground-truth labels while other parameters absorb unlabeled-domain knowledge under bounded aggregation; within each unlabeled client a student-teacher framework combines semantic self-training on high-confidence samples with label-free representation distillation on all samples, plus a sample-level DP extension.
AI.result: Across four evaluation protocols FedUDG consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: The objectives guide the model toward a transferable feature space, and DP-FedUDG quantifies the trade-off between privacy and out-of-distribution generalization.

title: Improved Sample Complexity Analysis For First Order Bilevel Reinforcement Learning
summary: Bilevel reinforcement learning optimizes an upper-level objective through the policy response to a lower-level reinforcement learning problem. Such problems arise when learning a reward model while adapting a policy to that reward. However, a gap remains between sample-complexity guarantees and practical actor--critic training. Tabular analyses restrict applicability to finite spaces, while continuous-state analyses often impose a uniform Polyak--Łojasiewicz (PL) condition. We show that this condition need not hold even for smooth positive policies with exactly representable values. We develop a single-loop, fully first-order method for continuous states and finite actions with specified multilayer neural actors and a persistently trained nonlinear critic built from fixed features. Under explicit initialization, regularity, feature-excitation, and value-realizability conditions, fixed reference-KL regularization yields local curvature, and we prove containment of the coupled iterates. Shared trajectories control sampling noise, while paired critic analysis controls normalized critic-error differences as the response perturbation shrinks. A joint descent and tracking argument establishes an improved $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\varepsilon^{-2})$ sample complexity for $O(\varepsilon)$ expected squared gradient norm of the upper objective induced by the selected regularized policy response, including critic training.

AI.tldr: The paper gives a single-loop, fully first-order actor-critic analysis for bilevel reinforcement learning with continuous states, proving an improved O~(eps^-2) sample complexity to reach O(eps) expected squared upper-objective gradient norm.
AI.motivation: Existing sample-complexity guarantees for bilevel RL either are tabular, or for continuous states assume a uniform Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition that the authors show need not hold even for smooth positive policies with representable values.
AI.method: The method is a single-loop first-order scheme with specified multilayer neural actors and a persistently trained nonlinear critic on fixed features, with fixed reference-KL regularization giving local curvature; the analysis relies on containment of coupled iterates, shared trajectories for sampling noise and paired critic analysis for response perturbation.
AI.result: Under explicit initialization, regularity, feature-excitation and value-realizability conditions, the method achieves O~(eps^-2) sample complexity for O(eps) expected squared gradient norm of the upper objective, including critic training.
AI.conclusion: The result closes part of the gap between sample-complexity theory and practical actor-critic training for bilevel RL, under the stated conditions.

title: InformedXRD: Reproducible Benchmarks and Physics-Informed Evaluation for Powder Diffraction Symmetry Classification
comment: Camera-ready version. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, Track on Evaluations and Datasets. 10 pages main text plus appendices and checklist (27 pages total). Code: this https URL benchmarks: this https URL checkpoints: this https URL
summary: Machine learning for powder diffraction (PXRD) symmetry classification is being trained at scale, yet the field lacks a common evaluation standard: papers report results on different subsets of experimental archives, with different target taxonomies, preprocessing, and metrics, and published models are rarely released in a form that permits rescoring. We present InformedXRD, an evaluation framework with three parts: (i) a machine-readable mapping from 230 space groups to 99 extinction groups, the finest classes powder diffraction can identify from systematic absences alone; (ii) a benchmark-construction method whose inclusion rules are specified as code and reproduce from a frozen snapshot, instantiated as RRUFF-473, RRUFF-325, and, as a small example, opXRD-98; (iii) a reporting protocol with prior-only frequency baselines, a label-permutation test, a hierarchy-aware error metric on the condensed translationengleiche subgroup graph, and stratified evaluation. We build on the mapping, RRUFF benchmarks, subgroup graph, and four ViT checkpoints released in our earlier work (Baggett et al., 2026). Using these checkpoints, a 1D residual CNN, and six architectures trained under the XRDBench recipe (Cao et al., 2025), we show that evaluation design changes what conclusions are justified: paired tests point in different directions at Top-1 and Top-5; paired Top-k tests do not separate the three leading XRDBench models, while hierarchy-aware analysis describes error distance and direction across all six; an input-blind frequency predictor matches the models on aggregate Top-k, yet a label-permutation test still detects pattern-specific evidence; and stratified analysis exposes a label-entropy confound that aggregate accuracy hides. All mapping tables, benchmark code, scripts, and checkpoints are released as shared infrastructure for PXRD-ML evaluation.

AI.tldr: InformedXRD is an evaluation framework for powder diffraction symmetry classification that supplies a space-group-to-extinction-group mapping, reproducible RRUFF-based benchmarks, and a reporting protocol with baselines and hierarchy-aware metrics.
AI.motivation: PXRD symmetry classification lacks a common evaluation standard, since papers use different archive subsets, label taxonomies, preprocessing and metrics, and models are rarely released in rescorable form.
AI.method: The framework contains a machine-readable mapping from 230 space groups to 99 extinction groups, a benchmark-construction method specified as code (RRUFF-473, RRUFF-325 and opXRD-98), and a reporting protocol with prior-only frequency baselines, a label-permutation test, a hierarchy-aware error metric on the subgroup graph and stratified evaluation.
AI.result: Evaluation design changes conclusions: paired tests disagree at Top-1 and Top-5, Top-k tests do not separate the three leading XRDBench models, an input-blind frequency predictor matches models on aggregate Top-k, the permutation test still detects pattern-specific evidence, and stratified analysis reveals a label-entropy confound.
AI.conclusion: The mappings, benchmark code, scripts and checkpoints are released as shared infrastructure for PXRD machine-learning evaluation.

title: Learning Gradients of Homogeneous Functions
summary: Homogeneous gradient functions have widespread significance, including applications in maximum energy subspace selection and retrieval problems. Euler's homogeneous function theorem specifies how the potential associated with a positively k-homogeneous gradient field can be recovered directly from the field itself. We use Euler's theorem to build on GradNets and propose a homogeneous gradient network architecture that is guaranteed to correspond to the gradient of a homogeneous function. Then, we describe how monotone homogeneous GradNets universally approximate the gradients of k-homogeneous convex functions. The inductive bias of homogeneous GradNets enables them to outperform baseline ICNNs by up to 7dB in our max energy subspace projection experiment and by up to 13% higher accuracy, 98% fewer parameters, and 70% fewer FLOPS in our amortized inner product search experiment.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a homogeneous GradNet architecture whose outputs are guaranteed to be gradients of a homogeneous function, and reports gains over ICNNs in energy subspace projection and amortized inner product search.
