AI.motivation: Homogeneous gradient fields matter for maximum energy subspace selection and retrieval, and Euler's theorem gives a way to recover the potential from such a field, which existing gradient architectures do not exploit.
AI.method: Building on GradNets and Euler's homogeneous function theorem, the authors design a homogeneous gradient network that corresponds to the gradient of a homogeneous function and show that monotone homogeneous GradNets universally approximate gradients of k-homogeneous convex functions.
AI.result: Homogeneous GradNets outperform baseline ICNNs by up to 7 dB in a max energy subspace projection experiment and, in amortized inner product search, reach up to 13% higher accuracy with 98% fewer parameters and 70% fewer FLOPS.
AI.conclusion: The inductive bias of homogeneity gives a parameter-efficient architecture for learning homogeneous gradient functions with universal approximation guarantees.

title: Generative Modeling with Continuous Flows: Sample Complexity of Flow Matching
summary: Flow matching has emerged as a promising alternative to diffusion-based generative modeling, offering a continuous-time ordinary differential equation formulation with fast sampling and a simple regression-based training objective. Despite its empirical success, some theoretical analyses idealize the learning procedure by assuming that the velocity field is obtained by exact empirical risk minimization. This assumption does not reflect the practical finite-dataset setting, where the empirical flow-matching loss is only approximately minimized by a finite number of stochastic-gradient updates. We develop an empirical-risk-minimizer-free analysis for flow matching that explicitly accounts for both finite-sample statistical error and finite-time empirical optimization error. Our analysis considers a finite dataset of \(N\) flow-matching samples and a learned parameter \(\theta_T\) obtained after \(T\) stochastic gradient updates on the empirical objective. Under regularity assumptions on the interpolation path, sub-exponential source and target distributions, approximation by a bounded-parameter smooth neural velocity class, empirical-loss optimization, and uniform flow stability, we prove a guarantee that holds with high probability over the finite training dataset and in expectation over the stochastic-gradient randomness. The resulting bound separates approximation error, statistical error from the finite dataset, tail error from unbounded source and target distributions, and empirical optimization error from approximate minimization of the finite-sample objective.

AI.tldr: The paper gives a finite-sample, finite-time analysis of flow matching that accounts for empirical risk not being exactly minimized, bounding error with high probability over the dataset and in expectation over SGD randomness.
AI.motivation: Existing flow-matching theory assumes exact empirical risk minimization, which does not reflect practice, where a finite number of stochastic gradient updates only approximately minimizes the empirical loss on a finite dataset.
AI.method: The analysis considers N flow-matching samples and the parameter theta_T after T SGD updates, under interpolation-path regularity, sub-exponential source and target distributions, approximation by a bounded-parameter smooth neural velocity class and uniform flow stability.
AI.result: The guarantee separates approximation error, statistical error from the finite dataset, tail error from unbounded distributions and empirical optimization error.
AI.conclusion: The bound gives an explicit decomposition of flow-matching error that holds without assuming exact empirical risk minimization.

title: Finite-Time Online Sample Complexity for Conditional Diffusion Models
summary: We study the finite-time training and sampling error of conditional diffusion models trained by online stochastic-gradient denoising score matching. Rather than assuming access to an exact empirical or population risk minimizer, we analyze the score network produced after a finite number of stochastic-gradient updates under an explicit localized Polyak--Łojasiewicz (PL) condition, stochastic-gradient regularity, and a trajectory-containment assumption. Our analysis separates the network approximation complexity from the online training-sample budget and propagates both errors through the reverse diffusion process. Under anisotropic smoothness, a joint intrinsic-dimensional structure for the data and conditioning variables, sub-exponential tails, and explicit approximation-class compatibility, we obtain a conditional score approximation error of order \[ \widetilde{\mathcal O}\!\left(M^{-\eta_{\mathrm{app}}}\right), \qquad \eta_{\mathrm{app}} = \frac{2\alpha_x} {2\alpha_x+d_x'+(\alpha_x/\alpha_y)d_y'}, \] where \(M\) denotes the approximation complexity, \(d_x'\) and \(d_y'\) are the intrinsic response and conditioning dimensions, and \(\alpha_x,\alpha_y\) are their corresponding smoothness exponents. For \(N=RB\) online denoising samples used by SGD, the finite-time optimization error is controlled explicitly in terms of the PL, smoothness, gradient-noise, and initialization constants. Combining these ingredients with reverse-process stability yields a total-variation bound that decomposes into terminal-initialization, time-discretization, approximation/localization, and finite-time optimization errors.

AI.tldr: The paper bounds the finite-time training and sampling error of conditional diffusion models trained with online SGD denoising score matching, yielding a conditional score approximation rate and a total-variation bound.
AI.motivation: Existing conditional diffusion guarantees usually assume exact risk minimizers, while practical models are trained with a finite number of stochastic gradient updates on an online sample stream.
AI.method: The analysis uses an explicit localized Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition, stochastic gradient regularity and trajectory containment, separates network approximation complexity from the online sample budget, and propagates errors through the reverse diffusion process under anisotropic smoothness and intrinsic-dimensional structure.
AI.result: The conditional score approximation error is of order O~(M^(-eta_app)) with eta_app = 2 alpha_x / (2 alpha_x + d_x' + (alpha_x/alpha_y) d_y'), and the finite-time optimization error is explicit in the PL, smoothness, gradient-noise and initialization constants; these combine into a total-variation bound.
AI.conclusion: The total-variation bound decomposes into terminal-initialization, time-discretization, approximation or localization and finite-time optimization errors.

title: Meta-memorization and memorization scaling laws in transformers
summary: Larger transformers can memorize more data, with a capacity (in bits) that scales roughly linearly with the number of parameters. Counterintuitively, larger models also memorize faster, requiring fewer repetitions of a sequence during training before it is memorized. We reproduce both memorization scaling laws in transformers trained on random binary sequences, showing that rapid memorization can arise even when data contain no semantic or compositional structure. Rapid memorization is due to a meta-memorization effect, where models trained to memorize a large set of random sequences learn to memorize novel sequences more quickly. The rate $r(t)$ at which models memorize grows with training time $t$ as a power-law $r(t) \sim t^{\beta}$ with a fixed exponent $\beta$ but an increasing upper cutoff across model scales. Meta-memorization enables even one-layer transformers to few-shot memorize a 100-bit sequence. This effect is partly explained by the formation of structured attention heads that convey position-invariant sequence information to MLPs where memorized sequences are stored. Meta-memorization is recapitulated in a simplified model of a dense associative memory where retrieval is constrained by an attentional bottleneck. Our results suggest transformers, through pre-training, acquire reusable mechanisms that enable highly efficient storage and retrieval of memories.

AI.tldr: The paper reproduces memorization scaling laws in transformers trained on random binary sequences and attributes faster memorization in larger models to a meta-memorization effect.
AI.motivation: Larger models are known to memorize more and faster, but it was unclear whether this needs semantic structure in the data.
AI.method: Transformers are trained on random binary sequences; the rate of memorization is tracked over training, attention-head structure is analyzed, and the effect is recapitulated in a simplified dense associative memory with an attentional bottleneck.
AI.result: Capacity scales roughly linearly with parameters, and memorization rate grows as a power law r(t) ~ t^beta with fixed exponent beta and a model-dependent upper cutoff; one-layer transformers can few-shot memorize a 100-bit sequence, and structured attention heads partly explain the effect.
AI.conclusion: Pre-training gives transformers reusable mechanisms for efficient storage and retrieval of memories, even without semantic or compositional data structure.

title: Beyond Validation Loss: Coverage and Reliability Dynamics in Robot Policy Pretraining
summary: In modern robot learning, generative robot policies are first pretrained through supervised learning from demonstrations, then refined through reinforcement learning, supervised finetuning, or other forms of posttraining. Yet conventional pretraining metrics, such as validation loss and average task success, provide an incomplete account of which policies support both effective direct deployment and subsequent posttraining. In this work, we study closed-loop pass@k, which evaluates the probability that k rollouts from the same initial condition attain at least one success. Thus, pass@1 measures mean task success; large-k pass@k measures whether success remains reachable under repeated sampling. Across a wide range of posttraining recipes, we show that large-k pass@k reveals posttraining differences not captured by pass@1. In particular, checkpoints with similar pass@1 but different large-k pass@k have different posttraining performance. Moreover, we show pass@k peaks at different checkpoints during supervised pretraining, revealing a coverage-reliability tradeoff over the course of training. Based on these observations, we propose two practical interventions: (1) a purely offline checkpoint-selection criterion that balances coverage and reliability without closed-loop evaluation, and (2) a generative data augmentation procedure that expands supervision beyond the finite demonstration set, preserving large-k pass@k while maintaining or improving pass@1 and raising the observed coverage-reliability Pareto frontier. Together, our results motivate evaluation, checkpoint selection, and training procedures that explicitly account for posttraining. Blog post, visualizations, and code are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that closed-loop pass@k reveals robot-policy differences invisible to pass@1 and proposes an offline checkpoint-selection criterion and a generative data augmentation procedure that improve the coverage-reliability trade-off.
AI.motivation: Validation loss and average task success give an incomplete picture of which pretrained generative robot policies will support both deployment and later posttraining.
AI.method: The authors measure closed-loop pass@k, the probability that k rollouts from one initial condition include at least one success, across posttraining recipes and over supervised pretraining checkpoints, and propose an offline checkpoint criterion balancing coverage and reliability plus generative data augmentation beyond the demonstration set.
AI.result: Checkpoints with similar pass@1 but different large-k pass@k perform differently after posttraining; pass@k peaks at different pretraining checkpoints; the augmentation preserves large-k pass@k while maintaining or improving pass@1 and raises the observed coverage-reliability Pareto frontier.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation, checkpoint selection and training should explicitly account for posttraining, since pass@1 alone misses coverage.

title: Search-Aware On-Policy Self-Distillation with Sibling Alignment for Generative Recommendation
summary: Generative recommendation retrieves items by autoregressively generating semantic IDs, typically via beam search. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) enhances training supervision by transferring privileged self-teacher knowledge at student-generated states. However, beam-search retention depends on competition among prefixes: visited states differ in importance, and initially reliable decisions may approach the pruning boundary as training evolves. Moreover, conventional distribution matching couples target-token confidence with preferences among competing continuations, potentially weakening relational supervision when the self-teacher strongly favors the target. To address these challenges, we propose Search-Aware On-Policy Self-Distillation (SA-OPSD), a framework that transfers privileged self-teacher knowledge to the states visited during the student's own beam search. Specifically, we introduce Evolving-Boundary Sampling, which prioritizes search-critical states by considering both current pruning-boundary proximity and initial-reference retention-margin decline under a controlled distillation budget. Furthermore, we develop Confidence-Decoupled Branch Distillation, which separates target-probability calibration from informative sibling relations to better preserve the teacher's preferences among competing branches. Experiments on Industrial, Office, and Instruments demonstrate strong performance for SA-OPSD.

AI.tldr: SA-OPSD applies on-policy self-distillation to the states visited during a generative recommender's own beam search, using boundary-aware sampling and decoupled branch distillation to improve semantic-ID recommendation.
AI.motivation: On-policy self-distillation for generative recommendation ignores that beam-search retention depends on competition among prefixes, and conventional distribution matching mixes target-token confidence with relations among competing continuations.
AI.method: Evolving-Boundary Sampling prioritizes search-critical states by pruning-boundary proximity and retention-margin decline under a distillation budget, and Confidence-Decoupled Branch Distillation separates target-probability calibration from sibling relations so the teacher's preferences among branches are preserved.
AI.result: The abstract reports strong performance on the Industrial, Office and Instruments datasets but gives no numeric results.
AI.conclusion: Distilling a privileged self-teacher at beam-search-visited states, with boundary-aware sampling and sibling alignment, is presented as an effective way to train generative recommenders.

title: Autoencoder Based Deep Clustering of Point Clouds
summary: Motivated by a problem in Generative Specification-Producing AIs (SPAIs), we focus on a problem of deep clustering of three-dimensional shapes specified by point clouds. After reviewing clustering and deep clustering, we study the fully unsupervised pipeline in which a FoldingNet autoencoder is first trained for reconstruction and then K-means++ is then applied to the resulting codewords. We report clustering accuracy (ACC), normalized mutual information (NMI) and adjusted Rand index (ARI) on ModelNet10 and ModelNet40 datasets, as a function of the number of clusters K. We also provide t-SNE visualizations of the codewords, and discuss the choice of K.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates a fully unsupervised pipeline that trains a FoldingNet autoencoder on point clouds and clusters the codewords with K-means++, reporting ACC, NMI and ARI on ModelNet10 and ModelNet40 across cluster counts.
AI.motivation: Deep clustering of 3D shapes given as point clouds is needed for Generative Specification-Producing AIs, and the paper reviews clustering and deep clustering before studying this pipeline.
AI.method: A FoldingNet autoencoder is trained for reconstruction, K-means++ is applied to the resulting codewords, and t-SNE visualizations of the codewords are used, with the choice of K discussed.
AI.result: The abstract reports clustering accuracy, NMI and ARI on ModelNet10 and ModelNet40 as a function of K but gives no numeric values.
AI.conclusion: The pipeline is an unsupervised baseline for point-cloud shape clustering, and the choice of K is discussed; the abstract states no further takeaways.

title: DyRadio: Spatiotemporal Diffusion for Dynamic Radio Map Reconstruction
summary: Accurate radio map (RM) reconstruction is essential for environment-aware wireless networks. Sampling-based methods, which infer radio conditions from sparse measurements, are widely adopted because they do not require explicit knowledge of transmitter configurations. However, in dynamic environments, time-varying propagation conditions cause RMs to evolve, complicating reconstruction from temporally distributed sparse observations. Although cross-frame observations provide complementary spatial information, their direct aggregation can introduce temporal state mismatch. Furthermore, unknown measurement noise adds to the reconstruction difficulties. To address these challenges, we propose DyRadio, a framework that integrates spatiotemporal RM reconstruction with unknown noise estimation. Specifically, a propagation-prior-guided, noise-conditioned spatiotemporal diffusion model (DM) jointly reconstructs consecutive RMs by capturing cross-frame dependencies, while adapting to measurement noise levels. To estimate the noise level, an iterative predictive likelihood method alternates between DM-based blind-area prediction and noise-level updates. The estimated noise level then conditions reconstruction of the complete RM sequence. Experimental results demonstrate superior reconstruction accuracy and robustness against measurement noise, with peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) improvements of 1.18-5.75 dB over the best-performing baseline across all evaluated settings.

AI.tldr: DyRadio reconstructs a sequence of dynamic radio maps with a noise-conditioned spatiotemporal diffusion model and an iterative predictive-likelihood estimator of unknown measurement noise, improving PSNR by 1.18 to 5.75 dB over the best baseline.
AI.motivation: Sparse measurements in time-varying environments complicate radio map reconstruction, and directly aggregating cross-frame observations causes temporal state mismatch, while unknown measurement noise adds further difficulty.
AI.method: A propagation-prior-guided, noise-conditioned spatiotemporal diffusion model jointly reconstructs consecutive radio maps using cross-frame dependencies, and an iterative predictive likelihood method alternates between diffusion-based blind-area prediction and noise-level updates, with the estimated level conditioning full-sequence reconstruction.
AI.result: Reconstruction accuracy and robustness to measurement noise are superior, with PSNR improvements of 1.18 to 5.75 dB over the best-performing baseline across all evaluated settings.
AI.conclusion: Joint spatiotemporal diffusion with noise estimation provides more accurate and robust dynamic radio map reconstruction for environment-aware wireless networks.

title: Sonny-ENS: demystifying machine-learning ensemble weather forecasting
comment: 25 pages, 6 figures, 7 Extended Data figures and 3 Extended Data tables; Supplementary Information (4 figures, 2 tables) included
summary: Every weather forecast is uncertain, and decisions from flood warnings to energy trading depend on how well that uncertainty is quantified. Machine-learning (ML) ensembles now quantify it better than the best physics-based ensemble, yet two things about them remain opaque: whether their skill requires hundreds to thousands of accelerator-days of training, and how a network with a simple source of randomness produces a spread that follows the flow. Here we introduce Sonny-ENS, an ensemble of three 68.9-million-parameter networks with Monte Carlo dropout, trained on the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) in 2.7 A40 GPU-days. On 2022, it has a lower CRPS than the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts ensemble (ENS) on 96% of 570 targets and an 8.3% lower mean CRPS at lead times of 1-10 days. It outperforms the operational GenCast on 69% of the targets, and a 51-member, 15-day forecast takes 69 s on one GPU. Ablations identify the ingredients of this skill, and a Kolmogorov-Arnold sparse autoencoder shows that dropout injects uncertainty mainly in the tropics, whereas the spread grows where the atmosphere is baroclinically unstable (spatial correlation 0.91 with the Eady growth rate). Skillful probabilistic weather forecasts are therefore within reach of a single GPU server.

AI.tldr: Sonny-ENS is a three-member ensemble of 68.9M-parameter networks with Monte Carlo dropout, trained on CRPS in 2.7 A40 GPU-days, that beats ECMWF ENS on CRPS for 96% of 570 targets in 2022.
AI.motivation: The paper asks whether skilful machine-learning ensemble weather forecasts require hundreds to thousands of accelerator-days of training, and how a simple randomness source yields a spread that follows the flow.
AI.method: Three 68.9M-parameter networks with Monte Carlo dropout are trained on the continuous ranked probability score, with ablations to identify the ingredients of skill and a Kolmogorov-Arnold sparse autoencoder to analyze where the spread comes from.
AI.result: On 2022 data it has lower CRPS than ECMWF ENS on 96% of 570 targets and an 8.3% lower mean CRPS at lead times of 1-10 days; it outperforms the operational GenCast on 69% of targets; a 51-member, 15-day forecast takes 69 s on one GPU; dropout mainly injects uncertainty in the tropics, and spread correlates 0.91 with the Eady growth rate.
AI.conclusion: Skilful probabilistic weather forecasts are within reach of a single GPU server.

title: Yielding Fairness: Coupled Learning and Fairness for Value-Weighted Ranking
summary: Risk screening and recommendation systems pass or block accounts that generate both value and loss. Under a blocked-value budget, a cap on expected value forgone through blocking, the optimal ranking orders accounts by expected value per unit expected loss, a ratio of conditional expectations. This rule can conflict with accepted harm or net-harm criteria, blocking accounts that another criterion would pass at the same budget. We call these cases account-level objections and define group complaint disparity as the difference between groups' normalized realized objections. Weighted binary cross-entropy (W-BCE) implements the value-per-loss order with one score. Objection penalties modify the ranking, while group multipliers scale those penalties differently by group, tracing tradeoffs between loss capture and complaint disparity. This preserves the value-budgeted ranking structure and makes the cost of reducing contestable blocks explicit. Across public recommendation, insurance, credit, and mortgage datasets, we compare undamped W-BCE with ordinary BCE using yield Gini, an area summary of loss capture versus blocked value. Logarithmic weight damping is evaluated separately. Held-out evaluations measure capture-disparity tradeoffs. Validation-selected group-aware complaint penalties improve complaint closure in some cohorts. A corrected comparison normalizes and enlarges candidate policy banks using validation-only price sweeps and retains all ten applicable sources. The source-level results do not establish a statistically significant average advantage over group-blind pricing at the fixed minimum retained loss capture. We also compare with blocked-count, blocked-value, and protected-loss parity postprocessors, which do not directly constrain realized objections, and measure objections in candidate-count and loss units.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes coupled fairness-aware ranking for value-weighted risk screening, using weighted BCE for the value-per-loss order plus objection penalties and group multipliers that trace the loss-capture versus complaint-disparity trade-off.
AI.motivation: Under a blocked-value budget the optimal value-per-loss ranking can conflict with accepted harm or net-harm criteria and creates group disparities in contestable blocks, which existing postprocessors do not directly constrain.
AI.method: Weighted BCE implements the value-per-loss order with one score, objection penalties modify the ranking, group multipliers scale penalties by group, and the approach is compared with ordinary BCE, logarithmic weight damping and blocked-count, blocked-value and protected-loss parity postprocessors on public recommendation, insurance, credit and mortgage datasets.
AI.result: The source-level results do not establish a statistically significant average advantage over group-blind pricing at fixed minimum retained loss capture; validation-selected group-aware penalties improve complaint closure in some cohorts.
AI.conclusion: The cost of reducing contestable blocks is made explicit, and the paper finds no robust average gain over group-blind pricing across the ten applicable sources.

title: Physics-Informed One-Step Generation on Long-short flow maps
summary: Physics-informed generative models should produce samples that are both data-aligned and physically valid, yet existing methods are often iterative and too slow for practical use. Achieving this with a one-step flow-map model is difficult because both data-distribution and physics-constraint learning are enforced only indirectly through surrogate objectives, making their joint learning fragile for long-range flow maps. We propose \textbf{Physics-Informed Long-Short Flow Maps with Direct Guidance (LSFM-DG)}, which makes direct target computation feasible by decomposing one-step generation into a long flow map for global evolution and a near-terminal short flow map with computable closed-form solutions and physics potentials. As the short flow map shrinks to zero, it provides both direct distributional and physical targets for learning the long flow map. This yields a unified one-step flow-map model that removes Jensen's gap, improves training stability, and achieves stronger data fidelity and physical consistency without distillation.

AI.tldr: LSFM-DG is a one-step physics-informed flow-map generator that splits generation into a long flow map for global evolution and a near-terminal short flow map with closed-form targets and physics potentials, removing distillation.
AI.motivation: Physics-informed generators are usually iterative and too slow, and one-step flow-map models learn data and physics constraints only through fragile surrogate objectives over long-range maps.
AI.method: The one-step generation is decomposed into a long flow map and a short flow map that shrinks to zero, whose closed-form solutions and physics potentials give direct distributional and physical targets for the long map, which removes Jensen's gap.
AI.result: The abstract reports stronger data fidelity and physical consistency with improved training stability, without distillation; no numeric results are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Direct target computation makes one-step flow-map generation practical while keeping samples both data-aligned and physically valid.

title: A Hybrid Anomaly Detection Method for Electric Vehicle Identification from Smart Meter Recordings
summary: In recent years, electric vehicles (EVs) have attracted much attention due to their potential to decarbonize the transport system. EV charging imposes challenges on power grids, such as load imbalance and voltage instability. Therefore, electricity distributors need to identify which users have an EV. Smart meter recordings can be effectively used for this purpose. The major issue associated with such data is the imbalance problem, where the majority of the data belongs to users without EVs. The existing methods for EV identification from smart meter recordings have framed it as a classification task. In this paper, we frame the problem as an unsupervised problem and propose a hybrid anomaly detection method that combines the power of prediction-based and reconstruction-based anomaly detection methods. The proposed model considers temporal and stochastic representation information of smart meter time series via prediction-based and reconstruction-based components, respectively. The performance of the proposed model is compared with state-of-the-art supervised and unsupervised methods. Its superiority is verified on real-world data.

AI.tldr: The paper frames electric-vehicle identification from smart-meter data as unsupervised anomaly detection and combines prediction-based and reconstruction-based components, reporting superiority over supervised and unsupervised baselines on real data.
AI.motivation: EV identification from smart-meter recordings has been treated as classification, which struggles with the strong imbalance where most users have no EV.
AI.method: A hybrid anomaly detection model uses a prediction-based component for temporal information and a reconstruction-based component for stochastic representation information of smart-meter time series.
AI.result: The abstract states the proposed model is superior to state-of-the-art supervised and unsupervised methods on real-world data, without numeric values.
AI.conclusion: Anomaly detection offers an unsupervised route to EV identification that copes with class imbalance, as verified on real-world data.

title: A Hybrid Anomaly Detection Method for Multivariate Time Series
summary: Multivariate time series are ubiquitous in monitoring smart systems such as power plants, smart houses, and servers. These systems use multiple sensors to collect the system's status over time. Those sensors represent the status of the whole system as one entity. Anomaly detection in such smart systems is of critical importance to prevent system failure and maintain functionality. But anomaly detection in such multivariate time series data is very challenging since this type of data includes both temporal and spatial information. Capturing both of these pieces of information is important to detect anomalies. In this paper, we propose a hybrid deep learning-based anomaly detection method, which captures both temporal and spatial information. We propose to take advantage of the feature extraction capabilities of 2d convolutional network in a variational autoencoder, alongside a prediction-based deep neural network of 2d convolutional networks and a gated recurrent unit network to capture both spatial and temporal information. Experiments on public data against state-of-the-art show the potential of our method.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hybrid deep anomaly detector for multivariate time series that combines a 2D-convolutional variational autoencoder with a prediction network using 2D convolutions and a GRU to capture spatial and temporal information.
AI.motivation: Anomaly detection in multivariate sensor data from smart systems must capture both temporal and spatial structure, which is hard for many existing methods.
AI.method: A 2D-convolutional VAE extracts features while a prediction-based deep network with 2D convolutions and a gated recurrent unit captures spatial and temporal patterns together.
AI.result: The abstract reports that experiments on public data against state-of-the-art methods show the potential of the method, without numeric results.
AI.conclusion: Combining reconstruction and prediction with spatial and temporal modelling is presented as a promising approach to multivariate time-series anomaly detection.

title: Stand-In Effects and Pooling Amplification: Design-Based Tests of Whether Biological World Models Use Actions
comment: 54 pages, 6 figures, 24 tables. Preregistrations: this https URL (M4) and this https URL (M5). Primary category cs.LG: a test for learned action-conditioned models; cross-listed for the statistical method (stat.ME) and the biological application (q-bio.QM)
summary: Action-conditioned world models are increasingly trained on data from randomized experiments, and whether their predictions respond to actions is usually checked by replacing or removing the actions and measuring the loss in accuracy. We show that such diagnostics report action effects where there are none: under autocorrelated designs, future actions stand in for history the model does not see, and a better model learns the stand-in better. When the design law is known, a conditional randomization test written as an e-value is valid in finite samples whatever the model, provided the resampler conditions on the full state the design used; resampling from a simpler law reproduces the false effect. We identify a second failure, specific to world models: when many sites share one action sequence (cells in a microscope field, pixels in a frame), the natural pooled score turns small model errors along the action contrast into overwhelming evidence against a true effect. In a pixel world, its median log e-value fell from $-17.3$ to $-6832$ as frames grew from 64 to 4096 pixels, while the oracle's rose. Tempering the score by a design effect estimated on training data changes the bet, not the validity. Our own preregistered analysis of optogenetic ERK experiments failed in exactly this way; a tempered statistic, selected on synthetic data and registered before the data were obtained, then rejected the null on a never-opened field ($E\approx 1.1\times10^{10}$). Every analysis is preregistered, fixed in a dated protocol before it was run, or labelled exploratory, and every reported result is generated from hashed result files.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that action-ablation diagnostics for action-conditioned world models can report false action effects under autocorrelated designs, and gives a finite-sample conditional randomization e-value test plus a tempered pooled score that fixes a pooling failure.
AI.motivation: Action-conditioned world models trained on randomized experiments are often checked by replacing or removing actions, but future actions can stand in for unseen history under autocorrelated designs, and pooling across many sites can produce overwhelming spurious evidence.
AI.method: When the design law is known, a conditional randomization test written as an e-value is valid in finite samples for any model if the resampler conditions on the full state used by the design; pooled scores are tempered by a design effect estimated on training data, with the statistic selected on synthetic data and preregistered.
AI.result: In a pixel world the median log e-value of the pooled score falls from -17.3 to -6832 as frames grow from 64 to 4096 pixels while the oracle's rises; the tempered statistic rejects the null on a never-opened field with E approximately 1.1 x 10^10 in the optogenetic ERK analysis.
AI.conclusion: Action-effect claims for world models require design-conditioned resampling and design-effect correction, and every analysis is preregistered, dated in a protocol, or labelled exploratory.

title: Wave Physics as Representation: Tensor-Structured Neural Reconstruction for Ocean Acoustic Fields
summary: Reconstructing three-dimensional (3D) complex ocean acoustic fields from sparse measurements is challenging due to highly oscillatory wave structures and restricted sensing patterns/routes. Learning-based approaches fall into two categories. First, purely data-driven models can learn complex field patterns, but do not explicitly exploit wave physics that may enhance interpretability and reduce training costs. Second, physics-informed methods impose a specified physical equation as a reconstruction constraint, but often require environment-dependent parameters that are difficult to acquire. As a result, practical 3D acoustic field reconstruction that is both physically grounded and robust to uncertain environmental information remains largely unexplored. This work takes an alternative route: instead of solving a fully specified wave equation, it extracts a structured representation from wave physics and learns its components from data. From the Helmholtz equation and normal mode propagation, we derive a structured spatial-angular tensor representation, termed the S/c representation. Under a low-rank specialization, it takes the form of a rank-(L,L,1) block-term tensor decomposition, which connects structured sampling patterns/routes used in ocean sensing to sufficient conditions for field recovery. Building on this tensor representation, we propose TIDAL, a neural reconstructor that uses the S/c representation as an inductive bias for structured decoding and aligns information aggregation with the sampling geometry. The neural learner removes the need for known model parameters required by conventional physics-based recovery methods. Experiments across three structured sampling geometries show that TIDAL achieves the best reconstruction performance and fastest inference among baselines, with benefits from the physics-derived representation under limited data and model capacity.

AI.tldr: TIDAL reconstructs three-dimensional ocean acoustic fields from sparse measurements using a physics-derived S/c tensor representation as an inductive bias, without requiring known environmental parameters.
AI.motivation: Purely data-driven models ignore wave physics, while physics-informed methods need environment-dependent parameters that are hard to obtain, leaving physically grounded reconstruction robust to uncertain environments underexplored.
AI.method: From the Helmholtz equation and normal-mode propagation the authors derive a spatial-angular S/c representation, which under low-rank specialization is a rank-(L,L,1) block-term tensor decomposition; TIDAL uses it for structured decoding aligned with sampling geometry.
AI.result: Across three structured sampling geometries TIDAL achieves the best reconstruction performance and the fastest inference among baselines, with benefits from the physics-derived representation under limited data and model capacity.
AI.conclusion: Learning components of a wave-physics representation from data offers a practical, physically motivated route to 3D acoustic field reconstruction without known model parameters.

title: Direct Covariance-to-Beamformer Mapping for Low-Latency Hybrid ISAC Beamforming with Subsequent DoA Estimation
summary: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) systems typically employ a two-stage beamforming pipeline, in which target directions are first estimated from the received covariance matrix and then used to compute the beamforming weights by solving non-convex optimization problems. Although effective, this approach introduces processing latency that can limit beam adaptation in dynamic environments. This letter proposes a beamforming deep neural network (BFDNN) for direct covariance-to-beamformer learning in ISAC systems. BFDNN is a compact regression network that maps covariance-matrix features directly to the hybrid beamforming weights produced by a hybrid ISAC beamformer, eliminating the direction-of-arrival (DoA) estimation stage during inference. Compared with MUSIC, classification-DNN, and regression-DNN based beamforming pipelines, BFDNN generates comparable beam patterns and higher effective spectral efficiencies while reducing the beamforming prediction latency by 25-30 times on the evaluated platform, demonstrating the potential of direct covariance-to-beamformer learning for low-latency ISAC beam updates. Moreover, the target directions can be inferred indirectly from the generated radiation pattern, yielding DoA accuracy competitive with that of dedicated learning-based methods in the evaluated scenario.

AI.tldr: BFDNN maps covariance-matrix features directly to hybrid ISAC beamforming weights, removing the DoA estimation stage and cutting beamforming prediction latency by 25 to 30 times on the evaluated platform.
AI.motivation: Two-stage ISAC beamforming estimates target directions from the covariance matrix and then solves non-convex optimization, which adds latency that limits beam adaptation in dynamic environments.
AI.method: BFDNN is a compact regression network that maps covariance-matrix features to the weights produced by a hybrid ISAC beamformer, with DoA recovered indirectly from the generated radiation pattern at inference.
AI.result: Compared with MUSIC, classification-DNN and regression-DNN pipelines it produces comparable beam patterns and higher effective spectral efficiency with 25 to 30 times lower prediction latency, and its DoA accuracy is competitive with dedicated learning-based methods in the evaluated scenario.
AI.conclusion: Direct covariance-to-beamformer learning shows potential for low-latency ISAC beam updates.

title: SparseLift: Automatically Optimizing Opaque Sparse Paths in Industrial-Scale Recommendation Model Training
summary: The sparse path, comprising sparse operations and collective communication, is a critical component of large-scale recommendation models. However, these operations are often represented as opaque nodes in the training computation graph, hindering whole-graph optimization. We present SparseLift, a low-overhead compiler for the sparse path of large-scale recommendation training. It exposes sparse computation and communication to whole-graph analysis to expand the optimization space and improve training efficiency. By analyzing model structure and runtime information, SparseLift reconstructs opaque nodes as analyzable subgraphs, recovering the resource semantics of sparse computation and communication within the graph. Building on the recovered semantics, we design incremental cost models and a constraint-aware planner to automatically select and organize subgraph optimizations into an execution plan that is reused during subsequent steady-state training. We evaluate SparseLift on an industrial video-platform recommendation task with 100B sparse parameters and the public DLRM benchmark. SparseLift improves steady-state throughput for ordinary industrial training steps by 16.5\% over the native baseline. On DLRM, it achieves $1.60\times$ and $1.26\times$ model-execution speedups over DLRM-Baseline and TorchRec, respectively.

AI.tldr: SparseLift is a compiler that reconstructs opaque sparse operations and communication in recommendation training graphs into analyzable subgraphs and plans their optimization, giving a 16.5% steady-state throughput gain on industrial training and 1.60x and 1.26x speedups on DLRM.
AI.motivation: Sparse operations and collective communication in large recommendation models appear as opaque graph nodes, which blocks whole-graph optimization.
AI.method: SparseLift recovers the resource semantics of sparse computation and communication from model structure and runtime information, uses incremental cost models and a constraint-aware planner to choose subgraph optimizations, and reuses the resulting plan during steady-state training.
AI.result: On an industrial video-platform recommendation task with 100B sparse parameters, steady-state throughput improves by 16.5% over the native baseline; on the public DLRM benchmark it achieves 1.60x and 1.26x model-execution speedups over DLRM-Baseline and TorchRec.
AI.conclusion: Exposing sparse paths to whole-graph analysis expands the optimization space and improves recommendation training efficiency.

title: MatMoE: Matryoshka Mixture-of-Experts with Dynamic Mixed-Precision Quantization for Efficient Inference
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture has been widely adopted in large language models (LLMs) since it reduces the computational cost through sparse expert activation. However, the massive parameter scale of MoE models hinders their deployment on resource-constrained edge devices. Although existing mixed-precision quantization reduces the model size, they are inherently static, fixing the bit-width of each expert across decoding steps. Such static schemes yield suboptimal performance as they overlook the dynamic variation in expert importance during decoding. Furthermore, they fail to adapt to the dynamic latency constraint driven by the fluctuating system utilization. To address these challenges, we propose MatMoE, a dynamic mixed-precision quantization framework for efficient MoE inference. MatMoE features: (1) a Matryoshka MoE PTQ algorithm that enables experts to operate flexibly at multiple precisions within a stringent memory budget; (2) a floor-and-compensation quantization method that eliminates redundant memory accesses in the Matryoshka representation; and (3) a dynamic bit-width allocation strategy that determines the precision for each expert based on their routing scores to satisfy the dynamic latency requirement. We implement our MatMoE system atop this http URL for both CPU and GPU platforms. Extensive evaluations across three modern MoE models and challenging benchmarks demonstrate that MatMoE achieves $4.0\% \sim 18.3\%$ higher accuracy than state-of-the-art static mixed-precision method. Compared to this http URL, MatMoE delivers $1.3\times \sim 3.7\times$ speedup on Raspberry Pi 5, and $1.2\times \sim 1.3\times$ speedup on NVIDIA RTX 4090 and Jetson AGX Orin.

AI.tldr: MatMoE is a dynamic mixed-precision quantization framework for MoE LLMs that uses Matryoshka-style multi-precision experts and per-token bit-width allocation, reporting 4.0% to 18.3% higher accuracy than static mixed-precision methods and 1.2x to 3.7x speedups on edge and GPU devices.
AI.motivation: Static mixed-precision schemes fix each expert's bit-width across decoding steps, overlooking changing expert importance and fluctuating latency constraints on resource-constrained edge devices.
AI.method: MatMoE uses a Matryoshka MoE PTQ algorithm allowing experts to run at several precisions within a memory budget, a floor-and-compensation quantization that avoids redundant memory accesses, and a dynamic bit-width allocation based on routing scores to meet latency requirements; it is implemented for CPU and GPU.
AI.result: Across three modern MoE models and challenging benchmarks it achieves 4.0% to 18.3% higher accuracy than the state-of-the-art static mixed-precision method, and 1.3x to 3.7x speedup on Raspberry Pi 5 and 1.2x to 1.3x on NVIDIA RTX 4090 and Jetson AGX Orin.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, routing-aware precision allocation improves both accuracy and speed of MoE inference under dynamic latency budgets.

title: Comparative Strategies for Handling Imbalanced QSAR Regression: A Case Study on hERG Activity Prediction
summary: Data imbalance frequently occurs in QSAR modeling, yet most studies focus on classification tasks, and few address regression tasks, as it is challenging to determine which regions of the data are sparse or dense. Data-level and algorithm-level imbalance-handling strategies can have different effects on model performance. In this study, we systematically compare various strategies across GCN and fingerprint-based machine learning models. To evaluate model performance more meaningfully, we partitioned the target region into several subregions based on both domain knowledge and data distribution. We focused on the region of greatest practical interest. Our results demonstrate that selecting models based on this interest-region metric leads to more reliable performance than using the total region metric. We also observed that different imbalance-handling strategies can have divergent effects depending on the model type. These findings highlight the importance of region-aware evaluation in regression QSAR modeling and provide practical guidance for selecting appropriate strategies for imbalanced datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper compares data-level and algorithm-level strategies for imbalanced QSAR regression on hERG activity and shows that region-aware metrics on the most practically relevant subregion select more reliable models.
AI.motivation: Imbalance handling is well studied for classification but rarely for regression QSAR, where sparse and dense regions are hard to identify, and total-region metrics can mislead model selection.
AI.method: Various imbalance-handling strategies are compared across GCN and fingerprint-based machine learning models, with the target range partitioned into subregions by domain knowledge and data distribution.
AI.result: Selecting models by the interest-region metric gives more reliable performance than by the total-region metric, and imbalance strategies have divergent effects depending on model type.
AI.conclusion: Region-aware evaluation is important in regression QSAR, and the findings give practical guidance for imbalanced datasets.

title: When Disagreement Labels Do Not Identify F1 Rankings
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Submitted to ESANN 2027, submission ES2027-34. Code and reproducibility artifact: this https URL
summary: Agreement labels cancel from an accuracy comparison but can change an F1 ranking. We specialize partial identification to an explicit audit after labeling disagreements: two agreement counts give exact bounds, certifying a ranking or a choice within a specified F1 tolerance under every completion. Across 3,200 frozen model pairs, shared completions tighten bounds and a 0.01 tolerance reduces labeling costs. A zero-loss (weak-winner) control attributes most savings to positive tolerance, not ties. Guarantees concern the evaluated batch, not future data.

AI.tldr: The paper gives exact partial-identification bounds for F1 rankings from two agreement counts after labeling disagreements, certifying rankings or F1-tolerance choices under every completion.
AI.motivation: Agreement labels cancel in accuracy comparisons but can change an F1 ranking, so an audit needs to certify rankings when some labels are unknown.
AI.method: After labeling disagreements, two agreement counts yield exact bounds on F1 across all completions; shared completions tighten bounds, and a positive F1 tolerance is used to reduce labeling cost, tested over 3,200 frozen model pairs with a zero-loss weak-winner control.
AI.result: Shared completions tighten the bounds and a 0.01 tolerance reduces labeling costs; most savings come from the positive tolerance rather than from ties, according to the zero-loss control.
AI.conclusion: The guarantees concern the evaluated batch only and do not extend to future data.

title: A sensor-driven physics-informed neural network for real-time occupant-centric space heating control
summary: Conventional space heating systems typically rely on single or sparse fixed-point temperature measurements, overlooking non-uniform indoor temperature distributions, transient thermal dynamics, and occupant-specific comfort requirements. This study explores an occupant-centric control strategy that aims to maintain the desired temperature around the occupant location. Spatially and temporally varying temperature fields, together with occupant mobility, make real-time local temperature estimation challenging. To address this challenge, we propose a control-oriented Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) model for indoor temperature-field prediction. Conventional PINNs rely on explicit time inputs and assume consistent temporal patterns across samples, which limits adaptability under variable initial conditions and heating sequences. The proposed model infers temporal dynamics implicitly from spatial coordinates and limited sensor measurements, improving robustness to changes in initial conditions and external disturbances. The method was validated across nine horizontal sensing planes in three controlled room-scale configurations. Against a validated COMSOL Multiphysics simulation, the PINN predicted the evaluated temperature fields with a maximum relative error below 1.85% across validation cases. These predictions supported an occupant-centric space heating control scheme. Compared with COMSOL-based offline control, the PINN-based system achieved an average prediction error of around 0.67%, and its rapid inference supports real-time occupant-centric control implementation. This work represents a move away from reliance on fixed-point temperature measurements in space heating control to an occupant-centric control strategy informed by real-time environmental feedback.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a physics-informed neural network that infers indoor temperature fields from spatial coordinates and sparse sensors, supporting occupant-centric space heating control with about 0.67% average error relative to COMSOL.
AI.motivation: Fixed-point temperature sensing overlooks non-uniform indoor temperature fields, transient dynamics and occupant mobility, and conventional PINNs need explicit time inputs that limit adaptability to varying initial conditions and heating sequences.
AI.method: A control-oriented PINN infers temporal dynamics implicitly from spatial coordinates and limited sensor measurements, validated on nine horizontal sensing planes in three room-scale configurations and used in an occupant-centric heating control scheme.
AI.result: Against a validated COMSOL simulation the PINN has a maximum relative error below 1.85% across validation cases, and the PINN-based system achieves an average prediction error of about 0.67% compared with COMSOL-based offline control, with rapid inference suitable for real-time control.
AI.conclusion: Moving from fixed-point measurements to occupant-centric control informed by real-time environmental feedback is shown to be feasible at room scale.

title: Robust EEG-based Emotion Recognition from Coarse Trial-level Labels under Intra-trial Affective Variability
summary: EEG-based emotion recognition has become an active research area in brain-computer interfaces. However, fine-grained affective annotation is costly, so most datasets provide only a global label for each long EEG trial. For practical emotion recognition, trials are commonly divided into short temporal windows, with the global label propagated to all windows for training. This practice treats trial-level emotion as temporally uniform, although affective responses may fluctuate within a trial. Consequently, windows that weakly reflect or deviate from the global emotional state may receive unreliable labels, posing a key challenge to robust EEG-based emotion recognition. To address this challenge, we propose VARY, a variability-aware robust learning framework for EEG-based emotion recognition from coarse trial-level labels. VARY incorporates a Two-stage Sample Selection (TSS) strategy to identify EEG windows with reliable emotional labels, and introduces MixAug, a data augmentation method tailored for EEG to improve model robustness under limited and unreliable supervision. We comprehensively evaluate VARY under the setting of label-noise learning on two public datasets, using three network architectures and multiple label-noise settings. Our method demonstrates superior performance, achieving a maximum accuracy gain of 11.54% on the DREAMER dataset and 5.39% on the SEED dataset compared with the best-performing baseline, highlighting the effectiveness of VARY in learning from unreliable trial-level labels under intra-trial affective variability.

AI.tldr: VARY is a variability-aware robust learning framework for EEG emotion recognition from coarse trial-level labels, using two-stage sample selection and EEG-specific MixAug augmentation, with gains up to 11.54% on DREAMER and 5.39% on SEED.
AI.motivation: Propagating a global trial label to all short windows assumes uniform emotion within a trial, so windows that deviate from the global state receive unreliable labels.
AI.method: Two-stage sample selection (TSS) identifies EEG windows with reliable emotional labels, and MixAug, a data augmentation tailored to EEG, improves robustness under limited and unreliable supervision; evaluation uses label-noise settings, three architectures and two public datasets.
AI.result: Compared with the best-performing baseline, the maximum accuracy gain is 11.54% on DREAMER and 5.39% on SEED.
AI.conclusion: Learning from unreliable trial-level labels under intra-trial affective variability is effective, as shown by the label-noise evaluation.

title: A Deep Reinforcement Learning Framework for Real-Time Electric Vehicle Charging Management in IoEV-Enabled Smart Cities
comment: 17 pages, 4 figures. Authors' accepted manuscript (paper ID 733916, AI2SD 2026 cycle), to appear in an indexed Springer Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems volume. Earlier preprint version deposited on Zenodo: this https URL
summary: The rapid growth of electric vehicles (EVs) in urban environments demands intelligent, decentralised charging management strategies that operate under strict real-time constraints. This paper proposes an Edge-Intelligent architecture in which each EV selects a charging station (CS) by querying a shared, centrally trained Deep Q-Network (DQN) policy over a lightweight MQTT publish-subscribe backbone; independent per-EV edge inference is the deployment target, not the configuration evaluated here. The reported simulation evaluates that shared DQN policy applied sequentially to each vehicle's observations within a single SUMO run, using MQTT for KPI telemetry while observations are obtained through TraCI. The system is evaluated on two real-world road networks from OpenStreetMap (Rabat Agdal-Hay Riad and Tangier, Morocco); the primary network carries four geolocated public charging stations with heterogeneous power levels (50 kW and 150 kW). Three traffic demand profiles (morning, midday, evening peak) are simulated, and four decision policies are compared: an Adaptive Heuristic, a Tabular Q-Learning agent, the proposed DQN agent, and a Double DQN variant. A multi-seed statistical protocol (7 seeds, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Cohen's d) evaluates the results. The DQN agent achieves a 6.8% relative improvement in charge rate and a 5.4% increase in delivered energy over the Adaptive Heuristic under Evening Peak demand ($p = 0.016$, Cohen's $d = 0.99$ and $1.51$), while showing no advantage in waiting time; on the second network the heuristic leads on waiting time, so the ranking is not stable across geographies. A scalability analysis shows linear state-space growth with station count and sub-millisecond inference; all runs include intermittent station outages under a Markov failure process.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an Edge-Intelligent EV charging architecture in which each EV picks a charging station using a shared DQN policy over MQTT, evaluated in SUMO on Moroccan road networks, where DQN beats an adaptive heuristic on charge rate and delivered energy under evening peak demand.
AI.motivation: Real-time EV charging management in smart cities needs decentralized, low-latency station selection, and the paper compares several decision policies across two OpenStreetMap networks.
AI.method: A shared, centrally trained DQN is applied sequentially to each vehicle's observations within a single SUMO run, with TraCI observations, MQTT for KPI telemetry, Markov station-outage failures, four policies (Adaptive Heuristic, tabular Q-learning, DQN and Double DQN) and a 7-seed protocol with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and Cohen's d.
AI.result: Under evening peak demand the DQN agent achieves 6.8% higher charge rate and 5.4% more delivered energy than the Adaptive Heuristic (p = 0.016; Cohen's d 0.99 and 1.51), with no waiting-time advantage; on the second network the heuristic leads on waiting time, and state-space growth is linear in station count with sub-millisecond inference.
AI.conclusion: The ranking of policies is not stable across geographies, so the DQN advantage is not general.

title: ReCoG: Relative Node Contexts for Multi-Domain Graph Pre-training
summary: The success of foundation models in language and vision has motivated Graph Foundation Models (GFMs), which learn transferable knowledge through multi-domain graph pre-training. Existing methods advance GFMs through feature unification and structural learning, and in doing so they rely on the raw graph structure to organize node contexts. However, we observe that removing a large proportion of edges from source graphs during pre-training improves cross-domain transfer accuracy across four representative methods. Our theoretical analysis identifies the raw graph structure as a source of conflict in cross-graph model sharing. We therefore advocate defining node contexts using criteria consistent across graphs. Achieving this requires (1) constructing node contexts consistently across graphs without a shared positional structure, such as the token order of text or the pixel grid of images, and (2) retaining the structural and neighborhood information of the original graphs. To this end, we introduce Relative Contexts for Graphs (ReCoG) for multi-domain graph pre-training. Specifically, we first construct attribute contexts to provide a comparison rule independent of the raw graph structure. Furthermore, we construct structural contexts based on common neighbors and semantic contexts based on neighborhood attribute summaries to retain the topological and neighborhood information of the original graphs. Since all graphs share these construction rules, we pre-train a single graph encoder by reconstructing node attributes over these contexts, without domain-specific modules. We conduct extensive experiments on 18 target datasets, which demonstrate the effectiveness of ReCoG. In particular, ReCoG exceeds the strongest baseline by 7.61 percentage points in mean 1-shot cross-domain node classification accuracy and by 4.47 points in cross-type transfer to heterophilous graphs.

AI.tldr: ReCoG builds node contexts from attribute, structural and semantic relations that do not depend on raw graph structure, enabling one encoder to pre-train across graph domains and improving 1-shot cross-domain node classification by 7.61 points over the strongest baseline.
AI.motivation: Graph foundation models rely on raw graph structure to form node contexts, which conflicts across graphs; removing many source edges was found to improve transfer for four representative methods.
AI.method: Attribute contexts give a comparison rule independent of raw structure, structural contexts use common neighbors and semantic contexts use neighborhood attribute summaries, and a single graph encoder is pre-trained by reconstructing node attributes over these contexts without domain-specific modules.
AI.result: Across 18 target datasets ReCoG exceeds the strongest baseline by 7.61 percentage points in mean 1-shot cross-domain node classification accuracy and by 4.47 points in cross-type transfer to heterophilous graphs.
AI.conclusion: Consistent, graph-independent node-context construction is an effective basis for multi-domain graph pre-training.

title: Silent Reward and Environment Defects in EV Charging Simulation Benchmarks: A Diagnostic Checklist
comment: 14 pages, 2 figures. Accepted for publication in Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics (BEEI), ISSN 2089-3191, e-ISSN 2302-9285 (accepted 8 September 2026; in press)
summary: Reinforcement-learning (RL) benchmarks built on microscopic traffic simulators such as SUMO are increasingly used to compare agent architectures for electric vehicle (EV) charging assignment. Unlike crashes, defects in the reward function, the environment's stochastic model, or the state encoding often fail silently: the simulation completes, produces plausible numbers, and the comparison is biased. We report five such defects, found by auditing a five-agent benchmark on OpenStreetMap road networks, stated generically: a shared random generator that desynchronises seed-paired comparisons, an ablation-specific reward clip applied unconditionally, a normalisation mismatch that zeroes a reward term, a per-timestep penalty that should fire once per event, and a state dimensionality documented but never wired into the network. We quantify three: a rejection counter inflated up to 125x across agents/cities, a reward term bounded at about $10^{-4}$ of its intended scale, and a 16.6%/16.3% greedy-action divergence from a state-encoding mismatch. Re-analysing a historical ablation, no A1-A2 effect survives family-wise correction; a 56-run campaign confirms the RNG defect's mechanism directly while showing its correction does not change that conclusion. We provide an eight-item checklist as a low-cost first-pass audit; in a later regeneration, three checks caught two new defects while three further process/artefact defects fell outside its boundary.

AI.tldr: The paper reports five silent defects found in an audit of a SUMO-based EV charging RL benchmark and offers an eight-item diagnostic checklist as a low-cost first-pass audit.
AI.motivation: RL benchmarks on microscopic traffic simulators can be biased by defects in reward, stochastic model or state encoding that fail silently, because the simulation completes and yields plausible numbers.
AI.method: The authors audit a five-agent benchmark on OpenStreetMap road networks, identify five defects (a shared random generator, an unconditional ablation-specific reward clip, a normalization mismatch, a per-timestep penalty that should fire once per event, and an undeployed state dimension) and quantify three of them.
AI.result: A rejection counter is inflated up to 125 times across agents and cities, a reward term is bounded at about 10^-4 of its intended scale, and a 16.6%/16.3% greedy-action divergence arises from a state-encoding mismatch; no A1-A2 effect survives family-wise correction in a historical ablation.
AI.conclusion: The eight-item checklist is a useful low-cost first pass, though in a later regeneration it caught two new defects while three process or artefact defects fell outside its scope.

title: Spectral Signatures of Memorization Basins in Diffusion Trajectories
summary: Diffusion models are known to reproduce individual examples from their training data as a form of memorization with implications for generalization, privacy, and downstream use. Recent work demonstrated that memorized training samples reside inside contiguous regions of the data/latent space known as basins of memorization -- once a denoising trajectory enters a basin, under finite perturbations it irreversibly reproduces a memorized example. Prior empirical work on such basins in trained models has primarily focused on classifier-free guidance based detection and mitigation strategies in text-to-image models, leaving basin entry and their formation largely uncharacterized. In this paper, we present a geometric characterization of memorization basins for conditional, unconditional, and rectified-flow-based diffusion models. We observe a characteristic signature in the local spectrum of the function geometry that distinguishes basin entry: the emergence of a dominant singular mode followed by a sharp spectral recovery. This signature appears at two timescales: along denoising trajectories during inference and over the course of training. We further investigate whether these geometric signatures can be used to intervene on memorization. During training, we suppress memorization by acting on the dominant mode. At inference, we develop methods to identify trajectories entering memorization basins and steer them away. We find that these interventions remain effective even with low-dimensional approximations of the underlying geometry, and demonstrate that geometry-informed steering extends to large-scale text-to-image diffusion models. Together, our results corroborate that local spectral geometry provides a common basis for characterizing memorization and for suppressing, detecting, and steering away from it across training and generation.

AI.tldr: The paper gives a geometric characterization of memorization basins in diffusion models, showing that entry into a basin leaves a spectral signature (a dominant singular mode followed by a sharp spectral recovery) that can be used to suppress, detect and steer away from memorization.
AI.motivation: Prior work on memorization basins focused on classifier-free guidance based detection and mitigation in text-to-image models and left basin entry and its formation largely uncharacterized.
AI.method: The authors analyze the local spectrum of the function geometry for conditional, unconditional and rectified-flow diffusion models, track the signature along denoising trajectories at inference and over training, suppress memorization during training by acting on the dominant mode, and steer trajectories that enter basins at inference, including with low-dimensional approximations of the geometry.
AI.result: The spectral signature appears at both timescales, interventions remain effective with low-dimensional approximations of the geometry, and the geometry-informed steering extends to large-scale text-to-image diffusion models.
AI.conclusion: Local spectral geometry provides a common basis for characterizing memorization and for suppressing, detecting and steering away from it across training and generation.

title: ReFrame: Silence-Aware Compute Reclamation for Full-Duplex Speech Models
summary: Full-duplex speech models execute dense model inference for every audio frame throughout a live interaction. This uniform framewise schedule creates sustained GPU load across dialogue states whose computation has strong, reusable temporal structure. ReFrame formulates full-duplex inference as a silence-aware computation problem. Mutual Silence Speculation (MSS) operates when both participants are silent: it evaluates multi-frame Temporal continuations, verifies text and hidden-state stability, and applies batched Mimi audio-token correction. Listening Frame Folding (LFF) operates while the user speaks and the agent listens: it processes already-arrived user frames through parallel Temporal execution and frame-batched audio-token generation while accepting only the verified prefix. Frame-Budget Reinvestment (FBR) assigns the released frame intervals to resumable external retrieval and language-model workers, then injects timely references through Moshi's conditioning interface. We instantiate ReFrame on five full-duplex models spanning Moshi-family, phase-structured, and flattened autoregressive generation. Across the complete 1,225-conversation FDBench, ReFrame reduces measured GPU execution time by 18.80-31.01% and retains 96.92-100% non-PAD text agreement on five different models. On HaluEval tests, FBR increases the number of correct generated spoken answers from 86 to 205 under the same auxiliary-service budget. ReFrame turns recurring dialogue structure into lower inference cost and higher end-to-end service capability.

AI.tldr: ReFrame is a silence-aware scheme for full-duplex speech models that reuses computation during mutual silence and listening periods, reducing measured GPU execution time while keeping text output largely unchanged and improving spoken answer quality through retrieval workers.
AI.motivation: Full-duplex speech models run dense inference on every audio frame, creating sustained GPU load even in dialogue states whose computation has strong, reusable temporal structure.
AI.method: Mutual Silence Speculation evaluates multi-frame continuations during joint silence with verification and batched Mimi audio-token correction; Listening Frame Folding processes already-arrived user frames in parallel while the agent listens and accepts only the verified prefix; Frame-Budget Reinvestment assigns the released frame intervals to resumable retrieval and language-model workers and injects their references through Moshi's conditioning interface. It is instantiated on five full-duplex models.
AI.result: On the 1,225-conversation FDBench, ReFrame reduces measured GPU execution time by 18.80 to 31.01 percent and retains 96.92 to 100 percent non-PAD text agreement across five models; on HaluEval tests, FBR raises correct generated spoken answers from 86 to 205 under the same auxiliary-service budget.
AI.conclusion: Recurring dialogue structure can be turned into lower inference cost and higher end-to-end service capability for full-duplex speech systems.

title: Missingness-Aware Prior-Data Fitted Network for Irregular Clinical Time-Series
summary: Clinical time series are irregularly observed with laboratory measurements recorded at uneven intervals and observation patterns often reflecting patient state, clinical concern, and site-specific practice. Consequently, missingness is not merely a nuisance factor but an informative signal for prediction. We propose a Missingness-Aware Prior-Data Fitted Network (MA-PFN) for irregular clinical time-series prediction. MA-PFN first learns a diffusion-based prior over joint laboratory value and observation-mask trajectories from source-domain electronic health records, capturing both physiological dynamics and measurement processes. Synthetic trajectories sampled from this prior are then transformed into context-query tasks to train a PFN-style conditional predictor. Once trained, the model performs prediction for new admissions in a single forward pass, requiring neither retraining nor parameter adaptation on target datasets. The framework naturally supports both imputation and forecasting through different context-query constructions. We conduct internal validation on a held-out MIMIC-III test set and external validation on eICU, evaluating both imputation and forecasting and assessing cross-domain generalization under shifts in patient populations, clinical practices, and observation mechanisms. MA-PFN achieves the best performance across all evaluated settings, with Overall/Macro nRMSD ranging from (0.193/0.186) for internal imputation to (0.297/0.297) for external forecasting, without target-domain adaptation. These results demonstrate that learning missingness-aware task priors enables accurate and transferable clinical time-series prediction under informative missingness.

AI.tldr: MA-PFN is a Prior-Data Fitted Network for irregular clinical time series that learns a diffusion prior over lab values and observation masks, so that missingness is modeled as informative and predictions for new admissions need only a single forward pass.
AI.motivation: Clinical time series are irregularly observed, and missingness reflects patient state and clinical practice, so treating it as a nuisance loses information; existing prediction needs retraining or adaptation on each target dataset to handle shifts.
AI.method: A diffusion-based prior is learned over joint laboratory value and observation-mask trajectories from source-domain EHR data; synthetic trajectories from this prior are converted into context-query tasks to train a PFN-style conditional predictor that supports imputation and forecasting through different context-query constructions.
AI.result: The model is validated internally on a held-out MIMIC-III test set and externally on eICU, achieving the best performance in all evaluated settings, with Overall/Macro nRMSD from (0.193/0.186) for internal imputation to (0.297/0.297) for external forecasting, without target-domain adaptation.
AI.conclusion: Learning missingness-aware task priors enables accurate and transferable clinical time-series prediction under informative missingness.

title: Privacy-Preserving ECG-HRV Emotion Classification for Mood Swing Detection using Federated Learning on Constrained Edge Devices
summary: This paper presents a privacy-preserving mood monitoring framework that classifies emotional states from ECG-derived heart rate variability (HRV) features. The framework is evaluated on three public datasets comprising 74 participants and further validated using a wearable device in a pilot study. Leave-One-Participant-Out cross-validation (LOPO-CV) is used to assess generalization to unseen individuals. A series of experiments investigates the impact of temporal windowing, HRV feature selection, and class balancing on both four-class valence-arousal and binary valence classification. Results show that class balancing substantially improves minority-class recall, while Logistic Regression consistently outperforms five alternative classifiers and achieves competitive performance against HRV-based baselines. Pilot validation using a Polar H10 wearable achieves 75% binary valence accuracy on an unseen individual without calibration, demonstrating the feasibility of real-world deployment. To preserve privacy, the framework is also implemented using federated learning on a six-node Raspberry Pi cluster. Federated Logistic Regression achieves performance comparable to centralized training without sharing raw physiological data. These results demonstrate the potential of interpretable and privacy-preserving mood monitoring for continuous mental health assessment in clinical and community settings.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a privacy-preserving mood monitoring framework that classifies emotional states from ECG-derived heart rate variability features, with logistic regression as the main classifier and federated learning used to keep raw physiological data local.
AI.motivation: Mood monitoring from physiological signals raises privacy concerns, and it is unclear how well HRV-based classifiers generalize to unseen individuals and to wearable deployment.
AI.method: The framework is evaluated on three public datasets with 74 participants using leave-one-participant-out cross-validation, studying temporal windowing, HRV feature selection and class balancing for four-class valence-arousal and binary valence classification; a wearable pilot uses a Polar H10, and federated logistic regression runs on a six-node Raspberry Pi cluster.
AI.result: Class balancing substantially improves minority-class recall and logistic regression outperforms five alternative classifiers; the Polar H10 pilot reaches 75 percent binary valence accuracy on an unseen individual without calibration, and federated logistic regression performs comparably to centralized training.
AI.conclusion: Interpretable and privacy-preserving mood monitoring is feasible for continuous mental health assessment in clinical and community settings.

title: The (Butter)fly Dream: Linear Separability of World-Model Rollouts in a Connectome-Constrained Visual Model
summary: Zhuangzi dreamt he was a butterfly and, on waking, could not tell which was the dream. We ask a version of his question of a model of the fly brain: placed inside a world generated by a world model, can a fixed brain tell that the world is a dream? We treat it as a question about what a connectome-constrained model trained on one task makes available beyond that task: do its responses make the defects of a dream linearly decodable? The observer is a published model of the fly visual system trained only for optic-flow estimation; reality is the MPI-Sintel movie on the model's 721-column retina; dreams are continuations of five real frames by three small world models (a persistence random walk, an MDN-RNN and an RSSM) at three temperatures. The judge is a classifier two-sample test on temporal statistics of cell-type responses, with sequence-level cross-validation. In the trained observer's responses all nine dreams are separable from reality (AUC 0.85-0.99, mean over 50 trained models), in those of the same network before training much less so (0.58-0.75 for the learned world models; paired difference 0.20-0.37), equally on sequences the observer never saw, and in an order unrelated to pixel error.
