Because these AUCs are near ceiling, we add graded probes made of each window's own real frames with only their order broken. Swapping one adjacent pair of the 14 generated frames gives 0.73 on the trained responses against 0.54 before training and 0.56 for pixel statistics; the trained curve reaches 0.75 at 1.1 swapped pairs of seven, the pixel statistics at 4.7, and the untrained network not at all. A detection horizon, the test on the first k generated frames, orders the world models where the full-length AUC saturates.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether a connectome-constrained fly visual model trained for optic-flow estimation can linearly separate real video from world-model rollouts, finding that its trained responses make dream artifacts decodable far better than an untrained network or pixel statistics.
AI.motivation: The question is whether a fixed brain model trained on one task makes information about the world's realism available beyond that task, and whether world-model dreams carry defects that a biological-style observer can detect.
AI.method: The observer is a published fly visual system model trained for optic-flow estimation on the MPI-Sintel movie with a 721-column retina; dreams continue five real frames using three world models (a persistence random walk, an MDN-RNN and an RSSM) at three temperatures; a classifier two-sample test on temporal statistics of cell-type responses with sequence-level cross-validation is used, plus graded probes that break the order of real frames and a detection horizon over the first k generated frames.
AI.result: With trained responses all nine dreams are separable from reality (AUC 0.85 to 0.99, mean over 50 trained models), versus 0.58 to 0.75 before training for the learned world models; swapping one adjacent pair of 14 generated frames gives AUC 0.73 on trained responses against 0.54 untrained and 0.56 for pixel statistics.
AI.conclusion: The trained connectome-constrained observer makes dream defects linearly decodable, and the detection horizon separates world models where the full-length AUC saturates.

title: A Self-Generated Floor on Adam's $\varepsilon$: Evidence from Power-Law Matrix Sensing
summary: In nonconvex Burer--Monteiro low-rank matrix sensing of $U^\ast \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times D}$ under power-law covariance $\Sigma = \mathrm{diag}(j^{-s})_{j=1}^V$, the precision-wall approximation predicts that Adam stalls when the smallest non-gauge Hessian eigenvalue drops below its denominator floor, giving $s^\ast(V,D) = [\log(1/\varepsilon_{\mathrm{eff}}) - \log V]/\log(VD) + \delta_{\mathrm{Adam}}$. If $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{eff}}$ were set by $\varepsilon_0$, lowering $\varepsilon_0$ from $10^{-10}$ to $10^{-12}$ would raise $s^\ast$ by $0.95\text{--}1.33$. Instead, across six values of $\varepsilon_0$ two decades apart, $10^{-2}$ to $10^{-12}$, the boundary follows the $\varepsilon_0$ slope down to $10^{-6}$, bends near $10^{-8}$, and is flat below $10^{-8}$, while warm-started L-BFGS and Gauss--Newton reach machine precision on stalled instances. We trace this saturation to a self-generated dynamical floor $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{dyn}} \propto \alpha$: high-curvature modes oscillate persistently near the adaptive edge of stability with amplitude $\propto \alpha(1-\beta_1)/(1+\beta_1)$ and leak gradient fluctuations of scale $\kappa\alpha$ into rare modes via measurement coupling, pinning $\sqrt{\hat{v}_V} \approx \kappa\alpha \gg \varepsilon_0$. Fitting a single threshold-crossing wall parameter $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{dyn}} = 4.76\times 10^{-9}$ (with the detection lag frozen at its companion calibration) predicts the saturated failure boundary for $D \ge 4$ across five $(V,D)$ scales to RMS $0.098$ (breaking down at $D = 2$), while shrinking $\varepsilon_0$ below $10^{-8}$ is ineffective and lowering the step size $\alpha$ reduces the floor directly.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that in Adam-based low-rank matrix sensing the stall boundary is set by a self-generated dynamical floor proportional to the step size, not by the nominal epsilon, so decreasing epsilon below about 1e-8 has no effect.
AI.motivation: A precision-wall approximation predicts Adam stalls when the smallest non-gauge Hessian eigenvalue falls below the denominator floor set by epsilon, but observed boundaries do not follow that prediction.
AI.method: The authors study nonconvex Burer-Monteiro matrix sensing with power-law covariance across six values of epsilon from 1e-2 to 1e-12, compare with warm-started L-BFGS and Gauss-Newton, analyze persistent oscillations near the edge of stability, and fit a single threshold-crossing wall parameter to the saturated failure boundary.
AI.result: The boundary follows the epsilon slope down to 1e-6, bends near 1e-8 and is flat below it, while warm-started L-BFGS and Gauss-Newton reach machine precision on stalled instances; the fitted floor of 4.76e-9 predicts the saturated boundary for D of at least 4 across five (V,D) scales with RMS 0.098, breaking down at D equal to 2.
AI.conclusion: Adam's effective epsilon floor is generated by the dynamics and scales with the step size, so reducing the step size is effective while reducing epsilon below 1e-8 is not.

title: Robust Remote ECG Monitoring under Energy Constraints: Anomaly Filtering versus Predictive Uncertainty
summary: Machine learning for remote electrocardiogram monitoring must handle noise and diseases absent from training under tight resource constraints. We investigate whether upstream unsupervised anomaly detection can improve monitoring decisions more efficiently than classifier-derived uncertainty. We evaluate five detectors on PTB-XL and BUT QDB and compare a two-stage filter-classifier system with Monte Carlo Dropout and deep ensembles under unseen-disease and noise conditions. Performance is averaged over five training seeds. We measure single-pass energy, latency, and graph memory on a microcontroller's central processing unit (CPU) and neural processing unit (NPU). Per-score neural network costs account for repeated evaluations but exclude scoring outside deployed graphs. Energy equations relate filtering and rejection to avoided classifier execution. Across four disease scenarios, Deep Support Vector Data Description (Deep SVDD) achieves the highest mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve within all tested finite CPU energy budgets. On the NPU, it leads at 1 mJ, while Monte Carlo Dropout has slightly higher means at 10 and 100 mJ. With a narrow CPU classifier, the Deep SVDD two-stage system increases the fraction of correctly classified or correctly rejected inputs by 15.0-19.4 percentage points over classification without rejection. Estimated energy per input is 1.93-6.99 mJ, compared with 52.53 mJ for Monte Carlo Dropout and 8.76-17.51 mJ for deep ensembles, at each method's retrospectively selected test accuracy peak. These results support upstream filtering for efficient remote monitoring, while independent validation and complete-system measurements remain necessary.

AI.tldr: The paper compares upstream unsupervised anomaly filtering with classifier-derived uncertainty for remote ECG monitoring on microcontrollers and finds that a Deep SVDD two-stage filter-classifier system gives the best accuracy within tight energy budgets.
AI.motivation: Remote ECG monitoring must handle noise and unseen diseases under tight energy and compute limits, and it is unclear whether anomaly detection can improve decisions more efficiently than uncertainty from MC Dropout or deep ensembles.
AI.method: Five anomaly detectors are evaluated on PTB-XL and BUT QDB and compared with a two-stage filter-classifier system, MC Dropout and deep ensembles under unseen-disease and noise conditions over five seeds; energy, latency and graph memory are measured on a microcontroller CPU and NPU.
AI.result: Deep SVDD has the highest mean AUROC within all tested finite CPU energy budgets and leads on the NPU at 1 mJ, while MC Dropout is slightly higher at 10 and 100 mJ; the Deep SVDD system raises the fraction of correct classifications or rejections by 15.0 to 19.4 percentage points, with 1.93 to 6.99 mJ per input against 52.53 mJ for MC Dropout.
AI.conclusion: Upstream filtering supports efficient remote monitoring, although independent validation and complete-system measurements are still needed.

title: Machine Learning Beyond Statistical Consistency for Hybrid AI
summary: We propose a new definition of machine learning, according to which a machine learns a function when it computes the function successfully, that is, when the value it returns for each input has a proper derivation in a formal system. We extend Gödel's Representability Theorem, which equates computation with derivation, to empirical targets in two ways: the theorem is extended to the computable reals, and the data are admitted into the system as empirical definitions that record what has been observed. We prove that a machine learns a true probability if and only if two conditions are met. The Truth Condition is that its estimate converges to the true probability, which is statistical consistency. The Assurance Condition is that the machine properly derives its own convergence inside the system. Learning thus lies beyond statistical consistency, for it requires a derivation of the convergence from the record. A global assumption about the data, such as the i.i.d. assumption, does not supply such a derivation, because it leads only to a circular one, as we show for PAC learning. On the other hand, the two conditions are met for the probability of a sentence over a finite ideal corpus. A real machine can approximate a true probability only if an ideal machine can learn it precisely, that is, only in a domain that meets the two conditions. Modern AI works in such a domain, and we offer this as a clue to its success. Modern AI is hybrid as well, in two senses: First, it performs two kinds of tasks, namely probabilistic ones such as predicting the next word and deductive ones such as proving and coding. Second, it combines two parts of different kinds, a statistical proposer and a deductive verifier, for proving and coding. Our framework explains both senses of hybridity in one formal system.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that a machine learns a function when it computes it with a formal derivation, and shows that learning a true probability requires both statistical consistency and an internal derivation of that consistency, which explains the hybrid statistical-plus-deductive structure of modern AI.
AI.motivation: Statistical consistency alone is taken as the criterion for learning, and the i.i.d. assumption is often used to justify convergence, yet the paper argues that such global assumptions do not supply a non-circular derivation of convergence.
AI.method: The authors extend Godel's Representability Theorem to computable reals and admit data as empirical definitions recording observations in a formal system, then prove a Truth Condition (convergence to the true probability) and an Assurance Condition (the machine derives its own convergence), and show the i.i.d. route is circular for PAC learning.
AI.result: The two conditions hold for the probability of a sentence over a finite ideal corpus, and a real machine can approximate a true probability only where an ideal machine can learn it precisely.
AI.conclusion: The framework explains both senses of hybridity in modern AI, namely probabilistic and deductive tasks and a statistical proposer paired with a deductive verifier, within one formal system.

title: ReWY: Faster Gradient Computation for Delta-Rule Attention Family
summary: Delta-rule linear attention underlies language models such as Kimi Linear and Qwen3-Next. Chunkwise implementations expose matrix parallelism, but their backward passes compute unnecessary auxiliary adjoints. We present ReWY, an algebraic reformulation that reduces this work before optimizing accelerator execution. Differentiating the chunk correction as one triangular residual system eliminates the inverse adjoint and reduces seven local WY matrix products to three. Two complementary transformations expose further reuse: centered matrix contractions replace pairwise vector-gate processing, and scalar-gate reductions reuse key-gradient products instead of forming a key Gram matrix. These identities simplify backward computation for DeltaNet, GDN, KDA, and GDN2 while preserving the recurrence and gradients in exact arithmetic, without changing the architecture or training objective. We implement the reduced graph on GPUs and Ascend NPUs. Under matched recomputation and full-saving policies, precision-qualified six-shape comparisons with frozen FLA references yield 1.15-1.81$\times$ geometric-mean complete low-level backward speedups on NVIDIA GPUs. All four operators achieve 1.18-1.70$\times$ on H100 and H200 while retaining original FP32 working matrices. A separate public-autograd evaluation on Ascend 950DT, including gradient conversions, yields 1.09-2.89$\times$ under available matched policies. Paired ablations establish further ReWY gains after optimizing the complementary contractions. Complete-gradient checks validate the recorded operator cases; supplementary full-model backward measurements assess integration into community FLA models and a GDN2 layer port. Code and reproduction materials: this https URL.

AI.tldr: ReWY is an algebraic reformulation of the backward pass for delta-rule linear attention that reduces seven local WY matrix products to three, giving 1.15 to 1.81 times geometric-mean backward speedups on NVIDIA GPUs without changing the model or the gradients in exact arithmetic.
AI.motivation: Chunkwise implementations of delta-rule linear attention, used in models such as Kimi Linear and Qwen3-Next, compute unnecessary auxiliary adjoints in the backward pass.
AI.method: The chunk correction is differentiated as one triangular residual system, which eliminates the inverse adjoint; centered matrix contractions replace pairwise vector-gate processing, and scalar-gate reductions reuse key-gradient products instead of forming a key Gram matrix; the reduced graph is implemented on GPUs and Ascend NPUs and applied to DeltaNet, GDN, KDA and GDN2.
AI.result: Under matched recomputation and full-saving policies, six-shape comparisons with frozen FLA references give 1.15 to 1.81 times geometric-mean complete low-level backward speedups on NVIDIA GPUs, with 1.18 to 1.70 times on H100 and H200 for all four operators; on Ascend 950DT the public-autograd evaluation gives 1.09 to 2.89 times.
AI.conclusion: Algebraic simplification of the backward graph yields practical speedups for delta-rule attention across GPU and NPU hardware while preserving the recurrence and gradients.

title: OC-OPD: Observation-coordinated Supervision for On-Policy Distillation
summary: Reverse and forward Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergences provide complementary supervision in on-policy distillation: reverse KL refines the student's active token rankings, and forward KL allocates mass to teacher-supported candidates. At student-generated prefixes, we form a four-observation matrix by treating the student and teacher as both candidate sources and evaluators. The diagonal self-observations measure uncertainty, while source-centered cross-observations recover the two KL objectives. We establish an exact identity equating the Fisher inverse-metric coupling of their logit gradients with the sum of these contrasts, yielding a common local descent direction for distinct positive distributions. Observation-coordinated on-policy distillation (OC-OPD) uses observations to set preferences, closed-form bargaining to coordinate gradients, and distributional discrepancy to scale the update. Across three heterogeneous student settings (non-thinking generation, thinking generation, and base-model initialization), OC-OPD achieves strong gains in mathematical reasoning and transfers effectively to out-of-distribution scientific question answering and code generation. Our code is publicly available at: this https URL.

AI.tldr: OC-OPD combines reverse and forward KL supervision in on-policy distillation through a four-observation matrix, yielding a common descent direction, and improves mathematical reasoning with transfer to scientific QA and code generation.
AI.motivation: Reverse KL refines the student's token rankings while forward KL allocates mass to teacher-supported candidates, but the two objectives can conflict when used together in on-policy distillation.
AI.method: At student-generated prefixes, student and teacher are treated as both candidate sources and evaluators to form a four-observation matrix; diagonal self-observations measure uncertainty and source-centered cross-observations recover the two KL objectives, with an exact identity linking their Fisher-coupled gradients, closed-form bargaining to coordinate gradients, and distributional discrepancy to scale the update.
AI.result: OC-OPD achieves strong gains in mathematical reasoning across three heterogeneous student settings (non-thinking generation, thinking generation and base-model initialization) and transfers to out-of-distribution scientific question answering and code generation.
AI.conclusion: Coordinating the forward and reverse KL objectives through observation-based preferences and a shared descent direction improves on-policy distillation.

title: Large-Scale Bayesian Optimisation Using Uncertainty-Calibrated Product-of-Experts Gaussian Process Models with Trust Regions
summary: The use of collections of independent local Gaussian processes (GP-ind) combined with trust regions is a widely adopted approach for large-scale and high-dimensional Bayesian optimisation (BO). However, this approach suffers from several limitations, including discontinuities at the boundaries of disjoint regions, an inability to capture long-range spatial correlations, potential information loss, and abrupt increases in computational overhead. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a novel BO algorithm, termed BO-pro-c-tr. The proposed method employs a product-of-experts Gaussian process model with uncertainty calibration (GP-pro-c) as its surrogate model and incorporates a one-to-many association strategy for integrating GP-pro-c with trust regions. Empirical results suggest that, when combined with the GP-LCB acquisition function, BO-pro-c-tr achieves an average reduction of 2.6% in simple regret and 34.9% in computational overhead relative to BO algorithms based on independent local GP models coupled with trust regions.

AI.tldr: BO-pro-c-tr is a large-scale Bayesian optimisation method that replaces independent local Gaussian processes with an uncertainty-calibrated product-of-experts GP inside trust regions, reducing simple regret and computational overhead relative to the independent-GP baseline.
AI.motivation: Collections of independent local GPs with trust regions suffer from discontinuities at region boundaries, an inability to capture long-range correlations, information loss and abrupt rises in computational overhead.
AI.method: The surrogate is a product-of-experts GP with uncertainty calibration (GP-pro-c), integrated with trust regions through a one-to-many association strategy, and paired with the GP-LCB acquisition function.
AI.result: Relative to BO algorithms built on independent local GPs with trust regions, BO-pro-c-tr reduces simple regret by an average of 2.6 percent and computational overhead by 34.9 percent.
AI.conclusion: Product-of-experts surrogates with uncertainty calibration are a practical improvement over independent local GPs for trust-region Bayesian optimisation at scale.

title: MIRA: Mutual Information guided calibration for Reliable Test-Time Adaptation
summary: Test-time adaptation (TTA) updates a deployed model using only unlabeled target data, but standard entropy-based methods often rely on deterministic confidence and can reinforce overconfident errors under distribution shift. We propose MIRA, Mutual Information guided calibration for Reliable Test-Time Adaptation, a source-free online adaptation method that uses lightweight last-layer Gaussian perturbations to probe prediction reliability. For each target batch, MIRA reuses a single feature extraction pass and samples perturbed classifiers around the source classifier, forming an efficient local predictive distribution. Rather than fitting a Bayesian posterior, MIRA treats the perturbation scale as a local probing radius and selects a batch-specific scale using mutual information (MI) and prediction agreement. The resulting perturbation-sensitivity signal identifies predictions that are confident and locally stable under classifier perturbations, while suppressing brittle predictions with high stochastic disagreement. MIRA then performs adaptation with an MI-confidence weighted entropy loss, which down-weights perturbation-sensitive or low-confidence samples before they drive entropy minimization. This weighted loss reduces the influence of brittle predictions that can otherwise cause harmful adaptation under distribution shift. The method requires no source data, retraining, model ensembles, or offline posterior fitting, and can be applied as a plug-and-play modification to entropy-minimization TTA. Experiments on distribution-shift benchmarks show improvements in accuracy, calibration, and negative log-likelihood, suggesting that mutual-information-guided perturbation probing and weighted adaptation yield more robust online TTA than deterministic confidence.

AI.tldr: MIRA is a source-free online test-time adaptation method that uses last-layer Gaussian perturbations and mutual information to down-weight brittle predictions in the entropy loss, improving accuracy, calibration and negative log-likelihood under distribution shift.
AI.motivation: Standard entropy-based test-time adaptation relies on deterministic confidence and can reinforce overconfident errors under distribution shift.
AI.method: For each target batch MIRA reuses one feature extraction pass, samples perturbed classifiers around the source classifier, selects a batch-specific perturbation scale using mutual information and prediction agreement, and performs entropy minimization with an MI-confidence weighted loss; it is applied as a plug-and-play modification to entropy-minimization TTA and needs no source data, retraining or ensembles.
AI.result: Experiments on distribution-shift benchmarks show improvements in accuracy, calibration and negative log-likelihood over deterministic-confidence entropy-based adaptation.
AI.conclusion: Mutual-information-guided perturbation probing and weighted adaptation give more robust online test-time adaptation than deterministic confidence.

title: Uncertainty-Aware 3D Position Reconstruction in CZT Drift-Strip Detectors
summary: Accurate three-dimensional interaction-position reconstruction is important for CZT drift-strip detectors, but conventional methods can suffer from degraded performance in challenging detector regions, while learned models provide limited information about prediction reliability. We investigate two uncertainty-aware approaches: deep ensembles of point-estimation networks and simulation-based inference (SBI), which estimates a posterior distribution over interaction position. Both approaches are trained on physics-based simulations and evaluated on both synthetic and experimental data. On synthetic data, uncertainty from both methods correlates with positioning error, with SBI showing a substantially stronger relationship. On experimental measurements, the deep ensemble achieves improved $z$-position resolution, while SBI provides more informative uncertainty estimates that highlight regions of reduced positional information and discrepancies between simulation and the physical detector. These results demonstrate the complementary strengths of ensemble-based reconstruction and posterior inference for uncertainty-aware detector position reconstruction.

AI.tldr: The paper compares deep ensembles of point-estimation networks with simulation-based inference for 3D interaction-position reconstruction in CZT drift-strip detectors and finds that the two methods give complementary strengths in accuracy and uncertainty.
AI.motivation: Conventional reconstruction degrades in some detector regions, and learned models provide limited information about the reliability of their predictions.
AI.method: Both an ensemble of point-estimation networks and a simulation-based inference model that estimates a posterior over the interaction position are trained on physics-based simulations and evaluated on synthetic and experimental data.
AI.result: On synthetic data both methods' uncertainty correlates with positioning error, with SBI showing a substantially stronger relationship; on experimental data the deep ensemble improves z-position resolution while SBI gives more informative uncertainty that highlights regions of reduced positional information and simulation-to-detector discrepancies.
AI.conclusion: Ensemble-based reconstruction and posterior inference are complementary for uncertainty-aware detector position reconstruction.

title: SensOFormer: Foundation Models for Particle Accelerators
summary: Large-scale scientific facilities, such as particle accelerators, are complex systems composed of thousands of interacting components that must operate collectively to support diagnostics and control, and ensure safe, reliable operation. These facilities rely on extensive sensor networks that generate large volumes of heterogeneous, incomplete, and noisy telemetry, often sampled at different rates across subsystems. In this paper, we adopt the foundation-model paradigm to learn general-purpose sensor representations from historical accelerator data through self-supervised pretraining. We introduce SensOFormer, a denoising masked transformer with a Perceiver-style encoder-decoder architecture designed to handle variable sensor sets, accommodate heterogeneous sampling rates, and learn robust representations from noisy measurements. The model is pretrained on multiple particle-accelerator datasets and transferred to downstream tasks, including missing-data imputation, anomaly detection, cavity identification, and fault identification. Through extensive evaluations and comparisons, we demonstrate that a single self-supervised model can learn reusable representations for diverse operational tasks in large-scale scientific facilities. Project page: this https URL.

AI.tldr: SensOFormer is a denoising masked transformer with a Perceiver-style encoder-decoder, pretrained self-supervised on historical particle-accelerator telemetry, whose single representation transfers to imputation, anomaly detection, cavity identification and fault identification.
AI.motivation: Accelerator sensor networks produce heterogeneous, incomplete and noisy telemetry sampled at different rates across subsystems, and existing approaches do not provide reusable general-purpose representations for diverse operational tasks.
AI.method: The model handles variable sensor sets and heterogeneous sampling rates and is pretrained on multiple particle-accelerator datasets with self-supervised denoising masked modeling, then transferred to downstream tasks.
AI.result: The abstract reports extensive evaluations and comparisons showing that one self-supervised model learns reusable representations across the listed downstream tasks, without specific numbers given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: A single self-supervised foundation model can serve diverse operational tasks in large-scale scientific facilities.

title: Scalar Smoothness Is One Point on a Besov Spectrum
summary: Studies of neural network generalization and robustness often summarize smoothness with a single number, such as a Lipschitz constant or a Hessian curvature statistic. However, Lipschitz constants summarize global worst-case sensitivity and Hessian statistics summarize local curvature; neither captures how model responses vary with the size, direction, and location of perturbations encountered in real-world deployment. To measure smoothness under these perturbations, we introduce a finite-difference roughness spectrum that profiles model responses across these conditions. Our roughness spectrum generalizes scalar smoothness measures, bringing Lipschitz sensitivity and directional Hessian curvature into a common framework across perturbation scales. We connect this spectrum to classical Besov theory, which describes how a function's variation changes with scale. Our theoretical analysis also proves that a larger output shift can cause less task damage than a smaller one, and that local curvature alone can miss the blocks most vulnerable to finite perturbations. In image classification, Roughness Source Control (RSC) suppresses margin roughness along noise directions and improves noise robustness in a comparison of 80 checkpoints across four model--dataset combinations. In post-training quantization, we identify blocks that need higher precision by measuring task-loss increases from perturbations matched to the size and direction of each block's quantization error. Our mixed-precision allocation achieves lower perplexity than the Hessian-based HAWQ-V2 baseline under the same GPTQ weights and bit budgets in all 14 settings across seven held-out large language models.

AI.tldr: The paper replaces scalar smoothness measures with a finite-difference roughness spectrum across perturbation scales, linked to Besov theory, and uses it to improve noise robustness in image classification and mixed-precision quantization of large language models.
AI.motivation: Scalar smoothness summaries such as the Lipschitz constant (global worst case) and Hessian curvature (local) do not capture how responses vary with the size, direction and location of perturbations met in deployment.
AI.method: A finite-difference roughness spectrum profiles model responses across perturbation sizes and directions, generalizes Lipschitz sensitivity and directional Hessian curvature, is connected to Besov theory, and drives Roughness Source Control for image classification and per-block mixed-precision allocation for post-training quantization.
AI.result: In image classification, Roughness Source Control improves noise robustness over a comparison of 80 checkpoints across four model-dataset combinations; the quantization allocation gives lower perplexity than HAWQ-V2 under the same GPTQ weights and bit budgets in all 14 settings across seven held-out LLMs.
AI.conclusion: Smoothness is better described as a spectrum over perturbation scales than as a single number, and the spectrum guides practical robustness and quantization decisions.

title: ECGJev: Question-Conditioned Option Scoring for 12-Lead ECG Interpretation
comment: 5 pages (4 pages plus ethics statement and references), 2 figures. Submitted to IEEE ISBI 2027. Zhuoyuan Li and Xidong Wu contributed equally
summary: Clinical interpretation of a 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) often requires answering targeted diagnostic questions with clear, quantifiable decisions. We introduce ECGJev, the first ECG framework built on a decision decoder, a pretrained language model trained to return a probability for every listed option. A question-conditioned bridge compresses frozen waveform and spectrogram features into 16 ECG tokens, and a two-stage procedure adapts the bridge and low-rank adapters on the decoder's native option readout using diagnostic labels alone, scoring all options for a question in one forward pass. Evaluated across four ECG benchmarks, ECGJev achieves the highest macro-F1 on CPSC2018 (80.46%), PTB-XL (71.68%) and Chapman (96.86%), and generalizes competitively to the small-sample PTB cohort. Concept probes and perturbation analyses further show that its predictions rely directly on the ECG input, remain stable under option-order and wording variations, and transfer zero-shot to unseen waveform concepts. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: ECGJev is a 12-lead ECG interpretation framework that uses a pretrained language model as a decision decoder, scoring all diagnostic options for a question in one forward pass, and reports the highest macro-F1 on CPSC2018, PTB-XL and Chapman.
AI.motivation: Clinical ECG interpretation often requires answering targeted diagnostic questions with clear, quantifiable decisions, which generic outputs do not directly provide.
AI.method: A question-conditioned bridge compresses frozen waveform and spectrogram features into 16 ECG tokens, and a two-stage procedure adapts the bridge and low-rank adapters on the decoder's native option readout using diagnostic labels alone.
AI.result: ECGJev achieves macro-F1 of 80.46 percent on CPSC2018, 71.68 percent on PTB-XL and 96.86 percent on Chapman, and is competitive on the small PTB cohort; concept probes and perturbation analyses show predictions depend on the ECG input, are stable to option order and wording, and transfer zero-shot to unseen waveform concepts.
AI.conclusion: Question-conditioned option scoring with a decision decoder gives accurate and robust ECG interpretation that relies on the input signal.

title: METER: Matched-Event Calibration for Short-Event EEG Microstate Transition Analysis
comment: 36 pages. Supplementary material (16 pages) included as an ancillary file. Abdul Basit and Eklavya Tomar contributed equally
summary: Short cognitive events contain unequal and often sparse transition evidence, so raw EEG microstate distances can reflect finite sampling rather than neural reconfiguration. We introduce METER (Matched-Event Transition Estimation against a Reference), a participant-relative framework that separates marginal occupancy from conditional next-state choice and evaluates each event against duration-conditioned events from a fixed participant-specific reference bank. METER-Jump integrates uncertainty in sparse target and reference transition tables, returning a randomized event rank for testing and a continuous standardized coordinate for association analysis. Using a reproducible three-state representation selected by spatial criteria, we evaluated METER with participant-fitted simulations, estimator ablations, map perturbations, and preprocessing sensitivities. Event-level false-positive rates were 0.044-0.056 across four heterogeneous null mechanisms. By contrast, global cutoffs learned under the participant-fitted null and transferred unchanged to other regimes produced false-positive rates from 0.004 under rare transitions to 0.234 under map perturbation; duration-conditioned ranks remained near 0.05. Detection probability was approximately 0.69 with fixed maps but fell to 0.22 after bootstrap-derived map-assignment perturbation. In 4,175 natural-reading events from 18 participants, no linguistic association survived multiplicity correction in the primary 30-ms analysis, although a 20-ms sensitivity changed one within-stream max-$T$ decision. METER therefore calibrates finite-event departures conditional on a defined microstate sequence, while map assignment, filtering, temporal smoothing, and reference construction remain separate sources of measurement uncertainty.

AI.tldr: METER calibrates EEG microstate transition tests for short events by comparing each event with duration-conditioned events from a participant-specific reference bank, keeping false-positive rates near the nominal level where global cutoffs fail.
AI.motivation: Short cognitive events contain sparse transition evidence, so raw microstate distances can reflect finite sampling rather than neural reconfiguration, and global cutoffs transfer poorly across regimes.
AI.method: METER separates marginal occupancy from conditional next-state choice and uses METER-Jump, which integrates uncertainty in sparse transition tables to return a randomized event rank and a continuous standardized coordinate; a three-state representation is evaluated with participant-fitted simulations, estimator ablations, map perturbations and preprocessing sensitivity analyses.
AI.result: Event-level false-positive rates are 0.044 to 0.056 across four null mechanisms, whereas global cutoffs give 0.004 to 0.234; detection probability is about 0.69 with fixed maps and 0.22 after map-assignment perturbation; in 4,175 natural-reading events from 18 participants, no linguistic association survived multiplicity correction in the primary 30 ms analysis.
AI.conclusion: Finite-event departures should be calibrated conditional on the microstate sequence, and map assignment, filtering, smoothing and reference construction remain separate sources of uncertainty.

title: Beliefs in feedback: Factored representations of interacting agents in transformers
summary: Complex systems, from ecosystems to brains, are usually modeled as modular components coupled through feedback rather than as indivisible wholes. Can a transformer trained on the joint behavior of a group of interacting agents be understood in the same way? In this work, we develop a computational-mechanics framework to study agents interacting in feedback loops. We formally prove that any joint stochastic process can be presented as resulting from the behavior of agents interacting in feedback, and the resulting process is generated by a hidden Markov model whose Bayesian beliefs factorize into separate components per agent. Furthermore, our experiments show that transformers trained on such feedback sequences make use of this separability, disentangling the beliefs about the underlying factors into separate subspaces of their residual stream. This representation is found to scale linearly (instead of exponentially) with the number of agents. Moreover, interventions show that these representations are causally efficacious, allowing for targeted steering of individual agents' beliefs by selectively inserting counterfactuals. However, coarse-graining the behavior is found to disrupt the factorization, and can force a higher-dimensional representation. Together, the results establish both the dimensional advantage of a factorized representation and the ability of transformers to exploit it, laying the groundwork for investigating traces of compositional predictive architecture in pretrained models.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that a transformer trained on joint behavior of feedback-coupled agents represents each agent's Bayesian beliefs in separate, linearly scaling subspaces of its residual stream, and that these beliefs can be steered causally.
AI.motivation: Whether a transformer trained on a group of interacting agents can be understood as modular components coupled through feedback, as complex systems often are, is an open question.
AI.method: The authors develop a computational-mechanics framework in which any joint stochastic process is shown to arise from agents interacting in feedback, generated by a hidden Markov model whose Bayesian beliefs factorize per agent, then train transformers on such sequences and probe their residual stream with interventions that insert counterfactuals.
AI.result: Transformers disentangle the per-agent belief factors into separate subspaces, with representation size scaling linearly rather than exponentially in the number of agents, and targeted counterfactual interventions steer individual agents' beliefs; coarse-graining the behavior disrupts the factorization and can force higher-dimensional representations.
AI.conclusion: Factorized representations offer a dimensional advantage, and transformers can exploit it, which supports looking for compositional predictive structure in pretrained models.

title: Same Function, Different Gradients: Evaluating Gradient Reliability under Reparameterization
summary: Gradients are no longer used only to train models: Gradient magnitudes are now measurement instruments, used to rank attention heads for pruning, to decide per-example clipping in private training, to allocate adapter rank budgets, and to debug models. Across these workflows, larger gradient magnitudes are taken to mean greater importance. Even for a fixed input--output function, these gradients are computed in one of many possible parameter coordinate systems. For example, attention scores depend on the query and key projections only through the paired product $W_QW_K^\top$. Scaling a head's query projection by $c$ and the corresponding key projection by $1/c$ therefore leaves every output logit unchanged. This change in parameter coordinates rescales the corresponding query and key gradient norms by $1/c$ and $c$, respectively. To test whether gradient-based decisions remain unchanged under these coordinate changes, we introduce Gradient Reliability under Reparameterization (GRR). GRR rewrites a trained model in new parameter coordinates that compute exactly the same function, verifies that predictions are unchanged, and then tests whether the decisions derived from the gradients are unchanged too. Our audits span GLUE classifiers, a ViT on CIFAR-10, GPT-2-medium and GPT-2-large, a 1.1B-parameter Llama-style model on WikiText-2, and six trained LoRA adapters. Empirically, predictions are preserved throughout, but both the gradients and the gradient-based decisions change. Across 66 GLUE attention audits, the median top-3 overlap of raw head-gradient rankings is only $1/3$, and rankings and pruning masks change even under the mildest rescalings we test. In the largest of 14 global-pruning audits, the shifted ranking selects head masks that differ in four of 22 pruned heads and reach $50.92\%$ and $94.84\%$ validation accuracy on one ELECTRA SST-2 model.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Gradient Reliability under Reparameterization (GRR) and shows that gradient magnitudes used for head pruning, clipping and rank allocation change under parameter rescalings that leave predictions unchanged, so gradient-based decisions are not reliable.
AI.motivation: Gradient magnitudes are now used as importance measures for pruning, private clipping and adapter budgets, yet they depend on the parameter coordinates chosen even for a fixed input-output function.
AI.method: GRR rewrites a trained model in new parameter coordinates that compute the same function, verifies that predictions are unchanged, and then tests whether gradient-derived decisions remain the same; audits cover GLUE classifiers, a ViT on CIFAR-10, GPT-2 medium and large, a 1.1B Llama-style model on WikiText-2 and six LoRA adapters.
AI.result: Predictions are preserved throughout, but gradients and decisions change: across 66 GLUE attention audits the median top-3 overlap of raw head-gradient rankings is only 1/3, and in the largest of 14 global-pruning audits the shifted ranking selects masks that differ in four of 22 pruned heads and reach 50.92 and 94.84 percent validation accuracy on one ELECTRA SST-2 model.
AI.conclusion: Gradient magnitudes are not invariant measurements of importance, so gradient-based decisions need checks under reparameterization before they are trusted.

title: Fragility Is Not Reducible to Hardness: Conditional Causal Difficulty for LLMs
summary: Large language models show large and seemingly arbitrary performance drops when a task is rewritten in ways that leave its requirements untouched. We recast task difficulty as a causal quantity: the treatment effect of meaning-preserving perturbations on a model. A meaning-preserving rewrite can only be observed to hurt a task the model can already solve, so we place the estimand on the principal stratum where the degradation occurs: the conditional causal difficulty (CCD), the probability that a randomly drawn twin breaks a solvable task. Because harder tasks tend to be more phrasing-sensitive, complexity enters as an effect modifier rather than a confounder, and we residualize it out to obtain complexity-residualized difficulty (CRD); zero for a task exactly as fragile as its complexity predicts, positive for anomalously fragile ones. Current benchmarks do not supply the data CCD requires, so we introduce GlassGSM and GlassMATH, augmenting GSM8K and MATH with twins built from perturbation families, raising fragility on GlassGSM by $\approx 12\times$ over GSM-IC-style distractors on the same problems ($3.7\%\to44.9\%$) while keeping the answer key unchanged. Our predictor Frail learns the per-perturbation break probability and reaches $0.613{\pm}0.023$ of the suite reliability ceiling on GlassGSM and $0.557{\pm}0.023$ on GlassMATH, against $0.171$/$0.401$ for a surface-feature baseline and $0.444$/$0.463$ for supervised baselines such as VAP3, and, at a $5\%$ curation budget on GlassGSM, doubles random recall of fragile items, matching an oracle ranking. Additionally, cross-fitted residualization leaves CRD uncorrelated with the declared proxy in practice. Code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper defines conditional causal difficulty as the probability that a meaning-preserving rewrite breaks a task the model can solve, introduces GlassGSM and GlassMATH benchmarks with such twins, and proposes the Frail predictor to estimate fragility.
AI.motivation: LLMs show large and seemingly arbitrary performance drops under meaning-preserving rewrites, and existing benchmarks do not supply the paired data needed to estimate fragility as a causal quantity.
AI.method: Task difficulty is recast as the treatment effect of meaning-preserving perturbations on the principal stratum where degradation occurs; complexity is residualized to obtain complexity-residualized difficulty; GSM8K and MATH are augmented with twins from perturbation families, and Frail learns the per-perturbation break probability.
AI.result: Fragility on GlassGSM rises to 44.9 percent from 3.7 percent for GSM-IC-style distractors on the same problems with answers unchanged; Frail reaches 0.613 and 0.557 of the suite reliability ceiling on GlassGSM and GlassMATH against 0.171 and 0.401 for a surface-feature baseline, and at a 5 percent curation budget doubles random recall of fragile items.
AI.conclusion: Fragility is a distinct, causally defined quantity that is not reducible to problem hardness, and it can be predicted and used for benchmark curation.

title: HQNN-CL: Regime-Aware Hybrid Quantum Neural Network with Continual Learning for Financial Forecasting
summary: Financial time-series forecasting is still difficult owing to the non-stationary nature of the market, regime changes, and catastrophic forgetting, which makes conventional deep learning models hard to adapt in the long term. To achieve uncertainty-aware robust financial forecasting in the face of changing market conditions, this study proposes a Hybrid Quantum-Classical Neural Network with Continual Learning (HQNN-CL). The proposed framework combines Gaussian Hidden Markov Model (HMM) based regime detection, BiLSTM temporal encoding, adaptive-depth parameterized quantum circuits, Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC), experience replay, and probabilistic forecasting in a single architecture. The framework was tested on four real-time stock datasets: Microsoft, Systems Limited, Teradata and Tata Consultancy Services, and compared with seven state-of-the-art forecasting models, including recurrent and Transformer-based models. The experimental results show that HQNN-CL has outperformed other methods on the Systems Limited (RMSE = 3.0149) and Teradata (RMSE = 0.8909) datasets and is within 0.32% and 0.40% of the best baseline method for Microsoft and Tata Consultancy Services, respectively. The proposed framework also generates well-calibrated probabilistic forecasts within the range of 89.5% to 96.5% empirical coverage rate, has zero catastrophic forgetting (BWT = 0.0000) for all sequential learning tasks, and consistently shows positive forward transfer. Ablation and statistical significance analyses also validate the performance of adaptive quantum feature learning and continual adaptation under heterogeneous market conditions, regime-wise.

AI.tldr: HQNN-CL is a hybrid quantum-classical forecaster that combines Gaussian HMM regime detection, BiLSTM encoding, adaptive quantum circuits and continual learning with EWC and replay, reporting wins on two of four stock datasets and zero backward transfer forgetting.
AI.motivation: Financial series are non-stationary with regime changes and catastrophic forgetting, which makes conventional deep models hard to keep adapted over the long term.
AI.method: The framework couples Gaussian HMM regime detection, BiLSTM temporal encoding, adaptive-depth parameterized quantum circuits, Elastic Weight Consolidation, experience replay and probabilistic forecasting, and is compared with seven forecasting baselines on Microsoft, Systems Limited, Teradata and TCS stock data.
AI.result: HQNN-CL outperforms the baselines on Systems Limited (RMSE 3.0149) and Teradata (RMSE 0.8909), is within 0.32 and 0.40 percent of the best baseline on Microsoft and TCS, achieves 89.5 to 96.5 percent empirical coverage, and has BWT of 0.0000 across sequential tasks.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid architecture gives competitive, well-calibrated forecasts with no measured forgetting, and the benefit of its quantum component is supported by ablation and significance analyses.

title: Bernoulli On-Policy Distillation: Don't Ignore High-Confidence Student Tokens
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures, Code: this https URL
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model on its own trajectories using token-level supervision from a stronger teacher. We show that standard sampled reverse-KL OPD systematically suppresses updates to high-confidence tokens, such that their weak gradient contribution does not necessarily imply weak or uninformative teacher supervision. We introduce Bernoulli On-Policy Distillation (Bernoulli OPD), which directly matches the teacher and student probabilities for that token. This yields a bounded probability space correction that preserves teacher-student disagreement while avoiding the additional confidence-dependent suppression induced by vanilla OPD. Fixed-rollout analyses show that Bernoulli OPD substantially restores optimization signal to high-confidence tokens while remaining sensitive to teacher-student disagreement. We further analyze the resulting model behavior through confidence distributions, answer calibration, policy movement, and training dynamics, showing that Bernoulli OPD's gains cannot be explained simply by longer reasoning, larger optimization steps, or more uniform imitation of the teacher. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Bernoulli On-Policy Distillation replaces the sampled reverse-KL objective with a direct match of teacher and student probabilities for each token, which restores gradient signal to high-confidence student tokens that vanilla on-policy distillation suppresses.
AI.motivation: Standard sampled reverse-KL on-policy distillation suppresses updates to high-confidence tokens, so a weak gradient does not imply weak teacher supervision.
AI.method: For each token the method directly matches teacher and student probabilities, giving a bounded probability-space correction that keeps teacher-student disagreement while removing confidence-dependent suppression; fixed-rollout analyses and studies of confidence distributions, answer calibration, policy movement and training dynamics are reported.
AI.result: Fixed-rollout analyses show substantial recovery of optimization signal on high-confidence tokens, and the gains cannot be attributed simply to longer reasoning, larger optimization steps or more uniform imitation of the teacher.
AI.conclusion: Not ignoring high-confidence student tokens improves on-policy distillation of language models.

title: NorthCUA Technical Report: Turbocharging Computer-Use Agents through Experience at Scale
summary: Scaling computer-use agents from individual actions to complex software work requires experience that connects decisions to complete outcomes. We present NorthCUA, an integrated system for turbocharging computer-use agents through experience at scale. Its Experience Flywheel supplies diverse executable tasks to the NorthCUA Harness, which sustains long interactions, records decisions, and checks task outcomes. The Flywheel uses these records to curate verified trajectories. For unsolved tasks, recursive self-improvement evolves reusable skills and preserves verified milestones so later attempts build on earlier progress. Staged Learning combines this experience with grounding data from the Flywheel to develop GUI competence through mid-training and long-horizon supervised fine-tuning. The policy then learns from fresh attempts in the same Harness through joint desktop-web reinforcement learning, closing the loop between experience production and policy improvement. The resulting Nano, Mini, and Pro family achieves state-of-the-art results among open-source models across GUI grounding, desktop execution, and Web interaction under the reported evaluation settings. For more responsive Web workflows, NorthCUA-Ultrafast pairs direct action selection with open-ended generation on pre-RL Nano, offering a measured quality-latency tradeoff. Together, these advances establish NorthCUA as a high-performing model family and a reusable foundation for agents that carry complex software work from intent to completion.

AI.tldr: NorthCUA is a system for computer-use agents that combines an experience flywheel of executable tasks, staged learning and joint desktop-web reinforcement learning, producing the Nano, Mini and Pro models reported as state of the art among open-source models, plus an Ultrafast variant for faster Web workflows.
AI.motivation: Computer-use agents need experience that links individual decisions to complete outcomes in order to handle complex, long-horizon software work.
AI.method: The Experience Flywheel supplies executable tasks to a harness that records decisions and checks outcomes and curates verified trajectories; recursive self-improvement builds reusable skills for unsolved tasks; staged learning uses mid-training and long-horizon supervised fine-tuning, followed by reinforcement learning on fresh attempts in the same harness.
AI.result: The Nano, Mini and Pro family achieves state-of-the-art results among open-source models on GUI grounding, desktop execution and Web interaction under the reported evaluation settings; NorthCUA-Ultrafast trades some quality for lower latency on Web workflows, with the measured tradeoff reported.
AI.conclusion: Closing the loop between experience production and policy improvement yields a reusable foundation for agents that carry complex software work to completion.

title: Mesh2Shell Neural Operator for Inverse Shape Optimization
summary: Physics-driven design seeks high-performing geometries, which need not conform to a learned shape category. Parametric and latent-space approaches facilitate surrogate-based optimization, but restrict deformations to prescribed shape families or learned decoders. We introduce the Mesh-to-Shell Neural Operator (M2S-NO) as the mesh-to-shell component of a category-agnostic inverse shape optimization framework. We separate the explicit mesh used for design from the volumetric representation used for physics prediction. M2S-NO maps oriented surface samples to a surface-centered shell representation, such as TruncatedSDF or HeatSDF. A separate problem-specific PDE neural operator (PDE-NO) maps this representation to physical fields. Objective gradients update mesh vertices through both operators, without a latent shape decoder. Preconditioning and remeshing support free-form deformation, while fixed interfaces are controlled directly on the mesh. Optional shell-space proposals enable topology changes. We evaluate geometric matching, jet-engine brackets, and neutron moderators, with independent FEM and OpenMC evaluation. Relative to the best training designs, M2S-NO reduces maximum bracket displacement by 14.3% and increases neutron-sensor current by 13.8%. Optimization also succeeds from an out-of-distribution bracket initialization, demonstrating the framework's geometric flexibility.

AI.tldr: M2S-NO maps oriented surface samples to a shell representation for a category-agnostic inverse shape optimization framework, with objective gradients updating mesh vertices through a PDE neural operator, reducing bracket displacement by 14.3 percent relative to the best training designs.
AI.motivation: Parametric and latent-space approaches restrict shape deformations to prescribed families or learned decoders, which limits the search for high-performing geometries.
AI.method: The Mesh-to-Shell Neural Operator converts the explicit design mesh into a surface-centered shell representation such as TruncatedSDF or HeatSDF, a separate problem-specific PDE neural operator maps that to physical fields, and gradients update mesh vertices through both operators with preconditioning, remeshing and optional shell-space proposals for topology changes.
AI.result: On jet-engine brackets, M2S-NO reduces maximum displacement by 14.3 percent and on neutron moderators increases neutron-sensor current by 13.8 percent, relative to the best training designs, with independent FEM and OpenMC evaluation, and optimization succeeds from an out-of-distribution bracket initialization.
AI.conclusion: Mesh-based, latent-free shape optimization can be geometrically flexible and effective across physics problems.

title: TSSDA: An Autonomous Agent for Constructing a Time-Series Text-to-SQL Benchmark
summary: As agents increasingly undertake data querying, Text-to-SQL serves as a foundational capability for database access. However, for text-to-SQL in time-series databases, high-quality benchmarks and large-scale training corpora remain scarce, limiting the systematic evaluation and domain adaptation of existing models and agents. Existing automated SQL generation approaches lack sufficient autonomy, leaving key challenges unresolved. First, numerous combinations of temporal syntax and functions complicate comprehensive coverage of valid queries. Second, as the corpus grows, generating valuable and diverse new data becomes increasingly challenging. Third, schema and data heterogeneity hinder reuse of temporal query structures, limiting generation efficiency. To address these challenges, we propose TSSDA, a Time-Series SQL (TSSQL) Generation Data Agent framework, and construct TERN, a comprehensive Time-sERies text-to-SQL beNchmark. First, to achieve broad coverage of valid queries, we systematically model TSSQL syntax and semantics to construct a data generation space. Next, to explore the space and improve diversity, we develop a Data Agent that autonomously orchestrates data generation. The agent comprises a planning and decision-making module and a query generation module, with online adaptation for continuous self-improvement. Finally, we introduce a temporal-aware memory that enables adaptive reuse of experience across heterogeneous data instances, improving generation efficiency. Comprehensive evaluations on TERN reveal the limitations of existing methods in performing Text-to-TSSQL tasks. Furthermore, extensive experiments demonstrate that TSSDA substantially improves coverage, diversity, and complexity.

AI.tldr: TSSDA is an autonomous data agent that generates a time-series text-to-SQL corpus and the TERN benchmark, using a modeled TSSQL generation space, a planning and query-generation agent, and temporal-aware memory to improve coverage, diversity and complexity.
AI.motivation: High-quality benchmarks and training corpora for text-to-SQL over time-series databases are scarce, and existing automated generation lacks autonomy, coverage of temporal syntax and reuse of query structure across heterogeneous schemas.
AI.method: The authors model TSSQL syntax and semantics to define a data generation space, build a Data Agent with a planning module, a query generation module and online adaptation, and add a temporal-aware memory for reusing experience across data instances.
AI.result: Evaluations on TERN reveal limitations of existing methods on Text-to-TSSQL tasks, and TSSDA substantially improves coverage, diversity and complexity of generated data, as stated in the abstract without specific figures.
AI.conclusion: An autonomous, memory-equipped generation agent can build broader time-series text-to-SQL benchmarks and training data than prior automated approaches.

title: When Is Personalized Federated Learning Worth Its Deployment Cost?
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures. Accepted and presented at UBMK 2026
summary: Personalized federated learning (PFL) may improve client-level performance, but deeper personalization increases deployment cost. We formulate personalization-depth selection as a utility-based empirical decision problem in which client utility equals Macro-F1 minus a cost-sensitivity weight times deployment cost, over six personalization depths labeled P0 through P5. We compare fixed policies with an offline per-client Oracle reference and report allocation maps over Dirichlet data heterogeneity and cost sensitivity. Although evaluated on this hierarchy, the formulation can accommodate any finite candidate set. On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and a PTB-XL subset, personalization shows empirical, setting-dependent decision regimes rather than a universal benefit: higher cost sensitivity shifts Oracle mass toward the global-only depth P0; low cost sensitivity can favor deeper actions. Patterns are grid observations (three seeds per cell), not theoretical boundaries. Best-uniform is competitive with Oracle assignment (6.5 percent plus or minus 7.8 percent relative regret; 95 percent confidence interval 5.9 to 7.1), whereas random and personalize-all incur much larger regret (189.3 percent plus or minus 367.1 percent and 409.0 percent plus or minus 803.2 percent). Under the same utility, Ditto full-model personalization is substantially suboptimal once cost is counted. The contribution is an offline characterization of when personalization depth is worth its cost, not a new PFL optimizer or deployment-time scheduler.

AI.tldr: The paper frames personalization depth selection for federated learning as a utility problem with cost weighting, showing that personalization benefit is setting-dependent and that a single best uniform depth is close to the offline oracle.
AI.motivation: Personalized federated learning can improve client performance but increases deployment cost, and there is no principled way to decide how deep personalization should go.
AI.method: Client utility is Macro-F1 minus a cost-sensitivity weight times deployment cost over six depths P0 to P5; fixed policies are compared with an offline per-client Oracle and allocation maps are reported over Dirichlet heterogeneity and cost sensitivity on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and a PTB-XL subset with three seeds per cell.
AI.result: Best-uniform is close to the Oracle with 6.5 percent plus or minus 7.8 percent relative regret (95 percent CI 5.9 to 7.1), while random and personalize-all incur much larger regret, and Ditto full-model personalization is substantially suboptimal once cost is counted.
AI.conclusion: The paper gives an offline characterization of when personalization depth is worth its cost, rather than a new optimizer or scheduler.

title: Value Forcing: Aligning Return Distributions at All Noise Levels
summary: Learning accurate value functions is central to reinforcement learning (RL), yet remains challenging because supervision is limited and indirect: ground-truth values are unavailable, and each transition in the data only provides an immediate reward that can be used to construct bootstrapped targets as supervision. This challenge is particularly pronounced when data is limited or reward signals are sparse, as is common in real-world applications such as robotics. We argue that the key to accurate value learning in this limited data regime is extracting richer learning signals from the available data. In this paper, we introduce Value Forcing, a new approach that uses flow matching to estimate return distributions and enables accurate value learning from limited data. Our key insight is that we can extract richer learning signals by enforcing Bellman consistency at every noise level. Empirically, Value Forcing improves the accuracy of estimating the return distribution, and prevents the distribution from collapsing to a single value, as occurs with prior methods. We instantiate Value Forcing with two practical value-learning algorithms: VF, an actor-critic method, and IVF, an implicit value-learning method. We evaluate both algorithms across $26$ long-horizon tasks in the offline RL setting and find that they outperform prior value-learning methods, with particularly large gains when data is limited. Our project website is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Value Forcing estimates return distributions with flow matching and enforces Bellman consistency at every noise level, improving value learning from limited data and preventing distributional collapse, and it is instantiated as VF and IVF.
AI.motivation: Value learning in RL relies on limited and indirect bootstrapped supervision, which is especially problematic when data is scarce or rewards are sparse, as in robotics.
AI.method: Flow matching models the return distribution, and Bellman consistency is enforced at every noise level to extract richer learning signals; two algorithms are built on this, VF as an actor-critic method and IVF as an implicit value-learning method.
AI.result: Across 26 long-horizon offline RL tasks, VF and IVF outperform prior value-learning methods, with particularly large gains when data is limited, and the approach improves return distribution accuracy and avoids collapse to a single value.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing consistency across noise levels is an effective way to learn accurate value distributions from limited offline data.

title: Restrained Diffusion Bridges: Targeted Denoiser Training and Refinement
summary: Diffusion models are often inaccurate in critical, data-sparse regions of the target distribution. Sampling from restrained distributions, biased distributions used in classical enhanced sampling to concentrate data near chosen configurations, can control where training data are collected but biases the learned distribution. We establish that this bias cancels exactly when forward noising from restrained data is conditioned on the restrained configuration at an appropriately chosen intermediate time. This allows a pretrained model fine-tuned on restrained data to achieve high accuracy in any chosen region of the target distribution, regardless of its probability, using standard denoising or flow matching objectives without importance weights. When no target data are available, Gibbs sampling enables inference from a model trained exclusively on restrained data.

AI.tldr: Restrained diffusion bridges fine-tune a diffusion model on data sampled from a restrained (biased) distribution, with the bias cancelled by conditioning forward noising on the restrained configuration at an intermediate time, giving high accuracy in chosen regions without importance weights.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models are inaccurate in critical data-sparse regions, and restrained sampling can concentrate data near chosen configurations but biases the learned distribution.
AI.method: The authors show that the bias cancels exactly when forward noising from restrained data is conditioned on the restrained configuration at an appropriately chosen intermediate time, and then fine-tune with standard denoising or flow matching objectives; Gibbs sampling is used when no target data are available.
AI.result: A pretrained model fine-tuned on restrained data achieves high accuracy in any chosen region regardless of its probability, and a model trained exclusively on restrained data supports inference through Gibbs sampling.
AI.conclusion: Restrained sampling with appropriately conditioned noising corrects its bias and lets diffusion models be accurate in targeted, low-probability regions.

title: Beyond Unit-Circle Eigenvalues: Invariant Bases for Stable State Space Dynamics
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 40 pages, 13 figures, 27 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Diagonal state space models process long sequences at linear cost, yet the same transition is applied at every step of a rollout, so an unconstrained recurrence holds no quantity fixed and the state decays or grows without bound. Current designs constrain one quantity, and preserving one does not guarantee preservation of the others, so a model can hold its norm to machine precision while momentum drifts by hundreds of percent. We claim that the conserved quantities of a diagonal recurrence are layered, that each layer requires a strictly stronger condition on the operator, and that a unit-modulus spectrum reaches only the outermost. Acting on the claim, we enforce the conditions required for every layer by construction. The generator of the Kronecker-Cayley transition (KC) is a graph Laplacian over object subspaces, $\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{L}\otimes I_m$, advanced by a Cayley transform, and the step stays diagonal at $O(N^3+N^2m)$ cost. The conserved set is exactly a $2m^2$-dimensional family of quadratic forms, held at every parameter value, so the quantities and the dynamics the construction reaches are fixed before training. On four conservation benchmarks, KC holds total mass at or near the reference floor while every diagonal baseline loses it by orders of magnitude. We further compare against mass correction and find that two correctors fail once the underlying prediction diverges, which shows that assembly rather than correction is necessary for a guarantee that holds across the rollout. A free modal basis trained under a conservation penalty conserves only by freezing its spectrum, whereas the assembled operator conserves with every mode but one free to rotate. Beyond these benchmarks, KC holds the linear momentum of three $N$-body systems and, at the operator level, the conserved quantity in molecular dynamics, chemical kinetics, pharmacokinetics and power-grid swing dynamics.

AI.tldr: KC is a diagonal state-space transition built from a Cayley-transformed graph Laplacian, which conserves a fixed family of quadratic invariants by construction and holds total mass near the reference floor where diagonal baselines lose it by orders of magnitude.
AI.motivation: An unconstrained diagonal recurrence holds no quantity fixed, and existing designs preserve only one invariant, so norm can be preserved while momentum drifts by hundreds of percent.
AI.method: The generator is H equal to L tensor I_m, with L a graph Laplacian over object subspaces, advanced by a Cayley transform, which keeps the step diagonal at O(N^3 + N^2 m) cost and conserves a 2m^2-dimensional family of quadratic forms at every parameter value; mass correction methods are compared as well.
AI.result: On four conservation benchmarks KC holds total mass at or near the reference floor while every diagonal baseline loses it by orders of magnitude; two correctors fail once the prediction diverges; KC also holds linear momentum on three N-body systems and conserves the relevant quantity in several physical and chemical dynamics settings at operator level.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing conservation through assembly of the operator, rather than post hoc correction, gives a guarantee that holds across the rollout.

title: ANCHOR: KL-Anchored Adaptation for Stable Offline-to-Online RL
comment: Accepted at the CoRL 2026 Workshop on Continually Self-Improving Robots. 37 pages
summary: Offline-to-online reinforcement learning (RL) follows the pretrain-finetune paradigm: an agent is first pretrained on historical data and then adapted through online interaction. We study offline-to-online adaptation without offline replay, where the agent must improve using only the pretrained model and newly collected experience. A key challenge is to avoid catastrophic failure, a sharp early performance collapse during online fine-tuning, while still achieving strong asymptotic performance. Through controlled experiments, we show that removing offline replay can induce catastrophic failure, while retaining strong conservative regularization from offline RL can suppress final online performance. We also find that common stabilization strategies do not reliably prevent early collapse, and that the critic-side mechanisms we test are insufficient on their own. Motivated by these findings, we propose ANCHOR, a simple adaptation method that anchors the actor to the offline-pretrained policy early in online fine-tuning, anneals this constraint over time, and retains only a small residual conservative critic regularizer. We provide a theoretical interpretation showing that KL anchoring helps preserve critic reliability across nearby occupancy distributions, with a two-phase regret bound explaining when anchoring should be maintained or relaxed. Across FrankaKitchen, AntMaze, and Adroit tasks, ANCHOR substantially reduces catastrophic failure while maintaining strong asymptotic performance. Ablations show that KL annealing and the residual conservative weight are important for balancing early stability and online adaptation, while additional analysis shows that ANCHOR is most beneficial when the pretrained policy contains useful behavior to preserve. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: ANCHOR adapts an offline-pretrained RL agent online without offline replay by anchoring the actor to the pretrained policy early in fine-tuning, annealing the constraint and keeping a small residual conservative critic regularizer, which substantially reduces catastrophic early collapse on FrankaKitchen, AntMaze and Adroit.
AI.motivation: Removing offline replay can cause catastrophic early collapse during online fine-tuning, while strong conservative regularization can suppress final performance, and common stabilization strategies do not reliably prevent early collapse.
AI.method: The actor is anchored to the offline-pretrained policy with a KL term early in online fine-tuning, the anchor is annealed over time, and a residual conservative critic weight is retained; a two-phase regret bound is given to explain when anchoring should be kept or relaxed.
AI.result: Across FrankaKitchen, AntMaze and Adroit tasks ANCHOR substantially reduces catastrophic failure while maintaining strong asymptotic performance; ablations show KL annealing and the residual conservative weight are important, and the method helps most when the pretrained policy contains useful behavior.
AI.conclusion: KL anchoring that is annealed over time balances early stability with online adaptation in offline-to-online RL.

title: Fuzzy-Enhanced Machine Learning Approach for Type 2 Diabetes Diagnosis
summary: Accurate diabetes prediction is critical for early clinical intervention, yet existing machine-learning pipelines often fail due to class imbalance, noisy physiological measurements, and redundant or weakly informative features. To address these unresolved limitations, this study establishes a unified fuzzy-evolutionary-ensemble framework designed to uncover a more discriminative feature space for type 2 diabetes prediction. The workflow integrates selective fuzzification of nonlinear clinical variables, SMOTE-ENN-based balancing and noise filtering, and Bat-Algorithm-driven evolutionary feature selection prior to training a Random Forest classifier. Applied to the Pima Indians Diabetes Dataset, the framework compresses the expanded fuzzy-numerical space into an optimized 10-feature subset and yields substantial performance gains: 96.11% accuracy, 95.14% precision, 98.00% recall, and a 98.23% F1-score. Relative to a baseline Random Forest using all 16 features (74.45% accuracy; 59.86% F1), the system achieves more than a 1.6-fold improvement in F1-score while preserving over 99% stability in majority-class detection and surpassing earlier published 16-feature models impacted by imbalance and weak feature relevance. Collectively, these results demonstrate that the integrated pipeline produces an enhanced fuzzy-numerical representation space that improves diabetes risk stratification and provides a scalable, uncertainty-aware foundation for diagnostic modeling across broader clinical datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a fuzzy-evolutionary-ensemble pipeline for type 2 diabetes prediction on the Pima Indians dataset that reports 96.11 percent accuracy and a 98.23 percent F1-score using a 10-feature subset.
AI.motivation: Diabetes prediction pipelines often fail because of class imbalance, noisy measurements and redundant features.
AI.method: The workflow applies selective fuzzification of nonlinear clinical variables, SMOTE-ENN balancing and noise filtering, and Bat-Algorithm-driven feature selection before training a Random Forest classifier.
AI.result: The framework reports 96.11 percent accuracy, 95.14 percent precision, 98.00 percent recall and 98.23 percent F1-score with 10 features, against a baseline Random Forest on all 16 features with 74.45 percent accuracy and 59.86 percent F1.
AI.conclusion: The integrated pipeline improves diabetes risk stratification on this dataset, and the authors suggest it as a basis for diagnostic modeling on broader clinical data, though the abstract does not establish this beyond the single dataset.

title: Discrimination, Calibration, and Ranking: A Unified Matrix Framework
comment: 88 pages, 8 figures. Lean 4 formalisation and experiment code: this https URL. Implemented in the aggmetrics package (version 0.3.0, subpackage this http URL)
summary: Discrimination, calibration, and ranking are the three pillars of classifier evaluation, yet no single algebraic language spans all three. A recent indicator-matrix account unifies discrimination measures (precision, recall, F1, Matthews correlation) across binary, multiclass, multilabel and related settings, using Boolean cell operations on indicator label matrices, generalised to soft labels by t-norms. Calibration measures (Brier score, log-loss) and ranking measures (nDCG, AUC) fall outside it. We close the gap with two further classes of cell operators: deviation operators phi(y - yhat), which give a Calibration Framework, and rank- and slice-dependent operators (positional gains for DCG, column concordance cells for AUC), which give a Ranking Framework. Both inherit the micro/macro/exemplar aggregation architecture. For calibration, the three Brier aggregations collapse to one scalar; the Murphy decomposition holds in matrix form (unbinned, binned and isotonic); and, within the Brier-type class-indexed family, a measure is skew-invariant if and only if it depends only on the class-conditional errors alpha_j and beta_j, the calibration analogues of recall and specificity. For ranking, raw DCG collapses across aggregations while nDCG does not; per-class nDCG and per-class AUC are related by a row-column duality; micro-AUC differs from pooled ROC-AUC; raw positional scores are never strictly proper, and nDCG and AUC need not be proper. The skew-invariant per-class building blocks share one class-conditional expectation template. Experiments on two multilabel benchmarks illustrate the distinctions. Many of the results are machine-checked in Lean 4; the proofs, the experiments and the this http URL package are public: this https URL
