The evaluation harness validates repairs using Verus and a change checker, recording solutions, execution traces, and resource usage. An initial evaluation of four general-purpose coding-agent harnesses achieved 75-85% success on focused tasks and 29-47% on full-module variants, highlighting the challenge of autonomous module-wide repairs. VerusWeave provides a reusable foundation for evaluating automated proof construction for concurrent software.

AI.tldr: VerusWeave is a benchmark of 75 focused tasks and 17 full-module variants for proof repair in concurrent Verus programs, in which agents fill removed proof annotations, and initial evaluation shows high success on focused tasks but much lower success on full modules.
AI.motivation: Existing Verus benchmarks offer limited coverage of concurrency-specific proofs that connect atomic operations to abstract protocols, and coding agents need such a benchmark to be evaluated on automated proof construction.
AI.method: Tasks are derived from four open-source projects by removing selected proof annotations while preserving executable code and specifications; the harness validates repairs with Verus and a change checker, recording solutions, execution traces and resource usage; four general-purpose coding-agent harnesses were evaluated.
AI.result: The four harnesses achieved 75-85% success on focused tasks and 29-47% on full-module variants.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark provides a reusable foundation for evaluating automated proof construction for concurrent software, and autonomous module-wide repair remains challenging.

title: When AI Agents Act on Our Behalf: A Taxonomy of Human-Agent Interaction Failure
summary: AI agents write and execute code, manipulate user interfaces, and transact on their users' behalf. We ask what forms failure takes in human-agent interaction, and how those forms change as agents act with greater autonomy. From 695 documented incidents in two public repositories, we developed 12 failure modes bottom-up within three interaction stages adapted from Amershi et al.'s guidelines, coding the autonomy at which each arose. What a person can do when an agent fails depends on how much the agent completes between points of user involvement--a property fixed at deployment. Therefore, the same model on the same task can fail differently under different configurations. All 12 modes appear at both low and high autonomy, and rising autonomy changes the form each failure takes. Users need controls between full delegation and full manual work, and neither incident records nor agent benchmarks reach the interaction where these failures occur.

AI.tldr: From 695 documented incidents, the authors derive 12 failure modes of human-agent interaction across three interaction stages and show that all 12 appear at both low and high agent autonomy, with rising autonomy changing the form each failure takes.
AI.motivation: As agents act with more autonomy, it is unclear what forms failure takes in human-agent interaction, and neither incident records nor agent benchmarks capture the interaction where these failures occur.
AI.method: The authors coded 695 incidents from two public repositories bottom-up into 12 failure modes within three stages adapted from Amershi et al.'s guidelines, recording the autonomy at which each failure arose.
AI.result: All 12 modes occur at both low and high autonomy; the form of each failure changes with autonomy; what a person can do after a failure depends on how much the agent completes between points of user involvement, a property fixed at deployment, so the same model on the same task can fail differently under different configurations.
AI.conclusion: Users need controls between full delegation and full manual work, and current incident records and agent benchmarks do not reach the interaction where these failures occur.

title: TADA: Technology Aware DNN Accelerator Performance and Energy Estimator
comment: 7 pages, 7 figures. Accepted at the 32nd Asia and South Pacific Design Automation Conference (ASPDAC '27), Tokyo, Japan, 2027
summary: Deep neural network (DNN) accelerators for edge inference must meet tight energy, latency, and area (EDP) constraints, and their optimal hardware architecture and dataflow configuration is typically identified through design space exploration (DSE). However, on-chip memory technology including cell type, bank organization, and process node, is rarely treated as a first-class citizen in DSE. For example, increasing memory capacity can reduce memory accesses through greater data reuse, but at the cost of higher area and access energy, thereby limiting the compute units budget. Consequently, memory technology can fundamentally shift the optimal accelerator architecture for a given area and EDP budget. Existing machine learning (ML)-based DSE methods require repeating simulation, data generation, and model training for each new memory technology. We present TADA, a memory technology-aware DNN accelerator performance and energy estimator that predicts system latency and energy for a given workload, hardware configuration, and memory technology. TADA is trained on a synthetic dataset that generalizes across memory technologies. The dataset spans current and future technology trends while enforcing physics-based guardrails to preserve realistic area-energy trade-offs. Each memory technology is represented by a technology signature, a vector of read energy, write energy, and storage capacity across a range of areas, provided as input alongside the workload and hardware configuration. Across 21 unseen technology curves spanning SRAM, STTRAM, ReRAM, PCM, FeFET, eDRAM, and CTT, TADA predicts system energy and latency with 1.5-4.4% and 0.7-1.2% mean absolute percentage error, respectively. In three pairwise case studies, it matches the simulator-selected memory technology at 98.7-100% of area budgets, with a mean EDP loss of at most 0.21%, while achieving over 10^4x higher evaluation throughput.

AI.tldr: TADA is a memory-technology-aware estimator that predicts latency and energy for DNN accelerators from workload, hardware configuration and a memory technology signature, trained on synthetic data and reaching low error on 21 unseen technology curves while evaluating over 10^4x faster than the simulator.
AI.motivation: Memory technology can shift the optimal accelerator architecture, but existing ML-based design space exploration must repeat simulation, data generation and training for each new memory technology.
AI.method: TADA is trained on a synthetic dataset spanning current and future technology trends with physics-based guardrails; each technology is encoded as a signature of read energy, write energy and storage capacity across areas, provided as input alongside the workload and hardware configuration.
AI.result: Across 21 unseen technology curves (SRAM, STTRAM, ReRAM, PCM, FeFET, eDRAM and CTT), TADA predicts energy and latency with 1.5-4.4% and 0.7-1.2% mean absolute percentage error; in three pairwise case studies it matches the simulator-selected technology at 98.7-100% of area budgets with a mean EDP loss of at most 0.21%, and achieves over 10^4x higher evaluation throughput.
AI.conclusion: TADA generalises across memory technologies and makes memory technology a practical first-class variable in accelerator design space exploration.

title: Agent Stack for ML Training Lifecycle: Generation, Validation, and Optimization
summary: Production model development requires repeated architecture design, platform integration, debugging, training, and evaluation. We present an agent stack deployed at LinkedIn with two independently usable agent loops: AutoTorch for model generation and migration, and AutoResearch for model optimization. AutoTorch generates PyTorch models and training pipelines for TensorFlow migration, XGBoost replacement, and new-model development. Executable validation hooks check platform API compliance, trainability, and conversion fidelity on sampled data, guiding iterative repair before engineer review and full-scale distributed training. AutoResearch explores architecture and training-configuration changes through expert-steered or autonomous experimentation. An external orchestrator manages parallel trials, experiment history, candidate selection, and wall-clock budgets across agent sessions. A shared runtime preserves execution state independently of agent reasoning and allocates GPUs separately from agent execution. Across ranking, content understanding, and recommendation workloads, AutoTorch completed generation and full-scale training in 92 of 115 workflow runs (80%). Of these, 77 (83.7%) produced models meeting post-training quality requirements. In a separate cohort, AutoResearch improved the primary task metric on held-out data for 28 of 100 production pipelines. Engineering teams estimate that the stack reduced elapsed end-to-end migration time from approximately eight weeks to two weeks, a 4x speedup.

AI.tldr: LinkedIn's agent stack has two agent loops, AutoTorch for model generation and migration and AutoResearch for model optimisation, with an external orchestrator and shared runtime; it completed most generation workflows and cut migration time from about eight weeks to two.
AI.motivation: Production model development repeatedly requires architecture design, platform integration, debugging, training and evaluation, which is slow when done manually.
AI.method: AutoTorch generates PyTorch models and training pipelines for TensorFlow migration, XGBoost replacement and new models, with executable validation hooks checking platform API compliance, trainability and conversion fidelity; AutoResearch explores architecture and training changes through expert-steered or autonomous experiments; an external orchestrator manages parallel trials, history and wall-clock budgets, and a shared runtime preserves execution state and allocates GPUs separately from agent execution.
AI.result: AutoTorch completed generation and full-scale training in 92 of 115 workflow runs (80%), and 77 of those (83.7%) met post-training quality requirements; AutoResearch improved the primary task metric on held-out data for 28 of 100 production pipelines; engineering teams estimate end-to-end migration time fell from about eight weeks to two, a 4x speedup.
AI.conclusion: The deployed agent stack reduces engineering effort in ML training lifecycles, with the largest reported gain in migration time.

title: On the Framing Effect of AI Red-Teaming Instructions: Evidence from Prior Exercises and Controlled Simulations
summary: AI red-teaming, adversarially probing generative AI systems to surface harms, has become a central evaluation method. However, prior work has highlighted that red-teaming is a fairly open-ended task, laden with myriad design choices that can shape its findings. In this work, we focus on the instructions used to conduct red-teaming exercises and hypothesize that they can significantly affect outcomes in a manner analogous to the framing effect in psychology, where the format in which information is presented greatly impacts how people respond. To understand whether and why instructions impact red-teaming outcomes, first, we analyze the range of ways in which instructions have historically been formulated, reviewing 228 instances of prior work. Second, based on takeaways from this review, we run controlled simulations that hold parameters such as the risk domain, the attacker, and the model under investigation fixed while varying only the instructions. From five real instruction templates used by industry and academic organizations, we derive 45 instruction frames across three risk domains and three levels of risk granularity, generating 100 variants per frame, and deploy each against five open-weights target models, for 22,500 attacks. Using a generalized linear mixed model, we find that certain instruction properties significantly predict attack success rates: the lowest and highest levels of risk granularity both outperform intermediate specificity, as do short and long instructions relative to medium-length ones. The presence of examples is associated with higher attack success rates, while supplying explicit harm definitions yields lower ones. As alignment evaluations become increasingly automated, our results suggest that humans continue to shape red-teaming outcomes substantially through the instructions they provide to scaffold the activity.

AI.tldr: Across 22,500 attacks, the paper shows that the wording of red-teaming instructions significantly affects attack success rates, with instruction granularity, length, examples and explicit harm definitions all having measurable effects.
AI.motivation: Red-teaming is an open-ended task whose design choices can shape findings, and the instructions used may act like a framing effect in psychology, but this had not been systematically examined.
AI.method: The authors reviewed 228 prior red-teaming instances, derived 45 instruction frames from five real templates across three risk domains and three granularity levels, generated 100 variants per frame, and ran them against five open-weight target models with a generalised linear mixed model.
AI.result: The lowest and highest risk-granularity levels both outperform intermediate specificity, and short and long instructions outperform medium-length ones; the presence of examples is associated with higher attack success, while explicit harm definitions are associated with lower success.
AI.conclusion: Humans shape red-teaming outcomes substantially through the instructions they write, which matters as alignment evaluations become more automated.

title: Online Fair Division of Chores with Upgrade Recourse
summary: We study the online fair division of indivisible chores among $n$ agents under upgrade recourse, where earlier assignments may be revised but each chore previously assigned to an agent must be replaced by a distinct chore that she finds no more costly. We show that a simple adaptation of round robin maintains envy-freeness up to one chore (EF1) together with a $(2-1/n)$-approximation of the maximin share (MMS), and that no deterministic algorithm without predictions can do better, even when all agents rank the chores in the same order. This stands in contrast to the allocation of goods, where the optimal MMS factor vanishes as $n$ grows and cannot be achieved together with EF1. Moreover, knowing only the number of chores modulo a period of length $O(n)$ (and nothing about the costs) suffices to improve upon this factor at the final configuration, while the same algorithm retains a factor below $3$ even if this information is wrong. On the other hand, envy-freeness up to any chore (EFX) essentially requires the exact number of chores: uncertainty between two consecutive values already rules out every finite approximation, and even exact knowledge does not allow EFX to be combined with an MMS guarantee better than the trivial factor of $n$.

AI.tldr: The paper gives an online fair-division algorithm for indivisible chores under upgrade recourse, where a simple round-robin adaptation achieves EF1 and a (2-1/n)-approximation of maximin share, and shows that EFX needs the exact number of chores.
AI.motivation: Online allocation of chores allows earlier assignments to be revised only by replacing each chore with one the agent does not find more costly, and the fairness guarantees achievable in this setting were unclear, in contrast with goods.
AI.method: The authors adapt round robin, prove a matching lower bound for deterministic algorithms without predictions, and study how partial information about the number of chores (modulo a period of length O(n)) or wrong predictions affect the MMS factor.
AI.result: The round-robin adaptation maintains EF1 with a (2-1/n)-approximation of MMS, which no deterministic algorithm without predictions can beat even with identical rankings; knowing the number of chores modulo O(n) improves the factor at the final configuration, and the algorithm keeps a factor below 3 even if this information is wrong; EFX is ruled out by uncertainty between two consecutive values of the count and cannot be combined with an MMS guarantee better than n.
AI.conclusion: Upgrade recourse makes fair chore division achievable with EF1 and a good MMS factor, while EFX demands exact knowledge of the number of chores.

title: Analog and hybrid computing in the 21st century
summary: Analog computers solve problems through physical representations of mathematical variables and relations, often using the dynamics of electronic circuits and their associated signals. Many analog computers directly represent nonlinear dynamical systems; they encode their solutions in the signals that they generate. Although most modern scientific computing relies on digital architectures with inherently discrete-valued representations and algorithmic approaches, the design constraints of such architectures increasingly limit both performance and energy efficiency. Analog systems can circumvent some of these constraints; they execute specific computations very efficiently by mapping them directly onto physical processes using smaller and simpler computing elements than the ones in digital architectures. In this article, we provide an interdisciplinary perspective on modern analog and hybrid (i.e., analog-digital) computing. We discuss how modern scientific computing workflows can leverage analog approaches in various applications, such as in simulating dynamical systems, performing optimization, and enabling more energy-efficient implementations of artificial intelligence.

AI.tldr: This perspective article reviews modern analog and hybrid analog-digital computing, arguing that physical representations of variables can solve dynamical systems, optimisation and energy-efficient AI tasks more efficiently than digital architectures in some cases.
AI.motivation: Digital architectures with discrete representations increasingly limit the performance and energy efficiency of scientific computing, and analog systems can circumvent some of these constraints.
AI.method: The article provides an interdisciplinary perspective on modern analog and hybrid computing and discusses how scientific computing workflows can use analog approaches.
AI.result: The abstract reports no experimental results; it identifies applications in simulating dynamical systems, performing optimisation and enabling more energy-efficient AI implementations.
AI.conclusion: Analog and hybrid computing are promising complements to digital scientific computing for specific computations.

title: Threat Modeling Intimate Partner Abuse in Agentic Systems
summary: Agentic systems are AI-powered technologies capable of autonomous action within digital environments, such as sending emails or making reservations. They are deeply connected to external tools as well as users' data and resources, making them vulnerable to attacks which exploit their access and capabilities. In this work, we apply the technology-facilitated abuse threat model, in the context of intimate partner violence and surveillance, to these systems, revealing threats that require deliberate investigation and mitigation. We categorize attacks based on system ownership: (1) Abuser-as-owner attacks demonstrate how agentic systems make existing forms of technology-facilitated abuse far easier and more scalable. (2) Victim-survivor-as-owner attacks show how agentic systems create a new attack surface which abusers can exploit. In light of these risks, we outline research and development directions for effective mitigation strategies.

AI.tldr: The paper applies the technology-facilitated abuse threat model to agentic AI systems in the context of intimate partner violence and surveillance, categorising attacks by who owns the system and outlining research and mitigation directions.
AI.motivation: Agentic systems that act with users' data, tools and resources open attack surfaces that could be used for technology-facilitated abuse in intimate partner violence, and these threats need deliberate investigation.
AI.method: Attacks are categorised by system ownership: abuser-as-owner attacks and victim-survivor-as-owner attacks.
AI.result: Abuser-as-owner attacks show that agentic systems make existing forms of technology-facilitated abuse far easier and more scalable; victim-survivor-as-owner attacks show that agentic systems create a new attack surface that abusers can exploit.
AI.conclusion: The paper outlines research and development directions for effective mitigation strategies against these risks.

title: Do Social Influence Pressures Move LLM Agents? Evidence from Delegated Audit Judgment
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are rapidly being integrated into complex professional workflows such as auditing and entrusted with judgments under human review. Human auditors are known to yield to social influence pressures from superiors, peers and clients, and this paper asks whether LLM agents yield to the same pressures and, if so, how they respond. In an experiment on twelve model settings, an LLM agent acting as a senior associate in audit analytical review forms an estimate and is then challenged without new evidence by colleagues inside the firm, by a reviewer from another firm and by the client's CFO, with and without a career inducement. Experimental findings show that LLM agents yield to pressure from the engagement partner, from peers and from a reviewer from another firm, but in most settings not to pressure from the client's CFO. Under a career inducement the LLM agents revise their estimates less, not more, and they name the inducement as a threat to independence. Furthermore, some models revise only toward the more conservative estimate, while others revise in both directions. LLM agents thus do not respond to social influence pressures as human auditors do, and LLM-based decision support systems should be designed with the differences in mind.

AI.tldr: In a controlled audit experiment across twelve model settings, LLM agents yield to challenges from the engagement partner, peers and an outside reviewer but mostly not to the client's CFO, and they respond to career inducements differently from human auditors.
AI.motivation: Human auditors yield to social influence from superiors, peers and clients, and it is unknown whether LLM agents used as decision support in auditing respond to the same pressures.
AI.method: An LLM agent acting as a senior associate in audit analytical review forms an estimate and is then challenged without new evidence by inside colleagues, an outside reviewer and the client's CFO, with and without a career inducement, across twelve model settings.
AI.result: LLM agents yield to pressure from the engagement partner, peers and the outside reviewer, but in most settings not to the CFO; under a career inducement they revise estimates less, not more, and name the inducement as a threat to independence; some models revise only toward the more conservative estimate while others revise in both directions.
AI.conclusion: LLM agents do not respond to social influence as human auditors do, so decision-support systems built on them should account for these differences.

title: Reflex: Fast Robot Policy Serving by Reusing and Correcting Past Actions
summary: Modern robot policies often perform expensive inference to generate action chunks, making serving a latency bottleneck for real-time control and a throughput bottleneck for multi-robot serving. Building on the success of caching in image, video, and audio generation, recent robot-policy advances have reported promising speedups by reusing intermediate denoising states to avoid redundant computation. Surprisingly, we find that such reuse often offers little advantage over simply running fewer denoising steps from fresh noise, without any cache. Moreover, accelerating denoising leaves the expensive policy backbone intact, which can account for 70% of GPU time. We present Reflex, a serving layer that turns past policy executions into a backbone-free path for future decisions. Rather than reusing intermediate computations, Reflex caches complete action chunks to bypass both the backbone and action head. This introduces two challenges: similar observations can demand different actions, and small action deviations (errors) in reuse can compound into execution stalls. Reflex addresses these through two-level cache correction. At the action level, it learns action-aware similarity from past policy decisions, assembles compatible chunks, and applies lightweight residual correction to limit action mismatch. At the execution level, it captures task progress and adaptively refreshes the original policy to limit accumulated errors and balance inference cost. Without modifying the underlying policy, Reflex improves inference latency by 1.4x to 11x and throughput by 2.0x to 2.2x on representative workloads and real robots, while preserving comparable task success.

AI.tldr: Reflex is a serving layer for robot policies that caches complete action chunks from past executions and corrects them with action-level residuals and execution-level refresh, improving latency by 1.4x to 11x and throughput by 2.0x to 2.2x without modifying the policy.
AI.motivation: Robot policy backbones often account for about 70% of GPU time, and reusing intermediate denoising states offers little advantage over simply running fewer denoising steps from fresh noise.
AI.method: Reflex caches complete action chunks to bypass both the backbone and action head, learns action-aware similarity from past decisions, assembles compatible chunks with lightweight residual correction, captures task progress, and adaptively refreshes the original policy to limit accumulated error.
AI.result: Without modifying the underlying policy, Reflex improves inference latency by 1.4x to 11x and throughput by 2.0x to 2.2x on representative workloads and real robots while preserving comparable task success.
AI.conclusion: Caching and correcting complete past action chunks is an effective serving strategy for robot policies, more so than reusing denoising states.

title: Faster Imitation by Re-timing Demonstrations Within the Controller Limit
summary: Imitation policies inherit the operator's pace, and re-timing the demonstrations to run faster works only until success collapses at two to three times demonstration speed. Recent methods attribute that collapse to distribution shift and answer it with finer rules for which segments may be sped up; we show it has a mechanical cause that segment selection cannot address. A low-level controller realises only a bounded displacement per control period, so merging consecutive commands produces sums outside that bound: training pairs that promise a transition the plant cannot deliver. The share of such pairs in the re-timed data, which we call the exceed share, tracks where the retrained policy collapses. The rule that follows has a single parameter: merge greedily while the sum stays realisable. Every command is then realisable by construction, the demonstrated geometry is preserved, and the speed-up lands only where the demonstrator left slack. On four simulated robomimic tasks, 200 held-out seeds per cell, a merge cap of two is at or above the frozen policy's success on all four, by 14 points on Square, and shortens the successful episodes. At matched tempo, uniform re-timing loses 9 and 16 points on Can and ToolHang, is within noise on the other two, and reaches zero on the hardest at 2x. Placement also matters: no shuffled, entropy-guided or speed-conditioned alternative beats the rule on three of the four tasks, by margins the exceed share alone does not explain; on the fourth, at a tempo the task absorbs, every placement lands in the same band. The same principle carries to a simulated humanoid whole-body tracker: re-timing 429 reference motions within its velocity envelope succeeds on 71% of clips at 2.3x, against 51% for uniform time scaling at 2x.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that imitation policies collapse when demonstrations are re-timed faster because merged commands exceed the controller's per-period displacement bound, and proposes a greedy merge rule with a single cap parameter that keeps every command realisable.
AI.motivation: Re-timing demonstrations faster works only until success collapses at two to three times speed, and prior work attributes this to distribution shift and answers with finer segment-selection rules.
AI.method: The authors define an exceed share, the fraction of training pairs whose merged command sum is unrealisable by the low-level controller, and propose a rule that merges consecutive commands greedily while the sum stays realisable, with a single merge-cap parameter; they test on four simulated robomimic tasks with 200 held-out seeds per cell, compare placement alternatives, and apply the principle to a simulated humanoid whole-body tracker.
AI.result: A merge cap of two matches or exceeds the frozen policy's success on all four tasks, by 14 points on Square, and shortens successful episodes; at matched tempo uniform re-timing loses 9 and 16 points on Can and ToolHang and reaches zero success on the hardest task at 2x; no alternative placement beats the rule on three of four tasks; on the humanoid, re-timing 429 reference motions succeeds on 71% of clips at 2.3x against 51% for uniform time scaling at 2x.
AI.conclusion: Collapse in re-timed imitation has a mechanical cause that segment selection cannot address, and respecting controller realisability allows speed-ups where the demonstrator left slack.

title: Learning from an Imitable Teacher: Competition Solution for the MetaFine Challenge
comment: 2026 CoRL MetaFine Open Competition 2nd place solution
summary: The MetaFine Open Competition (RoboFineMani workshop, CoRL 2026) evaluates fine-grained manipulation beyond binary success. Its five simulated tasks, from grasping a bottle by an instructed part to inserting letter-shaped pegs with 4 mm clearance, are scored on perception under lighting and camera changes, instruction understanding, and behavior. This report presents Team Friday's solution, which got second place with an overall score of 0.947, more than twice the $\pi_0$ baseline. Instead of fine-tuning a large vision-language-action (VLA) model, we train one 19M-parameter policy per task with a separate instruction classifier and focus on the data, all generated in the simulator by a privileged scripted teacher, including its corrections of the student's mistakes. By analyzing failed episodes, we find that a teacher that almost always succeeds can still teach a memoryless student badly: its pauses become stalls, its fixed habits become shortcuts, and it never shows the errors the student makes. Making the teacher \emph{imitable} raised the official score on letter insertion, the hardest task, from 0.44 to 0.82 with 32\% more data and the same architecture, and finally to 0.88. We summarize practical lessons on demonstration data and evaluation, which we hope will help in imitation learning for precise manipulation.

AI.tldr: Team Friday's second-place solution to the MetaFine challenge trains one 19M-parameter policy per task on simulator data from a privileged scripted teacher, and shows that making the teacher imitable raises letter-insertion performance from 0.44 to 0.88.
AI.motivation: The MetaFine challenge evaluates fine-grained manipulation beyond binary success, and the team sought an alternative to fine-tuning a large vision-language-action model.
AI.method: The team trains a small policy per task with a separate instruction classifier, generates all demonstrations in the simulator with a privileged scripted teacher that includes corrections of student mistakes, and analyses failed episodes to make the teacher easier for a memoryless student to imitate.
AI.result: The overall score is 0.947, more than twice the pi0 baseline and second place in the competition; making the teacher imitable raised the official score on letter insertion, the hardest task, from 0.44 to 0.82 with 32% more data and the same architecture, and finally to 0.88.
AI.conclusion: A teacher that almost always succeeds can still teach a memoryless student poorly, so the imitability of demonstrations matters; the paper summarises practical lessons on demonstration data and evaluation.

title: Discovering Models for Experimental Quantum Systems with Agentic AI
summary: A central obstacle in realizing color center cavity-QED-based quantum technologies is inhomogeneity, or disorder, among individual emitters. As the number of emitters increases, so does the complexity of the experimental data, making it difficult to quantify the present physical mechanisms of disorder. Here we introduce an artificial intelligence-driven model discovery framework in which a large language model (LLM)-based agent, equipped with tools and a structured workflow, proposes candidate Hamiltonian and Lindbladian models, generates computational tools, and quantitatively evaluates competing physical hypotheses. We apply the workflow to three previously published experimental cavity-QED datasets collected from color centers in diamond and silicon carbide. Across the experiments, the agent successfully identifies physical models for the system and characterizes the disorder. In assessing reproducibility, we find that run-to-run variability is concentrated primarily in the research plan generation step, while the computational analysis itself is substantially more consistent. Our results suggest that structured LLM agent workflows can support model discovery from quantum optical experimental data while simultaneously allowing for human expert supervision and collaboration.

AI.tldr: An LLM-based agent with tools and a structured workflow proposes Hamiltonian and Lindbladian models, generates analysis tools and evaluates competing hypotheses to identify and characterise disorder among colour-centre emitters in cavity QED from three published datasets.
AI.motivation: Inhomogeneity among emitters is a central obstacle to colour-centre cavity-QED technologies, and as emitter count grows, experimental data become too complex to quantify the physical mechanisms of disorder by hand.
AI.method: The LLM agent operates within a structured workflow to propose candidate Hamiltonian and Lindbladian models, generate computational tools and quantitatively compare competing physical hypotheses, applied to three published cavity-QED datasets from diamond and silicon carbide.
AI.result: The agent identifies physical models for the systems and characterises the disorder; run-to-run variability is concentrated mainly in research-plan generation, while the computational analysis is substantially more consistent.
AI.conclusion: Structured LLM agent workflows can support model discovery from quantum optical data while allowing human expert supervision and collaboration.

title: Log-Driven Semantic Tuning for Mixed Integer Programming Solvers
comment: 34 pages, 8 figures, 28 tables. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Automated configuration of mixed-integer programming (MIP) solvers largely relies on black-box optimization. Each trial requires an expensive solver run and provides only a scalar outcome, so tuning can require many such evaluations. Human experts take a different approach. They inspect solver logs, identify performance bottlenecks, and adjust the parameters that address them. We propose Log-Driven Semantic Tuning (LDST), which uses a large language model (LLM) to automate this process. LDST extracts compact diagnostics from solver logs, uses the LLM to propose sparse edits to the current best configuration based on parameter meanings and observed solver behavior, and validates each proposal before execution. A regime-adaptive objective selects the tuning signal according to the information available from a time-limited run, while a log-based completion signal estimates completion time from branch-and-bound tree growth recorded in ordinary solver logs, so that solved and unsolved runs share one time scale. On 215 instances from five benchmark sets, LDST reduces geometric-mean loss by 43.9% on easy instances and 16.7% on intermediate instances relative to the best of SMAC3, RBFOpt, and random search. In both regimes, LDST achieves a lower loss with 10 proposals than any of these baselines achieves with 50. Configurations that LDST tunes on a single instance also transfer better than baseline configurations to unseen instances of the same family.

AI.tldr: LDST uses an LLM to tune mixed-integer programming solver configurations by reading solver logs, proposing sparse validated edits to the best configuration, and reaching lower loss with 10 proposals than baselines reach with 50.
AI.motivation: Black-box tuning of MIP solvers needs many expensive runs that return only a scalar outcome, whereas human experts inspect logs to find bottlenecks and adjust the relevant parameters.
AI.method: LDST extracts compact diagnostics from solver logs and uses an LLM, guided by parameter meanings and observed behaviour, to propose sparse edits that are validated before execution; a regime-adaptive objective picks the tuning signal for a time-limited run, and a log-based completion signal estimates completion time from branch-and-bound tree growth.
AI.result: On 215 instances from five benchmark sets, LDST reduces geometric-mean loss by 43.9% on easy instances and 16.7% on intermediate instances relative to the best of SMAC3, RBFOpt and random search; in both regimes it reaches lower loss with 10 proposals than the baselines reach with 50; single-instance configurations transfer better to unseen instances of the same family.
AI.conclusion: Mimicking expert log-driven tuning with an LLM gives substantially more sample-efficient configuration search for MIP solvers.

title: Getting a Grip: Operating Human-Agent Software Teams Through Governed Messages
comment: Technical report. 45 pages, 9 figures, 27 tables. Data, code and corpus: this https URL
summary: Software is increasingly developed by teams in which several people direct many coding agents from different vendors. Such teams must establish who may request what from whom, which messages start work, which decisions bind, and who caused a change. We propose to govern a human-agent team through its message protocol and present yoars, a relay in which humans and agents are authenticated principals that exchange typed, addressed messages in rooms holding goals, decision rules, routing and an attributable, append-only record. This report gives the architecture, the full controlled study and the field material. In 926 controlled runs (899 analyzable), small agent teams built programs under varied room rules, some with a hostile member planting a backdoor. Revising which messages start work, bundled with limits on repeated messages, was followed by a drop in total coordination failure from 42% to 13% (p = .0063, adjusted p = .057 over nine registered tests). Instructed roles and votes did not reliably produce the intended process, and no defense inside the conversation reliably prevented the backdoor. An auditor read the records of 96 runs with a confirmed backdoor. In the 25 runs where the attacker had persuaded a teammate to write it, the auditor named the persuader in all 25, but it also flagged 24 of 40 honest runs. In a four-week field study, up to nineteen agents and two people developed a distributed system through yoars, producing 7,457 acts. Human attention and decision making emerged as the critical resource: requests waited mainly for the human-run coordinator and for approvals, while agents answered within minutes. Most governance requirements emerged from operation, and holding context dominated token cost. We report twenty-six failures of our own instruments, derive seven lessons and a checklist, and release the corpus, the redacted room ledger and the analysis scripts.

AI.tldr: The paper presents yoars, a relay that governs human-agent software teams through typed, addressed and attributable messages in rooms with goals and decision rules, and a controlled study and four-week field study show how message-protocol rules change coordination failures.
AI.motivation: Software teams increasingly direct many coding agents from different vendors, and they must establish who may request what, which messages start work, which decisions bind and who caused a change.
AI.method: Humans and agents are authenticated principals who exchange typed, addressed messages in rooms holding goals, decision rules, routing and an append-only record; 926 controlled runs with small agent teams tested varied room rules, some with a hostile member planting a backdoor; a four-week field study had up to nineteen agents and two people build a distributed system.
AI.result: Revising which messages start work, bundled with limits on repeated messages, reduced total coordination failure from 42% to 13% (p = .0063, adjusted p = .057 over nine registered tests); instructed roles and votes did not reliably produce the intended process and no in-conversation defence reliably prevented the backdoor; an auditor named the persuader in all 25 runs where a teammate was persuaded to write a backdoor but also flagged 24 of 40 honest runs; in the field study human attention and decisions were the critical resource.
AI.conclusion: Governance requirements emerge from operation, and the paper derives seven lessons, a checklist and released corpus, ledger and analysis scripts.

title: Architecting Fairness-Aware LLM Interactions
comment: Accepted at the IEEE/ACM ASE 2026 Journal Ahead Workshop (JAWs), October 12-16, 2026, Munich, Germany
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as decision-support tools but may generate stereotypical, discriminatory, or unfair responses. As LLMs become embedded in decision-critical software systems, fairness can no longer be treated as a downstream evaluation step, but must become an architectural concern of the interaction itself. Yet current fairness approaches operate as standalone evaluation techniques, lacking a reusable mechanism to verify and mitigate violations at runtime. We propose a fairness-assurance architecture grounded in three reusable design patterns, instantiated as a multi-agent framework that evaluates and iteratively refines LLM responses before delivery. A preliminary evaluation across eight configurations involving different LLM families shows that the architecture identifies fairness violations and iteratively produces compliant responses in all configurations, with behavior differing depending on the model-family composition. These results provide initial evidence for the joint instantiation of the proposed patterns and a first step toward architecting non-functional properties into LLM-based systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a fairness-assurance architecture built from three reusable design patterns, instantiated as a multi-agent framework that evaluates and iteratively refines LLM responses before delivery, with a preliminary evaluation on eight configurations.
AI.motivation: Fairness is usually a standalone evaluation step for LLMs, lacking a reusable runtime mechanism to verify and mitigate violations, yet LLMs are increasingly embedded in decision-critical systems.
AI.method: Three reusable design patterns are instantiated as a multi-agent framework that checks LLM responses for fairness violations and iteratively refines them before delivery.
AI.result: Across eight configurations involving different LLM families, the architecture identifies fairness violations and iteratively produces compliant responses in all configurations, with behaviour depending on model-family composition.
AI.conclusion: The results give initial evidence for the joint use of the patterns and a first step toward architecting non-functional properties into LLM-based systems.

title: Beyond Synthesis Conditions: Linking In-situ Growth Dynamics to Carbon Nanotube Forest Properties through Multimodal Machine Learning
summary: Machine learning for chemical vapor deposition (CVD) of carbon nanotubes (CNTs) has largely mapped static synthesis conditions to final properties, implicitly treating these conditions as a complete description of growth. Here, we test this assumption by integrating gas-flow conditions with in-situ time-resolve growth profiles (growth curves) of vertically aligned CNT forests. We introduce an observation-window analysis, in which prediction is evaluated as a function of observation time by providing models with the growth curve only up to progressively later times, to determine not only whether a property can be predicted, but when the necessary information becomes available during synthesis. Clustering of normalized growth curves revealed distinct growth patterns independent of final forest height. The gas conditions alone could predict the initial growth rate but not the growth lifetime and failed to capture the variation in yield (R^2<0). Adding the growth curve improved yield prediction (R^2~0.4-0.5), with the relevant information emerging during the intermediate and later stages of growth rather than at its onset. In contrast, density and G/D ratio, which forest height does not record, showed no consistent improvement. The maximum height and lifetime could be estimated with moderate accuracy midway through the 10-min growth. Permutation feature importance identified water vapor and H_2, both linked to catalyst activity, as the most informative gas variables. These results indicate that variation unexplained by synthesis conditions is not merely noise but reflects an evolving catalyst state, and they establish mid-growth decision points for autonomous synthesis, enabling early termination of unpromising batches and, ultimately, in-batch adjustment of growth conditions.

AI.tldr: Multimodal machine learning on gas-flow conditions and in-situ growth curves shows that carbon nanotube forest properties depend on information unavailable from synthesis conditions, and that yield and height become predictable at mid-growth decision points.
AI.motivation: Machine learning for CNT chemical vapour deposition has treated synthesis conditions as a full description of growth, and the authors test this by adding in-situ growth dynamics.
AI.method: The authors cluster normalised growth curves and introduce an observation-window analysis that provides models with the growth curve only up to progressively later times, measuring when prediction becomes possible, and use permutation feature importance on gas variables.
AI.result: Gas conditions alone predict initial growth rate but not growth lifetime and fail to capture yield (R^2 < 0); adding the growth curve raises yield prediction to R^2 of about 0.4 to 0.5, with relevant information emerging in intermediate and later growth; density and G/D ratio show no consistent improvement; maximum height and lifetime can be estimated with moderate accuracy midway through the 10-minute growth; water vapour and H2 are the most informative gas variables.
AI.conclusion: Variation unexplained by synthesis conditions reflects an evolving catalyst state rather than noise, and mid-growth decision points enable early termination of unpromising batches and in-batch adjustment of conditions.

title: ResMamba: A Dual-Path Convolution-Mamba Model for Music Genre Classification
summary: Music genre classification remains a fundamental yet challenging task in music information retrieval, requiring models that capture local time--frequency patterns and long-range temporal dependencies. To address this, we propose ResMamba, a hybrid architecture that augments a ResNet-style four-stage backbone with Mamba blocks. Building upon the selective structured state space sequence model, ResMamba first adapts the selective SSM into a 4D-compatible residual Mamba block that captures global dependencies at linear complexity. We then design the ConvMamba dual-path block, which combines this adapted Mamba branch with a parallel convolutional branch through a learned $1\times1$ fusion, jointly modeling global sequential context and local spectro-temporal patterns. Furthermore, we adopt a multi-scale fusion head that aggregates hierarchical representations across all four stages. Experiments on the GTZAN dataset demonstrate that our full ResMamba model achieves a 5-fold cross-validation accuracy of $88.99\% \pm 1.58\%$, surpassing the strongest published method in our comparison (88.64\%). All models are trained from scratch without any pretraining, external data, or data augmentation. Beyond GTZAN, ResMamba also generalizes to the larger FMA benchmarks under the same training protocol, attaining $64.52\% \pm 1.88\%$ on FMA-Small under 10-fold cross-validation --- the best published from-scratch result --- and $65.75\%$ on FMA-Medium under the official artist-level split, surpassing the widely cited SVM baseline of Defferrard \textit{et al.} (63\%).

AI.tldr: ResMamba is a hybrid ResNet-style network with Mamba blocks, including a ConvMamba dual-path block, that reaches 88.99% five-fold accuracy on GTZAN trained from scratch and reports the best from-scratch results on FMA-Small and FMA-Medium.
AI.motivation: Music genre classification needs models that capture both local time-frequency patterns and long-range temporal dependencies.
AI.method: ResMamba augments a four-stage ResNet-style backbone with a 4D-compatible residual Mamba block, a ConvMamba dual-path block combining a Mamba branch and a convolutional branch through a learned 1x1 fusion, and a multi-scale fusion head over all four stages; all models are trained from scratch without pretraining, external data or augmentation.
AI.result: On GTZAN, the full model reaches 88.99% plus or minus 1.58% five-fold cross-validation accuracy, above the strongest compared published method at 88.64%; on FMA-Small under ten-fold cross-validation it reaches 64.52% plus or minus 1.88%, described as the best published from-scratch result; on FMA-Medium under the official artist-level split it reaches 65.75%, above the SVM baseline of Defferrard et al. at 63%.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid convolution-Mamba design generalises from GTZAN to larger FMA benchmarks under the same from-scratch protocol.

title: HiPaper: A Human-AI Collaborative System for Academic Literature Triage and Scholarly Sensemaking
summary: Scholarly sensemaking requires researchers to iteratively retrieve, collect, and synthesize literature as their understanding evolves. However, existing scholarly tools provide only partial support for this process. Recent artificial intelligence (AI)-based systems generally rely on opaque submit-and-wait pipelines that it users' ability to inspect, revise, and validate intermediate outputs. In this study, we present HiPaper, a human-AI collaborative literature review system informed by a formative study with academic experts. HiPaper organizes scholarly sensemaking as a three-stage interactive workflow spanning Retrieval, Collection, andSynthesis, centralized on the human-in-the-loop paradigm that exposes intermediate AI-generated content for user inspection and intervention through a persistent workspace called Knowledge Pocket. Through this workflow, users can iteratively refine search intent, curate and organize papers with AI-enriched metadata and clustering, and conduct evidence-traceable synthesis over selected literature. Our user study with 14 Ph.D. students showed that HiPaper efficiently supports scholarly sensemaking by enabling human-AI collaboration in both familiar and unfamiliar domains. Furthermore, the findings highlight how staged interactions with intermediate AI-generated content successfully scaffold user interactions throughout the sensemaking process.

AI.tldr: HiPaper is a human-AI literature review system that organises scholarly sensemaking into Retrieval, Collection and Synthesis stages with a persistent Knowledge Pocket, so users can inspect and steer intermediate AI outputs; a study with 14 PhD students reports efficient support.
AI.motivation: Existing AI literature tools rely on opaque submit-and-wait pipelines that limit users' ability to inspect, revise and validate intermediate outputs, and only partly support iterative sensemaking.
AI.method: The system was informed by a formative study with academic experts and organises sensemaking as a three-stage interactive workflow with a human-in-the-loop design, in which users refine search intent, curate papers with AI-enriched metadata and clustering, and run evidence-traceable synthesis over selected papers.
AI.result: A user study with 14 PhD students showed that HiPaper efficiently supports sensemaking and human-AI collaboration in both familiar and unfamiliar domains, and that staged interaction with intermediate AI content scaffolds the sensemaking process.
AI.conclusion: Exposing intermediate AI-generated content for inspection and intervention supports sensemaking better than submit-and-wait pipelines.

title: Agent4FreeFem: A Verification-Guided Framework for Autonomous Topology Optimization
summary: Topology optimization has become an indispensable design tool in the aerospace, automotive, and mechanical engineering industries. Yet bringing a new problem from its description to an optimized result remains slow, expert-dependent, and unreliable: the workflow spans many manually connected stages, each new problem requires solver code to be written and debugged manually, and such code often fails or yields incorrect results. We present Agent4FreeFem, a pipeline driven by a large language model that turns a natural-language problem description into a set of verified optimization results without manual solver-code development or debugging. The pipeline keeps the problem definition unmodified, localizes errors using independent sources of evidence, and completes constrained repairs automatically, thereby providing efficient end-to-end automation, autonomous execution, and verifiable results. We evaluated Agent4FreeFem on a suite of single-physics and coupled multiphysics problems. Every case passed runtime verification and finished within the repair budget of each stage.

AI.tldr: Agent4FreeFem is an LLM-driven pipeline that turns a natural-language topology optimisation problem into verified results, writing and repairing FreeFem solver code without manual development, and passed runtime verification on every evaluated single-physics and coupled multiphysics case.
AI.motivation: Topology optimisation remains slow, expert-dependent and unreliable because each new problem needs manually written and debugged solver code, which often fails or gives incorrect results.
AI.method: The pipeline keeps the problem definition unmodified, localises errors using independent sources of evidence and completes constrained repairs automatically within a repair budget for each stage.
AI.result: Every case in a suite of single-physics and coupled multiphysics problems passed runtime verification and finished within the repair budget of each stage.
AI.conclusion: The pipeline offers end-to-end automation with autonomous execution and verifiable results for topology optimisation.

title: Microphone Geometry Aware Regional Target Speaker Extraction
summary: Regional target speaker extraction (RSE) aims to extract speech originating from a specified angular region, relaxing the requirement for precise target speaker location when performing location based speech extraction. However, existing RSE methods typically assume a fixed microphone array configuration and microphone number, limiting their applicability to unseen microphone geometries and varying numbers of microphones. In this work, we propose a geometry-aware RSE framework capable of extract with varying microphone array geometry and microphone numbers. Specifically, we introduce an attention-based multichannel front-end to encode inter-microphone phase information, together with a spatial audio reconstruction-based auxiliary objective to improve the front-end spatial representations quality. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework improves SI-SDRi by 5.1 dB over geometry-aware baselines across microphone arrays with four-microphones, while maintaining a performance gap of less than 0.6 dB compared with a tetrahedral geometry-specific baseline when evaluated on the tetrahedral microphone array.

AI.tldr: A geometry-aware regional target speaker extraction framework uses an attention-based multichannel front-end to handle unseen microphone geometries and varying microphone counts, improving SI-SDRi by 5.1 dB over geometry-aware baselines on four-microphone arrays.
AI.motivation: Existing regional target speaker extraction methods assume a fixed microphone array configuration and number of microphones, which limits their use on unseen geometries.
AI.method: An attention-based multichannel front-end encodes inter-microphone phase information, and a spatial audio reconstruction auxiliary objective is added to improve the quality of the spatial representations.
AI.result: The framework improves SI-SDRi by 5.1 dB over geometry-aware baselines across four-microphone arrays, and stays within 0.6 dB of a tetrahedral-geometry-specific baseline when evaluated on the tetrahedral array.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly encoding inter-microphone phase makes regional speaker extraction robust to changes in array geometry and microphone number.

title: Clockwork: Scheduling Compound AI Systems in Space Data Centers
comment: Accepted at the IEEE/ACM International Conference on Utility and Cloud Computing (UCC 2026). 10 pages, 5 figures
summary: Space data centers built on LEO constellations create an opportunity to serve Compound AI workflows close to where observations are captured. Serving such a workflow for an area of interest (AoI) requires deciding which orbital planes to provision and where to place each workflow component, while orbital motion continuously changes which satellites can serve the AoI. Provisioning must therefore be planned as a sequence of decisions over time, and these decisions are coupled because changing component placements or activating new planes incurs costs. To address this, we present Clockwork, a framework for scheduling Compound AI workflows on space data centers under end-to-end latency SLOs. Clockwork has two components: i) Castor jointly selects active planes and component placements for each constellation snapshot, while ii) Pollux connects Castor's candidate provisioning states across predicted orbital evolution to construct a low-cost schedule over time. On our experimental two-shell constellation, Castor serves 81% of instances at a 300 ms SLO, while Pollux reduces mean total scheduling cost by 56% on average and by up to 63% compared to heuristic baselines.

AI.tldr: Clockwork is a framework for scheduling compound AI workflows on LEO space data centers under end-to-end latency SLOs; it jointly chooses orbital planes and component placements and plans them over time as orbits evolve. On a two-shell constellation, Castor serves 81% of instances at a 300 ms SLO and Pollux cuts mean total scheduling cost by 56%.
AI.motivation: Serving an area of interest from a LEO constellation requires provisioning decisions that change as orbital motion alters which satellites can serve it, and these decisions are coupled because moving components or activating planes incurs costs. Existing approaches do not address provisioning as a sequence of coupled decisions over time.
AI.method: Clockwork has two components: Castor, which jointly selects active orbital planes and component placements for each constellation snapshot, and Pollux, which links Castor's candidate provisioning states across predicted orbital evolution to build a low-cost schedule over time.
AI.result: On the experimental two-shell constellation, Castor serves 81% of instances at a 300 ms SLO, and Pollux reduces mean total scheduling cost by 56% on average and by up to 63% relative to heuristic baselines.
AI.conclusion: Planning provisioning as a time-coupled sequence rather than per-snapshot decisions lowers scheduling cost for compound AI workflows in space data centers while meeting latency targets.

title: Illusion: Safeguarding Topology Confidentiality in LLM Multi-Agent Systems via Behavior-Preserving Obfuscation
summary: The communication topology of Large Language Model Multi-Agent Systems (LLM-MASs) governs how information propagates among agents and encodes critical domain knowledge and expert workflow design. It is valuable intellectual property and plays a decisive role in system utility and safety, yet remains vulnerable to inference attacks that stealthily reconstruct it from agent outputs. Existing defenses detect or mitigate such attacks but do not proactively conceal the topology itself. We propose \textit{Illusion}, a proactive topology obfuscation defense for LLM-MAS. \textit{Illusion} injects fake edges and fake messages to present attackers with a deceptive topology, while selecting low-impact candidates that preserve output-distribution equivalence and task-accuracy non-inferiority. The resulting fake edges are designed to be indistinguishable from genuine messages under black-box observation. Extensive experiments show that \textit{Illusion} reduces edge-level F1 from over 0.87 to 0.62 and graph similarity from over 0.94 to 0.71. It also largely preserves output distributions and task performance, and its fake edges resist both similarity-based and LLM-judge filtering, even under adaptive pruning.

AI.tldr: Illusion is a proactive topology obfuscation defense for LLM multi-agent systems that injects fake edges and fake messages to hide the true communication graph from attackers. It cuts edge-level F1 of topology reconstruction attacks from over 0.87 to 0.62 while largely preserving output distributions and task performance.
AI.motivation: The communication topology of LLM multi-agent systems encodes valuable domain knowledge and workflow design, yet it can be stealthily reconstructed from agent outputs by inference attacks. Existing defenses detect or mitigate such attacks but do not conceal the topology itself.
AI.method: Illusion injects fake edges and fake messages to present a deceptive topology, selecting low-impact candidates that preserve output-distribution equivalence and task-accuracy non-inferiority. The fake edges are designed to be indistinguishable from genuine messages under black-box observation.
AI.result: Edge-level F1 drops from over 0.87 to 0.62 and graph similarity from over 0.94 to 0.71. Output distributions and task performance are largely preserved, and the fake edges resist similarity-based and LLM-judge filtering, even under adaptive pruning.
AI.conclusion: Proactively concealing the topology is a practical defense for protecting the intellectual property and safety-relevant structure of LLM multi-agent systems without degrading their utility.

title: SNAPPerf: Software-Aware Tabular Foundation Model for Retraining-Free Performance Prediction of Configurable Systems
summary: Modern software systems expose hundreds of configuration options whose combinations can substantially affect execution time, memory and energy usage. Measuring software performance resulting from a configuration set requires running a realistic workload. Since the configuration space grows exponentially, exhaustive benchmarking is infeasible. Prior work therefore trains models on a small set of measured configurations to predict the performance of the rest. Yet these models are specific to a particular software version, hardware platform, and workload, so changes require new measurements and retraining, and such changes are becoming more frequent with coding agents. We challenge this per-system training assumption with SNAPPERF (Software-aware, No-retraining, Adaptive Prediction), a sample-efficient tabular foundation model specialized for configurable software. SNAPPERF is pretrained once on synthetic data. Each new update only requires a few measured configurations as context to predict the rest without any per-system training or hyperparameter tuning. Across 39,866 configurations from 12 real-world systems, spanning 6 domains and 4 performance metrics, SNAPPERF reduces prediction error by 38% over the prior state of the art at the same measurement budget, and by 25% over the best general-purpose tabular foundation model. It matches the state of the art's accuracy with 54% fewer measurements on average. These results suggest that knowledge about software can be encoded in pretraining data rather than in per-system models, opening a new research direction in software-aware pretraining.

AI.tldr: SNAPPerf is a tabular foundation model for predicting the performance of configurable software that is pretrained once on synthetic data and needs no retraining for new versions, hardware, or workloads. Across 39,866 configurations from 12 real systems it reduces prediction error by 38% over the prior state of the art at the same measurement budget.
AI.motivation: Performance models for configurable software are trained per system version, hardware and workload, so each change needs new measurements and retraining. This is costly because the configuration space grows exponentially and coding agents make software changes more frequent.
AI.method: SNAPPerf is a sample-efficient, software-aware tabular foundation model pretrained on synthetic data. For a new update it takes a few measured configurations as context and predicts the rest without per-system training or hyperparameter tuning.
AI.result: Across 39,866 configurations from 12 real-world systems, spanning 6 domains and 4 performance metrics, SNAPPerf reduces prediction error by 38% over the prior state of the art at the same budget and by 25% over the best general-purpose tabular foundation model. It matches the state of the art's accuracy with 54% fewer measurements on average.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge about software can be encoded in pretraining data rather than in per-system models, which suggests a new research direction in software-aware pretraining.

title: Testing concept-level audits of melanoma classifiers with diffusion counterfactuals and matched positive controls
comment: 25 pages, 7 figures, 9 tables. Under review at Scientific Reports. Code and data at this https URL
summary: Concept-based explanations of melanoma classifiers are rarely tested against controls with known targets. We built a counterfactual audit from a diffusion model conditioned on seven 7-point checklist concepts and tested it with such controls. Colour-calibrated start noise reduced colour outliers from 78.5-84.8\% to 6.6-13.3\%. Four of seven knobs were target-dominant but also changed other concepts. Quartile-based positive controls were confounded, and the audit failed its pre-specified rule. It recovered the targets of all 16 controls matched on the generator's pseudo-labels and of 12 of 12 controls labelled by a second evaluator, for three concepts; concept activation vectors recovered fewer (11 of 16). In 18 permuted-label classifiers, significant sweep responses and target rankings also arose, whereas standardised effect margins separated the controls from these null classifiers. The pigmentation sweep raised the melanoma logit in 15 of 15 ISIC 2020 classifiers (+3.12 on average) and 6 of 6 HAM10000 classifiers (+4.01), about four times the null response in scale-free units; the regression effect did not transfer. An exploratory decomposition, evaluated against the controls, suggested that knob cross-talk partly hides vascular responses. Matched controls and null classifiers are practical checks of concept audits.

AI.tldr: The paper tests concept-level audits of melanoma classifiers using diffusion-model counterfactuals with matched positive controls and permuted-label null classifiers. The audit recovers the targets of 16 of 16 matched controls, but the pre-specified rule fails and some concept effects are confounded by knob cross-talk.
AI.motivation: Concept-based explanations of melanoma classifiers are rarely tested against controls with known targets, so their reliability is unverified.
AI.method: A counterfactual audit is built from a diffusion model conditioned on seven 7-point checklist concepts, with colour-calibrated start noise to limit colour outliers. It is validated with quartile-based and matched positive controls, concept activation vectors as a comparison, and 18 permuted-label classifiers as nulls, using standardised effect margins.
AI.result: Colour-calibrated noise reduced colour outliers from 78.5-84.8% to 6.6-13.3%. Four of seven knobs were target-dominant but also changed other concepts. Quartile-based controls were confounded and the audit failed its pre-specified rule, while the audit recovered the targets of all 16 controls matched on pseudo-labels and 12 of 12 controls labelled by a second evaluator, compared with 11 of 16 for concept activation vectors. Standardised effect margins separated controls from null classifiers. The pigmentation sweep raised the melanoma logit in 15 of 15 ISIC 2020 classifiers (+3.12 on average) and 6 of 6 HAM10000 classifiers (+4.01).
AI.conclusion: Matched controls and null classifiers are practical checks for concept audits, which should be applied before their explanations are trusted.

title: Refining Roadside 4D Radar Vehicle Classification Using Point-Cloud Dispersion
summary: Roadside sensing infrastructure is essential for Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS), but cameras and legacy sensors are limited in range, weather robustness, and depth accuracy. 4D radar complements these modalities by resolving range, azimuth, elevation, and radial velocity under adverse conditions, though its sparse, noisy point clouds make reliable classification difficult. We present a roadside multi-sensor platform combining a 4D radar and stereo depth camera under synchronized acquisition, used to collect a real-world dataset. Our analysis reveals a substantial class-distribution discrepancy between modalities, most notably a strong radar confusion between passenger cars and motorcycles (49.01% and\ 48.60% of the dataset). To address this, we propose a Neyman-Pearson-based binary classifier on the temporally-smoothed 2D positional standard deviation of radar point cloud clusters, reducing classification error from 52.1% to 42.7%. This lightweight and edge-deployable approach improves radar-only classification reliability and lays the foundation for future camera-radar fusion.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a roadside multi-sensor platform combining 4D radar and a stereo depth camera and proposes a lightweight Neyman-Pearson classifier on the temporally smoothed positional spread of radar point-cloud clusters. It reduces radar-only vehicle classification error from 52.1% to 42.7%.
AI.motivation: Cameras and legacy roadside sensors are limited in range, weather robustness and depth accuracy, while 4D radar is robust but produces sparse, noisy point clouds that make classification difficult. Radar also shows a strong class-distribution mismatch with the camera.
AI.method: The authors collect a real-world dataset with synchronized 4D radar and stereo camera acquisition. They propose a Neyman-Pearson binary classifier on the temporally smoothed 2D positional standard deviation of radar point-cloud clusters.
AI.result: Radar confuses passenger cars and motorcycles strongly (49.01% and 48.60% of the dataset). Classification error falls from 52.1% to 42.7% with the proposed classifier.
AI.conclusion: The approach is lightweight and edge-deployable, improves radar-only classification reliability, and lays the groundwork for future camera-radar fusion.

title: A conditional generative model for T2-weighted prostate MRI with downstream evaluation in clinically significant cancer classificatio
summary: Scarce and unrepresentative training data limit the performance of prostate MRI prediction models. Synthetic T2-weighted (T2W) MRI may augment training data containing clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) and transition zone (TZ) lesions. In this retrospective, single-center, ethics-committee-approved study, we developed a conditional generative model for T2W prostate MRI extending MAISI-v2 with csPCa class, zonal, and lesion-mask-guided conditioning, incorporating a relative advantage weighted loss fine-tuned on 1,303 patients (1,654 lesions). Fidelity was assessed by incremental ablation, and downstream utility was evaluated with T2W-based csPCa classifiers across five simulated training-data scenarios, each testing 18 synthetic-data configurations. The proposed model reduced Fréchet inception distance (FID) from 13.28 (pretrained MAISI-v2) to $2.04 \pm 0.06$ internally (PI-CAI: $3.83 \pm 0.51$). Synthetic augmentation significantly increased AUC in all five scenarios (+0.027 to +0.088; adjusted $p = 0.016$--$0.043$), though cross-institutional augmentation of PI-CAI yielded a non-significant gain (+0.013; $p = 0.397$). Overall, our model improved T2W MRI fidelity, and synthetic images improved csPCa classification under simulated data constraints, although benefit did not transfer significantly across institutions.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a conditional generative model for T2-weighted prostate MRI by extending MAISI-v2 with clinically significant cancer, zonal and lesion-mask conditioning, and tests whether the synthetic images help csPCa classifiers. Synthetic augmentation significantly increases AUC in all five simulated scenarios, but the gain does not transfer significantly across institutions.
AI.motivation: Scarce and unrepresentative training data limit prostate MRI prediction models, and synthetic T2W images could augment training data containing csPCa and transition-zone lesions.
AI.method: The model extends MAISI-v2 with csPCa class, zonal and lesion-mask-guided conditioning and a relative advantage weighted loss, fine-tuned on 1,303 patients with 1,654 lesions. Fidelity is assessed by incremental ablation, and downstream utility by T2W-based csPCa classifiers across five simulated training-data scenarios, each testing 18 synthetic-data configurations.
AI.result: The model reduces Frechet inception distance from 13.28 for pretrained MAISI-v2 to 2.04 plus or minus 0.06 internally (3.83 plus or minus 0.51 on PI-CAI). Synthetic augmentation significantly increases AUC in all five scenarios (+0.027 to +0.088; adjusted p from 0.016 to 0.043), while cross-institutional augmentation on PI-CAI gives a non-significant gain (+0.013; p = 0.397).
AI.conclusion: The model improves T2W MRI fidelity and synthetic images improve csPCa classification under simulated data constraints, although the benefit does not transfer significantly across institutions.

title: Depth Anyviewpoint? Evaluating Monocular Depth Over Viewpoint Sequences
summary: Monocular depth estimation aims to predict depth maps from single RGB images (forgoing the need for stereo camera pairs) and has seen impressive leaps in performance in recent work due to the introduction of affine-invariant losses and the use of foundation model features. These monocular depth models predict affine-invariant depth, which describes the relative positions of objects in the scene instead of absolute depth. While these models demonstrate strong performance on single image benchmarks and qualitatively consistent predictions in video, their effectiveness at preserving consistent spatial structure has been less thoroughly explored. Many potential real-world applications, such as handling video streams as input, rely on coherent three dimensional consistency in scenes. Further, anchoring relative depth predictions to a metric reference for a given scene is a key challenge for applying monocular depth models to real-world situations. We develop a novel evaluation protocol for monocular depth models using video sequences with moving camera positions to test the consistency of prediction across variation in viewpoint. We demonstrate this methodology over diverse, real-world video sequences where we are able to anchor depth model output to metric depth values using structure from motion. Our work demonstrates open challenges in the development of broadly applicable monocular depth foundation models, particularly with their ability to provide temporal consistency over long time frames. We also identify challenges in the straightforward adoption of structure-from-motion as a metric grounding tool for monocular depth estimation models.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an evaluation protocol for monocular depth models using video sequences with moving cameras to test spatial consistency across viewpoints. Using structure from motion to anchor predictions to metric depth, it shows open challenges in temporal consistency over long time frames for depth foundation models.
AI.motivation: Monocular depth models predict affine-invariant depth and perform well on single-image benchmarks, but their ability to preserve consistent 3D structure across viewpoints and video has been little explored. Anchoring relative depth to metric scale is also a key challenge for real-world use.
AI.method: The authors develop a novel evaluation protocol using video sequences with moving camera positions to measure prediction consistency across viewpoint changes. They anchor depth model outputs to metric depth values using structure from motion.
AI.result: The methodology is demonstrated on diverse real-world video sequences, where the depth outputs can be anchored to metric values. The abstract does not report specific quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: Open challenges remain for broadly applicable monocular depth foundation models, particularly temporal consistency over long horizons, and structure from motion has limits as a metric grounding tool for depth estimation.

title: Learning from high-resolution 2D images to reconstruct 3D microstructures
summary: High-resolution three-dimensional (3D) microstructure characterization remains difficult to undertake at scale because volumetric imaging at the required spatial resolution is expensive, time-consuming or destructive. In many settings, however, fine-resolution two-dimensional (2D) imaging and lower-resolution volumetric measurements are both readily available. We introduce a Privileged Cross-modal Relational Distillation (PCRD) framework that leverages fine-resolution 2D observations during training to improve specimen-specific 3D reconstruction from lower-resolution volumetric imaging alone. We demonstrate PCRD on pultruded carbon fiber-reinforced polymer composites, using scanning electron microscopy as the privileged modality and micro-CT as the inference input. The framework transfers spatial organization by matching similarity distributions defined around corresponding spatial anchors in the teacher and student representations, avoiding direct alignment of heterogeneous feature vectors. In 2D cross-sectional reconstruction, PCRD improves mAP by 1.66 percentage points over direct micro-CT training. Independent 3D validation against high-resolution synchrotron X-ray CT data shows close agreement in fiber volume fraction, diameter and local spacing. The PCRD reconstruction matches 89.97% of the reference fiber centerline length, compared with 75.08% for the interpolated low-resolution volume.
