AI.tldr: PCRD is a privileged cross-modal relational distillation framework that uses fine-resolution 2D SEM images during training to improve 3D reconstruction of composite microstructures from micro-CT alone. It improves 2D cross-sectional mAP by 1.66 points over direct micro-CT training, and its 3D reconstructions agree closely with synchrotron CT reference data.
AI.motivation: High-resolution 3D microstructure characterization is expensive, slow or destructive, while fine 2D images and lower-resolution volumes are often available. Existing transfer approaches do not exploit the fine 2D observations for the 3D inference task.
AI.method: PCRD transfers spatial organization by matching similarity distributions around corresponding spatial anchors in teacher and student representations, avoiding direct alignment of heterogeneous feature vectors. It is demonstrated on pultruded carbon fiber-reinforced polymer composites with SEM as the privileged modality and micro-CT as the inference input.
AI.result: In 2D cross-sectional reconstruction, PCRD improves mAP by 1.66 percentage points over direct micro-CT training. Independent 3D validation against high-resolution synchrotron X-ray CT shows close agreement in fiber volume fraction, diameter and local spacing, and the reconstruction matches 89.97% of the reference fiber centerline length versus 75.08% for the interpolated low-resolution volume.
AI.conclusion: Privileged fine-resolution 2D observations used during training can improve specimen-specific 3D reconstruction from lower-resolution volumetric imaging alone.

title: Forecasting Earth Surface Change in Embedding Space
summary: Repeated satellite imagery permits understanding of how our planet changes over time, letting us predict its future and plan mitigating actions. Most existing studies that rely on a time series of satellite observations forecast the spectral values at each pixel for a future target date. However, clouds, shadows, and sensor noise often corrupt these observations, so that spectral forecasters waste much of their capacity on low-level features or noise rather than real change. With the advent of Earth foundation models, we argue that forecasting in embedding space is a feasible and more effective alternative. To this end, we design a token space that handles irregular histories from different sensors and foundation models and supports forecasts at any query date. Tokens from this space are inputs to our proposed forecaster, E$^2$Forecast, which is a transformer with two branches: a Gaussian branch that directly predicts a mean point forecast and per-dimension standard deviations, and a rectified-flow branch that generates forecast ensembles. On Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 benchmarks, forecasting embeddings instead of spectral values halves the cosine distance (from 0.20 to 0.10) and greatly reduces overconfidence, lowering the z-score standard deviation from 2.63 to 1.22. By comparing new observations with its forecasts, E$^2$Forecast can also detect anomalous changes without labels or retraining, raising F$_1$ from 41.58 to 48.70 on a global benchmark. This consistent superiority is validated on nine remote sensing foundation models. Beyond change detection, we believe our approach advances the field by permitting effective reuse of diverse pretrained task heads. Our code is publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: E2Forecast forecasts Earth surface change in an embedding space rather than per-pixel spectral values, using a transformer with a Gaussian branch and a rectified-flow branch. On Sentinel benchmarks it halves the cosine distance (0.20 to 0.10) and detects anomalous change without labels, raising F1 from 41.58 to 48.70 on a global benchmark.
AI.motivation: Spectral forecasters of satellite time series spend capacity on clouds, shadows and sensor noise rather than real change, and existing approaches do not handle irregular histories from different sensors and foundation models.
AI.method: The authors design a token space that handles irregular histories from different sensors and foundation models and supports forecasts at any query date. E2Forecast is a transformer with a Gaussian branch that predicts a mean and per-dimension standard deviations and a rectified-flow branch that generates forecast ensembles.
AI.result: On Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 benchmarks, forecasting embeddings halves the cosine distance from 0.20 to 0.10 and lowers the z-score standard deviation from 2.63 to 1.22, reducing overconfidence. Anomaly detection without labels or retraining raises F1 from 41.58 to 48.70 on a global benchmark. The superiority holds across nine remote sensing foundation models.
AI.conclusion: Forecasting in embedding space is more effective than forecasting spectral values, and it allows reuse of diverse pretrained task heads beyond change detection.

title: SVD-Prune: Spectral Vision Token Pruning under Extreme Compression
comment: Accepted at WACV 2027. Code available at this https URL
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models process hundreds of visual tokens, making visual representations a major computational bottleneck. We argue that visual token pruning should be formulated not as identifying individually important tokens, but as preserving the dominant low-rank spectral structure of the visual representation. Based on this formulation, we introduce SVD-Prune, a training-free framework that leverages Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and statistical leverage scores for globally informed token selection. SVD-Prune is architecture-agnostic and can be applied at different stages of the multimodal pipeline, including encoder-side, decoder-side, and hybrid configurations Extensive experiments across VLM and VLA benchmarks demonstrate strong robustness under extreme compression. SVD-Prune reduces the visual token. SVD-Prune cuts the visual token budget by up to 99.3%, while, at a 16-token budget, encoder-side pruning lowers inference FLOPs by 82.4% and achieves a 4.18x end-to-end speedup, including pruning overhead.

AI.tldr: SVD-Prune is a training-free visual token pruning method that preserves the dominant low-rank spectral structure of visual representations using SVD and statistical leverage scores. It cuts the visual token budget by up to 99.3%, and at a 16-token budget encoder-side pruning lowers inference FLOPs by 82.4% with a 4.18x end-to-end speedup.
AI.motivation: VLMs and VLA models process hundreds of visual tokens, which makes visual representations a major computational bottleneck. Pruning individually important tokens is the wrong formulation when the goal is to keep the global structure of the representation.
AI.method: SVD-Prune uses singular value decomposition and statistical leverage scores for globally informed token selection. It is architecture-agnostic and can be applied at the encoder side, the decoder side, or in hybrid configurations of the multimodal pipeline.
AI.result: The method shows robustness under extreme compression across VLM and VLA benchmarks. It cuts the visual token budget by up to 99.3%. At a 16-token budget, encoder-side pruning lowers inference FLOPs by 82.4% and gives a 4.18x end-to-end speedup including pruning overhead.
AI.conclusion: Framing visual token pruning as preservation of low-rank spectral structure gives strong efficiency gains under extreme compression without training.

title: Peripheral prototypical contrastive loss for supervised medical image segmentation
summary: Robust segmentation of biomedical images remains challenging primarily due to ill-defined object boundaries. Although several loss functions have recently been proposed to enhance object boundary recognition, concerns remain about the susceptibility to unstable annotations resulting from boundary ambiguities. Here, we introduce the Peripheral Prototypical Contrastive (PPC) loss, which leverages prototypical contrastive learning to improve boundary recognition and enable stable training even under noisy annotation conditions. The PPC loss utilizes prototype features obtained from local regions near object boundaries, focusing specifically on ambiguous areas that have been challenging for existing approaches. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets demonstrated that the PPC loss consistently improve segmentation performance even under conditions with noisy labels. A newly proposed strategy, which adaptively determines the local region for prototype calculation, enhanced robustness and outperformed existing methods. Our findings indicate the potential of the PPC loss in facilitating scalable and reliable medical image segmentation, including the development of foundation models with imperfect annotations.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Peripheral Prototypical Contrastive loss for medical image segmentation, which uses prototypes from regions near object boundaries to improve boundary recognition. It consistently improves segmentation across multiple datasets, including under noisy labels.
AI.motivation: Biomedical segmentation is hard mainly because object boundaries are ill-defined, and existing boundary losses are sensitive to unstable annotations caused by boundary ambiguity.
AI.method: The PPC loss uses prototypical contrastive learning with prototype features from local regions near object boundaries, focusing on the ambiguous areas. A newly proposed strategy adaptively determines the local region used for prototype calculation.
AI.result: The PPC loss consistently improves segmentation performance across multiple datasets, including conditions with noisy labels. The adaptive region strategy enhances robustness and outperforms existing methods.
AI.conclusion: The PPC loss shows potential for scalable and reliable medical image segmentation, including foundation models trained with imperfect annotations.

title: Lie Routing Vision Language Models for View-Robust 3D Understanding
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have made substantial progress in 3D scene understanding from multi-view RGB observations. Yet a fixed object and query can elicit inconsistent target-related responses across camera viewpoints, a phenomenon we characterize as viewpoint-induced semantic drift. We introduce LieVLM, a Lie routing framework for view-robust 3D understanding. Motivated by the rotational component of viewpoint change, Lie routing adapts visual representations by applying local $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ transformations to projected features within learned three-dimensional subspaces. Geometry tokens extracted by VGGT predict local rotation parameters and channel-wise routing coefficients. A closed-form Padé--Cayley map transforms projected visual features, whose identity-relative corrections are projected back and gated into the original visual and geometry features. This design retains the pretrained semantic and direct spatial context while learning view-dependent feature adjustments. Experiments on 3D captioning, grounding, detection, and spatial reasoning show consistent improvements over additive fusion across training scales and backbones. Controlled ablations examine the roles of geometric conditioning and transformation structure. Viewpoint analyses further reveal systematic variation in the predicted routing states alongside more localized target responses and stronger task performance across viewpoint changes.

AI.tldr: LieVLM is a Lie routing framework that makes multimodal LLMs robust to viewpoint changes in 3D scene understanding by applying local SO(3) transformations to projected visual features. It yields consistent gains over additive fusion on 3D captioning, grounding, detection and spatial reasoning across training scales and backbones.
AI.motivation: A fixed object and query can elicit inconsistent target-related responses across camera viewpoints, a phenomenon called viewpoint-induced semantic drift. Motivated by the rotational component of viewpoint change, the authors seek view-dependent feature adjustments.
AI.method: Lie routing applies local SO(3) transformations to projected features within learned three-dimensional subspaces. Geometry tokens from VGGT predict local rotation parameters and channel-wise routing coefficients, and a closed-form Pade-Cayley map transforms the features. The corrections are projected back and gated into the original visual and geometry features.
AI.result: Experiments on 3D captioning, grounding, detection and spatial reasoning show consistent improvements over additive fusion across training scales and backbones. Controlled ablations examine geometric conditioning and transformation structure, and viewpoint analyses show systematic variation in routing states with more localized target responses.
AI.conclusion: Gated, geometry-conditioned rotational routing preserves pretrained semantic and spatial context while learning view-dependent adjustments that reduce viewpoint-induced drift.

title: The DynaCell Evaluation Suite for Dynamic 3D Virtual Staining of Live Cells
comment: 64 pages: 10-page main text with 4 figures and 1 table, plus references and a 49-page appendix with 15 figures and 25 tables. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, Track on Evaluations and Datasets
summary: Understanding how cells respond to perturbations over time is central to cell biology and drug discovery. Live-cell imaging captures the dynamics of perturbation-induced phenotypes in individual cells. While fluorescence imaging can visualize specific molecular phenotypes, labeling and repeated illumination often affect cell health. Virtual staining offers an alternative by predicting these fluorescence images from images acquired without fluorescent labels. Although many virtual staining models have been developed, their performance on volumetric time-lapse data remains poorly characterized. We address this gap with an evaluation suite for 3D time-lapse virtual staining of live cells. The suite combines paired 3D time-lapse images acquired with and without fluorescent labels, a set of baseline models, and three metric tiers measuring pixel-level fidelity, organelle segmentation performance, and single-cell phenotype similarity. Using this evaluation suite, we study metric and model behavior across 3 cell types, 2 microscopes, 4 organelles, and 3 perturbation states. We find that regression baselines better predict the spatial localization of target organelles, whereas the generative baseline better captures the distribution of phenotypes across cells. These differences expose trade-offs between structural and phenotypic fidelity that are obscured by single-metric evaluation and suggest how virtual staining models can be developed for diverse downstream tasks such as localization, segmentation, tracking, and phenotypic profiling. We release the curated datasets, baseline checkpoints, and evaluation code as part of DynaCell, a broader framework for image-based profiling of cell-state dynamics.

AI.tldr: DynaCell is an evaluation suite for 3D time-lapse virtual staining of live cells that combines paired labelled and unlabelled volumes, baseline models and three metric tiers. It shows that regression baselines better localize organelles while the generative baseline better captures the phenotype distribution across cells.
AI.motivation: Virtual staining can predict fluorescence images from label-free images and avoid label-induced cell damage, but the performance of these models on volumetric time-lapse data is poorly characterized.
AI.method: The evaluation suite pairs 3D time-lapse images acquired with and without fluorescent labels, includes a set of baseline models, and measures pixel-level fidelity, organelle segmentation performance and single-cell phenotype similarity. The study covers 3 cell types, 2 microscopes, 4 organelles and 3 perturbation states.
AI.result: Regression baselines better predict the spatial localization of target organelles, whereas the generative baseline better captures the distribution of phenotypes across cells. Single-metric evaluation obscures these trade-offs between structural and phenotypic fidelity.
AI.conclusion: Models should be developed and judged with multiple metric tiers for downstream tasks such as localization, segmentation, tracking and phenotypic profiling. Curated datasets, baseline checkpoints and evaluation code are released as part of DynaCell.

title: Findings-aware Language-Image Pretraining for CT Volume Interpretation
summary: Computed tomography (CT) provides diverse patient information and various clinical tasks, for which numerous deep learning models have been investigated. Recent years have seen the development of vision-language foundation models that can comprehensively extract clinical features, driven by representation learning that combines CT volumes with radiology reports. Existing approaches typically adopt Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP)-based representation learning, where pairs from different cases are, in principle, treated as negative pairs such that the volume and report embeddings are pushed apart. In the biomedical imaging, however, treating different cases as negative pairs is not always appropriate, particularly when clinical similarity exists. In this study, we propose a supervised representation learning framework grounded in clinical knowledge from language foundation models, rather than the weak supervision used in CLIP. Specifically, we utilized a large language model to extract abnormal finding phrases from reports. We then explicitly constructed the target features that the image encoder should output, as the semantic representation of the extracted findings using a biomedical text embedding model. Our Findings-aware Language-Image Pre-training (FiLIP) outperformed weakly supervised approaches in multi-label zero-shot finding classification in both in-domain and external-domain evaluations, and also proved effective when fine-tuned for the downstream task of radiology report generation.

AI.tldr: FiLIP is a supervised language-image pretraining framework for CT volumes that replaces CLIP-style negatives with target features built from abnormal findings extracted from reports by an LLM and embedded with a biomedical text model. It outperforms weakly supervised approaches on multi-label zero-shot finding classification and transfers to radiology report generation.
AI.motivation: CLIP-based pretraining treats different cases as negative pairs, which is not appropriate in biomedical imaging when clinically similar cases exist. Existing approaches rely on weak supervision.
AI.method: A large language model extracts abnormal finding phrases from radiology reports. The target features that the image encoder should output are then built explicitly as embeddings of these findings from a biomedical text embedding model, grounded in clinical knowledge from language foundation models.
AI.result: FiLIP outperforms weakly supervised approaches in multi-label zero-shot finding classification in both in-domain and external-domain evaluations. It is also effective when fine-tuned for radiology report generation.
AI.conclusion: Supervised, clinically grounded target construction is a better basis for CT vision-language pretraining than weak CLIP-style contrastive supervision.

title: AgiWorld: An Agentic Video World Model for Building Persistent Worlds
summary: Recent interactive video world models generate visually compelling videos from a single image, following user-provided camera motion and text prompts. However, such low-level control demands substantial user effort to realize a high-level intent, and the generated world struggles to remain persistent as the exploration proceeds. In this work, we present AgiWorld, an agentic video world model that explores and builds a persistent world from a single image and a free-form instruction. For high-level planning, our agent AgiWorld-Agent designs the world and the journey through it in a world state and directs the exploration. For low-level realization, our video world model AgiWorld-WM generates the video chunk by chunk and stores it with its geometry in a spatial memory, from which the agent updates its world state. This closed loop keeps the world faithful to the user's intent and keeps the agent's world state consistent with the generated content throughout the exploration. We co-design the two levels around the shared spatial memory and an interface of metric camera trajectories and structured prompts. In AgiWorld-WM, to handle occlusion and accumulated geometric errors in the spatial memory over long rollouts, we propose occlusion-aware history selection, which retrieves past views by surface visibility, and reliability-based memory maintenance, which prefers reliable geometry and earlier observations. AgiWorld-WM achieves state-of-the-art overall performance on world revisiting and exploration benchmarks, and qualitative results and ablations show that AgiWorld builds persistent worlds from free-form instructions over minute-long journeys. Persistence thus arises not from the video model alone but from its closed loop with the agent.

AI.tldr: AgiWorld is an agentic video world model that builds a persistent world from a single image and a free-form instruction, with a planning agent and a video generator linked through a shared spatial memory. It achieves state-of-the-art overall performance on world revisiting and exploration benchmarks and builds persistent worlds over minute-long journeys.
AI.motivation: Interactive video world models need low-level camera control that demands substantial user effort to realize high-level intent, and the generated worlds struggle to stay persistent as exploration proceeds.
AI.method: AgiWorld-Agent designs the world and the journey in a world state and directs exploration. AgiWorld-WM generates video chunk by chunk and stores it with its geometry in spatial memory. The two levels share the spatial memory and an interface of metric camera trajectories and structured prompts. Occlusion-aware history selection retrieves past views by surface visibility, and reliability-based memory maintenance prefers reliable geometry and earlier observations.
AI.result: AgiWorld-WM achieves state-of-the-art overall performance on world revisiting and exploration benchmarks. Qualitative results and ablations show persistent worlds built from free-form instructions over minute-long journeys.
AI.conclusion: Persistence arises from the closed loop between the agent and the video model rather than from the video model alone.

title: Exploiting Textual Semantics for Robust Cross-View Object Correspondence
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. 12 figures, 12 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Cross-view object correspondence (CVOC) aims to establish associations of the same target between query and search videos captured from different viewpoints. Existing methods often rely on visual cues for CVOC. Despite recent progress, these methods struggle in complicated scenarios with substantial viewpoint changes and appearance variations, due to lacking sufficient target information. Addressing this, we introduce TeSCo, a framework that exploits rich Textual Semantics of an object, in addition to its visual cues, for cross-view object Correspondence. Our key insight is, textual description of a target, by capturing diverse attributes such as category, texture, and color, provides viewpoint- and appearance-invariant semantics, which are complementary to visual cues and can hence enhance correspondence robustness in complicated scenes. Inspired by this, TeSCo first generates a textual expression of the target from the given query view using a vision-language model, and then extracts textual feature to enhance visual features for localization in the search view. To realize this, we introduce a text-conditioned cross-modal fusion (TCF) module that incorporates the textual feature into visual features with text-guided modulation, producing more robust multimodal target representation for object correspondence. Since not all textual cues are equally compatible with the target in current search-view frame, we propose an iterative textual feature refinement (ITFR) module that progressively adjusts textual feature using search-view information before the TCF module, enabling search-view-aware textual semantics to be fused into visual features and leading to better performance. In extensive experiments on Ego-Exo4D and HANDAL-X, TeSCo demonstrates state-of-the-art results and largely outperforms other models, validating its efficacy. Our code is released at this https URL.

AI.tldr: TeSCo improves cross-view object correspondence by generating a textual description of the target with a vision-language model and fusing its features with visual cues. It achieves state-of-the-art results on Ego-Exo4D and HANDAL-X.
AI.motivation: Existing cross-view correspondence methods rely on visual cues and struggle under large viewpoint changes and appearance variation, because they lack sufficient target information.
AI.method: TeSCo generates a textual expression of the target from the query view using a vision-language model and extracts textual features. An iterative textual feature refinement module adjusts these features using search-view information, and a text-conditioned cross-modal fusion module injects them into visual features through text-guided modulation.
AI.result: On Ego-Exo4D and HANDAL-X, TeSCo demonstrates state-of-the-art results and largely outperforms other models.
AI.conclusion: Textual semantics, which are invariant to viewpoint and appearance, are complementary to visual cues and make correspondence more robust in complicated scenes.

title: GEAR: Generative Editing for Scene-Conditioned Outfit Retrieval for VR Travel
summary: In virtual environments, choosing appropriate outfits requires contextual harmony with surrounding scenes, yet bridging the visual gap between 3D ambient views and catalog garment assets remains challenging. This paper investigates scene-conditioned outfit retrieval for interactive 3D environments, where a user's egocentric view serves as the retrieval signal. We present GEAR (Generative Editing for Asset Retrieval), a framework that bridges the cross-domain gap by synthesizing intermediate visual queries rather than predicting direct compatibility. GEAR uses a vision-language model to describe suitable clothing from a captured scene, employs an instruction-guided diffusion model to render the concept onto a standardized reference character, and utilizes the cropped clothing region to retrieve existing 2D outfit assets via embedding similarity. An interactive Unity prototype demonstrates real-time scene capture, asset retrieval, and in-engine 3D avatar fitting. We benchmark GEAR against direct visual similarity, aesthetic scoring, and VLM-based reranking on a controlled dataset using automated Swiss-system pairwise judgments, where GEAR achieves competitive top-ranked performance (mean Elo@5 of 1012.75 and top-10 overlap of 0.180) alongside 0.539 pairwise agreement. Furthermore, a user study across 20 virtual travel scenes demonstrates that GEAR achieves the highest overall participant preference in both visual appeal (34.5%) and contextual suitability (34.5%).

AI.tldr: GEAR retrieves outfits for a user's egocentric view in VR by generating intermediate visual queries with a VLM and an instruction-guided diffusion model, then retrieving 2D outfit assets by embedding similarity. It achieves the highest overall participant preference in a 20-scene user study and is competitive on automated ranking metrics.
AI.motivation: Choosing outfits in virtual environments requires contextual harmony with the scene, but the visual gap between 3D ambient views and catalog garment assets makes direct retrieval difficult.
AI.method: A vision-language model describes suitable clothing from the captured scene, and an instruction-guided diffusion model renders that concept onto a standardized reference character. The cropped clothing region is used to retrieve existing 2D outfit assets by embedding similarity. An interactive Unity prototype demonstrates real-time capture, retrieval and avatar fitting.
AI.result: Against direct visual similarity, aesthetic scoring and VLM-based reranking, GEAR achieves a mean Elo@5 of 1012.75 and a top-10 overlap of 0.180, with 0.539 pairwise agreement. In a user study across 20 virtual travel scenes, it earns the highest preference for visual appeal (34.5%) and contextual suitability (34.5%).
AI.conclusion: Generating an intermediate visual query bridges the cross-domain gap better than direct compatibility prediction for scene-conditioned outfit retrieval in VR.

title: IMUdrape: Generating Garment-Mounted Virtual IMU Data from Text through Physics-Based Cloth Simulation
comment: 34 pages, 7 figures, 15 tables. Under review. Project page: this https URL
summary: Inertial sensors are moving into clothing, from sensorized sportswear to garments instrumented with hundreds of IMUs. Sewn into clothing, a sensor no longer moves rigidly with the body: loose fabric slides, twists and swings, so a garment-mounted sensor records the motion of the fabric as well as that of the body, and this extra motion differs from one garment to the next. Models for such sensors need training data recorded with the deployed garment, yet labeled data are scarce. Virtual IMU data generated from videos or text have eased this scarcity for body-attached sensors, but existing generators attach their virtual sensors rigidly to the body. We present IMUdrape, which generates garment-mounted virtual IMU data from text through physics-based cloth simulation. IMUdrape synthesizes motion from activity descriptions, reconstructs the target garment as a sewing pattern from photographs, places virtual IMUs at the deployment's real sensor positions, and simulates the garment with an intersection-free contact solver, so that every simulation yields paired garment and body signals. On four real datasets with clothing-mounted sensors, IMUdrape improves on existing virtual-data approaches for both activity recognition and full-body pose estimation. With one real subject, its data improve recognition macro-F1 by 7% to 46% over real data alone and by 2% to 11% over body-mounted virtual data from the same motion. When the garment is simulated on recorded motion, the pose error without any real training data falls by 30% to 33% relative to generated motion, and garment data remain 12% more accurate than body data. IMUdrape thus reduces the amount of real data that garment-mounted sensing requires.

AI.tldr: IMUdrape generates virtual IMU data for garment-mounted sensors from text using physics-based cloth simulation with an intersection-free contact solver, producing paired garment and body signals. It improves activity recognition and pose estimation over existing virtual-data approaches on four real datasets.
AI.motivation: Sensors sewn into clothing move with the fabric as well as the body, and this motion differs between garments. Training data recorded with the deployed garment is scarce, while existing virtual IMU generators attach sensors rigidly to the body.
AI.method: IMUdrape synthesizes motion from activity descriptions, reconstructs the target garment as a sewing pattern from photographs, places virtual IMUs at the real sensor positions of the deployment, and simulates the garment with an intersection-free contact solver, so each simulation yields paired garment and body signals.
AI.result: With one real subject, its data improve recognition macro-F1 by 7% to 46% over real data alone and by 2% to 11% over body-mounted virtual data from the same motion. On recorded motion, pose error without real training data falls by 30% to 33% relative to generated motion, and garment data are 12% more accurate than body data.
AI.conclusion: Garment-mounted virtual data reduces the amount of real data needed for garment-mounted sensing.

title: TERA: Task-Evidence Restoration for Underwater Object Detection under Bandwidth-Constrained Transmission
summary: Underwater object detectors are typically evaluated on pre-transmission images, overlooking additional degradation from bandwidth-constrained downscaling and compression. We introduce AquaTX, a controlled benchmark built from real underwater detection datasets with seen and held-out codecs. We also propose TERA, a metadata-blind receiver-side framework combining task-guided pixel restoration and dual-state feature correction while keeping the detector frozen. Under seen compound degradation, TERA improves mean average precision (mAP50:95, averaged over IoU thresholds from 0.50 to 0.95) from 37.7 to 50.0 on DUO-TX and from 31.5 to 41.3 on RUOD-TX relative to the frozen detector without restoration. TERA also preserves clean-input performance and remains competitive with detector fine-tuning under the held-out AVIF codec. These findings support transmission-aware evaluation and task-guided restoration for underwater object detection. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: TERA is a receiver-side framework that restores underwater images degraded by bandwidth-constrained downscaling and compression while keeping the detector frozen, and it is evaluated on a new AquaTX benchmark. It raises mAP50:95 from 37.7 to 50.0 on DUO-TX and from 31.5 to 41.3 on RUOD-TX under seen compound degradation.
AI.motivation: Underwater object detectors are typically evaluated on pre-transmission images and ignore the extra degradation introduced by bandwidth-constrained downscaling and compression.
AI.method: AquaTX is a controlled benchmark built from real underwater detection datasets with seen and held-out codecs. TERA is a metadata-blind receiver-side framework that combines task-guided pixel restoration and dual-state feature correction while keeping the detector frozen.
AI.result: Under seen compound degradation, TERA improves mAP50:95 from 37.7 to 50.0 on DUO-TX and from 31.5 to 41.3 on RUOD-TX relative to the frozen detector without restoration. It preserves clean-input performance and remains competitive with detector fine-tuning under the held-out AVIF codec.
AI.conclusion: Transmission-aware evaluation and task-guided restoration are effective for underwater object detection under bandwidth constraints.

title: Blueprint2CAD: Benchmarking Foundation Models on Engineering Drawing-to-CAD Render Correspondence
summary: Engineering drawings specify mechanical parts through orthographic projections. Recognizing which part a drawing depicts underlies part search, design reuse, and digitization, yet no public benchmark measures whether vision models can do it. We introduce Blueprint2CAD, a benchmark for drawing-to-render correspondence: given an orthographic line drawing and a shaded render, usually from another viewpoint, decide whether they show the same part. Its data layer, BlueCAD-30K, applies an open drafting pipeline to 29,925 Zero-to-CAD models, adding view-aligned renders, clean and dimensioned drawings from six viewpoints, and surface-type metadata. Frozen encoders retrieve the matching part from a 10,000-model gallery with up to 65% Recall@1 when viewpoints are known but 43% when they are not, and the four encoders we test lie within six points of each other: viewpoint, not backbone, is the bottleneck. Six zero-shot vision-language models reach only 0.52-0.67 verification accuracy, with model-specific Yes/No biases that chain-of-thought shifts but does not remove; a quick LoRA fine-tuning on in-domain pairs improves verification accuracy by a few points but sharpens these biases and leaves the viewpoint failure intact.

AI.tldr: Blueprint2CAD is a benchmark for deciding whether an orthographic engineering drawing and a shaded render show the same mechanical part, built on BlueCAD-30K with 29,925 models. Viewpoint, not the backbone, is the bottleneck for frozen encoders, and six zero-shot vision-language models reach only 0.52 to 0.67 verification accuracy.
AI.motivation: Engineering drawings specify mechanical parts, and recognizing which part a drawing depicts underlies part search and design reuse, but no public benchmark measures whether vision models can do this.
AI.method: The data layer applies an open drafting pipeline to 29,925 Zero-to-CAD models, adding view-aligned renders, clean and dimensioned drawings from six viewpoints, and surface-type metadata. Frozen encoders retrieve matches from a 10,000-model gallery, six zero-shot VLMs are evaluated for verification, and a quick LoRA fine-tune is tested on in-domain pairs.
AI.result: Frozen encoders reach up to 65% Recall@1 when viewpoints are known and 43% when they are not, and the four encoders lie within six points of each other. Zero-shot VLMs reach 0.52 to 0.67 verification accuracy with model-specific Yes/No biases that chain-of-thought shifts but does not remove. LoRA fine-tuning improves accuracy by a few points but sharpens these biases and leaves the viewpoint failure intact.
AI.conclusion: Viewpoint mismatch between drawing and render is the main obstacle for drawing-to-CAD correspondence, and fine-tuning alone does not resolve it.

title: Evaluating Synthetic Skin Lesion Images for Classifier Training: A Safety-Aware Algorithm
comment: 57 pages, 12 figures. Code to reproduce all experiments, along with links to the full Zenodo dataset and the synth-curator package, can be found at this https URL
summary: Skin cancer classifiers need large sets of annotated images, which are scarce, especially for rare lesion types. AI-generated images can fill the gap, but a generator produces images of widely varying quality, so selecting which images to retain is important. That choice usually rests on a single quality score, most often the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), which has not been tested against what a classifier needs and cannot tell whether the generator memorizes its training photographs. We test that practice with a tournament of 16 quality metrics. Each metric alone selects a training subset from a pool of 275,472 images generated by a diffusion model (EDM2), and a classifier trained on each subset scores the metric per class. The tournament shows that no single metric serves every class: FID computed on Inception features gives the best classifier for one lesion type and no measurable advantage over random sampling for another, and the generation setting it prefers is also the one closest to the training images. We turn these per-class measurements into a safety-aware evaluation algorithm that weights each metric by its measured value in each class and removes images too close to a real training image. On the held-out ISIC-2018 test set, the algorithm improves Macro-$F_2$, a recall-weighted measure of classification performance, over the FID baseline for a Swin-B classifier by +0.0136 to +0.0164 across four safety thresholds (Bonferroni-corrected $p < 0.02$) and over random sampling by about +0.03, though not for ResNet-50. Tightening the threshold improves a memorization-safety score with no measurable change in utility, but every curated set remains less safe than random sampling. The results show a modest but statistically significant gain on the primary classifier, and offer a practical, safety-aware procedure for evaluating and using synthetic data.

AI.tldr: The paper tests 16 quality metrics for selecting synthetic skin lesion images from an EDM2 diffusion generator and proposes a safety-aware selection algorithm that weights each metric per class and removes images too close to real training images. It improves Macro-F2 over the FID baseline for a Swin-B classifier by +0.0136 to +0.0164, but not for ResNet-50.
AI.motivation: Synthetic images for rare skin lesion types could fill data gaps, but selection usually relies on FID, which has not been tested against what a classifier needs and cannot reveal memorization of training photographs.
AI.method: Each of 16 quality metrics alone selects a training subset from a pool of 275,472 generated images, and a classifier trained on each subset is scored per class. The safety-aware algorithm weights each metric by its measured value in each class and excludes images too close to a real training image, with evaluation on held-out ISIC-2018 at four safety thresholds.
AI.result: No single metric serves every class. FID on Inception features gives the best classifier for one lesion type and no measurable advantage over random sampling for another. The algorithm improves Macro-F2 over the FID baseline for Swin-B by +0.0136 to +0.0164 (Bonferroni-corrected p below 0.02) and over random sampling by about +0.03, but not for ResNet-50. Tighter thresholds improve a memorization-safety score without a measurable utility change, yet every curated set remains less safe than random sampling.
AI.conclusion: The gain on the primary classifier is modest but statistically significant, and the procedure offers a practical safety-aware way to evaluate and use synthetic data.

title: Gnomon4D: Learning Where and When to Focus for Geometric Motion-Grounded World-Action Modeling
summary: World-action models (WAMs) use video-generation priors to jointly predict future observations and robot actions. Yet RGB futures entangle physical state changes with appearance, while frame-wise depth and point maps lack temporal correspondence. Existing 4D approaches either keep motion implicit in visual features or translate predicted traces into actions through a separate interface. We present Gnomon4D, a WAM that jointly generates future video, robot actions, and GeoDelta, a video-aligned 4D geometric motion field encoding the cross-frame image-plane displacement and depth change of embodiment and object points. By placing embodiment motion and object responses in a shared space, GeoDelta exposes their motion relations to the action expert at inference. Interaction-Salient Attention (InSAttn) uses these relations to focus spatial readout on task-relevant interaction regions, while Transition-Anchored Aggregation (TransAgg) aggregates evidence around changes in their relative motion, such as grasp and release. GeoDelta describes surface motion independently of embodiment-specific controls, providing a shared human--robot quasi-action for action-free pretraining on EgoManip-5000H followed by robot mid-training on Robot-30H. Gnomon4D leads on RoboTwin~2.0, VLABench, and RoboDojo, and outperforms the strongest real-robot baseline by 7.0 and 16.0 percentage points under in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings, respectively.

AI.tldr: Gnomon4D is a world-action model that jointly generates future video, robot actions and GeoDelta, a video-aligned 4D geometric motion field, so that embodiment and object motion are represented in a shared space. It leads on RoboTwin 2.0, VLABench and RoboDojo and beats the strongest real-robot baseline by 7.0 and 16.0 points in-distribution and out-of-distribution.
AI.motivation: RGB futures entangle physical state change with appearance, and frame-wise depth or point maps lack temporal correspondence. Existing 4D approaches either keep motion implicit or translate predicted traces into actions through a separate interface.
AI.method: GeoDelta encodes cross-frame image-plane displacement and depth change of embodiment and object points. Interaction-Salient Attention focuses spatial readout on task-relevant interaction regions, and Transition-Anchored Aggregation pools evidence around changes in relative motion such as grasp and release. Action-free pretraining on EgoManip-5000H is followed by robot mid-training on Robot-30H.
AI.result: Gnomon4D leads on RoboTwin 2.0, VLABench and RoboDojo and outperforms the strongest real-robot baseline by 7.0 and 16.0 percentage points under in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Exposing motion relations between embodiment and objects to the action expert through a shared geometric motion field improves world-action modeling, particularly under distribution shift.

title: Fast-Slow Evolutionary Occupancy Prediction via Controlled Dynamics
summary: 3D semantic occupancy prediction provides dense geometric and semantic scene representations for autonomous driving, where both high accuracy and low response latency are crucial for safe downstream forecasting and planning. Existing methods usually exhibit different accuracy-latency characteristics. Performance-oriented models provide stronger geometric and semantic predictions, while deployment-friendly models provide faster responses. This motivates EvoOcc, a fast-slow evolutionary occupancy prediction framework that jointly exploits their complementary strengths to improve the accuracy-latency balance without changing the upstream architectures. EvoOcc models evolutionary occupancy prediction as a continuous time controlled dynamical system, enabling flexible adaptation to variable slow system delays and irregular fast system arrivals. The framework further decomposes the evolution process into dual state evolution where ego state evolution compensates for the deterministic coordinate shifts and scene state evolution models the genuine geometric and semantic scene changes. Extensive experiments on three different fast-slow system pairs and irregular prediction arrivals show that EvoOcc consistently improves over fast system baselines while maintaining much lower latency than the slow system, indicating a favorable accuracy-latency balance and stable behavior under practical inference situations.

AI.tldr: EvoOcc is a fast-slow framework for 3D semantic occupancy prediction in autonomous driving that combines a slow accurate model and a fast deployable model as a continuous-time controlled dynamical system. It improves over fast-system baselines while keeping much lower latency than the slow system.
AI.motivation: Performance-oriented occupancy models are accurate but slow, while deployment-friendly models respond quickly but are less accurate, and both accuracy and latency matter for safe driving.
AI.method: EvoOcc models evolutionary occupancy prediction as a continuous-time controlled dynamical system, handling variable slow-system delays and irregular fast-system arrivals. It decomposes evolution into ego state evolution, which compensates for deterministic coordinate shifts, and scene state evolution, which models genuine geometric and semantic changes. The upstream architectures are left unchanged.
AI.result: Experiments on three fast-slow system pairs and irregular prediction arrivals show consistent improvement over fast-system baselines, with much lower latency than the slow system.
AI.conclusion: The framework gives a favourable accuracy-latency balance and stable behaviour under practical inference conditions.

title: QFacePlacement: From Arbitrary Tensorization to Semantic Spatial Correspondence in Modern Face Verification
comment: Accepted at 11th International Conference on Computer Vision & Image Processing (CVIP)
summary: Quantum-inspired computer vision often reshapes high-dimensional features into tensors and applies tensor-network models. In face verification, this can be misleading: modern embeddings are optimized for cosine similarity, and tensorization alone does not establish the low-rank structure needed for tensor trains or matrix-product operators (MPOs). We study model placement through two controlled interfaces. First, cross-model embedding alignment requires a 512 x 512 operator to map AdaFace embeddings into ArcFace space. Dense Ridge and Procrustes mappings remain strong, while deterministic TT-SVD and MPO compression underperform even with basis changes and low-rank residuals. At a 64K-parameter storage budget, mean directional AUC is 0.9297 for dense Ridge, 0.8952 for rank-64 SVD, 0.8685 for the best low-rank-MPO hybrid, and approximately 0.649 for raw MPO. Second, before global pooling, we construct a 7 x 7 x 7 x 7 probe-gallery correspondence tensor from local AdaFace descriptors. A geometry-aware symmetric tensor train with bond dimension 2 uses 122 trainable parameters, compared with 2,403 for a dense linear matcher, while attaining an LFW AUC of 0.9802. Yet compression does not translate into better low-false-acceptance performance: on CFP-FP, TAR at FAR = 0.001 is 0.0102 versus 0.1734 for global cosine matching, and on CPLFW it is 0.7805 versus 0.8737. These results suggest that quantum-inspired factorization is most credible when the chosen interface provides task-aligned axes and compressible structure. They also show why aggregate AUC must be assessed alongside operational low-FAR metrics.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that tensorizing face embeddings does not by itself give useful low-rank structure, and it compares a dense cross-model alignment, low-rank and MPO compressions, and a geometry-aware symmetric tensor train on a correspondence tensor. The tensor train reaches an LFW AUC of 0.9802 with 122 parameters, but it fails at low false-acceptance rates on CFP-FP and CPLFW.
AI.motivation: Quantum-inspired computer vision often reshapes features into tensors without showing that they have the low-rank structure that tensor networks need, and modern face embeddings are optimized for cosine similarity.
AI.method: Two controlled interfaces are studied. First, a 512 by 512 operator maps AdaFace embeddings into ArcFace space, compared among dense Ridge and Procrustes mappings, TT-SVD, MPO compression and low-rank hybrids. Second, a 7x7x7x7 probe-gallery correspondence tensor is built from local AdaFace descriptors before global pooling and matched with a geometry-aware symmetric tensor train with bond dimension 2.
AI.result: At a 64K-parameter storage budget, mean directional AUC is 0.9297 for dense Ridge, 0.8952 for rank-64 SVD, 0.8685 for the best low-rank MPO hybrid, and about 0.649 for raw MPO. The tensor train uses 122 trainable parameters versus 2,403 for a dense linear matcher and reaches an LFW AUC of 0.9802. On CFP-FP, TAR at FAR 0.001 is 0.0102 versus 0.1734 for global cosine matching, and on CPLFW it is 0.7805 versus 0.8737.
AI.conclusion: Quantum-inspired factorization is credible only when the interface offers task-aligned axes and compressible structure, and aggregate AUC must be read alongside low-FAR operating metrics.

title: CellPlex: Benchmarking Single-Cell Spatial Proteomics Prediction from H&E
summary: Spatial proteomics measures tens of proteins in every cell of a tissue section, but its cost confines it to small research cohorts, whereas hematoxylin and eosin (H\&E) slides exist for nearly every patient. Inferring single-cell spatial proteomics from H\&E would bring its analyses to routine pathology, and a growing number of virtual staining models pursue this goal. Each is evaluated on its own cohort, panel and pixel-level metric, and released models transfer poorly to new cohorts, leaving open which approach to build on and which proteins H\&E can reveal. We introduce CellPlex, a benchmark that poses the task at the level of the cell: seven cohorts with same-section H\&E and multiplexed immunofluorescence, from colorectal and breast cancer to lymph-node metastases, bone marrow and glioma, with 717 samples, 44.8 million cells and 149 proteins, processed by one pipeline into per-cell targets. Pathology foundation models (PFMs) are adapted with one cell-level protocol, specialist models are fine-tuned under a matched budget, and all are scored on the same cells. Adapted PFMs are the most accurate models on every cohort, ahead of the specialists even after fine-tuning, but keep less than half of their accuracy on cohorts they were not trained on. Which proteins can be predicted depends on the tissue, not on how many cells were measured for them. By fixing the cells, targets and splits on which predictions are judged, CellPlex sets a common standard for inferring costly molecular measurements from routine H\&E and shows how far H\&E can stand in for spatial proteomics. We will release the data, splits, evaluation code and baselines as a testbed for developing and comparing future pathology foundation models and virtual staining methods.

AI.tldr: CellPlex is a benchmark for predicting single-cell spatial proteomics from H&E slides across seven cohorts with 717 samples, 44.8 million cells and 149 proteins. Adapted pathology foundation models are the most accurate on every cohort but keep less than half their accuracy on unseen cohorts.
AI.motivation: Spatial proteomics is costly and confined to small cohorts, while H&E slides are available for nearly every patient. Virtual staining models are each evaluated on their own cohort, panel and pixel-level metric, and released models transfer poorly, leaving open which approach to build on.
AI.method: Seven cohorts with same-section H&E and multiplexed immunofluorescence are processed by one pipeline into per-cell targets. Pathology foundation models are adapted with one cell-level protocol, specialist models are fine-tuned under a matched budget, and all are scored on the same cells.
AI.result: Adapted pathology foundation models are the most accurate on every cohort, ahead of the specialists even after fine-tuning, but keep less than half of their accuracy on cohorts not seen in training. Which proteins can be predicted depends on the tissue rather than on the number of cells measured for them.
AI.conclusion: Fixing the cells, targets and splits gives a common standard for inferring costly molecular measurements from routine H&E and shows how far H&E can substitute for spatial proteomics.

title: Latent Spectral Prompting for Multimodal Hyperspectral Object Tracking
comment: Accepted at the IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV 2027)
summary: Hyperspectral videos provide rich spectral signatures for robust tracking under challenging conditions such as camouflage and low illumination. However, limited hyperspectral annotations and the large RGB-hyperspectral domain gap hinder the direct use of modern temporally pretrained RGB trackers. We propose SProTrack, a multimodal framework that transfers temporal knowledge from pretrained RGB trackers to the hyperspectral domain through latent spectral prompting. The key idea is to decouple temporal modeling from spectral adaptation, allowing temporal dynamics to be inherited from RGB foundation models while hyperspectral information is learned from unlabeled data in a self-supervised manner. Unlike band-selection methods that discard most spectral information or prompt-based approaches that rely on local-search crops, SProTrack learns a global, scene-level spectral representation from the full hyperspectral frame using an autoencoder. This latent representation is used to guide spectral prompt extraction while a pretrained RGB tracker preserves strong temporal modeling on RGB-compatible inputs. By encoding spectral-spatial structure into compact latent prompts, SProTrack bridges the RGB-hyperspectral modality gap without extensive retraining or dense supervision. Experiments on HOT2020 and HOT2023 demonstrate that SProTrack achieves the best overall performance, with strong results across all spectral domains.

AI.tldr: SProTrack is a multimodal hyperspectral tracker that transfers temporal knowledge from pretrained RGB trackers through latent spectral prompts learned by a self-supervised autoencoder over full hyperspectral frames. It achieves the best overall performance on HOT2020 and HOT2023.
AI.motivation: Limited hyperspectral annotations and the large RGB-hyperspectral domain gap prevent direct use of modern temporally pretrained RGB trackers, and existing band selection discards spectral information while prompt methods rely on local-search crops.
AI.method: The temporal modeling of a pretrained RGB tracker is kept and decoupled from spectral adaptation. An autoencoder learns a global, scene-level spectral representation from unlabeled hyperspectral frames, and this latent representation guides spectral prompt extraction that encodes spectral-spatial structure into compact latent prompts.
AI.result: Experiments on HOT2020 and HOT2023 show that SProTrack achieves the best overall performance, with strong results across all spectral domains.
AI.conclusion: Latent spectral prompting bridges the RGB-hyperspectral modality gap without extensive retraining or dense supervision.

title: MedHEB: Benchmarking Medical Embeddings Across Heterogeneous Clinical Evidence
summary: Clinical evidence is inherently relational: medical images are interpreted with prior studies, cross-modal examinations, reports, and localized findings, and retrieving relevant evidence is therefore central to clinical interpretation. Recent foundation models increasingly encode these heterogeneous sources into shared embedding spaces, yet existing embedding evaluation often focuses on isolated matches, leaving unclear whether current models retrieve relevant evidence across changes in modality, appearance, and granularity. We introduce MedHEB, a unified benchmark with 107 retrieval tasks from 54 datasets, including both in-distribution and held-out-source evaluation, across three axes: evidence form (2D images, 3D volumes, text), pairing type (image--image, image--text, text--text, and modality-bridging visual matching), and relevance granularity (global, question-conditioned, region-level). Under a single ranking protocol, MedHEB varies clinically relevant evidence definitions to test whether embedding proximity remains meaningful across heterogeneous evidence, including modality-bridging visual retrieval and region-level text-to-region retrieval. Across representative models, performance is uneven across retrieval families: models strong on conventional image--text or text--text retrieval are less reliable on modality-bridging and region-level tasks. Current embedding spaces capture some clinical relationships well but do not yet provide balanced retrieval across heterogeneous evidence. We further provide MedEmb, an MLLM-based reference embedding model trained on the MedHEB ID split, as a reproducible baseline for unified 2D--3D--text medical retrieval. We release MedHEB with preprocessing scripts, evaluation code, access manifests, and MedEmb to support research on clinically meaningful medical embeddings.

AI.tldr: MedHEB is a benchmark of 107 retrieval tasks from 54 datasets for medical embeddings across 2D images, 3D volumes and text, including modality-bridging and region-level retrieval. Models strong on conventional image-text or text-text retrieval are less reliable on modality-bridging and region-level tasks, and the MedEmb baseline is released.
AI.motivation: Clinical retrieval requires relating prior studies, cross-modal examinations, reports and localized findings, but existing embedding evaluation mostly covers isolated matches and does not test whether proximity holds across changes in modality, appearance and granularity.
AI.method: MedHEB spans three axes: evidence form (2D images, 3D volumes, text), pairing type (image-image, image-text, text-text and modality-bridging visual matching) and relevance granularity (global, question-conditioned and region-level). It uses a single ranking protocol with in-distribution and held-out-source evaluation. MedEmb, an MLLM-based reference embedding model, is trained on the MedHEB ID split.
AI.result: Performance is uneven across retrieval families. Representative models that are strong on conventional image-text or text-text retrieval are less reliable on modality-bridging and region-level tasks.
AI.conclusion: Current embedding spaces capture some clinical relationships well but do not yet give balanced retrieval across heterogeneous evidence. MedHEB, its scripts, code, access manifests and MedEmb are released to support research on medical embeddings.

title: INTERACT: Learning Interaction-Aware World Dynamics from Driving Videos for Autonomous Driving
summary: Safe autonomous driving requires more than recognizing the current scene: the ego vehicle must anticipate how surrounding traffic participants will evolve under its own motion. However, existing end-to-end driving models typically encode scenes into dense visual or BEV features, leaving object-level interactions implicit. We propose (INTERACT INTERaction-aware Action-Conditioned Trajectory learning), a three-stage framework that learns a slot-based object-centric world model from unlabeled driving videos and transfers it to trajectory planning. INTERACT first learns recurrent slots that group dense visual features into temporally structured scene-entity representations without object annotations. It then infers latent ego actions from slot context and video transitions, and uses them to condition future slot prediction, capturing how ego motion and surrounding entities co-evolve. Finally, the learned slots, latent actions, and future slot predictions are distilled into a trajectory planner to guide trajectory generation and selection. Extensive experiments on NAVSIM and nuScenes validate the effectiveness of INTERACT. In particular, it achieves state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM, with improvements in safety-critical collision metrics.

AI.tldr: INTERACT learns a slot-based object-centric world model from unlabeled driving videos, conditioned on latent ego actions, and distils it into a trajectory planner. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM with improvements in safety-critical collision metrics.
AI.motivation: End-to-end driving models encode scenes as dense visual or BEV features, which leaves object-level interactions between the ego vehicle and other traffic participants implicit, even though safe driving requires anticipating how they evolve under the ego motion.
AI.method: The three-stage framework first learns recurrent slots that group dense visual features into temporally structured entity representations without object annotations. It then infers latent ego actions from slot context and video transitions to condition future slot prediction. Finally, slots, latent actions and future slot predictions are distilled into a trajectory planner that guides trajectory generation and selection.
AI.result: INTERACT achieves state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM, with improvements in safety-critical collision metrics. Experiments on nuScenes are also reported.
AI.conclusion: Object-centric, action-conditioned world dynamics learned from unlabeled video provide a useful signal for safer trajectory planning.

title: Flat Features, Detailed Images? Simple Detail Control for Diffusion Transformers
summary: Prompt engineering is commonly used to encourage text-to-image models to generate more detailed images. However, it does not provide reliable, continuous, or disentangled control. We analyze feature tokens produced with and without detail-enhancing prompts across six diffusion transformers and observe a common pattern: these prompts tend to increase the entropy of each token's energy distribution while largely preserving its ordering. That is, flattening the distribution increases the level of detail. Motivated by this counter-intuitive finding, we introduce a simple training-free approach that continuously adjusts the level of detail according to a scalar. Specifically, it shifts the squared channel magnitudes of each token toward a higher entropy distribution with a time-aware scheduler to concentrate the intervention at intermediate sampling steps. Across extensive experiments on different types of diffusion transformers, we show that our approach provides continuous control over detail metrics while largely preserving image quality and semantic structure. It requires only a few lines of code and adds negligible inference time overhead.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that detail-enhancing prompts mainly flatten the energy distribution of diffusion transformer features while keeping its ordering, and proposes a training-free method that shifts squared channel magnitudes toward higher entropy with a time-aware schedule. This gives continuous control over detail metrics while largely preserving image quality and semantic structure.
AI.motivation: Prompt engineering is the usual way to encourage more detailed images from text-to-image models, but it offers no reliable, continuous or disentangled control.
AI.method: Feature tokens with and without detail-enhancing prompts are compared across six diffusion transformers. A training-free approach then shifts the squared channel magnitudes of each token toward a higher-entropy distribution, scaled by a scalar and concentrated at intermediate sampling steps by a time-aware scheduler. It requires only a few lines of code.
AI.result: Across diverse diffusion transformers, the approach gives continuous control over detail metrics while largely preserving image quality and semantic structure, with negligible inference overhead.
AI.conclusion: Flattening the token energy distribution is a simple, disentangled handle on the level of detail in diffusion transformers.

title: SeMo3D: Unifying 3D Generation, Editing, and Completion via Selective Modeling
summary: 3D generation, editing, and completion are typically treated as regenerating the complete 3D asset under task-specific constraints, even when only a local region needs modification. This leads to task isolation, inconsistency in content that should remain unchanged, and dependence on task-specific paired data. We address these issues with a key observation: the three tasks all synthesize a designated region while keeping the rest intact---the full region for generation, the target region for editing, and the missing region for completion. We term this paradigm Selective Modeling and build SeMo3D upon it; it naturally unifies the three tasks, preserves unchanged content by construction, and enables training without paired editing or completion data, since any 3D asset can be partitioned into a selected region and its context. For training, we propose region-selective denoising, which randomly selects regions of varying sizes on standard 3D assets and applies noise and loss only to them, jointly learning all three tasks. For architecture, we propose Omni3DiT, a multi-condition 3D diffusion transformer that distinguishes regions to create from those to retain and fuses image, text, and point guidance for fine-grained control. Experiments across three benchmarks show SeMo3D surpasses state-of-the-art methods on all tasks, delivering multimodal controllability in generation and strong consistency and accuracy in editing and completion. SeMo3D further serves as a unified modeling tool for agents, enabling efficient 3D creation through natural-language interaction. Project page: this https URL.

AI.tldr: SeMo3D unifies 3D generation, editing and completion by synthesizing only a selected region while keeping the rest intact, trained with region-selective denoising and a multi-condition diffusion transformer, Omni3DiT. It surpasses state-of-the-art methods on all three tasks across three benchmarks and serves as a tool for agents.
AI.motivation: The three 3D tasks are usually treated as regenerating the whole asset under task-specific constraints, which causes inconsistency in unchanged content and depends on task-specific paired data.
AI.method: Selective Modeling synthesizes a designated region with the rest kept intact. Region-selective denoising randomly selects regions of varying sizes on standard 3D assets and applies noise and loss only to them, so all three tasks are learned jointly without paired editing or completion data. Omni3DiT distinguishes regions to create from regions to retain and fuses image, text and point guidance.
AI.result: SeMo3D surpasses state-of-the-art methods on all tasks across three benchmarks, with multimodal controllability in generation and strong consistency and accuracy in editing and completion.
AI.conclusion: Selective modeling unifies 3D generation, editing and completion, and it also enables efficient natural-language 3D creation for agents.

title: AVID: A 5T fMRI Dataset for Benchmarking Auditory-induced Visual Mental Imagery Decoding
comment: This is the camera-ready version accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Abstract shortened to respect the arXiv limit of 1920 characters. Please see the PDF for the full abstract
summary: Visual mental imagery (VMI) decoding uses brain activity to reconstruct internally generated visual scenes, providing a potential pathway for externalizing internal experiences and developing neuroprosthetic communication interfaces. However, progress is limited by the lack of dedicated, training-scale VMI datasets. Current VMI paradigms often rely on visual prompts or short-term memory images, introducing visual and mnemonic confounds that make it difficult to disentangle neural activity associated with endogenous image construction from signals driven by prior or concurrent visual input. Furthermore, existing VMI datasets offer limited descriptive control over individual visual attributes, making it difficult to systematically assess fine grained visual details. To address these gaps, we introduce AVID, the first dedicated training-scale 5.0 Tesla functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) resource for auditory-induced VMI decoding. AVID comprises approximately 67 hours of dense recordings from nine participants. The dataset is structured into two complementary splits: a scene-level complex split using naturalistic Mandarin descriptions and a controlled simple split with explicitly specified visual attributes. We further formalize a standardized evaluation protocol that decouples source-image consistency from semantic alignment, allowing for a more nuanced assessment of imagery reconstruction. Baseline qualitative and quantitative results show that current reconstruction pipelines remain limited on AVID, although the most successful reconstructions preserve recognizable scene level semantics from spoken descriptions. By combining dedicated training-scale neural recordings and standardized evaluation resources, AVID provides both a data foundation for imagery-specific model development and a benchmark for evaluating VMI decoding with substantially reduced sensory contamination.

AI.tldr: AVID is a 5.0 Tesla fMRI dataset of about 67 hours from nine participants for decoding auditory-induced visual mental imagery, designed to avoid visual and short-term memory confounds. It includes complex Mandarin scene descriptions and simple attribute-controlled splits, and baseline reconstructions remain limited but preserve recognizable scene semantics.
AI.motivation: Visual mental imagery decoding lacks training-scale datasets, and existing paradigms use visual prompts or short-term memory images that confound endogenous image construction with sensory input. Existing datasets also offer limited control over individual visual attributes.
AI.method: Imagery is induced by auditory description rather than visual prompts. The dataset has two splits: a scene-level complex split with naturalistic Mandarin descriptions and a controlled simple split with explicitly specified attributes. A standardized protocol separates source-image consistency from semantic alignment.
AI.result: Baseline qualitative and quantitative results show that current reconstruction pipelines remain limited on AVID. The most successful reconstructions preserve recognizable scene-level semantics from the spoken descriptions.
AI.conclusion: AVID provides a data foundation for imagery-specific model development and a benchmark with reduced sensory contamination for evaluating VMI decoding.

title: BGD-SF PolySegNet: boundary-guided dynamic selective fusion network for robust polyp segmentation in colonoscopy images
comment: 26 pages, 9 figures, 8 tables, Submitted to PLOS ONE
summary: Effective polyp segmentation in colonoscopy images is crucial for early detection of colorectal cancer, a leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide. While current deep learning models perform well on traditional Dice benchmarks, border segmentation remains difficult. Most methods use boundary information only as an additional loss signal during training, which prevents the network from explicitly learning border-guided feature selection or mask refinement. This paper introduces BGD-SF PolySegNet, a boundary-guided encoder-decoder architecture that controls three phases of the segmentation pipeline: dynamic multi-scale context aggregation, selective skip-feature fusion, and final mask refinement. The architecture comprises a pretrained EfficientNet-B4 backbone and three proposed modules: Boundary-Guided Dynamic Cascaded Multi-Scale Context Aggregation (BGD-CMSCA), Boundary-Guided Selective Attention Fusion (BG-SAGF), and a Multi-Level Boundary Guidance Head (MBGH). The model is trained on 3,535 annotated images from Kvasir-SEG, BKAI-IGH NeoPolyp-Small, and PolypGen, and evaluated on four held-out benchmark datasets. On the internal test set, BGD-SF achieves a Dice of 0.887, IoU of 0.839, mask-derived Boundary F1 of 0.531, HD95 of 30.32, and ASSD of 18.10, improving Boundary F1, HD95, and ASSD by 15.7%, 27.5%, and 34.6% over the strongest CNN baselines. External validation on CVC-ClinicDB, CVC-ColonDB, ETIS-Larib, and CVC-300 yielded Dice scores of 0.891, 0.776, 0.863, and 0.885, respectively. The model runs at 35 FPS with 22.51M parameters. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests confirm statistically significant mask-derived Boundary F1 improvements over six of seven ablation variants (p < 0.001; small-to-moderate effect sizes, r = 0.215-0.434), demonstrating that integrating boundary guidance as an active architectural component measurably advances polyp boundary delineation.

AI.tldr: BGD-SF PolySegNet is a boundary-guided encoder-decoder for polyp segmentation that guides context aggregation, skip-feature fusion and mask refinement with boundary information. It reaches a Dice of 0.887 internally, improves boundary metrics over the strongest CNN baselines, and runs at 35 FPS with 22.51M parameters.
AI.motivation: Most segmentation methods use boundary information only as an extra loss during training, which prevents the network from explicitly learning boundary-guided feature selection or mask refinement, and border segmentation remains hard.
AI.method: The model uses a pretrained EfficientNet-B4 backbone with three modules: Boundary-Guided Dynamic Cascaded Multi-Scale Context Aggregation (BGD-CMSCA), Boundary-Guided Selective Attention Fusion (BG-SAGF) and a Multi-Level Boundary Guidance Head (MBGH). It is trained on 3,535 images from Kvasir-SEG, BKAI-IGH NeoPolyp-Small and PolypGen.
AI.result: On the internal test set, Dice is 0.887, IoU 0.839, mask-derived Boundary F1 0.531, HD95 30.32 and ASSD 18.10, improving Boundary F1, HD95 and ASSD by 15.7%, 27.5% and 34.6% over the strongest CNN baselines. External Dice is 0.891 on CVC-ClinicDB, 0.776 on CVC-ColonDB, 0.863 on ETIS-Larib and 0.885 on CVC-300. Boundary F1 improvements are significant over six of seven ablation variants.
AI.conclusion: Integrating boundary guidance as an active architectural component measurably improves polyp boundary delineation.

title: Latent Diffusion-GAN: Adversarial Learning in the Autoencoded Latent Space
summary: Diffusion models are powerful generative frameworks for producing high-quality images by denoising latent variables from random noise. However, training with likelihood-based objectives, such as denoising score matching, can lead to locally over-smoothed high-frequency details, including fine textures and sharp edges, thereby limiting perceptual fidelity and structural detail. Adversarial training with GANs enhances sharpness but typically requires additional discriminator networks, increasing computational costs and destabilizing training. To this end, we propose Latent Diffusion Generative Adversarial Networks (LD-GAN), a novel framework that seamlessly integrates adversarial learning into diffusion models without modifying their original pipeline. LD-GAN leverages the pretrained variational autoencoder (VAE) in latent diffusion models as an energy-based discriminator, enabling adversarial training without extra parameters and preserving the structured latent priors learned from large datasets. We also introduce a structural consistency energy that aligns encoder and decoder feature representations, thereby enhancing perceptual quality and compatibility with the pretrained latent space. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LD-GAN significantly improves sample fidelity, perceptual sharpness, and diversity over state-of-the-art baseline methods across various generation tasks while ensuring efficient training dynamics.

AI.tldr: LD-GAN adds adversarial training to latent diffusion models by using the pretrained VAE as an energy-based discriminator, adding no extra parameters and keeping the original pipeline. It improves sample fidelity, perceptual sharpness and diversity over state-of-the-art baselines across various generation tasks.
AI.motivation: Likelihood-based diffusion objectives can over-smooth high-frequency details such as fine textures and sharp edges, while GAN-based sharpening needs extra discriminator networks that raise cost and destabilize training.
AI.method: The pretrained VAE of the latent diffusion model serves as an energy-based discriminator, so adversarial learning needs no additional parameters and preserves the latent priors learned from large datasets. A structural consistency energy aligns encoder and decoder feature representations to improve perceptual quality and compatibility with the latent space.
AI.result: LD-GAN significantly improves sample fidelity, perceptual sharpness and diversity over state-of-the-art baselines across various generation tasks, with efficient training dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Adversarial learning can be integrated into diffusion training in the autoencoded latent space without extra discriminator networks.

title: UniCross3D: Unified Cross-View and Cross-Domain Diffusion for Consistent Single-Image 3D Generation
summary: Reconstructing detailed geometry and realistic appearance from a single RGB image is essential yet fundamentally challenging due to inherent ambiguities such as occlusion, lighting variations, and texture-geometry entanglement. While recent diffusion-based generative models have significantly improved novel view synthesis, existing approaches suffer from two critical limitations: lack of cross-view geometric consistency and insufficient cross-domain semantic alignment. To address these issues, we introduce UniCross3D, a unified cross-view and cross-domain diffusion framework designed explicitly for consistent and physically coherent 3D generation. UniCross3D features two novel contributions: (1) a cross-view latent regularization that enforces cross-view geometric consistency across synthesized viewpoints by penalizing latent variance, and (2) a cross-domain mutual information objective grounded in the physics of image formation, explicitly aligning synthesized color and normal maps. Extensive experiments demonstrate that UniCross3D achieves significantly improved view consistency and semantic alignment over state-of-the-art methods and yields higher-fidelity reconstructions, particularly under challenging textures and ambiguous viewpoints.

AI.tldr: UniCross3D is a diffusion framework for single-image 3D generation that enforces cross-view geometric consistency through latent variance regularization and cross-domain alignment of color and normal maps via a mutual information objective.
