It achieves better view consistency and semantic alignment than state-of-the-art methods and yields higher-fidelity reconstructions.
AI.motivation: Single-image 3D reconstruction is ambiguous due to occlusion, lighting and texture-geometry entanglement, and diffusion-based novel view synthesis lacks cross-view geometric consistency and cross-domain semantic alignment.
AI.method: A cross-view latent regularization penalizes latent variance across synthesized viewpoints to enforce geometric consistency. A cross-domain mutual information objective, grounded in image formation physics, explicitly aligns synthesized color and normal maps.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show significantly improved view consistency and semantic alignment over state-of-the-art methods, and higher-fidelity reconstructions, particularly for challenging textures and ambiguous viewpoints.
AI.conclusion: Unifying cross-view and cross-domain constraints in one diffusion framework yields more consistent and physically coherent 3D generation from a single image.

title: ReinSeg: Retrieval-Guided Bounded Multimodal Refinement for 3-D Road Anomaly Segmentation
summary: 3-D road anomaly segmentation is essential for risk-aware perception in autonomous driving. Its central challenge is to rank sparsely observed hazards ahead of abundant normal road structures while preserving point-wise metric localization. LiDAR provides accurate 3-D point support, whereas surround-view imagery offers complementary semantic context for separating unexpected hazards from challenging normal structures. We propose ReinSeg, a retrieval-guided bounded multimodal refinement framework for point-wise road anomaly segmentation. Occupied LiDAR bird's-eye-view cells retrieve scene-specific context from a shared memory of eight surround-view images without supplying calibration variables to the retrieval module. A relative-norm-bounded residual returns this context to the LiDAR point features, so the frozen LIDO anomaly-scoring interface is preserved, and the refinement is optimized with in-distribution semantic labels only. On the Spotting the Unexpected (STU) benchmark, ReinSeg improves validation average precision from 27.54\% to 35.67\% and reduces the false-positive rate at 95\% anomaly recall from 34.85\% to 10.61\%, shrinking the high-recall screening set from 67.54 to 20.55 million points. Relative to REL, AP is 24.99 percentage points higher and FPR95 is 0.99 points lower. Matched interfaces and component isolation show that retrieved scene imagery and the relative-norm bound are both essential, and ReinSeg stays above LiDAR-only performance under missing, corrupted, or misaligned camera inputs while running at 21.8 frames per second. These results establish bounded retrieval of scene-specific visual evidence as an effective route to reliable 3-D road-hazard perception.

AI.tldr: ReinSeg is a retrieval-guided, norm-bounded multimodal refinement framework for point-wise 3D road anomaly segmentation that retrieves scene context from surround-view images for LiDAR points. It raises validation AP from 27.54% to 35.67% and lowers FPR95 from 34.85% to 10.61% on the STU benchmark while running at 21.8 fps.
AI.motivation: Road hazards are sparse among abundant normal road structures, and LiDAR gives accurate 3D points but limited semantic context, while surround-view imagery can separate unexpected hazards from challenging normal structures.
AI.method: Occupied LiDAR bird's-eye-view cells retrieve scene-specific context from a shared memory of eight surround-view images without calibration variables. A relative-norm-bounded residual returns this context to LiDAR point features, which preserves the frozen LIDO anomaly-scoring interface, and training uses only in-distribution semantic labels.
AI.result: On the STU benchmark, validation AP rises from 27.54% to 35.67% and FPR95 falls from 34.85% to 10.61%, shrinking the high-recall screening set from 67.54 to 20.55 million points. Relative to REL, AP is 24.99 points higher and FPR95 0.99 points lower. ReinSeg stays above LiDAR-only performance with missing, corrupted or misaligned cameras and runs at 21.8 frames per second.
AI.conclusion: Bounded retrieval of scene-specific visual evidence is an effective route to reliable 3D road-hazard perception.

title: Computer Vision Applications for Art History: Reflections and paradigms for future research
comment: 8 pages. Published in the Proceedings of EVA London 2021 (Electronic Visualisation and the Arts), BCS Electronic Workshops in Computing (eWiC), under CC BY 4.0
summary: One of the contributing factors to the continuing debate among art historians over the use of computational methods in art history research is that they do not consider the core of today's art history research questions. The lack of close collaboration between the two involved research communities makes the definition of contemporary art-historical methods as well-defined computer vision problems extremely difficult. For that purpose, it is devised as a methodology to study articles in art history journals from a computer science perspective. The objective is to identify which image features art historians utilise within their research and describe them in immediate and meaningful terms to the computer vision research community. Finally, some paradigms that could serve as a new starting point for exploring how computer vision applications for art history can address the core of today's art history research are given.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a methodology that studies articles in art history journals from a computer science perspective to identify which image features art historians use and to describe them in terms usable by computer vision researchers. It concludes with paradigms for computer vision applications that address core art-historical research questions.
AI.motivation: Art historians debate computational methods partly because these methods do not address today's core research questions, and the close collaboration needed to define art-historical problems as computer vision problems is lacking.
AI.method: The authors analyse articles in art history journals from a computer science perspective, identifying the image features art historians use and expressing them in immediate and meaningful terms for the computer vision community.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative results. Its outputs are the identified image features and a set of proposed paradigms for future research.
AI.conclusion: The proposed paradigms can serve as a new starting point for computer vision applications that address the core of contemporary art-historical research.

title: Probe-Guided Gradient Balancing for Multimodal Learning
summary: Jointly trained multimodal networks frequently underutilize weaker modalities, as faster-learning modalities dominate the shared fusion objective and suppress gradients reaching slower ones. Most existing approaches throttle dominant modalities, whereas directly boosting weaker modalities often fails because monitoring signals derived from the joint loss remain dominated by stronger modalities. We propose Probe-Guided Gradient Boosting (PGGB), a gradient modulation approach that boosts weaker modalities while preserving the strength of dominant ones. PGGB attaches lightweight linear classifiers to stop-gradient features from each modality to estimate representation quality independently. The gap between these scores, termed the utilization gap, provides an imbalance signal used to adaptively scale weaker-modality gradients through bounded and smoothed modulation. PGGB is composable with throttling methods, as it leaves the loss function and fusion architecture unchanged. Experiments across eight benchmarks spanning four domains and 2-4 modalities demonstrate that PGGB outperforms state-of-the-art methods on highly imbalanced multimodal datasets while remaining competitive under low or negligible imbalance. We further establish bounded scaling, self-attenuation, and a descent bound for standard SGD under smoothness and bounded-variance assumptions. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: PGGB is a gradient modulation method for multimodal learning that estimates the representation quality of each modality with lightweight linear probes on stop-gradient features and boosts weaker modalities through bounded, smoothed scaling. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods on highly imbalanced datasets across eight benchmarks and is composable with throttling methods.
AI.motivation: Faster-learning modalities dominate the shared fusion objective and suppress gradients to slower ones. Throttling dominant modalities is common, but boosting weaker modalities fails when monitoring signals from the joint loss are still dominated by stronger modalities.
AI.method: Linear classifiers attached to stop-gradient features of each modality estimate representation quality independently. The gap between these scores, termed the utilization gap, is an imbalance signal that adaptively scales weaker-modality gradients through bounded and smoothed modulation. The loss and fusion architecture are unchanged.
AI.result: Across eight benchmarks spanning four domains and 2 to 4 modalities, PGGB outperforms state-of-the-art methods on highly imbalanced datasets and remains competitive under low or negligible imbalance. Bounded scaling, self-attenuation and a descent bound for standard SGD are established under smoothness and bounded-variance assumptions.
AI.conclusion: Probe-guided boosting of weaker modalities addresses modality imbalance without changing the loss or architecture, and it complements throttling approaches.

title: VerdictAD: Few-Shot Anomaly Detection via Decision-Guided Refinement
comment: Preprint with 5 tables and 7 figures. Code and experimental logs available at this https URL
summary: Detecting defects in real-world industrial inspection often requires learning from only a few normal images per category. Recent few-shot anomaly detection methods have achieved strong performance by measuring feature differences between query images and normal references. However, visual differences do not always indicate genuine defects, as normal appearance variations can also produce high anomaly scores. Conversely, structural or logical anomalies may not produce strong local feature differences, making them difficult to detect. To address this limitation, we introduce VerdictAD, a training-free framework that refines existing anomaly detectors through visual decisions. Rather than replacing existing detectors, VerdictAD adopts a typed decision model to assess the query image and its local regions against a few normal references. By directly producing structured decision probabilities without text generation, the model provides complementary evidence for refining anomaly responses at different spatial scales. Building on this capability, we introduce two modules: Global Verdict Refinement (GVR) uses image-level decisions to refine the overall anomaly score, while Local Verdict Refinement (LVR) aggregates regional decisions to refine the anomaly map. Combined with a simple DINOv2-based detector, VerdictAD achieves competitive performance in one-shot and few-shot anomaly detection. More importantly, as a plug-and-play framework, it consistently improves existing anomaly detectors across MVTec AD, VisA, and MVTec LOCO AD, achieving strong results across one-shot and few-shot settings. Our code and experimental logs are publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: VerdictAD is a training-free framework that refines existing few-shot anomaly detectors with visual decisions, using global and local verdict modules driven by a typed decision model. It consistently improves existing detectors across MVTec AD, VisA and MVTec LOCO AD, and a DINOv2-based version is competitive in one-shot and few-shot settings.
AI.motivation: Visual differences do not always indicate defects because normal appearance variation can produce high anomaly scores, while structural or logical anomalies may produce weak local feature differences.
AI.method: The typed decision model assesses the query image and its local regions against a few normal references and directly outputs structured decision probabilities without text generation. Global Verdict Refinement uses image-level decisions to refine the overall anomaly score, and Local Verdict Refinement aggregates regional decisions to refine the anomaly map.
AI.result: Combined with a simple DINOv2-based detector, VerdictAD achieves competitive performance in one-shot and few-shot anomaly detection. As a plug-and-play framework it consistently improves existing detectors across MVTec AD, VisA and MVTec LOCO AD in one-shot and few-shot settings.
AI.conclusion: Decision-based refinement gives complementary evidence that improves existing anomaly detectors without training.

title: OctreeSplat: Hierarchical Octree-Guided Feed-Forward Gaussian Splatting
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has shown considerable potential for novel view synthesis (NVS) and 3D reconstruction. Feed-forward methods avoid costly per-scene optimization, but fixed image or spatial resolutions limit their ability to allocate primitives according to local complexity. We present OctreeSplat, a hierarchical octree-guided feed-forward Gaussian splatting. OctreeSplat extracts multi-view features and geometric priors from a frozen visual foundation model (VFM), constructs a hierarchical octree, and predicts densification scores. The resulting representation allocates Gaussian primitives at spatially varying densities according to local complexity. Stochastic solids volume rendering improves depth rendering, strengthens geometric supervision, and supports surface reconstruction. When camera parameters are available, an optional test-time optimization (TTO) module improves agreement between predicted and ground-truth parameters. Training updates only 76 million additional parameters and requires 35 GPU-hours. Experiments on Replica, TUM, Tanks and Temples, and DTU demonstrate competitive RGB view synthesis, depth synthesis, and surface reconstruction. OctreeSplat reduces the number of Gaussian primitives while maintaining high reconstruction quality.

AI.tldr: OctreeSplat is a feed-forward Gaussian splatting method that builds a hierarchical octree guided by a frozen visual foundation model and allocates Gaussian primitives according to local complexity. It reduces the number of primitives while keeping high reconstruction quality on Replica, TUM, Tanks and Temples and DTU.
AI.motivation: Feed-forward Gaussian splatting avoids per-scene optimization, but fixed image or spatial resolutions limit how primitives can be allocated according to local complexity.
AI.method: Multi-view features and geometric priors are extracted from a frozen VFM, a hierarchical octree is constructed, and densification scores are predicted to place Gaussians at spatially varying densities. Stochastic solids volume rendering improves depth rendering and supports surface reconstruction. An optional test-time optimization module improves agreement with ground-truth camera parameters when they are available. Training updates 76 million parameters and takes 35 GPU-hours.
AI.result: Experiments on Replica, TUM, Tanks and Temples and DTU show competitive RGB view synthesis, depth synthesis and surface reconstruction, while the number of Gaussian primitives is reduced.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive octree-guided allocation makes feed-forward splatting more efficient without sacrificing reconstruction quality.

title: PriCBMs: Multi-granular Concept Bottleneck Vision-Language Models for Visual Privacy Recognition
summary: Widespread image sharing on social media has increased the need for visual privacy recognition to identify inadvertently exposed privacy information. However, multi-label visual privacy recognition presents two challenges. First, privacy categories represent high-level semantic attributes and do not have a one-to-one correspondence with visual objects. Different visual objects may involve the same privacy category, while the same type of object may contain different types of privacy-sensitive information. In this setting, direct prediction methods generally lack explicit guidance for identifying category-relevant privacy cues, leaving this process implicit in the learned image-to-label mapping and potentially limiting classification performance. Second, privacy cues are often distributed across image regions and may not be adequately represented by whole-image features. To address these challenges, we propose Privacy Concept Bottleneck Models (PriCBMs). By introducing privacy-related concepts as intermediate semantic representations, PriCBMs first identify category-relevant privacy cues through visual-concept matching and then predict privacy categories based on concept responses. This process makes privacy predictions more interpretable. To improve the quality of these concepts, we design a concept selection strategy based on target-category relevance, cross-category discriminability, and semantic diversity. Meanwhile, we introduce a global-region modeling module to capture localized privacy evidence while retaining global context. Experiments on VISPR and FineViP show that PriCBMs outperform evaluated competitors across all four multi-label metrics. Ablation studies and concept-quality analyses support the effectiveness of the proposed design. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: PriCBMs are multi-granular concept bottleneck vision-language models for multi-label visual privacy recognition that predict privacy categories from privacy-related concept responses. They outperform the evaluated competitors on VISPR and FineViP across all four multi-label metrics, and make predictions more interpretable.
AI.motivation: Privacy categories are high-level attributes that do not map one-to-one to visual objects, and privacy cues are spread across image regions, so direct image-to-label prediction lacks explicit guidance and whole-image features may miss localized evidence.
AI.method: Privacy concepts serve as intermediate semantic representations, and visual-concept matching identifies category-relevant cues before categories are predicted from concept responses. Concepts are selected by target-category relevance, cross-category discriminability and semantic diversity, and a global-region modeling module captures localized evidence while keeping global context.
AI.result: PriCBMs outperform the evaluated competitors on VISPR and FineViP across all four multi-label metrics. Ablation and concept-quality analyses support the design.
AI.conclusion: Concept bottleneck modelling offers a more interpretable route to multi-label visual privacy recognition, with better performance than direct prediction.
